name: acl2
desc: Logic and programming language in which you can model computer systems
why: A Lisp-based theorem prover used to model and formally verify real hardware and systems, a genuinely deep rabbit hole.

brief.what_it_is: ACL2 is a logic and programming language, built on a dialect of Common Lisp, in which you write models of computer systems and then use an accompanying theorem-proving tool to prove properties about those models. The homepage describes it as "A Computational Logic for Applicative Common Lisp" and places it in the Boyer-Moore family of provers. The input is ACL2 definitions and theorems, typically organised into files called books, and the output is machine-checked proofs or failed proof attempts. The page is for Version 8.7, dated March 20, 2026.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to model computer systems and prove properties of those models, and it credits the Boyer-Moore provers with the 2005 ACM Software System Award. It also points to a large shared library of community books so users can reuse existing definitions and lemmas.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal proof machinery. It does describe the usage model: you write definitions and theorems, collect them into books, and can certify and reuse community books that others have written. Extensions include ACL2(r) for real numbers via non-standard analysis, ACL2(p) for parallel evaluation, and the Eclipse-based ACL2 Sedan (ACL2s), which adds termination-proof automation and counterexample generation.

commands_seen.context: Shown on the homepage as the first step for building the ACL2+Books manual locally from the source distribution.

Builds the ACL2+Books manual locally; the placeholder is the path to your ACL2 executable. The page says it uses ccl by default and that sbcl is also acceptable, and that it may take several minutes or longer depending on which books are already certified.
Referenced as the ACL2 terminal command for reading documentation, as in 'the ACL2 :DOC command at the terminal'. Mentioned in prose, not shown as a standalone command line.

brief.install_notes: The homepage links to an 'Obtaining, Installing, and License' page, which I did not fetch. Community books are downloaded and installed separately, per the installation instructions. Building the full manual from source requires a local ACL2 binary and, by default, Clozure Common Lisp (ccl), with SBCL also acceptable. ACL2s is distributed separately by Pete Manolios's group and ships a standard executable ACL2 image for Windows. The brew executables are listed as acl2 and acl2p, where acl2p is the parallel-evaluation build.
brief.standout: It is a theorem prover where the models are written in an executable Lisp dialect, so the same artefact can be run and proved, and it has a large community library of reusable proven books. The homepage's own emphasis is that the manual and books are at least as large as the system itself.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the homepage shows: it is on Version 8.7 with the page dated March 20, 2026, and the authors and community maintain books and documentation. I did not check a repository commit date or release history.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not describe hardware or systems verification. The scout note's claim that it is used to model and verify real hardware and systems is not supported by the text I read, though that is a known use. The homepage warns newcomers not to wander into the full manual and to start with the START-HERE topic. Building the manual is slow. ACL2s, the Eclipse-based variant, is distributed by a different group and is not the same as the base ACL2 executable.
quotes: ACL2 is a logic and programming language in which you can model computer systems, together with a tool to help you prove properties of those models.
If you are a newcomer to ACL2, we do not recommend that you wander off into the full documentation.
ACL2 is freely available under the terms of the LICENSE file distributed with ACL2.
fetch_log: https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~moore/acl2/ — fetched OK; homepage text returned with version 8.7, the feature summary, and a build command. I did not follow the 'Obtaining, Installing, and License' link, the manual links, or the START-HERE page because the fetched text did not include their URLs.

judge.reason: ACL2’s executable Lisp models and machine-checked proofs open a deep, distinctive rabbit hole in formal verification, including real hardware and systems.

name: aalib
desc: Portable ASCII art graphics library
why: Renders graphics as ASCII art via a portable library, a classic image-to-text transform with some charm.

brief.what_it_is: AA-lib is a portable ASCII art graphics library. It takes graphics drawing calls through a standard API and renders them as text characters, so programs can produce images on any terminal. The homepage describes it as a library that works on a terminal of any kind. The Homebrew package installs five executables built on it: aafire, aainfo, aalib-config, aasavefont and aatest.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is simplicity: video cards, low-frequency monitors and crashing graphical apps cause many problems, and AA-lib is offered as the answer. The homepage says it gives old hardware more power.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps beyond the package. The download page (dated 2001) lists release candidate sources of version 1.4, plus a separate VGA library and text library that the DOS port requires, and an OS/2 patch. The Homebrew formula's executables are aafire, aainfo, aalib-config, aasavefont and aatest.
brief.standout: It is a 1990s-era text-mode rendering library whose origin story is a Linux penguin logo shown on Hercules monitors, converted to ASCII with a font-bitmap approximation table. The same author later made XaoS, a fractal zoomer, and the BB demo to show off the library.
brief.status: quiet. The newest news item is dated Apr 25 2001 (version 1.4rc4). The homepage says the project is moving from its original home to SourceForge and points to SourceForge news, which I did not fetch. I found no release or commit data for a recent version.
brief.caveats: The README is thin and the site is old. The online documentation and tuning pages were named but I found no URLs for them, so I did not follow them. Only release candidates from 2001 appear on the download page, and I could not confirm a current stable release. The site has a copyright notice from 1997 but I found no license text, so I cannot state the license. The Homebrew formula's caveats were empty.
quotes: AAlib is an portable ascii art GFX library.
I vote for simplicity.
It works on a terminal of any kind, it is fast and portable, it gives to you standard API.

name: acpica
desc: OS-independent implementation of the ACPI specification
why: Intel's reference ACPI interpreter lets you explore the firmware tables and bytecode hiding inside every machine.

brief.what_it_is: ACPICA (ACPI Component Architecture) is an OS-independent C implementation of the ACPI specification. Its kernel-side parts are an AML interpreter, a table manager, a namespace manager, a resource manager, fixed and general-purpose event support, and hardware support, plus optional AML disassembler and debugger modules. It also ships user-space tools: the iASL ACPI source compiler and disassembler, AcpiExec (a simulator/executer), acpidump (dumps system ACPI tables to ASCII), acpixtract (the inverse of acpidump), and AcpiHelp. It takes in ACPI firmware tables and AML bytecode, or ASL source for iASL, and produces ASCII table dumps, disassembled source, or compiled AML. The brew executables also include acpibin, acpiexamples and acpisrc, which I did not see described in the pages I read.
brief.why_it_exists: The project describes ACPI as moving power management from the BIOS to the operating system, with the firmware describing the machine in tables that the OS must interpret. ACPICA provides a reference implementation so that OS developers do not have to write that interpreter and table handling from scratch.
brief.how_it_works: ACPICA isolates all operating-system dependencies in a relatively small translation layer called the OS Services Layer, so the bulk of the code stays independent of any single OS. Per the site, a new OS needs no source changes inside ACPICA itself, only the services layer and initialization calls in its startup routine. The components run in both kernel mode and user mode.
brief.install_notes: No brew-specific setup was described. The site says source packages are provided for Microsoft Windows (the Windows package includes Visual C++ project files and ACPI utilities) and for UNIX. There is no stand-alone Linux source package; ACPICA updates for Linux arrive periodically as patches to be merged into the kernel tree. The GitHub repo has a Makefile at the root, but I did not read build instructions, so I cannot say what the build needs beyond ANSI C.
brief.standout: The same ACPICA code runs inside kernels and in user-space tools, and the site says almost every operating system except Windows uses it to enable ACPI. The package also includes an ASL compiler and AcpiExec, a simulator that lets you run firmware bytecode without the target hardware. The site also documents a 'slack mode' that tolerates AML control methods that forget an explicit return, a bug it says Windows masks.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub page shows about 15,522 commits, 641 stars and 443 forks, but I did not see a last-commit date or a release date. The acpica.org site says ACPICA is 'actively maintained and updated' with releases 'approximately on a monthly to quarterly basis', but its newest news item is dated August 27, 2024 and the news list is otherwise older.
brief.caveats: Dual licensed under BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0-only, per the GitHub About panel and the CONTRIBUTING file. No stand-alone Linux source package; Linux support comes as kernel patches. The GitHub URL I was given returned the CONTRIBUTING.md text rather than a README, and the repo file listing shows no README, so the usage details here are thin. The site's feature list says ACPI 5.0 support, while its news says ACPI 6.4 support arrived in 2021, so the spec version coverage is unclear. The site does not mention macOS. The scout note's claim that it lets you explore firmware tables and bytecode is consistent with the tool list, but I saw no usage examples to confirm it.
quotes: ACPICA is actively maintained and updated.
AML stands for ACPI Machine Language. This is a binary pseudo-code format, which the operating system's ACPI AML interpreter parses to discover the machine's properties.
It is a dual license, so your contribution may be included in downstream projects under any of the two alternative licenses.
fetch_log: https://github.com/acpica/acpica: worked, but returned the CONTRIBUTING.md text plus the repo sidebar (About, stars, license), not a README. The file listing shows dev_docs, documents, generate, source, tests and zephyr folders and no README.
https://www.acpica.org: worked; returned the overview, what's included, system requirements, environments, news and FAQ. Some page markup was noisy, but the text was readable.

judge.reason: ACPICA lets you inspect and disassemble your machine’s firmware tables and run ACPI bytecode in a simulator, opening up a hidden layer of everyday computers.

name: abnfgen
desc: Quickly generate random documents that match an ABFN grammar
why: Generates random documents from ABNF grammars, a strange way to fuzz and see grammars come alive.

brief.what_it_is: abnfgen is a command-line tool written in C that takes a grammar written in Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF, RFC 4234) and emits many random documents that match it. The input is a grammar file; the output is text printed to stdout, or with -d and -n, a directory of numbered files such as demo/0001.tst. The page's example turns the grammar 'ring = 1*12("ding" SP) "dong" CRLF' into output like 'DInG DiNg doNg'. It is not a parser or validator, though it doubles as a rough check that a grammar is syntactically correct.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Jutta Degener, uses it to stress-test parsers she has written and to show what a grammar can produce. The page lists three uses: verifying an ABNF grammar's syntactical correctness, illustrating a grammar with non-obvious examples, and testing software that consumes documents described by a grammar. The page is dedicated in memoriam to Peter Naur and John Backus.
brief.how_it_works: It expands the grammar's rules at random, bounded by a maximum recursion depth (adjustable with the -y runtime option). The page says it differs from standard ABNF in three ways. Single quotes give case-sensitive literals. A number in curly braces before an alternative, such as {2}, sets the relative chance that branch is taken. Numeric codes like %d13 are emitted as UTF-8 Unicode. The -l flag turns these extensions off.

commands_seen.context: Shows the example grammar file before running the tool on it.
Generates random documents from the grammar file; the example prints 'DInG DiNg doNg'.
Prints the quick-reference usage summary (the page points here for a quick reference).
Unpacks the 0.21 source tarball during the build from source.
Standard autotools configure step, run inside the unpacked abnfgen-0.21 directory.
Builds the abnfgen binary with gcc.
Tutorial step: runs the tool on the ABNF-definition-of-ABNF section extracted from RFC 4234 and prints one random output.
Creates the directory demo and writes 100 random grammars into demo/0001.tst through demo/0100.tst.

commands_seen.cmd: for i in demo/*; do ./abnfgen $i > /dev/null 2>&1; done
commands_seen.context: Tutorial step: feeds the generated grammars back into abnfgen to see whether it crashes. The page reports segfaults only in version 0.1.

brief.install_notes: The page describes building from source rather than only giving brew install. You need a C compiler and a Unix-like environment. The steps are: download abnfgen-0.21.tar.gz, unpack it, run ./configure, then make. The configure output on the page shows gcc and autotools being checked. The page does not mention accounts, runtimes or runtime configuration beyond the -d, -n, -y, -l and -_ options it mentions.
brief.standout: It is a grammar-driven generator aimed at breaking parsers rather than at producing text for people. The author's testing advice is unusual: bias rules with {N} weights toward short output, reuse familiar identifier names, and inject occasional noise rules to shake out parser bugs. It is also a small, self-described alpha tool with a 2016-era tribute on the front page.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage says the release was last updated June 3rd, 2023, with version 0.21 as the current release and the latest change listed as 'Stop ignoring {chance} annotations for repetitions.' The page calls the tool 'in alpha' and names Jutta Degener as the maintainer. I did not check a repository or a commit log, so the date is from the page alone.
brief.caveats: The page calls the tool alpha. It targets Unix-like systems with a C compiler, so Windows is not mentioned. The author's own tutorial shows early versions segfaulting on generated input and notes that recursion-depth handling is still 'broken' in some cases. Other known limits from the page: output size is not limited (only recursion depth is), the 'full coverage' option is easy to satisfy, and chance annotations 'probably don't quite work everywhere'. Generated documents are often small or unreadable. The page licenses the tool as 'copyrighted, free for any use', which is not a formal open-source license. I did not see one named on the page.
quotes: The tool is in alpha and, while copyrighted, free for any use.
I tend to use it to stress-test parsers I've written, and they ususally produce about a week's worth of painful crashes and bugs to find for about a day of work getting the grammar just right.
In retrospect, that's a bit of a hack.
Given an Augmented Backus-Naur form (ABNF) grammar (Wikipedia, RFC 4234), abnfgen quickly generates lots of random documents that match that grammar.

judge.reason: A little-known grammar-driven generator turns ABNF into randomized parser tests, making a formal language tangible and offering a distinctive route to finding bugs.

name: abcl
desc: Armed Bear Common Lisp: a full implementation of Common Lisp
why: Common Lisp running on the JVM is a real door into an old language on an unusual host.

brief.what_it_is: Armed Bear Common Lisp (ABCL) is an implementation of ANSI Common Lisp that runs on the Java Virtual Machine. It has both an interpreter and a compiler, and the README says it compiles Lisp code directly to Java byte code for execution. You start it with a command that opens a Lisp REPL, where you type Lisp forms and get results. It also works as a JSR-223 scripting engine inside a Java application, and offers Java-to-Lisp integration APIs. The version described is 1.9.2.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it was originally started as a scripting language for the J editor. The README frames it as a conforming ANSI X3J13 Common Lisp that runs in a JVM, and says that any behavior other than conformance should be reported as a bug.
brief.how_it_works: Lisp source is compiled to Java byte code and run on the JVM, so it can call Java libraries and be embedded in Java programs. The homepage describes using ABCL as a scripting engine in any Java application, or implementing parts of an application in Lisp through the integration APIs.

Unpack the binary release and make sure java is on your PATH; the README says Java 8, 11, and 17 are strongly supported. The README's own test table reports about 63 failures out of 21,902 ANSI tests for 1.9.2, and says Maxima's test suite passes.

The homepage was a landing page rather than a README, so I took the README from the GitHub repository; I guessed that URL from the homepage's GitHub link.

name: abcmidi
desc: Converts abc music notation files to MIDI files
why: Turns ABC text notation into MIDI, a small but genuine text-to-music transform.

brief.what_it_is: abcMIDI is a package of C command-line programs for working with abc music notation, a plain-text format for tunes. Its headline program, abc2midi, takes an abc text file and writes a MIDI file. The package also includes abc2abc, which transposes and rewrites abc files, midi2abc, which goes the other way from MIDI to abc, and mftext, which prints a MIDI file as readable text. Other members are abcmatch, which finds common elements across a collection of tunes, midicopy, which copies parts of a MIDI file into a new one, midistats, and yaps, an older PostScript renderer.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents abcMIDI as the maintained continuation of James Allwright's 1990s tools for abc notation, with Seymour Shlien taking over maintenance. The homepage frames the programs as the engines behind graphical front-ends such as runabc and EasyAbc.

name: adplay
desc: Command-line player for OPL2 music
why: Plays AdLib OPL2 chip music from the 1990s DOS era in the terminal, a real trip into how old sound cards worked.

brief.what_it_is: AdPlay/UNIX is a console-based player for AdLib and Sound Blaster OPL2 music files, the UNIX frontend of the AdPlug project. You start it with one or more music files as parameters, and it plays them through the terminal. AdPlug's core library reads a large number of old game and tracker music formats (the homepage lists over 60, including A2M, CMF, D00, RAD, S3M and ROL) and renders them with an emulated OPL2 chip. The homepage notes that the library can also drive real hardware, but the UNIX player's README says only emulated OPL2 output is supported.
brief.why_it_exists: AdPlug's homepage describes it as a free, cross-platform, hardware independent AdLib sound player library that plays sound data 'directly from its original format' so that no OPL chip is required for playback. AdPlay/UNIX is the stand-alone console front end built on that library.
brief.how_it_works: AdPlug has a separate replayer for each supported file format, so each game or tracker format is interpreted on its own terms instead of being converted to MIDI or WAV first. The OPL2 register writes are then sent to an emulator, and AdPlay/UNIX lets you pick among output devices, per its README. The README says only emulated OPL2 output is supported in the UNIX player.

name: ad
desc: Adaptable text editor inspired by vi, kakoune, and acme
why: A small editor inspired by acme and kakoune with an unusual design, though editors are a crowded niche.

brief.what_it_is: ad (pronounced A.D.) is a text editor written in Rust that combines vi/kakoune-style modal editing with the extensibility of Plan 9's Acme. Its README says that inside ad, text is something you can execute as well as edit. Editing is done in the terminal, and the editor exposes its state through a virtual filesystem interface (fsys, built on a 9p implementation) so external client programs can interact with it. The README does not say exactly what input and output formats it handles beyond text buffers and its command language.
brief.why_it_exists: The author used vim and kakoune for years but wanted acme's approach of running arbitrary external programs from inside the editor and driving it through a simple protocol, without acme's mouse-first design. The README says the goal is a small, usable editor that can be hacked on, and that it is not trying to replace vim, kakoune, or emacs as a massively hackable editor.
brief.how_it_works: Editing is built from a set of internal modules: a gap buffer for buffer state, a 'dot' module for selections and vim-like motions, and an 'exec' module implementing the core of the sam editing language, now split into its own crate called structex. Other modules include a 9p-backed virtual filesystem (fsys and ninep), a minimal LSP client, a custom character-stream regex engine, tree-sitter syntax highlighting with regex fallback, and a trie for sequence-based keybindings. The README describes these as a non-exhaustive list of the more interesting internals.

The homepage describes AdPlug as only the backend, with frontends built on top of it: AdPlay/UNIX, AdPlay/DOS, and plugins for Winamp and XMMS. name: afflib
desc: Advanced Forensic Format
why: Advanced Forensic Format library opens the door to disk image forensics and how evidence containers are structured.

brief.what_it_is: AFFLIB is a C library and set of command-line tools for the Advanced Forensic Format (AFF), an on-disk format for storing computer forensic data and its metadata in one or more files. The tools convert disk images between raw/dd, splitraw, AFF, AFD (multiple AFF files in a directory) and AFM (an AFF file annotating a raw file). They also compare images, copy images with verification and a chain-of-custody segment, find and repair errors in AFF files, print file info and statistics, and emit XML metadata or an XML "diskprint" fingerprint. The executables listed for the package are affcat, affcompare, affconvert, affcopy, affcrypto, affdiskprint, affinfo, affix, affrecover, affsegment, affsign, affstats, affuse, affverify and affxml.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames AFF as a way to keep forensic data, metadata, digital signatures for chain of custody and long-term integrity, and on-the-fly encryption together in one open format, so privacy-sensitive disk images can be stored or shared, for example on the Internet. It describes AFF as unencumbered by copyright or patent protection.
brief.how_it_works: AFF stores a disk image and its metadata in a purpose-built container file (AFFv3), with optional digital signatures and on-the-fly encryption and decryption for processing. The toolkit reads and writes that container and converts it to and from other image layouts. The README notes that AFFv4 will instead be based on ZIP64.

name: afl++
desc: American Fuzzy Lop++
why: A coverage-guided fuzzer that evolves inputs to break programs, a fascinating way to watch software get taken apart.

brief.what_it_is: AFL++ is a fuzzing framework: a tool that generates many mutated inputs and feeds them to a target program to find crashes and hangs. You compile the target with AFL++'s compiler wrappers (afl-cc, afl-c++), then run afl-fuzz against it with a directory of seed inputs. The fuzzer mutates those inputs and keeps the ones that reach new code paths. Crashes and hangs are written to crashes/ and hangs/ under the output directory, and afl-fuzz shows a status screen while it runs. The package also ships helpers such as afl-cmin and afl-tmin for corpus minimization, afl-showmap for coverage maps, and afl-plot for graphs, plus binary-only instrumentation modes (QEMU, Unicorn, QBDI).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says AFLplusplus is the daughter of American Fuzzy Lop by Michal 'lcamtuf' Zalewski and was created to merge the best features developed for the AFL family that were never merged into AFL, which the homepage says has not been updated since November 2017. The README calls it 'a superior fork to Google's AFL - more speed, more and better mutations, more and better instrumentation, custom module support, etc.'
brief.how_it_works: Targets are built with instrumentation (LLVM mode, afl-as, or the GCC plugin) so the fuzzer can observe which code paths each input exercises. afl-fuzz then mutates seed inputs and keeps those that discover new coverage. The README also describes a CMPLOG option (AFL_LLVM_CMPLOG=1 with afl-clang-fast), which the README recommends for comparisons; its mechanism was not explained in the pages read.

name: agda
desc: Dependently typed functional programming language
why: A dependently typed language where types are proofs, a genuinely strange way to program and prove things.

brief.what_it_is: Agda is a dependently typed functional programming language and interactive proof assistant. It lets you write programs whose types can depend on values, such as a type of vectors indexed by length, and then check proofs about those programs. The homepage describes an interactive Emacs interface that helps the programmer write code, and the brew description calls it a dependently typed functional programming language. Input is Agda source code; the checker verifies types and proofs, and the compiler produces executables. The package installs four executables: agda, agda-mode, agda2hs, and als.
brief.why_it_exists: The wiki frames Agda as a foundational tool for constructive mathematics based on Per Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, and as a system for writing and checking proofs interactively. It is positioned alongside other dependent-type proof assistants such as Rocq, Epigram, Matita and NuPRL.
brief.how_it_works: Agda type-checks programs and proofs written in dependently typed functional style, supporting inductive families, parametrised modules, mixfix operators and Unicode. The main interactive workflow runs through an Emacs interface (agda-mode) that assists the programmer while writing the program. The GitHub README points to a 'Quick guide to editing, type checking and compiling Agda code' as the entry point for this workflow.
brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the brew caveats say that to use installed Agda libraries you must run: mkdir -p $HOME/.config/agda, then copy $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/agda/share/agda/example-libraries to $HOME/.config/agda/libraries and example-defaults to $HOME/.config/agda/defaults. Redo this after upgrading from an earlier version. The Agda Pad lets you try Agda in the browser without installing. The Agda Standard Library is a separate download with its own wiki page.
brief.standout: Types are proofs: a single language is both the programming language and the proof checker, so a program can carry a machine-checked specification in its type. Agda also has an interactive editor-driven workflow in Emacs, with Unicode syntax and mixfix operators, which makes it feel quite unlike mainstream languages. The agda2hs executable, bundled here, translates Agda code to Haskell.

name: afsctool
desc: Utility for manipulating APFS and ZFS compressed files
why: Exposes APFS and HFS compression internals on macOS, a close call but a real look at filesystem compression.

brief.what_it_is: afsctool is a command-line utility for macOS that applies Apple File System Compression to files, decompresses files that are already compressed, or reports information about compressed files. The original blog describes it as working on HFS+ compression on Mac OS 10.6 or later. This GitHub fork (RJVB/afsctool) also covers APFS, adds LZVN and LZFSE support, and builds a second executable, zfsctool. Input is one or more file or folder paths on the command line, and output is compression statistics or the compressed or decompressed files on disk.
brief.why_it_exists: The blog post frames it as a way to use AFSC (Apple File System Compression) on existing files, which the author says Finder does not let you do directly. The blogger's own example is compressing a large World of Warcraft install, and a commenter reports running it nightly as a cron job over ~/Library mail and sync directories to save SSD space.
brief.how_it_works: Per the fork README, afsctool compresses files by writing them back in compressed form, with an undo path if something goes wrong and an optional backup while compressing. Parallel modes -j and -J let you set a worker-thread count; -j parallelises only the compression step while disk I/O runs with exclusive access, and -J parallelises all steps. zfsctool takes a different route: ZFS compression is set per dataset, so it recompresses by changing the dataset's compression property, rewriting the files, and resetting the property, which also affects other files written during the rewrite.

name: ahcpd
desc: Autoconfiguration protocol for IPv6 and IPv6/IPv4 networks
why: Autoconfiguration protocol for IPv6 addressing, a rarely examined door into how networks configure themselves without DHCP.

brief.what_it_is: ahcpd is a daemon that automatically configures IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, name servers and NTP servers on a network. It is an implementation of the Ad-Hoc Configuration Protocol (AHCP), an autoconfiguration protocol for IPv6 and dual-stack IPv6/IPv4 networks. It does not set default routes, because it is meant to run alongside a routing protocol such as Babel or OLSR. One or more servers hold the configuration (prefixes, name servers, NTP servers, leases in a lease database), and clients on the link ask for it. Output is addresses and settings handed to client interfaces.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says AHCP is meant to replace router discovery and DHCP where it is difficult or impossible to configure a server in every link-layer broadcast domain, for example mobile ad-hoc networks. The GitHub README says DHCP and IPv6 autoconfiguration do not work in wireless mesh networks, though the protocol could also be used on wired networks.
brief.how_it_works: A server is started with a configuration file that lists IPv6 and IPv4 prefixes, a lease directory, name servers and an NTP server, and it hands out leases from those prefixes. Clients run ahcpd as root with no config file and receive IPv4 and IPv6 addresses within seconds. The server checks the kernel for time synchronisation, and without it hands out only short leases and is very conservative about releasing them. For redundancy, several servers can share one network if they serve disjoint IPv4 address ranges.

commands_seen.context: Installs the Debian/Ubuntu package from the mainstream repository (the homepage says the package ships without init scripts).
Clones the latest, possibly unstable, sources from the author's git server; the homepage also mentions a GitHub mirror.

brief.install_notes: Beyond apt-get or brew, you can build from source with make and make install (run as root). Building for BSD or OpenWRT needs different make variables. A server needs a configuration file at /etc/ahcpd.conf that sets mode server, one or more prefix lines (IPv6 and/or IPv4), lease-dir, name-server and ntp-server, plus a lease directory the server can write. The server does not have to run as root if it can write the lease database and pidfile. The server's clock should be synchronised with Mills' NTP implementation, since SNTP clients usually won't satisfy the kernel time-sync check. Clients need no config file. Packages are also listed for Fedora Extras, Arch Linux and OpenWRT.
brief.standout: Instead of a central DHCP server on every link, it lets a few servers in a mesh hand out IPv4, IPv6, DNS and NTP settings without router advertisements, and it leaves routing to a separate protocol. Its requirement that servers prove time synchronisation through the kernel before handing out long leases is a distinctive design choice.

Its tools capture 802.11 frames from a wireless card in monitor mode and export them to text files for other tools. brief.how_it_works: The tools work at the level of the wireless card. Monitoring tools capture packets, and Attacking tools inject frames via packet injection to perform replay, deauthentication, and fake-AP attacks. Testing tools check whether a card and its driver can capture and inject. Cracking tools recover WEP and WPA PSK keys from captured traffic.

name: alda

why: A text-based music programming language that turns plain notation into sound, a genuine door into live-coded composition.

brief.what_it_is: Alda is a text-based programming language for music composition. You write a score as a plain text file using markup-like notation for parts, octaves, notes, rests and chords, then play it with the alda command-line tool. Input is text, either a score file, a string passed on the command line, or lines typed into an interactive REPL. Output is sound: a separate player process renders the music as MIDI using General MIDI instruments. The changelog also shows alda export writing MIDI files and alda import reading MusicXML.

The README links a blog post by the author for the history and rationale, as an alternative to graphical sheet-music programs.
brief.how_it_works: A score is a text file in Alda's syntax, run by the alda client. The client talks over OSC to a background player process (JVM, Kotlin/Java) that produces the MIDI output. Since 2.0 the client parses the score into an AST before generating events. The REPL keeps a live session going, so you can enter code and hear it immediately, and the README says Alda can also be driven programmatically for algorithmic composition and live coding.

name: alive2
desc: Automatic verification of LLVM optimizations
why: Uses SMT solving to prove or disprove that LLVM optimizations are correct, a door into formal verification of compilers.

brief.what_it_is: Alive2 is a set of libraries and tools for analysing and verifying LLVM code and transformations. It takes LLVM IR, either a source and a target IR file or a single file with functions named src and tgt, or an unoptimized IR file that it runs through an -O2-like pipeline without interprocedural passes. It then uses an SMT solver to check whether the transformation refines the original, reporting 'Transformation seems to be correct!' or a counterexample with concrete input values. It also ships clang and opt plugins, drop-in compiler wrappers (alivecc, alive++), and an LLVM IR interpreter (alive-exec).
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as automatic verification of LLVM optimizations, citing its PLDI 2021 paper as the technical introduction. The sponsor section says it is meant to make LLVM less buggy, and a list of LLVM bugs it has found is kept in BugList.md.
brief.how_it_works: Alive2 has its own IR, a symbolic executor, an LLVM-to-Alive2-IR converter, and a refinement check (the optimization verifier) built on an SMT abstraction layer, with Z3 as the prerequisite solver. For translation validation it converts the before and after IR and checks refinement, so an optimizer run is validated after the fact instead of proving the optimizer correct as a whole. The README says it is UB-precise and that undef inputs can be excluded with -disable-undef-input.

brief.install_notes: Prerequisites: recent cmake, gcc or clang, re2c, and Z3; LLVM is optional and hiredis is optional for caching. Standalone build needs only cmake, Ninja and Z3 (use -DZ3_INCLUDE_DIR and -DZ3_LIBRARIES if CMake finds the wrong Z3). Translation validation for opt and clang needs an LLVM build with RTTI and exceptions on (-DLLVM_ENABLE_RTTI=ON), built from LLVM main, and Alive2 must be pointed at it via CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH. The README also suggests clang as the compiler when the default is gcc. Caching needs a Redis server on localhost that Alive2 uses alone. No account is needed. Not needed: you can try alive-tv in a browser at https://alive2.llvm.org/ce/ without building.
brief.standout: It checks whether a specific optimizer transformation preserves meaning, and returns a concrete counterexample when it does not, instead of a proof of the compiler as a whole. It also runs as a drop-in clang/clang++ wrapper, so an entire build can be checked pass by pass.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release version or date and I could not see a last-commit date from the README alone. It does describe current activity: it is aimed at LLVM top of tree, the maintainers run the LLVM unit-test validation daily, and it is supported by several sponsors.
brief.caveats: Does not support interprocedural transformations and may produce spurious counterexamples on them. Translation validation tracks LLVM top of tree closely, so older LLVM sources may require reverting to an older Alive2 commit. Builds on macOS can hit linker issues (chained fixups, flat namespace), and the README suggests setting CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET to 11.0 or less. alive-exec is described as highly experimental: the function cannot take inputs, use memory, depend on undefined behaviour, or loop too many times. The opt wrapper's timeout is not supported on macOS. The README's example path for the alive binary reads ~/alive/build in one place, which looks like a typo for ~/alive2/build. The README does not state a licence.

Sat4j is the cross-platform SAT solver, with optional native solvers (minisat, lingeling/plingeling, glucose). The same JAR can be embedded as an API in other applications. name: algol68g
desc: Algol 68 compiler-interpreter
why: A working Algol 68 interpreter opens a door into a historical language with a strange, almost alien syntax.

brief.what_it_is: Algol 68 Genie (a68g) is a free, GPL-licensed interpreter for Algol 68, a historical programming language. You give it Algol 68 source code and it runs the program, with runtime checks and a GDB-style debugger available during execution. It also offers arbitrary-precision integer, real and complex arithmetic. On Linux or FreeBSD it can optionally partially precompile well-debugged code to object code that is dynamically linked at runtime. The project describes itself as essentially feature-complete and ships with a Revised Report, a programming guide and example programs.
brief.why_it_exists: The project's stated aim is to preserve Algol 68 for educational and scientific-historical reasons, by providing a recent implementation written from scratch along with extensive documentation. The author wants people to be able to study the language and its context-dependent two-level grammar, and also use it for medium-sized programming tasks.
brief.how_it_works: It is an interpreter, like Python, that checks for uninitialised objects, out-of-range subscripts or values, dangling references and similar problems as the program runs. Its one extension to the language is Charles Lindsey's 1976 partial parametrization proposal, which gives the imperative language a functional sub-language. On Linux and FreeBSD, the optional precompilation step produces object code that the interpreter links in at runtime.
brief.install_notes: Downloads on the homepage are a source tarball (algol68g-3.13.4.tar.gz, 690 kB) for Linux or BSD, and a source archive with a WIN64 binary (algol68g-3.13.4.win64.zip, 2.2 MB) for Windows 11. The Windows binary is linked against the GNU Scientific Library, GNU plotutils and R mathlib, and the page says to run it from a command-line shell such as PowerShell. Precompiled binaries for major distributions are linked from a separate page. Detailed installation instructions are in the documentation, which I did not open. The brew formula name is algol68g and the executable is a68g.
brief.standout: It is one of the most complete Algol 68 implementations, and it was written from scratch rather than derived from an older compiler. Its hand-coded parser for the W-grammar is the basis of ga68, the Algol 68 front-end that was merged into GCC 16.1 as experimental, according to the homepage.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists version 3.13.4 with a date of 15 October 2026, the copyright line reads 2001-2026, and the page says recent releases mainly concern maintenance and additions to the runtime library. A post dated May 2026 covers GCC's Algol 68 support. Version 3 revisions have been released since 2022.
brief.caveats: The page says the project is not intended to modernise Algol 68; it aims to preserve the original language. The optional precompilation is available only on Linux and FreeBSD. Version 3 is developed on Debian and tested on FreeBSD and Windows 11. The Windows binary is run from a command-line shell rather than from a GUI. The homepage does not state the Windows binary's dependency details beyond the libraries named above. Many of the homepage's listed links, including the documentation PDF, the browsable source and the GitHub or SourceForge mirrors, were not followed.
quotes: It is an interpreter like Python, offering many runtime-checks and a GDB-style debugger.
The interpreter implements one extension to the language – Charles Lindsey's partial parametrization proposal published in 1976, that gives the imperative language Algol 68 a functional sub-language.
Note that responsibility for Algol 68 still lies with IFIP Working Group 2.1, and that it is not the intention of this project to modernise the language.

name: allureofthestars

brief.what_it_is: Allure of the Stars is a near-future science-fiction roguelike with tactical squad combat, written in Haskell on the LambdaHack engine. The player manually controls each member of a squad, though the homepage says the best tactic is often to scout with one character and let the others guard key areas. The game is turn-based but fine-grained: projectiles fly over time at varying speeds and can be sidestepped or shot down. It can be played in a browser at allureofthestars.com/play, and the Homebrew formula installs an executable called Allure.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as an attempt to make a roguelike that feels like a shared experience with a band of trusted friends, where players fight as one organism with minimal communication and build their own story. The homepage describes the UI as deliberately sparse so the player's imagination does most of the sensory work, "like when reading a book, but with less words and more action."
brief.how_it_works: The homepage lists the design differences from classic roguelikes. Factions and actors all obey the same rules (field of view, skill checks, equipment and terrain use), and combat is deterministic, with randomness coming only from AI decisions and procedural generation. There is almost no HP regeneration, and each character has 10 equipment slots. Each faction has one shared, unlimited inventory that sits at a physical place on the map and can be ransacked. Several levels advance simultaneously while others are frozen, and all are persistent.
brief.install_notes: Homebrew installs the Allure executable. The homepage also offers official binaries for Linux and Windows, a Homebrew formula with Mac OS X binaries, and a browser version at http://allureofthestars.com/play, which needs no install. The README and manual were not reachable, so no configuration or first-run steps are known.
brief.standout: Few terminal or roguelike games combine real-time-feeling projectile flight, per-character tactical control of a squad, deterministic combat, and faction inventories that exist as physical objects on the map. name: amfora
desc: Fancy terminal browser for the Gemini protocol
why: A terminal browser for the Gemini protocol, a small alternative internet worth a look even if it is one of several.

brief.what_it_is: Amfora is a terminal browser for the Gemini protocol, a small internet protocol that is separate from the Web. You give it a gemini:// address and it fetches and renders the page inside your terminal, with styled headings, links, tabs, bookmarks, and history. It also handles Gemini input prompts, client certificates, and TOFU certificate checks. Its output is text drawn in the terminal, and it can download pages or hand non-text files to other applications.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the aim is to be "the best looking [Gemini](https://geminiquickst.art/) client with the most features... all in the terminal." It is scoped to Gemini only and does not support Gopher or other non-Web protocols; the README points to Bombadillo for those.
brief.how_it_works: Amfora is written in Go. It uses cview, a fork of tview, for the terminal interface, with tcell underneath for low-level terminal control. It uses the author's forked go-gemini library for the protocol, and Viper for configuration and TOFU certificate storage. Feed support covers RSS, Atom, and JSON Feed, and page subscriptions notify you when a page changes.

name: ancient
desc: Decompression routines for ancient formats
why: Decompression routines for long-dead file formats, a fascinating way into old binary formats and their quirks.

brief.what_it_is: Ancient is a C++ library and command-line tool that decompresses data made by old compression formats, mostly from Amiga and Atari machines in the 1980s and 1990s, plus some newer formats used in those systems. You feed it a compressed file and it detects the format in most cases and writes out the decompressed data. The README lists dozens of formats, including ByteKiller, Pack-Ice, PowerPacker, StoneCracker, DMS, XPK wrappers, and Unix compress/pack, along with gzip and bzip2. It also includes decompressor backends for Zip and LZH that are not built in yet, and it does not handle archives or self-extracting executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says most of these algorithms can still be downloaded, but the original implementations were written only for the machines they ran on, and some ports are incomplete, poor quality, or direct translations of M68K assembly. The project aims to provide clean modern implementations, a BSD-style license in place of unclear or missing licenses, and testing against a cache of about 10k files that used these formats.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives little detail on internals. It says the compression format is detected automatically in most cases, with some corner cases where detection is unreliable because of weaknesses in the old formats. It says the tests use a cache of roughly 10k real files plus a small batch of generated test files drawn from public domain sources. Several decompressors were re-implemented using reference code (Harri Hirvola's HA for SASC/SHSC, Lhasa for some LZH variants), and the README says no code was reused from them.
brief.install_notes: The README has no installation or build instructions. It says the code should compile cleanly on most C++17 compilers and is tested on clang and MSVC. It describes two entry points: a simple command-line application (see main.cpp) and a simple API (see api/ancient/ancient.hpp). No commands are shown in the README. Some formats have weak password protection that the code can bypass, for DMS and PowerPacker PX20. The project says it does not do real cryptography.
brief.standout: It is a single decompressor covering a large number of obscure Amiga and Atari formats, many of which exist nowhere else as clean modern code, and it is tested against thousands of real files. The author also cleared up licensing: many of the original implementations have unclear or missing licenses, and some ports are of doubtful legality, so this project rewrites them under BSD-style terms.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release date, changelog, or last-commit information. It says the author is 'slowly adding new stuff' and invites requests for new formats, which suggests the project is still being worked on, but I did not check the commit history or releases page.
brief.caveats: The README says detection is not fully reliable for some formats because of weaknesses in the old formats. Several formats are marked 'verification missing': PP 1.1, FLT!, Dupa, and PARA. Archive files and self-extracting executables are not supported. Zip and LZH decompressors exist only as backends, not as usable archive readers. PPC-only XPK compressors are not planned. The README gives no license name for the project itself beyond the claim of BSD-style licensing, and it says the BZIP2 randomization tables carry the bzip2 license. The homepage was reachable.

Provide a clean, modern implementation of the algorithms

name: ansilove
desc: ANSI/ASCII art to PNG converter
why: Renders old BBS ANSI art files into PNG, a satisfying look at a forgotten art form and its formats.

brief.what_it_is: AnsiLove/C is a command-line converter that turns ANSI and ASCII text-mode art files from the BBS and artscene era into PNG images. It takes files in formats such as ANS, PCB, BIN, ADF, IDF, TND and XB, reads any SAUCE metadata record, and writes a size-optimized 4-bit PNG, optionally with Retina @2x or custom scale output. The project is by Frederic Cambus, Stefan Vogt and Brian Cassidy, and the latest release listed on the homepage is 4.2.2 from June 10, 2026.

brief.how_it_works: The tool loads the input through the libansilove library, which parses the text-mode escape sequences or raw video-memory dump for the detected format and draws each character cell using embedded binary font dumps, with iCE colors and SAUCE hints where enabled. It then writes the canvas out as a PNG. The README says the renderer uses a 4-bit palette to keep files small.

name: apktool
desc: Tool for reverse engineering 3rd party, closed, binary Android apps
why: Decodes closed Android APKs into smali and resources, a solid door into how apps are taken apart, though fairly well known.

brief.what_it_is: Apktool is a command-line tool for reverse engineering closed, binary Android apps. You give it an APK file and it decodes the resources and manifest to nearly their original form and disassembles the code into smali, which lays the app out as a project folder. After you edit that folder, the same tool rebuilds it into an APK. The homepage transcript shows version 3.0.3 in use.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to take third-party, closed Android apps apart so people can inspect and modify them, for example to localize an app or add features. It also says it is not for piracy.
brief.how_it_works: Running decode (d) on an APK writes out a project-like folder with decoded resources, manifest and smali code, and it copies unknown and original files across. Running build (b) on that folder reassembles the smali into classes.dex, rebuilds the resources and packages a new APK. The homepage also describes an analyze mode: attaching -m to a decode command skips rebuilding and just unpacks resources and manifest for inspection.

name: apkid

brief.what_it_is: APKiD is a command-line tool that reports how an Android APK was built and protected. It takes an APK, a DEX file, or a directory as input (a FILE argument, optionally recursive) and scans it with YARA rules. It outputs which compilers, packers, obfuscators, and other notable traits it recognizes, per classes.dex entry, either as text or as JSON (-j), or written to a directory with -o. The README's example output shows a line like ' |-> compiler : dx'. It is written in Python and installs from PyPI.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says APKiD 'gives you information about how an APK was made' and calls it 'PEiD for Android', after the Windows tool that identified packers and compilers in PE executables. The author also points to detecting pirated and malicious apps and to fingerprinting AppShielding and mobile RASP SDKs.
brief.how_it_works: It applies a set of YARA rules to APK and DEX contents to match signatures of known compilers, packers, and obfuscators. The README says new detections are added as rules, and the Hacking section says the rules must be compiled with prep-release.py before they take effect. The README does not describe the matching internals beyond this.

name: anyquery
desc: Query anything with SQL
why: Runs SQL across many external sources like apps and APIs, a fun door into treating everything as a database.

brief.what_it_is: Anyquery is a SQL query engine, built on SQLite, that exposes apps, files, and databases as tables you can query with one dialect. brief.how_it_works: Anyquery runs on SQLite and uses plugins to turn each external service or file type into a table, so you can JOIN across them. It runs locally and the homepage says API tokens never leave the machine. It can run as an MCP server so LLM clients can query your data, or as a MySQL-compatible server so tools like Metabase and TablePlus can connect.

name: aravis
desc: Vision library for genicam based cameras
why: Opens the GenICam camera protocol family, a door into industrial machine vision hardware with real hands-on potential.

brief.what_it_is: Aravis is a glib/gobject based C library for video acquisition from GenICam cameras. According to its README it implements the gigabit ethernet (GigE Vision) and USB3 protocols used by industrial cameras. It also ships a basic ethernet camera simulator and a simple video viewer. The inputs are cameras on the network or USB, and the output is video frames and camera control through the library API.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it simply as a library for video acquisition using GenICam cameras, the standard interface family for industrial cameras. The README gives no further motivation.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals beyond naming the protocols it implements (GigE Vision and USB3) and its glib/gobject foundation. The Documentation section points to the stable docs for installation, performance tuning, and API reference. The viewer is built on GStreamer1 and Gtk+3, and the GStreamer plugin is an optional add-on to the library.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no install commands. Dependencies: the library needs zlib, libxml2 and glib2, with optional USB support via libusb1. The GStreamer plugin also needs GStreamer1. The simple viewer needs GStreamer1, Gtk+3 and the library dependencies. Required versions are in meson.build, and the README says it is possible to build only the library with minimal dependencies. The docs cover installing on Linux, macOS and Windows. The brew caveat (not from the README) says that for GStreamer to find the bundled plugin you must set GST_PLUGIN_PATH to $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/aravis/lib/gstreamer-1.0. Real camera use also requires camera hardware on the network or USB, and the docs mention system tuning for best performance.
brief.standout: It bundles a fake GigE camera simulator alongside the real library, so you can test acquisition code without hardware. The README also has an unusual contribution rule: contributions to the GigE Vision and USB3 Vision protocol code must not be based on the A3 specification documents, because A3 forbids their use for open source implementations.

name: arcade-learning-environment
desc: Platform for AI research
why: Runs classic Atari ROMs as an RL environment, a real research platform that lets you watch emulated games learn.

brief.what_it_is: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) is a framework for building AI agents that play Atari 2600 games. It is built on the Stella emulator and separates emulation details from agent design. An agent sends an action, such as a joystick input, and the environment returns the screen image, the game score, and an end-of-game signal. The README describes Python, Gymnasium, C++, and WebAssembly interfaces, and says ROMs are packaged inside the pip package. Over 50 games are shown in a linked video, and automatic score and end-of-game extraction covers more than 100 games.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the ALE exists to give researchers and hobbyists a platform for developing general AI agents on Atari 2600 games. It points to the JAIR paper 'The Arcade Learning Environment: An Evaluation Platform for General Agents' for the project's goals.
brief.how_it_works: The Python bindings wrap the Stella emulator core, which is kept separate from rendering and sound so emulation stays fast with few dependencies. The agent loop calls ale.act(action) to step the game, then reads the screen with getScreenRGB(). In Gymnasium, gym.make('ALE/Breakout-v5') wraps this into the standard reset/step API. A C++ vectorizer can run several ROMs at once.

commands_seen.context: Installs the ALE Python package from PyPI. The README says to make sure pip is up to date first, or the install may fail.
Installs Gymnasium with the Atari extras, which the README says pulls in the necessary modules and ROMs for ale-py.
First step of the C++ build from source with CMake.
Configures the C++ build in Release mode.

Installs the WebAssembly build of the ALE from NPM for use in browsers.

brief.install_notes: Python: CPython 3.11 to 3.15 is supported. Free-threaded CPython builds (the t ABI, e.g. python3.14t) are not supported because OpenCV has no compatible wheels, which preprocessing needs. C++: requires a C++17 compiler, and the README assumes vcpkg is installed. Optional CMake flags include -DSDL_SUPPORT=ON/OFF (off by default, toggles display_screen and sound), -DBUILD_CPP_LIB=ON/OFF (on by default), and -DBUILD_PYTHON_LIB=ON/OFF (on by default). WebAssembly: install via NPM or use the standalone zip from release artifacts. No account or hardware setup is mentioned. ROMs ship in the pip package, so there is no separate ROM download step described.
brief.standout: Its Gymnasium integration makes an Atari game a standard environment in a few lines, and a C++ vectorizer runs many ROMs in parallel. It also runs in the browser through WebAssembly. The README also documents the evaluation protocol through the Machado et al. 2018 citation, which covers sticky actions and game mode and difficulty flavours.
brief.status: Appears actively maintained, but the fetched README has no release date or commit date, so this is inferred. Evidence: it supports Python 3.14 and 3.15, uses the maintained Gymnasium fork, lists a 2024 CALE citation, and is hosted under the Farama Foundation with a docs site. I did not check release or commit history.
brief.caveats: Free-threaded CPython is unsupported. The C++ SDL display and sound support is off by default. The README does not discuss ROM licensing, even though ROMs are bundled in the pip package. The scout note says the project lets you 'watch emulated games learn', but the README frames it as a research framework. Watching comes from render_mode='human' in Gymnasium, not from a dedicated feature.
quotes: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) is a simple framework that allows researchers and hobbyists to develop AI agents for Atari 2600 games.
Emulation core uncoupled from rendering and sound generation modules for fast emulation with minimal library dependencies.
Atari roms are packaged within the pip package.

name: argus
desc: Audit Record Generation and Utilization System server
why: Network audit record generation server from the Argus project, a door into flow-level network monitoring that most people never see.

brief.what_it_is: Argus (Audit Record Generation and Utilization System) is a network flow sensor. It reads live traffic from a network interface, or packets from a pcap capture file, and writes flow records in Argus's own binary format, which the README says covers all network activity, not just IP. The package is split in two: the argus sensor, which generates the flow data, and argus-clients, which holds the tools that read and process it, such as ra, rasum and racluster. The homepage describes the sensor as the component that generates flow data and the clients as the component that processes it. The Homebrew formula installs the sensor and its argus-* helper programs; ra and the other client tools are not in the executables list.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Argus as the original network flow monitoring technology, developed since 1984, meant to audit all network activity for operations, security analysis, performance monitoring and forensics. The homepage adds that it was modeled on the telephone network's Call Detail Record and is used for ML data sources and endpoint detection.
brief.how_it_works: The sensor processes packets from an interface or capture file and aggregates them into flow records using configurable flow keys (the README names a classic 5-tuple key and a Layer 2 matrix key). Records carry many metrics, including packet dynamics, jitter and throughput. Output goes to a file, which the client tools then read, filter, summarise or cluster; the README also describes a real-time mode where tools such as ratop watch flows live.

commands_seen.context: Monitor interface eth0 live and write flow records to a file (needs root for capture).
Read flows from a pcap file instead of a live interface and write them to an Argus file.
View the flow records with ra, which comes from the separate argus-clients package.
Capture on eth0 with a BPF-style filter so only TCP flows are recorded.

Configure the source build (from the GitHub README's build steps).

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: the GitHub README lists prerequisites of libpcap, flex and bison, a C compiler (gcc or clang) and zlib development libraries, then ./configure, make and sudo make install. Packages exist for RedHat, Debian, Suse and Ubuntu (argus-server and argus-clients). Live capture needs root (sudo). Configuration lives in /etc/argus.conf, with ARGUS_MONITOR_ID, ARGUS_FLOW_TYPE, ARGUS_FLOW_KEY, ARGUS_INTERFACE and ARGUS_OUTPUT as example keys. The homepage notes that clients 3.0 cannot read 5.0 data, so the sensor and clients should be matched to the same major version.
brief.standout: It is among the oldest flow-monitoring systems, with a flow-record model intended as a superset of NetFlow, IPFIX and flow-tools, and over 175 attributes per record. It is also unusual in covering non-IP traffic and in being described as ported to more than 20 platforms, including real-time OSes.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage lists a v5.0.2 release dated Feb 18, 2025, a v5.0 release in June 2024, and new projects in 2024 (Endpoint, Private Passive DNS). The GitHub README badge shows version 5.0.4. I did not see commit dates or a releases page, so the exact latest activity is unconfirmed.

Version conflict: the homepage names v5.0.2 as the latest release, while the README badge says 5.0.4. The homepage warns that the v5.0.2 encapsulation capture feature should be enabled in argus.conf with some thought. The client tools (ra and the rest) are in a separate package and are not among the executables listed here. Some claims, such as 'proven at scale from 1G to 100G+' and the 175-attribute count, are the project's own and I did not verify them. The homepage is a marketing front page with little technical detail, so most technical content comes from the GitHub README.

name: argyll-cms
desc: ICC compatible color management system
why: Colour management suite that profiles real monitors with a sensor, a hands-on look at how colour is measured.

brief.what_it_is: Argyll CMS is an open source, ICC compatible color management system, distributed as a collection of C source code that compiles into a set of command line tools. It creates ICC profiles for scanners, cameras and film recorders, and calibrates and profiles displays and RGB and CMYK printers, using its own drivers for color measurement instruments. It also builds device links, including 3D LUTs and video calibration standards, and accepts spectral sample data with a choice of illuminants and observer types. Gamut mapping and profile linking use the CIECAM02 appearance model.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Graeme Gill, frames it as making serious color management available on platforms other than MSWin and OS X. The project is funded by donations, which he says are what let him keep working on it.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers prebuilt executables for Microsoft Windows, Apple OS X and Linux x86, plus source code, and tells users to read the notes on installing after downloading. Nothing on the homepage describes accounts, runtimes or first-run configuration. Some Linux distribution packages are modified and may behave differently from the upstream release, so the author asks users to retest with the unmodified download before reporting bugs. The brew entry lists 47 executables, including dispcal, dispread, colprof, spotread and targen.
brief.standout: It drives color measurement instruments directly through its own driver code, so a sensor can profile a real monitor from the command line. The homepage also says it contains what it calls the fastest portable 8 bit raster color conversion engine available anywhere.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage says it was last updated 2026/2/4 and lists current version 3.5.0 dated 4th February 2026, with downloads for that version.
brief.caveats: Licensed under AGPL, and the author points commercial users to a separate non-GPL licence for icclib and cgatslib. The author says there is little prospect of native Wayland display calibration support and recommends X11 for Linux users who need a color managed display. Instrument problems should go to the Argyll author or mailing list, not the instrument vendor. The brew caveats field was empty. I did not fetch the online documentation, so no command syntax was checked.
quotes: ArgyllCMS is an ICC compatible color management system, available as Open Source.
Argyll is a collection of source code that compiles into a set of command line tools, licensed under an AGPL license.
So my current advice for people wanting to use a color managed display on Linux is to stick to X11.

name: ares
desc: Automated decoding of encrypted text
why: Automatically chains through encodings and ciphers to decode text, a fun puzzle-solving transform for exploring classical crypto.

brief.what_it_is: Ciphey is a command-line tool and Rust library that takes encoded or encrypted text and works out the chain of decoders needed to recover the plaintext, with no key, cipher name, or hint supplied. It searches through combinations of encodings and classical ciphers such as Base64, hex, Caesar/ROT13, Vigenere, and Morse, several layers deep. Input is text pasted or read from a file, and the output is the candidate plaintext, the decoder path used (for example Base64 → Hexadecimal → caesar), and any key it found. It runs under a time limit, five seconds by default.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as the next generation of Ciphey, a Python decoding tool that the same author plans to replace. The pitch is speed: Ciphey is 'very fast', and the old tool 'could run forever' with no answer and no signal that it had given up.
brief.how_it_works: An A* search tries chains of decoders, running fast ones like Base64 first and ordering the rest with a heuristic from the cipher_identifier crate. Candidate outputs are checked for plaintext by an English checker (trigram and dictionary based), LemmeKnow (a Rust port of pyWhat that recognises more than 120 formats), and a common-password check, and the search stops at the first candidate that passes. Decoders run in parallel with Rayon, and results are cached in ~/.ciphey/database.sqlite.

brief.install_notes: cargo install ciphey is the main route. Prebuilt binaries for Linux x86_64, macOS (Intel and Apple silicon), and Windows x86_64 are on the GitHub releases page, each with a .sha256 checksum. Building from source needs a Rust toolchain. On first run, a short setup asks for a colour theme, how results are shown, and whether to use a wordlist, then writes ~/.ciphey/config.toml. The Ares-era README also mentions a BERT-based 'enhanced detection' option that needs a one-time download of a roughly 500MB model and a free Hugging Face account, enabled with 'ciphey --enable-enhanced-detection'; the current README does not mention it. A Dockerfile exists per the older README (git clone, then docker build .). The brew formula gives no extra install steps.
brief.standout: Most decoders need you to name the cipher, or they brute-force one at a time. This tool searches chains of decoders with no key or hint, and its crib mode (-r with a regex like flag\{) suits CTF work. It also reports what the plaintext is (for example an IP address, a TOTP URI, or a password in a mount command), not just the decoded string.
brief.status: Unknown as to exact dates: neither page shows a last-commit or release date. Evidence of ongoing work: the current README mentions an MCP server and a crates.io 0.12.0 release that is behind master, plus a Notion doc and a Discord bot. The Ares-named page carries an older README (Dec 2022 screenshot, 16 decoders), so the two pages are at different points in the project's history.
brief.caveats: Name mismatch: the brew formula is named 'ares' with executable 'ares', but the README describes the 'ciphey' crate and binary, and says Ares was the old name. Check the binary name after install. The bee-san/Ares URL serves an older README for the same project, and the current README lives at bee-san/Ciphey. Plaintext detection is imperfect: very short phrases, non-English text, JSON, and unusual flag formats can be missed or misidentified. The default timeout is 5 seconds. The library API on master differs from the crates.io 0.12.0 release (a git dependency is needed for the newer functions). The MCP feature is not in a crates.io release yet. Licence is MIT. The homepage fetch did not fail, but the content may not match what the brew formula's description implies. The decoder count differs between sources: 16 in the Ares-era README, 24 in the current one.

Paste in text that's been encoded or encrypted. Ciphey works out how and hands you the plaintext.
No key, no cipher name, no hints.
One of the big issues with Ciphey is that it could run forever. If it couldn't decode your text, you'd never know!

name: arping
desc: Utility to check whether MAC addresses are already taken on a LAN
why: A door into ARP: asking the LAN who has an address and seeing duplicate MACs answer back.

brief.what_it_is: Arping is a command-line ARP utility, written in C, that checks whether an IPv4 address on the local network segment is in use and reports which MAC address answers for it. It sends ARP who-has requests to the LAN and prints the is-at replies it gets back. The README also describes a second mode that goes the other way: pinging a raw MAC address with a broadcast ICMP echo, sent in an Ethernet frame addressed only to that MAC, to learn which IP it uses. The Homebrew description says it checks whether MAC addresses are taken, but the README's main framing is IP-to-MAC probing.
brief.why_it_exists: Thomas Habets wrote it because plain ping fails when a host blocks ICMP, or when you are on a non-routable net, and ARP cache entries are a more reliable signal. He also gives a catch-22 use case: someone with a block of real IANA addresses cannot ping an address before taking it, and cannot pick a free one without knowing which are taken.
brief.how_it_works: For an IP target, arping broadcasts an ARP 'who-has' request and waits for an 'is-at' reply, which the README shows with tcpdump captures. For a MAC target, it sends an ICMP echo request to a broadcast IP (255.255.255.255 or an address given with -T) inside an Ethernet frame addressed to the target MAC, and the target's echo reply reveals its IP. The README notes that many OSes do not answer broadcast pings the expected way, so -T may need tuning, and it suggests a brute-force loop over -T addresses.

brief.standout: It explains ARP-level probing clearly with real tcpdump traces and a candid FAQ. The MAC-ping trick, which sends an ICMP broadcast inside a unicast frame to a chosen MAC, reveals an IP for a host that may ignore ICMP otherwise. The author is open about its limits, down to the libnet quirks and timing accuracy.

brief.caveats: Round-trip times are imprecise, sometimes off by milliseconds, because the program only sees packets once the kernel hands them over. It does not answer for localhost or your own MAC. The author tests on Debian, Ubuntu on ARM, and OpenBSD, and says other platforms should work but are not regularly tested. Licence is GPLv2. The author says the MAC-scan brute force may be added someday, but 'don't hold your breath'.

Arping tries to drop all possible privileges as early as possible, but this is a network debugging tool, which generates low-level network packets that ordinary users have absolutely no business generating.

name: arss
desc: Analyze a sound file into a spectrogram
why: Turning a sound file into a spectrogram is a satisfying audio-to-image transform, if an old one.

brief.what_it_is: ARSS (Analysis & Resynthesis Sound Spectrograph) is a command-line program that analyses a sound file into a spectrogram image. It can also synthesise a spectrogram, or any other user-created image, back into a sound. Its spectrograph uses a base-2 logarithmic frequency scale and a filter bank rather than the usual short-time Fourier transform. The homepage describes uses such as time stretching, pitch shifting, filtering with an image editor, and drawing sounds by hand.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a tool for treating sound as an image, so that sounds can be stored as pictures, edited in image-editing programs, and turned back into audio. The author's stated aim is to leave room for experimentation: "Who knows what else, there's a lot of room for experimentation".
brief.how_it_works: Analysis runs the signal through overlapping logarithmic-scale Hann-window filter bank bands, then takes the magnitude of the analytic signal in each band as an envelope; each envelope becomes a horizontal line in the image, with amplitude mapped linearly to intensity. Synthesis upsamples each image line to the output sample rate and modulates it with either sine waves at each band's centre frequency or noise passed through the filter bank.

commands_seen.context: Compile command given in a July 2008 news item for building ARSS from source on Mac OS X. Links the libm and FFTW3 libraries and produces the arss binary.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs a C compiler (gcc), the math library, and FFTW3 (the -lfftw3 flag). The homepage gives no other setup steps. A 2008 news item mentions a Mac OS X Universal Binary with a double-click installer from a third party, and an AppleScript front end, also third party. Those are old and I did not check whether they still exist. The brew formula supplies the arss executable.
brief.standout: Instead of the STFT that most spectrographs use, ARSS uses a filter bank with envelope detection, closer to how analogue spectrographs worked. Because the image is a plain editable array of envelopes, the same tool that analyses also resynthesises, so you can paint or edit a spectrogram and hear the result.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage says "This site is in hiatus. Last updated on February 23rd, 2009". The latest release mentioned is ARSS 0.2.3 from May 30, 2008. The homepage says ARSS is "now superseded by Photosounder", a GUI program released December 17, 2008. The brew formula was not checked for a version date.
brief.caveats: The homepage is an old, hiatus-era project page with news dated 2008 to 2009, and it has no docs or install guide beyond the single gcc line. Platform details are dated: the Mac notes refer to PowerPC and Universal Binary builds. The author states the noise-synthesis volume may be "way off" for logarithmic bases other than 2 with linear frequency scale. The homepage's licence was not stated in the text I read. The Documentation, Download and Code pages were not followed because the page text did not expose their URLs.

name: arturo
desc: Simple, modern and portable programming language for efficient scripting
why: A modern, unusual scripting language with a distinctive design, worth a look for language enthusiasts.

brief.what_it_is: Arturo is an independently developed, modern, general-purpose scripting language, written in Nim, that runs on a bytecode VM. Scripts are plain text files run with the arturo executable. The README's sample is a recursive factorial function plus a loop that prints results, showing the syntax. The homepage says it ships a built-in web server, UI toolkit, databases, cryptography, HTTP clients and templating, and that scripts can be bundled into standalone executables. The homepage lists Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD, plus a JS web build.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the language is 'vaguely related to various other ones' including Logo, Rebol, Forth, Ruby, Haskell, D, Smalltalk, Tcl and Lisp, and the homepage pitches it as 'The Swiss Army Knife for ultra-efficient coding'. The author named it after a pet Emperor Scorpion, a quiet and docile creature, as a hint at what the language aspires to be.
brief.how_it_works: The README's core principles are that code is just a list of words, symbols and literal values, and that words and symbols within a block are interpreted according to context. There are no reserved words or keywords. The homepage says the language has an optimized bytecode VM with no warm-up or compilation step before a script runs.

name: asn1c
desc: Compile ASN.1 specifications into C source code
why: ASN.1 is the hidden grammar behind telecom and certificates, and this compiler is a real door into it.

brief.what_it_is: asn1c is a command-line compiler that takes ASN.1 module files (ASN.1 is the schema language used for telecom and X.509 certificate formats) and generates C source code. The generated C is described as C++ compatible. You pass it one or more .asn1 modules, and by default it writes .c and .h files, one set per ASN.1 type. The generated code serializes native C structures into BER, DER, OER, PER, or XER data and deserializes them back.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says ASN.1 is used in practice for X.509 certificates in HTTPS, phone-to-network control data, and car-to-car communication, and that no open source compiler supports the whole ASN.1 family. It calls asn1c 'arguably the most evolved open source ASN.1 compiler.'
brief.how_it_works: The compiler runs in three stages: it parses the ASN.1 file into a syntax tree, 'fixes' that tree by checking for semantic errors and rewriting it into canonical form, then compiles the tree into the target language. Options -E, -F, and -P print the output after each stage. The generated API pairs encoders with decoders by transfer syntax, for example der_encode() with ber_decode() for BER and DER, and uper_encode() with uper_decode() for UPER.
