name: cppinsights
desc: See your source code with the eyes of a compiler
why: Shows what the compiler actually does to your C++ code, templates and lambdas expanded, a genuinely revealing way to see your source.

brief.what_it_is: C++ Insights is a Clang-based command-line tool, also served as a web page at cppinsights.io, that takes a C++ source file and rewrites it as the compiler's internal view of the same code. The README calls this a source-to-source transformation: the output is C++ rather than assembly. Its examples show compiler-generated special member functions, lambdas, range-based for-loops, structured bindings, the implicit upcast from Derived to Base, and the deduced types behind auto and decltype. The homepage only exposes Source, Insight and Console panes, and the README says the goal is compilable output, though that is not always possible. The homepage footer credits Andreas Fertig and says the site is powered by Flask and CodeMirror.
brief.why_it_exists: The author found that C++ AST dumps and Compiler Explorer assembly are not in the language he writes, and that showing a student an AST and saying 'this is all there was' was unsatisfying. He wanted a view of the compiler's work expressed in C++ itself.
brief.how_it_works: It is a Clang-based tool, so it parses with Clang and uses Clang's AST to decide what to rewrite. The transformation is then printed back out as C++ source. The README warns that results are only as good as Clang's understanding of the AST, and that output is not guaranteed to compile.

name: cppad
desc: Differentiation of C++ Algorithms
why: Automatic differentiation for C++ algorithms; a genuine math idea, though it is a library rather than something to play with.

brief.what_it_is: CppAD is a C++ template library that computes derivatives of any algorithm you can write in C++. You write your function using its AD scalar and vector types, and it records the operations and produces derivative values from them, with no hand-derived formulas. Input is ordinary C++ code that computes function values; output is function values plus derivatives of arbitrary order, Jacobians, Hessians, and sparsity patterns. It is a library for other programs to link against, not a command-line tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the core idea as Algorithmic Differentiation: automatically creating an algorithm that computes derivative values from an algorithm that computes function values. The docs point to autodiff.org for research and promotion of AD.
brief.how_it_works: CppAD uses operator overloading of a template class AD, so ordinary arithmetic on AD objects is recorded as a sequence of operations. That recording is stored in an ADFun object, which can then evaluate function values and derivatives of any order, and sparsity patterns, using the base type. The docs also describe optimizing the recorded sequence, dynamic parameters that are not differentiated, atomic functions for user-defined derivatives, and multi-threading support with OpenMP, Boost, and POSIX threads.
brief.install_notes: The README says the preferred way to test and install is with cmake; an autotools procedure exists but is deprecated and will eventually be removed. The docs have an Install page, and the user guide's install section lists get_optional.sh scripts (get_adolc.sh, get_cppadcg.sh, get_colpack.sh, get_fadbad.sh, get_ipopt.sh, get_sacado.sh) for optional third-party packages. These were seen only as file names in the navigation, not as commands. The docs also mention a cmake configuration step for choosing the test vector class, but I did not see a verbatim command. Homebrew installs no executables for this package, so you would be using it from C++ code.
brief.standout: It is a genuine math idea, not a toy: it differentiates whatever C++ code you already have by operator overloading, and the docs go further with sparsity-pattern-driven sparse Jacobians and Hessians, and atomic and checkpoint functions for user-defined derivatives. It is a library for building numerical programs, not something to play with at a prompt.

The README says the autotools path is deprecated. The homepage I fetched was the user guide rather than a README, and the brew description and the scout note were the only context I had for the package name.

name: cppp
desc: Partial Preprocessor for C
why: A partial C preprocessor from an old-school hacker, handling only some directives, which makes it a quirky window into macro processing.

brief.what_it_is: cppp is a small command-line tool that applies a subset of C preprocessor conditionals. You run it with macro names defined (-D) or undefined (-U) on the command line, and it reads C source on input and writes C source on output. Conditionals (#ifdef, #ifndef, #if, #elif, #elifdef, #elifndef) that test those symbols are resolved and removed or simplified. Everything else is left in place, and macros it does not know about are treated as indeterminate. It does not expand macros or do the rest of the preprocessor's work.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Brian Raiter, wrote it for legacy codebases where #ifdef statements have built up over time and hurt legibility. He first wrote it as a learning exercise, then said it later saved him from a tedious and error-prone cleanup.
brief.how_it_works: Symbols given with -D are treated as defined and symbols given with -U as undefined. Conditionals that test those symbols are applied, and partly determined #if expressions are rewritten to keep only the undecided part. Numeric constants assigned with -D (for example MYLIB_VERSION=0x0102) can be used in arithmetic comparisons, which are then evaluated.

commands_seen.context: Example from the page: defines FOO, so the FOO branch is kept and the #else branch is dropped.
Example from the page: defines BAR only, so the nested BAR test is resolved against that.
Example from the page: undefines FOO and BAZ, so the #ifdef FOO branch is removed and the #ifndef BAZ branch is kept.
Example from the page: undefines FOO only, which leaves the BAR and BAZ tests partly unresolved in the output.
Example from the page: assigns a numeric value, so the #if MYLIB_VERSION >= ((1 << 8) | 13) test evaluates to false and the older API branch is kept.
Example from the page: assigns a newer numeric value, so the same #if test evaluates to true and the newer API branch is kept.

brief.standout: It is a deliberately partial preprocessor: it only resolves conditionals, and anything it cannot decide is passed through unchanged. That makes it a good way to see how #if and defined() evaluation works, and it is useful for stripping configuration branches out of old code.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows a cppp-2.9 tarball and no release date or commit history. I did not open the Sourcehut page, so I cannot say when the last change was made.

A test that depends on another macro's value stays unresolved unless that macro is also given on the command line. name: creduce
desc: Reduce a C/C++ program while keeping a property of interest
why: Automatically shrinks a crashing C program to a minimal case, a fascinating look at test-case reduction, though deprecated.

brief.what_it_is: C-Reduce is a command-line tool for shrinking C or C++ source files. You give it a large program and a test script (the interestingness test) that says whether the program still has some property, such as triggering a compiler bug. It repeatedly tries smaller variants and keeps the ones that still pass the test, and it outputs a much smaller C/C++ program with the same property. The README says it also reduces programs in other languages such as JavaScript and Rust, though it is built for C/C++.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is intended for people who discover and report bugs in compilers and other tools that process C/C++ code, who need a minimal test case to report.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes the reduction loop only briefly: it searches for smaller versions of the input that keep the property of interest. Each run of the interestingness test happens in a fresh temporary directory containing a copy of the file being reduced. With more than one core it runs candidate compiler invocations in parallel and may kill them when they are no longer useful. The README does not explain the reduction passes in detail; INSTALL.md mentions an internal clang_delta tool built against LLVM/Clang.

name: crcany
desc: Compute any CRC, a bit at a time, a byte at a time, and a word at a time
why: A generator for any CRC variant that shows the bit-level machinery behind checksums in a way few people have seen.

brief.what_it_is: crcany is a C suite of programs that compute any CRC from its parameter set (the Greg Cook / Ross Williams model format) and can generate C code for it. It takes a CRC definition, either by catalogue name or as parameters, plus data bytes, and outputs the checksum. It can also combine two CRCs, given the CRC of each sequence and the length of the second, to get the CRC of the concatenation. A companion tool generates .c and .h files for one or many CRC definitions.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's stated motivation is to "Provide once and for all a definitive reference for how to compute and combine any CRC with any of bit, byte, or word-at-a-time algorithms, on any big or little-endian architecture."
brief.how_it_works: It computes a CRC bit at a time, as a hardware shift register would. For byte-at-a-time, it first uses the bit-at-a-time routine to build a 256-entry table of CRCs for all byte values. For word-at-a-time, it expands the byte table into n-1 further tables, where n is the word size in bytes, with separate little-endian and big-endian flavors.

commands_seen.context: Compiles the crcany, crctest, crcall, crcadd, and mincrc executables from the repository root.
Tests CRC calculation and generated CRC code against the full list of catalogued CRCs.

brief.install_notes: Build from source with make; the README names no other dependencies, accounts, or runtimes. Generated code defaults to the host's integer sizes and endianness, and can be forced to 32- or 64-bit words and big- or little-endian. The README gives no usage syntax for the crcany binary itself.
brief.standout: It treats the CRC as a single parameterized algorithm and generates optimized C for any width up to 64 bits, rather than hard-coding one polynomial. It also includes CRC combination, which lets you join checksums of separate blocks without re-reading the data.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release or version notes and I saw no commit dates. It does have a working build and test target and a full catalogue of CRC definitions.
brief.caveats: The README documents no usage syntax for crcany itself, so anyone writing examples will need to read the source or run it. Code generation is limited to CRCs up to 64 bits; the bit-wise calculation goes up to 128 bits on 64-bit machines. The getcrcs tool scrapes Greg Cook's website for definitions. The README does not name a C compiler requirement or a platform list beyond the endianness discussion.
quotes: _crcany_ can compute a CRC in three different ways.
Provide once and for all a definitive reference for how to compute and combine any CRC with any of bit, byte, or word-at-a-time algorithms, on any big or little-endian architecture.
This code is under the zlib license, permitting free commercial use.

name: crosstool-ng
desc: Tool for building toolchains
why: Building cross-compilation toolchains from scratch reveals how compilers, libcs, and targets are actually assembled.

brief.what_it_is: Crosstool-NG is a generator for cross toolchains, the set of compiler, assembler, linker and C library that builds code for a different target machine than the one it runs on. Per the homepage it supports many architectures and components and has a menuconfig-style interface for choosing them. The README says the toolchain it produces will compile, assemble and link the code being developed, and that some pieces, such as static libraries, can end up inside the resulting binaries. Its command is ct-ng, which the README says is actually a make(2) script underneath. The README does not spell out the exact inputs and outputs beyond this, so treat the specifics of the configuration step as coming from the homepage description only.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage calls it a versatile (cross) toolchain generator with a simple yet powerful menuconfig-style interface. The README's framing is that toolchains are an essential component of a software development project and that the project aims at building them.
brief.how_it_works: ct-ng is a make-driven script, and the README warns that ct-ng --help prints make's help instead, with no clean workaround. The install docs describe a working directory where you run ct-ng help, which suggests you configure and build from there. The docs index lists sections on configuring, building the toolchain, toolchain types and how a toolchain is constructed, but I did not open those pages, so I cannot describe the build mechanism beyond that.

name: cryptol
desc: Domain-specific language for specifying cryptographic algorithms
why: A domain-specific language for specifying cryptographic algorithms that can be checked against implementations with formal tools.

brief.what_it_is: Cryptol is an interpreter for version 3 of the Cryptol language, a domain-specific language for writing executable specifications of cryptographic algorithms. You feed it Cryptol source and interact with it through a REPL, where you can evaluate expressions and run checks. The `:check` command tests predicates against randomly generated test vectors, in the style of QuickCheck. The `:prove` command calls out to SMT solvers such as Yices, Z3, or CVC5 to prove predicates for all possible inputs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the Cryptol specification language was designed by Galois for the NSA Laboratory for Advanced Cybersecurity Research as a public standard for specifying cryptographic algorithms. It argues that a Cryptol reference specification can serve as the formal documentation for a cryptographic module.
brief.how_it_works: Cryptol specifications are fully executable, so designers can run and experiment with them as the design changes. `:check` runs predicates on random inputs, QuickCheck-style. `:prove` and `:sat` hand the question to an external SMT solver, with Z3 as the default. The README also says Galois builds tools that consume Cryptol specs and C or Java implementations, letting you verify that an implementation meets its spec, though this takes some work and is described on the SAW website rather than here.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux, and Windows are on the GitHub releases page; Windows also has .msi installers. Z3 must be on your PATH, since Cryptol uses it by default for type checking and for :sat and :prove. Building from source needs GHC (9.6.7, 9.8.4, or 9.12.2, easiest via ghcup), GMP, and ncurses. Cryptol reads its library files from the embedded copy by default. To override them, copy the lib directory into $HOME/.cryptol or set CRYPTOLPATH.
brief.standout: Specifications are executable, so the same file can be run, randomly tested with :check, and proven with an SMT solver with :prove. It is aimed at cryptographers and implementers rather than general programmers. Galois also links it to implementation-verification tooling (SAW).

name: csmith
desc: Generates random C programs conforming to the C99 standard
why: Generates random valid C programs to find compiler bugs, a strange and genuinely clever way to stress-test toolchains.

brief.what_it_is: Csmith is a random generator of C programs. You run the csmith command, optionally with options, and it writes one randomly generated C program to standard output, which you redirect to a .c file. The README says the output is free of undefined behaviors and also produces statistics about each generated program. The generated programs are meant to be compiled and run, and their output compared across compilers.
brief.why_it_exists: The primary purpose is to find compiler bugs with random programs, using differential testing as the test oracle. The README also says it can serve anyone who needs a test suite of C programs and doesn't want to write them by hand.
brief.how_it_works: Csmith generates a random C program for each run. You compile that program with two or more compilers (for example gcc and clang), run both binaries, and compare their outputs. Any difference points to a bug in one compiler, or in the unlikely case, in Csmith itself. The README says to repeat this in scripts to amplify the testing and to apply timeouts, since generated programs might contain infinite loops.

name: cryptominisat
desc: Advanced SAT solver
why: A capable SAT solver is fascinating to feed puzzles, but solvers are a known niche and this is mostly a tool for experts.

brief.what_it_is: CryptoMiniSat is a SAT solver, a program that decides whether a Boolean formula can be satisfied. It takes a CNF file in DIMACS format, extended with XOR clauses, and prints 's SATISFIABLE' with a variable assignment ('v' lines) or 's UNSATISFIABLE'. It runs from the command line and also has C++, Python (pycryptosat) and C/Rust wrappers that support assumptions and repeated solve calls. A loop that bans each model it finds can enumerate all solutions, and it can write XLRUP proofs that an independent checker verifies.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as an advanced incremental SAT solver for users who need to embed or drive SAT solving from code, not just run one-off files. The homepage describes it as a modern, multi-threaded, feature-rich, simplifying solver, and asks users to cite its SAT 2009 paper.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. The homepage, which describes the CryptoMiniSat 4 era, says the solver simplifies the instance during search (inprocessing) using variable elimination, subsumption, vivification and failed-literal probing. It also says XOR clauses are recovered and manipulated, and that redundant clauses are removed based on tracked usefulness. The current build pulls in the CaDiCaL and CaDiBack solvers as dependencies.

name: cuba
desc: Library for multidimensional numerical integration
why: Real multidimensional numerical integration from particle physics, a genuine research tool you could run at home.

brief.what_it_is: Cuba is a C/C++, Fortran, and Mathematica library for multidimensional numerical integration. You give it an integrand function and integration bounds, and it returns the integral's value along with an error estimate and a χ²-probability that indicates how reliable that error estimate is. It offers four interchangeable routines (Vegas, Suave, Divonne, and Cuhre) with nearly identical calling conventions, so you can swap one for another to cross-check results. It can also integrate vector-valued integrands and parallelizes the sampling automatically in Fortran and C/C++.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a tool for numerical integration in particle physics: different methods suit different integrands, so a researcher needs several routines with a common interface to compare results and to reach high precision when needed. The page describes the library as developed at the Max Planck Institute for Physics in Munich by Thomas Hahn.
brief.how_it_works: Vegas, Suave, and Divonne are Monte Carlo or stratified-sampling methods that draw quasi-random (Sobol or Korobov) or pseudo-random (Mersenne Twister or Ranlux) points, using importance sampling, globally adaptive subdivision, or numerical-optimization-guided partitioning. Cuhre is deterministic: it uses a cubature rule on subregions and, in each iteration, halves the subregion with the largest error along the axis with the largest fourth difference. The page notes that Cuhre is usually the only practical choice for relative accuracies much below 1e–3.

commands_seen.context: Instruction on the homepage for the prebuilt MathLink executables: after downloading, gunzip the file and then make it executable with this command.

brief.install_notes: Source is distributed as a tarball (latest Cuba-4.2.2.tar.gz, about 744 kB); the page says the source compiles with gcc. The C functions can be called from Fortran directly without adapter code. Prebuilt Mathematica MathLink executables (version 4.2) are offered for Linux x86-64, macOS x86-64, and Cygwin/Windows, each as a gzipped file that needs gunzip and chmod 755. Windows native builds are not supported: Cuba 3 and later use fork(2), so Windows users are pointed to Cygwin. Third-party wrappers exist for Maple, REDUCE, R, Python, Julia, and Rust. The page does not give a Homebrew-specific procedure.
brief.standout: Four quite different algorithms share one calling interface, so cross-checking one integral against another is a matter of changing a routine name. The page also flags that most questions concern bounds other than the unit hypercube, and answers it by scaling the integrand with a Jacobian rather than changing the bounds, which it shows in a Fortran snippet.

The page lists no newer release. I did not check a code repository for later commits, so the status is inferred from the homepage only.

Upward of 75% of all questions regarding Cuba have to do with how to choose bounds different from the unit hypercube in Fortran, C, and C++. The solution is not to choose bounds but to scale the integrand.

name: ctl
desc: Programming language for digital color management
why: A small programming language for color transforms in film and VFX pipelines, an odd domain with a real design of its own.

brief.what_it_is: CTL (Color Transformation Language) is a small domain-specific programming language for describing digital color transforms as programs. A color management system includes an interpreter that loads a CTL program and runs it on the pixels of an input image, producing a transformed output image. The command-line tool ctlrender applies a CTL transform to image files, for example ctlrender -ctl transform.ctl input.exr output.exr. Parameters such as exposure can be set to adjust a transform.
brief.why_it_exists: The README argues that general-purpose languages like C, C++ or Python are poor for sharing color transforms, because recipients may need to compile code, portability is hard to guarantee, bugs can crash a host application, and malware protection is difficult. CTL is restricted to the operations color transforms need, which the author says improves portability, protects host applications and users, and allows efficient interpreters.
brief.how_it_works: A color management system with CTL support runs an interpreter that loads a specific CTL program and applies it to the original image, which is the program's input, producing the transformed image as output. Two parties with the same CTL program and the same parameter settings get identical results, so transforms are shared by distributing the program. The language is limited to single-pixel operations, so it cannot express neighborhood operations such as blurs or whole-image statistics.

desc: Build compacted de Bruijn graphs from references or reads
why: Builds compacted de Bruijn graphs from sequencing reads, real genomics software that is a close call for a home break.

brief.what_it_is: Cuttlefish 3 is a command-line tool that builds compacted de Bruijn graphs, where each vertex is a maximal unitig, from reference FASTA sequences or sequencing reads (FASTQ, gzipped input accepted). It can build an uncolored graph or a colored graph over a collection of genomes, and the colored output records which input sources cover which stretch of each unitig, written alongside the unitig FASTA. The binary also has commands for comparing graphs, querying colors, cleaning up, and probing.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as fast, parallel graph construction that stays feasible at collection scale, claiming it has built the colored graph of 150,000 bacterial genomes on a single machine. The homepage says the tool is designed for collections too large to keep in RAM.
brief.how_it_works: Partition buckets, blocked edge matrices, and collation buckets live on disk, so peak RAM tracks the worker set rather than the graph size. Partitioning, local contraction, discontinuity contraction, and final collation all run multi-threaded under a worker budget set by the user (the -t flag). The working directory passed with -w holds the intermediate external-memory files.

name: cweb
desc: Literate documentation system for C, C++, and Java
why: Knuth's literate programming system, weaving code and documentation into a single source file, is a genuinely odd and historic idea.

brief.what_it_is: CWEB is a literate programming system for documenting C, C++, and Java programs. You write one source file, foo.w, that mixes prose documentation with code. CTANGLE reads that file and produces a compilable program file, foo.c. CWEAVE reads the same file and produces foo.tex, a prettily printed, cross-indexed document for TeX. The homepage describes two programs, ctangle and cweave, and the brew package provides those two executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The authors frame it as treating a program as a communication to human beings rather than as a set of instructions to a computer. The homepage says WEB was developed by Donald E. Knuth while he wrote TeX, and that CWEB adapts it to C (Silvio Levy, 1987) and later to C++ and ANSI C.
brief.how_it_works: CTANGLE extracts the code from the .w file into a compilable .c file. CWEAVE typesets the documentation and code into a .tex file with cross-references and an index. Since version 3.61 the weaver can also produce PDF with clickable links, either through standard TeX with dvipdfm or through pdfTeX.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers the CWEB software by anonymous ftp from ftp.cs.stanford.edu, in the ~ftp/pub/cweb directory, as cweb.tar.gz. The page does not describe a build procedure, and it does not mention the brew package. For PDF output you need TeX plus either dvipdfm or pdfTeX. The page points to the Makefile for examples of the PDF workflow. The page also links the CWEB development project maintained by Andreas Scherer, which the authors say carries the current news and newer versions.
brief.standout: The source file is a hypertext document as much as a program, and the page presents the cross-indexed typeset output as a core deliverable. The authors also say CTANGLE and CWEAVE are now finished and will not change, which is an unusual stance for a developer tool.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage says CTANGLE and CWEAVE are stable and the authors do not intend to change CWEB unless a devastating bug is found. The most recent version it names is 3.64, with a 3.6 cover edition and a 2001 printing. The page carries no release dates. Ongoing development of CWEB 4.0 is referred to the separate CWEB development project, which I did not fetch.
brief.caveats: The homepage is an authors' page for the 1993 Knuth and Levy book, and its details may be dated. The book is out of print. The page warns that identifiers such as and, compl, not, or, xor, and not_eq became reserved in newer C++, so old .w files may format strangely; the fix is a line like @s not_eq normal. The authors describe some non-catastrophic infelicities as permanent features. I did not check the brew formula or how well the build works on other platforms.
quotes: The main idea is to regard a program as a communication to human beings rather than as a set of instructions to a computer.
The authors do not intend to change CWEB henceforth unless some devastating new bug is discovered.
If you are in the software industry and do not use CWEB but your competitors do, your competitors will soon overtake you---and you'll miss out on a lot of fun besides.

name: cyme
desc: List system USB buses and devices
why: Lists USB buses and devices with the descriptor trees, a readable door into the USB hardware layer.

brief.what_it_is: Cyme is a command-line tool that lists the USB buses and devices on the host machine, including full device descriptors. It is described as a cross-platform replacement for lsusb, targeting Linux, macOS and Windows. It takes no input beyond the host's USB hardware and its own config file, and prints a list, a tree, lsusb-style output, or JSON, with filtering, configurable display blocks and coloured or ASCII output. It also has a `cyme watch` subcommand for hotplug events. It can be used as a Rust library as well.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, an embedded developer who uses a USB listing tool often, found lsusb's verbose dump too verbose, its tree lacking useful data, and its behaviour poor outside Linux. The project began as a replacement for a barely working lsusb script and as a Rust learning project, and grew into a cross-platform lsusb.
brief.how_it_works: The default build uses a pure Rust profiler built on nusb, which reads the system USB tree and device descriptors. On Linux it can also use udev for driver and USB ID lookup. Older or alternative backends are available: libusb, which is what lsusb uses, and macOS system_profiler parsing. The README says the libusb backend uses control messages to gather the same information lsusb does.

name: cvs-fast-export
desc: Export an RCS or CVS history as a fast-import stream
why: Converts decades-old CVS repository history into a git fast-import stream, a fossil-digging tool.

brief.what_it_is: cvs-fast-export is a command-line converter that reads RCS files or a CVS project repository (directories of ,v master files) and writes a Git fast-import stream to standard output. It groups the per-file commits and tags into per-project changesets, then emits them in topological order. The package also includes cvssync, which mirrors masters from a remote CVS host, and cvsconvert, which runs a trial conversion and checks it against the original. A DOT-format graph of the commit DAG for graphviz can also be produced.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as a way to export an RCS or CVS history as a fast-import stream, and the man page says that plain conversions contain fossils that reposurgeon is good at cleaning up. The author frames the tool as the first stage of a conversion, with reposurgeon used for sanity checks and polishing.
brief.how_it_works: Changesets are formed by coalescing per-file revisions that share a commitid, or, when there is no commitid, that have identical comments, authors and dates within a time-fuzz window (default 300 seconds). Tags become lightweight Git tags, found by a two-pass search for an existing snapshot or else a synthetic commit. HEAD is renamed to master, and .cvsignore files are translated to .gitignore. The program does not expand CVS $-keywords and does not re-encode file contents or comments.

commands_seen.context: Typical invocation: convert the CVS or RCS masters in the current directory and write the fast-import stream to stream.fi.
Alternative invocation that feeds the master filenames to stdin, one per line.
Example from the man page: fetch the CVS masters for groff from a remote CVS host into a local directory named groff.
Example from the man page: convert the fetched groff masters into the stream file groff.fi.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the Homebrew formula is described in the material I read. The GitLab project lists the package names cvs-fast-export, cvs-fast-export-tools and cvs-fast-export-doc. The docs I read state no runtime requirements, first-run configuration or accounts. The man page mentions that a -A authormap file can be supplied to map usernames to Git identities, but that is optional. I did not fetch the README.html or the cvsconvert/cvssync pages.
brief.standout: Rather than trying to reconstruct changesets from shared tags, it groups changesets only by commitid or by matching metadata within a time window, and it warns when history is ambiguous instead of guessing. It is built to hand off to reposurgeon, and it can emit cvs-revisions properties that reposurgeon uses as reference-lifting hints.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage is a resource page for version 2.6, dated 06 Oct 2026, and its Recent Changes entry reads 'Improve handling of vendor branches.' The man page was last updated 2026-10-06. The GitLab project was created June 10, 2015, and the author is Eric S. Raymond.
brief.caveats: Nothing here installs or runs on Windows; the docs say nothing about Windows support. CVS vendor branches are a known source of trouble, and the program warns about some cases but not all, so output can be wrong for those. $-keywords are not expanded, which leaves unreliable $-header data. Memory use is proportional to the total volume of attributions, comments and blobs in the repository. History from before commitids (CVS older than 1.12) can be ordered wrongly because of clock skew. Incremental dumps must reanalyse the whole repository. CVSNT extension fields are ignored. The license is GPL v2 or later, per the GitLab page.

This tool is best used in conjunction with reposurgeon(1).

name: dafny
desc: Verification-aware programming language
why: A verification-aware language where you prove programs correct, a rare door into formal methods that most developers never open.

brief.what_it_is: Dafny is a verification-aware programming language with a built-in static verifier. You write code together with specifications (pre- and postconditions, loop invariants, termination conditions) in Dafny itself, and the verifier checks that the implementation meets those specifications, flagging errors and showing counterexamples as you type. When you are done, Dafny compiles the verified code to C#, Go, Python, Java, or JavaScript so it can fit into an existing toolchain. Input is Dafny source; output is verification results plus compiled code in the target language.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to reduce the risk of costly late-stage bugs that testing typically misses, by making verification an integral part of development rather than a separate afterthought.
brief.how_it_works: The verifier runs continuously while you edit, similar to a language server checking a file, and reports errors or counterexamples inline. Specifications are written in the same language as the program, so the proof obligations live next to the code. The README does not describe the underlying solver or proof engine in detail.
brief.install_notes: The README suggests installing Dafny in Visual Studio Code and following the Dafny tutorial, or downloading the Dafny CLI for command-line work. Binary downloads are offered for Windows, macOS, GNU/Linux, and FreeBSD. No command lines, runtime prerequisites, or first-run steps appear in the README I read. The Homebrew formula's executable is named dafny.
brief.standout: Few developers ever meet formal verification, and Dafny is one of the more approachable doors into it: the verifier runs live in the editor, and the output still compiles to mainstream languages. Its design draws from Euclid, Eiffel, CLU, ML, and Coq/VeriFast, which is a distinctive lineage for a practical tool.
brief.status: Maintained as far as the materials show: the project has an active GitHub repository with an issue tracker, a Zulip community channel, a reference manual, a standard library, and IDE plugins. I did not find a last-release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so recency is not confirmed.
brief.caveats: Verification is a real learning curve; the README points to a tutorial and course lectures rather than a quick start. The compiler targets are C#, Go, Python, Java, and JavaScript, and the README notes more are to come. The README and docs site describe a Coco parser subdirectory under third-party license terms. The homepage link in the catalogue points to the README on GitHub rather than the project site.
quotes: Dafny is a verification-ready programming language. As you type in your program, Dafny's verifier constantly looks over your shoulder, flags any errors, shows you counterexamples, and congratulates you when your code matches your specifications.
Dafny will give you assurance that your code meets the specifications you write, while letting you write both code and specifications in the Dafny programming language itself.
Dafny makes rigorous verification an integral part of development, thus reducing costly late-stage bugs that may be missed by testing.

name: daemontools
desc: Collection of tools for managing UNIX services
why: D. J. Bernstein's supervision suite is a classic old-school design for keeping services alive, a door into Unix process management worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: daemontools is a collection of tools for managing UNIX services, according to the homepage. Its central program, supervise, starts a service and restarts it if it dies, and it needs only a directory containing a run script that runs the service. multilog handles logging: it saves error messages to one or more logs, can timestamp each line, can include or exclude lines matching patterns for each log, and rotates logs to limit disk use. The package also ships further programs (svscan, svscanboot, svc, svok, svstat, tai64n, tai64nlocal, setuidgid, envuidgid, envdir, softlimit, setlock, fghack, pgrphack, readproctitle), which the homepage lists by name only.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit motivation beyond describing the tools. It frames the problem as keeping UNIX services running and capturing their error output in managed logs.
brief.how_it_works: supervise watches one service directory and runs its run script, restarting the service whenever it exits. multilog receives the service's error output and writes it to one or more logs, optionally timestamping lines and filtering them by pattern. If the disk fills, multilog pauses and retries without losing data.
brief.install_notes: The Homebrew caveat says services are stored in $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/etc/service/. The homepage has a 'How to install daemontools' section and a 'How to start daemontools' section, but I did not fetch those sub-pages, so I have no install or first-run commands to report.
brief.standout: The supervision model is minimal: a service is just a directory with a run script, with no config format. multilog's rule that a full disk pauses logging and retries without dropping data is a specific, deliberate design choice.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows no release date, version, or last-updated note, and the Homebrew metadata gives no version date either. The page's own voice is that of a long-standing personal project by D. J. Bernstein.
brief.caveats: I read only the homepage. Its section titles point to install, start, and per-program pages whose contents I did not retrieve, so the list of commands is empty and the install steps are unverified. The homepage itself has no visible licence statement, and I did not check for one. The Homebrew scout note calls the design 'classic old-school'; that is an editorial comment, not something the homepage states.
quotes: daemontools is a collection of tools for managing UNIX services.
supervise monitors a service. It starts the service and restarts the service if it dies.
all supervise needs is a directory with a run script that runs the service.
If the disk fills up, it pauses and tries again, without losing any data.
fetch_log: https://cr.yp.to/daemontools.html: fetched OK, returned page text with section titles and the 'What is it?' description; per-program and install pages were not followed.

judge.reason: Its tiny directory-and-run-script supervision model, paired with unusually careful log rotation and retry behavior, makes a worthwhile Unix process-management design to explore.

name: d2
desc: Modern diagram scripting language that turns text to diagrams
why: Diagram scripting language is a neat text-to-picture transform, but it is popular and mostly a diagram tool.

brief.what_it_is: D2 is an open-source command-line tool and Go library that turns text written in its own declarative diagram language into diagrams. You write a .d2 file describing shapes, containers, and arrows, and the d2 command renders it to SVG, PNG, PDF, PPTX, GIF, or ASCII. It bundles three layout engines and a built-in autoformatter, and it can watch a file and live-reload a browser preview as you edit. The homepage also describes an online playground and editor extensions for VS Code, Vim, and Obsidian.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to "get a mental model from your head onto the screen, then make edits with your team" with simple syntax and no drag-and-drop diagram editor. The README calls it "A modern diagram scripting language that turns text to diagrams."
brief.how_it_works: A .d2 file is parsed into a graph of shapes, containers, and connections, with variables, imports, and globs for reuse. The chosen layout engine (dagre by default, elk, or the opt-in tala) positions the nodes, and the renderer writes the result as SVG or another export format. Sketch mode, LaTeX labels, and fonts are handled by bundled Go ports of rough.js, MathJax, and Source Sans Pro-based rendering.

Quickstart: creates a minimal one-line D2 source file.
Quickstart: renders in.d2 to out.svg, opens a browser window, and live-reloads on changes to in.d2.
Alternative install from source if Go is installed; the README notes this does not include the manpage.

Install page: the step to confirm the installation worked.
Lists the bundled layout engines; d2 layout <name> shows that engine's configuration options.

brief.install_notes: The README's primary path is the curl-to-shell install script, which the README itself says to pair with a review of its behavior (--dry-run). It also says the OS package manager is preferred for security, and the homepage says D2 is included in Homebrew and Winget. Installing from source needs Go; precompiled binaries are on the GitHub releases page; a release-from-source route with manpages is documented in docs/INSTALL.md. The README says D2 needs no browser to run and can work entirely server-side, and no account is mentioned. Fonts can be swapped by supplying your own .ttf files. Editor support needs the separate VS Code or Vim extensions.
brief.standout: The homepage claims D2 is the only text-to-diagram language that can produce animated diagrams, and it also advertises a hand-drawn sketch mode and an offline CLI with watch mode. Its layout engines are native Go ports (dagre, elk, and the TALA engine aimed at software architecture diagrams), so the tool needs no external runtime. The README also lists a large community ecosystem of plugins, including Pandoc filters, MkDocs, VitePress, and a Postgres ERD importer.
brief.status: Maintained, with evidence but no dates. The README shows active CI, a weekly race-test workflow, a release badge, a changelog, and a next.md file for upcoming changes. The homepage is a current docs site with a Discord and blog. I did not see a last-release date or last-commit date, so I cannot give an exact date.
brief.caveats: The install script is curl piped to sh; the README itself recommends the package manager for better security. The README says D2 makes no network connection after installation, except for periodic version checks against GitHub. TALA is bundled but opt-in. The README says the editor extensions for VS Code and Vim exist, but the homepage says the Vim and VS Code support has 'more coming soon,' so coverage may be incomplete. The license is Mozilla Public License 2.0. The 'only language that can animate diagrams' claim is the project's own marketing statement and I did not verify it against other tools.

Create beautiful diagrams in minutes. Simple syntax. Endlessly customizable.
D2 is the only language that can produce animated diagrams from text.
D2 does not use an internet connection after installation, except to check for version updates from Github periodically.

name: damask-grid
desc: Grid solver of DAMASK - Multi-physics crystal plasticity simulation package
why: A real crystal plasticity solver you can run at home, a genuine materials-science simulation rabbit hole.

brief.what_it_is: DAMASK (the Düsseldorf Advanced Material Simulation Kit) is a multiphysics crystal plasticity simulation package. The grid solver, which is the part this formula installs as damask_grid and DAMASK_grid, takes a geometry file (a .vti grain structure on a regular grid), a load case YAML file, and a material YAML file, then runs a spectral (FFT) solve. Its output is an HDF5-based result file (DADF5). The wider package also includes a Python library for pre- and post-processing, a mesh solver that is still under development, and an integration into the commercial MSC Marc FEM code.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage argues that treating mechanics in isolation is no longer sufficient for emergent advanced high-strength materials, where deformation interacts with displacive phase transformation, significant heating, and potential damage evolution. DAMASK is meant to handle these coupled multiphysics problems using crystal plasticity with a modular approach where additional field equations are solved in a fully coupled way using a staggered approach.
brief.how_it_works: The grid solver is set up with a Geometry file and a Load Case file, plus a materialpoint configuration in YAML that defines constitutive models and homogenization. The docs describe it as a spectral (FFT) solver on a regular grid with mixed periodic boundary conditions, as opposed to the FEM-based mesh solver and MSC Marc. Parallelism is via OpenMP threads (OMP_NUM_THREADS) and/or MPI, where MPI decomposes the domain along the z-axis into layers of roughly equal height.

commands_seen.context: Basic grid solver invocation from the usage docs; the three flags --load, --geom and --material are all mandatory. Curly brackets are placeholders for file names.
Environment variable set before running damask_grid to control the number of OpenMP threads.
Runs the grid solver over n_proc MPI processes, decomposing the domain along the z-axis; MPI and OpenMP can be combined.
Optional flag listed in the docs (shown as a flag, not a full command) to configure the numerics algorithms.
Optional flag setting the job name, which becomes the DADF5 result file name; default is {grid}_{load}_{material}.
Optional flag for the working directory; the docs spell the flag this way, with the typo included.
Restarts the simulation at increment N from a snapshot file in the working directory.
Reports the solver version and usage instructions.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the docs point to curated downloads: a complete grid simulation setup as grid.tar.xz, curated materialpoint configurations as config.tar.xz, and a mesh setup as mesh.tar.xz. The usage docs also mention a DAMASK Python library (import damask) for pre- and post-processing, and the Jupyter notebook tutorials. I did not see explicit pip or Python install steps, a license file, or any hardware requirements in the pages I read. The MSC Marc route needs a commercial MSC Marc licence and a Mentat setup with a DAMASK_Marc.f90 subroutine; I did not need that route for the grid solver.
brief.standout: It is a free, open-source spectral FFT crystal plasticity solver with a documented Python toolchain (texture generation, Voronoi polycrystals, load case generation, IPF plots, r-value calculation) and an academic citation with a DOI, which is unusual for a materials simulation code you can install with one formula. Results are stored in HDF5 with a ParaView integration, and the project asks users who make ParaView plots to overlay its logo.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage and docs look current and the GitHub mirror exists with issues and discussions enabled, but I did not find a release date or last commit date in the pages I fetched. The citation DOI points to a 2018 paper. Development happens on a private GitLab instance that requires registration, and GitHub is a read-only mirror.
brief.caveats: The development repo is private (registration required); GitHub is a read-only mirror, so outside contributions go through issues and discussions. The mesh solver is explicitly under development and the docs warn it lacks features and has convergence issues. The MSC Marc integration is commercial and fiddly (material IDs are zero-based, state variable 2 links to material.yaml, and DAMASK does not check thermal consistency with material.yaml). Marc restarts only support last converged increment. The formula installs only the grid solver executables. I did not fetch the license page, so the free and open source claim rests on the homepage feature list.

treating mechanics in isolation is no longer sufficient to study emergent advanced high-strength materials.
Warning: The mesh solver is under development. It lacks features and has convergence issues.

name: dash-mpd-cli
desc: Download media content from a DASH-MPEG or DASH-WebM MPD manifest
why: Downloads DASH streams from manifests, a window into how adaptive video is actually assembled.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line application, written in Rust and MIT-licensed, that downloads audio or video described by a DASH MPD manifest. Input is an MPD URL. It selects the best-matching alternative by bitrate, codec and similar criteria, fetches the segments over HTTP, HTTPS or HTTP/2, and muxes audio and video together using an external tool (mkvmerge, ffmpeg, VLC or MP4Box). It can also download subtitles in WebVTT, TTML, SRT, tx3g, SMIL and wvtt. Output is a local media file, with the container chosen from the output filename extension (for example .mp4, .mkv or .webm).
brief.why_it_exists: The author built it to watch a news programme from a public broadcaster's replay service at the gym, where the network was sometimes poor. The README frames it as a way to download streaming video or audio for local use, and it builds on the dash-mpd-rs library.
brief.how_it_works: It parses the MPD XML and chooses a representation by bitrate, codec, language, resolution, stream id and role. It then requests the media segments over HTTP(S) and calls an external muxer to combine them. The muxer is picked by output extension, in a preference order: for .mkv, mkvmerge then ffmpeg then MP4Box; for .mp4, ffmpeg then VLC then MP4Box; for .webm, VLC then ffmpeg. A --muxer-preference option overrides this order.

commands_seen.context: Homebrew install, listed as the install route on macOS and Linux.
Builds and installs the binary from crates.io into the Cargo bin directory, typically $HOME/.cargo/bin.
Runs the prebuilt container with Podman, mounting the current directory as /content and writing foo.mp4 to it.

Optional step, needed only on Windows and macOS before running the container with Podman.

Example of the muxer preference flag, not a standalone command: for AVI output, try VLC first, then ffmpeg.
Listed under similar tools as a comparable way to download from a DASH manifest; not part of dash-mpd-cli itself.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt binaries are on GitHub releases for Linux AMD64 (static musl), Windows AMD64 and macOS aarch64. Alternatives are cargo install or a container image at ghcr.io/emarsden/dash-mpd-cli (about 220 MB, Podman or Docker, multiarch including arm64, armv7 and riscv64). The README treats the container as the safest route because it bundles every helper. Native installs need external tools depending on use: mkvmerge (MKVToolNix) for .mkv; ffmpeg or VLC for .mp4; MP4Box (GPAC) optionally for wvtt subtitles and as a fallback muxer; mp4decrypt (Bento4) or shaka-packager for DRM; xsltproc for MPD rewriting. Non-standard install locations can be given with flags such as --ffmpeg-location, --vlc-location, --mkvmerge-location, --mp4box-location, --mp4decrypt-location and --shaka-packager-location. No account is mentioned.
brief.standout: Compared with yt-dlp, ffmpeg, VLC or streamlink, the README claims it handles multi-period manifests, XLink elements and xHE-AAC audio that those tools reportedly fail on. It can also read cookies from installed browsers, add Basic or Bearer auth for both manifest and CDN, and rewrite the MPD with a user XSLT stylesheet before downloading.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub README shows a CI badge, a crates.io badge, a deps.rs dependency-status badge and a published container image, which suggests active upkeep. I did not see a release date or last-commit date on either page, so I cannot confirm recency.
brief.caveats: Live (dynamic) MPD streams are not really supported. Pseudo-live streams work with --enable-live-streams, and --sleep-requests may help with live. Not supported: HLS m3u8, XLink with actuate=onRequest, and Microsoft Smooth Streaming. DRM decryption needs mp4decrypt or shaka-packager installed plus a key via --key. Android (termux), FreeBSD and OpenBSD need the cookies feature disabled, and OpenBSD support for the external decryptors is poor. Static musl builds do not work with OpenSSL, so they use rustls, which can fail some handshakes. The README warns that redistributing media you did not produce may breach IP law and that circumventing DRM may be prohibited in some countries.
quotes: A commandline application for downloading media content from a DASH MPD file, as used for on-demand replay of TV content and video streaming services.
dash-mpd-cli is written in the Rust programming language, meaning that it’s high performance and protected from a variety of vulnerabilities that can affect more traditional software.

The author is not the morality police nor a lawyer, but please note that redistributing media content that you have not produced may, depending on the publication licence, be a breach of intellectual property laws.

name: dbus
desc: Message bus system, providing inter-application communication
why: The message bus underneath many desktops is a protocol door most people never look through, though the formulae is commonly known.

brief.what_it_is: D-Bus is a message bus system that lets applications send messages to one another on the same computer. It runs as a bus daemon (dbus-daemon) with a system instance for events such as new hardware or printer queue changes, and a per-login-session instance for general user-application IPC. Applications connect to the daemon and exchange messages through it, though two applications can also talk directly over a one-to-one framework. The reference implementation includes dbus-daemon and the libdbus library.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says D-Bus is a simple way for applications to talk to one another, and that it also coordinates process lifecycle so that a single-instance application or daemon is simple and reliable to write, and so that services can be launched on demand when needed.
brief.how_it_works: Applications connect to a message bus daemon, either the system bus or a per-session bus, and exchange messages through it. The reference library libdbus has no required dependencies, and the reference bus daemon's only required dependency is the expat XML parser. Higher-level bindings for Qt, GLib, Java, C#, Python and others wrap libdbus and add their own dependencies.
brief.install_notes: The fetched homepage and project page contained no command lines. The Homebrew formula's caveats, which were not from the README or docs, give these steps. To start the session bus now and at login: brew services start dbus. To start the system bus, run sudo cp -f $(brew --prefix dbus)/org.freedesktop.dbus-system.plist /Library/LaunchDaemons and then sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/org.freedesktop.dbus-system.plist. To restart an already running system daemon: sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/org.freedesktop.dbus-system. The system-bus steps need root and are a manual install on macOS.
brief.standout: The bus is also a process-lifecycle tool: it enforces single-instance applications and launches services on demand when something calls them. The reference daemon needs only expat, and the protocol has been declared stable.
brief.status: Maintained. The wiki page was last edited Feb 27 2025. The wiki says the current stable branch is 1.16.x and is recommended, the legacy 1.14.x branch gets security fixes until mid 2026, and a 1.17.x development branch is in progress. The GitLab project page loaded but showed no README text or release dates.
brief.caveats: The low-level libdbus is not designed for application authors; the wiki recommends higher-level bindings or reimplementations instead. Remote communication is only unencrypted TCP/IP, intended for use behind a firewall with shared NFS home directories. The 1.17.x development branch has no security support. The wiki says the Windows port is mostly finished and supports Vista, 8, 10 and server variants with MSVC, mingw or Cygwin. The GitLab page shows spam restrictions on new accounts. The brew-only system bus setup requires sudo and launchctl.
quotes: D-Bus is a message bus system, a simple way for applications to talk to one another.
it makes it simple and reliable to code a "single instance" application or daemon, and to launch applications and daemons on demand when their services are needed.
Get on D-Bus today!

name: dbacl
desc: Digramic Bayesian classifier
why: Digram-based Bayesian text classifier from the early days of spam filtering; old-school and uncommon, though mostly a classic utility.

brief.what_it_is: dbacl is a set of lightweight UNIX/POSIX command-line utilities that classify text documents using Bayesian statistics. You train it on example document collections, and it computes the posterior probability that a new text resembles each one, then makes a decision based on misclassification costs you choose. The executables listed are bayesol, dbacl, hmine, hypex, mailcross, mailfoot, mailinspect and mailtoe. dbacl is also the name of the core utility. The homepage does not describe the exact input and output formats.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as a simple, powerful, easily integrated set of tools for automatic text classification. The homepage lists uses such as junk email filtering, web page screening, automated answering machines, email prioritization, topical news gathering, and even playing chess.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says dbacl computes posterior probabilities with Bayesian methods, combining prior beliefs with observed text, and then chooses the mathematically optimal class under arbitrary misclassification costs. The name suggests a digram (two-character sequence) model, but the homepage does not spell out the mechanism. The tutorial and man page are linked from the homepage, but I could not get their addresses from the fetched text.
brief.install_notes: The homepage has a Download link and a CVS link, but I did not follow them. Nothing about dependencies, configuration, or first-run steps appeared on the homepage. The brew formula lists eight executables.
brief.standout: Unlike most spam filters of its era, it is a set of small Unix tools meant to be composed in shell scripts, not a single application. Its digram-based Bayesian approach is a classic early-spam-era design.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows no release date, last-commit date, or changelog, and the scout note calls it old-school and uncommon. Links to Forums and CVS suggest an older SourceForge-era project, but I could not confirm whether it is still maintained.
brief.caveats: The homepage is the only page I could read, and it is thin on specifics. It gives no commands, install steps, platform list, or benchmarks. The Brew formula has no caveats. The homepage says the project is GPL-licensed Free Software. The page links to CVS, which suggests an older source-control setup.
quotes: The dbacl project consist of a set of lightweight UNIX/POSIX utilities which can be used, either directly or in shell scripts, to classify text documents automatically, according to Bayesian statistical principles.
The dbacl utilities cannot do all these tasks directly, but by concentrating on simple, powerful, and easily integrated tools these applications become possible.
The dbacl utilities are Free Software distributed under the terms of the GNU General Public License (GPL).

name: dcraw
desc: Digital camera RAW photo decoding software
why: Decodes proprietary camera RAW formats, a fascinating look at undocumented file formats reverse engineered across many cameras.

brief.what_it_is: dcraw is a single-file command-line program, written in ANSI C, that decodes raw sensor data from digital cameras. It takes proprietary camera raw files (the page names CRW, CR2, MRW, NEF, RAF and others) and writes decoded image pixels, with an option for TIFF output that includes metadata. It can also extract embedded thumbnails and display camera metadata. The author says the source is about 10,500 lines and uses only standard C libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's stated mission is to "Write and maintain an ANSI C program that decodes any raw image from any digital camera on any computer running any operating system." He wrote it because camera vendors' raw decoders were Windows and Mac only and closed source, which left other operating systems and programmers without a way to read the files.
brief.how_it_works: The page says dcraw reads each manufacturer's undocumented raw format, reverse-engineered from cameras, and decodes the sensor data. It then reconstructs color from the single color per pixel of the sensor using a choice of interpolation methods (Bilinear, VNG, PPG, AHD); Foveon X3 sensors get a different treatment. Auto-exposure stretches the output so that one percent of pixels come out white by default.

commands_seen.context: Build command with optional external libraries (JasPer, libjpeg, lcms2) for JPEG/JPEG 2000 and color management support.
Build command that avoids all external library dependencies.
Quick metadata read; the FAQ says it is much faster than ExifTool but gives less information.

Pipes dcraw's output through cjpeg to produce a JPEG file.
First thing to try if output shows repeating patterns; the FAQ says to try this before -f.

Writes TIFF output with metadata (the FAQ says this is available in versions 8.25 and later).

brief.install_notes: Installed through Homebrew as the formula dcraw. Building from source needs a C compiler and gcc, with optional libraries JasPer, libjpeg and lcms2, or the -DNODEPS flag to skip them. For Windows the page points to prebuilt EXE files from Sergio Namias, or to building with DJGPP or the Win32 API. Multilingual builds use an install script in a tarball from the author's directory. No accounts, hardware or first-run configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: Its decades-long reverse engineering of undocumented camera formats, with a 'dcraw.c' file that the author calls documentation the camera makers refused to provide, makes it a reference that many commercial raw converters have reused. Its refusal to become a library, in favor of a single standalone C program that others wrap, is a deliberate and unusual design choice.
brief.status: unknown. The page shows no release date, changelog, or last-updated stamp. The news items date from 2003 to 2006, but the supported camera list includes bodies from around 2017 and the author describes dcraw as something he will "maintain", which suggests ongoing work. The brew description and the scout notes are the only other sources.
brief.caveats: Licence is a permissive 'free for all uses' rather than a named open-source licence, and the author asks for credit. Output looks dark unless you use 8-bit mode or read the FAQ. Vista's 32MB memory limit on old DOS-API builds can cause 'Out of memory' errors. Only camera raw formats are covered, not scanner files (NEF from scanners is not supported). The author also sells a paid $800 test suite. The homepage is written in a fairly dated style and the camera list has notes such as 'hack' and 'DIAG RAW' for some models that need camera-side changes first.

It's small (about 10,500 lines), portable (standard C libraries only), free (both "gratis" and "libre"), and when used skillfully, produces better quality output than the tools provided by the camera vendor.
Dcraw is not perfect, so if it cannot do something, that does not mean that the task is impossible.

name: dcmtk
desc: OFFIS DICOM toolkit command-line utilities
why: The DICOM toolkit opens a door into medical imaging formats and network protocols that few developers have ever touched.

brief.what_it_is: DCMTK is the OFFIS DICOM toolkit, a package of source code, documentation and build instructions for a set of software libraries and applications that implement part of the DICOM/MEDICOM medical imaging standard. The README describes it as sub-packages covering data encoding and decoding (dcmdata), image processing (dcmimgle), networking (dcmnet), JPEG and JPEG-LS compression, presentation states, structured reporting, radiology objects, a database server (dcmqrdb), and a modality worklist server (dcmwlm). The executables listed in the package metadata (for example dcmdump, dcm2img, storescu, storescp, findscu, movescu, echoscu, img2dcm, xml2dcm, dsr2html) are the command-line tools built from these libraries. The README does not describe what each tool takes in or emits, so that detail is inferred from the tool names and is unverified.

name: ddcutil
desc: Control monitor settings using DDC/CI and USB
why: Talks DDC/CI to monitors over I2C, a hidden channel that lets you drive brightness and inputs from software on hardware you own.

brief.what_it_is: ddcutil is a Linux command-line program for querying and changing monitor settings such as brightness, color levels, and input source. It talks to the monitor's Virtual Control Panel over I2C using DDC/CI, or over USB for monitors that offer that interface (the README cites Eizo ColorEdge and Apple Cinema). It builds both a command-line executable called ddcutil and a shared library called libddcutil, and the command-line tool does not depend on the library. A separate GUI, ddcui, is built on Qt and is described on the same site.
brief.why_it_exists: The project was inspired by color profile management: calibration is relative to the monitor's current color settings, such as red gain, so ddcutil can save those settings at calibration time and restore them when the calibration is applied.
brief.how_it_works: Most monitors other than laptop panels expose a Virtual Control Panel that implements the Monitor Control Command Set (MCCS). ddcutil sends DDC/CI commands to that panel over an I2C bus, normally exposed by the video driver as /dev/i2c-n devices. For monitors that provide a USB interface to the VCP, it uses the USB Monitor Control Class Specification instead.

name: deark
desc: File conversion utility for older formats
why: Extracts and converts obscure legacy file formats, a rewarding dive into forgotten binary structures.

brief.what_it_is: Deark is a free, open-source, portable command-line utility that decodes certain older or obscure file formats. It either converts them to a more modern or more readable format, or extracts embedded files from them. It can also print detailed technical information about a file's contents and metadata with -d. Input is a legacy file such as an image, icon, font, archive, disk image, or executable-packed file. Output is usually written as files named output.* (or into a ZIP or TAR archive with -zip or -tar).
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to turn files in forgotten or obsolete formats into something modern or readable, and to pull embedded files out of them. The author also notes that Deark contains a lot of knowledge about third-party formats (structures, algorithms, tables, palettes) that is otherwise scattered.
brief.how_it_works: Deark autodetects the format of the input file and hands it to a format-specific module; -m selects a module by hand when detection fails or a special-purpose module like copy is wanted. Each module decodes the format and writes the converted or extracted items as output files, with many options controlling names, timestamps, and containers. The README notes that archive formats are best converted to ZIP with -zip -ka so filenames and paths are kept. The formats.txt file lists the modules.

name: decker
desc: HyperCard-like multimedia sketchpad
why: A HyperCard-style multimedia sketchpad with a scripting language revives an old-school authoring environment that few developers have touched.

brief.what_it_is: Decker is a multimedia authoring platform for making interactive documents that combine sound, images, hypertext, and scripted behavior. You paint, draw, record sound, and wire up navigation between cards, using widgets like buttons, fields, sliders, canvases, and grids, with optional scripting in Lil. Decks can be saved as a single self-contained .html file that runs in a browser (Web-Decker), or run in the native C application (Native-Decker) on MacOS, BSD, Linux, Haiku, and Windows. Lilt, the command-line Lil interpreter, can read, write, and execute decks headlessly.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches Decker as a single holistic environment for digital arts and crafts, where you could write a zine, build an adventure game, make a utility, or doodle pixel art, and which erases the divide between users and authors. It presents HyperCard's index-card model as a key inspiration, alongside Bitsy, Twine, Flash, VisualBasic, and TiddlyWiki.
brief.how_it_works: A deck is a set of cards holding widgets, and every interactive behavior is built from those widgets. Scripts run in a sandbox that prevents low-level host access so Web-Decker and Native-Decker behave the same; an opt-in 'Danger Zone' exposes non-portable operations. Decks are stored in a line-oriented text format, which the README says works well with Git and SVN, and Lilt can manipulate them programmatically.

name: decompose
desc: Reverse-engineering tool for docker environments
why: Reverse-engineers running docker environments into compose files, a useful way to see how a stack was assembled.

brief.what_it_is: decompose is a command-line tool that reverse-engineers a running Docker environment. It takes the network connections of your containers and exports them as a graph or structured file: graphviz dot, structurizr DSL, compose YAML, PlantUML, a pseudographical tree, a JSON stream, statistics (node, connection and listen-port counts), or CSV with columns name, listen and outbounds. Its input is the live Docker daemon (via DOCKER_HOST and related variables), and its output goes to stdout by default. It can also load saved JSON streams and merge them.
brief.why_it_exists: The author needed to visualize and inspect a large dockerized legacy system (more than 470 containers) with no schemes and very little documentation. The README says the closest existing tools did not fit: some only produce compose YAML, and others take links and ports from compose configuration, which can miss connections.
brief.how_it_works: It collects connections from the containers rather than reading compose files. On Linux as root it uses nsenter, which works even for scratch-based containers. As non-root or on other OSes it runs netstat inside each container, and containers without netstat yield no connections. Unix-socket matching on Linux needs root and uses inode matching. Output formats are sorted, so they can be committed to version control and diffed.

Full scanning as root on Linux needs sudo, since the nsenter path requires it. The README does not describe a first-run setup beyond this.

name: depqbf
desc: Solver for quantified boolean formulae (QBF)
why: Solver for quantified boolean formulae, a niche corner of logic and complexity theory you can actually run and feed problems.

brief.what_it_is: DepQBF is a command-line solver for quantified boolean formulae (QBF) in prenex conjunctive normal form. It reads a QBF from a file, such as a QDIMACS input, and reports whether the formula is satisfiable (exit code 10) or unsatisfiable (exit code 20). It can also print a partial assignment for the outermost quantifier block with --qdo, or a resolution trace in QRP format with --trace. It is also usable as a C library (libqdpll.a, API in qdpll.h) and through a Java wrapper called DepQBF4J.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents DepQBF as a research system from Florian Lonsing's group, built to implement and evaluate QBF solving ideas from their papers. The site frames it as a search-based solver beyond traditional QCDCL, and it is aimed at users who want to run and feed QBF problems.
brief.how_it_works: It is a search-based solver built on QDPLL with conflict-driven clause learning and solution-driven cube learning (QCDCL) using generalized axioms. Since version 6.0 it calls PicoSAT and Nenofex as oracles to check satisfiability of formulas that arise during axiom applications. It computes the standard dependency scheme of the formula, a compact graph representing which variables depend on which, to find independent variables and widen decision freedom, and since version 5.0 it runs dynamic blocked clause elimination interleaved with the search.

name: deheader
desc: Analyze C/C++ files for unnecessary headers
why: Eric Raymond's tool to find unnecessary C headers, a quirky static analysis with a clever trial-and-compile approach.

brief.what_it_is: deheader is a command-line tool, written by Eric S. Raymond, that analyzes C and C++ source files and reports which #include lines can be removed while the code still compiles. It takes one or more source files or a directory (it recurses, skipping dot-directories), and prints a report of removable headers, duplicate includes, and standard headers that portability may require but that are missing. With -r it also rewrites the sources to delete the unneeded includes. It exits 1 when removable includes are found, 2 when a file could not be compiled and analyzed, and 0 otherwise.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it helps find unneeded includes, which can substantially improve compilation time on large C++ projects, and that it sometimes exposes dependencies and cohesions developers did not know about.
brief.how_it_works: For each foo.c, foo.cc or foo.cpp, the test is whether "rm foo.o; make foo.o" returns a zero status, with the build command overridable via -m. Under CMake (when a CMakeLists.txt is detected) it runs "make clean" instead, since foo.o is a phony target there. Inclusions inside #if/#ifdef/#else/#endif blocks are left alone, except headers guarded only by S_SPLINT_S, and each test compile works on a temporary backup of the source that is restored afterward.

name: der-ascii
desc: Reversible DER and BER pretty-printer
why: A reversible DER and BER pretty-printer that lets you edit ASN.1 certificate and X.509 structures as text and round-trip them back to binary.

brief.what_it_is: DER ASCII is a small, human-editable text language for writing DER or BER encodings of ASN.1 structures, including deliberately malformed variants. It ships two command-line tools. ascii2der takes DER ASCII text and emits the binary encoding. der2ascii goes the other way, taking a binary DER or BER input and producing a DER ASCII text disassembly that can be edited and reassembled. The README also presents it as a readable view of DER structures.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the tools exist to make test inputs without manually fixing up length prefixes: disassemble an existing DER or BER structure, adjust it as text, and reassemble it to binary. It also says the format is meant to emit invalid encodings as well as valid ones.
brief.how_it_works: ascii2der tokenizes the text and emits byte strings in sequence. Tokens cover quoted strings, UTF-16 and UTF-32 literals, hex and bit-string literals, integers, OIDs, booleans, tag expressions like [0] or [UNIVERSAL 2 PRIMITIVE], and curly-brace blocks that get length prefixes computed automatically, with options such as indefinite, long-form:N and adjust-length:N for deliberately odd lengths. der2ascii is a heuristic disassembler: it greedily parses BER elements, recurses into constructed bodies, and decodes known tags like INTEGER, OID, BOOLEAN, BIT STRING and BMPString, falling back to hex literals when parsing fails. The language spec notes that the disassembly is not unique, so the same bytes can have more than one text form.

commands_seen.context: Install command from the README that builds and installs both ascii2der and der2ascii from the Go module.

brief.install_notes: The README's only install instruction is the go install line above, which implies a Go toolchain is needed. No accounts, hardware, or configuration are mentioned. The README does not describe a first-run step. Homebrew installs the same two executables (ascii2der, der2ascii).
brief.standout: It is reversible by design: the text form keeps every encoding variation (indefinite lengths, non-minimal lengths, constructed BER strings), and it can deliberately encode broken input such as wrong length prefixes or wrong constructed bits. Most ASN.1 printers normalize, which is the opposite goal. The disassembler also has a special case for X.509 mistakenly using BIT STRING for SubjectPublicKeyInfo and signatures.

desc: Device firmware update based USB programmer for Atmel chips
why: Talks the USB DFU protocol to flash Atmel chips directly, a real door into firmware and microcontroller hardware.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line tool, dfu-programmer, that flashes Atmel microcontrollers over USB using the Device Firmware Upgrade (DFU) protocol. It talks to a chip that is already running a DFU-capable bootloader, so the chip must be in that bootloader mode first. name: dhcpdump
desc: Monitor DHCP traffic for debugging purposes
why: Watching DHCP traffic live is a direct door into a protocol every network runs and almost nobody inspects.

brief.what_it_is: dhcpdump is a command-line tool that parses DHCP packets captured from a network interface and prints them in readable form. This fork, based on dhcpdump 1.8, adds a session-tracking full-screen TUI (-t) that groups DHCP traffic by client and then by transaction (XID), showing the message flow (DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK and so on) and a derived state such as waiting, offered, bound, NAK, or timed out. It can work on live interfaces (-i) or on a saved capture (-r), and the README says the parser was split into a reusable decoder library separate from the CLI.
brief.why_it_exists: The fork exists to collect in one place the bug-fixes and improvements made to dhcpdump 1.8 over more than ten years, since the original project had gone quiet. The README frames it as a consolidated, maintained continuation rather than a new tool.
brief.how_it_works: It captures or reads packets, filters for DHCP, and decodes the DHCP options (including VLAN 802.1Q and QinQ 802.1ad tagged traffic) into text. In the TUI, transactions are keyed by XID inside each client's session, and each transaction's state is derived from the messages seen so far.
