name: diffoci
desc: Diff for Docker and OCI container images
why: Diffs container images layer by layer, a handy lens into the structure of OCI image formats.

brief.what_it_is: diffoci is a command-line tool that compares two Docker or OCI container images and reports where they differ. Its inputs are image references: registry names such as alpine:3.18.2, local Docker images via docker:// prefix, Podman images via podman://, or images in the containerd store. The output is a table of differing entries (type, name, and a digest or message for each input). In --semantic mode it ignores timestamps, build histories, file ordering inside tar layers, and image name annotations. With --report-dir it writes the conflicting files to a directory so you can inspect them with diff -ur or diffoscope.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to help with reproducible builds: you build an image from published source, then check whether your result matches the official binary image.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe internals in detail. It says diffoci is not aware of file formats inside layers, so differences like timestamps inside a nested scripts.tar are reported as-is and are not filtered by --semantic. Layer-level diffs are shown as length mismatches and whiteout entries, and file-level diffs by content digest.

name: difftastic
desc: Diff that understands syntax
why: Syntax-aware diffing parses code into trees, a clever transform, though well known among diff tool users.

brief.what_it_is: Difftastic is a command-line diff tool, installed as the executable difft, that compares two files by their syntax rather than line by line. It parses each file into a syntax tree using tree-sitter, then reports what actually changed, so an inner expression that is merely wrapped or reformatted is not shown as a deleted and re-added line. It takes two files (or a single file containing git merge conflict markers) and prints a human-readable diff with real line numbers from both files. It supports over 30 programming languages and several file formats such as HCL, HTML, JSON and YAML; unrecognised extensions fall back to a line-oriented diff with word highlighting.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames it around the problem that a line-oriented diff misleads people: a reformatter splitting code across lines, or a wrapper added around an expression, produces noisy diffs that hide what really changed. The homepage says it produces accurate diffs that are easier for humans to read.
brief.how_it_works: Files are parsed with tree-sitter into syntax trees, and the comparison is treated as a graph problem solved with Dijkstra's algorithm. The README says that when parse errors are found it falls back to a line-oriented diff by default, to avoid claiming two syntactically different files are the same; a DFT_PARSE_ERROR_LIMIT environment variable can allow a few parse errors. The author's blog post and the manual's internals section describe the design.

brief.standout: Structural diffing is a well-known idea among diff tool users, but difftastic is notable for treating the problem as a shortest-path search over a graph, and for choosing to fall back to a line diff on parse errors rather than risk declaring different files equal. It also diffs merge-conflict files directly and offers a fast AST-equality check with a useful exit code.

brief.caveats: The README lists known issues: it scales relatively poorly on files with many changes and can use a lot of memory; its side-by-side display can be confusing; and it has regular releases that fix crashes. name: direwolf
desc: Software "soundcard" AX.25 packet modem/TNC and APRS encoder/decoder
why: A software soundcard turning audio into AX.25 packets and APRS, a delightful audio-to-data transform you can hear.

brief.what_it_is: Dire Wolf is an open-source software TNC (terminal node controller) and packet modem for amateur radio. It runs on Windows, Linux (including Raspberry Pi), and macOS. It takes audio from a radio through a computer's soundcard interface, or from SDR software such as gqrx, rtl_fm, or SDR#, and decodes AX.25 packets and APRS frames from it. It also encodes packets and transmits them back out through the radio. Without extra software it can act as an APRS tracker, digipeater, Internet gateway (IGate), or APRStt gateway, and it can serve as a virtual TNC for applications such as Xastir, YAAC, and Winlink Express over KISS (TCP, serial, or Bluetooth) or AGW interfaces. The package also ships a set of companion programs, including decode_aprs, gen_packets, atest, kissutil, the telem-*.pl and telem-*.py telemetry scripts, and coordinate converters such as ll2utm and utm2ll.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Dire Wolf as a replacement for the expensive hardware Terminal Node Controller of the early packet radio days. Its argument is that a computer soundcard with software decoding gives better receive performance at lower cost than a TNC built around an old modem chip.
brief.how_it_works: Radio audio goes into the computer's soundcard, and Dire Wolf does the modem work in software using digital signal processing. It supports several modem types: 300 bps AFSK for HF, 1200 bps AFSK for VHF/UHF, 2400 and 4800 bps PSK, 9600 bps GMSK/G3RUH, plus AIS and EAS SAME reception. FX.25 adds forward error correction in a form that remains compatible with ordinary AX.25 receivers. Version 1.7 added IL2P, a different FEC scheme with less overhead, which is not compatible with AX.25.

CentOS 6 and 7 need cmake 3.1 or later from EPEL. macOS: install Xcode Command Line Tools and Homebrew, then brew install cmake, portaudio, and hidapi, then build from source the same way as Linux. There is no brew install direwolf line in the README. name: dislocker
desc: FUSE driver to read/write Windows' BitLocker-ed volumes
why: FUSE driver that reads and writes BitLocker volumes, a fascinating look at encrypted on-disk formats.

brief.what_it_is: Dislocker is a Linux tool for opening BitLocker-encrypted Windows volumes. It takes a BitLocker partition (or a BitLocker To Go USB stick) plus the user's key material, such as a password or recovery key, and exposes the decrypted contents. The README describes two routes: dislocker-fuse presents a virtual NTFS file through a FUSE mount, and dislocker-file writes the decrypted volume out as a flat NTFS image file. The README covers Vista, 7, 8, 8.1 and 10 volumes, using AES-CBC or AES-XTS at 128 or 256 bits, with or without the Elephant diffuser.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the software was "designed to read BitLocker encrypted partitions under a Linux system." It also explains BitLocker To Go's dual format, a FAT32 filesystem sitting alongside an encrypted volume, so the same tool handles both kinds of media.
brief.how_it_works: dislocker is a library with several binaries built on top of it. dislocker-fuse decrypts on demand through FUSE: once keys are unlocked, a file named dislocker-file appears in the mount point, and that file is a virtual NTFS partition that can be mounted normally. Writes to it go through to the underlying BitLocker volume. dislocker-file instead decrypts the whole volume into a separate flat file, which is detached from the original, so writes affect only the copy. The README notes that this file is the same size as the volume and can take a long time to create.

commands_seen.context: Configures the build from the source directory, per the README's build section (INSTALL.md is referenced for full steps).
Builds only the dislocker-fuse target, the binary the README says you use to mount a BitLocker volume. Other binaries can be built the same way by naming their make target.

The dislocker-find script needs the library built with Ruby bindings. The README does not describe any other accounts or runtimes. I did not fetch INSTALL.md or BUILD.md.
brief.standout: The BitLocker To Go section explains why the same tool works on both internal drives and USB sticks. A FAT32 filesystem and an encrypted volume occupy the same partition, and dislocker treats the whole partition as the BitLocker volume. The fuse route also gives you a live, writable view of the decrypted disk without making a full copy, which is different from the flat-file route.

name: ditaa
desc: Convert ASCII diagrams into proper bitmap graphics
why: Turns ASCII box-and-line drawings into bitmap diagrams, a clean transform from text shapes into pixels.

brief.what_it_is: ditaa is a small command-line utility written in Java that converts ASCII-art diagrams (drawings made of characters like | / - +) into bitmap images. It reads a text file containing the diagram and writes out a rendered image, PNG by default. It can also process HTML files, replacing the contents of pre class='textdiagram' blocks with generated tags. The homepage describes the project as open source under the GPL.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Stathis Sideris, gives several reasons: hack value ('I wanted to know if/how it could be done and how easily'), modernising old ASCII diagrams in legacy FAQs, embedding diagrams in text-based formats like HTML, DocBook, LaTeX and code comments, and keeping diagrams as editable text that can be re-rendered by newer versions.
brief.how_it_works: ditaa interprets the ASCII drawing as a series of open and closed shapes, then renders those shapes as graphics. Extra markup extends what it can draw: colour codes (cXXX hex or named codes like cRED), tags such as {d}, {s} and {io} for special symbols, dashed lines when a line contains = or :, round corners when / and \ join corners, and a * point marker. Colour applies only inside closed shapes, and text inside dark fills is switched to white.

name: distcc
desc: Distributed compiler client and server
why: A distributed compile protocol that farms compiler jobs across machines, an old networked idea worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: distcc is a free distributed C/C++ compiler front-end. It takes a normal build command, usually make -j with CC=distcc, and sends each compile job across the network to volunteer machines running the distccd daemon. Each job travels as complete preprocessed source, and the compiled object comes back to the client. It is not a compiler itself; it hands work to gcc or clang on the servers. In pump mode, preprocessing is also moved to the servers, which requires matching system headers on client and server. It is licensed under GPL v2.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says distcc should always generate the same results as a local compile, be simple to install and use, and often be two or more times faster than a local compile. Its author contrasts it with other distributed build systems that need a shared filesystem, synchronized clocks, or identical libraries and headers on every machine.
brief.how_it_works: The client runs the preprocessor locally and ships the preprocessed source for each job to a distccd server, which runs the compiler and returns the object file. Shipping work takes network time but little client CPU, so remote jobs are essentially free for the client when used with make -j. In pump mode (added in distcc 3.0), the preprocessing step also runs on the servers, so the client does not preprocess at all.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: the upstream route is download, then ./configure && make && sudo make install on each machine. The client needs DISTCC_POTENTIAL_HOSTS set to the list of servers, and the build is wrapped with pump and CC=distcc. Servers need an appropriate compiler installed. brief.standout: Most distributed build systems need shared filesystems, synchronized clocks, or matched toolchains. distcc sends the preprocessed source over the wire, so any volunteer machine with a compiler can join. The pump mode goes further by moving preprocessing off the client as well. It is an early-2000s design that still shows up in the 'related tools' lists of its own site.

name: dns2tcp

why: Tunnels TCP through DNS queries, a vivid door into how DNS can carry arbitrary traffic past firewalls.

brief.what_it_is: dns2tcp is a set of command-line tools that tunnels a TCP session inside DNS packets. Per the Debian package description, it encapsulates TCP in DNS queries and replies, and the client does not need root privileges. The brew metadata lists two executables, dns2tcpc (client) and dns2tcpd (server). I did not read the upstream README, so details on exactly what goes in and out are not confirmed.
brief.why_it_exists: The Debian description frames it as a way to carry a TCP session over DNS, claiming this produces smaller packets than IP-over-DNS and so improves throughput. The motivation to get past restrictive networks is the scout note's framing, not something I confirmed in the package text.
brief.how_it_works: The Debian description says only that it encapsulates a TCP session in DNS packets, and that this yields smaller packets than IP-over-DNS. I did not find a mechanism explanation in the pages I read.
brief.install_notes: Installable via Debian packages (dns2tcp 0.5.2-4 in sid, with builds for many architectures) and, per the brew metadata, via Homebrew. brief.standout: Tunnelling TCP over DNS queries, rather than IP-over-DNS, is the notable choice, and the Debian text claims it gives smaller packets and better throughput. The client running without root is also worth noting.
brief.status: Packaged and maintained in Debian: the package page shows version 0.5.2-4 in sid with two named maintainers and builds for many architectures. I found no upstream release date or last-commit date, so upstream activity is unknown.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a Debian package listing, not the project's own site, and it gives no usage docs. name: dnscrypt-proxy
desc: Secure communications between a client and a DNS resolver
why: A window into encrypted DNS transport and resolver trust, a protocol most people never inspect despite it running on every machine.

brief.what_it_is: dnscrypt-proxy is a local DNS proxy written in Go that sits between your machine and upstream DNS resolvers. It accepts ordinary DNS queries on localhost and forwards them over encrypted transports: DNSCrypt v2, Post-Quantum DNSCrypt, DNS-over-HTTPS, Anonymized DNSCrypt, and ODoH. Answers come back to the client as ordinary DNS responses. The dnscrypt.info homepage itself is the protocol's project site, not the tool's page, and the tool's README is on GitHub.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames DNSCrypt as a protocol built for privacy, security, and performance from the ground up, which encrypts and authenticates DNS between client and resolver and uses signatures to prevent spoofing. It argues that DNSCrypt needs no certificate authorities, that anyone can run a resolver, and that its traffic is harder to block than DoH.
brief.how_it_works: Per the homepage, DNSCrypt clients are configured with a resolver IP address and a public key, so encryption starts from the first packet without a plaintext hostname lookup, and each resolver has a static public key verified by signatures rather than a CA. The README says the proxy measures the speed of the resolvers you list and balances traffic across the fastest ones. It can also cache answers, filter ads and malware, and hide client IPs via Tor, SOCKS proxies, or Anonymized DNS relays.
brief.install_notes: The README points to pre-built binaries for many platforms, including macOS arm64 and x86_64, and says signature-verification steps are in the GitHub wiki installation page. The Homebrew caveats (not from the README) say to point the system DNS to 127.0.0.1 through Network settings, that the default listens on 127.0.0.1 port 53, that the config lives at $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/etc/dnscrypt-proxy.toml, and suggest checking with: sudo tcpdump -i en1 -vvv 'port 443' (replace en1 with your interface). Port 53 and changing system DNS need admin rights.
brief.standout: The homepage pitches a protocol that starts encrypting from the first packet and has no CA dependency, while the proxy bundles many transports, Tor and relay support, and local cloaking/filtering into one binary. Few DNS tools cover this range of transports and anonymization options together.
brief.status: unknown. The README mentions DNSCrypt 2026 and a v2.1.10 release note, has a live build-status badge and a latest-release link, and the Homebrew formula is present, but I did not see a release date or last commit date in the fetched text.
brief.caveats: The homepage fetch returned only the protocol marketing copy, with no install or usage details. The README gives no commands, so the only usage lines come from Homebrew metadata. Changing system DNS to 127.0.0.1 affects the whole machine's resolution, and the README does not say how to undo it. The README does not state a license in the fetched text. Hot-reloading is disabled by default from v2.1.10.
quotes: A flexible DNS proxy, with support for modern encrypted DNS protocols such as DNSCrypt v2 including Post-Quantum DNSCrypt (DNSCrypt 2026), DNS-over-HTTPS, Anonymized DNSCrypt and ODoH (Oblivious DoH).
Load balancing: pick a set of resolvers, dnscrypt-proxy will automatically measure and keep track of their speed, and balance the traffic across the fastest available ones.
Cloaking: like a HOSTS file on steroids, that can return preconfigured addresses for specific names, or resolve and return the IP address of other names.
DNSCrypt clients are configured with an IP address and a public key. Encryption starts from the very first query.

judge.reason: A local proxy makes DNS privacy tangible, exposing an unusual mix of CA-free encryption, anonymized relays, and newer protocols like ODoH and post-quantum DNSCrypt.

name: dnsperf
desc: Measure DNS performance by simulating network conditions
why: A DNS load tester from the OARC crowd that opens a real door into how resolvers behave under pressure.

brief.what_it_is: dnsperf and resperf are two command-line DNS benchmarking tools from DNS-OARC. dnsperf reads a file of DNS queries and sends them to DNS servers, measuring latency and throughput. resperf ramps up the query rate and watches how the response rate holds up, to simulate a caching DNS service. The tools take a query data file and a target server, and output latency and throughput metrics; the homepage says the output is concise and that latency data can feed detailed graphs. Sample query data is published alongside the releases.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the tools make it simple to gather accurate latency and throughput metrics for DNS, so network operators can benchmark their naming and addressing infrastructure and plan upgrades. The README adds that they are meant to simulate typical Internet conditions.
brief.how_it_works: dnsperf "self-paces" the query load to simulate network conditions, and newer versions are multithreaded, with each dnsperf client needing two cores. resperf systematically increases the query rate and monitors the response rate to find where a caching resolver stops keeping up. Per-query latency reporting is available in newer versions.

name: dnstop
desc: Console tool to analyze DNS traffic
why: Live console view of DNS traffic on the wire; a readable door into DNS that most people never watch.

brief.what_it_is: dnstop is a console tool that analyzes DNS traffic. It is a libpcap application, similar to tcpdump, that reads packets either from a live capture device or from a tcpdump savefile. It displays live tables of DNS traffic: source IP addresses, destination IP addresses, query types, response codes, opcodes, and top, second, and third level domains. It supports both IPv4 and IPv6.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a way to "Stay on Top of Your DNS Traffic" and to help find especially undesirable DNS queries, using filters for unknown or invalid TLDs, queries whose name is already an IP address, PTR queries for RFC1918 address space, and responses with code REFUSED.
brief.how_it_works: It captures packets with libpcap, as tcpdump does, and decodes them as DNS. It aggregates what it sees into the ranked tables listed above and can restrict the display to the filtered query classes. Input is either the live capture device or a saved tcpdump capture file.
brief.install_notes: The homepage shows no install steps, commands, or configuration. Live capture needs access to the capture device, which typically means running with elevated privileges, but the page does not say so. The executable is named dnstop.
brief.standout: It is a live, ranked-table view of DNS traffic on the wire, which most people never watch. It also ships built-in filters aimed at spotting bad or suspicious DNS (invalid TLDs, IP-as-name queries, RFC1918 reverse lookups, REFUSED responses).

name: dnstwist
desc: Test domains for typo squatting, phishing and corporate espionage
why: Generates typosquatted domain variants and resolves them, a window into DNS and how phishing domains get found.

brief.what_it_is: dnstwist is a Python command-line tool that takes a domain name and generates lookalike variants of it using several fuzzing algorithms (homoglyph, hyphenation, and others), plus optional dictionary words and TLDs. By default it then does DNS lookups on each variant and reports which ones resolve, along with their DNS records. Output goes to the terminal, CSV, or JSON, or can be limited to bare permutations with no lookups. Optional modes fetch each live site and compare its HTML fuzzy hash (ssdeep or TLSH) or headless-Chromium screenshot pHash against the original, and can add GeoIP country and rogue MX detection.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to "See what sort of trouble users can get in trying to type your domain name" and to "Find lookalike domains that adversaries can use to attack you." It is meant as a source of targeted threat intelligence for defenders such as SOC and incident response teams.
brief.how_it_works: It permutes the input domain with its fuzzers, then resolves each permutation to see whether it is registered. With --lsh it fetches the HTTP content of resolving domains, normalizes the HTML, and compares a fuzzy hash to the original site's hash as a similarity percentage. With --phash it uses headless Chromium to take screenshots and compares perceptual hashes. The README also notes that the homoglyph fuzzer is built from Unicode characters that can actually be registered.

For GeoIP, the GeoIP2 library is used by default, and the country database path must be set in the $GEOLITE2_MMDB environment variable; otherwise it falls back to the older GeoIP Legacy. Proxies are picked up from standard <scheme>_proxy environment variables. The --phash mode needs Chromium installed. Heavy runs may need an external resolver via --nameservers, including DNS-over-HTTPS.

name: dnsviz
desc: Tools for analyzing and visualizing DNS and DNSSEC behavior
why: Visualizing DNSSEC chains of trust is a great door into DNS internals that almost nobody looks at.

brief.what_it_is: DNSViz is a tool suite for analysing and visualising the Domain Name System, including its DNSSEC security extensions. It is driven from a single command-line tool, dnsviz, with subcommands that run in a pipeline. probe takes domain names and sends DNS queries to recursive or authoritative servers, writing the results as JSON. grok takes that JSON and assesses the named domains, and graph or print turn the assessment into an image, an interactive HTML page, or plain text. The README says the tool suite also powers the web analysis at dnsviz.net.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as a tool suite for analysis and visualisation of DNS behaviour, including DNSSEC, and notes that it powers the Web-based analysis at dnsviz.net. It also documents pre-deployment testing, so operators can check a zone or its delegation before changes go live.
brief.how_it_works: probe records raw queries and responses as JSON, so the collection step is separate from analysis. grok then assesses the recorded data, and graph (Graphviz-based, per its dependencies) or print renders the result. The stages can be piped together, and the trust anchor can be supplied as a root or zone DNSKEY file to show authentication status. For pre-deployment work, the -x, -N and -D options supply zone files, server addresses, future delegation records or DS records, and the README says BIND's named is started to serve local zone files.

name: dnstracer
desc: Trace a chain of DNS servers to the source
why: Walking the DNS delegation chain from root to authority is a clear door into how DNS resolution actually works.

brief.what_it_is: dnstracer is a command-line Unix tool that takes a domain name (or PTR/SOA/CNAME query) and walks the DNS delegation chain from the root servers down to the authoritative servers that hold the answer. It prints a tree of each server it asked, the name and IP of that server, whether it gave an authoritative answer, cached data, a lame-server response, or nothing (shown as * * *). The homepage's examples show a trace for www.mavetju.org starting from a clean resolver, and a trace started from a chosen server with -s.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a way to find "where a given Domain Name Server (DNS) gets its information from, and follows the chain of DNS servers back to the servers which know the data." It is aimed at debugging and understanding delegation, caching, and broken servers.
brief.how_it_works: It starts at a resolver (127.0.0.1 by default, or a server given with -s, where a dot means A.ROOT-SERVERS.NET) and queries each server in turn, following referrals to the next level of the hierarchy. Each answer or referral is shown as a branch, and additional records or failed lookups are noted. The author says addresses without additional records are fetched with gethostbyname(), that multiple additional records are each tested, and that there are three retries by default before a * is printed.

commands_seen.context: Basic full trace of a name from a clean resolver, walking root, then .org, then the zone's own servers; the author notes this example produced about 480 lines.

Reverse (PTR) lookup; the name must use the .in-addr.arpa or ip6.int suffix.

Full trace used to show multiple additional records being tested and the difference between authoritative and cached (non-authoritative) answers.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond brew install is described on the page. It is a plain command-line tool with a single executable, dnstracer. No accounts, runtimes or configuration steps are mentioned. The default starting point is 127.0.0.1, so it assumes a local resolver is running unless -s is given.
brief.standout: Instead of asking one resolver for an answer, it shows the whole referral tree, with every server tried at each level and whether each one answered authoritatively, from cache, or as a lame server. name: dolt
desc: Git for Data
why: A SQL database with Git-style versioning and branching for data is a genuinely unusual database with a twist.

brief.what_it_is: Dolt is a SQL database that can be forked, cloned, branched, merged, pushed and pulled the way a Git repository can. You connect to it with any MySQL-compatible client to read or change schema and data. Version control is exposed in SQL through system tables, functions and stored procedures, and through a Git-like command line (`dolt`) that can import CSV files, commit, push to a remote, and merge a teammate's changes. The output is a database whose tables carry commit history, branches and cell-level diffs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as Git for data: "Git versions files. Dolt versions tables. It's like Git and MySQL had a baby." The project also says it is useful for agent memory, especially in multi-agent and multi-machine workflows, and that it powers Beads and Gas Town.
brief.how_it_works: Dolt exposes Git-style operations inside SQL. Read operations are system tables named dolt_<thing> such as dolt_log, dolt_status and dolt_diff_<table>, and write operations are stored procedures named after the CLI command, such as dolt_add and dolt_commit, with options passed as arguments in the same way as on the command line. The `dolt sql-server` command runs a MySQL-compatible server on port 3306 by default, and the CLI's `dolt sql` gives a built-in MySQL-style client.

Options in the README: the install script (needs sudo), Arch Linux `pacman -S dolt`, Homebrew, MacPorts `sudo port install dolt`, Windows .msi from GitHub releases, Chocolatey `choco install dolt`, or Docker images dolthub/dolt and dolthub/dolt-sql-server. Building from source needs Go and a working C compiler, because Dolt depends on cgo; the build is `go install ./cmd/dolt`, with output in ~/go/bin. After install, set user.name and user.email with dolt config --global. Databases live in whatever directory you create them in, and each one is a directory. To use a GUI, the README uses TablePlus with MySQL as the connection type and root as the user.

name: doltgres
desc: Dolt for Postgres
why: A Postgres-compatible database with git-style versioning of data, a strange twist on a familiar system.

brief.what_it_is: Doltgres is a Postgres-compatible SQL database that adds Git-style version control to data. You connect to it with any Postgres client and read or change schema and data as usual. You can also branch and merge, fork and clone, and push and pull the database the way you would a Git repository. Version control is exposed through SQL system tables, functions, and procedures rather than a Git-style CLI. It is the Postgres-flavored version of Dolt, from the same creators.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as Dolt for Postgres: 'Git versions file, Doltgres versions tables. It's like Git and Postgres had a baby.' It aims to give Postgres users versioned tables without giving up the Postgres wire protocol and SQL.
brief.how_it_works: Doltgres emulates a Postgres server and parses Postgres SQL into an AST. That AST is converted into a form the Dolt engine can interpret. It uses the same SQL engine and storage format as Dolt, which the README says gives version control at OLTP database performance. Version control operations are invoked as SQL, for example dolt_add, dolt_commit, and the dolt.status and dolt.log system tables.

name: doltlite
desc: SQLite fork with Git-style version control via prolly trees
why: SQLite with git-style versioning built on prolly trees, a strange and genuinely original database idea to explore.

brief.what_it_is: DoltLite is a fork of SQLite that replaces SQLite's B-tree storage engine with a content-addressed prolly tree, giving Git-style version control over a SQL database. The parser, planner and VDBE stay upstream-derived; below SQLite's btree.h seam, a single-file chunk store backs the prolly trees. Version control is exposed as dolt_* SQL functions and virtual tables such as dolt_commit, dolt_branch, dolt_merge, dolt_diff_<table> and dolt_log. It ships as a doltlite CLI shell, a doltlite-remotesrv sync server and a libdoltlite C library with bindings for Python, Ruby, Node, Rust, Go and other languages. Stock SQLite files are still opened on the original B-tree engine.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to bring Dolt's versioned, prolly-tree design to embedded, local-first use: DoltLite "can be embedded in any language enabling local-first use cases for Dolt." The linked blog post "Why DoltLite?" gives the longer rationale, which I did not fetch.
brief.how_it_works: Each database is one content-addressed chunk-store file rather than SQLite pages. Prolly trees are built from immutable nodes with rolling-hash boundaries, the same design the README says Dolt uses. Branches, commits, diffs and merges operate on those trees, and each connection selects its own branch.

Language bindings are installed through each ecosystem's package manager (pip, gem, npm, composer, dotnet, cargo, go get, SwiftPM, Gradle). brief.standout: It puts Git-style branches, merges, diffs and conflict resolution inside an ordinary embedded SQL database that is one file, instead of a separate server like Dolt. Merge conflicts exist only inside the transaction that produced them and never reach disk, and the built-in vec1 vector index is versioned and merges like the rest of the data.

name: dosbox-x
desc: DOSBox with accurate emulation and wide testing
why: Accurate DOS emulation is a window into old hardware and software, though DOSBox is a known name.

brief.what_it_is: DOSBox-X is an open-source, cross-platform DOS emulator for running DOS games and applications on modern Windows, Linux, and macOS, and as a DOS program itself. It emulates a PC of the IBM PC/XT/AT class, and also NEC PC-98, AX, and DOS/V systems. The README says it also runs Windows 1.0 through Windows ME as guest systems, with Windows 3.x and 9x officially supported. It is a fork of DOSBox, taken from DOSBox SVN Daum in mid-2011, and it is a separate project now.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the original DOSBox focuses on DOS games and uses game-oriented kludges, while he wanted changes that real DOS systems and non-game software need. The stated goal is accurate enough emulation to support historical preservation, testing, and new DOS development, covering pre-2000 DOS and Windows 9x hardware.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes the program as a set of incremental changes on top of the DOSBox codebase, with many options to tweak the virtual machine, from an original IBM PC up to late-1990s configurations. Behaviour is set through a .conf file and command-line options, and a GUI drop-down menu and built-in configuration tool are included. Emulation covers CPUs up to Pentium III and MMX, IDE and disk controllers, 3dfx Voodoo and Glide, NE2000 networking, and FluidSynth and MT-32 MIDI.

name: dovi_tool
desc: CLI tool for Dolby Vision metadata on video streams
why: Reads and edits Dolby Vision RPU metadata inside video bitstreams, a rare look into hidden structure in video files.

brief.what_it_is: dovi_tool is a command-line tool for Dolby Vision metadata. It reads the RPU (Reference Processing Unit) metadata carried in HEVC video streams and in Matroska files that contain HEVC, and it can print, export, plot, generate, and edit that metadata. It also converts between Dolby Vision profiles (for example to profile 8.1 or 8.4), demuxes dual-layer files into base and enhancement layers, muxes them back together, and injects or removes RPU data. Outputs include JSON, CSV, binary RPU files, PNG plots, and HEVC bitstreams. The repo also hosts the dolby_vision Rust crate and the C-compatible libdovi library.

brief.how_it_works: Subcommands operate on binary RPU files or on HEVC bitstreams. Extraction and injection work by locating RPU NAL units inside the HEVC stream. Conversion modes (-m 0 to 5) rewrite the RPU for a target profile, and the editor and generate commands take JSON configuration files that describe the metadata to write. The README does not describe the internal parsing approach in detail.

name: dovi_convert
desc: Dolby Vision Profile 7 to 8.1 MKV converter
why: Rewrites Dolby Vision metadata between profiles, a peek into how HDR layers are structured in files.

brief.what_it_is: dovi_convert is a command-line tool that converts Dolby Vision Profile 7 MKV files, typically UHD Blu-ray rips, into Profile 8.1 MKV files. You point it at a file or a directory. It first scans and analyzes the files, flags Complex FEL files, and skips them by default. For the rest, it removes the Profile 7 Enhancement Layer and keeps the dynamic metadata (RPU), without re-encoding the video. It needs ffmpeg, mkvtoolnix, mediainfo and dovi_tool, and it can install missing ones itself.
brief.why_it_exists: Many streaming devices, including Apple TV, Nvidia Shield, Amazon Fire, Zidoo players and Plex clients, cannot process the Profile 7 Enhancement Layer. They either fall back to HDR10 or strip the layer blindly and damage the picture. The README says the tool analyzes files first, converts only what is safe, and keeps the dynamic metadata so Dolby Vision still plays correctly. The author's personal need for this conversion was the driver behind the project.
brief.how_it_works: The tool scans each file to identify the video format and the FEL type. Files with Complex FEL, where the enhancement layer carries brightness expansion, are skipped unless you force the conversion. Converted files keep the RPU dynamic metadata and drop the enhancement layer. Originals are backed up automatically, and the --delete flag removes them permanently.

name: dotslash
desc: Simplified executable deployment
why: Turns executables into small manifest files that fetch binaries on demand, a curious idea about what a runnable file can be.

brief.what_it_is: DotSlash is a command-line tool, invoked as `dotslash`, that replaces a set of platform-specific, heavyweight executables with one small, readable text file. You make the file executable and give it a `#!/usr/bin/env dotslash` shebang. The file is a JSON-like manifest (the README example uses `//` comments) that lists, per platform, the download URL, size, hash digest, archive format and the path inside the archive. When you run the file, DotSlash fetches, decompresses and verifies the right binary for your platform. The homepage also says it provides tools for generating DotSlash files from GitHub releases.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to keep executables in source control without bloating the repository, so build toolchains and other tools can be checked into the repo. That reduces dependence on the host environment and helps with reproducible builds.
brief.how_it_works: The manifest names a platform-keyed set of entries, each with a provider URL, a blake3 digest and size, and the archive path of the binary. On first run DotSlash downloads, decompresses and verifies the matching archive, which is the small delay the README mentions, and later runs are near-instant. The README points to a docs page on execution for the details, which I did not fetch.

brief.standout: Instead of a shell wrapper plus several binaries, a single text file is the executable, and it fetches the correct binary per platform on demand. Storing the manifest in git keeps the repo small while still vendoring tools like Node.js.

name: dragonbox
desc: Reference implementation of Dragonbox in C++
why: Reference implementation of an elegant shortest float-to-string algorithm, a close call showing how numbers become text.

brief.what_it_is: Dragonbox is a C++ library that converts a floating-point number into the shortest decimal digits that will read back as the same number. Given a nonzero finite float or double, its to_decimal function returns a decimal significand, a decimal exponent, and optionally a sign flag. A separate to_chars function, shipped with the library, turns those integers into a text string such as 1.234E0 for the input 1.234. The core dragonbox.h header is header-only. The string-generation part adds dragonbox_to_chars.h and dragonbox_to_chars.cpp. The package is not a command-line tool and has no executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a successor to Schubfach, a float-to-string algorithm by Raffaello Giulietti, and as inspired by Grisu and Grisu-Exact. It promises three things: round-trip correctness, the shortest output length, and correct rounding among the shortest candidates. The name comes from the pigeonhole principle, which Schubfach calls the drawer principle and which is also known as Dirichlet's box principle. Dragonbox keeps the box idea and adds Grisu's dragon.
brief.how_it_works: Dragonbox does not produce the final string. It computes the decimal significand and exponent that a string generator then formats, and the README says the string step is not officially part of the algorithm. The README says the algorithm is explained in a paper at other_files/Dragonbox.pdf, which includes a mathematical proof. It also says the proof was checked with verification programs in the test and meta directories. The README does not describe the internal arithmetic in more detail.

commands_seen.context: Clones the repository before building it from source with CMake.
Run from a build directory to generate platform-specific build files for the library.

Creates a separate build folder so that the test subproject can be built on its own.

brief.install_notes: Not a Homebrew-style CLI. The library is C++11 or later, and every function is constexpr since C++20. Header-only use needs only dragonbox.h. For string output, add dragonbox_to_chars.h and dragonbox_to_chars.cpp. Setup can be manual, or done through CMake with FetchContent_Declare and FetchContent_MakeAvailable, then target_link_libraries against dragonbox::dragonbox or dragonbox::dragonbox_to_chars. A system install can use find_package(dragonbox). The benchmark subproject runs MATLAB scripts and must have its working directory set to subproject/benchmark. Non-Visual Studio generators need that set by hand.
brief.standout: The output is guaranteed to be the shortest, correctly rounded string that round-trips, and the README presents this as a tie-break-aware refinement of Schubfach. The policy system is also unusual: sign handling, trailing-zero handling, rounding mode for parsing and for formatting, and the cache size are all compile-time choices. The README also says the fmt library uses an almost identical implementation.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release version or last-commit date. Its benchmarks are dated 03/30/2024, which is the only date evidence. I did not check the commit history or releases page.
brief.caveats: to_decimal is only defined for finite nonzero inputs. Behavior with infinities, NaN, or zeros is undefined, although to_chars and to_chars_n accept any input. Each policy combination creates a separate template instantiation, which can bloat binaries. The compact cache is about 20 percent slower, and the README says it has no effect on float. The README says the Schubfach comparison is not completely fair. The Clang and MSVC benchmark images are not described in text. Licensing is dual Apache 2.0 with LLVM exceptions or Boost 1.0, with third-party code in subproject/3rdparty excluded. The main implementation is described as hard to read, and the README points to a simpler version in subproject/simple for porting.

name: dqlite
desc: Embeddable, replicated and fault-tolerant SQLite-powered engine
why: A replicated SQLite engine using the Raft protocol; a real door into distributed consensus, though it is a library.

brief.what_it_is: dqlite is a C library that implements an embeddable, replicated SQL database engine with high availability and automatic failover. It extends SQLite with a network protocol so that several instances of an application can connect and act as one highly available cluster, with no external database needed. Applications link it in and use it like SQLite, and the nodes replicate data among themselves using the Raft consensus algorithm. The homepage describes the output as a fast, persistent SQL database with automatic leader election and failover. The README does not document a client API or a standalone server binary; the demo it points to lives in the Go bindings.
brief.why_it_exists: The name stands for "distributed SQLite". The homepage frames it for edge and IoT deployments, where appliances in remote locations cannot be quickly monitored, managed, or replaced, so the data needs to survive machine loss and fail over quickly.
brief.how_it_works: Each node runs an asynchronous, single-threaded event loop built on libuv, and nodes talk to each other over a custom wire protocol designed around SQLite primitives and data types. Writes are replicated across the cluster with the Raft algorithm, so data survives loss of machines as long as a majority remains. The homepage says the Raft implementation is C-Raft, a separate hand-tuned C implementation.

name: dumbpipe
desc: Unix pipes between devices
why: Pipes stdin and stdout between devices through peer connections, a clever revival of the Unix pipe across the network.

brief.what_it_is: Dumbpipe is a command-line tool that connects two machines directly and pipes data between them, like a Unix pipe that works across the network. You run `dumbpipe listen` on one machine, which prints a ticket (a long node identifier). On the other machine you run `dumbpipe connect <ticket>` and feed it stdin, and the bytes come out on the listener's stdout. It also has TCP and Unix-socket variants that forward local ports or sockets across the connection. Per the homepage there are no accounts and no configuration, and it works regardless of where the two machines are.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says that in 2023 it is hard to connect two devices directly, and dumbpipe is meant to solve that. The GitHub README frames it as a netcat-style tool that uses 256-bit endpoint IDs instead of IP addresses, so it is somewhat location transparent.
brief.how_it_works: It is a thin wrapper around the iroh Rust crate, which creates QUIC connections over a 'magic socket'. Iroh does NAT hole punching where it can and falls back to a meshed network of relay nodes that carry UDP traffic over HTTP when a direct connection is impossible (the homepage estimates this is 10-20% of connections). Connections are encrypted with TLS and can multiplex streams, and custom ALPN strings let you talk to other iroh protocols.

name: dvanalyzer
desc: Quality control tool for examining tape-to-file DV streams
why: Examines raw DV tape-to-file streams for errors, a rare look at how digital video bits are laid down on tape.

brief.what_it_is: DV Analyzer is a technical quality control and reporting tool that examines DV streams, the raw DV data produced when a DV tape (miniDV, DVCam, DVCPro) is transferred to a file. It reports errors introduced in the tape-to-file transfer, such as video error concealment information, invalid audio samples, timecode inconsistency, inconsistent use of arbitrary bits in video DIF blocks, and DIF structural problems. It also reports patterns in the DV stream, such as changes in DV time code, changes in recording date and time markers, and first and last frame markers within individual recordings. The input is a DV file and the output is a per-frame analysis and report.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the tape-to-file reformatting of DV is a point where permanent errors are of particularly high risk, and that most capture tools only report errors when they are significant, such as a lost frame, while other documented errors go unreviewed. The tool is meant to enable automated quality control and to verify the accuracy and integrity of the reformatting on a frame-by-frame basis. It was initially funded, designed and led by AVPreserve and is developed by MediaArea.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes the tool as analyzing and reporting audio, video, subcode, and structural errors within a DV file, and as interpreting the temporal metadata carried in every DV frame (time code, recording date and time, recording markers). It has views and documents that present this information, and the homepage links to a case study with sample DV files and explanations of detected errors, including Final Cut Pro XML temporal metadata, video error concealment, audio errors, DIF incoherency, and STTS fluctuation. I did not find a description of the internal implementation.
brief.install_notes: Binaries are provided for Windows, macOS, Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, RedHat Enterprise Linux, CentOS, Fedora, openSUSE, ArchLinux, Flatpak, and other systems, per the homepage. The homepage lists version 1.4.2 and links to a ChangeLog and to very recent snapshots. The GitHub repository has separate CLI and GUI history files, which suggests both a command-line and a graphical interface exist, but I did not verify this from a README. I saw no hardware, account, or runtime requirements, and no first-run steps.
brief.standout: Few tools look at the raw DV bitstream this closely; most capture tools only flag gross failures like dropped frames. It is aimed at digital preservation QC and reads the per-frame temporal metadata that DV carries. It is produced by MediaArea with AVPreserve's original funding and is GPL-licensed.

name: dwarfs
desc: Fast high compression read-only file system for Linux, Windows, and macOS
why: A read-only compressed filesystem that lets you mount huge archives and explore how deduplicated, block-based storage really works.

brief.what_it_is: DwarFS is a read-only, compressed file system for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS and Windows. You feed mkdwarfs a directory and it writes a single .dwarfs image file. The dwarfs driver then mounts that image as an ordinary folder, and dwarfsextract can unpack it if you need real files. dwarfsck lists the contents of an image and can print per-file checksums. The README pitches it as a mountable archive that opens instantly with no full extraction and no temporary files.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Marcus Holland-Moritz, started it in 2013 to store several hundred Perl versions, about 30 GB, in a fraction of their size. Cromfs compressed well but was slow to build and often crashed, and SquashFS never reached its compression rates. The README says other read-only compressed file systems do not exploit redundancy well, and DwarFS is built for fast random reads together with space savings.
brief.how_it_works: According to the README, DwarFS clusters files by similarity using a similarity hash function, so redundancy across file boundaries can be exploited. It segments analysis across file system blocks to shrink the uncompressed file system, which saves memory when mounted. A categorization framework lets different file types or fragments be handled differently, for example skipping compression on incompressible files or using FLAC for PCM audio. The tools are highly multi-threaded.

Release pages have prebuilt, statically linked binaries for several architectures, and the README says they should run without dependencies. Universal binaries bundle all the tools into one executable, but they decompress on each run, and they need Linux kernel 3.17 or later. The FUSE driver on Linux needs the fuse3 tools installed separately. Building from source uses CMake and Ninja, with dependency lists in the CI Dockerfiles for Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch and openSUSE, and a FreeBSD setup script. Building from the release tarball needs fewer dependencies than building from git. On Windows, you need WinFsp and the README recommends vcpkg with MSVC. Static builds are described as discouraged and unsupported.
brief.standout: Its folly-free rewrite is unusual: the author removed the Facebook folly dependency, forked the needed parts of fbthrift, and rewrote thrift code generation in Python, which the README says also made some binaries smaller. The published benchmarks are striking but self-reported, including a Perl corpus compressed to 0.310 GiB with lzma against 12.17 GiB for tar.gz. Its categorizer and similarity clustering go beyond what SquashFS does, and it is designed for random reads in large collections.

name: dwarf
desc: Object file manipulation tool
why: An object file manipulation tool that opens the door to ELF and DWARF debug structures.

brief.what_it_is: dwarf-ng is a command-line object file manipulation tool and hex editor, described as being in the spirit of gdb. It opens raw files and ELF (32 and 64-bit), PE (PE32 and PE+), and Mach-O (macOS 32 and 64-bit) executables, and lets you read and edit section headers and raw data. It can also create new file headers, inject headers and code or data into a file, and be used as a compiler back-end to produce executables or object files. Input is a file; output is printed hex, strings, numbers, and edited or saved files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a little but powerful tool for reading and editing object files at the header and raw-byte level, the way gdb works on a running program, and for building or patching binaries directly.
brief.how_it_works: You open a file (probed for its type, or opened raw with oO) and get a shell-like prompt where commands follow a gdb-like syntax: a letter for the operation, optional ? for help, and arguments such as an address or block size. Format-specific structures are exposed as variables such as $elf, $ph[0..n], $sh[0..n] for ELF, $mac and $lc for Mach-O, and $pe and $sect for PE, which can be printed, assigned, and used in expressions. Config files /etc/dwarfrc and ~/.dwarfrc are read in that order, and a work_on_tmpcopy option controls whether edits go to a temporary copy.

brief.what_it_is: Dynare is a platform for building and running economic models, mainly DSGE (dynamic stochastic general equilibrium) and OLG (overlapping generations) models. The author says you write the model almost as you would on paper, and Dynare handles the solving. The homepage lists solving and estimating a model, computing optimal policy, identification and sensitivity analysis, and perfect-foresight simulation as tasks. It runs on top of MATLAB, GNU Octave, or Julia. The homepage does not say what the inputs or outputs look like in detail.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to make macroeconomic modelling easy to use: write the model in near-paper form and let the tool do the solving and estimation work.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the mechanism. The package metadata lists a dynare-preprocessor executable, which suggests a preprocessing step that translates the model file before it runs in the host language, but I could not confirm this from the pages I read.
brief.install_notes: The Homebrew caveat says that to get started, you open Octave and type: addpath $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/dynare/lib/dynare/matlab. So the Homebrew install needs GNU Octave (or MATLAB) plus that addpath step before Dynare is usable. The homepage's 'Platforms' section names MATLAB, GNU Octave, and Julia as hosts. I did not see documentation on other setup steps.

name: dwarfutils
desc: Dump and produce DWARF debug information in ELF objects
why: Dumping and producing DWARF debug info lets you see how compilers describe programs, a real window into binaries.

brief.what_it_is: libdwarf is a C library, and dwarfdump is the command-line tool built alongside it, for reading DWARF debugging information out of object files. dwarfdump takes an object file and prints its DWARF data in readable form, covering DWARF2, DWARF3, DWARF4, and some DWARF5. The README says libdwarf reads files from disk and does not read running programs or shared objects. The Homebrew formula is named dwarfutils and provides the dwarfdump executable. The homepage says the old producer interfaces for creating DWARF were removed, and no replacement producer API is described in what I read, so the 'produce' part of the formula description is doubtful.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the project for programmers working on compilers and debuggers, and anyone reading or writing DWARF, and traces it to SGI's IRIX toolchain before it was open-sourced. The README's stated goal is portable, ABI-independent access to DWARF2 through DWARF5 data that detects corruption and avoids crashes or leaks however corrupted the input is.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain internals beyond the stated goal. For DWARF held in memory rather than in a file, a caller uses dwarf_object_init_b() with three access structs, and a worked example is at src/bin/dwarfexample/jitreader.c. Testing is the other described mechanism: about twenty thousand regression checks compare the last good dwarfdump against the latest build, and fuzzing has driven many fixes.

commands_seen.context: Gets the current source from GitHub into a libdwarf-code directory (homepage).
Autotools configure step, run from the base of the source tree (homepage).
Builds libdwarf and dwarfdump after configure (homepage).

Runs the full test script, including release builds and regression tests; the homepage says this takes about 35 minutes on a modern host and expects a PASS message at the end (homepage).

brief.install_notes: Homebrew installs it as dwarfutils. Building from source needs a C compiler conforming to the 1989 C standard or later, with long long support. The README says no library other than libc is needed to build or use libdwarf or dwarfdump. zlib and libzstd are optional, but needed to read compressed sections; on Ubuntu the packages are zlib1g-dev and libzstd-dev, and on FreeBSD they come from pkg. The README says libelf is not required as of version 0.8.0. Autotools-from-git builds also need autoconf, automake, libtool, and pkg-config. The author recommends meson over cmake and configure. On FreeBSD, python3 must be on PATH. On Windows the README recommends msys2 or cygwin.
brief.standout: The project publishes its own hardening record: a public vulnerability list, Coverity scans with a claimed zero-defect status, and regression testing on a big-endian s390 machine provided by IBM. It came out of SGI's IRIX developer tools and was open-sourced in 1994 for libdwarf and 1999 for dwarfdump.
brief.status: maintained. The README, updated 19 September 2026, lists version 2.3.3 released 22 September 2026, with 2.3.2 on 7 July 2026, 2.3.1 on 4 March 2026, and 2.3.0 on 1 February 2026. The homepage has a matching release table. I did not see a commit date. These dates are as the pages state them.

It has no dwarfdump usage example, and the flags I saw (--print-debug-names, --print-debug-addr, --print-machine-arch) appear only in prose and release notes, so I did not record them as commands. The regression tests expect a known-good dwarfdump in the distribution, which may not run on every platform. The README does not compare dwarfdump with readelf or objdump. name: ebook2cw
desc: Converts ebooks to morse code
why: Turns any ebook into Morse code audio you can listen to, a delightful transform from text into radio-style sound.

brief.what_it_is: ebook2cw is a command-line program that converts a plain text file (ASCII, ISO 8859-1, or UTF-8), such as an ebook, into Morse code audio in MP3 or OGG format. You pass it the text file and options for speed, tone frequency, waveform, chapter splitting, and ID3 tags, and it writes audio files. A separate GUI, ebook2cwgui, is optional. The page lists Windows, Linux, FreeBSD and Mac OS X as supported platforms.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Fabian Kurz (DJ5CW, ex DJ1YFK), wrote it so anyone can make a CW audio book to their own liking. He says earlier hams had made Morse audiobooks, but distributing them as finished audio files limited flexibility and needed a lot of bandwidth.
brief.how_it_works: The program reads the text and turns each character into Morse using built-in code tables (ISO 8859-1 by default, UTF-8 with -u). Inline text commands such as |f400, |w60 and |S1000 change tone, speed, or insert silence mid-text, and prosigns can be written in angle brackets like <AR>. Output is split into numbered files at chapter markers or by duration or word count. Settings can also be stored in an ebook2cw.conf file.

commands_seen.context: Windows example from the Usage section: converts Book.txt at 40 wpm, splitting chapters at the word Chapter and writing Book-0000.mp3, Book-0001.mp3, and so on.
Performance section: suggested settings (sample rate 22050, MP3 bitrate 32) if an MP3 player fails on the default settings.

Sets CW speed in words per minute (default 25).
Sets effective speed for spaces (Farnsworth spacing).
Adds background noise at an SNR from -10 to 10; negative values must be quoted.
Test mode: runs without generating any files.

brief.install_notes: Official downloads include a Windows EXE (with OGG/MP3 support), an MP3-only and an OGG-only EXE, a static Linux binary, and source tarballs for the program and GUI. Packages exist for Debian, Ubuntu (PPA ppa:kamalmostafa/ebook2cw), FreeBSD ports, and ArchLinux, and the Mac OS X build is described in separate instructions. On Windows, ebook2cw.conf and map files go in the same folder as the executable; on Linux they are also read from ~/.ebook2cw/. The GUI needs ebook2cw.exe saved alongside it or on the executable path.
brief.standout: It is a text-to-Morse converter that writes ordinary MP3 or OGG files and can be built as a CGI, which the Learn CW Online site uses to generate Morse on demand. Character mapping lets accented letters be sent as simpler Morse equivalents, and inline commands change speed or pitch mid-text.
brief.status: Maintained. ebook2cw 0.8.5 was released 16 Aug 2023, and the homepage was last modified 21 Apr 2024. The GUI, ebook2cwgui 0.1.2, dates from January 2013. I did not check the git repository's commit history.

The GUI was designed for Windows 95 through 7, and its Mac OS X support is marked not tested. The author notes copyright varies by country and points to public-domain sources such as Project Gutenberg. The software is GPLv2.

name: easyrpg-player
desc: RPG Maker 2000/2003 games interpreter
why: An interpreter for old RPG Maker games, a fun reimplementation of a forgotten engine.

brief.what_it_is: EasyRPG Player is a free, open-source game interpreter that plays games made with RPG Maker 2000 and 2003, and EasyRPG-format games. It reads the original game data through the liblcf parser library and draws the game on screen with SDL, with audio, fonts, and images handled by the libraries listed in its requirements. The input is an existing RPG Maker game project folder, and the output is the playable game on your screen. The Player does not ship games; you point it at a game you already have. It is one part of the wider EasyRPG Project, which also includes an editor and the OpenRTP asset collection.
brief.why_it_exists: The EasyRPG project describes itself as a community effort to create a free, open source role playing game creation tool compatible with RPG Maker 2000/2003 games, with the homepage pitch "Play your own RPG games anywhere". The Player is the playback half of that effort, so that games made for the old engine can run on platforms beyond Windows.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the Player uses the liblcf (LCF parser) library to read RPG Maker game data, then runs the game logic and rendering itself. It has a screen backend on SDL3 or SDL2, with optional libraries for extra fonts, music formats, and MIDI. It is also built to target Emscripten, which is how the browser version is made. The README does not go deeper into the internals.

commands_seen.context: Run from inside an RPG Maker 2000 or 2003 game project folder, the same folder that contains RPG_RT.exe. The README gives this as a plain instruction, not as a full command line with flags.

brief.install_notes: The README lists required libraries: liblcf, SDL3 or SDL2 (2.0.14 or later), Pixman, libpng, zlib, and fmtlib (6 or later). Recommended extras include FreeType2 with HarfBuzz, mpg123, WildMIDI, FluidSynth, Vorbis or Tremor, opusfile, libsndfile, libxmp, SpeexDSP or libsamplerate, lhasa, and nlohmann_json (required for Emscripten). Running it needs a game project folder, which you supply yourself. Build steps are in docs/BUILDING.md, which I did not open. Daily prebuilt binaries are at ci.easyrpg.org. The Homebrew formula's own description and executable name match this project.
brief.standout: It is a clean-room interpreter for a niche engine that is now mostly forgotten, and it runs the original game data rather than requiring a port or a re-export. The README also notes a browser build, so these games can run in a web page as well as natively.
brief.status: Appears maintained, though I have no dated evidence. The README points to active daily CI builds, supports the newer SDL3, and the homepage copyright reads 2007-2026. I did not see a last-release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so I cannot confirm the exact recency.
brief.caveats: You must supply your own RPG Maker 2000/2003 game data. The Player does not include games. The SDL 1.2 backend still works but is deprecated, and the README asks that no new platform code be added for it. The build needs several third-party libraries, so compiling from source is not trivial. Licensing: the Player is GPLv3, and the bundled fonts each carry their own licenses (Baekmuk, Shinonome, ttyp0, WenQuanYi, Teenyicons). I did not read the build document or the wiki, so I cannot speak to build pain beyond the dependency list.

brief.what_it_is: e2fsprogs is the set of userland utilities for the ext2, ext3, and ext4 Linux filesystems. The homepage describes it as the filesystem utilities for ext2, with support for ext3 and ext4. The executables listed include mke2fs and mkfs.ext2 for making filesystems, e2fsck and fsck for checking them, resize2fs for resizing, debugfs for interactive inspection, dumpe2fs for dumping superblock and group info, tune and label tools such as e2label, and helpers such as badblocks, blkid, chattr, lsattr, filefrag, e2image, e2undo, and uuidgen. name: eccodes
desc: Decode and encode messages in the GRIB 1/2 and BUFR 3/4 formats
why: Decodes GRIB and BUFR weather message formats, a door into how forecast data is actually packed.

brief.what_it_is: ecCodes is a package from ECMWF that provides an API and a set of command-line tools for decoding and encoding weather messages in WMO GRIB edition 1 and 2, BUFR edition 3 and 4, and (decode only) the GTS abbreviated header. The command-line tools give quick access to messages, and C, Fortran 90 and Python interfaces expose the main functionality. It reads and writes binary meteorological message files, and the tools print or change their contents using a key/value model. The executables include grib_ls, grib_dump, grib_get, grib_set, grib_copy, grib_to_netcdf, the matching bufr_ and gts_ tools, and codes_info and codes_count.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents ecCodes as the successor to GRIB-API, offering a simple key/value way to access data from several formats. It is now the primary GRIB encoding and decoding package at ECMWF, and GRIB-API is no longer maintained as of December 2018.
brief.how_it_works: Messages are accessed through key/value functions, so a caller asks for a named key such as a field attribute and gets its value, or sets one. The grib_ functions are kept, and a new codes_ family with the same interface and behaviour works across all supported formats. The command-line tools were built to mirror the old GRIB-API tools' options and behaviour, with bufr_dump as the main difference because it emits JSON.

name: edbrowse
desc: Command-line editor and web browser
why: A text-mode browser built around the ed editor, a genuinely odd way to browse the web.

brief.what_it_is: Edbrowse is a combination editor, browser, and mail client that is 100% text based, with an interface similar to /bin/ed. It can edit several files at once and render HTML, and it can be driven from scripts: a batch job or cron job can fetch pages, submit forms, and send email without a human present. It can also query databases over ODBC. The executables listed are edbrowse plus plugins for chrome, mpv, telnet, and zip.
brief.why_it_exists: It was written for blind users, and the inspiration came from author Karl Dahlke's years as a blind computer user; the site describes it as a command-line philosophy piece in its own right. Many sighted users now use it for its scripting capabilities, which the site says can be found nowhere else.
brief.how_it_works: You drive it with ed-style line commands rather than a mouse or full-screen menus, and it renders HTML into text you can edit. The homepage says the JavaScript engine has changed over time: a home-grown engine, then SpiderMonkey in 3.1.1, then duktape, then quickjs, and now quickjs-ng. The README does not explain the rendering pipeline further.

commands_seen.context: From the README: converts the user's guide to plain text with lynx so you can read it in an editor, since the guide is best read in a browser and edbrowse is not yet installed.

Nodes started with the same token find each other over libp2p, and the README warns that it can take up to five minutes for connections to form. Automatic IP assignment, an embedded DNS server and the blockchain (described as a lightweight ledger) keep network state among peers instead of on a server.

name: endlessh
desc: SSH tarpit that slowly sends an endless banner
why: An SSH tarpit that drips an endless banner to trap bots, a delightful door into how SSH banners and connection handling actually work.

brief.what_it_is: Endlessh is a small standalone C program that acts as an SSH tarpit. It listens on a port and, for each connecting client, slowly sends an endless stream of random SSH banner lines, one line every few seconds by default, so the client stays stuck. Its input is incoming TCP connections on the listening port, and its output is the drip of banner lines plus optional log messages to stdout or syslog. It is meant to sit on the port that bots probe while the real SSH server moves elsewhere.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's aim is to move the real SSH server to another port and let script kiddies get stuck in the tarpit instead of bothering a real server. The README says it keeps SSH clients locked up for hours or even days at a time.
brief.how_it_works: The tarpit works inside the banner phase, before any cryptographic exchange, so the program needs no crypto libraries. It is a single-threaded C program that uses poll() to hold many clients at once. Each line is randomized in length up to a configurable maximum, and lines are sent with a configurable millisecond delay.

why: Encrypted archives built on a small, auditable Ed25519 and Curve25519 design by skeeto, a fun crypto-internals read.

brief.what_it_is: Enchive is a command-line tool for encrypting files to yourself for long-term archival. You generate a keypair once with `keygen`, then `archive` encrypts a file to the public key, producing a `.enchive` file that reveals nothing about its format. `extract` decrypts it with the secret key and passphrase, reproducing the original file. Without filenames, it reads from standard input and writes to standard output. The README says it has no external dependencies and runs on Linux, BSD, macOS and Windows.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls it a focused, simple alternative to more complex solutions such as GnuPG or encrypted filesystems. Its author says he is not aware of any tool that does everything Enchive does, and that GnuPG comes close but cannot derive a key pair from a passphrase.
brief.how_it_works: To encrypt, it generates an ephemeral Curve25519 keypair, runs Diffie-Hellman against the master public key, and uses the hashed shared secret to key ChaCha8. It writes the 8-byte IV, the 32-byte ephemeral public key, the ciphertext, and an HMAC-SHA256 of the plaintext. The master key can be derived from a passphrase with an scrypt-like memory-hard function, defaulting to 512MB for the secret key (D=29), so the key can be remembered rather than stored.

brief.standout: The format is built to be unrecognizable: encrypted files have no magic numbers and look like random data. Keys can be derived from a passphrase with a memory-hard function, so you can carry the archive key in your head. Each file gets a fresh ephemeral Curve25519 key, which the README uses to justify a shortened IV. The whole thing is one small C program with no dependencies.

name: enzyme
desc: High-performance automatic differentiation of LLVM
why: Automatic differentiation performed on LLVM IR is a genuinely odd and deep compiler idea worth understanding.

brief.what_it_is: Enzyme is an automatic differentiation plugin for LLVM. It takes existing code in the form of LLVM IR, which the homepage says can come from C, C++, Swift, Julia, Rust, Fortran, and TensorFlow, and produces the derivative or gradient of a chosen function. You mark the function with a call to __enzyme_autodiff. When the Enzyme pass runs, that call is replaced with the generated derivative function. The GitHub README also describes it as working on MLIR and as plugin for statically analyzable code.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the goal is to create gradients of existing source code without much additional work, instead of rewriting that code for machine learning. Working at the LLVM level lets one tool cover several languages and reuse LLVM's optimizer.
brief.how_it_works: Enzyme runs in four parts: an optional preprocessing phase, a new interprocedural type analysis that deduces the underlying types of memory locations, an activity analysis that determines which values can affect the derivative, and an optimization pass that generates derivative functions and replaces calls to __enzyme_autodiff. The homepage says it differentiates code after optimization rather than before, which it claims yields substantially faster derivatives than tools that differentiate before optimization.

name: epics-base

Built from source, it provides a soft IOC (Input/Output Controller) that runs a Channel Access server, and the records it serves are listed from an interactive epics> prompt. The homepage's own description says such systems can span tens or hundreds of networked computers, controlled from a central room or remotely.

The homepage adds that EPICS 7's pvAccess protocol carries the newer structured data. The README does not explain the record or database model in detail.

name: eprover
desc: Theorem prover for full first-order logic with equality
why: A serious first-order logic theorem prover you can drive from the terminal, a real window into automated reasoning.

brief.what_it_is: E is an automated theorem prover, written in C and distributed under the GNU GPL, for many-sorted first-order logic with equality. The README says it can also take polymorphic higher-order logic when built with --enable-ho. You feed it a problem file, a specification plus a conjecture, in formats it detects automatically (LOP, TPTP-2 or TPTP-3). It runs a search and, if it succeeds, reports a proof, optionally in a proof-object format that the bundled checkproof tool can verify. The package also ships helper programs for strategy scheduling, parallel runs, proof filtering, and a knowledge-base (ekb_*) toolset.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames E as an equational theorem prover for stating a mathematical specification and a conjecture and letting the machine search for a proof. It is candid that this can run for a long time: 'which will then run forever, using up all of your machines resources. Very occasionally it will find a proof for the conjecture and tell you so ;-).'
brief.how_it_works: By default the prover runs a single strategy, or with --auto it picks a heuristic strategy based on the problem, pruning the axiom set for large inputs, which the README says may cost completeness. The --satauto variant keeps completeness. The --auto-schedule modes run a series of strategies in sequence, assuming a 300-second budget unless --cpu-limit says otherwise, and --auto-schedule=n spreads them across n cores. Proof objects can be written out and checked with checkproof.

brief.what_it_is: ERFA (Essential Routines for Fundamental Astronomy) is a C library of core astronomy algorithms, based on the SOFA library published by the International Astronomical Union. It is a code library, not an application: programs call its functions, which compute astronomical quantities such as coordinate transformations and time-scale conversions. Its inputs are numeric values passed in by the calling program, and its outputs are computed results returned through those functions. The README does not list the individual functions, and it does not say which downstream tools use it.

It is a renamed and relicensed derivative of SOFA version 20210512 for v2.0.0, with functions prefixed era instead of iau and C macros prefixed ERFA_. It adds runtime functions for version info (eraVersion, eraSofaVersion) and for reading and setting leap seconds (eraGetLeapSeconds, eraSetLeapSeconds), declared in erfaextra.h.

name: erg
desc: Statically typed language that can deeply improve the Python ecosystem
why: A statically typed language aimed at Python's ecosystem is unusual, though its pitch is more pragmatic than strange.

brief.what_it_is: Erg is a statically typed programming language whose compiler lives in this repository, along with its documentation. It takes Erg source files (.er) and checks them at compile time, using a type system with dependent and refinement types, so errors like out-of-range list indexing or unit mismatches are reported before running. The README's examples run through Python, and it also ships a REPL and an Erg Language Server (ELS, behind a feature flag). The README does not spell out the output format, so treat the exact artifacts it produces as unstated.
brief.why_it_exists: The README pitches Erg at people who want Rust-like robustness without Rust's verbose type specifications and memory management, and at people who are frustrated with Python but cannot throw away their Python code. It also names an ML-style simplicity goal and a Scala-style blend of object-oriented and functional programming.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the compiler's internals. It says Erg is internally compatible with Python and imports Python modules with the pyimport keyword, which it claims works at zero cost. Side effects are marked with a trailing ! on names and methods, and the compiler rejects calling a procedural method inside a function.

name: esbmc
desc: Efficient SMT-based context-bounded model checker for C, C++, and Python
why: SMT-based bounded model checker that hunts bugs in C and Python by reasoning about all execution paths.

brief.what_it_is: ESBMC is an open-source bounded model checker that takes source code (C, C++, CUDA, CHERI-C, Kotlin/Java, Python, Rust, Solidity, and PLC ladder diagrams) and encodes it into SMT formulas solved by an SMT solver such as Bitwuzla, Z3, or Boolector. It explores a finite prefix of program execution with all possible inputs, and reports either VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL, VERIFICATION FAILED with a concrete counterexample trace, or a budget-exhausted result. Users pass a source file and flags such as --incremental-bmc, --k-induction, or --multi-property; the input is the program plus optional assertions, and the output is the verdict and a counterexample trace (optionally as GraphML witnesses).
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a mature, permissively licensed tool that 'automatically detects or proves the absence of runtime errors' and checks user-defined assertions in single- and multi-threaded programs. The homepage pitches it as 'push-button' verification that needs no pre- or postconditions. It is a fork of CBMC v2.9 (2008) that the homepage says has diverged substantially.
brief.how_it_works: Programs are compiled through a language frontend (Clang for C/C++, CPython's parser via ast and ast2json for Python, Soot/Jimple for Java/Kotlin) and turned into GOTO form. Loops are unwound to a bound, with unwinding assertions inserted for soundness, and the resulting verification conditions are encoded as SMT and sent to a solver. For concurrency, ESBMC explores thread interleavings explicitly under a context bound, using a lazy depth-first search by default or encoding all interleavings into one formula. Unbounded proofs come from k-induction (base case, forward condition, inductive step) or incremental BMC.
