brief.install_notes: The homepage offers downloads for Linux (x86_64 and ARMv8), Windows, and macOS. FreeBSD has no prebuilt binary and needs the build guide. Ubuntu users can use the PPA (22.04 and 24.04). Homebrew installs bundled Z3 and Bitwuzla. The GitHub releases page has Ubuntu and Windows binaries. Users need math.h installed (build-essential usually provides it). Building from source is documented at esbmc.github.io/docs/development/building.
brief.standout: It is bounded but aims for proofs, combining incremental BMC, k-induction with a forward condition, and an interval-analysis domain in one run. It is also one of the few BMC tools to cover Python, Solidity, and Kotlin/Java alongside C/C++, and the homepage claims it is the first BMC-based Python verifier. Its --all-witnesses mode enumerates every failing input vector, not just one counterexample.
brief.status: Maintained, based on recent activity. The homepage has news items dated late September 2026 and mentions around 80 pull requests landed in early August 2026. The README lists a current release and a Homebrew package, but I did not see an explicit last-release date or last-commit date in the pages I read.
brief.caveats: Bounded by default: bug-finding within the bound is complete, but unbounded proofs depend on k-induction converging, and counterexamples can be spurious if models are abstracted. Verification needs a bound on loops; the --no-unwinding-assertions option can assume away paths past the bound. The Python frontend's README example uses type annotations. Some options (--bitwuzllob, --neurosym) need a special build and external programs, and incremental strategies are rejected for them. FreeBSD has no downloadable builds. The homepage has an ARM64 limitations link. The homepage also has an explicit 'ESBMC is a fork of CBMC v2.9' framing and a claim of being 'the first' for Python, which are the authors' own claims and not independently checked. Licensing is Apache 2.0 according to the README, with a COPYING file for third-party code.

It automatically detects or proves the absence of runtime errors (e.g., bounds checks, pointer safety, overflow) and verifies user-defined assertions without requiring pre- or postconditions.
ESBMC is push-button: one invocation produces VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL, VERIFICATION FAILED (with a concrete counterexample trace) or a budget-exhausted result.

name: erlang@27
desc: Programming language for highly scalable real-time systems
why: Erlang's actor model and hot code loading are strange and worth a look, though it is a mainstream runtime.

brief.what_it_is: Erlang is a programming language, with its runtime and the OTP library and tooling set, for building massively scalable soft real-time systems that need high availability. Its runtime has built-in support for concurrency, distribution and fault tolerance. You write functional code with pattern matching and recursion, run it in an interactive shell, and spawn lightweight processes that communicate by sending and receiving messages. OTP adds libraries, design principles, a distributed database, cross-language interfaces, and debugging and release-handling tools. The package installed here, erlang@27, is the OTP 27 line; the homepage is pitched at OTP 29.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes Erlang as used in telecoms, banking, e-commerce, computer telephony and instant messaging, where systems must stay up and handle huge numbers of concurrent activities. Its framing is practical functional programming for a parallel world.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage's examples show lightweight processes created with spawn, with messages passed using ! and received with receive. One example runs a parallel map-reduce by spawning a process per number and collecting replies. The page does not explain the runtime internals.

name: etsh
desc: Two ports of /bin/sh from V6 UNIX (circa 1975)
why: Two ports of the 1975 Sixth Edition Unix shell let you run a living piece of computing history in a terminal.

brief.what_it_is: Etsh is a set of ports of the original V6 UNIX Thompson shell (/bin/sh from V6 UNIX, May 1975), maintained by J.A. Neitzel. The homepage describes two shells: etsh, an enhanced but backward-compatible port, and tsh, an unenhanced port. It also describes glob, a port of the V6 global command. The homepage says nothing about what osh or sh6 are, though both appear among the installed executables. You run it in a terminal as an ordinary interactive shell, and it runs shell scripts and command files written in the V6 Thompson shell language.
brief.why_it_exists: The project exists to preserve and run the 1975 Thompson shell so people can use it. The homepage frames it as UNIX history: "Two ports of the 1975 Sixth Edition Unix shell let you run a living piece of computing history in a terminal" is the brew scout note, and the site adds a History section and a link list for UNIX history.
brief.how_it_works: The shells are ports of the V6 Thompson shell's command language, which the homepage calls a predecessor and subset of the Bourne and C shell languages. The Thompson shell supports pipelines (| or ^), sequential and asynchronous commands (; and &), I/O redirection, globbing, and $1-style parameter substitution. The utilities if, goto, and fd2 are built into etsh and are external programs for tsh. The homepage gives no further internals.
brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the homepage describes source tarballs (etsh-5.4.0.tar.gz or .tar.xz) with SHA512 checksums and signify signatures, signed by the author's signify key, which is published on the site. It also lists an etsh-current development branch in CVS. No runtime, account, or configuration requirements appear on the homepage. Example RC files are linked for configuring etsh interactively, but I did not open them.
brief.standout: It is a faithful revival of a 1975 shell rather than a reimagining, and it ships both a strict port (tsh) and an enhanced one (etsh) so you can run the original behavior or a backward-compatible upgrade. The author also publishes a gopher hole alongside the web site and signs releases with signify.
brief.status: Apparently maintained. The homepage gives copyright 2003-2025, lists release 5.4.0 with signed checksums, says the author develops and maintains the project, and asks users to try the latest release before reporting bugs. No release date appears on the homepage, and I did not check a changelog or repository.
brief.caveats: The brew description says ports of /bin/sh from V6 UNIX, but the homepage does not say which platforms are supported. Only etsh and tsh are described in detail, and the brew executables list also includes osh, sh6, and glob-related names that the homepage does not explain. I did not follow the Usage, Sources, or NOTES pages, so there are no verified commands and no details on the dialect differences from modern shells. UNIX is a trademark of The Open Group, which the site notes.

Bug reports are certainly welcome, but please try upgrading to the latest release before reporting any bug as it may have already been fixed.

name: espeak-ng
desc: Speech synthesizer that supports more than hundred languages and accents
why: Formant speech synthesis from the terminal, with a fascinating hand-built approach to voice across hundreds of languages.

brief.what_it_is: eSpeak NG is a compact open-source text-to-speech synthesizer for Linux, Windows, Android and other systems, supporting more than 100 languages and accents. As a command-line program it takes text from a file or stdin and speaks it aloud; it can also write the speech out as a WAV file. It is also available as a shared library (a DLL on Windows) and as a SAPI5 engine for Windows screen readers. The project is written in C and is based on the eSpeak engine by Jonathan Duddington.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a small, broadly multilingual synthesizer: formant synthesis lets many languages fit in a small footprint, at the cost of sounding less natural than recording-based synthesizers. It is a cleaned-up fork of eSpeak, started in late 2015 with the intention of tidying the existing codebase, adding features, and improving the supported languages.
brief.how_it_works: It uses formant synthesis, a method that generates speech from modelled vocal-tract resonances rather than from recorded human speech, which is why the data for many languages stays small. The README says it also supports Klatt formant synthesis and can use MBROLA diphone voices as a backend, in which case eSpeak NG converts text to phonemes with pitch and length information. Its text-to-phoneme output can also be used as a front end for another speech engine.

It can speak through MBROLA diphone voices and can also emit phonemes, so it works as a front end rather than only a standalone speaker. name: evtx
desc: Windows XML Event Log parser
why: Parses Windows binary event logs into readable records, a window into an opaque format most Unix people never open.

brief.what_it_is: A cross-platform Rust parser for Windows XML EventLog (.evtx) files, the binary event log format Windows writes. It takes .evtx files as input and emits each record as XML or JSON (or JSON Lines). It ships as a Rust library crate, a command-line tool called evtx_dump, Python bindings (pyevtx-rs / PyPI 'evtx'), and a browser-based viewer called EVTX Web that runs the same core as WebAssembly and handles files locally.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a formal motivation. It frames the project around speed and format coverage: it calls itself 'a cross-platform parser for the Windows XML EventLog format' and claims to be faster than other implementations.
brief.how_it_works: The README says XML and JSON outputs are both built directly from a shared intermediate representation, so no XML-to-JSON conversion step happens. Parsing is multithreaded by default, which means records can come out of order unless you pass -t 1. It also has some basic recovery for missing records or chunks. Optional WEVT_TEMPLATE support can pull message templates out of provider DLL/EXE/SYS files into an offline cache and use them to render records.

The WEVT_TEMPLATE template features need the Cargo feature 'wevt_templates' at build time, though the README says release binaries may already include it. No accounts or external services are needed. The Python bindings are a separate package on PyPI. The browser viewer needs no install and works offline after first load.

name: ettercap
desc: Multipurpose sniffer/interceptor/logger for switched LAN
why: ARP poisoning and LAN interception make it a vivid door into how switched networks trust every packet.

brief.what_it_is: Ettercap is a multipurpose sniffer, interceptor and logger for switched LANs, and the project describes itself as a comprehensive suite for man in the middle attacks. It sniffs live connections, filters and modifies content on the fly, and actively and passively dissects many protocols. It also does host discovery and passive OS fingerprinting. It runs against traffic on the LAN it is attached to. The package ships four executables: ettercap (the main program, with text, curses and GTK interfaces), ettercap-pkexec, etterfilter (compiles filter scripts that ettercap uses), and etterlog (processes log files).
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no motivation beyond describing itself as a suite for man in the middle attacks. Its technical paper explains each attack method in detail, so it reads as documentation of how switched networks can be intercepted.
brief.how_it_works: Host discovery sends an ARP request for each IP in the local netmask and collects the replies. For ARP poisoning, ettercap sends forged ARP replies so that two victims each cache the attacker's MAC address as the other's, then records packets and forwards them to the real destination. Its unified sniffing method keeps kernel IP forwarding off and has ettercap re-send packets that are addressed to its MAC but carry other IPs. Filter scripts written in a small language are compiled with etterfilter and can drop or rewrite traffic.

It walks through ARP poisoning with a worked MAC and IP example, explains kernel-specific caching quirks (a Linux 2.4 ARP behaviour and a Solaris workaround using a spoofed ICMP echo), describes port stealing by flooding the switch, and covers an SSH1 man-in-the-middle. name: execline

brief.how_it_works: Scripts are run through the execlineb program used as an interpreter. Each command in a script chains directly into the next program rather than being evaluated by an interpreter loop, so the script effectively execs programs in sequence. The homepage does not spell out the mechanism further, and the design-and-grammar page was not followed.

name: f3
desc: Test various flash cards
why: Tests flash cards for fake capacity, a satisfying way to catch counterfeit storage by writing and reading back data.

brief.what_it_is: f3 is a command-line tool for checking whether a flash drive or memory card holds the capacity and performance it claims. f3write takes a mounted path, fills all free space with 1GB files named N.h2w, and f3read checks those files byte-for-byte against the pseudorandom data that was written. The output is a per-file count of ok, corrupted, changed and overwritten sectors, plus average read and write speeds. A separate tool, f3probe, works on the raw block device (for example /dev/sdX) and reports the drive's usable size next to its announced size, and f3fix can then create a partition that matches the usable size. The homepage is only a table of contents, so this summary is drawn from the GitHub README and the Usage page.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says f3 is meant to see 'if they live up to claimed specifications' and that 'F3 stands for Fight Flash Fraud, or Fight Fake Flash.' The Usage page frames it as a free, open answer to counterfeit flash cards that advertise far more capacity than they hold.
brief.how_it_works: f3write fills free space with H2testw-compatible N.h2w files, and f3read validates them. Because each sector records what it should contain and where it should sit, f3read can tell a corrupted sector from one that was overwritten at the wrong address, which is how a fake card that wraps around is exposed. f3probe writes only a small number of blocks, about half the drive or 2GB at most, and uses a model of fake-drive behaviour (limbo, wraparound, chain) to find the real size quickly. The docs say f3probe is still marked experimental.

name: exult
desc: Recreation of Ultima 7
why: A recreation of Ultima 7 engine is a fascinating look at how old games were engineered, though it needs game data files.

brief.what_it_is: Exult is an open-source engine that recreates Ultima VII (The Black Gate, with Serpent Isle as a sequel) for modern operating systems. It takes the original game's data, graphics, and plot files as input, which the user must supply from their own legal copy, and it outputs a playable game that runs natively on Windows, macOS, and Android. The project also ships Exult Studio, a level and content editor, and tools for the game's SHP graphics format.
brief.why_it_exists: The project's introduction says that as computers evolve, classic games risk being lost, and that Ultima VII, a two-part early-1990s RPG, still has a large following and is considered by many to be one of the most immersive games ever made. Exult aims to keep it running on modern systems.
brief.how_it_works: Exult is a reimplementation of the game engine that reads the original Ultima VII data, graphics, and music files rather than including them. The site's news says the engine was ported from SDL2 to SDL3 in its development tree, and that a 2026 release changed the Windows installer's helper DLL to be compiled with MSVC. The brew caveat notes that audio is configured in ~/Library/Preferences/exult.cfg, and that CoreAudio or an audio pack (use_oggs) can be selected there.
brief.install_notes: The Homebrew formula contains only the game engine, so you must supply your own legal copy of the Ultima VII game files for it to fully work. Audio is configured in ~/Library/Preferences/exult.cfg: set driver to CoreAudio for CoreAudio, and set use_oggs to yes to use the audio pack. The Windows installer can also download the audio packs and several mods. The homepage does not describe a first-run wizard.
brief.standout: Unlike a remake with new assets, Exult is a pure engine that depends on the original game files, and it has grown into a whole toolkit: an editor (Exult Studio), GIMP and Aseprite plug-ins for SHP files, an Android port, and a community Ultima VI remake mod that runs on the Exult engine.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage news runs to 27 March 2026 (Windows 1.12.1-1 re-release), 8 January 2026 (1.12.1 hotfix), and 11 May 2025 (1.12), with a development tree in progress. The project also notes that releases now come roughly every two years, with occasional hotfixes in between.
brief.caveats: You must provide your own legal copy of the Ultima VII game data, and the engine does not include it. Antivirus programs falsely flagged the Windows installer, which the project says was a gcc compile issue and has since been rebuilt with MSVC. The 2020 and 2022 news lists known issues, such as the antimagic rain from the cube generator not dissipating quickly enough and the game quitting rather than returning to the menu after the ending. Support for very old Windows versions (95, 98, ME, NT, 2000) ended with 1.6, and a legacy download exists for them. The homepage does not state a license.

name: faketty
desc: Wrapper to exec a command in a pty, even if redirecting the output
why: Tricks programs into thinking their redirected output is a terminal, a small door into how tty detection actually works.

brief.what_it_is: faketty is a small command-line wrapper binary written in Rust. You put it in front of any command, and it runs that command inside a pseudoterminal (pty) while still sending the command's stdout and stderr to whatever you redirect them to, such as log files. The README's example is `faketty bazel build :target >log/out 2>log/err`. The output lands in the log files, but the program still sees a terminal and formats its output as if a person were watching.
brief.why_it_exists: When a program's output is redirected to a pipe or file, many programs detect that it is no longer a terminal and drop progress bars or colored text. The README says faketty lets you log stdout and stderr separately without changing what the output looks like compared with running in a terminal. It also explains that the standard tool script(1) can fake a terminal but uses a single pty, so it cannot keep stdout and stderr separate.
brief.how_it_works: faketty execs the given command inside a pty, so the process sees a real terminal with width, height and similar properties. Because the README says faketty 'preserves distinct stdout and stderr streams', unlike script(1), it keeps the two streams apart so each can go to its own destination. The README does not describe the internal mechanism for doing that separation beyond this.

commands_seen.context: The README's install command, which uses Cargo to install the crate from crates.io.
Main usage example: runs bazel build inside a pty, with stdout going to log/out and stderr going to log/err. The README labels 'bazel build :target' as the command to run.
Not a faketty command. The README uses it to describe the closest existing equivalent, script(1), which faketty is similar to except that it keeps stdout and stderr distinct.

brief.install_notes: The README gives only `cargo install faketty`, which means a Rust toolchain with Cargo is needed. The Homebrew formula lists the faketty executable, but the README does not mention brew. No accounts, hardware, or first-run configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: Most wrappers for fooling tty detection use one pseudoterminal, so stdout and stderr get merged. faketty points out that script(1) has this limit and keeps the two streams separate, so you can log errors apart from normal output while the program still believes it is talking to a terminal.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a crates.io version badge and a GitHub Actions CI build-status badge, but it gives no release date, last commit date, or maintenance note, and I did not fetch the crates.io page or the commit history to check.
brief.caveats: The README says nothing about supported platforms. Because it depends on ptys, it is probably limited to Unix-like systems, but I did not confirm this. Its usefulness depends on the target program's behavior, since programs that check other things besides tty status may still act differently. The README includes no limitations section, so other gaps are unknown.
quotes: This allows logging the stdout and stderr (separately) of a process, without the output being different from what you'd see in the terminal if you weren't logging anything.
However, `script` only uses a single pty, which makes it impossible to demultiplex stdout and stderr to different places.
The `faketty` command in this repo is similar to `script --quiet --return --command '...' /dev/null` except that it preserves distinct stdout and stderr streams.

name: fastani
desc: Fast whole-genome similarity (ANI) estimation
why: Real genomics software estimating whole-genome similarity, a legitimate science rabbit hole though a bit specialised.

brief.what_it_is: FastANI is a command-line tool that estimates whole-genome Average Nucleotide Identity between genome assemblies without doing expensive sequence alignment. It takes FASTA or multi-FASTA genome files (gzip-compressed is fine), either one query against one reference, one query against a list of references, or many queries against many references. It writes tab-delimited rows giving query, reference, ANI value, count of bidirectional fragment mappings, and total query fragments. An optional --matrix flag also writes a PHYLIP-style lower-triangular ANI matrix.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it was built for fast, alignment-free ANI computation, so that large numbers of genome pairs can be compared. It follows the workflow of Goris et al. 2007 but is much faster, and the authors point to a 90K prokaryotic genome study as evidence for its use in finding species boundaries.
brief.how_it_works: Rather than running BLAST-style alignments, FastANI uses Mashmap, a MinHash-based sequence mapping engine, to find orthologous mappings between genomes and estimate alignment identity. It then averages identity over bidirectional fragment mappings to produce the ANI value. The README reports accuracy on par with the BLAST-based ANI solver and a two to three orders of magnitude speedup.

The visualization step needs R with the genoPlotR package. The repo includes a script to randomly split a reference database into chunks for running parallel processes across nodes.
brief.standout: It replaces alignment-based ANI with a MinHash mapping step borrowed from Mashmap, and the README claims BLAST-level accuracy at two to three orders of magnitude more speed. It also documents its own asymmetry: A-to-B and B-to-A ANI can differ slightly, and the --matrix option averages the two values.

name: fastga
desc: Pairwise whole genome aligner
why: Pairwise whole genome aligner from a respected bioinformatics group; real science you can run on your own genomes.

brief.what_it_is: FastGA is a command-line pairwise whole-genome aligner from Gene Myers and Chenxi Zhou. Given two genome assemblies as FASTA (or gzipped FASTA, or ONEcode sequence files), it finds all local DNA alignments between them and by default streams them to stdout in PAF format. It can also write PSL or its own binary .1aln format, and the package includes utilities to convert, inspect, plot, and filter those alignments and to manage the intermediate genome databases and indexes.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a fast way to find all local alignments (over 100bp at 70% or more similarity) between two high-quality, nearly complete genomes, with compact storage of the results. It assumes assemblies of at most several thousand contigs at Q40 or better.
brief.how_it_works: FastGA converts each FASTA into a genome database (.1gdb plus a hidden 2-bit sequence file) and builds a truncated suffix-array-like genome index (.gix) for each genome, then compares the two indexes directly. It finds 'adaptamer' seeds, chains them within diagonal bands, and runs a wave-based local aligner (from daligner) on the chains. Alignments are stored as trace-point encodings in a .1aln file, which ALNtoPAF or ALNtoPSL later expand into PAF or PSL on demand.

commands_seen.context: Basic comparison of two genomes (FASTA, gzipped FASTA, or ONEcode sequence); PAF goes to stdout by default, using 8 threads.
README example: verbose mode, 16 threads, and PSL output. The README notes that optional arguments may be placed anywhere, so -psl can be appended to a command already typed.
Single-source mode: compares A against itself, skipping self-matches, for repeat detection or finding homologous regions between haplotypes.
Soft-masks A with the union of two .1ano interval files and masks B with its implicit upper/lower-case mask, per the README's masking example.
Converts a FASTA into a genome database A.1gdb in the same directory. The README recommends replacing FASTA files with GDBs, since GDBtoFA can reproduce the FASTA exactly.
Builds A.1gdb in the current directory from a FASTA in another path, per the README's example.

Usage line from the README for converting a .1aln file to PSL on stdout.

brief.install_notes: Installs through Bioconda with pixi (pixi global install fastga), conda (conda install fastga or conda create -n envname fastga), or micromamba, after the conda-forge and bioconda channels are set up. A Docker/Podman container is available from quay.io/biocontainers/fastga. The Bioconda page lists Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) and macOS (x86_64 needs 11.0 or later, plus osx-arm64) builds, with dependencies on zlib. The README also describes building from source with a Makefile, and notes that for the ONEalnTEST build several modules (GDB, ONElib, alncode, align, gene_core) must be compiled in. No accounts or API keys are mentioned. Disk space matters: GIX indexes occupy about 13-14 GB per gigabase, so the README recommends building them only when needed and removing them afterwards with GIXrm.
brief.standout: The alignment output is a compact trace-point encoding (the README's example: 635,000+ local alignments in 44.5 MB) that can be expanded to PAF or PSL later, and the tool compares two genome indexes directly instead of querying one genome's index with the other's sequences. The seed method is credited to Martin Frith's adaptamer idea, and the README reports about 5 minutes wall clock for two 2 Gbp bat genomes on 8 cores.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the sources show. The README header gives a last update of December 30, 2025, with version 1.5 adding ANO annotation files and version 1.4 adding a C library for reading .1aln files. The Bioconda page lists versions 1.5-0, 1.5-1, and 1.5.20260729-0. I did not check the GitHub commit history or release tags directly.
brief.caveats: Index size is large: about 14 GB of GIX per gigabase of genome. The PSL output is almost 15 times the size of the .1aln file, and the -m, -x, -s, and -S options slow ALNtoPAF by about 10 times and enlarge output by almost 100 times. Alignments depend on source paths recorded in the .1aln file, so moving GDBs breaks ALNtoPAF unless ALNreset is run. The README says FastGA's results are asymmetric: FastGA A B does not give the same alignments as FastGA B A unless the -S option is used. It is designed for near-complete, high-quality assemblies, and the authors say sensitivity for distant genomes and satellite repeats still needs work. The README reports a BSD-like license, which I got from the Bioconda recipe page, not from a LICENSE file I read. The scout note's claim that the group is 'respected' is an opinion I did not verify. I did not see a docs site beyond the README.

Note carefully, that one has the option to keep the results in the very disk efficient ALN format, and then convert it to any of PAF, PSL, or other desired alignment format on demand.
Beware, the -m, -x, -s and -S options increase the time taken by ALNtoPAF by a factor of 10 and the file size by a factor of almost 100 !

name: fantom
desc: Object oriented, portable programming language

name: faust
desc: Functional programming language for real time signal processing
why: A functional language for signal processing that compiles DSP code to many targets, a genuinely distinctive way to make sound.

brief.what_it_is: Faust (Functional Audio Stream) is a functional programming language for real-time audio signal processing and synthesis, built at GRAME in Lyon. You write DSP code in the Faust language, and the Faust compiler translates it into C++, C, LLVM IR, WebAssembly, Rust and other targets. Wrapper scripts called architectures then turn the generated code into plugins (VST, AU, LV2, CLAP and others), standalone apps, mobile or web apps, and objects for Max, Pure Data, SuperCollider and similar hosts. The README describes it as 'fully compiled', and the homepage calls it an alternative to C++ that is much simpler to learn.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Faust as a way to design synthesizers, instruments and audio effects in a functional language, then ship the same DSP specification to many platforms without rewriting it by hand. It has been developed at GRAME since 2002.
brief.how_it_works: A Faust program is a DSP specification that the compiler translates to sample-level code for the chosen language. The master branch can emit LLVM IR and use an LLVM JIT, which lets libfaust be embedded in C++ programs and used by tools such as FaustLive. The faust2... scripts combine the generated code with a chosen architecture file (JACK, ALSA, Qt, VST, and so on) to produce a finished binary or plugin.

commands_seen.context: README example: compiles a Faust file into a JACK application with a Qt interface.
README tip: type faust2 in a terminal and press Tab to auto-complete and list every faust2... tool.
Maintainer-side: updates the libraries submodule to its latest version before committing it to the main repo. Not something a user needs to run.

brief.install_notes: Since release 2.5.18 the build and install is CMake-based. The README points to the GitHub wiki (BuildingSimple tutorial) for compiling from source. Official packages are on the GitHub releases page. Each faust2... script needs its own dependencies installed, for example faust2jaqt needs JACK and Qt. Faust libraries live in a separate repo included as a git submodule, so a source checkout needs submodules. No account or license key is mentioned. The browser tools (Faust Playground, Online Faust IDE) need no install.
brief.standout: Compile-to-everything from one functional DSP source is the core trick. Also notable: the Faust Web IDE and Playground run the compiler in the browser, so you can try a DSP program with no install, and the web tooling is a live part of the project, with 2026 news including a Godot integration and an experimental Rust port (faust-rs) that adds forward and reverse-mode automatic differentiation.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage news runs through September 2, 2026 (Google Summer of Code projects finalized). Three CI badges (Ubuntu, macOS, Windows) appear in the README. I did not check the GitHub commit date or the latest release tag, so this rests on the news and CI links.

name: fastme
desc: Accurate and fast distance-based phylogeny inference program
why: Infers phylogenetic trees from distance matrices, real evolutionary biology you can run on your own data.

brief.what_it_is: FastME is a software package that infers phylogenetic trees from distance matrices. It takes a square PHYLIP distance matrix, or DNA, protein, or PHYLIP alignments from which it estimates distances, and outputs a tree. It implements Balanced Minimum Evolution (BME), a distance criterion closely related to Neighbor Joining, and refines the tree with NNI and SPR rearrangements. The homepage also hosts a web submission form for running analyses online.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the goal of the BME framework is to identify the phylogenetic tree that minimizes the total estimated evolutionary distance among taxa, and that FastME is aimed at accurate, fast reconstruction on large datasets where likelihood-based approaches may be computationally demanding.
brief.how_it_works: After building an initial tree, FastME refines the topology with rearrangement operations, Nearest Neighbor Interchange (NNI) and Subtree Pruning and Regrafting (SPR), to find trees with shorter total branch lengths at a computational cost comparable to NJ. It accepts DNA sequences, protein sequences, or precomputed distance matrices and offers several distance estimation methods. Bootstrap support and parallel computation are also listed.

commands_seen.context: Quoted from the web form's BioNJ pipeline description: the BioNJ mode preserves PHYLIP distance options and runs FastME with these flags and no refinement, with bootstrap consensus made by PHYLIP Consense.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond brew install was on the homepage. The homepage has a Download link and a User guide link, but I did not follow them. The online service accepts PHYLIP alignments or square PHYLIP distance matrices, 1 to 100 data sets, and a Newick starting topology is optional.
brief.standout: It is a distance-based method that starts from an NJ-like tree and then searches for a better BME tree with SPR moves, aiming for likelihood-like accuracy at distance-method speed. The package is also published with a web front end that exposes model choices and bootstrapping.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows the 2015 MBE paper (FastME 2.0, Lefort, Desper, Gascuel) and a live execution API check, but gives no release date, last commit, or version.
brief.caveats: I read only the homepage, which is a web page rather than a repository README, so I have no install instructions, licence, or platform details. The web service page notes that submitting an analysis is subject to Terms of Use. The homepage text does not state a licence.
quotes: FastME is a software package for the fast and accurate inference of phylogenetic trees from distance matrices.
Compared to classical Neighbor Joining approaches, FastME improves tree accuracy through efficient topological optimization procedures.

Thanks to its combination of speed, scalability, and accuracy, FastME is widely used for phylogenetic reconstruction, particularly for large datasets where likelihood-based approaches may be computationally demanding.

name: fedify
desc: CLI toolchain for Fedify
why: A toolchain for ActivityPub's federated social protocol is a real door into a protocol most people never look at.

brief.what_it_is: fedify is a command-line toolchain from the Fedify project, used for building ActivityPub federated server apps and for debugging ActivityPub servers in general. Its main job is fedify lookup: you give it an object URL or an actor handle such as @user@example.com, and it fetches and prints the ActivityPub object, as a readable dump, compacted or expanded JSON-LD, or raw JSON. It also scaffolds new Fedify projects with fedify init, and runs fedify inbox, a temporary public ActivityPub inbox for watching what your server sends out. The sample config file also has relay and nodeinfo sections, but I did not see the commands for those in the text I read.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the fedify command is a CLI toolchain for Fedify and for debugging ActivityPub-enabled federated server apps. It is primarily aimed at developers who use Fedify, but it says it works with any ActivityPub-enabled server.
brief.how_it_works: For lookup, the tool fetches the URL or resolves the handle over HTTP, then parses the JSON-LD and prints it in the chosen format. With -a/--authorized-fetch, it generates a one-time key pair, starts a temporary ActivityPub server to publish the public key, and signs the request. For fedify inbox, it starts an ephemeral server with a one-time actor, exposes it through a short-lived public DNS name with HTTPS, and logs incoming activities to the console.

Starts an ephemeral ActivityPub inbox server on a public HTTPS address that stays up until you press ^C.

brief.install_notes: Several routes are documented: npm or Bun (npm install -g @fedify/cli), Homebrew (brew install fedify), Scoop on Windows (scoop install fedify), Deno (deno install -gA --unstable-fs --unstable-kv -n fedify jsr:@fedify/cli, with --unstable-temporal added on Deno versions before 2.7.0), mise (mise use -g github:fedify-dev/fedify), or a pre-built executable from the GitHub releases page placed on your PATH. There is no hardware or account requirement mentioned. Configuration is optional TOML: system-wide, ~/.config/fedify/config.toml (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME), a project-level .fedify.toml, or a file passed with --config. Config needs Fedify 2.0.0 or later, and command-line flags override it.
brief.standout: Two things stand out. fedify inbox gives you a throwaway public ActivityPub actor and inbox, so you can see exactly what your server sends. The lookup command's authorized fetch tries RFC 9421 and falls back to draft-cavage HTTP Signatures (double-knocking), and it also resolves FEP-ef61 portable objects (ap:// URIs with DIDs). Most ActivityPub tooling does not do any of these.

name: fastk
desc: K-mer counter for high-fidelity shotgun datasets
why: A k-mer counter from genomics research; real science to run at home, though a close call for a general audience.

brief.what_it_is: FastK is a k-mer counter from Gene Myers, written in C, aimed mainly at high-quality DNA data such as Illumina reads or PacBio HiFi reads. It takes CRAM, BAM, SAM, fasta, or fastq files (gzipped fasta/fastq allowed), or Dazzler databases, and the type is read from the file extension. For a chosen k (default 40), it always writes a .hist histogram of k-mer frequencies. With options it can also write a sorted table of canonical k-mers with counts (.ktab), a per-read count profile (.prof), or a profile of each read relative to another dataset's table. A suite of companion tools (Histex, Tabex, Profex, Logex, Symmex, KmerMap, Fastmerge, Fastcat and the Fastrm/Fastmv/Fastcp file tools) reads, merges, filters and converts these outputs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says FastK is optimized for high-quality assembly datasets and handles arbitrarily large inputs on modest memory. It also says profiles can be produced during the underlying sort, which the author calls much more efficient than building a k-mer hash after the fact, as other counters require.
brief.how_it_works: FastK treats a k-mer and its reverse complement as one, storing the lexicographically smaller form as canonical, and sorts the k-mers to count them. Profiles are recorded during that sort in a compressed form (about 4.7 bits per base for a 50X HiFi assembly, per the README). Output is split into a stub file plus hidden per-thread part files, which Fastrm, Fastmv and Fastcp handle as a unit, and Fastmerge and Fastcat merge or splice slices for HPC runs.

name: fernflower
desc: Advanced decompiler for Java bytecode
why: JetBrains' Java bytecode decompiler; a real window into reconstructing source from compiled classes.

brief.what_it_is: Fernflower is JetBrains' analytical decompiler for Java bytecode. It takes .class files, and .zip or .jar archives (directories are scanned recursively), and writes reconstructed Java source files into a destination directory. Optional library jars can be supplied so that class relationships resolve without being decompiled. It runs from the command line as a Java program, and it is also bundled inside IntelliJ IDEA to show source when debugging or navigating class files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls it 'the first actually working analytical decompiler for Java and probably for a high-level programming language in general.' Its renaming feature targets obfuscated bytecode: the README says obfuscators give classes and members 'short, meaningless and above all ambiguous names,' and recompiling such code 'leads to a great number of conflicts.'
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the internal decompilation algorithm. It does describe the inputs and controls: a long list of -<option>=<value> flags (mostly 0/1 toggles, such as hides bridge methods, decompile enumerations, and decompile lambda expressions to anonymous classes), an optional per-method time limit (mpm), and an optional renamer. The renamer, enabled with ren=1, renames elements that are reserved words or shorter than three characters to names like class_<n>, method_<n>, field_<n>. A custom renamer implementing IMemberIdentifierRenamer can be supplied with urc.

commands_seen.context: General stand-alone usage synopsis from the README; sources are class, zip or jar files or directories, and the last argument is the output directory.

README example: decompiles a binary directory with hide-empty-super (hes) and hide-empty-default-constructor (hdc) turned off, using rt.jar as a library source for context, and writes to c:\Temp\source\.
README example: turns on decompile generic signatures (dgs) and mixes a jar and a single class as sources, writing output to c:\Temp\source\.
Development build step from the README; generates an executable start-up script in build/install/engine/bin.

brief.install_notes: The README does not mention Homebrew. It says releases are published in the IntelliJ Community repository (https://www.jetbrains.com/intellij-repository/releases), so a release jar is the expected artifact. Running it means invoking java -jar fernflower.jar, which needs a Java runtime. To build from source, run ./gradlew :installDist from the repository, then use the script in build/install/engine/bin. No accounts or hardware are needed. Whether the Homebrew 'fernflower' executable wraps the jar that way is not confirmed by the README.
brief.standout: Its own README treats the renamer as a first-class feature. The renamer is pluggable through an interface, and it can use library jars for context so that renames avoid conflicts with external classes. The options list also includes Java-language reconstruction choices such as record patterns and switch with patterns, which are unusual for a decompiler.
brief.status: Maintained by JetBrains, though the README gives no release date or recent-commit evidence. The credits say JetBrains has maintained it 'since 2014' and that its original author Stiver has passed away. Releases are published through the IntelliJ repository and bugs go to the IntelliJ YouTrack. Overall, it appears active, but the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: The README is written as if the reader is already a Java developer, and it says most options are 'aimed at professional reverse engineers.' Some defaults are workarounds for compiler bugs. The -e library example points at rt.jar, a legacy file that modern JDKs no longer ship. The README describes Windows-style paths in its examples. The Homebrew formula's executable name matches the README but its invocation is not documented here. The license is Apache 2.0.

name: fennel
desc: Lua Lisp Language
why: A Lisp that compiles to Lua with macros and a REPL, a genuinely unusual door into language design.

brief.what_it_is: Fennel is a Lisp-syntax programming language that compiles to Lua and is built around a macro system. It takes Fennel source files (.fnl) or code typed into its REPL and produces plain Lua code, which runs anywhere Lua runs. It can be run as a command-line script, embedded as a single fennel.lua file inside a Lua program, or precompiled ahead of time with the compiler. The site claims full two-way Lua compatibility, so Fennel can call any Lua function or library and vice versa.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches Fennel as bringing together the simplicity, speed, and reach of Lua with the flexibility of Lisp syntax and macros. The Rationale page on the site is said to explain why it was created, but I did not fetch it.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler turns Fennel forms into Lua source, and macros run at compile time, so the shipped Lua has no runtime dependency on Fennel. name: flif
desc: Free Loseless Image Format
why: A progressive lossless image format with interlacing tricks, a fascinating file format, but deprecated and no longer maintained.

brief.what_it_is: FLIF (Free Lossless Image Format) is a lossless raster image format and its reference implementation: an encoder (the flif command), a decoder library (libflif, and a decode-only libflif_dec), and an example viewer (viewflif). It takes ordinary pixel images (greyscale, RGB, RGBA, palette, up to 16 bits per channel) and writes .flif files that decode back to the identical pixels. It also has a lossy preprocessing option on the encoder side, and animation support. The package also ships apng2flif and gif2flif converters and a dflif tool. The homepage and README describe it as a format that compresses better than PNG and lossless WebP, BPG, JPEG 2000 and JPEG XR.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches FLIF as a single format that works well on any kind of image, so end users do not have to pick PNG for line art, JPEG 2000 for medical images, and so on. It also aims for progressive decoding, so a partial download gives a usable preview.
brief.how_it_works: FLIF is based on MANIAC (Meta-Adaptive Near-zero Integer Arithmetic Coding), a variant of CABAC in which the contexts are decision-tree nodes learned dynamically at encode time rather than a fixed multi-dimensional array of quantized local image information. Its interlacing generalizes PNG's Adam7, so any prefix of a compressed file can serve as a reasonable lossy version of the whole image, and the interlacing is accounted for in the pixel estimation and the context model, which keeps the overhead small.

brief.standout: Interlacing is treated as a model feature rather than a bolt-on. The encoder accounts for it in both pixel estimation and the MANIAC context model, so interlaced files are often no bigger, and sometimes smaller, than non-interlaced ones for photographs. It is also one of the few lossless formats built around a learned decision-tree context model instead of fixed contexts.

name: flecs
desc: Fast entity component system for C & C++
why: An entity component system library is a plumbing-adjacent tool, but it opens a door into simulation architecture worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Flecs is a fast, lightweight Entity Component System library for C and C++, aimed at games and simulations with very large numbers of entities. You define components as plain data types, attach them to entities, and write systems (functions) that run over every entity matching a query. It is a library you compile into your program, not a standalone tool: the input is your C or C++ code, and the output is the running simulation loop, which the README drives with ecs_progress. It also has a web-based Flecs Explorer for monitoring and controlling a running app.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames ECS as a way to organize code and data so that games are 'larger, more complex and are easier to extend', and presents Flecs as a fast, portable implementation of that pattern.
brief.how_it_works: Entities are identifiers, components are datatypes added to entities, and systems are functions that run for all entities matching a component query. Storage is described as cache-friendly archetype/SoA, which the README says can process millions of entities every frame. Systems run inside a pipeline via ecs_progress, and the README mentions a lockless scheduler for running work across CPU cores.

name: flint
desc: C library for number theory
why: A serious C library for number theory that lets you play with real algebraic computation at home.

brief.what_it_is: FLINT (Fast Library for Number Theory) is a C library for number theory, released under the GNU LGPL version 3 or later. It provides arithmetic in the integers, rationals, algebraic, real, complex and p-adic numbers, finite fields and number fields, plus univariate and multivariate polynomials, power series and matrices. Its functions include primality testing, integer factorisation, multivariate polynomial GCD and factorisation, FFTs, special functions, exact and approximate linear algebra and LLL. Input is C calls on library types; output is the computed numbers, polynomials, matrices and so on.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents FLINT as a fast, mature number theory library for all operand sizes, from single-word to multi-gigabyte, which many computer algebra systems use as a back end. It also says its developers have published more than 20 papers describing new algorithms first implemented in or on top of FLINT.
brief.how_it_works: The page says FLINT picks automatically between basecase, intermediate, asymptotically fast and special-purpose algorithms depending on the size and structure of the problem. Many algorithms are multithreaded and some key functions use SIMD acceleration. Real and complex numbers use ball arithmetic, which gives arbitrary precision with rigorous error bounds.

name: flix
desc: Statically typed functional, imperative, and logic programming language
why: A language blending functional, imperative and logic programming with Datalog-style constraint solving, uncommon enough to explore.

brief.what_it_is: Flix is a statically typed programming language that combines functional, imperative, and logic programming, with a focus on algebraic effects and handlers. It takes Flix source files (.flix) and compiles them to JVM bytecode, with a built-in build tool, package manager, test runner, REPL, and language server. The homepage also describes it as a whole-program optimizing compiler, and it offers an embedded first-class Datalog for fixpoint and graph-reachability problems. It can call Java and Maven libraries directly.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Flix as an effect-oriented language: by explicitly modelling side effects in the type system, it aims to enforce modularity, aid program reasoning, and let programmers write their own control structures through user-defined effects and handlers. It is developed at Aarhus University with contributors from Waterloo, Tübingen, and Copenhagen.
brief.how_it_works: Every expression is annotated with an effect set (for example \ {} for pure, \ IO for impure), and the compiler infers and tracks these, including through higher-order functions via effect polymorphism. Library effects such as Clock, Http, and Logger have default handlers, so programs can run without handler boilerplate, and users can wrap them with middleware like retries or circuit breakers in with clauses. The compiler is whole-program: it uses monomorphization, inlining, closure elimination, tail call elimination, and tree shaking, and the homepage shows JVM bytecode to back this up.

name: flye
desc: De novo assembler for single molecule sequencing reads using repeat graphs
why: A real genome assembler using repeat graphs for long reads, a genuine science tool you can run at home with sample data.

brief.what_it_is: Flye is a de novo genome assembler for single-molecule long reads from PacBio (CLR, HiFi, corrected) and Oxford Nanopore (regular, HQ, corrected). You give it raw base-called reads in FASTA or FASTQ format, optionally gzipped, and it returns a directory containing assembly.fasta (contigs, plus scaffolds if enabled), assembly_graph.gfa or .gv (the final repeat graph), and assembly_info.txt (per-contig length, coverage, circularity, repeat status and graph path). The README describes it as a complete pipeline that takes raw reads and outputs polished contigs, with a special metagenome mode (--meta). It is a command-line tool written in C++ with a Python driver.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as an assembler for long, error-prone single-molecule reads that works from small bacterial projects up to mammalian-scale genomes. Its core idea is that repeat graphs, built from approximate sequence matches, tolerate the higher noise of these reads better than de Bruijn graphs, which need exact k-mer matches.
brief.how_it_works: Flye counts k-mers and keeps only the solid ones, then extends contigs by chaining overlapping reads and aligns reads back to these draft contigs with minimap2 to call a consensus. It builds a repeat graph from those contigs, collapses repeats longer than the minimum overlap, and resolves them using read information and graph structure; unbranching paths become the output contigs. A final polishing stage realigns all reads and applies a maximum-likelihood correction to each alignment bubble.

brief.install_notes: Install with conda install flye (Bioconda), or fetch a release from GitHub. Building from source needs Python 2.7 or 3.5+ with setuptools, a C++ compiler with C++11 support, GNU make, git, and core OS development headers such as zlib. The README says Python 2 was dropped in 2.9.5. Platforms are Linux and macOS. No accounts, GPUs or special hardware are needed. If the ARM build fails, the INSTALL doc points to an issue about modifying minimap2 compile parameters. No configuration or first-run setup is described beyond the optional test script. The sample E. coli datasets are downloaded from Zenodo, and a bacterial run is practical on a laptop-class machine; the benchmark table lists about 2 GB RAM and 2 CPU hours for E. coli at 50x PacBio. Human-scale runs need hundreds of GB of RAM and thousands of CPU hours.
brief.standout: It uses a repeat graph rather than a de Bruijn graph, so it works directly on noisy raw reads without prior error correction, and it reports each unique graph edge as a contig. The Zenodo sample datasets and the README's benchmark table make it easy to run a real bacterial assembly at home. The repo is also a Pevzner-lab project with peer-reviewed papers behind it (Nature Biotechnology 2019 and Nature Methods 2020 for metaFlye).
brief.status: Maintained, judging from the README. The latest listed release is 2.9.6 on 2 May 2025, and the README has a dated changelog going back to 2021. I could not see commit history or issue activity from the pages I fetched.
brief.caveats: Flye produces collapsed haploid assemblies of diploid genomes, which is stated as a current limitation; the README points to HapDup for phased haplotypes and strainy for heterozygous bacteria or metagenomes. Mixing read types in one run is not supported. The --subassemblies and --trestle modes are deprecated and slated for removal. The --plasmids option is unused and kept only for backward compatibility. Flye is designed mainly for uncorrected reads, and CLR input is assumed to be properly split subreads, so badly converted FASTQ may need pbclip. Only Linux and macOS are supported. The scout note's claim that this runs at home on sample data holds for bacterial-scale genomes; large genomes need large RAM and long runs. The README was not checked for licence beyond the BSD line.

name: foremost
desc: Console program to recover files based on their headers and footers
why: Carves files out of raw disk images by header and footer signatures, a clear window into how file formats are recognised.

brief.what_it_is: Foremost is a console program that recovers files from raw data by looking for their headers, footers, and internal data structures, a technique called data carving. It takes image files made by tools such as dd, Safeback, or EnCase, or it can read a drive directly. Header and footer signatures can come from a configuration file, or you can pick built-in file types on the command line. The output is the recovered files.
brief.why_it_exists: Foremost is a data carving tool for recovering files when the filesystem metadata is gone or unusable. The homepage says it was originally developed by the United States Air Force Office of Special Investigations and The Center for Information Systems Security Studies and Research, and was later opened to the general public.
brief.how_it_works: Foremost scans the raw bytes of an image or device for known header signatures and footer signatures, then cuts out the data between them. Built-in types go further and parse each format's internal data structures, which the homepage says makes recovery more reliable and faster than simple signature matching.
brief.standout: Built-in file types parse the format's internal structures rather than relying only on byte signatures, which the homepage presents as the reason for better reliability and speed. The same engine also accepts user-defined header and footer rules from a configuration file.

name: form
desc: Symbolic manipulation system
why: A symbolic manipulation system from high-energy physics that few developers have ever touched, with a fascinating old-school heritage.

brief.what_it_is: FORM is a symbolic manipulation system. It reads symbolic expressions from program files and applies algebraic transformations to them, such as pattern-matching rewrites on symbols and functions. The answers come back as text in a mathematical notation. Its README stresses that expression size is limited by disk space rather than RAM.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents FORM as a tool that has been essential for many state-of-the-art High Energy Physics computations. Its original author is Jos Vermaseren of NIKHEF, the Dutch institute for subatomic physics.
brief.how_it_works: You write a FORM program in a text file with declarations such as Symbol and CFunction, then a Local expression and rewrite statements such as id ... = ..., and end with Print and .end. The README's examples show a repeat loop that rewrites x^10 into 34 + 55*x, and a pattern that reorders the arguments of f(1,2,x,3,4) to give f(3,4,1,2). The README does not describe the internal mechanism beyond the disk-backed expression size.

name: fluid-synth
desc: Real-time software synthesizer based on the SoundFont 2 specs
why: A real-time SoundFont synthesizer that can be driven from MIDI or the terminal, a good instrument to poke at, though fairly well known.

brief.what_it_is: FluidSynth is a real-time software synthesizer based on the SoundFont 2 specification. It generates audio from MIDI events, read from MIDI input devices, using a SoundFont as its instrument bank, so it works as the software equivalent of a hardware MIDI synth. It can also play MIDI files. It has no graphical interface of its own. It ships a built-in command line shell and a shared library that other programs can embed.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that FluidSynth came out of an online multi-user game project that wanted SoundFont-based music: wavetable synthesis is cheap on CPU, and small MIDI files plus SoundFonts are easier to download than audio. Since sound had to work on Linux, macOS and Windows with any sound card, the team needed a software SoundFont synthesizer.
brief.how_it_works: The README says it reads and handles MIDI events from MIDI input devices and renders them to audio using a SoundFont. Its design goal was to stay self-contained, with no platform-specific libraries and no external dependencies, so it could be embedded as a plugin, loaded dynamically, or wrapped in language bindings and game frameworks. The homepage adds real-time effect control through SoundFont 2.04 modulators and support for SoundFont 3 (Vorbis-compressed SF2), DLS Level 1 and 2, and playback of MIDI files.
brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the README points to the wiki page BuildingWithCMake for building from source, which implies CMake. I did not open the wiki, so I cannot confirm the build steps or dependencies. The README and homepage mention no accounts, hardware, or first-run configuration. The shell and the MIDI input setup are described only at a high level.
brief.standout: It is a self-contained SoundFont 2 synthesizer that is meant to be embedded as much as used. The homepage notes that several GUI frontends and music programs (QSynth, wxFluid, LMMS, MusE, Denemo and others) are built on its API, while FluidSynth itself has no GUI.

name: fplll
desc: Lattice algorithms using floating-point arithmetic
why: Lattice reduction algorithms are a real mathematical door, though the tool is mostly a library for specialists.

brief.what_it_is: fplll is a C++ library, with two command-line programs, for lattice reduction. You give it a lattice basis as a matrix of integer row vectors, typically on stdin or as a file, and it outputs a reduced basis. It can also run LLL, BKZ, HKZ, slide, self-dual BKZ and HLLL reduction, and solve shortest-vector (SVP) and closest-vector (CVP) problems. The companion program latticegen prints random test matrices of several kinds (knapsack, NTRU-like, q-ary, and others) for fplll to consume.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the library is named for LLL, the Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász algorithm, which is central to the code, and that it implements floating-point LLL variants 'offering different speed/guarantees ratios'. The aim is a practical, fast set of lattice reduction algorithms with the guarantees stated.
brief.how_it_works: Reduction works on floating-point orthogonalization (Gram-Schmidt data), with several floating-point types available: double, long double, dd, qd, dpe and MPFR. A 'wrapper' picks an estimated best sequence of LLL variants to give a guaranteed output as fast as possible, and the user does not have to choose. BKZ includes the BKZ-2.0 improvements (extreme enumeration pruning, block preprocessing, early termination). SVP uses Kannan-Fincke-Pohst enumeration.

name: fpart
desc: Sorts file trees and packs them into bags
why: Packs file trees into equal-sized bags using bin-packing, a neat algorithmic trick for splitting backups onto media.

brief.what_it_is: Fpart is a UNIX command-line tool that crawls directories and file trees and splits them into a set number of partitions, aiming for similar sizes and file counts. It takes paths (or piped input such as find or du output) and writes partitions as file lists to stdout or to numbered output files, which other programs can consume. It never copies, splits, or modifies the data itself. It is written in C under a BSD license. A companion tool, fpsync, uses fpart's lists to run rsync, cpio, or tar jobs in parallel; the README says fpsync is provided in the tools/ directory as a demonstration.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames fpart as a way to sort file trees and pack them into bags called partitions, so large trees can be handled in pieces. The changelog credits Jean-Baptiste Denis with suggesting the idea.
brief.how_it_works: Fpart uses a bin-packing algorithm to spread files or directories across partitions, with options for a number of partitions, a file count per partition, or a size limit per partition. In live mode (-L) it emits each partition as soon as it is complete, and hooks (-w before, -W after) run a shell command with variables such as FPART_PARTFILENAME, so a transfer can start while the crawl is still running. The README is explicit that fpart only reads the filesystem and never splits files, so a directory with one huge file cannot be balanced.

name: fragroute
desc: Intercepts, modifies and rewrites egress traffic for a specified host
why: Rewrites and fragments outgoing packets, a hands-on door into how IDS evasion and TCP fragmentation actually work.

brief.what_it_is: fragroute is a command-line tool that intercepts outbound (egress) traffic destined for a specified host and rewrites it according to a small ruleset language. The ruleset can delay, duplicate, drop, fragment, overlap, print, reorder, segment, source-route, or otherwise alter each outgoing packet, with minimal support for randomized or probabilistic behaviour. The page names libdnet, libpcap, and libevent as required libraries. It implements most of the attacks described in the 1998 Secure Networks paper "Insertion, Evasion, and Denial of Service: Eluding Network Intrusion Detection."
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it to help test network intrusion detection systems, firewalls, and basic TCP/IP stack behaviour. The page says it was "written in good faith to aid in the testing of network intrusion detection systems, firewalls, and basic TCP/IP stack behaviour."
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals. It says the tool intercepts and modifies egress packets bound for one target host, and that the behaviour is driven by a ruleset file. The homepage does not describe the ruleset syntax, so the fragroute(8) manpage would be needed for details.
brief.install_notes: The page lists the download as fragroute-1.2.tar.gz, so it is built from source rather than installed from a package. Required libraries are libdnet, libpcap, and libevent (libevent is needed on non-Windows platforms only). Supported platforms are BSD (OpenBSD, FreeBSD, NetBSD, BSD/OS, Mac OS X), Linux, Solaris, and Windows 2000. On Solaris, a TUN/TAP driver is listed for sparc64 and x86. On Windows 2000, the page says the CIPE-Win32 driver is required for fragroute, and WinPcap is required for fragtest. An OpenBSD earlier than 3.1 needs a loopback MTU patch. Build steps are in an INSTALL document the page links to, which I did not fetch.
brief.standout: It is a hands-on way to see how IP fragmentation, TCP segmentation, overlapping fragments, and reordering can evade IDS reassembly. Because it rewrites real outbound packets rather than simulating them, it can test how a target device handles them. The author also lists ideas such as simulating one-way latency, loss, and retransmissions, and evading passive OS fingerprinting.
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage shows the current version as 1.2 but gives no release date, last commit, or changelog. The references to 1998 and Windows 2000 suggest the project is old, and the page reads as a long-stable personal distribution page rather than an active project. I did not check a source repository for recent activity.
brief.caveats: The author's note says "Please do not abuse this software." The page gives no license. The platform list is dated and includes components such as CIPE-Win32, WinPcap, and the Solaris TUN/TAP driver, so a modern system may need substitutes or patches. The homepage mentions a TCP Daytona implementation that the author will not release. brief.what_it_is: freeDiameter is an open source C implementation of the Diameter protocol, which carries Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) payloads. The README splits it into parts: libfdproto, a shared library for parsing and manipulating Diameter messages and dictionaries; libfdcore, a shared library holding the framework core (peer connections, watchdogs, basic routing, extension loading); freeDiameterd, a small daemon that parses the command line and starts the framework; and extensions that add server applications, advanced routing, or peer management. The README does not spell out a full input/output contract, but in use it takes Diameter peer traffic and a configuration file, and it acts as a server or agent node.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Diameter as the successor to RADIUS for AAA traffic and says it is an extensible protocol, with a base protocol (RFC 3588) that every node must support plus application documents such as NAS (RFC 4005) and EAP (RFC 4072). freeDiameter provides a working implementation of that stack.
brief.how_it_works: Applications link libfdcore or run freeDiameterd, which initializes the framework, opens network connections to other Diameter peers, and runs the Base Protocol duties such as watchdogs and routing. Features beyond that base come from extensions that libfdcore loads at startup. The README says that clients which must become Diameter-aware should link libfdcore directly rather than run the daemon.

name: frege
desc: Non-strict, functional programming language in the spirit of Haskell
why: A Haskell-inspired language running on the JVM; uncommon and worth a curious afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: Frege is a purely functional, non-strict (lazy) programming language described by its author as a Haskell for the JVM. It compiles Frege source to Java (the README says it produces a .class and a .java file per module) and runs on the Java Virtual Machine. Frege code can call any Java library, and Java code can call Frege functions. The compiler is the fregec executable. The README says most vanilla Haskell code runs unmodified or with minor changes, and that the standard library supports almost all of Haskell 2010.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents Frege as a way for Java programmers to learn a pure functional paradigm and for Haskell programmers to use their skills on the JVM, while keeping access to Java's libraries. It says Frege keeps Haskell's guarantees, such as purity, thread safety and lazy evaluation, even when it calls Java code.
brief.how_it_works: Functions are checked by a strong static type system with global type inference, so purity is carried in the types. Pure functions are described as stateless and safe to cache automatically, and the README suggests the compiler could use this for optimizations such as precalculation, deferred execution and common subexpression elimination. Main is typed IO (), and the type system requires any caller of an IO function to also be IO, so impurity propagates up the call chain. Calling Java from Frege requires declaring the Java types in Frege terms.
brief.install_notes: The README requires at least JDK 7 to compile and run programs. The compiler, an Eclipse plugin and provisional documentation are downloaded from the GitHub releases page. Getting started at the command line is covered on the project wiki's Getting Started page, which I did not fetch. Build tool support is listed for Maven, Gradle, Leiningen, SBT and Bazel. Editor support includes the Eclipse plugin, a VS Code plugin and an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that is still under development. The README also points to an online REPL at try.fregelang.org, so you can try it without installing anything.
brief.standout: Purity is encoded in the type system, and the README uses a Hello World with a pure greeting function and an IO main to show the idea of islands of purity in a sea of imperative code. Most of the compiler, standard library, REPL and documentation tool are written in Frege itself, which the README offers as evidence of stability.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release version or date, and I did not check the releases or commit history. The copyright line says 2011-2022. The README also links a Travis CI badge at travis-ci.org and a Freenode IRC channel, both of which may be out of date. The project appears to have been active through about 2022 and to be quiet since, but I could not confirm this from the page.
brief.caveats: The README says the documentation is provisional. Some Haskell differences remain, listed on a wiki page I did not fetch. The Hoogle instance for Frege is disabled due to domain issues. The IntelliJ plugin is still under development. The README says Frege requires JDK 7 or later. Code that uses JVM-specific features will not run on other Haskell compilers.

name: fst

brief.what_it_is: A Rust crate (library, not a standalone program) that provides ordered sets and maps built on finite state transducers. You feed it keys, typically already sorted, and it builds a compact automaton that stores them and can be searched directly. Lookups, prefix and range queries, and fuzzy queries run against that automaton, and large structures can be memory-mapped. The brew formula lists an `fst` executable, but the README describes only the library API and shows no command-line tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to index very large key collections compactly while keeping them easy to search, citing the author's blog post on indexing 1.6 billion keys with automata and Rust.
brief.how_it_works: Keys are stored as paths through a finite state machine, and values are emitted as output along those transitions, so the machine maps keys to values as it runs. Sharing common prefixes and suffixes is what keeps the storage compact. Searches are made by running an automaton, such as a Levenshtein automaton for fuzzy matching, over the transducer, and memory maps make range queries fast.
brief.install_notes: Not a brew-installed tool in any meaningful sense: the README's installation is adding `fst = "0.4"` to a Cargo.toml under [dependencies], so it needs a Rust toolchain and Cargo. The fuzzy Levenshtein automaton requires enabling the `levenshtein` cargo feature, which is disabled by default and adds a utf8-ranges dependency. The optional `transducer` feature integrates with regex-automata DFAs.
brief.standout: Sorted keys become a compact, searchable automaton rather than a hash or tree of strings, so the same structure answers exact lookup, range queries, and typo-tolerant fuzzy searches. The README's example queries a set of short words for everything within one edit of "foo".

name: fwknop
desc: Single Packet Authorization and Port Knocking
why: Single Packet Authorization hides services behind an encrypted packet knock, a fascinating and under-known take on port knocking.

brief.what_it_is: fwknop (FireWall KNock OPerator) is a Linux, BSD and macOS tool that implements Single Packet Authorization (SPA), a stronger successor to port knocking. It keeps a firewall in a default-drop stance so the protected service, typically SSH, shows no open port. A client sends one encrypted, HMAC-authenticated packet describing the access it wants, and the fwknopd server passively sniffs that packet with libpcap. If the packet decrypts, verifies and is not a replay, the server temporarily opens the firewall for that client. The project ships a client binary, fwknop, and a server daemon, fwknopd.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames SPA as next-generation port knocking that fixes its known weaknesses: replay attacks, the difficulty of using asymmetric ciphers or HMACs, and DoS by spoofing an extra packet into a knock sequence. The stated goal is that exploitable services like SSHD cannot even be seen by nmap, so attackers cannot run password crackers or 0-day exploits against them.
brief.how_it_works: The client encrypts the SPA payload with Rijndael (key derived via PBKDF1, CBC mode) or with GnuPG, then appends an HMAC in an encrypt-then-authenticate arrangement. The server checks the HMAC before decrypting, and rejects replays by SHA-256 digest comparison. For iptables, ACCEPT rules go into custom chains and are removed after a configurable timeout. The README also covers NAT (DNAT/SNAT) and port randomization.

brief.standout: SPA sends one encrypted packet and the server listens passively with libpcap, so there is no listening port to connect to and nothing to scan. The HMAC is applied after encryption, and the server verifies it before any decryption or GnuPG code runs, to reduce padding-oracle-style exposure.

name: futhark
desc: Data-parallel functional programming language
why: A data-parallel functional language compiling to GPU code, an unusual language with real depth and little mainstream awareness.

brief.what_it_is: Futhark is a small, statically typed, purely functional array language in the ML family, built for data-parallel code. You write array functions in Futhark, and its ahead-of-time optimising compiler turns them into GPU code (via CUDA, HIP, or OpenCL) or multi-threaded CPU code. The homepage's example is a one-line average over an array of 64-bit floats: def average (xs: []f64) = reduce (+) 0 xs / f64.i64 (length xs). The compiler output can be a Python module that drives PyOpenCL, or plain C that any language with a basic FFI can call. It is developed at DIKU, the University of Copenhagen.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as "nicer than writing CUDA or OpenCL by hand". The stated intent is to use it only for small, compute-intensive parts of a larger application, not to replace general-purpose languages.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler is described as heavily optimising and ahead-of-time, emitting CUDA, HIP, OpenCL, or multi-threaded CPU code, or C and Python modules. The language supports nested data-parallelism and automatic differentiation, and offers imperative-style in-place array updates while keeping purity through alias analysis and consumption effects.

name: fwup
desc: Configurable embedded Linux firmware update creator and runner
why: Builds and applies embedded Linux firmware images, a glimpse into how devices get their updates.

brief.what_it_is: fwup is a command-line utility for embedded Linux devices that applies whole-image software updates. You feed it a configuration file (fwup.conf) that describes partitions, filesystems, and update tasks, and it packs the resources into a .fw file, which is a ZIP archive that can optionally be cryptographically signed. On the device or host side, fwup takes a .fw file and writes it to a memory card or device, or to an image file, and can verify archives and signatures. The README also describes a helper script, img2fwup, that converts a raw image file into a .fw file.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames fwup as an update tool for systems that replace entire root filesystem images, such as A/B partition swaps, recovery partitions, and trial-update/failback schemes. It says distribution of update archives is deliberately not a feature: users call fwup from external media, the network, or a tool like Ansible. The author also says the goal is to make updates fast enough for development and reliable enough for production, and that it aims to beat dd(1) on write speed and reliability.
brief.how_it_works: A configuration file defines file-resources, mbr or gpt partition tables, and task blocks with event handlers (on-init, on-resource, on-finish, on-error) and actions such as fat_write, raw_write, and uboot_setenv. fwup embeds a processed copy of that config and each resource's BLAKE2b-256 hash into the archive, then streams through the archive in one pass when applying, checking writes as it goes. The README says scripts are kept intentionally limited so that failure cases are easier to reason about, and it recommends the A/B 'write to unused slot, then flip at the end' pattern.

On Linux, prebuilt .deb (AMD64, ARM64, Raspbian armhf) and RPM packages are on the GitHub releases page, and Alpine, Arch (AUR fwup-git), Buildroot, and Yocto (meta-fwup) are also listed. On Windows, use chocolatey (choco install fwup) or download fwup.exe and put it on your PATH. Building from source is documented per platform (Linux, OSX, Windows, Raspbian, BSD) and needs the regression tests run. Using the tool on real devices or SD cards requires sudo on Linux (no sudo on OSX/Windows). The README also points to asdf-fwup for version pinning with asdf or mise. No account or hardware is needed to build or run archives; the target device only needs a matching layout.
brief.standout: Unlike a general-purpose flasher, fwup is built around the archive: one ZIP can hold several tasks, the first matching task is applied based on conditions read from the target (file exists, partition offset, U-Boot variable, path on device), and tasks can be signed and verified. It also has delta updates via VCDIFF and xdelta3 (still labelled BETA), and it ships a config language with scoped blocks and include() fragments.
