name: fwupd
desc: Firmware update daemon
why: A door into the firmware update path of real devices, with LVFS metadata and vendor blobs worth inspecting.

brief.what_it_is: fwupd is a Linux firmware update daemon, with fwupdmgr as its command-line client. It detects devices that have firmware fwupd supports, downloads update metadata from the Linux Vendor Firmware Service (LVFS) by default, and applies firmware updates to those devices. Updates that can be applied live happen immediately, and others are staged to run at the next boot. The README also mentions optionally reporting update success or failure back to LVFS. The README does not mention the brew executables dbxtool or fwupdtool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the project aims "to make updating firmware on Linux automatic, safe, and reliable." It is meant to give Linux users a single path for vendor firmware updates, backed by LVFS as the source of firmware.
brief.how_it_works: The daemon is configured by default to download firmware metadata and capsules from LVFS, and fwupdmgr refresh pulls the latest metadata. Enterprises can restrict updates with an approved-updates list: ApprovalRequired=true in the remote config, plus ApprovedFirmware in fwupd.conf, which holds container checksums. If Passim is installed and enabled, fwupd republishes downloaded metadata on 0.0.0.0:27500 so other clients on the LAN can fetch it via mDNS/LLMNR; P2pPolicy=none in /etc/fwupd/daemon.conf turns this off.

name: gammaray
desc: Examine and manipulate Qt application internals at runtime
why: Inspecting and modifying a running Qt application's internals is a real window into live program structure, though it is a dev tool.

brief.what_it_is: GammaRay is an introspection tool for running Qt applications, written by KDAB and released under GPL-2.0-or-later. It uses Qt's QObject introspection mechanism to let you browse the object tree, view and edit properties, invoke slots, and watch signal/slot connections while the program runs. It works on a local workstation or remotely on an embedded target, and you can attach it to an application that is already running. Its output is an interactive view of the application's internals, including specialised views for Qt Quick scene graphs, model/view proxy chains, state machines, and QGraphicsView scenes.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it augments the instruction-level debugger so developers can work 'at a much higher level, with the same concepts as the frameworks you use', which matters most for complex Qt frameworks such as model/view, state machines and scene graphs. The homepage adds that a debugger does not understand these internal structures, while GammaRay can present them in a meaningful way.
brief.how_it_works: GammaRay exploits Qt's QObject introspection mechanism, so it runs alongside the target application rather than replacing the debugger. The README and INSTALL.md say it relies on Qt private headers, and on Android a probe is built into the app and reached over a forwarded socket on port 11732 by a GammaRay GUI.

name: garble
desc: Obfuscate Go builds
why: Obfuscates Go binaries, a useful window into how compiled programs can be hidden and what makes them hard to read.

brief.what_it_is: Garble is a command-line tool that obfuscates Go builds by wrapping the Go toolchain. You run it in place of go build, and it takes your Go source packages (including the standard runtime) and produces a binary that behaves like a normal build but reveals much less about the original source. It also provides garble test to run tests on obfuscated code, garble run to obfuscate and execute a simple program, garble reverse to de-obfuscate text such as panic stack traces, and garble bug to file a pre-filled bug report. The README says it requires Go 1.27 or later.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's stated goal is to produce a binary that works as well as a regular build but has as little information about the original source code as possible. It targets cases where Go binaries are shared with end users and the source is private or paid for, and it also covers sharing obfuscated source for private Go libraries, since Go plugins have shortcomings, and reducing binary size (the -tiny flag claims about 15% smaller).
brief.how_it_works: Garble wraps calls to the Go compiler and linker. It replaces identifiers and package paths with short base64 hashes, replaces position information with short base64 hashed filenames, and strips build, module, and debug information. With the -literals flag it also rewrites literal expressions such as strings into more complex expressions that resolve to the same value at run time, and obfuscates //go:embed files, which are decoded at run time. Builds are deterministic per package, keyed on garble version, Go version, source, and build parameters, which is what makes garble reverse work on stack traces.

brief.install_notes: Installed with go install mvdan.cc/garble@latest (or @master). Requires Go 1.27 or later. garble build uses whichever go is first on $PATH; to use a different Go version the README points to GOTOOLCHAIN. Garble uses its own cache, defaulting to a directory under the user cache dir such as ~/.cache/garble, which can be moved with the GARBLE_CACHE environment variable. Garble also requires git on the machine to patch the linker. No accounts or hardware are mentioned.
brief.standout: Garble is built to stay coupled to cmd/go and the build cache, obfuscating one package at a time so incremental builds only redo changed code, and it stays reversible: given the same seed and inputs, garble reverse can map obfuscated panic stack traces back to original names. The -tiny flag removes panic and fatal error printing from the runtime entirely, trading debuggability for size.
brief.status: unknown for release and commit dates, since the fetched README carries no dates. Signals of active upkeep in the text: it targets Go 1.27, it cites issues up to #984, it has a CI badge, and it invites new contributors. I would call it actively maintained by inference, not by a dated record.
brief.caveats: Exported methods are never obfuscated, because interfaces may need them. There is no supported way to exclude specific files or packages from obfuscation. Go plugins are unsupported. Obfuscation is not encryption: with -literals the executable contains the decoding key, and embedded filenames stay visible. Constant-expression literals cannot be obfuscated. Literal obfuscation can slow programs down. With -literals, -ldflags values must be unpatterned. -tiny means panics print no stack trace and the program simply exits, which makes crashes harder to debug and makes reverse mostly useless. APIs such as runtime.GOROOT and runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo do not work in obfuscated binaries, which can affect timezone loading. Initialization order can change because import paths are obfuscated. The README says garble build takes about twice as long as go build. The first build is slow because every package is obfuscated once. The runtime/cgo and crypto/internal/fips140 packages are excluded. Custom -seed values must be kept, because losing one makes garble reverse stop working.
quotes: Produce a binary that works as well as a regular build, but that has as little information about the original source code as possible.
This is obfuscation, not encryption: the executable contains the decoding key, so its contents can still be recovered.

name: gcl
desc: GNU Common Lisp
why: GNU Common Lisp is an old-school Lisp environment, a worthwhile visit to a classic language implementation.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Common Lisp (GCL) is a free implementation of Common Lisp, the official Common Lisp of the GNU project. It takes Lisp source or code typed at its REPL and produces native object code by using the system's C compiler. It can also save custom Lisp images. The homepage describes it as 'An implementation of Common Lisp' and gives 2.7.1 as the latest stable release.
brief.why_it_exists: The page presents GCL as the GNU project's Common Lisp, built to support free software Lisp applications such as Maxima, ACL2 and Axiom. Its history section says it began as AKCL and was released as GCL in 1994, mainly to support the Maxima computer algebra system.
brief.how_it_works: GCL uses the system C compiler to compile Lisp to native object code, which the README credits for good performance and easy portability. On most platforms it can load native object code modules directly into its Lisp core, and those modules persist in custom images made with save-system. The README also describes a stratified garbage collector (SGC) that uses native page fault handling for recent allocations.

The homepage also says a function call costs about the same as a C function call through a pointer, and it has a source-level debugger (dbl) for interpreted code that works with an Emacs window.

name: gecode

brief.what_it_is: Gecode is an open source C++ toolkit for building constraint-based systems and applications, with a constraint solver at its core. You state variables and constraints over integers, Booleans, sets, and floats, and its search engines look for assignments that satisfy them. It also provides a C++ modeling layer, and the brew formula ships fzn-gecode and mzn-gecode, which indicates MiniZinc and FlatZinc front ends. The homepage says it supports MiniZinc, but I did not see the executables described in either page I fetched.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches Gecode as open, efficient, and modular: a solver with state-of-the-art performance that can be extended with new constraints, branching strategies, search engines, and variable domains.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage lists advanced branching heuristics (accumulated failure count, activity), several search engines (parallel, interactive graphical, restarts), automatic symmetry breaking (LDSB), and no-goods from restarts. Parallel search uses multiple cores. The README also points to a worker-control guide for asynchronous control of parallel-search worker allocation.

name: gemmi
desc: Macromolecular crystallography library and utilities
why: Macromolecular crystallography tools let you read real protein structure files, a close call on whether utilities go far enough.

brief.what_it_is: GEMMI is a C++ library for macromolecular crystallography, shipped with a command-line program also named gemmi that bundles many small subcommands. It reads and writes coordinate files (PDB, mmCIF, mmJSON), CIF/STAR files, reflection data (MTZ and SF-mmCIF, plus XDS_ASCII), CCP4/MRC density maps, and restraint or monomer-library CIF files. Output is usually a converted or modified file, a text report, or a histogram in the terminal. The project also has Python bindings, partial WebAssembly bindings, and an online viewer and stats pages.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says GEMMI can help if you work with macromolecular models, refinement restraints, crystallographic reflections, density maps, crystallographic symmetries, or just CIF/STAR files, where the C in CIF stands for Crystallographic. It is an open-source project of CCP4 and Global Phasing Ltd, which the README describes as two major providers of software for macromolecular crystallography.
brief.how_it_works: The command-line program is a set of small subcommands (for example validate, grep, convert, set, mtz, map, sfcalc), each run as gemmi followed by the subcommand name. The grep subcommand parses CIF syntax rather than doing plain text matching, so it prints values from both name-value pairs and loops. The docs say the whole compressed PDB mmCIF archive can be searched in roughly 10 to 30 minutes on an average computer, and that output pipes into standard Unix tools such as sort, awk, and uniq.

name: geogram

brief.what_it_is: Geogram is a C++ programming library of geometric algorithms, aimed at developers building geometry tools. The brew formula also installs a set of executables: geobox, geocod, geodump, geoshade, vorpalite, vorpaview, and several geogram_demo_* programs. brief.how_it_works: The library is organised as a set of C++ modules: low-level exact predicates and Delaunay/Voronoi code, mesh and geometric-search data structures, and higher-level processing algorithms built on them. desc: Opinionated dialect of Scheme designed for Systems Programming
why: A Scheme dialect built on Gambit with systems-programming leanings, offering an unusual take on Lisp for low-level work.

brief.what_it_is: Gerbil Scheme is a Scheme dialect built on the Gambit runtime and compiler, with its own macro system, module system, and standard library. It is aimed at systems programming. You write Gerbil source files or type expressions into an interactive interpreter (gxi), and the compiler (gxc) produces native code. The distribution also ships tools such as gxpkg for packages, gxtest for tests, gxprof for profiling, gxtags for tags, and gxhttpd, an HTTP server.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls Gerbil an opinionated, some might even say tendentious, dialect of Scheme for systems programming, and says one way to think of it is as the C++ to Marc Feeley's C. The author says it began as his private Scheme and was released publicly at the prompting of friends, with a self-hosting source bootstrap on Gambit.
brief.how_it_works: The macro system is based on quote-syntax and provides a full meta-syntactic tower with a native syntax-case implementation. The module system resembles PLT/Racket modules, but per the README Gerbil modules are single-instantiation, which supports high-performance ahead-of-time compilation and compiled macros. The README says the system is entirely self-hosted, bootstrapping from source on Gambit with a precompiled macro system and compiler.

name: gforth
desc: Implementation of the ANS Forth language
why: A standards-following Forth with a stack-based mindset that rewires how you think about programs.

brief.what_it_is: Gforth is the GNU Project's implementation of the Forth language, a stack-based programming language. You run it as an interactive interpreter or batch-process Forth source files, and it compiles code to a fast direct or indirect threaded form using GCC. The homepage describes it as fully ANS/Forth 2012 compliant, with a large set of built-in words and libraries such as an object-oriented package written in plain ANS Forth. Input is Forth source or keystrokes at the prompt, and output is text on the terminal, files, or the program's own results.
brief.why_it_exists: The Gforth project's stated goal is to develop a standard model for ANSI Forth: to conform to the standard, to model its implementation-dependent parts, and to become widely accepted. The project also wants to be similar to earlier systems like fig-Forth and F83, powerful, efficient, free, and easy to port.
brief.how_it_works: The gforth binary is built on a virtual-machine generator called Vmgen, with primitives written in a small specification language and compiled through GCC into direct or indirect threaded code. Release notes describe two engines: gforth-fast, which is quicker, and gforth, the debugging engine that gives precise backtraces for signals such as illegal memory access but runs roughly 1 to 2 times slower. Dynamic and static superinstructions are used to speed up common sequences.

The 0.7.0 release notes say the runtime needs libtool and gcc (for the libcc C interface), and gdb for the SEE disassembler on some platforms. Debian and Ubuntu users can use a third-party net2o apt repo, and Docker or podman images exist. The homepage lists Windows, MacOS, and GNU/Linux as supported, plus the Gforth EC embedded variants for R8C, 4stack, MISC, and 8086.
brief.standout: Forth is a stack-based language with no conventional syntax, and Gforth is a full ANS-standard implementation with two execution engines, a debugger-friendly build, and a generator-based VM. Its embedded-control variants run on very small controllers such as 8086, R8C, and 4stack, which is unusual for a GNU project. The OO package being written in plain ANS Forth is also notable.

name: geph4
desc: Modular Internet censorship circumvention system to deal with national filtering
why: A censorship circumvention system is a fascinating door into how national filtering and tunnelling work, though this is the older version.

brief.what_it_is: geph4-client is the command-line client for Geph, a circumvention tool built to get past national internet filtering. You give it an exit server name plus credentials (the README example uses username and password, with auth-password), and it opens a tunnel to a Geph exit server, relaying through bridge servers when the exit is blocked. What comes out is local SOCKS5 and HTTP proxies on 127.0.0.1 (ports 9909 and 9910 by default), and optionally a system-wide VPN through a TUN device on Linux or WinDivert on Windows. It also has sync, binder_proxy and debugpack subcommands, mostly used by the GUI or for exporting debug logs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes Geph as a modular Internet censorship circumvention system designed specifically to deal with national filtering. The homepage frames it as a VPN built from the ground up to resist ISP-level censorship, rather than one that plays cat-and-mouse with censors.
brief.how_it_works: connect builds a ClientTunnel that keeps a sosistab2 Multiplex session alive over several routes, some through bridges and some direct, and switches to the best working route; in China only bridge routes are used because all exits are blocked. Local proxies forward requests into that tunnel, and VPN mode sends packets over the same unreliable datagram connection. sync fetches subscription and exit information through domain fronting and checks the exit list against a public record on the Mel blockchain.

commands_seen.context: Installs the client from crates.io; the README says to install Rust first.
Lists the available subcommands and flags.
Typical connect invocation, using a public example account and a named exit server.

commands_seen.context: Starts connect in VPN mode on Linux, which needs root; the $(which ...) lets root find the binary.
Exports Geph's debug logs as an SQLite database to the given directory.

brief.install_notes: Install the Rust toolchain first (the README links rust-lang.org/tools/install), then run cargo install geph4-client. Running in VPN mode needs root or sudo. On Linux, tun-route uses iptables to route traffic into a TUN device. On Windows, --vpn-mode windivert uses WinDivert. The README gives no accounts or configuration steps beyond the credentials passed to connect. The example credentials are public demo accounts.
brief.standout: Instead of one fixed server, the client keeps a multiplex of routes and rotates the bridge servers it uses, so blocked bridges get swapped out. It also checks the exit list against a public blockchain record, so a compromised central binder cannot quietly feed it bad exits.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README has no release date, last-commit date or deprecation notice, and I could not see either from the pages I loaded. The homepage admits the service is still centralized ("Yes, but not for long!") and says decentralization integration with Earendil is in development. name: git-annex
desc: Manage files with git without checking in file contents
why: Tracks large file contents outside git with a distributed, location-aware model; a strange and deep design worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: git-annex is a command-line tool, written in Haskell, that manages large files with git without storing their contents in git. You run git-annex inside a git repository. Each file's content is stored under .git/annex/objects and tracked by a checksum-based key, while git holds only a symlink pointing at that content. It takes existing files and commands such as add, get, drop, move, copy, and sync, and it records which repositories hold which content. Its output is a git repository whose annexed files can be fetched from or sent to other repositories, USB drives, ssh remotes, or cloud storage (special remotes such as S3). The homepage also describes an optional git-annex assistant that acts as a folder synchroniser.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says git-annex lets you 'Bring the power and distributed nature of git to bear on your large files' and is 'designed for git users who love the command line'. Its use cases are archiving many offline drives (Bob) and a nomad who syncs files across a laptop, USB drive, and server (Alice).
brief.how_it_works: git-annex stores file contents in the annex under .git/annex/objects and commits only symlinks to git. Each repository records which other repositories hold each file's content, so commands like get and drop can find or verify copies and report which drives to plug in. The numcopies setting and --auto options let git-annex decide when to fetch or drop content to reach a target number of copies. The homepage describes this location tracking as letting 'every drive know what is on every other drive'.

commands_seen.context: Run inside a new git repository (after git init) to turn it into an annex; the walkthrough also shows git annex init "portable USB drive" to add a description.
Adds the files in the current directory to the annex; the content is checksummed and only a symlink is staged for git.
Fetches the content of annexed files in the current directory from another repository that has them.
Removes local content of an annexed file, but only after verifying another repository still has a copy; the file stays in the work tree as a broken symlink.
Replaces the content symlink with a real copy so the file can be edited; git annex lock reverses it.
Copies content to the named remote and then drops it locally, freeing space.

commands_seen.cmd: git annex initremote mys3 type=S3 chunk=1MiB encryption=shared
commands_seen.context: Creates a special remote (S3 here) with shared encryption; S3 credentials are read from AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY environment variables.
Sets the global default minimum number of copies before content can be dropped.
Fetches content only for files that have fewer than two copies, letting git-annex decide what to get.
Verifies data integrity (checksums for SHA backends) and checks that numcopies is satisfied; bad content is moved to .git/annex/bad/ rather than deleted.

brief.install_notes: The install page lists packages for many systems, including apt-get install git-annex on Debian/Ubuntu, pacman -S git-annex on Arch, and brew install git-annex on macOS (Homebrew). Other entries include FreeBSD (pkg install hs-git-annex), termux on Android, and PyPI (uv tool install git-annex). The Windows section has no command shown. Building from source is possible in Haskell; the install page says 'Experienced users should not find it too hard'. Special remotes such as S3 need their own credentials set in environment variables, and git-annex prompts if they are missing. Ssh remotes need full shell access or the git-annex-shell command on the remote host.

name: ghostscript

brief.what_it_is: Ghostscript is an open-source interpreter for the PostScript language and PDF files, distributed as the command-line program gs and as a library. It takes PostScript, PDF, and (via sibling tools) PCL, XPS, and image files as input and renders them to raster images such as PNG, JPEG, and TIFF, or converts them to PDF, PostScript, text, or other output devices. The homepage describes it as a PostScript interpreter layer plus a graphics library. The GitHub README describes the repository as GhostPDL, the umbrella source tree for the whole family.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames GhostPDL as a unified package of interpreters and a shared graphics library for rendering, converting, and manipulating documents across every major page description language and many image formats. The homepage pitches it at SaaS document pipelines, print production, and PDF compression.
brief.how_it_works: Each interpreter (Ghostscript for PostScript and PDF, GhostPCL, GhostXPS) sits on one shared graphics library and can be built separately or together. When run as GhostPDL, it detects the input language from file signatures and heuristics, with no flag needed for mixed job streams. Output goes through a chosen device, selected with -sDEVICE=, such as png16m for raster or pdfwrite for PDF.

name: git-cinnabar
desc: Git remote helper to interact with mercurial repositories
why: Lets git speak Mercurial remotes by translating between the two object models, a genuinely odd piece of plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: git-cinnabar is a git remote helper that lets git talk to Mercurial repositories. You run git clone with an hg:: URL (a local path, or http, https or ssh) in place of a git:// URL, and then use git as usual. Git-cinnabar translates between git commits and Mercurial changesets, and it keeps metadata that maps between the two. The README says the main focus is mozilla-central and related Mercurial repositories, including Mozilla workflows such as the try server. The executables are git-cinnabar and git-remote-hg.
brief.why_it_exists: The README contrasts it with other git-to-Mercurial helpers: 'Contrary to other such helpers ... it doesn't use a local mercurial clone under the hood.' Its main aim is to make Mozilla's large Mercurial repositories usable from git.
brief.how_it_works: Instead of running a local Mercurial clone, it talks to the Mercurial repository directly and stores git-cinnabar metadata that maps git commit SHA-1s to Mercurial changeset SHA-1s, in both directions. The git commands hg2git and git2hg use that mapping. Mercurial branches and bookmarks can be exposed as git refs in several styles, set with the cinnabar.refs configuration.

The Cargo route needs cargo install --locked git-cinnabar followed by git cinnabar setup. name: global-arrays
desc: Partitioned Global Address Space (PGAS) library for distributed arrays
why: A PGAS distributed array library is an interesting model of global memory, but it is mostly plumbing for HPC.

brief.what_it_is: Global Arrays (GA) is a library for distributed dense arrays that presents them as one global array. Application code, written against its C, Fortran, or GA++ C++ interface, reads and writes array sections with one-sided Get, Put, and Accumulate calls and does atomic read-increment operations, without needing to know which node holds the data. The library bundles the ComEx communication runtime, the MA memory allocator, parallel I/O libraries (DRA, EAF, SF), and TCGMSG/TCGMSG-MPI. The homepage says it supports both blocking and non-blocking primitives.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes GA as a Partitioned Global Address Space programming model that gives shared-memory-like access to distributed arrays. The README frames it as augmenting the message-passing model with that shared-memory-style access.
brief.how_it_works: GA uses ComEx, its communication runtime, to abstract inter-node communication, and ComEx replaced ARMCI starting with GA v5.4. The default ComEx ports use MPI, and most ComEx implementations use on-node shared memory for faster communication within a node. The homepage says GA supports location consistency.
brief.install_notes: Neither the homepage nor the GitHub README I read includes build or install steps, required dependencies, or configuration. The README links to a full manual on readthedocs, which I did not fetch, so build details (MPI, compilers, configure options) remain unverified. The homepage links to release notes and a download page, but I did not see a version number.
brief.standout: Its PGAS model is built on one-sided operations over dense arrays, with an MPI-based communication layer that also uses shared memory inside a node. It has been around long enough to carry its own ARMCI-to-ComEx transition and a bundled set of parallel I/O libraries.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage has a Latest Release section but shows no version or date. name: gluon
desc: Static, type inferred and embeddable language written in Rust
why: A statically typed, embeddable, type-inferred language in Rust is an uncommon design worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: Gluon is a small, statically typed, functional programming language built to be embedded inside Rust applications, with type inference so types are rarely written out. Source programs go in, and the gluon virtual machine evaluates them; a command-line gluon_repl executable can run a file or start an interactive REPL with -i. The homepage shows a short example that imports std.json, derives Serialize and Deserialize on a record type, parses a JSON string, updates the record, and prints it back as pretty JSON. The REPL supports :t for types and :i for information about a name, and it tab-completes identifiers.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames gluon as a language 'designed for application embedding', with the goal of being 'similar to Lua' in that it is meant to be included in another program to extend its functionality. Its stated inspirations are Lua, Haskell and OCaml.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the library is split into a parser, a type checker, and a virtual machine plus compiler, and each part can be used on its own. It uses a Hindley-Milner based type system with some extensions. Values are marshalled to and from Rust with little boilerplate, so Rust functions can be passed straight into gluon, and each executing gluon thread gets its own garbage-collected heap.

name: glulxe

brief.what_it_is: Glulxe is the reference interpreter for Glulx, a portable virtual machine for interactive fiction. It takes a Glulx game file (usually compiled from Inform 6 source, often with a .ulx extension, or packaged in a Blorb .gblorb or .blb) and runs it, using a Glk library for input and output. It is a C program, and the homepage says it must be built against a Glk library. The Glulx VM itself is specified separately, currently at version 3.1.3, and the homepage also lists Quixe (a pure JavaScript Glulx interpreter for browsers) and Lectrote (Quixe packaged as a desktop app) as other ways to run the same games.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents Glulx as a 32-bit successor to the Z-machine. Per the homepage, it uses 32-bit data and addresses so game files can reach four gigabytes, and it has native Glk I/O so games can use any capability Glk provides, which the Z-machine lacks.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes Glulxe as a Glk program that executes Glulx bytecode, with the VM spec defining the opcodes, and it notes that Inform games are compiled to Glulx files by the standard Inform 6 compiler. The page does not explain interpreter internals beyond a note that memory-range checking is on by default since 0.5.0 and that a debugger module exists but is not compiled in by default.
brief.install_notes: The homepage does not give a build command. It says Glulxe is 'a Glk program, it must be built with a Glk library' and points to the Glk home page for that library. Source is offered as a 0.6.1 C tarball and a git repository, and ports are archived on the IF Archive. Brew installs the binary 'glulxe' per the formula metadata, so the Glk library question may be handled by the formula, but I did not verify that. The homepage also says Glulx games are played through the glulxe binary; no account or runtime is required.
brief.standout: Glulx is a 32-bit sibling of the Z-machine that the author treats as a documented, versioned spec with a public test suite of small games exercising each opcode and feature (glulxercise, unicodetest, memheaptest and others). The interpreter, spec, compiler and browser ports all sit on one site, with a 'Local Variable Mess' note on deprecating 8- and 16-bit locals, so the lineage is unusually visible.
brief.status: Quiet, not abandoned. The homepage says 'Last updated October 22, 2023'. Glulxe 0.6.1 is the current version named on the page, and the spec is at 3.1.3. The 'What's New' list is dated only by year (for example April 2020 for the Glk copyright transfer), and the author says he still acts as maintainer. I did not check the git repository or IF Archive dates.

name: gmssl
desc: Toolkit for Chinese national cryptographic standards
why: An open toolkit for Chinese national cryptographic standards like SM2, SM3 and SM4 is a rare window onto a different crypto world.

brief.what_it_is: GmSSL is an open-source cryptography library and command-line toolkit, written in C and built with CMake, that implements the Chinese national commercial cryptography standards: SM2, SM3, SM4, SM9 and ZUC. The README is in Chinese and says it was developed independently at Peking University. It also covers TLCP (GB/T 38636-2020), TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 with the RFC 8998 SM4-GCM-SM3 suite, X.509 certificates, CRLs, CSRs, PEM/PKCS #8 keys, SM2 digital envelopes, and some post-quantum signature schemes. Inputs are data, keys, certificates and protocol traffic; outputs are ciphertexts, digests, signatures, certificates and TLS sessions, through a `gmssl` CLI or a C library (libgmssl). Language bindings are provided as separate sub-projects.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says GmSSL is a domestic commercial cryptography library that gives full coverage of the national (GM/guomi) algorithms, standards and secure communication protocols, and that it is meant to make it easier to build products that must pass Chinese cryptographic product certification. It also supports Chinese cryptographic hardware (SDF PCI-E cards and servers, SKF USB keys).
brief.how_it_works: The library is organised around the national algorithms and protocols, with the TLS stack written as a state machine that supports non-blocking mode. GmSSL 3 can be configured to include only the national algorithms and the TLCP protocol, and it avoids dynamic memory allocation so it can run on bare-metal MCUs and SoCs. Hardware keys are reached through SDF or SKF interfaces, and the SoftSDF sub-project offers a software SDF module for development and testing.

name: gnirehtet
desc: Reverse tethering tool for Android
why: Reverse tethering that routes an Android phone's network through adb, a clever hack on USB networking.

brief.what_it_is: Gnirehtet is a command-line tool that gives an Android phone the internet connection of the computer it is plugged into over USB, a setup the README calls reverse tethering. It takes the phone's traffic, relays it through adb to a relay server on the computer, and sends it out through the computer's network. It needs no root on either the device or the computer, and runs on GNU/Linux, Windows and macOS. It relays TCP and UDP over IPv4 only; IPv6 is not supported. The Android side is a small APK that the tool installs, and the app has no UI of its own.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a way for devices to use the internet connection of the computer they are plugged into, without root access. The name is the word tethering reversed, and the project's own joke is "rev <<< tethering" (in Bash).
brief.how_it_works: The computer runs a relay server (Rust or Java) and sets up an adb reverse tunnel, adb reverse localabstract:gnirehtet tcp:31416, to the phone. A small APK on the phone is started with an adb shell command and forwards the phone's TCP and UDP traffic through that tunnel to the relay, which passes it to the computer's network. The README does not go into further detail about the protocol.

GMT supplements add about 50 more specialized tools, and it supports over 30 map projections. It can also be called from MATLAB/Octave, Julia, Python, C and C++ through wrapper libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames GMT as a free, open source toolbox for Earth, ocean and planetary science that lets researchers process data and produce publication-quality illustrations, automate workflows and make animations. brief.how_it_works: GMT is a set of command-line programs that are chained together in scripts to read data, transform it and draw the result. Since GMT 6 it has also been rebuilt as an API that the language wrappers call.

Separate installers exist for macOS and Windows. The README says it installs on UNIX, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and OpenBSD, and also on Windows, Cygwin and virtual machines. name: gnmic
desc: GNMI CLI client and collector
why: A gNMI client for streaming telemetry from network gear, a door into the OpenConfig protocol routers speak.

brief.what_it_is: gnmic is an open-source gNMI command-line client written in Go, maintained under the OpenConfig project. You point it at a network device's gRPC gNMI endpoint and it can run Capabilities, Get, Set and Subscribe RPCs against that device. It can also run as a collector that takes gNMI telemetry streams from many targets, processes them, and writes them to outputs such as Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, InfluxDB, Kafka, NATS and ClickHouse. The homepage says it is open source under Apache 2.0.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as streaming telemetry that works: start with one command to query or change a device, then grow into a telemetry pipeline. The README describes it as a gNMI CLI client with full support for Capabilities, Get, Set and Subscribe plus collector capabilities.
brief.how_it_works: Each gNMI RPC has its own subcommand (capabilities, get, set, subscribe, with sub as a short form), and the RPC options are set through local and global flags. Targets can be given directly with -a or loaded at runtime from files, Docker, Consul or HTTP sources. In collector mode, updates pass through event processors that filter, enrich, convert and transform them before export. Prompt mode loads YANG modules so flags that take XPATH values get auto-suggestions. Configuration can come from flags, environment variables or a config file.

brief.install_notes: The homepage and README both use the one-line curl installer (bash -c "$(curl -sL https://get-gnmic.openconfig.net)"). The README also says statically linked pre-built binaries for major OS and architectures are published on the GitHub releases page. Platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows via WSL, containers, and a Kubernetes operator. Nothing in the pages mentions an account, license key or runtime needed to run the binary. Source builds need Go 1.21+ and the repo's make tooling. Your device must expose gNMI, and the examples assume user admin with a password and TLS turned off via --insecure. name: gnu-prolog
desc: Prolog compiler with constraint solving
why: A real Prolog compiler with finite-domain constraint solving is an old-school logic language worth a long afternoon of puzzles.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Prolog is a free Prolog compiler with a finite-domain (FD) constraint solver, developed by Daniel Diaz. It takes Prolog and constraint programs and compiles them to stand-alone native binaries, similar to how gcc turns C source into an executable. It also ships an interactive top-level interpreter with a debugger, and the gprolog, gplc and related tools are its command-line front ends. The homepage describes the Prolog part as ISO-conformant with many extensions such as global variables, DCGs, sockets and OS interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to combine the power of constraint programming with the declarativity of logic programming, in a free, native-code system. It was inspired by the author's earlier systems wamcc (Prolog to C via the WAM, slowed by gcc compile times) and clp(FD) (a single-primitive FD constraint design), and development began in January 1996 under the name Calypso.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler is based on the Warren Abstract Machine. A Prolog program is first compiled to a WAM file, then translated to a machine-independent low-level language called mini-assembly, then to the target machine's assembly, and finally to a native object and executable. Unused built-in predicates are excluded at link time, which keeps executables small. The FD solver defines all high-level constraints in terms of a single low-level primitive, which the homepage says makes constraints compilable and lets users define their own.

commands_seen.context: From the Reporting Bugs section: the homepage asks bug reporters to run this to report the GNU Prolog version.
From the Reporting Bugs section: suggested Unix command for reporting the machine type in a bug report. It is a general shell command, not a GNU Prolog one.

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers a source tarball (gprolog-1.5.0.tar.gz) and mentions a configure step, since bug reports should include the operands given to configure and its output. Binary options are a Mac OS X installer package made with MacPorts (installs to /opt/local/ and /opt/local/bin), and Windows 32-bit and 64-bit auto-install setups built with MSVC++ or MinGW. Windows builds are also described in src/WINDOWS and src/WINDOWS-OLD inside the source tree. The page does not mention Homebrew specifically, so the brew formula details are not confirmed here. Notepad++ users can import a UDL file for syntax highlighting.
brief.standout: Native-code output for a Prolog system, with the FD solver built on one primitive that users can extend, plus a claimed performance comparable to commercial solvers. Its compiler design avoids gcc's compile-time cost by generating assembly directly.
brief.status: Appears maintained but the homepage shows no release date. It lists gprolog-1.5.0 as the current stable version and has a copyright line of 1999-2021. The page also mentions a GIT repository on GitHub and separate unstable and old-version directories. Last release date and last commit are unknown from this page alone.
brief.caveats: Platform support is broad but varies: Linux, BSDs, Solaris, macOS and Windows (Cygwin, MinGW, MinGW64, MSVC++) on x86, plus ARM, PowerPC, SPARC, alpha and MIPS entries that may be older. The homepage does not give a licence name, only that it is free software. The homepage's own macOS binary was built on Big Sur, so newer macOS may depend on a source build. Windows builds have separate instructions in the source tree. The manual is available in many formats, but I did not open it.
quotes: GNU Prolog is a free Prolog compiler with constraint solving over finite domains developed by Daniel Diaz.
GNU Prolog accepts Prolog+constraint programs and produces native binaries (like gcc does from a C source).
The key feature of the GNU Prolog solver is the use of a single (low-level) primitive to define all (high-level) FD constraints.

name: gnu-units
desc: GNU unit conversion tool
why: A units converter with a surprisingly large built-in database of physical constants and odd units, fun to explore in a pinch.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Units is a command-line converter for quantities between systems of measurement. You give it a quantity with a unit (for example "mile") and a target unit, and it prints the multiplicative factor both ways. It also handles nonlinear conversions such as Fahrenheit to Celsius and wire gauge, and sums of units such as feet plus inches. Beyond conversion, it works as a scientific calculator that tracks units through expressions with sums, products, quotients, powers and roots. Units are defined in an external data file that ships with the program, and users can supply their own or add to the standard one.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a converter that can also keep dimensional consistency in long calculations, so mixed units do not silently go wrong. The author describes it as handling conversions that simple multiplicative tools cannot, such as affine temperature scales.
brief.how_it_works: Units are defined as entries in a text data file (the README says the definitions are generally found in /usr/share/units/). The program reads that file, so the unit vocabulary can be extended or replaced without changing the program. Expressions are checked for dimensional consistency as they are evaluated, which is how it can report results like a definition in K from an expression involving W/m^2 and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

The data file is also an external, editable text file, so the built-in list of odd units and constants is something you can read and extend.

name: gnu-smalltalk
desc: Implementation of the Smalltalk language
why: A GNU Smalltalk environment opens a door into a live object-oriented language with a long, influential history.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Smalltalk is a free implementation of the Smalltalk-80 language, with a command-line virtual machine called gst. You give it Smalltalk source as files on the command line or on standard input, and it compiles and runs that code. Output is printed to the terminal, and results of top-level expressions are echoed at the st> prompt unless you use -q. The homepage describes it as running on most Unix systems and anywhere a POSIX-compliance library is available. The manual says the goal is a complete system for writing scripts in Smalltalk, and it also has a GTK-based GUI environment (GTK and VisualGST).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says an uncommon feature is that it is well-versed to scripting tasks and headless processing. The manual says it emphasizes rapid prototyping over the graphical environment of other Smalltalks, and aims to be a language for scripts that is clear, aesthetically pleasing, and philosophically appealing, in place of tasks usually given to scripting languages.
brief.how_it_works: gst runs a virtual machine on a binary image file (gst.im). On startup it checks that the image is up to date against the kernel source files, and rebuilds it from those files if it is stale. Files given on the command line run in order and then it exits. The manual also describes a larger startup sequence: site-pre.st, ~/.st/pre.st, the snapshot, then ~/.st/init.st. The class reference in the library docs is generated by a Smalltalk program from the library source.

commands_seen.context: Invocation synopsis from the user's guide. Files are run in order and gst exits at end of file. With no file, gst reads standard input.
Runs a file as a script with arguments, described as equivalent to gst -q file -a args...
Shebang line for a Smalltalk script file that runs directly. The manual also shows a #! /bin/sh variant that uses an exec "gst" line.
Runs the regression test suite from the top-level source directory. Any output other than the names of the test files indicates a problem.
Typed at the st> prompt to exit. Ctrl-d also exits when reading from standard input.

brief.install_notes: The brew formula installs three executables: gst, gst-blox, and gst-config. I saw documentation only for gst; I did not find docs for gst-blox or gst-config. No accounts, hardware, or extra runtimes are mentioned. On first run gst builds gst.im from the kernel files, and it can load ~/.st/kernel overrides, ~/.st/pre.st and ~/.st/init.st. The SMALLTALK_IMAGE and SMALLTALK_KERNEL environment variables and the --no-user-files flag also change this. Images only load on systems with the same pointer size, so an x86-64 image will not load on 32-bit x86.
brief.standout: Most Smalltalks are built around an interactive graphical image. This one treats the image as a snapshot you can rebuild from source, and it aims at scripting and headless use. The manual also says the class reference is generated from the library source by a Smalltalk program. The language follows the Blue Book closely, with a few extensions such as generators built on continuations, namespaces, and a built-in Perl-style regex engine.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched pages do not show a release date or last commit. The homepage footer reads 'Updated: $Date: 2019/11/11' and the copyright line says 2007, but those dates belong to the web page, not to project activity. The homepage links to a Savannah project page and FTP release sites, which I did not fetch.
brief.caveats: The VM is GPL, so programs that bundle it must also be GPL. The system class libraries are LGPL, and the manual gives a specific reading of how LGPL applies to images. The manual says the startup sequence is complicated. Ctrl-c during startup aborts it. The regex engine is 8-bit clean and does not fully support Unicode even when the I18N package is loaded. The GUI is GTK-based and the manual describes it only briefly. Several package entries in the manual's package list are empty.

An uncommon feature of it is that it is well-versed to scripting tasks and headless processing.

name: gnuastro

why: Real astronomy data analysis utilities you can run on actual telescope images at home.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Astronomy Utilities (Gnuastro) is an official GNU package of command-line programs and library functions for manipulating and analysing astronomical data. The homepage says that the programs can be used from the shell, and that each has a full entry in the Info manual and a man page. name: gocryptfs
desc: Encrypted overlay filesystem written in Go
why: An encrypted overlay filesystem whose layered design of encrypted names and blocks is worth understanding.

brief.what_it_is: gocryptfs is an encrypted overlay filesystem written in Go, built on the go-fuse FUSE library. You mount a directory of encrypted files as a plain-looking folder. Each plaintext file is stored as one corresponding encrypted file on disk, and the encrypted store can live on any disk, USB stick, or synced folder such as Dropbox. Input is a password (or master key) plus a cipher directory; output is a mounted plaintext view. The on-disk layout has a 18-byte header per non-empty file and 32 bytes of overhead per 4kB block.
brief.why_it_exists: The project was inspired by EncFS and aims to fix its security problems while keeping good performance. The homepage argues that file-based encryption, unlike whole-disk encryption, lets encrypted files sync efficiently with tools like Dropbox or rsync, and lets the encrypted store grow with available disk space.
brief.how_it_works: Forward mode encrypts each file's contents with AES-GCM (or XChaCha20-Poly1305 when chosen at init) and encrypts file names with EME wide-block encryption using a per-directory IV, with the password run through scrypt. Reverse mode instead exposes an encrypted view of a plaintext directory, using AES-SIV for deterministic encryption. The README and homepage point to a separate Security or Cryptography design document for the full scheme, which I did not fetch.

name: godap
desc: Complete TUI (terminal user interface) for LDAP
why: A TUI for LDAP that opens a door into directory protocols most developers never touch.

brief.what_it_is: godap is a terminal user interface (TUI) for LDAP, written in Go. You point it at a directory server (usually an Active Directory domain controller), authenticate with a password, NT hash, Kerberos credential, or client certificate, and browse the directory as an expandable object tree. It takes a hostname or IP plus bind options and renders the directory interactively, with attribute formatting, colors, and emojis. It can also search, create, edit, move, and delete objects and attributes, inspect and edit DACLs and userAccountControl, edit ADIDNS records, view GPOs, and export subtrees or results to JSON.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls it "A complete terminal user interface (TUI) for LDAP." The author says it started as a side project and grew into a practical tool, and the main focus is Active Directory; for other LDAP servers the README suggests setting the --backend flag.
brief.how_it_works: It runs as a single binary that connects over LDAP, LDAPS, or StartTLS, optionally through a SOCKS4/4a/5 proxy. The explorer loads objects on demand, and entries are cached in memory while the program is open (-M/--cache, default true). Authentication goes through the RedTeamPentesting/adauth library; per the v2.12.0 release notes, the default -u/-p bind is NTLM via the Sicily path and --simple forces a simple bind. Kerberos supports CCACHE, password, NT hash, AES key, or PKINIT, and the SPN is derived from the target host.

name: goresym
desc: Go symbol recovery tool
why: Recovers symbols from stripped Go binaries, a satisfying way into how Go's runtime metadata is laid out.

brief.what_it_is: GoReSym is a command-line Go symbol parser that reads a compiled Go binary and prints JSON (or a flat text listing with -human) describing it. It reports program metadata such as CPU architecture, OS, endianness and compiler version, plus function names with start and end addresses and source locations, file and line-number data, and embedded type and interface structures. It is cross-platform and handles ELF, Mach-O and PE files, and it can recover this information from stripped or partly damaged binaries.
brief.why_it_exists: Go binaries that are stripped, or packed with tools such as UPX, lose much of the symbol information that reverse engineers rely on. The README frames GoReSym as a way to recover that metadata from the runtime structures Go embeds in every binary, for reverse-engineering work. It also points to a Mandiant blog post on Go symbol recovery.
brief.how_it_works: It is built on the upstream Go compiler's debug/gosym and runtime code, which it extends to find and parse the pclntab and moduledata structures even when section layout is unusual or the binary is stripped. It can scan for the pclntab by a signature near runtime_modulesinit and repair a modified pclntab magic. Type recovery walks typelinks from the moduledata table, and the internal structures it parses are defined in objfile/internals.

commands_seen.context: Builds the GoReSym binary from source using a recent Go compiler.
Example run: -t recovers type names, -d includes standard Go package names along with user packages, and -p prints file paths embedded in the pclntab. Output is JSON by default.

brief.install_notes: Pre-built linux, macos and windows binaries are on the GitHub Releases tab. To build from source, run go build with a recent Go compiler. No accounts or extra runtimes are mentioned. The README also describes an optional IDAPython script, IDAPython/goresym_rename.py, which reads GoReSym's JSON output and sets symbols and labels in IDA Pro.
brief.standout: Most symbol tools depend on intact symbol tables. GoReSym instead reads the runtime's own metadata, so it can still work on stripped binaries, UPX-mangled files and binaries with split data sections. The README also says the project keeps pace with new Go runtime releases, with Go 1.24 support listed in its changes.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The README's Changes section lists Go 1.24 parsing support, and the project has an MIT license and a Releases tab. I did not see a release date or last-commit date, so recent activity is inferred from that changelog entry alone.
brief.caveats: Type parsing requires the Go runtime version to be detected correctly. For some stripped binaries you must pass -v with the version string, and the README warns that type parsing will fail if that version is wrong. Types cannot be extracted from Go versions before 1.5. The pclntab parser covers layouts from 1.2 onward, and the README says the pclntab version can lag the runtime version. The source is partly copied from the Go tree with exported internals, and the README says the maintainers keep these modifications by hand, which makes upgrading the Go dependency work. The README does not state a platform limit for the tool itself beyond the supported architectures and file formats.
quotes: GoReSym is a Go symbol parser that extracts program metadata (such as CPU architecture, OS, endianness, compiler version, etc), function metadata (start & end addresses, names, sources), filename and line number metadata, and embedded structures and types.

name: gotestwaf
desc: Tool for API and OWASP attack simulation
why: Generates OWASP-style attack traffic to probe WAFs, a window into how filters misjudge requests.

brief.what_it_is: GoTestWAF is an open-source command-line tool, written in Go, that simulates API and OWASP-style attacks against a web application security product such as a WAF, API gateway, IPS, or API security proxy. It takes a target URL and generates malicious HTTP requests from YAML test cases, with payloads placed in bodies, headers, URL parameters, paths, and API formats (REST, SOAP, XMLRPC, gRPC, GraphQL). It then classifies each response as blocked, bypassed, or unresolved and writes a scored report to the console, as a PDF, HTML, or JSON file.
brief.why_it_exists: Wallarm's blog argues that WAF evaluation usually focuses on false positives while ignoring false negatives, and that no simple tool lets a developer, QA engineer, or security engineer produce a report of WAF coverage. GoTestWAF was open-sourced to fill that gap.
brief.how_it_works: Each YAML test case lists payloads, encoders (Base64, Base64Flat, JSUnicode, URL, Plain, XML Entity), and placeholders (places in the request such as URLPath, URLParam, Header, JSONBody, SOAPBody, gRPC, RawRequest), and GoTestWAF sends every payload-encoder-placeholder permutation, so 2 payloads x 3 encoders x 1 placeholder yields 6 requests. A response is marked blocked when it has a block status code (default 403) or matches a block regex, and bypassed when it has a pass status code (default 200 or 404) or matches a pass regex. With --openapiFile, it builds valid requests from an OpenAPI 3.0 spec and substitutes attack vectors into them.

Use --network="host" or put GoTestWAF and the target on the same Docker network, and the README says the IP running GoTestWAF must be whitelisted on the security solution. Running natively needs Go installed (the repo can be built with go build). For native runs, PDF reports need Google Chrome; without Chrome, use --reportFormat html. Chrome as the HTTP client (--httpClient=chrome) on Linux needs --cap-add=SYS_ADMIN in Docker. There is no account or license key required in the README; without --noEmailReport or --email the tool prompts for an email address, which can be skipped by pressing Enter.

The OpenAPI mode sends attacks inside requests that are valid for the app's own API description, which makes the bypass results more meaningful than raw fuzzing.

brief.what_it_is: gotpm is a command-line tool for using a TPM 2.0 chip, shipped from the same repository as the go-tpm-tools Go module. name: gource
desc: Version Control Visualization Tool
why: Turns a repository's history into an animated tree of contributors, a striking visualisation of version control.

brief.what_it_is: Gource is a command-line visualisation tool that turns a version-controlled project's history into an animated tree. The project's root directory sits at the centre, directories are branches, files are leaves, and contributors appear on the tree at the times they made changes. It reads history from Git, Mercurial, Bazaar and SVN directly, and can also parse logs from several third-party tools for CVS repositories. Running plain `gource` inside a repository shows its log. Output is an on-screen animation, and the homepage notes that video output can be piped to ffmpeg.

brief.how_it_works: Gource generates or reads a log of commits (built in for Git, Mercurial, Bazaar and SVN, or from third-party tool output for CVS), then replays that log as an animated directory tree. Each contributor is drawn working on the tree at the timestamp of their commit. The homepage changelog mentions options such as --start-date, --stop-date, --output-stream and --file-idle-time, which control the date range, output and file display.

name: gpac
desc: Multimedia framework for research and academic purposes
why: A research multimedia framework that dissects containers and streaming protocols like MP4 and DASH, a real door into how media is structured.

brief.what_it_is: GPAC is an open-source multimedia framework written in C, with a library (libgpac) and command-line tools. It can process, analyse, package, stream, encode, decode and play back audio, video, subtitles, metadata, encrypted media, 2D/3D graphics and ECMAScript. Media goes in as files, pipes, sockets, HTTP or capture devices, and comes out as remuxed or segmented files, streams, or playback. Its best-known tool is MP4Box, a command-line MP4 manipulator for importing and extracting media, inspecting files, DASH segmentation and RTP hinting. The gpac command is a direct interface to its filter engine, which lets you chain any combination of filters. The project also ships MP4Box.js, a JavaScript library for parsing and writing MP4 in browsers and Node.js.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents GPAC as a standards-focused framework for processing, inspecting, packaging, streaming and playing media, aimed at video enthusiasts, academic researchers, standardization bodies and professional broadcasters. Its own description says it is best known for its MP4/ISOBMFF capabilities. The 2025 MP4Box.js post frames the project's core mission as giving developers high-quality, efficient, modular building blocks for multimedia workflows.
brief.how_it_works: Features are packaged as processing modules called filters, and the filter engine manages stream flow between them. The gpac application exposes that engine directly, so you can build a pipeline from any filters. MP4Box is a front end that uses the same engine, and most GPAC applications are built on it. The README says the tools are mostly wrappers around libgpac, which can be embedded in other projects.

name: gpsd
desc: Global Positioning System (GPS) daemon
why: A daemon that multiplexes GPS receivers over a simple protocol, a real door into talking to satellite hardware.

brief.what_it_is: gpsd is a service daemon that monitors one or more GPS (or AIS) receivers attached to a host computer through serial or USB ports. It reads the raw receiver output and makes location, course and velocity data available to query over TCP port 2947, in a format the project says is much easier to parse than the NMEA 0183 sentences most GPS receivers emit. The distribution also includes a linkable C service library, a C++ wrapper, a Python module, and auxiliary diagnostic tools such as cgps, gpsmon, gpspipe and gpsdecode.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that with gpsd, multiple location-aware applications can share access to one sensor without contention or loss of data, and that it replaces the NMEA 0183 parsing each client would otherwise do. The project also points to a long-running critique of GPS standards and vendors, and argues for a simpler protocol.
brief.how_it_works: The daemon watches the attached serial or USB receivers and, under Linux, binary packages install hotplug scripts that start gpsd and tell it which device to read when a USB device appears. gpsd then deduces the baud rate and whether the device is GPS or AIS by inspecting the data stream. Clients connect to TCP 2947 and exchange JSON requests and responses, described in the gpsd_json(5) man page.

commands_seen.context: From the project homepage: the suggested way to install gpsd on Debian-based distributions, including Ubuntu, through the regular package manager.

Not from the project pages. This is the Homebrew formula caveat text supplied with the package metadata. It tells the user to manually add a GPS device to the running daemon via gpsdctl, because gpsd does not auto-detect device addresses on macOS.

brief.install_notes: The project does not release binary packages; the INSTALL page is for people running distributions with binary package systems, and BUILD covers building from source. Release tarballs are on the Releases page. On Debian/Ubuntu, apt install gpsd is suggested. On Homebrew, after starting the daemon you must force-add your GPS device with gpsdctl, as shown in the commands list. No accounts or special hardware are required to install, though you need a GPS or AIS receiver to get any data.
brief.standout: Under Linux it normally runs with zero configuration: plugging in a USB receiver triggers hotplug scripts that launch the daemon and feed it the device, and it works out baud rate and receiver type on its own. It is also very widely deployed, with the homepage saying it underlies the Android map location service and appears in drones, marine navigation and driverless-car stacks.

Documentation is spread over many pages, and the README itself is thin; the homepage is the main source.

name: gpsim
desc: Simulator for Microchip's PIC microcontrollers
why: A PIC microcontroller simulator lets you run and step firmware with simulated pins, a great way to watch hardware execute.

brief.what_it_is: gpsim is a software simulator for Microchip PIC microcontrollers, licensed under GPL v2 or later with some libraries under LGPL. You load a PIC program (the README's examples are assembler source plus stimulus files) and run it on the simulated chip, with simulated stimuli tied to its I/O pins. It offers a command-line interface like gdb and a GTK GUI. The homepage describes breakpoints, single-stepping, disassembly, memory inspect and change, and a trace buffer, and it lists a register viewer, source browser, breadboard viewer, and scope viewer among its screenshots.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames gpsim around three goals: accuracy ("designed to be as accurate as possible", covering the core, I/O pins, and internal peripherals so that you can test the PIC "the same way you would in the real world"), speed, and usefulness. It also aims to offer debugging features normally found only in in-circuit emulators.
brief.how_it_works: Peripherals and external hardware are modelled as stimuli and modules that connect to the simulated I/O pins. The homepage says modules are loadable libraries that are distributed separately, and it lists bundled ones: pull-up/pull-down resistors, USART, switch, logic gates, LEDs, PAL video emulator, rotary encoder, I2C EEPROM, and an LCD module. A continuous trace buffer records simulator activity, and read/write breakpoints can fire on register values.

name: gql
desc: Git Query language is a SQL like language to perform queries on .git files
why: A SQL-like language for querying git internals, turning the repository itself into a queryable database.

brief.what_it_is: GitQL (the Homebrew formula is named gql, and the executable is gitql) is a SQL-like query language and small engine that runs queries directly against a local git repository's data. You write statements like SELECT author_name, COUNT(author_name) FROM commits, and it returns rows from tables such as commits, branches, tags, refs and diffs_changes. Nothing is converted or imported into a separate database; the engine reads the .git data on the fly and prints the result. The README also describes an in-memory query SDK that the tool is built on.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches GQL as a way to query .git data with familiar SQL syntax, without creating database files or converting .git into another format. The README frames the wider project as an SDK for running SQL-like queries over any kind of data.
brief.how_it_works: The engine parses a SQL-like statement, then resolves the FROM clause against tables it builds from the repository, such as commits, branches, refs, tags and diffs_changes. It evaluates the query in memory, using the expression, function and aggregation layers from the GitQL SDK, and the data is computed on the fly rather than stored. Keywords are case-insensitive. The SDK exposes customizable schema, data provider, functions, types and values, according to the README's SDK documentation list.

name: grap

brief.what_it_is: Grap is a language for describing graphs so they can be typeset inside documents. name: graphqlite
desc: SQLite graph database extension
why: A graph database bolted onto SQLite; an unusual database twist worth a look for the Cypher-style queries.

brief.what_it_is: GraphQLite is a SQLite extension that adds graph database capabilities using the Cypher query language. You load it into an ordinary SQLite connection and then create nodes, traverse relationships, run graph algorithms, and write graph patterns, all in a single .db file alongside your other data. Input is Cypher text (via a cypher() SQL function, the Python Graph class, or the Rust crate). Output is query rows, returned as JSON through SQL in the raw SQL interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a way to get graph capabilities without a separate database server, network configuration, or migration scripts: your graph lives in a single .db file next to the rest of your application data.
brief.how_it_works: It is a SQLite loadable extension, and Cypher queries are passed through the cypher() SQL function. Properties are stored in an EAV model with separate tables for text, integer, real, boolean, and JSON values. Graph algorithms such as pageRank are exposed as Cypher functions or Python methods. The README does not go deeper on internals; the homepage lists architecture and query dispatch as explanation pages I did not follow.

name: grex
desc: Command-line tool for generating regular expressions
why: Given example strings, it synthesizes a regular expression that matches them, a satisfying inversion of the usual regex workflow.

brief.what_it_is: grex is a generator for regular expressions. You give it example strings, the test cases, and it returns a single regular expression that matches all of them. The output is anchored with ^ and $ by default, so it matches only the inputs given and nothing else. The Homebrew package is the Rust command-line tool, which prints the pattern to stdout. The homepage is the demo site for grex-js, a WebAssembly build of the same Rust library for browsers and Node.js.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes writing regexes by hand as a often complicated and tedious task, and wants grex to produce a correct starting expression automatically. The project began as a Rust port of the JavaScript tool regexgen by Devon Govett, whose development had apparently ceased.
brief.how_it_works: grex builds a deterministic finite automaton from the input strings, then reduces it with Hopcroft's DFA minimization algorithm. The minimized automaton is treated as a system of linear equations and solved with Brzozowski's algebraic method, which yields the final regex. The README notes that this aims for the shortest regex but often produces something longer than needed, so hand-tuning is still expected.

commands_seen.context: Basic CLI use. Test cases are passed as arguments; the output for these inputs is ^[a-c]$.
The -r flag turns repeated substrings into {min,max} quantifiers. The output for these inputs is ^b(?:a{1,3})?$.

Reads test cases from a Unix pipe, with - standing for stdin.
Reads one test case per line from a file, as an alternative to passing arguments.
Escapes non-ASCII characters as \u{...} sequences and converts astral code points to surrogate pairs, for older JavaScript engines.
Combines the digit, whitespace and word flags with their negated forms, replacing the matching character classes with \d, \s, \w, \W and similar.

name: grin
desc: Minimal implementation of the Mimblewimble protocol
why: A minimal Mimblewimble implementation is a rare look at an unusual cryptocurrency protocol design.

brief.what_it_is: Grin is an in-progress implementation of the Mimblewimble protocol, a privacy-preserving digital currency built by developers around the world. The README describes it as a clean, minimal codebase that aims to stay that way. The homepage frames Grin as a currency with no amounts and no addresses, where transactions can be aggregated and relayed through a subset of peers before broadcast. The brew formula installs a single executable named grin. The README does not say what the command takes in or prints, so input and output formats are unknown from these pages.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents Grin as a privacy-preserving currency that is not controlled by any company, foundation or individual, with fair distribution and no ICO, pre-mine or founder's reward. The homepage says Mimblewimble lets past transaction data be removed without losing security, so the chain does not collapse under stored data.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the protocol hides amounts and gives scaling advantages, and that transaction fees depend on the number of outputs created or destroyed and total transaction size. Proof of work uses Cuckoo Cycle in two variants, Cuckaroo (ASIC-resistant) and Cuckatoo (ASIC-targeted), with a one-minute block time and a smooth difficulty adjustment curve. The homepage adds that a new transaction is relayed among a subset of peers before wide broadcast to hide its origin. The detailed mechanism is in doc/intro.md, which I did not fetch.

The README does not mention first-run configuration.

The project also keeps its implementation deliberately small and says so in its philosophy section.

name: gromacs
desc: Versatile package for molecular dynamics calculations
why: Molecular dynamics you can run at home, watching atoms move under real physics, is serious science worth a long weekend.

brief.what_it_is: GROMACS is a free, open-source molecular dynamics package that simulates the Newtonian equations of motion for systems of hundreds to millions of particles. It is built mainly for biomolecules such as proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, though its homepage says many groups also use it for polymers and fluid dynamics. Input is clear-text topology and parameter files plus run settings, and output is trajectories and energies that analysis tools can read. The suite ships with a large set of command-line tools under the gmx program, such as gmx grompp and gmx mdrun, and the docs say no scripting is required.
brief.why_it_exists: The About page frames it as a versatile package for high-performance molecular dynamics and output analysis, and it stresses speed, with the nonbonded interactions that usually dominate a simulation calculated extremely fast. It is run by a community-driven development team.
brief.how_it_works: The README-level pages do not explain the core integration algorithm in detail; they point to the manual. What they do describe is the execution model: compute kernels use SIMD intrinsics on CPUs and CUDA, OpenCL or SYCL on GPUs, CPU and GPU work can run at once with load balancing, and parallelism uses either MPI or the built-in thread-MPI for single workstations.

The install guide assumes a C99 and C++17 compiler (gcc 11+, clang 14+ or MSVC 2019+) and CMake 3.28 or later. An FFT library is required: FFTW 3, Intel MKL, or the bundled FFTPACK fallback. Optional extras include CUDA (toolkit 12.1+, GPU compute capability 5.0+), SYCL, OpenCL, HIP, MPI (MPI 3.0 standard), and hwloc. name: guile
desc: GNU Ubiquitous Intelligent Language for Extensions
why: GNU's Scheme implementation with a long history as an embeddable extension language, worth exploring though not obscure.

brief.what_it_is: Guile is GNU's implementation of the Scheme programming language, with an efficient compiler and virtual machine. It can run standalone Scheme programs or be embedded in C and C++ applications as an extension language. It supports the Revised5 and most of the Revised6 Scheme reports plus many SRFIs, and ships a module library that includes an HTTP server and client, XML parsing, and object-oriented programming. The homepage's examples show scripts that print text, print the date using an SRFI-19 module, and serve a plain-text response over HTTP on port 8080.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Guile is designed to help programmers build applications that users or other programmers can extend with plug-ins, modules, or scripts. It calls itself the GNU Ubiquitous Intelligent Language for Extensions and the official extension language of the GNU project.
brief.how_it_works: Guile compiles Scheme to bytecode for its virtual machine. The homepage says its parsing and compiling tools are exposed as part of the standard module set, so new source languages can be added without writing C. Compiler front-ends already exist for ECMAScript and Emacs Lisp, with Lua support described as underway.
brief.install_notes: The homepage does not describe installation. The Homebrew caveats say that after installing, you can place Guile libraries under $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/share/guile/site/3.0 (source), $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/lib/guile/3.0/site-ccache (compiled), and $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/lib/guile/3.0/extensions (extensions). They recommend adding these to your shell profile: export GUILE_LOAD_PATH="$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/share/guile/site/3.0", export GUILE_LOAD_COMPILED_PATH="$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/lib/guile/3.0/site-ccache", and export GUILE_SYSTEM_EXTENSIONS_PATH="$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/lib/guile/3.0/extensions". The Homebrew formula installs guile, guild, guile-config, guile-snarf, and guile-tools.
brief.standout: Guile is a general-purpose Scheme that is also designed to be embedded, and it can host other languages. Its ECMAScript and Emacs Lisp front-ends are built on the same parsing and compiling tools it exposes to module authors. The homepage also presents it as a way for end users to share features as scripts instead of patches.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists GNU Guile 3.0.11 released December 1, 2025, a bug-fix release with some new features. Earlier releases are 3.0.10 (June 24, 2024) and 3.0.9 (January 25, 2023). I did not check the repository commit history.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not mention a license. It describes Lua support as underway, not finished. The examples are Scheme and do not cover embedding in C. The Homebrew formula's install paths and environment variables are specific to the 3.0 series. The scout note mentions a long history, which I did not verify beyond the GNU project affiliation.
quotes: Guile is designed to help programmers create flexible applications that can be extended by users or other programmers with plug-ins, modules, or scripts.
Guile is the GNU Ubiquitous Intelligent Language for Extensions, and the official extension language of the GNU project.
Guile empowers users with "practical software freedom"

name: guile-fibers

brief.what_it_is: Fibers is a Guile Scheme library that adds lightweight, Go-like concurrency in the style of Concurrent ML. You write fibers with spawn-fiber, run them under run-fibers, and pass messages between them over channels with put-message and get-message. The README's example is a client and server that exchange messages over two channels, and it prints the messages it receives as it runs. Input is Scheme code that uses the library, and output is the program's own results, such as the printed message traces.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Fibers 'provides Go-like concurrency for Guile Scheme, in the tradition of Concurrent ML.' The project is an attempt to bring CML-style channel-based concurrency to Guile.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. It shows that fibers run inside a run-fibers call, that spawn-fiber starts a new fiber, and that fibers communicate through make-channel, put-message, and get-message. The manual's index lists sections for API reference, pitfalls, examples, and project status, but I could not read their contents.
