name: gts
desc: GNU triangulated surface library
why: A GNU library for triangulated surfaces and geometry operations, a real computational geometry toolkit though mostly hidden as a dependency.

brief.what_it_is: GTS (GNU Triangulated Surface Library) is a C library for working with 3D surfaces meshed from interconnected triangles. It offers object-oriented structures for topology, 2D Delaunay and constrained Delaunay triangulation, boolean set operations (union, intersection, difference) on surfaces, surface refinement and coarsening, isosurface extraction, and metric operations such as area, volume and curvature. Its inputs are triangulated surface files (its own GTS text format, plus STL via converters), and its outputs are transformed or analysed surfaces, converted files (DXF, OOGL, STL) and triangulations. The Debian-style executable list includes delaunay, gts-config, gts2dxf, gts2oogl, gts2stl, gtscheck, gtscompare, gtstemplate, happrox, stl2gts and transform.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the initial goal was to provide 'a simple and efficient library to scientists dealing with 3D computational surface meshes', written in C with an object-oriented design based mostly on GTK+.
brief.how_it_works: The library is organised as a GTK-style object hierarchy (points, vertices, segments, edges, triangles, faces, surfaces) with inheritance and virtual functions. Boolean operations and point-in-surface tests use Simulation of Simplicity (SoS) to handle degenerate geometric cases, and the floating-point predicates use fast adaptive arithmetic adapted from Jonathan Shewchuk's work. Bounding-box and Kd-trees support point location and intersection tests.
brief.install_notes: The homepage lists a 'Debian packages' page, sample files, Python bindings, a Darcs repository and daily snapshots, and an installation instructions document, but I did not open these, so I have no build commands. Release notes say the library builds with glib 1.2.8 or later, with glib 2.4 or later autodetected, and that pkgconfig is preliminarily supported. The gts-config script is provided for compiling against the library, in the style of glib. Windows support was added in stages: MinGW, Cygwin and Microsoft C were each mentioned as preliminary.
brief.standout: It is a real computational geometry toolkit with robust exact-style predicates and SoS-based boolean operations, but it is mostly invisible to users because it usually arrives as a dependency. Its 2002 marching tetrahedra isosurface method was added to avoid the topological defects of marching cubes.
brief.status: quiet. The newest item on the homepage is Release 0.7.6 dated March 29th 2006, and the news section has no entries after that. The homepage says version control moved from CVS to Darcs in 2005. I could not check a repository or the Debian package, so I cannot confirm whether later work exists.
brief.caveats: The homepage looks dated, with 2006 as its latest release and SourceForge-era hosting. The library is LGPL-licensed. Release notes say boolean operations could still fail with nested closed loops inside one another, and that results could contain degenerate faces that block later boolean operations until they are collapsed. Release 0.7.6 forces LC_ALL=POSIX in its executables to avoid locale-dependent floating-point issues. The homepage gives no installation instructions in the main text, and the homepage was reached without errors.
quotes: GTS stands for the GNU Triangulated Surface Library.
Careful attention is paid to performance related issues as the initial goal of GTS is to provide a simple and efficient library to scientists dealing with 3D computational surface meshes.
Robust set operations on surfaces (union, intersection, difference).

judge.reason: A substantial computational-geometry toolkit whose robust mesh booleans, adaptive predicates, and isosurface extraction make triangulated surfaces worth exploring despite its age.

name: h26forge
desc: Tool for making syntactically valid but semantically spec-noncompliant videos
why: Generates syntactically valid but spec-breaking H.264/H.265 video to probe decoders, a wonderful way to see how codecs fail.

brief.what_it_is: H26Forge is a command-line tool, written in Rust, for generating and modifying H.264 (AVC) video files that are syntactically valid but break the spec's semantic rules. It can take an existing Annex B H.264 file and randomly mutate its syntax elements, or apply edits from a Python script to those elements. It can also generate new Annex B H.264 streams from random syntax elements, written to a file or streamed over RTP. The output is meant to be fed to video decoders to see how they fail. The README mentions only H.264. The scout note's mention of H.265 is not supported by this README.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as domain-specific infrastructure for analyzing, generating, and manipulating syntactically correct but semantically spec-non-compliant H.264 files. Its motivation document, MOTIVATION.md, says it simplifies a previously manual proof-of-concept (PoC) generation process. The accompanying paper is "The Most Dangerous Codec in the World: Finding and Exploiting Vulnerabilities in H.264 Decoders" (USENIX Security 2023).
brief.how_it_works: Per the README, the tool has three modes: random mutation of syntax elements in an existing Annex B file, programmatic modification of syntax elements via a Python script, and generation of Annex B H.264 from random syntax elements. The syntax element ranges are controlled by a JSON config file (config/default.json, or config/chrome.json for browser-oriented output). The README says the spec is 844 pages and the tool parses bitstreams into syntax elements and reproduces frames, so its generated streams are structurally valid but violate semantic rules. The README does not give deeper internals.

Build with ./make.sh on Linux/Mac or ./make.bat on Windows. The README does not say whether Homebrew installs Python or other extras. brief.standout: It turns syntax-level fuzzing into a targeted tool for building spec-breaking streams, and the README's trophy list ties it to real CVEs in Apple, Firefox, FFmpeg/VLC, and Pixel hardware decoders. It also includes a conformance harness against ITU vectors, so the user can see which parts of the spec the generator still gets wrong.
brief.status: Status is not clear from the README. It cites a 2023 paper and a trophy list running through CVE-2024-27793, which suggests active work through 2024. The README has no release date or changelog, and I did not check the commit history. I would call it unknown rather than maintained or abandoned.

name: gzrt
desc: Gzip recovery toolkit
why: Recovers data from corrupted gzip archives by scanning deflate streams, a good window into how compressed formats actually break.

brief.what_it_is: gzrecover is a command-line program from the gzip Recovery Toolkit (gzrt) that tries to salvage data from a corrupted .gz file. It reads a damaged gzip archive, either from a named file or from standard input, and skips over bad bytes. It writes whatever it can read to a new file named with a .recovered suffix (any .gz is stripped), or to standard output with -p. The output is not guaranteed to be good, so the author says it must be checked by hand.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it after a backup restore failed: bad sectors had corrupted the archive, and gzip stopped about 10% of the way through, so almost everything was lost. The README's framing is that gzip 'craps out' on the first error, and gzrecover is meant to get past bad data and keep what it can.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internal algorithm. It says gzrecover 'attempts to skip over bad data in a gzip archive', that it reports where it finds bad bytes when run with -v, and that it runs slower than gunzip, more so the more corrupt the file. It does not say it scans deflate streams, so that detail comes from the scout note and is unverified here. For tarballs, the workflow is to run gzrecover first and then pass the .recovered output to GNU cpio, since GNU tar cannot handle format errors.

commands_seen.context: Builds the gzrecover program from the unpacked gzrt source directory. The README says to install by copying the binary manually to a directory of your choice.
Suggested way to check whether GNU cpio is installed and at version 2.6 or higher, which is needed only for recovering compressed tar files.
Runs recovery on a corrupted gzipped tarball. Per the README's example, it writes my-corrupted-backup.tar.recovered alongside the input.
Extracts files from the recovered tar stream with GNU cpio, which tolerates format errors that GNU tar rejects. The README's example uses this after gzrecover.

brief.install_notes: You need zlib, which you may already have; build and install it first if not. Unpack the gzrt sources, cd into the gzrt directory, and run make. There is no make install step: the README says to copy the binary manually to a directory of your choice. For compressed tar archives you also need GNU cpio 2.6 or higher, which the README says is only needed if you don't already have it. The README mentions a 0.8 release (2013-10-03) and a GitHub repository, but the GitHub link's URL was not given on the homepage, so I did not follow it. The brew formula's executable is gzrecover.
brief.standout: Rather than trying to decompress the whole stream, it treats a corrupt gzip file as something to scan past its damage and keep what can be read. It pairs with cpio for tarballs because cpio tolerates errors that tar does not, which is a practical recovery chain for backups.
brief.status: quiet. The latest release listed is 0.8, dated 2013-10-03, and the copyright line runs 2002-2013. The page shows no commits or releases after that, and I did not check the GitHub repository's activity.
brief.caveats: Output is not guaranteed to be valid and the author warns it 'is likely to recover some bad data', so everything must be checked by hand; the bigger the file, the more likely it extracts something. Runtime grows with corruption and can be long, and cpio can produce very verbose errors and run for a long time. The README gives no platform list; the build is a plain make with zlib, and the docs assume a Unix-style shell. The program is GPL-licensed, but the copyright notice also says 'All Rights Reserved' under a separate line. Also, before recovering, check that the file was not transferred by FTP in ASCII mode, which the author says causes 99% of corruption reports.
quotes: gzip craps out 10% of the way through your archive.
99% of "corrupted" gzip archives are caused by transferring the file via FTP in ASCII mode instead of binary mode.

name: h3
desc: Hexagonal hierarchical geospatial indexing system
why: Uber's hexagonal geospatial index; a clever tiling system you can poke at for geometry and mapping.

brief.what_it_is: H3 is an open-source C library, developed at Uber, that indexes latitude/longitude points into a hexagonal grid. You give it a coordinate and a resolution from 0 to 15, and it returns a cell ID, a 64-bit index shown as a hex string. Given a cell ID, it can return the cell's hexagon boundary vertices or its center coordinate. The homepage describes it as a discrete global grid system, and the README says it is a hexagonal grid that can be approximately subdivided into finer hexagonal grids.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says H3 exists so that data can be joined across disparate datasets and aggregated at different levels of precision, and that the grid enables algorithms such as nearest neighbors, shortest path, and gradient smoothing. The README frames it as combining the benefits of a hexagonal grid with the hierarchical subdivisions of Google's S2 library.
brief.how_it_works: Each point is mapped to a cell at a chosen resolution, and each cell ID encodes its place in the hierarchy. The README says the hexagons can be approximately subdivided into finer hexagons, so cells nest across resolutions, though not perfectly. The command-line tools wrap the C API: latLngToCell takes coordinates and a resolution, and cellToBoundary and cellToLatLng take a cell index. The README does not explain the underlying projection or the indexing math beyond this.

name: halide
desc: Language for fast, portable data-parallel computation
why: A DSL that separates what an image computation does from how it is scheduled, a genuinely interesting idea, though it is a compiler toolchain.

brief.what_it_is: Halide is a programming language for writing high-performance image and array processing code, embedded in C++ with a Python binding as well. You write an algorithm as a set of functions over x and y, then write a separate schedule that sets tiling, vectorization, parallelism, and where intermediate results are stored or recomputed. Halide turns this into an in-memory pipeline that it compiles to an object file for ahead-of-time use, or JIT-compiles and runs in the same process. It targets many CPU architectures, operating systems, and GPU compute APIs including CUDA, OpenCL, Metal, and Vulkan.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it exists to make it easier to write high-performance image and array processing code on modern machines. The publication titles frame the core idea as decoupling algorithms from schedules, so the same computation can be reorganized for different hardware without rewriting what it computes.
brief.how_it_works: A pipeline is built through Halide's C++ API as an in-memory representation rather than parsed from a separate source file. Scheduling calls such as tile, vectorize, parallel, and compute_at are applied to the same Func objects that hold the algorithm, so changing the schedule changes execution order and locality while the algorithm stays the same. The result is then compiled for the chosen target, either to an object file or JIT-compiled in-process.

name: hack-browser-data
desc: Command-line tool for decrypting and exporting browser data
why: Decrypts browser credential stores, which reveals how browsers protect local secrets, though it is security-sensitive and a bit narrow.

brief.what_it_is: HackBrowserData is a command-line tool (executable hack-browser-data) that decrypts and exports data from browsers on Windows, macOS and Linux. It reads local browser profile files, decrypts them with the user's keys, and writes passwords, cookies, history, bookmarks, credit cards, downloads, localStorage, sessionStorage and extensions to output files. Output is JSON by default, with CSV and a Cookie-Editor cookie format also available. It covers most Chromium-based browsers and Firefox on all three OSes, and Safari on macOS.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a tool for security research. The disclaimer says it is 'only intended for security research' and that users are responsible for their own legal liability. It is also part of the 404Team StarLink-Galaxy project.
brief.how_it_works: It locates each browser's profile directory, reads the SQLite and key files (including through a locked-file bypass for live files on Windows), and decrypts them using the platform's secret store, such as DPAPI on Windows, the macOS Keychain (or a keychain password passed with --keychain-pw), or Linux keyring-based keys. For Chrome 127+ cookies on Windows it needs a separate C payload for App-Bound Encryption. The README also describes a cross-host workflow: dumpkeys exports master keys from the origin host as JSON, archive packs the relevant files into a zip, and restore decrypts them offline on another machine, even for browsers the analyst's OS cannot run.

commands_seen.context: Builds the binary from source on the local platform (Go 1.20+ required).

Cross-host step 2 on the origin host: packs only the files needed for decryption into a zip.
Cross-host step 3 on the analyst host: decrypts the copied data offline using the exported keys.

brief.install_notes: Most users are told to download a release binary from the GitHub releases page. Building from source needs Go 1.20 or newer and git clone of the repo. Windows builds for Chromium 127+ App-Bound Encryption cookies need Zig 0.13+ (the Makefile calls zig cc; brew install zig on macOS, scoop install zig on Windows) and then make payload followed by make build-windows; MinGW-w64 gcc is an option if make payload is bypassed. Safari extraction on macOS needs Full Disk Access granted in System Settings → Privacy & Security. Some Chromium browsers on macOS prompt for the current user password, or you can pass --keychain-pw. No accounts or servers are required.
brief.standout: It is built for offline, cross-machine decryption. dumpkeys exports the platform-bound master keys once, so the data can be decrypted on a different OS, including for browsers such as Sogou or QQ that only ship on Windows. Compared with simple password dumpers, it covers many Chromium forks and Safari, and it has a Cookie-Editor export format. name: hashcash
desc: Proof-of-work algorithm to counter denial-of-service (DoS) attacks
why: Proof-of-work stamps from the 1997 anti-spam scheme; a clear door into the idea behind Bitcoin mining and cost-based DoS defence.

brief.what_it_is: Hashcash is a proof-of-work algorithm and stamp format. A sender computes a stamp that takes a tunable amount of CPU work, and anyone can verify it cheaply. The input is a text to be stamped, such as an email, and the output is a stamp that proves the work was done. The homepage says the algorithm works with a cryptographic hash such as SHA1 or SHA256, and that a stamp can be checked by counting leading zeros with ordinary tools like sha1sum. The same name also covers an email anti-spam tool that attaches stamps to mail, and a library form of the code.
brief.why_it_exists: It is a denial-of-service counter-measure: it adds a small, unavoidable cost to actions that are cheap to spam, such as sending mail. The homepage frames it as 'payment in burnt CPU cycles' that can throttle abuse of un-metered resources while preserving privacy, and as a stop-gap until electronic cash is widely used.
brief.how_it_works: The sender searches for a value that makes a hash of the stamped data have a set number of leading zero bits, which is a partial hash collision. Each extra bit doubles the average work, and verification is a single hash. The cypherspace page gives the example of a 20-bit collision taking about 6 seconds on a machine testing 180,000 hashes per second. The homepage notes that the work needed should rise a couple of bits a year as machines get faster.
brief.install_notes: Neither page gives installation steps or commands. The cypherspace page, which is the older location, lists prebuilt tool binaries for Windows win32 and redhat9-i386 (rpm and tgz formats), a .src.rpm buildable on any Unix RPM platform, and source with a Visual C++ project file. It also lists a Windows GUI build, and third-party versions in Java, a browser applet, RISC-OS, Emacs (hashcash.el), and Perl. The homepage says the site is moving to hashcash.org, so some links may be stale. The brew metadata lists two executables, hashcash and sha1, but neither page mentions sha1.
brief.standout: The verification step is so simple that a human can check a stamp by counting leading zeros with sha1sum, and the whole scheme can be re-implemented from scratch in a few lines. Its design, from 1997, is the ancestor of the proof-of-work idea that Bitcoin mining later used, and the homepage says that is now its most widely used role.
brief.status: Unknown, leaning quiet. The homepage has a 'hits since nov 03' counter and the cypherspace page has a 'new 1-Sep-2003' counter, and the paper is dated Aug 2002. The pages show no release version or recent commit dates, and I did not check a source repository. The site is described as being 'slowly moving' to a new domain.
brief.caveats: Most of the material is old, dating from about 2002 to 2003, and the binaries listed are for Windows and RedHat 9. The homepage says Microsoft released an incompatible hashcash spec (email postmark) that hashes the body too, uses a modified SHA1, and uses multiple sub-puzzles. The homepage also warns that hashcash 'suffers from a high rate of inflation' as machines get faster, so the difficulty must keep rising. The sha1 executable from the brew metadata is not documented on either page.
quotes: A hashcash stamp constitutes a proof-of-work which takes a parameterizable amount of work to compute for the sender.
Hash cash is payment in burnt CPU cycles by calculating n-bit partial hash collisions on chosen texts.
Verification can be done by a human eye (count leading 0s) even with availability of common preinstalled command line tools such as sha1sum.

name: hamlib

brief.what_it_is: Hamlib is a C library, with a command-line and network-daemon layer on top, that gives programs one consistent API for controlling amateur radio transceivers, rotators and amplifiers. The library's generic API (libhamlib.so) is what applications link against, and it contains the per-device backends. Control goes over serial (RS-232), USB-to-serial or, in later work, IP connections. The bundled executables (rigctl, rigctld, rotctl, rotctld and others) are front ends that let a user or script send control commands to a rig or rotator. The README also mentions distance, bearing and grid-square conversion helpers and bindings for Perl, Python and TCL.
brief.why_it_exists: The project exists so that application authors can write radio-control software once, against a shared API, instead of learning each manufacturer's serial protocol. The README says the goal is to provide "stable, flexible, shared libraries that enable quicker development of amateur radio equipment control applications."
brief.how_it_works: A generic front-end API sits over per-model backends, one for each protocol family such as yaesu, and the library maps common calls onto each device's serial or network protocol. The network daemons (rigctld, rotctld) expose that control over a TCP socket, so any language that can open a socket can drive the hardware, and the README notes even netcat works. Contributors add support by writing backends and rig model definitions, and the supported-radio list is kept on the project wiki.

name: hashlink
desc: Virtual machine for Haxe
why: Virtual machine running Haxe bytecode; an unusual runtime that opens a corner of language implementation.

brief.what_it_is: HashLink is a virtual machine for Haxe, the cross-platform language. The Haxe compiler turns source into HashLink bytecode (.hl) using the -hl flag, and the hl runtime executes it through a JIT. Alternatively, the same bytecode can be converted to C (HL/C) and compiled with gcc or a similar compiler into a native executable. The runtime also ships with standard library support for file I/O, regular expressions, networking, and Unicode strings, plus optional libraries for compression and image decoding (fmt), OS dialogs (UI), and SDL windowing and OpenGL (SDL).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a fast, optionally native-compiled runtime for Haxe, with a case study of Northgard, a commercial 3D game originally built on Adobe AIR that moved to HashLink. The author framing is that HL/JIT gives fast development iteration and HL/C gives the best release performance.
brief.how_it_works: Haxe compiles to strictly typed HashLink bytecode. HL/JIT runs that bytecode in a just-in-time virtual machine for quick builds during development. HL/C instead translates the bytecode to C, which is compiled with gcc for release builds, and both paths share the same runtime and semantics. The runtime uses a mark-and-not-sweep garbage collector and has performance features such as typed virtuals for anonymous object access and static dispatch when no override exists.

name: healpix
desc: Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization of a sphere
why: Equal-area sphere pixelization used in cosmology surveys, a real scientific tool worth an afternoon of curiosity.

brief.what_it_is: HEALPix is a pixelization scheme for the sphere and a software package built around it, distributed in C, C++, Fortran 90, IDL, Java and Python. It splits a sphere into pixels of identical area, and the package adds spherical harmonic transforms, filtering, pixel queries, median filtering, mask handling and map rotation, with FITS as the usual file format. Inputs are typically full-sky maps and harmonic coefficients, and outputs are maps, coefficients and images, including Google Earth/Sky images and DomeMaster planetarium images. The homepage's feature list is the only description of the tools; the executables list in the metadata names command-line programs that the pages I read do not describe.
brief.why_it_exists: It was built for cosmic microwave background satellite data (WMAP, and Planck), which needed full-sky maps at arcminute resolution and fast, accurate statistical analysis. The homepage says its use has since spread well beyond the CMB field.
brief.how_it_works: The sphere is hierarchically tessellated into 12 base curvilinear quadrilaterals, and each pixel divides into four at the next resolution level. Pixels lie on lines of constant latitude, which makes spherical harmonic integrals scale as about N^1/2 rather than N, according to the homepage. The harmonic transforms come from a shared optimised library called libsharp.
brief.install_notes: The downloads page recommends the source package from the SourceForge Download page under GPLv2 and says to follow its installation directions. Source is also browsable in a SourceForge SVN repository. Prebuilt packages exist for macOS (MacPorts, Homebrew) and Linux (RPM), with variable delays. The download is free with no registration, though the page suggests subscribing to the Healpix-users mailing list for updates. Python users get it through healpy, configured and installed via pip. Fortran codes on Apple ARM chips need CFITSIO 4.1.0 or higher. The 3.83 notes mention support for the Intel ifx compiler and Python 3.10 and above. I saw no hardware or account requirements.
brief.standout: The equal-area, iso-latitude grid is what makes it fast for harmonic analysis, and the homepage says so directly, which is less common than a plain area-equalizing claim. The base-12 recursive quartering scheme also reaches a stated resolution down to 0.4 milli-arcseconds.
brief.status: Maintained, though releases are infrequent. The latest software release listed is HEALPix 3.83 on 2022-11-18, with 3.82 on 2022-07-29 and 3.81 on 2022-01-25. The downloads page was last edited 2024-11-15, and its notes mention a 2024-09-27 IDL library update and healpy 1.18.0 support. I did not check a commit log.
brief.caveats: The pages give no command-line usage, so I have no verified command lines and no flag details. The executables list comes from the Homebrew metadata and was not checked against documentation. The software is GPLv2. Publications using it are expected to cite Górski et al. 2005 and footnote the website. The Fortran build needs a recent CFITSIO on Apple ARM. The homepage is thin on install detail, which means the build steps live in the source package, which I did not fetch.

name: hatari
desc: Atari ST/STE/TT/Falcon emulator
why: An Atari ST emulator lets you watch 1980s software and hardware run, a good way to poke at old machine internals.

brief.what_it_is: Hatari is an emulator of the Atari ST, STE, TT and Falcon home computers, running on GNU/Linux, BSD, Mac OS X, Windows and other systems supported by the SDL library. It emulates the hardware closely enough to run most old ST games and demos, and it can also be run in a browser. It needs a TOS image file, which you either dump from a real Atari or replace with the free EmuTOS. Optional inputs include a host directory mounted as an ST drive and images from an original Atari hard disk.
brief.why_it_exists: Unlike many other Atari ST emulators that aim to give a good environment for GEM applications, Hatari tries to emulate the ST hardware as closely as possible so that it can run most of the old ST games and demos.
brief.how_it_works: It emulates the ST and STE hardware, including tricks such as raster interrupts, border effects and PSG sample sound. A joystick can be emulated with the cursor keys or a real PC joystick. For TT and Falcon it adds emulation of the Videl video chip and the DSP 56001, which the site describes as still in development and experimental.
brief.install_notes: Hatari needs a fast machine: 1 GHz or more for ST/STE emulation and more than 2 GHz for Falcon emulation, running a POSIX-compatible OS that supports SDL. Before it runs you need a TOS image, either dumped from your own Atari or EmuTOS, because the image cannot be shipped with Hatari. The site points to a downloads page for required libraries and packages. Some binary packages exist but not for all architectures, so you may need GNU C to compile from source.
brief.standout: Its accuracy-first goal sets it apart from GEM-focused Atari ST emulators: it targets the hardware itself so that demo-scene and game tricks work. It can also mount a host directory as an ST drive.

name: harbour
desc: Portable, xBase-compatible programming language and environment
why: An xBase dialect with a living dBASE lineage, a real old-school environment, though this formula is deprecated.

brief.what_it_is: Harbour is an open, free-software implementation of an xBase-compatible programming language, described as cross-platform, multi-threaded, object-oriented and scriptable. It ships as a compiler plus runtime libraries, with several UI and database backends, its own build system (hbmk2), and a collection of libraries and bindings for popular APIs. You write Harbour source (.prg files) and compile it into native apps for GNU/Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, BSD and other *nix systems. The bundled executables are harbour, hbmk2, hbpp, hbrun, hbformat, hbi18n, hbnetio, hbtest, hb3rdpat.hbs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Harbour as the free software successor to Clipper/xBase: backward compatible with Clipper/xBase code and 100% compatible with Clipper compilers, so existing xBase applications can run on modern platforms from one code base.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler turns Harbour source into C-level output that is then built with a C compiler, using Harbour's own make system (hbmk2, driven by .hbp/.hbc project files) to handle the build. Optional third-party components are wired in through HB_WITH_* environment variables. Native RDDs, SQL and ODBC support sit in the runtime, alongside JSON, SSL, TCP/IP and XML support and Console, TUI, GUI, service/daemon and web app targets.

name: helib
desc: Implementation of homomorphic encryption
why: A homomorphic encryption library where you can compute on ciphertexts, a genuinely strange idea to dig into.

brief.what_it_is: HElib is an open-source C++17 library, under the Apache License v2.0, that implements homomorphic encryption. It provides the BGV scheme (with bootstrapping) and the CKKS approximate-number scheme. Data goes in encrypted as ciphertexts, and arithmetic such as add, multiply, and shift runs directly on those ciphertexts, so the results stay encrypted. The library depends on the NTL mathematical library, and the README describes it as an 'assembly language for HE' with low-level routines.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that since mid-2018 HElib has been under extensive refactoring for Reliability, Robustness & Serviceability, Performance, and most importantly Usability for researchers and developers working on HE and its uses. The stated goal is to make homomorphic evaluation practical and usable, with an emphasis on performance.
brief.how_it_works: The README names the techniques used: Smart-Vercauteren ciphertext packing and Gentry-Halevi-Smart optimizations, along with automatic noise management and multi-threading. It also supports Ptxt (plaintext) objects that mirror the functionality of Ctxt (ciphertext) objects. The README points to a design report (eprint 2020/1481) for further detail.

commands_seen.context: Configure the recommended package build, which bundles HElib with NTL and GMP in one relocatable folder; run from a build directory inside the repo.
Compile HElib; the output lands in the relocatable helib_pack folder. The 16 is an example thread count.
Optional: run HElib's tests. Requires configuring with -DENABLE_TEST=ON.

Configure the examples directory against an installed HElib; the examples are built with pure CMake.

Run the example test suite; the tests are written in bats and require bats-core and a successful examples build.
Run the example tests with DEBUG set so the artifacts they generate are kept for inspection.

brief.install_notes: The brew formula is not the only route. The README and INSTALL.md describe two source builds. The package build (option 1, recommended) fetches and compiles GMP and NTL itself, and needs m4 >= 1.4.18 and, on Linux, patchelf >= 0.14.3. The library build (option 2) needs you to build GMP >= 6.2.1 and NTL >= 11.5.1 yourself, with NTL configured using NTL_GMP_LIP=on SHARED=on NTL_THREADS=on NTL_THREAD_BOOST=on. Prerequisites are g++ >= 11.3.0 (or Apple clang >= 14), cmake >= 3.22, GNU make >= 4.3, pthreads, and git >= 2.36 if you run the test suite. Optional Intel HEXL acceleration needs AVX512DQ and AVX512-IFMA CPUs, a static build, and HEXL >= 1.2.1. Tested platforms are Ubuntu 22.04 and recent macOS releases. No account or runtime configuration is mentioned.
brief.standout: HElib is one of the reference implementations of BGV and CKKS and is aimed at people who want to program against the scheme directly, not at a turnkey product. The README pitches it as an assembly language for homomorphic encryption, so you work with ciphertext and plaintext objects and low-level operations.
brief.status: Status is unknown from what I read. The README shows a passing 'Build and Test' CI badge and INSTALL.md lists tested platforms up to macOS Ventura 13.4.1 and Ubuntu 22.04, which suggests active work. I did not see a release date or last-commit date on the pages I fetched, and I did not open CHANGES.md to check.
brief.caveats: HEXL acceleration is experimental, only works on specific Intel CPUs, and is only supported for static library builds with -DPACKAGE_BUILD=OFF and -DBUILD_SHARED=OFF. Building as a shared library fails unless NTL was also built as a shared library. The build is C++ with several dependencies (NTL, GMP) and needs a fairly recent toolchain. The README links a separate CKKS-security.md for the security status of the CKKS implementation, which I did not read. The examples are BGV-focused, and the README says more are expected later. The brew formula's description says only 'Implementation of homomorphic encryption', and brew reports no executables, so this is a library, not a command-line tool.

HElib is an open-source (Apache License v2.0) software library that implements homomorphic encryption (HE).

name: hebcal
desc: Perpetual Jewish calendar for the command-line
why: Perpetual Jewish calendar with astronomical calculations for the command line; a niche but genuinely computational tool.

brief.what_it_is: Hebcal is a command-line program that prints the days of the Jewish calendar for a given secular (Gregorian) year, or for a single month or date within it. You can switch on or off the Hebrew date, Jewish holidays, the weekly sedra, the day of the week, and the days of the Omer. It can also add candle-lighting, havdalah, fast times, zmanim, sunrise and sunset, and daily learning schedules such as Daf Yomi. Input is a year, month, day, or YYYY-MM-DD date, plus optional location and timezone; output is plain text, tab-delimited, or ISO dates.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a perpetual Jewish calendar for the command line, meant for generating calendars for PDAs and personal calendars. The README says the original motivation for the algorithms was the Tur Shulchan Aruch.
brief.how_it_works: The key routines were originally translations of Dershowitz and Reingold's Lisp calendar code for GNU Emacs. Candle-lighting times were later rewritten using Derick Rethans's timelib, and the program was ported from C to Go in version 5. Sunset and sunrise come from solar calculations based on a city from a built-in database (hebcal cities), or on latitude, longitude, and timezone you supply with --geo and -z.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, building from source needs Go 1.18 or higher and GNU make 3.79 or later, then make clean all. The default city ('New York') is set when the program is compiled. Set HEBCAL_CITY to pick a different default city, and HEBCAL_OPTS to prepend options (for example --geo and -z) to every run. Running hebcal info shows the current settings.
brief.standout: It is a small, opinionated, old-school program with a very large option set. It covers many learning cycles (Daf Yomi, Mishna Yomi, 929, Rambam, Psalms, Pirkei Avot and more) and sunrise/sunset zmanim from the command line, and it is explicit about the Julian-to-Gregorian switchover of 1752. Its README is candid that the sun-time routines are approximate.

name: hercules
desc: System/370, ESA/390 and z/Architecture Emulator
why: An emulator for System/370 and z/Architecture mainframes, letting you boot period operating systems on a machine that never existed.

brief.what_it_is: Hercules is an open source software emulator of IBM System/370 and ESA/390 mainframes, plus the 64-bit z/Architecture. The SDL 4.x 'Hyperion' build covered here runs on Linux, Windows, Solaris, FreeBSD and Mac OS X. The emulated machine is driven by a Hercules Configuration File, and the project documents a 3270 console and emulated devices. Its companion utilities, listed in the brew metadata, handle DASD disk and tape image files (for example dasdinit, maketape, tapecopy, hetinit). What comes out is an emulated mainframe console on which period operating systems such as MVS, VM or DOS/VS can be booted.
brief.why_it_exists: The project exists so people can run period mainframe operating systems and software on ordinary PCs without IBM hardware. The homepage frames it as a tool for systems programmers and hobbyists, and quotes users describing the nostalgia and learning value of running MVS on a personal machine.
brief.how_it_works: Hercules emulates the processor and I/O of the System/370, ESA/390 and z/Architecture machines in software, using a configuration file to define the virtual hardware. Devices are backed by host files that the bundled dasd and tape utilities create and convert. The README points to a separate Overview install page and a Configuration File page for the details, which I did not open.
brief.install_notes: Install is from source: the README says build instructions are in the source files BUILDING and INSTALL (Unix) or README.WIN64 (Windows), and the README links to a separate 'Building External Packages' step described as important. The repo README also links platform-specific build notes for AIX, BSD, OS X, MinGW, MSVC and Solaris, and some Windows notes are marked obsolete. Windows pre-built zip binaries from SoftDevLabs contain only the Hercules binaries, so the user must install the Microsoft Visual C++ 2008 runtime manually or use a SoftDevLabs installer that bundles it. The README also covers running Hercules in a no-UI daemon mode and building as setuid root for HercIFC. A Hercules Configuration File is needed to define the machine before an operating system can be IPLed; the README does not spell out first-run steps in what I read.
brief.standout: It is a long-running open source emulator that spans three generations of IBM mainframe architecture, and the SDL fork adds its own fixes and features (QDIO/OSA networking, a redesigned I/O subsystem) on top of the original code base. It also includes a built-in 3270 console, so the experience is a real mainframe operator console rather than a simplified simulator.
brief.status: Maintained, by the project's own account: the README says this SDL 4.x version is 'currently the only actively maintained version' and the homepage says a dedicated crew is constantly working on it. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so I cannot confirm recency from the evidence. The repo README's Travis CI badge points to travis-ci.org, a service that has since been retired, which may suggest the CI setup is dated.
brief.caveats: The homepage states this SDL version is not created, owned, maintained or copyrighted by Software Development Laboratories, despite the 'SDL' name. The git repository is described as bleeding edge and may contain bugs and experimental code. Minimum Windows is Windows Vista, and Non-Windows host support is listed only as '(varies)'. Building from source is needed for most platforms, and Windows users must handle the VC++ 2008 runtime themselves. Documentation is the project's web pages, which the homepage calls the only accurate source; some pages, such as System Messages, are marked obsolete. Licensing is the Q Public Licence, which the README says is OSI approved open source. IBM, System/370, ESA/390 and z/Architecture are IBM trademarks, as noted on the homepage.

Hercules is a systems programmer's dream come true.

name: hexapoda
desc: Colorful modal hex editor
why: A modal hex editor is a niche but pleasant way into binary files; standout only in its modal, colourful approach, not deeply strange.

brief.what_it_is: Hexapoda is a terminal hex editor for binary files, described on its homepage as a colorful modal hex editor. It opens a file and shows its bytes, with each byte colored by its value. Editing is modal and selection-first, in the style of Kakoune and Helix. The homepage lists inspection of the selection as signed, unsigned, binary, fixed-point, UTF-8 and color. It can also search, mark offsets, and jump to offsets. Replacing and deleting bytes are supported; inserting bytes is not yet.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit motivation. It presents hexapoda as a hex editor that borrows the modal, selection-first editing model of Helix and Kakoune, with colour to make byte values easier to read.
brief.how_it_works: Editing is selection-first: you select bytes, then act on them, as in Helix. Multiple selections are supported, and a selection can be split into #-byte chunks. The repeat action (bound to * by default) repeats an action a set number of times, using the primary register as the count, so the count can come from a value in the file. The homepage says hexapoda uses ijkl for cursor movement by default and that keybinds are configurable.

name: hesiod
desc: Library for the simple string lookup service built on top of DNS
why: Hesiod is a real but obscure lookup service layered on DNS, a door into MIT-era naming, though this is only the library.

brief.what_it_is: Hesiod is a C name service library, release 3.2.1, for a simple string lookup service layered on top of DNS. A client program asks the library for a name and a type, and the library turns that into an ordinary DNS query under the configured domain. The answers are plain text records (TXT, or CNAME pointing at a TXT record) held on the central name servers. The README describes the data as general name service for a variety of applications. The Homebrew entry names one executable, hesinfo, but the README does not describe it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Hesiod "can provide general name service for a variety of applications" and is based on the Berkeley Internet Name Daemon (BIND). It does not give a longer motivation.
brief.how_it_works: Clients read a hesiod.conf file that sets rhs (the domain suffix) and lhs (a label, default .ns); the rhs value can be overridden by the HES_DOMAIN environment variable. Administrators make their name servers authoritative for ns.your.domain and load a zone file containing TXT records such as haynes.group and CNAME records such as 2638.gid pointing at them. A lookup therefore resolves through normal DNS to a text string.

commands_seen.context: Prepares the source directory for building; accepts options.
Lists the configure options.
Builds the Hesiod library.
Alternative build target, same as make per the README.

brief.install_notes: Needs a vaguely ANSI C compiler; the README says gcc will do. Beyond building, each client machine needs a hesiod.conf in sysconfdir (default /usr/local/etc/hesiod.conf) with rhs and lhs lines, and the central DNS servers need a named.boot primary line and a named.hesiod zone file with SOA, NS and Hesiod TXT/CNAME data. The README's example uses rhs=.your.domain and lhs=.ns. No account or hardware is required.
brief.standout: It is a 1980s-style naming scheme that reuses DNS as its transport, so no new server protocol is needed; the zone data is just TXT and CNAME records. The README is candid that the .ns label is a historical accident that it would not choose today.

name: hfsutils
desc: Tools for reading and writing Macintosh volumes
why: Reads and writes classic Macintosh HFS disk volumes, a fascinating dead filesystem you can poke at from a modern shell.

brief.what_it_is: hfsutils is a set of tools for reading and writing volumes in Apple's classic HFS (Hierarchical File System) format, the native Macintosh disk format, from UNIX and other systems. It includes command-line programs named on the page (hformat, hmount, hls, hcopy, and others) that are meant to work like mtools does for MS-DOS disks. It also has an X-based graphical browser (xhfs), a Tcl package offering a scriptable HFS shell, and a C library for low-level volume access. Input is an HFS volume such as a floppy, SCSI disk, CD-ROM, Zip disk, partitioned medium, or image file; output is files read from or written to that volume. The page does not mention the hvol executable that Homebrew lists, so I could not confirm what it does.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants to manipulate Macintosh volumes from UNIX and other systems without a Mac. The page describes the package as 'a comprehensive software package being developed to permit manipulation of HFS volumes from UNIX and other systems.'
brief.how_it_works: The page does not explain the internals. It says the C library can be linked into other programs, for example to build a Macintosh Resource Manager on top of it, and that the command-line tools follow the mtools model. The Tcl interface is described as more efficient than calling the external programs.
brief.install_notes: The page names no Homebrew-specific steps. To build the Tcl and X tools you need the Tcl and Tk libraries; the page asks for the most recently patched Tcl 7.6 and Tk 4.2, and warns that other versions may not work. The Tcl and Tk interfaces are optional, so you can build only the command-line tools. The page links an FTP download for source but I did not follow it.
brief.standout: It reads and writes a volume format that is now mostly dead, and it is meant to be used the way mtools is used for DOS disks. It also has a scriptable Tcl HFS shell and a linkable C library, so it works as a toolkit as well as a set of commands.

name: hivex
desc: Library and tools for extracting the contents of Windows Registry hive files
why: Extracts contents from Windows Registry hive binaries, a genuine door into a binary format most developers never open.

brief.what_it_is: Hivex is a C library, with bindings for OCaml, Perl, Python and Ruby, that reads Windows Registry hive files, the binary files Windows keeps under C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM32\CONFIG. It takes a hive file on disk and gives you a handle for walking its tree of keys, subkeys and typed values. Three command-line tools sit on top: hivexget prints one subkey's values or a single named value, hivexml exports the hive as XML, and hivexsh is an interactive shell for navigating it. Reading is the default; writing needs an explicit open flag and an explicit commit.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that, unlike other tools in this area, hivex does not use the textual .REG format, because parsing that is as much trouble as parsing the original binary format. Its stated aim is to be secure against buggy or malicious registry files. It is a subproject of libguestfs, where it lets you examine or merge changes into the Registry of Windows guests in disk images.
brief.how_it_works: You open a hive with hivex_open, which returns a handle, then move through nodes (keys) from hivex_root and read their (key, value) pairs by name or by listing them. Each value has a type such as REG_SZ, REG_DWORD or REG_BINARY, but the docs warn that the type field is often unrelated to the real contents. Writes are buffered: nothing reaches the file until hivex_commit is called, and new blocks are appended to the end of the file instead of reusing freed space.

commands_seen.context: From the hivexget(1) SYNOPSIS: lists all the (key, value) pairs under that subkey in a format similar to regedit. The path is relative to the top of the hive, so HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM is not valid.
From the hivexget(1) SYNOPSIS: prints one named value raw, with no escaping. Use @ for the default value. Strings are converted to UTF-8, multi-strings go one per line, and numbers print in decimal.

brief.standout: It is a small, defensive parser for a format Microsoft has never documented, and the docs are unusually frank about what the author does not understand. Its write path avoids rewriting structures in place: it appends new blocks and leaves unreachable blocks behind rather than risk corrupting the hive.

name: hidapitester
desc: Command-line tool to exercise USB HID devices via HIDAPI
why: Lets you send raw reports to any USB HID device from the shell, opening up the strange world of HID descriptors.

brief.what_it_is: hidapitester is a command-line program for poking at USB HID devices through the HIDAPI library. You give it a list of ordered arguments: filters to find a device (vendor/product ID, usage page, usage, serial), then actions such as opening it, sending Output or Feature reports, reading Input reports, or fetching the report descriptor. Output goes to the terminal as device listings and hex dumps of the report bytes. The README says the goal is to exercise every API call in hidapi from the shell. Prebuilt binaries are published for macOS, Linux (x86_64 and Raspberry Pi), and Windows 64-bit.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a simple, low-dependency tool for testing every API call in hidapi, with default builds fully static and needing no system-installed hidapi. The scout note adds that it lets you send raw reports to any USB HID device from the shell.
brief.how_it_works: The program parses its arguments left to right as a sequence of commands and runs them in order, so filters set up the next --open and reads and writes follow it. Report bytes are passed as comma-separated lists, and the first byte is the report ID when report IDs are used. Buffer length is set separately with --length, and reads block for a configurable --timeout in milliseconds, or loop forever with the -forever variants.

name: hmmer
desc: Build profile HMMs and scan against sequence databases
why: Profile hidden Markov models scanning sequence databases is real bioinformatics you can run at home on protein families.

brief.what_it_is: HMMER is a suite of command-line tools for biosequence analysis using profile hidden Markov models (profile HMMs). You can build a profile from your own multiple sequence alignment with hmmbuild, then search sequence databases with hmmsearch. You can scan a sequence against a curated profile database such as Pfam with hmmscan. You can also start from a query sequence instead of a profile, as BLAST does, using phmmer or the iterative jackhmmer. The package's executable list also includes nhmmer and nhmmscan for DNA, plus alignment, conversion, and database tools. Inputs are sequence files and profile or alignment files, and outputs are search hits and alignments.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says HMMER is for searching sequence databases for homologs and for making sequence alignments, and it is built to detect remote homologs as sensitively as possible. It frames profile HMMs as the way to do this, noting that they were first introduced at significant computational expense, but that as of HMMER3 it is essentially as fast as BLAST.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes the method only at a high level: it uses probabilistic models called profile HMMs, built from conserved protein domains or DNA elements or from a multiple sequence alignment, and it relies on the strength of those underlying probability models for sensitivity. It does not explain the internal algorithm further. The user guide PDF was linked but could not be read as text.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers the latest version v3.4 as a source download, plus precompiled packages and archived older versions. No build requirements, dependencies, or first-run steps appear on the homepage. The user guide, which would likely cover these, could not be read.
brief.standout: Profile HMMs give HMMER good sensitivity for remote homologs that plain pairwise search can miss, and HMMER3 claims that this is now about as fast as BLAST. It is a whole toolkit of about nineteen executables covering build, search, scan, alignment, and database preparation, not a single tool.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the homepage shows: it lists v3.4 as the latest version, and it links a blog about HMMER3 and an EBI-hosted search server. No release date or last-commit date was visible, so the exact activity level is unknown.

name: hsd
desc: Handshake Daemon & Full Node
why: Handshake full node is a door into a decentralised naming system where domains are rooted in a blockchain rather than DNS.

brief.what_it_is: HSD (Handshake Daemon) is the reference full-node implementation of the Handshake protocol, a peer-to-peer root naming system. It takes in blockchain and peer-network data and serves a validated root zone: it runs a built-in recursive resolver and an authoritative nameserver (ports 5349 and 5350 by default) so local tools like dig can resolve Handshake names. It also provides a wallet server, command-line tools (hsd-cli, hsw-cli), and RPC and REST APIs for querying the node, bidding on names, and claiming DNS names with DNSSEC proofs. The homepage describes the broader project as a decentralised naming and certificate-authority experiment.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Handshake aims to replace centralised root naming and certificate authorities with a system where every peer validates and manages the root zone, and it argues that charging an economic cost for names (through HNS coin auctions) deters the spam and sybil attacks that pushed earlier decentralised systems toward central operators.
brief.how_it_works: Names are registered through on-chain auctions: an open transaction starts bidding, bids are placed with a hidden lockup value, bids are later revealed, and the winner registers the name with sendupdate. Existing DNS owners can instead publish a DNSSEC ownership proof (a TXT record commitment, then sendclaim) that is mined on-chain and matures after about 30 days (4,320 blocks), allowing them to skip the auction. The README says the built-in resolver is JavaScript, with optional native libunbound bindings for better performance and DNS conformance.

commands_seen.context: Returns basic node info; the README says it works once hsd is installed globally.

Sends the open transaction that starts the auction for the name handshake.

brief.install_notes: The README points to docs/install.md for the install guide. It is installed as an npm package with Node.js, and the README says to install unbound first if you want native libunbound bindings, since those must be present before installing hsd. Mining needs hs-client. Claiming an existing DNS name requires DNSSEC already enabled on that name, and running your own zone requires BIND-style key tools (dnssec-keygen, dnssec-signzone) or the bns package. The README's examples use testnet addresses and settings, so mainnet configuration is not covered in what I read.
brief.standout: Rather than a blockchain that only moves money, it treats the chain as a root zone that any peer can validate, and it lets existing DNS owners prove ownership with DNSSEC instead of buying names at auction. The project's own page also says it has no official foundation or controlling entity.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a CI build badge and a coverage badge, and it says the testnet airdrop is live, but it gives no release version, date, or last-commit date, and the homepage does not say when it was last updated. I could not confirm whether it is actively maintained.
brief.caveats: The homepage calls Handshake an experimental protocol. The README warns that HSD does not protect against theft or lost funds from bugs or user error. Some ports and examples are public-facing or testnet-only, and the README flags binding the resolver to 0.0.0.0 as public. Claims need DNSSEC set up correctly (no CNAMEs or wildcards, and every label must be a zone cut), and a claim takes about 30 days to mature. The JavaScript resolver is slower and less DNS-conformant than the libunbound build. Code is MIT-licensed, with Bcoin copyright notices as well. The Homepage says 'Multiple implementations may exist', so HSD is one of several.

every peer is validating and in charge of managing the root DNS naming zone

name: hqx
desc: Magnification filter designed for pixel art
why: A pixel-art magnification filter based on hand-tuned lookup rules, turning small images into clean enlargements with a pleasing transform.

brief.what_it_is: hqx is a C library and command-line tool that enlarges pixel art by a factor of 2, 3, or 4 (hq2x, hq3x, hq4x). It takes a source bitmap and writes a larger image with smoothed diagonal edges. The CLI reads an image file such as a PNG and writes the scaled result to another file. The library version works on 32-bit RGB buffers that the caller allocates. The README describes the filter as built for line graphics and cartoon sprites rather than photographs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames hqx as one of Maxim Stepin's pixel-art scaling algorithms, the kind used in emulators such as Nestopia, bsnes, ZSNES, Snes9x and FCE Ultra. The filter was meant to be fast enough to process 256x256 images in real time.
brief.how_it_works: For each source pixel, the filter examines its 3x3 neighbourhood and compares the centre with its 8 neighbours in YUV colour space, with more tolerance on brightness (Y) than on chroma (U and V). Each neighbour is labelled 'close' or 'distant', which gives 256 possible patterns. A 256-entry lookup table maps each pattern to a precomputed way of blending the source pixels into the output. The table was built by determining the most probable edge geometry for each pattern and rasterising it at 3x resolution with anti-aliasing.

name: homeworlds

why: Framework for Binary Homeworlds, a strange abstract two-player space game with a C++ engine you can play and extend.

brief.what_it_is: A C++ framework for Binary Homeworlds, a two-player strategy game played with Icehouse pieces in four colors and no board. The repository provides a C++14 core library (ApplyMove, AllMoves, InferMove, AIMove over GameState and WholeMove types), a command-line player and analyzer (homeworlds-cli), a wxWidgets graphical interface (homeworlds-wx), a Python extension (libhomeworlds), and a partial archive of SuperDuperGames.org game transcripts with a converter script. brief.how_it_works: Pieces on the table represent star systems and spaceships, and the goal is to eliminate the enemy's homeworld ships by capture, catastrophe, or attacking the binary star system. The library represents states as GameState and moves as WholeMove, generates all legal moves, and can infer a full move from a partial entry such as "build g1". The GUI works by tracking mouse drags of pieces from the start position to the end position and deducing the move. The AI picks the best move from the full move list, and the README notes it cannot look far ahead because of the high branching factor.

name: ht
desc: Viewer/editor/analyzer for executables
why: A terminal hex editor and disassembler for executables that lets you walk through binary structure, a classic door into reverse engineering.

brief.what_it_is: HT (HT Editor, ht) is a terminal-based viewer, editor and analyzer for text, binary and especially executable files. You point it at a file and it shows the raw bytes in a hex view, or parses the file's structure (headers, sections, symbols, imports, relocations) and disassembles its code. It can also run a code and data analyser over the image, add labels and comments, search with regex or expressions, and run block operations that rewrite bytes. It reads many executable formats (ELF, PE32/PE64, Mach-O, MZ, NE, LE, COFF, XBE, PEF, Java class) and writes changes back to the file.
brief.why_it_exists: HT is a free-software tool for inspecting and modifying executables, which the README calls 'a file viewer, editor and analyzer for text, binary, and (especially) executable files'. The homepage frames it as a classic reverse-engineering tool, and the scout note calls it a door into reverse engineering.
brief.how_it_works: The loader parses the file's format, then the code and data analyser follows branch sources and destinations recursively, finds procedure entries, and creates labels and xrefs. You can extend the analysis by hand: press 'c' to continue code analysis at the cursor, 'n' to name an address, and '#' to add comments. Search and block operations use a built-in expression evaluator with functions such as readbyte(ofs) and readstring(ofs, size), and analysis state is saved in a FILENAME.htcfg file beside the target.

name: httm
desc: Interactive, file-level Time Machine-like tool for ZFS/btrfs
why: Time-machine-style browsing of ZFS and btrfs snapshots, a clever look at filesystem internals.

brief.what_it_is: httm is a command-line tool, written in Rust, that lists the unique past versions of a file found on filesystem snapshots and backups, showing each version's size, date and location. You give it file paths (or pipe paths on stdin) and it prints every distinct version, deduplicated by modify time and size. It also has four interactive modes (browse, select, prune, restore) for picking a version and restoring or pruning it. It works with ZFS, btrfs and NILFS2 snapshots, Restic repositories and Time Machine backups, and can also be pointed at rsync-ed copies on ext4, XFS or NTFS. Output can be plain lines, null or tab delimited, JSON or CSV.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants a command-line Time Machine. ZFS, BTRFS and NILFS2 snapshots are not designed to find unique versions of a single file, so httm does that search. The README says httm 'might change the way you use snapshots' and 'the Time Machine concept (because httm is very fast!)'.
brief.how_it_works: httm reads the snapshot directories for the dataset holding each path and compares the versions it finds, deduplicating by modify time and size, or by checksum if you ask for that verification level. It can also list deleted files and browse files behind deleted directories, and it can map snapshot mounts by file. Restores can be guarded by taking a pre-restore snapshot, and roll-forward avoids destroying interstitial snapshots. The README does not describe the internals in more detail.

name: hy
desc: Dialect of Lisp that's embedded in Python
why: A Lisp dialect embedded in Python with macros and Python interop is an unusual language to try for a short while.

brief.what_it_is: Hy is a Lisp dialect embedded in Python. It takes Lisp-syntax source, either typed at a REPL or in .hy files, and transforms it into Python abstract syntax tree (AST) objects, so Python libraries can be called from Lisp code. You start an interactive REPL with the command hy, or run a program with hy myprogram.hy. The package also installs hy2py and hyc, though the README does not describe what those two do.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as wanting Lisp and Python to get along: "Lisp and Python should love each other. Let's make it happen." The practical pitch is that Hy gives you "the whole beautiful world of Python at your fingertips, in Lisp form."
brief.how_it_works: Hy reads Lisp forms and compiles them into Python AST objects, which then run on the Python runtime. Because the output is Python AST, Python modules and functions are directly usable from Hy code. The README gives no further detail on the compiler internals or macro system.

name: hyphy
desc: Hypothesis testing using Phylogenies
why: Phylogenetic hypothesis testing software that lets you run real evolutionary analyses on sequence trees at home.

brief.what_it_is: HyPhy (Hypothesis Testing using Phylogenies) is an open-source package for comparative sequence analysis, built on stochastic evolutionary models. It takes a sequence alignment plus a phylogenetic tree (FASTA, NEXUS, Phylip or MEGA input, per the 2.5 README) and runs statistical tests that detect natural selection, recombination, co-evolution and rate variation across genes and lineages. Output is machine-readable JSON, which the companion HyPhy Vision site renders as interactive trees and site plots. It ships as a command-line tool (hyphy), a scripting language called HBL, and a shared library callable from Python and R.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as a suite of advanced phylogenetic methods for detecting and testing natural selection, recombination, co-evolution and rate variation. The 2.5 README frames it as software for analysing genetic sequences with techniques from phylogenetics, molecular evolution and machine learning, and notes that it powers the datamonkey.org web server.
brief.how_it_works: Each analysis is a named method (for example MEME, FUBAR, FEL, BUSTED, aBSREL, RELAX, GARD) that fits a codon or nucleotide substitution model to an alignment and tree and then tests hypotheses about selection or recombination. Results are written as JSON, which HyPhy Vision parses for visualisation. The homepage lists the analyses as: MEME for episodic site-specific positive selection, FUBAR/FEL/SLAC for pervasive selection, BUSTED/aBSREL for gene-wide and branch-specific selection, RELAX for relaxed or intensified constraint, and GARD for recombination breakpoints.

brief.what_it_is: iccDEV is a set of command-line tools, C/C++ libraries, and bindings for reading, validating, converting, and applying ICC colour profiles. The Homebrew formula exposes 20 executables, including iccDumpProfile (dump and validate a profile), iccToJson/iccFromJson and iccToXml/iccFromXml (convert between binary ICC and editable text), iccApplyNamedCmm and iccApplyProfiles (run colour values or TIFF images through profile chains), iccRoundTrip and iccPawgReport (assessment), and iccDumpProfileGui (a graphical viewer). Inputs are ICC profiles (including ICC iccMAX profiles), text colour data, TIFF/PNG/JPEG images, and .cube LUTs; outputs are text, JSON or XML, transformed colour values, converted images, or DeviceLink profiles. It is also packaged as a Python module (iccdev on PyPI), a MATLAB package, a WebAssembly npm package, a Docker image, and an MCP server for AI assistants.
brief.why_it_exists: The ICC, the body that promotes open, vendor-neutral, cross-platform colour management, publishes this as its reference-style open source toolkit for the ICC profile format and the iccMAX profile specification. The README says the project was formerly known as DemoIccMAX.
brief.how_it_works: The tools are built on shared libraries (IccProfLib and related code) that parse and write profile tags, then apply profile chains through a CMM (colour management module) using a chosen rendering intent. The npm package is the same command-line tools compiled to WebAssembly: each tool is a module that is called with callMain() on files written into an in-memory file system. The Python and MATLAB packages wrap the same libraries in-process, or call the command-line tools for JSON, XML and dump helpers.

name: icarus-verilog
desc: Verilog simulation and synthesis tool
why: A Verilog simulator that lets you design and watch digital circuits run in software, a real door into hardware design.

brief.what_it_is: Icarus Verilog is a free compiler for Verilog HDL, the hardware description language used to design digital circuits, written by Stephen Williams. You feed it Verilog source files, and it parses them into an internal netlist, elaborates and optimizes that netlist, and then emits output through a selectable code generator. The README's own example compiles a small hello-world module with `iverilog hello.vl` and runs the result as `./a.out`, which prints the message and finishes. The shipped executables are iverilog (the driver), iverilog-vpi, and vvp (the runtime). The README says it compiles all of IEEE 1364 Verilog, plus a growing subset of SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800).
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the project as an attempt to compile all of the Verilog HDL as described in the IEEE 1364 standard, and it notes that 'it's not quite there yet.' It also describes the project as 'a GPL Verilog for Linux', per its credits section, which suggests it was started to give Verilog users a free toolchain.
brief.how_it_works: A preprocessor (ivlpp) handles `include and `define, then a parser builds a 'pform' that is elaborated into a netlist with scope and parameter passes followed by structural and behavioural passes. Optimization passes such as constant propagation run on the netlist, and the target chosen with -t generates the output. The README describes this as a compiler that 'generates code employed by back-end tools' rather than a traditional simulator, and the default vvp target produces a program that runs the simulation.

name: idris2
desc: Pure functional programming language with dependent types
why: A dependently typed language where types can carry proofs about programs, a genuine door into a different way of thinking.

brief.what_it_is: Idris 2 is a purely functional programming language with first-class types, from the Idris project. You write programs and type definitions in .idr source files, and the idris2 compiler checks them against those types, including dependent types where a type can mention a value, such as the length of a list. The compiler then produces an executable. Its package workflow uses an .ipkg project file, and the pack tool fetches libraries from the pack collection.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes Type-Driven Development: treat the type as the plan for a program, and let the compiler and type checker guide you to a complete program that satisfies it. The more expressive the type you start with, the more confidence you can have that the program is correct. Types are first-class, so they can be passed to and returned from functions like any other value, which lets you state relationships between values, make assumptions explicit and checked, and formally prove properties of behaviour.
brief.how_it_works: Types are ordinary values in the language, so a function's type can express properties such as two lists having the same length or a list being non-empty, and the compiler checks those before the program runs. The README does not go deeper into the mechanism. The INSTALL file says the compiler generates code through a Scheme backend, with Chez Scheme by default and Racket as an option.

name: ifuse
desc: FUSE module for iOS devices
why: Mounts an iPhone as a filesystem via usbmuxd and AFC; a door into Apple's device protocols over USB.

brief.what_it_is: ifuse is a command-line FUSE filesystem for iOS devices. You give it a mountpoint and it mounts a directory from a connected iPhone or iPad onto your computer, so you can browse and copy files with ordinary tools. By default it exposes the Media partition (/var/mobile/Media, holding music and pictures). It can also mount the Documents or sandbox container of a named app, and on jailbroken devices it can mount the root filesystem. It talks to the device through libimobiledevice, using usbmuxd over USB and the AFC file protocol.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the wider libimobiledevice project as an effort to let Linux users talk to iOS hardware without iTunes, with the goal to 'allow penguins to talk to fruits'. ifuse is the piece that makes the device's files appear as a normal mounted folder.
brief.how_it_works: ifuse connects to the device through usbmuxd and libimobiledevice, then opens an AFC session that serves files from the chosen directory. It registers that session as a FUSE filesystem via libfuse 3 on Linux or macFUSE on macOS. Reads and writes from the mountpoint are translated into AFC calls. The README says the device is reached through usbmuxd, so that daemon must be running.

brief.install_notes: On macOS: install Xcode command line tools, then install automake, autoconf and libtool with MacPorts or Homebrew. Build and install libplist, libimobiledevice-glue, libusbmuxd and libimobiledevice first. Install macFUSE from its releases page, then allow the macFUSE system extension under Settings > Privacy & Security > Security. That change needs a restart. On Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): apt-get install build-essential, pkg-config, checkinstall, git, autoconf, automake, libtool-bin, libplist-dev, libimobiledevice-dev, libfuse3-dev and usbmuxd. You may need to run 'sudo modprobe fuse' and add your user to the fuse group ('sudo adduser $USER fuse'), then log out and back in. Build with autogen.sh (git) or configure (release tarball), then make and make install. The homepage also offers a Homebrew route for the wider stack (brew install libimobiledevice), but the ifuse README gives the source build steps. No account or signing is mentioned. The device must be trusted and connected by USB.
brief.standout: It is a small, focused FUSE front end over a reimplemented native protocol stack, so you can browse an iPhone's files from a shell with no Apple software. The 'Jailbreak' option to mount the root filesystem is also unusual. The homepage frankly notes that GNOME's GVFS already provides device access, which makes ifuse redundant there.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists ifuse 1.2.0, dated 2025-10-14, as the current download. The README was updated 2026-04-22, and it already points to a 1.2.1 bug-fix release. The homepage download list had not caught up with 1.2.1 when I read it.
brief.caveats: The README warns that version 1.2.0 has a serious bug that corrupts data. The regression came in with commit 36956a and was fixed in 1.2.1 (commit 903a29). The homepage still lists 1.2.0 as the download, so use 1.2.1 or later. The tool needs usbmuxd running and the device trusted. Linux and macOS are the documented platforms (macOS needs macFUSE). Windows is not covered by the ifuse README. By default AFC only exposes the Media chroot. The README says AFC was not built to reach the root filesystem, so --root should be used with care. The README says some jailbreaks (for example blackra1n) do not install AFC2, so --root will not work there. On GNOME, GVFS already offers device access. The license is LGPL-2.1.

name: ike-scan
desc: Discover and fingerprint IKE hosts
why: A door into IPsec IKE handshakes, letting you fingerprint VPN gateways and see how they negotiate.

brief.what_it_is: ike-scan is a command-line scanner that finds hosts speaking IKE, the key exchange protocol behind IPsec VPNs, and fingerprints them. You give it IP addresses, CIDR ranges, hostnames, or a file of targets. It sends IKE phase-1 Main Mode or Aggressive Mode requests and prints the hosts that respond, either with a handshake or a notify message. With --showbackoff it also records response timing for fingerprinting, and the package includes psk-crack, which runs offline pre-shared-key cracking on material ike-scan captures.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says ike-scan "discovers IKE hosts and can also fingerprint them using the retransmission backoff pattern" and lists discovery, fingerprinting, transform enumeration, user enumeration, and pre-shared key cracking as its functions. The author wrote it to learn IKE from the RFCs and a book, and it is maintained as an NTA Monitor project.
brief.how_it_works: ike-scan builds an ISAKMP header and an SA payload with a set of transforms (by default 8 combinations of DES/3DES, MD5/SHA-1 and MODP 768/1024), sends it over UDP to port 500, and rate-limits outbound traffic (default 56000 bits per second). Responses are matched to hosts by IKE cookie rather than source IP, and a handshake response shows the chosen transform. Backoff fingerprinting times the retransmissions from a host that completes a handshake and compares the intervals against a text file of known patterns, ike-backoff-patterns.

brief.install_notes: Standard GNU autotools build: git clone, autoreconf --install, ./configure (or ./configure --with-openssl), make, make check, make install with root or sudo. The README recommends the OpenSSL option if you plan to do pre-shared key cracking, and says it needs OpenSSL headers and libraries, for example libssl-dev on Debian. Windows users can use Cygwin, or a standalone Windows binary with cygwin1.dll present; a README-WIN32 file covers the differences. No accounts or runtime services are mentioned.
brief.standout: Fingerprinting by retransmission timing: hosts that complete a handshake retransmit on a backoff schedule that differs by implementation, and ike-scan matches the timings against a pattern file that users can extend. The README also says ike-scan never answers the responses it receives, so the Main Mode handshake never completes, and that some implementations do not log incomplete handshakes.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README has active-looking CI badges (build, coverage, CodeQL) and a GitHub issues and pull-request workflow, but it shows no release date or last-commit date, and I did not fetch the releases or commits pages. Its supported-platforms list is dated (Debian Woody, Windows NT 4.0 / Cygwin 1.5.12, Mac OS X Darwin 7.7.0), so the list may be stale.
brief.caveats: Built for Unix-like systems; the README says it works on Windows through Cygwin or a standalone binary, and the Windows section points to a separate README-WIN32 file. Any packet loss breaks backoff fingerprinting because every response must be seen. Some VPN servers ignore long packets, and custom transform sets can push packets past the MTU and cause fragmentation. Aggressive Mode is needed for PSK cracking with psk-crack. Only hosts that send a handshake can be fingerprinted by backoff, not hosts that send a notify. The author says some implementations won't log these scans, so the owners may not notice. The README gives no licence in the fetched text. The brew metadata says the package includes psk-crack and gives no separate usage examples for it.
quotes: ike-scan discovers IKE hosts and can also fingerprint them using the retransmission backoff pattern.
ike-scan does not respond to any of the IKE responses it receives, so the IKE main mode handshake will never complete.
