name: imagejs
desc: Tool to hide JavaScript inside valid image files
why: Hides JavaScript inside valid image files, a clever polyglot trick that opens a door into file format ambiguity.

brief.what_it_is: imagejs is a small C command-line tool that packages a JavaScript file into a valid image file, so the output is still a working picture. You give it an output format and a .js file, and it writes an image named after the input plus the format extension (for example code.js.bmp). The README lists bmp, gif, webp, pnm and pgf as output options, and says it can also embed code into an existing gif, bmp or webp file with -i. The bmp output with -l can be viewed as a line of pixels. The README's opening line says only gif and bmp are supported, which conflicts with the later list of formats.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a proof of concept for turning image uploads into a code-execution vector. Its background section says an attacker who can't run a script tag on a site, but can upload a profile picture, could carry script in that image. The idea came from Ajin Abraham's 2014 post on GIFs serving JavaScript, and the author ported it to C and added bitmap support.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the internal mechanism. It says the tool writes the JavaScript into the image file while keeping the file a valid image in the chosen format. For gif, bmp and webp it can embed the code into an existing image with -i. With -l, bmp output stores the code as a line of pixels that can be opened and viewed.

name: immudb
desc: Lightweight, high-speed immutable database
why: An immutable database with cryptographic verification of history, a twist worth an afternoon of poking at tamper-evident storage.

brief.what_it_is: immudb is an open-source database written in Go that adds cryptographic proof and verification to its stored history. It can be used as a key-value store, a document store, or a SQL relational database, and it accepts records, text, images, JSON, and blobs. Writes only add new versions; existing records are never changed or deleted, and reads can come back with a proof that clients check themselves. It runs as a standalone server with gRPC, PostgreSQL wire protocol, and REST access, or embedded in a Go program as a library.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says traditional database transactions and logs are mutable, so there is no way to know for sure whether data has been compromised, and immudb is positioned as a way to store critical data without fear of it being tampered with. The homepage pitches it as a practical alternative to a blockchain or a hosted ledger service, with throughput far beyond blockchains.
brief.how_it_works: Per the tech specs table, the core is a cryptographic commit log with a parallel Merkle tree, plus sync or async indexing on an extended B-tree. Clients verify proofs on their own without trusting the server, and the homepage says the server continuously checks disk and memory consistency. SQL users can call functions such as immudb_verify_row, immudb_verify_tx, and immudb_history to query proofs directly.

Docker and Helm (repo at https://packages.codenotary.org/helm) are also supported. Data storage can be pointed at S3 or an S3-compatible service such as MinIO through IMMUDB_S3_* environment variables, including role-based and Fargate credentials. The README says that when running in Docker you should expose ports 3322 and 9497, while the homepage's docker run example publishes 3322 and 8080 instead. The web console is served with the default immudb/immudb credentials on the online demo, but that is a demo only. The Go embedding guide is in docs/EMBEDDING.md in the repo.
brief.standout: Verification happens on the client side, so a client can check proofs without trusting the server, and the same proof system is exposed through ordinary SQL functions and a PostgreSQL wire endpoint that ORMs like Rails or Django can talk to. It is also the same engine whether you run it as a server or embed it as a Go library with no process at all.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The homepage has a blog post dated 3 September 2026 about release 1.11.2, and it lists a 2026 post about coding agents as recent. The README describes recent 1.11.x changes (structured audit logging, DIFF OF, PostgreSQL compatibility, security hardening). The homepage shows 9.0k and the README mentions 157M Docker Hub pulls. I did not find a last-commit date, so the exact activity level is unverified.
brief.caveats: The license is Business Source License 1.1 (the homepage says 'Source available'), which is not an OSI open-source license, so check the terms before commercial use. The README says there is no official Rust SDK; the crates.io immudb crate is unofficial and unmaintained by the authors, so Rust users are pointed to PostgreSQL clients or generating gRPC code from the protobuf files. The PostgreSQL compatibility layer has known gaps: no generated columns, no stored procedures or PL/pgSQL, only B-tree indexes (no GIN or GiST), no ARRAY/ENUM/composite types. Performance figures come from the author's own benchmark on a 4-core E3-1275v6 with SSD, and the roadmap lists data pruning and compression as not yet built. The PostgreSQL-compatible server logs a warning when run without TLS because cleartext password auth is used. The homepage has a cookie-consent banner about Google Analytics, which is unrelated to the project itself.
quotes: immudb is a database with built-in cryptographic proof and verification. It tracks changes in sensitive data and the integrity of the history will be protected by the clients, without the need to trust the database.
Traditional database transactions and logs are mutable, and therefore there is no way to know for sure if your data has been compromised. immudb is immutable.
You can add new versions of existing records, but never change or delete records. This lets you store critical data without fear of it being tampered.

name: imessage-exporter
desc: Command-line tool to export and inspect local iMessage database
why: Opens and inspects the hidden local iMessage database, a good look at how a consumer app stores data.

brief.what_it_is: imessage-exporter is a Rust command-line tool, also published as a library crate, that reads the local iMessage database (on a Mac, chat.db) or an iOS device backup directory. It exports conversations to txt or html, with optional copying and conversion of attachments, and it can run diagnostics on the database. The README says the binary performs read-only operations. Output goes to ~/imessage_export by default, or to a directory you choose with -o.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to save, back up, archive and migrate iMessage history in open, portable formats, giving users "full ownership and control over your communication history." It also lists data-retention and legal-compliance use. The stated aim is "the most comprehensive and accurate representation of iMessage data available."
brief.how_it_works: The tool opens the SQLite message database and maps handles (phone numbers and emails) to names using the macOS Address Book or a contacts database found in an iOS backup. It then renders each conversation as txt or html, and can copy attachments and convert formats such as HEIC to JPEG and CAF or MOV to MP4. The README says its reverse engineering drew on the typedstream format and the payload_data plist format, and it credits SQLiteFlow and Xplist for that work.

name: inchi
desc: IUPAC International Chemical Identifier
why: Turning molecules into canonical text strings is a real chemistry idea worth an afternoon, though the library itself is fairly plain.

brief.what_it_is: InChI is an open-source structure-based chemical identifier, developed by IUPAC and the InChI Trust. It takes a chemical structure, described by its atoms, bond connectivity, tautomeric, isotope, stereochemistry and charge information, and produces a textual InChI string with those information layers. The README also describes a hashed 27-character InChIKey derived from the InChI, intended for compact storage and search. The repository ships the inchi-1 command-line executable and a C library (libinchi) with the inchi_main demo program. The README's MOLfile and SDfile references suggest molecule files are a main input, but it does not spell out the full input and output workflow.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames InChI as a standard identifier for chemical databases that facilitates information management across chemistry. It says the identifiers are strictly unique, non-proprietary and freely accessible, and that they enable linking chemistry on the web, advancing the FAIR data principles by improving findability and interoperability.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes InChI as layered: the connectivity layer comes first, then tautomeric, isotope, stereochemistry and charge information, each as a separate part of the string. The InChIKey is the hashed, fixed-length form of the InChI. Beta options such as EnhancedStereochemistry rewrite the stereo layers from MOLfile V3000 stereo collections (STEABS, STEREL, STERAC), and the README says those collections are ignored without that option. The README gives no further internal algorithm detail.

name: inform6
desc: Design system for interactive fiction
why: Inform 6 is a classic interactive fiction language with a deep, quirky history, and writing a text adventure is a real door into an unusual craft.

brief.what_it_is: Inform 6 is a compiler for Inform, a C-like design language for writing interactive fiction (text adventures), created by Graham Nelson and first released in 1993. You feed it Inform 6 source files together with the Inform 6 library, and it produces a Z-machine story file that a Z-machine interpreter can run. The README says Inform 6 is now considered stable, with only bug fixes and minor non-breaking features added, and it is also the code generator used by Inform 7. The Homebrew package also ships punyinform, pblorb, and scanblorb helpers, but the README I read does not describe them.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a continuation of a community tradition: after Infocom's Z-machine format was reverse-engineered in the late 1980s, Nelson's Inform made it practical for hundreds of free games to be written by the rec.arts.int-fiction community. name: inko
desc: Safe and concurrent object-oriented programming language
why: A young concurrent object-oriented language with its own ownership model, unusual enough to be worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Inko is a statically typed, object-oriented programming language for concurrent software. Source code goes in as .inko files, which are compiled to native machine code through LLVM and statically linked against a small runtime library written in Rust. The runtime handles process scheduling and non-blocking IO. The language is built around single ownership with move semantics, borrowing through ref and mut, lightweight processes that communicate by messages, and Result-based error handling with try and throw. The homepage and README do not name a version or describe a command-line interface beyond the inko executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Inko exists to make concurrent software easy to build 'without having to worry about unpredictable performance, unexpected runtime errors, data races, and type errors.' The README adds that it aims to be 'a compelling alternative to the likes of Ruby, Erlang, and Go', and not to compete with C and Rust.
brief.how_it_works: Memory is managed deterministically: values start out owned and are dropped when they go out of scope, with no garbage collector. Values can be borrowed immutably with ref or mutably with mut, and moved, and the compiler checks these uses. Concurrency uses lightweight processes defined as async types, which are isolated and communicate by sending messages. The compiler requires data sent between processes to be unique (uni), which removes the need for deep copying.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no install steps. It points to the 'Installing Inko' guide in the Inko manual at https://docs.inko-lang.org/manual/main/setup/installation/. The compiler uses LLVM as its backend, so an LLVM toolchain is probably needed, but I did not confirm the exact requirements from the guide, and I did not read that page.
brief.standout: Single ownership with move semantics and borrowing, applied without a garbage collector, is the unusual part. The concurrency model is described as inspired by Erlang and Pony, with compile-time checks that message data is unique, so the data is moved between processes and not copied.
brief.status: unknown. Neither the homepage nor the GitHub README shows a release version, release date, or last-commit date. The project has an active-looking site, a Discord server, and a GitHub repository, and nothing in the pages suggests it has been abandoned. The scout note calls it a young language.
brief.caveats: The README does not state a version, so the language may still change. Compilation depends on LLVM. The README says Inko does not aim to compete with low-level languages such as C and Rust on performance. Source is under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. Several homepage snippets are deliberately incorrect, such as one Stack example that includes a commented type error, so they are illustrations and not runnable as written. The install guide was not read.
quotes: A language for building concurrent software with confidence
Inko doesn't rely on garbage collection to manage memory. Instead, Inko relies on single ownership and move semantics.
Inko aims to be an efficient language, though it doesn't aim to compete with low-level languages such as C and Rust.

name: interface99
desc: Full-featured interfaces for C99
why: Brings polymorphic interfaces to C99 via macros, a clever hack worth a look though it is a single library.

brief.what_it_is: Interface99 is a single C99 header (interface99.h) that adds polymorphic interfaces to plain C, in the style of Rust traits and Go interfaces. You declare an interface with a list of vfunc lines and call interface(Shape); the macros generate a vtable struct and an interface object struct holding a void *self and a const vptr. You then write ordinary functions for each concrete type, call impl(Shape, Rectangle); to generate the vtable, and build interface values with DYN_LIT or DYN and dispatch them with VCALL. It supports multiple inheritance, superinterfaces, marker interfaces, default implementations, and dynamic dispatch on self. It depends on the Metalang99 preprocessor library for its macro machinery.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants interfaces with minimal boilerplate in pure C, without maintaining vtables by hand, and wants the generated layout to be predictable. The README says it is inspired by Rust and Golang, and that it is meant to stay small: it implements only the software interface concept, not wider OOP features like GObject or COS.
brief.how_it_works: Interface99 is built on Metalang99, a preprocessor metaprogramming library, so the interface and impl macros expand to C structs and vtable instances at compile time. An impl(Iface, T) expansion fills each vtable slot with T_func if the implementer defines it, otherwise falls back to a default Iface_func defined with vfuncDefault. VCALL(obj, func, args...) expands to obj.vptr->func(obj.self, args...), and VSELF(T) casts the untyped self parameter to a typed pointer inside the implementation.

Calls a superinterface method through the subinterface's vtable. Not a shell command.

brief.install_notes: No shell install command is given. Add interface99 and metalang99/include to the include directories and set -ftrack-macro-expansion=0 (GCC) or -fmacro-backtrace-limit=1 (Clang). With CMake, the recommended route is FetchContent_Declare pointing at the GitHub release tarball vx.y.z, then target_link_libraries(MyProject interface99). By default interface99/CMakeLists.txt downloads Metalang99 v1.13.5 from GitHub releases, and you can override that by declaring Metalang99 earlier. Precompiled headers are optional. Needs a standard C99 compiler; the README says no standard library, VLA, or compiler-specific features are required. The README lists GCC, Clang, MSVC, and TCC as tested, and says C++11 and later also works.
brief.standout: The clever part is that impl(Shape, Rectangle) takes no vtable body: the macro fills each slot by name lookup, using Rectangle_perim if it exists or a default Shape_perim otherwise, so adding an implementation is one line. The README also says it has formal code generation semantics, so the data layout is specified rather than left to the compiler. Its error messages are kept readable by building on Metalang99's resilient macro expansion, with the author saying nearly 95 percent of errors make sense.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a CI badge for C/C++ CI, a release procedure that mentions CHANGELOG.md and GitHub Releases, and a pinned Metalang99 v1.13.5, but it gives no release date, version number, or last-commit date. The fetched page was the GitHub repository view, which did not show those dates, so I could not confirm whether it is active.
brief.caveats: Needs Metalang99 as a second dependency, so it is not a single header on its own. Requires -ftrack-macro-expansion=0 on GCC or -fmacro-backtrace-limit=1 on Clang for readable errors. Multiple dispatch is listed as not implemented and unlikely to be. VCALL and its friends break go-to-definition in IDEs and do not highlight function signatures, which the author calls a deliberate trade for concision. Default implementations must follow a strict <iface>_<func> naming convention, and custom overrides need the odd *_CUSTOM () macro. The README does not state a license in the parts I read.
quotes: Full-featured interfaces inspired by Rust and Golang. Multiple inheritance, superinterfaces, and default implementations supported. No external tools required, pure C99.
Minimum boilerplate. Forget about maintaining virtual tables -- just write impl(Shape, Rectangle) and Interface99 will do it for you!
Predictable. Interface99 comes with formal code generation semantics, meaning that the generated data layout is guaranteed to always be the same.
From my experience, nearly 95% of errors make sense.

name: iodine
desc: Tunnel IPv4 traffic through a DNS server
why: Tunnels IPv4 traffic through DNS queries, a striking door into how DNS can be bent to carry arbitrary data.

brief.what_it_is: iodine is a command-line tunnel that carries IPv4 traffic inside DNS queries and replies. You run iodined on a server you control, which owns a delegated subdomain and listens for DNS on UDP port 53, and run iodine on the client, which creates a TUN/TAP interface. The client takes an optional relaying DNS server and the tunnel domain as arguments, and the two ends share a password. The result is a point-to-point IPv4 link that rides on whatever DNS the client can reach. The README says the bandwidth is asymmetric, with limited upstream and up to 1 Mbit/s downstream.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is usable where internet access is firewalled but DNS queries are allowed. The name is a pun: it starts with IOD (IP Over DNS), and iodine has atomic number 53, the DNS port.
brief.how_it_works: The client sends upstream data encoded in the labels of DNS queries, using Base32, Base64, Base64u or Base128 depending on what the relay accepts, and the upstream encoding is autodetected. Downstream data comes back in DNS replies, mainly using the NULL and PRIVATE record types, which carry data without encoding. The server holds each reply until the next query arrives (what the README calls lazy mode), so it always has a query ready to answer with, and the client sends periodic pings to keep that going. Login uses challenge-response with an MD5 hash, and the server drops packets that do not come from the address used at login.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the README needs a TUN/TAP device on every platform (on macOS 10.6 and later, -d utunX uses the built-in utun). Server setup needs a real domain you control, with an NS delegation for a subdomain (for example t1.mydomain.com) pointing at a host with a public IP, plus a BIND zone-file example in the README. Dynamic-DNS hosts work too. Client and server must run the same iodine version, since the protocol is not compatible across versions. Windows needs the OpenVPN TAP32 driver, per the README's portability section. Building from source needs meson, and the tests need the check library.
brief.standout: It uses the DNS NULL record type to send downstream data without encoding, which the README says gives over a kilobyte of payload per reply. Its lazy-reply design and automatic probing of fragment size and request type make it much faster than typical DNS tunnels.
brief.status: Quiet: the homepage lists 0.8.0 as the latest release, dated 2023-04-17. I did not find a commit date in the GitHub README, so I cannot say more about maintenance.
brief.caveats: The README says the tunneled traffic is not encrypted at all and can be read or altered relatively easily, so it recommends running a VPN or SSH inside it. Bandwidth is asymmetric, with downstream up to about 1 Mbit/s per the homepage, and round trips add latency, which the performance tables show. Server and client must run the same protocol version. Some DNS relays break or throttle NULL and TXT, and the README says the -T and -M options may be needed. Its DNS forwarding with -b is not transparent (zone transfers will not work). Routing all traffic through the tunnel takes manual host-route and NAT setup. The code is ISC-licensed, and the README's warranty disclaimer is the standard ISC one.
quotes: iodine lets you tunnel IPv4 data through a DNS server. This can be usable in different situations where internet access is firewalled, but DNS queries are allowed.
The name iodine was chosen since it starts with IOD (IP Over DNS) and since iodine has atomic number 53, which happens to be the DNS port number.
Note: server and client are required to speak the exact same protocol. In most cases, this means running the same iodine version.

name: io
desc: Small prototype-based programming language
why: A small prototype-based language with everything as objects; a compact, strange window into a different model of programming.

brief.what_it_is: Io is a dynamic, prototype-based programming language. The README places it in the same family as Smalltalk and Self and says that everything is a message send from one object to another. You type Io expressions into a REPL or pass it a script file, and it prints evaluated values back, for example 1 + 1 gives ==> 2 and List clone append(30, 10, 5, 20) sort gives list(5, 10, 20, 30). The README's examples build objects by cloning other objects and adding slots at runtime, with no classes involved. The current master branch compiles to a single WASI binary (io_static) that runs under wasmtime, Node, or browsers, and there is a browser REPL.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit motivation beyond describing Io as a dynamic prototype-based language in the Smalltalk and Self family, where objects are created by cloning and extending other objects rather than from classes. The homepage calls it a small prototype-based language with everything as objects.
brief.how_it_works: Every operation is a message sent from one object to another, and new objects are made with clone and then extended by setting slots, as in Contact := Object clone and Contact fullAddress := method(...). On the current master branch, Io targets WebAssembly; the native addon system (DynLib, AddonLoader, Eerie) is not available there, and host integration goes through a bidirectional JavaScript bridge in which Io code can call JS functions and JS can call Io methods.

name: ipmitool
desc: Utility for IPMI control with kernel driver or LAN interface
why: A door into IPMI, the out-of-band management backdoor hiding in almost every server, though the tool itself is plain plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: ipmitool is a command-line utility for talking to the BMC (baseboard management controller), the separate service processor in IPMI-capable hardware. It sends IPMI request messages and parses the responses. It can read sensor data and print sensor values, display the System Event Log, print FRU inventory, read and set LAN configuration, and control remote chassis power. It reaches the BMC through the local system interface on Linux or over the network via IPMI-over-LAN (lan and lanplus interfaces). The package also ships ipmievd, a daemon that listens for BMC events and logs them to syslog.
brief.why_it_exists: Written by Duncan Laurie, who began it while between projects at Sun Microsystems: remote chassis power control was the first goal, and it grew into a general tool. The README says it is for system administrators who like the simplicity and scriptability of command-line utilities, and for people debugging or developing their own BMC implementations. It is explicitly not meant as enterprise management software.
brief.how_it_works: ipmitool builds IPMI requests (netfn, command, and payload) and sends them over an interface: the Linux OpenIPMI kernel driver through /dev/ipmi0, or RMCP/RMCP+ packets over UDP port 623 for LAN access. The README also documents IPMB bridging, where the driver encapsulates a request with the send message command (0x34) and retrieves the reply with get message (0x33), tracking request and response pairs. Commands can be run one at a time, in an interactive shell, or from a script file with exec.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: you need IPMI hardware (a BMC) and, for the local interface on Linux, the OpenIPMI kernel modules ipmi_msghandler and ipmi_devintf, plus ipmi_si or the older per-type driver modules, with the device node /dev/ipmi0 pointing at the driver's dynamically assigned major number (check /proc/devices for 'ipmidev'). The package includes the sample scripts ipmi.init (boot-time device setup) and bmclanconf (LAN configuration over the system interface). IPMIv2.0 LAN access (lanplus) needs an OpenSSL library with the required encryption functions. The build is autotools-based (configure.ac, Makefile.am, and a bootstrap script that the README mentions adding Mac support to). The README does not walk through a source build, so I did not read INSTALL.
brief.standout: The README documents IPMB bridging and dual-bridged commands in unusual depth, with concrete addresses and channel numbers, and it is candid about where the tool fails (for example, fru print cannot pass through two levels of encapsulation). Its design is plain, scriptable, and openly modest: it is a probe and control tool rather than a fleet manager.
brief.status: maintained. The Codeberg repo shows 2,186 commits, 9 branches and 28 tags, with the latest commit on master dated 2026-03-30 (a fru fix that resolves issue #81). It has 12 open issues and 10 open pull requests, and CI runs on Codeberg via .woodpecker.yml. The README says the project moved from GitHub (2018 to 2023) and SourceForge (up to 2018). Latest release date was not checked.

Originally it supported Solaris, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD, but as of 2025 the maintainers no longer check changes against those systems, and CI only builds on Ubuntu Noble, Ubuntu Plucky, Ubuntu Questing, and Fedora 39, 41 and 42. The IPMI-over-LAN feature can be 'dangerous' to enable on some buggy BMCs, and shared management NICs that intercept port 623 carry extra security risk. Some commands fail under double bridging because of payload size. You need actual IPMI hardware to do anything useful. The README states a BSD license in the background section. Warnings about default passwords appear only implicitly in the examples (admin).

name: ios-webkit-debug-proxy
desc: DevTools proxy for iOS devices
why: A door into the remote debugging protocol iOS exposes over USB, letting you talk to Safari's inspector from a desktop.

brief.what_it_is: ios_webkit_debug_proxy (iwdp) is a command-line proxy that takes in the debugging traffic iOS devices expose over USB through the usbmuxd daemon and re-exposes it over websocket. Developers can then send commands to MobileSafari and UIWebViews on real and simulated iOS devices. It serves a device list at localhost:9221, and each device's tabs on its own port (9222 onward). The output is a set of JSON endpoints and websocket URLs that DevTools-style frontends can connect to.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way for developers to reach MobileSafari and UIWebViews on real and simulated iOS devices from a desktop. It notes that recent Chrome DevTools and Safari's WebKit inspector protocols have diverged, so newer Chrome DevTools no longer works with Safari directly.
brief.how_it_works: The proxy talks to usbmuxd, which handles the USB connection to each attached device, and bridges that to websocket clients. Each attached device gets its own port, assigned first-come-first-serve and preserved across detach and reattach until the proxy restarts. The -f flag selects which DevTools frontend HTML page is served, and -c sets the device-to-port mapping.

name: ipsw

name: jack
desc: Audio Connection Kit
why: A low-latency audio connection kit that lets programs patch audio between each other, a door into live audio routing.

brief.what_it_is: JACK (JACK Audio Connection Kit) is a sound server API plus a pair of daemon implementations that provide real-time, low-latency connections for audio and MIDI data between applications. Programs connect to it as clients, and the server moves audio and MIDI between them so one program's output can feed another program's input. The homepage describes it as a professional tool for routing audio between software and sharing devices, with a cross-platform API for developers. The executable named in the metadata is jackd.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the problem as wanting to send one program's audio output to another, or to several others, and then record the result in the first program. It also pitches JACK to developers who need a cross-platform API for device sharing and inter-application audio routing that is easy to learn and use.
brief.how_it_works: JACK runs as a server daemon that drives a processing graph of clients, each of which runs once per audio cycle. The JACK2 README (jackdmp, a C++ implementation for multiprocessor machines) says it uses a data-flow activation model that lets clients run simultaneously when they are independent in the graph, and lock-free graph access so connections can change without interrupting the audio stream. The server can run in synchronous mode, waiting for all clients each cycle, or asynchronous mode, reusing the previous cycle's output for clients that miss a deadline.
brief.install_notes: The README and homepage give no install steps, no runtime or hardware requirements, and no first-run configuration beyond the brew install already named in the metadata. The README does mention that JACK2 is a separate implementation (jackdmp) from the original JACK1 server, which may matter when choosing a build, but it does not say which one the Homebrew formula installs.
brief.standout: Unlike a plain audio router, JACK is a real-time server that treats audio and MIDI as one routing graph that any program can join. JACK2 adds a lock-free graph and an asynchronous mode that reuses the previous cycle's output, so a late client yields a partial result rather than a dropout for everyone.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched pages show no release date, last-commit date, or version. The JACK2 README carries a Travis CI badge pointing to travis-ci.org, which is a legacy hosting address, so it may be stale, but I could not confirm that from the pages I read.
brief.caveats: The README describes JACK2 as aimed at multiprocessor machines and does not say which platforms it supports. The fetched pages give no usage examples, so I could not show how to start jackd or connect a client. Install and configuration details were not in the pages I read. The Travis CI badge points to a legacy service, so the project's current CI status is unclear.
quotes: JACK Audio Connection Kit (or JACK) is a professional sound server API and pair of daemon implementations to provide real-time, low-latency connections for both audio and MIDI data between applications.
Have you ever wanted to take the audio output of one piece of software and send it to another?

name: jaguar
desc: Live reloading for your ESP32
why: Live reloading on ESP32 via the Toit language is a neat workflow, though it leans toward toolchain plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: Jaguar is a live-reloading workflow for ESP32 boards programmed in Toit. The host side is a command-line tool called jag, and a small Toit application that jag installs on the ESP32. You point jag at a Toit source file, it compiles the program and sends it to the device over WiFi, and the device stops the old version, installs the new one in flash, and restarts it from main. The README says the cycle takes under two seconds, with no reflashing over serial and no reboot. The device-side piece also runs an HTTP server and can keep named containers running at boot.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's framing is that flashing over serial, rebooting the device, and waiting for it to rejoin the network makes embedded iteration slow, and Jaguar removes those steps so you can 'iterate quickly and learn fast'.
brief.how_it_works: Jaguar runs a small HTTP server on the ESP32 that listens for incoming requests. Each request carries a compiled Toit program, which is relocated and installed in flash on the device. Before installing, Jaguar stops any old version of the program and frees its resources, then the new version starts again from main.

Linux archive installs need the embedded jag binary placed on PATH by hand. Hardware: an ESP32 connected by serial cable for the first flash, then WiFi. On Linux you need access to /dev/ttyUSB0, usually via the uucp or dialout group (sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER, then log out and back in). Go users can run go install github.com/toitlang/jaguar/cmd/jag@latest with Go 1.16+. Building from source needs the Toit repo checkout (JAG_TOIT_REPO_PATH), ESP-IDF sourced from the patched copy inside Toit's third_party directory, then make. The Toit VS Code extension finds the SDK automatically if jag is on PATH.
brief.standout: The device runs a tiny HTTP-served Toit program that accepts new compiled programs over WiFi and swaps them in place, so there is no reflash in the loop. Its per-run options are also useful: -D jag.wifi=false lets an app take over the WiFi radio for something like a soft access point, and a UART proxy can carry Jaguar commands over the serial cable.

name: janet
desc: Dynamic language and bytecode vm
why: A small Lisp-like language with a bytecode VM and PEG grammar support, unusual and fun to explore.

brief.what_it_is: Janet is a dynamic, functional-and-imperative programming language with a bytecode virtual machine, mostly written in standard C99. You run it by typing code into its REPL or by passing it a script file such as janet myscript.janet, and it prints results or program output. Its syntax is prefix notation in the Lisp style. The homepage says the whole language (core library, interpreter, compiler, assembler, PEG) is under 1MB. Projects can be exported as standalone executables with the companion build tool jpm.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches Janet as a system scripting language and as a language to embed in other programs, and says it suits rapid prototyping and other domains where dynamic languages shine. It positions itself as embeddable but with more included out of the box than most embeddable languages, such as threads, networking, an event loop, subprocess handling and PEG.
brief.how_it_works: The janet binary runs as a bytecode VM: source is read, compiled, and executed, and the compiler can also write an image file with the --compile option. Janet is embedded by adding a single C source file and a single header (janet.c and janet.h) to a host project. Parsing Expression Grammars are built into the core library rather than supplied as a separate package.

name: jasmin
desc: Assembler for the Java Virtual Machine
why: Writing JVM bytecode by hand exposes the machine beneath Java, a strange and instructive way to see how programs really run.

brief.what_it_is: Jasmin is an assembler for the Java Virtual Machine. It takes ASCII source files written in a simple assembler-like syntax that uses JVM instruction mnemonics, and converts them into binary Java .class files that a Java runtime can load. The source file's .class directive decides where the output class file goes. The assembler does little checking: it does not verify that referenced classes exist or that type descriptors are well formed.
brief.why_it_exists: Jasmin was created by Jon Meyer as a companion to his O'Reilly book 'Java Virtual Machine', so readers could try out JVM features directly. The homepage says it has since become the de-facto standard assembly format for Java and is used in dozens of compiler classes around the world.
brief.how_it_works: Source is tokenized on whitespace into directives (names starting with '.'), instructions (standard JVM opcode mnemonics), and labels. Class and method names use class-file conventions, so java/lang/String rather than java.lang.String, and methods are written as one token such as java/io/PrintStream/println(Ljava/lang/String;)V. The assembler emits a class file; with -g it adds line-number information for debuggers.

brief.standout: Jasmin is a thin, literal assembler: it maps almost one-to-one onto class-file structure and deliberately skips verification, so you can hand-write bytecode that a compiler would never emit and see what the JVM does with it. The guide is candid that it is a teaching and experimentation tool, not a macro assembler.

brief.caveats: The assembler does no compile-time checking of class references or descriptors, so mistakes show up only at runtime or in the verifier. Numeric support is limited: no scientific notation, character literals, or octal. String escape support is basic, with only \n and \t documented. Labels cannot start with a digit or contain = : . " -. Methods get no implicit return and must end with one. The guide doesn't cover every instruction; the JVM spec is needed for that. The homepage's 'Download' link to SourceForge was not followed, so I have no version number or licence statement. The homepage's copyright line is 2004, Jonathan Meyer.

name: jbigkit
desc: JBIG1 data compression standard implementation
why: JBIG1 bilevel image compression is a neat window into a fax-era standard, though the tool itself is plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: JBIG-KIT is a C software implementation of the JBIG1 lossless compression standard (ITU-T T.82 / ISO/IEC 11544), aimed at bi-level images such as scanned documents. It is a portable library for encoding and decoding JBIG1 streams, plus ready-to-use command-line converters that work like netpbm's tools: they take PBM/PGM bitmaps in and write JBIG data out, and reverse the process. The package has two variants: jbig.c implements nearly all of the standard but holds the full uncompressed image in memory, while jbig85.c implements the ITU-T T.85 profile with low memory use for embedded and fax work. The homepage says it is also usable for grayscale images up to 6 bits per pixel.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a ready-to-embed reference implementation of JBIG1, a lossless bi-level standard that the author says beats G4 fax compression on typical scanned documents by about 1.1 to 1.5 times, and that is widely used in fax products, printer firmware and document management systems.
brief.how_it_works: JBIG1 uses arithmetic coding over pixel neighbourhoods (templates) and can encode an image progressively as a low-resolution layer followed by resolution-enhancement layers, so a viewer can show a coarse version while the rest arrives. The library is built to decode incomplete and growing streams and to handle several streams at once, with no global or static variables. The homepage does not go into further mechanism detail.

name: jigdo
desc: Tool to distribute very large files over the internet
why: Jigdo's template-based distribution of huge files from many mirrors is a clever, forgotten transfer scheme worth understanding.

brief.what_it_is: Jigdo (Jigsaw Download) is a command-line toolkit for distributing very large files, such as CD or DVD images, over the internet. The publisher runs jigdo-file on the image and on a set of source files. It produces a small human-readable .jigdo description file and a binary .template file. A user gives the .jigdo file to a download client, which fetches the pieces of the image from one or more mirrors and reassembles the exact image. The homepage says the goal is downloading images as easy as clicking a direct download link in a browser. The three executables named in the brew metadata are jigdo-file, jigdo-lite and jigdo-mirror. The homepage describes the tool family in general and does not document these three executables individually.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it exists to make downloading very large images as easy for users as a direct browser download link, while avoiding the hosting problems server administrators have with such large files. The man page adds that it was made primarily for ISO9660 and UDF images but could also serve large audio, video or software packages.
brief.how_it_works: jigdo-file scans the image with a rolling checksum inspired by rsync and finds the regions that match known input files. Matched data is left out of the template and replaced with a checksum reference, while unmatched data such as directory information is compressed into the template. The .jigdo file is an INI-style text file that maps each part's checksum to one or more labelled server locations, so mirrors can be added by editing it. Format v1 uses MD5 checksums. Format v2, added in 0.8.0, uses SHA256 and is not readable by pre-0.8.0 tools.

The mirror layout is a plain text file that can be edited without rebuilding the image.

name: joern
desc: Open-source code analysis platform based on code property graphs
why: Code property graph platform lets you query source and binaries as a graph, a genuinely different way to take code apart.

brief.what_it_is: Joern is an open-source platform for analyzing source code, bytecode, and binary executables. It turns code into code property graphs (CPGs), a graph representation of the program, and stores them in a custom graph database. You then mine that graph with search queries written in a Scala-based domain-specific query language, through an interactive shell (the `joern` REPL) or a server mode with a REST API. Input is source or binaries; output is query results, and it can also run scanners built on those queries.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is developed 'with the goal of providing a useful tool for vulnerability discovery and research in static program analysis.' The homepage frames it as 'The Bug Hunter's Workbench' and says it uncovers attack surface, sloppy coding practices, and variants of known vulnerabilities.
brief.how_it_works: Language frontends (the *2cpg tools) parse code, tolerating missing build environments, and build a CPG that layers syntax, control flow, data flow and call information into one graph. The docs say it is 'a language-agnostic intermediate representation,' and that the graph is extended by 'CPG passes.' Analysts then query the graph, including a taint-analysis engine that tracks attacker-controlled data statically. Queries can be wrapped into scanners (joern-scan) and run in CI.

name: john-jumbo
desc: Enhanced version of john, a UNIX password cracker
why: The enhanced John the Ripper gives a hands-on look at hashing formats and cracking internals, a strong door into security thinking.

brief.what_it_is: John the Ripper jumbo is the community-enhanced build of John the Ripper, a password security auditing and password recovery tool. You give it password hash files or encrypted files, and it tries guesses across several cracking modes (wordlist, rules, and others) to recover the plaintext. Beyond the core crypt(3) types, jumbo supports hundreds of hash and cipher formats, including Windows NTLM, macOS and web-app hashes, SSH and GnuPG private keys, ZIP, RAR and 7z archives, PDFs, Office documents, and disk images. Cracked passwords print to the terminal and are saved to a potfile, and larger encrypted files are first converted with a bundled *2john helper whose output is fed into jumbo.

Values are dual-ported objects, so the string form and the internal form can both be used without repeated conversion.

name: john
desc: Featureful UNIX password cracker
why: John the Ripper is a famous password cracker, but its format-cracking depth makes it a real window into hash internals.

brief.what_it_is: John the Ripper is a free, open-source password security auditing and password recovery tool for many operating systems. You give it password hash files (such as a Unix passwd or shadow copy, or exported hashes from other formats) and it tries guesses against them using wordlists, rules, and other cracking modes, printing any passwords it recovers. The 'jumbo' build adds support for hundreds of hash and cipher types, including web-app and database hashes, SSH and GnuPG private keys, archives (ZIP, RAR, 7z), PDFs, Office documents, and disk images. Output is cracked plaintext shown in the terminal and saved to a pot file.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as a password security auditing tool, and the README says its primary purpose is to detect weak Unix passwords. The README also says it was built to combine several cracking modes in one fast, configurable program that runs the same way across platforms.
brief.how_it_works: John runs a set of cracking modes (wordlist, rules-based mangling, incremental and others) against the hashes in the files you pass it, auto-detecting the hash type. Cracked results go to a pot file ($JOHN/john.pot), which is also used to skip hashes already cracked on later runs. Sessions save state to john.rec on abort or every 10 minutes, so they can be resumed with --restore. Jumbo users run a bundled *2john helper first to convert larger files (archives, documents, keys) into hashes that John can load.

Packages exist in several Linux distributions, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, and as an Ubuntu snap. Downloads come with GPG signatures.

name: joker
desc: Small Clojure interpreter, linter and formatter
why: A small Clojure interpreter with linter and formatter; an unusual lisp dialect worth an afternoon of poking.

brief.what_it_is: Joker is a small interpreted dialect of Clojure, written in Go, that also works as a Clojure and ClojureScript linter and formatter. You can run scripts written in its .joke files, use it as a REPL, or pipe source in on stdin. Linter mode takes a source file and prints warnings and errors as file:line:column messages. Format mode reads Clojure source and writes pretty-printed code to standard output. A task runner reads public functions from a tasks.joke file and runs them by name.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants a Clojure-flavoured language that is suitable for scripting, with lightweight, fast startup, because Clojure itself is not good at that. The README also states a goal of good error messages and stack traces, and of providing tooling for Clojure and its dialects.
brief.how_it_works: Joker is an interpreter. The README says it executes bytecode by default and has a VM, documented in VM.md. Lint mode reads and parses every form in a file and reports Read error, Read warning, Parse error, Parse warning or Exception. Settings go in a .joker config file that is found by walking up the directory tree, and it can list known macros, ignored namespaces and rules. The core namespaces are built in, and the README says a gen_code step pre-builds them into the executable to speed up startup.

name: jolie
desc: Service-oriented programming language
why: A service-oriented language where programs are microservices and communication is first-class, a genuinely different way to think about code.

brief.what_it_is: Jolie is a programming language for building systems out of services. Per the homepage, the basic building blocks are services that can be relocated and replicated as needed, and a composition of services is itself a service. Jolie is contract-first: types and interfaces (for example requestResponse and oneWay operations) are declared up front, and the interpreter handles data transformations between types. The homepage's sample takes a JSON HTTP request with a name field and returns a greeting string. The brew package ships a set of executables, including jolie, joliec, joliedoc, joliemock, metaservice, and converters such as wsdl2jolie, openapi2jolie, jolie2java, and jolie2wsdl; those names come from the package metadata, not from the homepage.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Jolie as a way to make the concepts of service-oriented computing into linguistic constructs, so that the building blocks of software are services rather than objects or functions. It is pitched at microservices and APIs, and at keeping a monolith's logic unchanged while it is split across machines.
brief.how_it_works: A Jolie program is a service with input ports (location, protocol, interfaces) and a main block that handles operations. The same logic can run locally or remotely, and one program can be exposed over several protocols at once (the homepage shows HTTP/JSON, SOAP, and a binary protocol called SODEP on separate ports). Native operators express workflow: the homepage example 'login( credentials )() { checkCredentials }; { publish( x ) | edit( y ) }' uses ';' for sequence and '|' for parallel. Fault handling uses scope and install so handlers can be changed at runtime. Java and JavaScript code can be embedded, and new protocols can be added through a Java API.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps. Its Download page is linked from the navigation, but both guessed paths (download.html and download) returned 404, so I could not verify the install process, runtime requirements, or first-run steps. The homepage links to a tutorial titled 'Get Started Now' for a first project, which I did not reach.
brief.standout: Jolie makes the service itself the unit of code: the same program can move from local to remote or be split across machines without changing its logic, and a composition of services is again a service you can expose. The language also has built-in sequence and parallel operators and runtime-updatable fault handlers for parallel code, which is not common in mainstream languages.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows a copyright range of 2014-2024 and a News section, but I found no release date, commit date, or maintenance note on the pages I could read.
brief.caveats: I could not reach the Download or Docs pages, so platform support, install steps, and build requirements are unverified. The homepage claims formal semantics and use in research and teaching but gives no details. Licensing: the website text is CC BY 4.0 and the code samples are GPL v2, per the footer; the language's own license was not stated on the homepage. The brief's executable list comes from package metadata, not from documentation I read. The homepage's 'Vision' and 'About' pages were not fetched.
quotes: Jolie crystallises the programming concepts of service-oriented computing as linguistic constructs.
The basic building blocks of software are not objects or functions, but rather services that can be relocated and replicated as needed. A composition of services is a service.
Jolie is a contract-first programming language, which puts API design at the forefront.

name: joyce
desc: Emulates the Amstrad PCW on Unix, Windows and macOS

brief.what_it_is: JOYCE is an emulator of the Amstrad PCW, the all-in-one word processor computer, for Unix, Windows and Mac OS X, written in SDL. It runs the PCW's CP/M environment and emulates its hardware, and it incorporates ANNE, an emulator of the later PcW16. The homepage mentions PCW disc images in DSK format, host folders mapped as emulated drives, and host joysticks, and output goes to an emulated PCW screen, with printer output that can be written to PDF or PNG files. The page covers the emulator and its downloads, plus a set of PCW hardware and software reference material.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit mission statement. It is the author's own project page (John Elliott's site, seasip.info) and is framed around keeping the PCW machine and its software usable, with a large reference archive of hardware, file formats and public-domain catalogues alongside the emulator.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals beyond saying it is written using SDL and that it incorporates ANNE for the PcW16. Its update history mentions a Z80 emulation, a MYZ80 hard drive emulation, and a GSX graphics driver, but it does not describe the architecture in detail.
brief.install_notes: The homepage lists Downloads and a FAQ, but the text I received did not include their URLs, so I did not follow them. From the page alone I found no install steps, runtimes or accounts. The brew executables are dskconv, dsklabel, lsgotek, xanne and xjoyce. The homepage mentions a configuration script in its history, and says the Windows build is a separate pack. Source builds on Linux and macOS are implied by the history notes about GCC, libpng and C++17 compile fixes.
brief.standout: It is a full hardware-level emulator of a 1990s word-processor appliance that also runs CP/M, and it has been kept current through a long run of releases. It also comes with an unusually deep archive of the machine's documentation and a security fix against malicious CP/M programs touching host files.

name: julius
desc: Two-pass large vocabulary continuous speech recognition engine
why: A classic open speech recognition engine; worth poking at to see how decoding actually works, though it's old and niche.

brief.what_it_is: Julius is an open-source large vocabulary continuous speech recognition (LVCSR) decoder, written for speech researchers and developers. It takes live microphone or network audio, or a list of audio files, and needs a language model (word N-gram in ARPA format, or a rule-based grammar) plus an acoustic model (HTK ASCII HMM definitions, or a DNN-HMM). It outputs recognized word sequences and can also produce N-best lists, word graphs, confusion networks, forced alignments and confidence scores. It runs as a command-line program, a server, or a library with a simple API, and the README says it is mainly for Linux and other Unix, with Windows, Mac and Android also supported.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Julius has been developed as research software for Japanese LVCSR since 1997, continued through the IPA Japanese dictation toolkit project, the Continuous Speech Recognition Consortium (CSRC) and the Interactive Speech Technology Consortium (ISTC). Its stated goal is a high-performance, small-footprint decoder that runs in real time on everything from micro-computers to cloud servers.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes a 2-pass tree-trellis search built on word N-gram and context-dependent HMMs. It uses a tree-organized lexicon, 1-best or word-pair context approximation, rank and score pruning, N-gram factoring, cross-word context handling, enveloped beam search, and Gaussian pruning and selection. The search is kept independent of model structure, so shared-state triphones, tied-mixture models and DNN front ends can be swapped in.

name: judy
desc: State-of-the-art C library that implements a sparse dynamic array
why: A sparse dynamic array library with a clever trie-based design; an unusual data structure worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Judy is a C library that implements a sparse dynamic array. Per the homepage, Judy arrays are declared with a null pointer and consume memory only when populated, yet can grow to use available memory. The API uses simple insert, retrieve, and delete calls, and sort, search, count, and sequential access are built in. The page says Judy can replace arrays, sparse arrays, hash tables, B-trees, binary trees, linear lists, skiplists, and some sort and search and counting code. The homepage does not describe the inputs and outputs in detail.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Judy as a scalable, high-performance, memory-efficient way to get dynamically sized and associative arrays without rework for expansion or contraction. It says tuning and configuring are not required, and in fact not even possible.
brief.standout: The homepage claims a single structure can stand in for many common data structures (hash tables, B-trees, skiplists, and others) while needing no tuning. It also says the array is unbounded, sized only by machine memory, and allocates only for populated elements. The scout note calls the design trie-based, but the homepage I read does not confirm that.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage footer reads 'Modified: 11/10/04' and '© 2004 Judy Team', so the site has not been updated in a long time. I did not check the Downloads or News pages for a later release, and brew provided no version info.
brief.caveats: The homepage is short and marketing-toned, with no code sample, platform list, or license on this page. Its only technical content is in linked pages (a 10-minute and a 3-hour technical description, Documentation, Downloads, Errors, Glossary) that I did not follow, because the fetch returned text with the link URLs stripped. The 'state-of-the-art' wording is the project's own phrasing from 2004. The homepage was reachable.

name: juman
desc: Japanese morphological analysis system
why: A Japanese morphological analyser from Kyoto University, a rare piece of old NLP worth taking apart for its lattice-based segmentation.

brief.what_it_is: JUMAN is a Japanese morphological analyser from Kyoto University's Language Media Processing Lab. It takes Japanese text (UTF-8 since version 7.0) and splits it into morphemes, one per line, giving each token's surface form, reading, dictionary base form, part of speech and conjugation info, with an EOS line closing each sentence. The homepage's sample shows it handling informal and non-standard spellings such as ビミョーだ, ありがとー and 行きたぁぁぁい. The executable is juman, and it reads from stdin, e.g. juman < sample.txt.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it was built to give many researchers studying computational analysis of Japanese a common morphological analysis tool, and that school grammar is poorly suited to computers, so the grammar definitions and the connection rules between words can be changed easily by the user.
brief.how_it_works: The fetched pages do not describe the segmentation algorithm; the 'lattice-based' framing in the scout notes is not confirmed by anything I read. The repository tree does show makemat (source for connectivity rules), makeint (dictionary conversion) and makepat (a Patricia database), and the sample output carries auto-acquired tags such as 自動獲得:Wikipedia and 既知語帰着, which suggests dictionary lookup plus connection-rule scoring, but I did not verify that from the text.

name: kaitai-struct-compiler
desc: Compiler for generating binary data parsers
why: Describe a binary format in YAML and generate parsers for it, a strong tool for taking file formats apart.

brief.what_it_is: Kaitai Struct is a declarative language for describing binary data layouts, such as file formats and network packet formats, in a .ksy file. The ksc compiler takes that .ksy file and generates source code for a parser in one of the supported programming languages. The generated code reads the described structure from a file or stream and exposes its fields through an API. The site lists C++/STL, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Lua, Nim, Perl, PHP, Python, Ruby, and Rust as targets, with Swift listed among runtime libraries. The project also ships an IDE, a visualizer, and a library of format descriptions.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says that reading and writing binary formats is hard, especially for interchange formats that must work across platforms and languages, and that hand-written parsing code is repetitive, error-prone, and hard to debug. The goal is to describe the format once and use it from any supported language.
brief.how_it_works: You write a .ksy file that declares the format, using fields such as seq with types like u2 and u4, plus endianness and nested types. You can check the parse with the visualizer, then compile the .ksy with ksc into a source file for your target language. You add the small KS runtime library for that language to your project, and the generated class parses the data and gives access to its fields.

commands_seen.context: Homebrew install of the compiler on macOS or Linux, listed as the Homebrew option under Downloading and installing.

Windows users get an MSI installer, or a portable universal .zip. The .zip and MSI need Java, with LTS 21 recommended and Java 8 as the minimum, and the universal build bundles its jars and launcher scripts. Building from source needs git, Java, sbt, and a POSIX shell for tests. Your project also needs the KS runtime library for its language. The runtimes are described as small.

name: katago
desc: Neural Network Go engine with no human-provided knowledge
why: A Go engine learning from self-play alone is a real AI rabbit hole, though it is somewhat known in the Go community.

brief.what_it_is: KataGo is an open-source Go engine (board game) that uses a neural network trained purely by self-play. It runs as a command-line GTP engine with no graphical interface of its own: a GUI or analysis tool launches it and sends it moves over the Go Text Protocol. It takes a neural network weights file (.bin.gz) plus a config file, and returns move choices, win rates, estimated score, and territory ownership. It also has a JSON-based analysis engine for batch evaluation of whole games. The brew formula installs the engine binary, not the training run.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a strong Go bot that reaches top levels from scratch with no outside data, improving only via self-play, and as a tool for players and developers that estimates score and territory rather than only win rate. The homepage also hosts KataGo's public distributed training run, where volunteers contribute GPU time to self-play.
brief.how_it_works: KataGo is an AlphaZero-like self-play system with many added enhancements, written in C++. It uses Monte-Carlo Graph Search, which extends MCTS to graphs instead of trees, and it has six neural-network backends (OpenCL, CUDA, TensorRT, ROCm, ONNX Runtime, Eigen CPU, plus Metal on macOS via Homebrew). The README points to arXiv 1902.10565 and docs/KataGoMethods.md for the methods.

name: keyd
desc: Key remapping daemon for Linux
why: A key remapping daemon that works at the kernel input layer, a fascinating look at how keyboards become events on Linux.

brief.what_it_is: keyd is a key remapping daemon for Linux. It runs system-wide and intercepts keyboard input at the kernel input layer (evdev, with uinput for output), then emits remapped events through a virtual keyboard device. Its config is a plain INI-style file, usually /etc/keyd/default.conf, with sections like [ids] and [main] and bindings such as capslock = overload(control, esc). It supports layers, oneshot modifiers, tap/hold overloading, per-keyboard config, and Unicode output. Optional per-application remapping is marked experimental.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Linux lacks a good key remapping solution, and that people usually have to chain tools like xcape and xmodmap, which tie the result to X11. keyd is meant to be a single display-server-independent daemon that works at the kernel level.
brief.how_it_works: keyd reads raw events from physical keyboards through evdev and applies the mappings from its config. It then writes the results to a virtual device created through uinput, which is why the same config works in a VT, under X, or under Wayland. Because it sits below the display server, libinput sees a single virtual keyboard, and the README notes that this can break libinput's disable-while-typing trackpad behaviour unless a quirks override is added.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no Homebrew instructions. Its installation options are: build from source with a C compiler and Linux kernel headers (git clone, make, sudo make install), or install a distro package (Debian 13 and later, Ubuntu 25.04 and later, Arch extra, Alpine, Fedora COPR, Gentoo GURU, openSUSE, Void). After installing, enable the systemd service, put the config in /etc/keyd/default.conf, and run sudo keyd reload. Optional extras are python (for application-specific remapping), python-xlib (X support), and dbus-python (KDE support). The README says master is the development branch and tagged releases are the stable ones.
brief.standout: Layers, oneshot modifiers, and tap/hold overloads are usually found only in QMK-style keyboard firmware, and keyd brings them to the OS level with a short config format. The README also says the core is written in C in under 2000 lines, aiming at a sub-millisecond input loop.

Application-specific remapping is marked experimental. The README warns that master may break between releases.

name: kim-api
desc: Knowledgebase of Interatomic Models (KIM) API
why: Knowledgebase and API for interatomic potentials in molecular simulation, real science but mostly infrastructure for researchers.

brief.what_it_is: OpenKIM is a curated repository of interatomic potentials (also called force fields or models) for atomistic simulation, with a Knowledgebase of Interatomic Models (KIM) API that lets many simulation codes load these models without modification. The site lists about 1,532 models, 40 model drivers, 26 test drivers, and 220,789 tests, and offers search by element and by material. The kim-api package is the software layer: it takes a model name from the knowledgebase and provides a common interface so that codes such as LAMMPS, ASE, DL_POLY, and GULP can call it. Each potential is checked for coding integrity and benchmarked against material properties.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the goal as helping users "discover and use the best potentials for their research" through a "simple plug-and-play API". The KIM API docs describe a standard Portable Model Interface so one implementation of a model can run in several simulators unmodified.
brief.how_it_works: The KIM API defines the Portable Model Interface (PMI) for models and the Simulator Model Interface (SMI) for packaging a model's native simulator input, parameters, and metadata (supported species, units). A portable model can carry its code and parameters together, or carry only parameters and use a separate model driver library. Bindings exist for C++, C, Fortran, Python, and Julia.

name: kimwitu++
desc: Tool for processing trees (i.e. terms)
why: A term-rewriting tree processor from the compiler toolkit era, obscure and a little old-school strange.

brief.what_it_is: Kimwitu++ is a meta tool for processing trees (terms), used mainly to generate software, especially compilers. It has its own input language for defining a tree structure and functions that operate on the tree. From that input it generates a set of C++ files, which are then compiled and bound into a program with a C++ compiler. It is the successor to Kimwitu and is licensed under the GNU GPL v2 or later.
brief.why_it_exists: The project page presents it as a tool for building compilers, where a parser (for example lex and yacc) handles the grammar and Kimwitu++ builds the abstract syntax tree that later passes work on. Its successor relationship to Kimwitu is the only other framing the page gives.
brief.how_it_works: Kimwitu++ offers two mechanisms for processing the tree: unparse rules, for code generation, and rewrite rules, for transformations. Each rule is tailored to a node structure by pattern matching, and all rules are applied to the tree recursively. Views let different rules apply to the same kind of node in different contexts, C++ code can be embedded in rules, and a C++ class is generated for each node type that users can extend with their own methods.

brief.standout: Instead of being a library, it is a generator: a small input language describes the tree and its operations, and it emits C++ classes with pattern-matched rewrite and unparse rules. Its pairing with lex and yacc places it in the classic compiler-toolkit lineage, which is far from most current tooling.

brief.what_it_is: Kissat is a SAT solver: a program that takes a Boolean formula and reports whether some assignment of true/false to its variables satisfies it, usually in CNF form, and returns a satisfying assignment or an unsatisfiability answer. The README describes it as a "keep it simple and clean bare metal SAT solver" written in C. It is a port of CaDiCaL back to C, with new data structures and different scheduling of inprocessing. The README does not document input or output formats or command-line usage beyond the build step.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a simpler, cleaner C solver built from CaDiCaL's ideas, with better data structures, better scheduling of inprocessing, and optimized algorithms. brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. The release notes name several techniques: clausal congruence closure (congruence.c), bounded variable addition (factor.c), fast variable elimination during preprocessing (fastel.c), vivification of clauses, local search for initial phases, and probing and elimination on a scheduled interval. These come from the NEWS file, not the README.

name: klee
desc: Symbolic Execution Engine
why: Symbolic execution engine that finds inputs driving programs down hidden paths; a strange and rewarding way to watch code think.

brief.what_it_is: KLEE is a symbolic virtual machine, a dynamic symbolic execution engine built on the LLVM compiler infrastructure. It executes LLVM bitcode modules with support for symbolic values, so inputs can be treated as unknowns rather than fixed data. It also includes a POSIX/Linux emulation layer, aimed at uClibc, that can make parts of the operating system environment symbolic. Replay tools can run computed inputs on native programs, including setting up files, pipes, environment variables, and command-line arguments. The homepage licenses it under the UIUC open source license. The brew metadata lists executables kleaver, klee, klee-exec-tree, klee-replay, klee-stats, klee-zesti, ktest-gen, ktest-randgen, and ktest-tool, but I did not read docs for what each one does.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents KLEE as a research and practical tool for symbolic execution, citing the OSDI 2008 paper as the reference for what it is and can do. The README gives no separate problem statement.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the core engine executes LLVM bitcode with symbolic values, and a separate POSIX/Linux emulation layer handles the operating system side. Computed inputs can be saved and replayed on native code. The fetched pages do not explain in detail how path exploration or constraint solving works.
brief.install_notes: The Getting Started page lists several routes: a web interface (KLEE Web) for running small examples in a browser, Docker images, a Snap Store package (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian and others), Arch Linux and openSUSE Tumbleweed packages, Nix, a FreeBSD package (pkg install klee, or building the security/klee port), and Homebrew. For manual installs, the recommended route is building from source against LLVM 18, and the page also covers building other KLEE configurations and their dependencies. I did not fetch the build instructions themselves, so I have no details on dependencies or build steps.
brief.standout: It is a symbolic virtual machine that treats parts of the operating system environment as symbolic and can replay the generated inputs on native binaries, which goes beyond a pure bitcode analyzer. The project also has a browser-based KLEE Web demo, which lowers the barrier to first contact.

name: koka
desc: Compiler for the Koka language
why: A functional language with effect types and reference counting that avoids garbage collection, a genuinely different way to think about code.

brief.what_it_is: Koka is a strongly typed functional-style language with effect types and handlers, and its compiler. The compiler takes Koka source files (.kk) and compiles them, by default through generated C code, into runnable programs. The README also mentions JavaScript and WebAssembly backends. Koka tracks the side effects of every function in its type, so pure and effectful code are distinguished. Effect handlers let users build control abstractions such as exceptions, async/await, or probabilistic programs as ordinary libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents Koka as a research language from Daan Leijen and collaborators, built on a small set of well-studied features (first-class functions, a polymorphic type and effect system, algebraic data types, effect handlers) with precise effect typing that makes programs easier to reason about for humans and compilers. The Perceus reference counting work is framed as a way to get fast, garbage-collector-free memory management.
brief.how_it_works: Koka uses evidence passing to compile effect handlers, and Perceus compiler analysis for reference counting, which lets it emit C code without a garbage collector or runtime system. Perceus also does reuse analysis, so functional-style code can update memory in place when possible. The README reports benchmarks against OCaml, GHC, Swift, Java and C++ on allocation-heavy tests, and says these show Koka is competitive, not a precise head-to-head.

brief.standout: Few mainstream languages compile to C with no garbage collector while tracking effects in the type system. Effect handlers as the one general mechanism for exceptions, async and similar features also sets it apart from typical functional languages.

name: kona
desc: Open-source implementation of the K programming language
why: An open-source implementation of the terse K array language, a rare and dense corner of array programming worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: Kona is an open-source implementation of the k programming language, a terse, ASCII-based array language in the APL and LISP tradition. Its fundamental data construct is a list rather than APL's multi-dimensional arrays. It targets k3, an older Kx Systems version that is no longer sold, and is described as a reimplementation that is unaffiliated with Kx. You run it as an interactive interpreter from a terminal (the executable is named k), or on Windows by double-clicking k.exe.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to keep the k3 language alive after Kx stopped distributing it, since k3 has been unavailable for about 20 years. It also positions k as the preferred APL dialect for people in finance and data-heavy analysis who care about performance.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the interpreter's internals. It does say the C code deliberately imitates Arthur Whitney's terse style, and points to a 11-line buddy memory allocator by Whitney versus a roughly 750-line conventional C version as an example.

name: kraftkit
desc: Build and use highly customized and ultra-lightweight unikernel VMs
why: Builds ultra-lightweight unikernel VMs, a fascinating corner of systems work, though it leans toward a CLI wrapper for tooling.

brief.what_it_is: KraftKit, shipped as the kraft command-line tool, builds and runs unikernels: small single-purpose virtual machines that bundle an application with a minimal library OS (Unikraft). It takes an application, either a Dockerfile-based rootfs described by a Kraftfile or a pre-built image from the Unikraft catalog, and produces a unikernel image that it can run locally under QEMU, Xen or Firecracker, or push as an OCI package. The README also describes a Go SDK for building unikernels programmatically, and the tool includes local networking, volume and compose-style commands. The homepage help output also lists a large set of Unikraft Cloud commands, but the README says that cloud CLI is a separate product.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames unikernels as a lighter, faster, more secure and greener alternative to containers and general-purpose VMs, and says KraftKit exists to make building and managing these specialized applications easy at every stage, from construction to production. The docs say the tool was modeled on popular package managers and build tools with the explicit aim of making it easy to build and manage an application as a unikernel.
brief.how_it_works: You place a Kraftfile in a repo that points at an existing Dockerfile (rootfs) and a start command, then run kraft run . to build and launch it. kraft fetches Unikraft components and libraries, configures and builds them for a target platform and architecture (the GitHub Actions example uses qemu and x86_64), and runs the result on a hypervisor. The README describes the local instance manager as daemonless.

name: knock
desc: Port-knock server
why: A port-knocking server, a door into the idea of hiding services behind a sequence of packets that most people have never seen used.

brief.what_it_is: knock is a port-knocking server and client. The server, knockd, uses libpcap to sniff a network interface for a configured sequence of port hits (knocks). When it sees the sequence, it runs a command bound to that sequence, such as an iptables rule that opens a port. The knock client is a small command for sending those hits. Input is raw network traffic on the server's interface; output is whatever command the server is configured to run. The README does not document the config file format or client usage.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames port-knocking as a way for a server to watch its interfaces for a special "knock" sequence and then act on it. It notes that the knock hits do not need to land on open ports, because libpcap reads the raw traffic.
brief.how_it_works: knockd watches raw interface traffic with libpcap rather than listening on a socket, so knock packets can target closed ports. The README's example is a DENY-policy firewall: the client sends four TCP SYN packets to a fixed port sequence, the server runs an iptables command to open port 22 for that client, and a second four-port sequence closes it again. The README does not explain how the sequence is configured.
