name: kraken2
desc: Taxonomic sequence classification system
why: Real k-mer taxonomic classification of sequencing reads, a genuine bioinformatics tool, though it needs large reference databases.

brief.what_it_is: Kraken 2 is a taxonomic sequence classifier written in C++ with Perl and shell scripts, plus a newer Python wrapper called k2. It takes DNA (or, with a protein database, amino acid) sequence reads or assemblies in FASTA or FASTQ form, optionally compressed with gzip, bzip2 or xz. It assigns each sequence a taxonomic label by looking up its k-mers in a prebuilt or custom reference database, and writes a per-sequence classification file plus an optional sample-level report of counts per taxon. The README itself is short and points to docs/MANUAL.html (version 2.1.6) for usage.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes Kraken 2 as 'the second version of the Kraken taxonomic sequence classification system' and says it is a rewrite of Kraken 1 that is not backwards compatible. The manual says Kraken 2 was created because Kraken 1's large k-mer/LCA list needed a lot of memory, and it cites the original Kraken, KrakenUniq and protocol papers.
brief.how_it_works: Kraken 2 stores only minimizers of k-mers in a compact probabilistic hash table, mapping each minimizer to the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of the genomes containing it. Query reads are reduced to minimizers and looked up, and the manual notes the hash table can occasionally return a false positive in under 1% of queries, which confidence thresholds can compensate for. The k2 wrapper adds multi-database classification (merging per-database results by LCA) and HTTP-based NCBI downloads.

The manual says the install path is ./install_kraken2.sh, which needs a C++11-capable g++, Bash, Perl, and Linux utilities such as sed, find and wget. The k2 wrapper needs only Python 3's standard library. OpenMP is needed for multithreading. Standard database builds need about 100 GB of disk (the manual's 2018 figures were 42 GB library, 26 GB taxonomy and 29 GB hash table). Running needs enough RAM to hold the database (about 29 GB for the default as of Jan 2018), unless --memory-mapping is used. The manual recommends against NFS for the database and notes that NCBI downloads may need proxy environment variables or --use-ftp. The Homebrew formula is the usual route; the manual's install steps are for source builds.
brief.standout: Instead of storing every k-mer, Kraken 2 stores only minimizers and accepts a small false-positive rate in exchange for speed and lower memory. The manual also describes two ways to shrink a database for low-memory machines: larger k relative to minimizer length, and hash-based downsampling via --max-db-size.
brief.status: maintained. The README links to a Bioconda recipe and a usegalaxy.eu tool. The manual is titled Version 2.1.6, and its k2 section refers to version 2.17.0, so the docs are not fully consistent. I did not see a last-commit or release date, so recent activity is unconfirmed.
brief.caveats: The manual says macOS and other non-Linux systems are not explicitly supported by the developers. On macOS, the default GCC lacks OpenMP, which limits the tool to single-threaded runs. The standard database needs roughly 100 GB of disk and about 29 GB of RAM or more, so the scout note about large databases holds. Classification is probabilistic, so false positives occur in under 1% of queries. The manual says zstd input is not yet supported. RDP databases are unavailable because their URLs no longer work. The manual says the --threads option on download-library can get the client kicked off NCBI's servers. I did not find the license in the pages I read.

name: kwok
desc: Kubernetes WithOut Kubelet - Simulates thousands of Nodes and Clusters
why: Simulates thousands of fake Kubernetes nodes, a surprising way to watch a control plane behave at scale.

brief.what_it_is: KWOK (Kubernetes WithOut Kubelet) is a toolkit for building Kubernetes clusters whose nodes are simulated rather than real. It ships two executables: kwok, which simulates the lifecycle of fake nodes, pods, and other Kubernetes API resources, and kwokctl, a CLI that creates and manages clusters whose nodes are simulated by kwok. Input is a cluster-creation or node-configuration request; output is a Kubernetes API that kubectl, helm, and other standard clients can talk to, with fake nodes that report status and pods that never actually run. The homepage says a cluster of thousands of nodes can be set up in seconds on a laptop.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage positions KWOK against kubemark and kind. Kubemark runs a kubelet that does not run containers, so it behaves exactly like a kubelet and needs a lot of memory to simulate many nodes and pods. KWOK simulates only the node's behavior, so it uses very little memory. Against kind, the homepage says kwokctl can stand in for kind when you don't need pods to actually run.
brief.how_it_works: kwok simulates each fake node and pod's lifecycle against the Kubernetes API, rather than running a kubelet or containers. kwokctl sets up a cluster using a chosen runtime (binary, docker, podman, nerdctl, lima, finch, or kind-based variants) and wires those simulated nodes into it. The README does not describe the internal mechanism in more detail than that.
brief.install_notes: Binaries are published for linux, darwin, and windows on amd64 and arm64. Alternatively, pre-built images can be run once a container runtime is installed; the homepage lists Docker, Podman, or Nerdctl, while the GitHub README lists Docker or Nerdctl. kwokctl needs a runtime chosen from its support matrix: the binary runtime is recommended and works on linux, darwin, and windows (amd64 and arm64), while docker and podman are recommended on linux and supported on darwin amd64/arm64 and windows amd64 with varying test coverage. nerdctl is unsupported on darwin and windows. lima, finch, and the kind-* variants are marked work in progress or not fully tested on several platforms. The README does not give exact install commands, and the brew formula notes contain no caveats.
brief.standout: Instead of running a kubelet for each fake node, KWOK simulates node behavior directly, so the API server and controllers see realistic nodes at a memory cost far below kubemark's. The point is to test the control plane at scale: the project pitches it as a way to see how a Kubernetes control plane behaves with thousands of nodes and tens of thousands of pods on a laptop.
brief.status: unknown. Neither the homepage nor the GitHub README shows a release date, last commit, or version number, so I cannot confirm recent activity from these pages. The project is hosted under kubernetes-sigs and its homepage and runtime matrix read as current, but that is not a maintenance signal in itself.
brief.caveats: Simulated pods are not real: the homepage notes that curling a pod's IP in a KWOK cluster returns nothing, so KWOK cannot test workloads that need to serve traffic or run containers. The performance figures (reliably 1k nodes and 100k pods; creating 20 nodes or pods per second) are the project's own claims and come with no methodology in these pages. Runtime support is uneven: the matrix marks lima and finch as work in progress, nerdctl as unsupported on darwin and windows, and several kind-* combinations as only partly tested or unsupported. The homepage and README disagree on whether Podman is a supported image runtime. The brew formula has no caveats.
quotes: KWOK is a toolkit that enables setting up a cluster of thousands of Nodes in seconds.
kubemark is a kubelet that does not actually run a container.

kind runs Kubernetes in Docker, creating a real cluster. If you deploy a nginx pod to a kind cluster, you could curl to its IP address and get an HTTP response containing its HTML page. But in a KWOK cluster, you get nothing because the pod isn't real.

name: kuto
desc: Reverse JS bundler
why: A reverse JavaScript bundler unpacks minified web apps back into source, a satisfying way of taking something apart.

brief.what_it_is: Kuto is a command-line tool that takes a large ES module JavaScript bundle and splits it into a 'main' file plus a 'corpus' of static chunks. Its output is the main file and the corpus directory, and running it again on a rebuilt bundle reuses existing corpus files where possible and deletes unused ones. It also has a 'kuto info' command that gives basic information about an ES module. Correction to the scout note: Kuto does not unpack minified apps back into source. It splits a bundle, and it works best on output from another bundler.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Kuto makes updating your site's JS smaller by re-using code you've already shipped. The author says the tool started as a way to learn about side-effects through 'kuto info': "This is the origin of the tool; I wanted something that could inform me about side-effects."
brief.how_it_works: Kuto parses the input with acorn and works at the statement level, moving large enough statements into static parts that have no side-effects. Clients can cache those parts forever, and Chromium also caches the bytecode of previously shipped files. Kuto needs the previously generated output to be kept around so the next run can reuse the existing corpus.

commands_seen.context: Run after installing to learn more about the tool (per the README's Usage section).
Splits a JS bundle into a 'main' part and a corpus of code written to out/.
Mentioned inline in the Notes section as giving basic information about an ES Module; no full example given.
Best Practice section: builds Kuto itself by bundling with esbuild, splitting with kuto, then minifying with esbuild.

brief.install_notes: Requires Node 16+. The README says to install via "kuto" and then run npx kuto, without giving an exact install command. esbuild is optional: if it is installed, split and info will transparently compile TS and similar files, but it is not a peerDependency. To get reuse across builds, keep the old generated output in the output dir or point to it with the -c flag, which can be a directory, a local main file, or a URL fetched with fetch().
brief.standout: Kuto moves code-splitting to the end of the build instead of the start. It takes an already-bundled file and reuses previously shipped chunks across deploys, so returning visitors download less. The author describes it as "Think of it as doing code-splitting 'last', rather than first."
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README has no release date, last-commit date, or maintenance note. The only signal is a GitHub Actions Tests badge.
brief.caveats: Kuto works best on large (>1mb) single ESM bundles. The README says an IIFE or webpack output is one giant statement, so it gives little benefit there. Old generated output must be kept, or the -c flag must point to it, or the reuse step does not work. The -d dedup flag is off by default because the README calls it dangerous. The -k flag's author says it 'will probably evolve over time'. The README does not state a license. The scout note's claim that it unpacks minified apps back into source is inaccurate.
quotes: It reduces your download size by re-using code you've already shipped.
Ideally, Kuto operates on a large output bundle from another tool.
Think of it as doing code-splitting 'last', rather than first.

judge.reason: Post-bundle splitting reuses shipped code across deploys and can preserve browser bytecode caches—a genuinely unusual twist on ordinary code splitting.

name: lammps
desc: Molecular Dynamics Simulator
why: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulator, real physics you can run at home on your own molecules and materials.

brief.what_it_is: LAMMPS (Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator) is a classical molecular dynamics simulation code focused on materials modeling. You feed it an input script of commands describing atoms, interaction potentials, the simulation box and the run, and it prints progress to the screen and writes a logfile named log.lammps, plus whatever output files the script asks for. The docs describe it as open-source under GPLv2.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs say it was designed to run efficiently on parallel computers and to be easy to extend and modify. It was originally developed at Sandia National Laboratories, with most funding from the US Department of Energy, and now includes contributions from many groups.
brief.how_it_works: The executable reads commands from an input file (given with -in) or from standard input and runs the molecular dynamics steps they describe. Parallel runs are launched with mpirun or mpiexec, and the processors command controls how MPI tasks map onto the simulation box. Multi-threading per MPI task is set with the OMP_NUM_THREADS environment variable or the package command.

commands_seen.context: Basic serial run: reads the input script in.file from the current directory. The docs recommend the -in form.
Same run using the serial executable name from the traditional build system, which is one of the names the brew formula installs.
Parallel run on 4 MPI tasks using the lmp_mpi executable.
Parallel run on 4 MPI tasks using mpiexec with the lmp executable name.
Installs the prebuilt Ubuntu/Debian package, which provides an executable named lmp.
Fedora install of the OpenMPI build; afterwards run module load mpi/openmpi-x86_64 before mpirun.
OpenSuse install of the prebuilt package, which includes OpenMPI support.
Gentoo install; Gentoo downloads the source and compiles it on the machine.
Lists the compilation options, packages and styles included in the binary, as the install pages recommend.

brief.install_notes: The brew formula provides lmp_mpi and lmp_serial. The docs point to several non-brew routes: static Linux x86_64 tarballs from download.lammps.org (no MPI, no python module), Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora, EPEL, OpenSuse, Gentoo and Arch AUR build scripts, plus a Conda route and CMake or make source builds. Optional packages such as KIM need extra steps. Using openkim.org potentials needs the openkim-models package or KIM-API download commands. I did not read the source-build pages, so the prerequisites are unverified.
brief.standout: It is a long-running, DOE-backed materials MD code that is extensible through its own styles and plugin mechanism and is available as a large set of prebuilt packages. Its docs are unusually thorough, with a full command reference and a list of benchmarks.
brief.status: Maintained as far as the docs show. The manual is stamped 30 Sep 2026 and the git info reads 30Sep2026, and the docs carry both stable and develop branch versions. I did not check the GitHub release or commit history directly.
brief.caveats: The static Linux binaries are not built for MPI. Several distro packages are maintained by third parties, and the LAMMPS developers say they have no control over those packages' timing or configuration. Some examples and accelerator features need optional packages compiled in. Parallel runs need the correct MPI launcher, and the redirection operator < may fail under mpirun. Floating-point round-off means trajectories can diverge across processor counts. The license is GPLv2. The homepage is the documentation site, not a project landing page, and it does not mention Homebrew.

In theory you should get identical answers on any number of processors and on any machine.

name: landrun
desc: Lightweight, secure sandbox for running Linux processes using Landlock LSM
why: Runs processes under Landlock LSM restrictions, a good door into kernel sandboxing you rarely see.

brief.what_it_is: Landrun is a command-line sandbox for Linux. You put it in front of any command, such as `landrun --rox /usr --ro /etc --connect-tcp 443 nc kernel.org 443`, and it runs that command under Landlock restrictions. You list which paths the process may read, write, or execute, and which TCP/UDP ports it may bind or connect to. The command's output is the same as it would be unsandboxed, and any access outside the rules is denied by the kernel. It is written in Go and needs no root privileges.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a practical way to sandbox any command with fine-grained filesystem and network controls, with "No root. No containers. No SELinux/AppArmor configs." It describes itself as "Think firejail, but with kernel-level security and minimal overhead."
brief.how_it_works: Landrun wraps the Landlock Linux Security Module, which lets an unprivileged process restrict itself and its future children. It builds a ruleset from the --ro, --rox, --rw, --rwx, --bind-tcp, --connect-tcp, --bind-udp, --connect-udp and --unix flags, then applies it before running the target command. The README targets Landlock ABI v10 by default and uses the go-landlock package (v0.10.0). Its --best-effort mode falls back to whatever ABI the running kernel supports. The README also covers IPC scoping for abstract UNIX sockets and signals, which is on by default, and audit logging of denials.

commands_seen.context: Quick install via the Go toolchain (Go 1.24 or later).
Basic syntax as given in the README.
Example 1: exec access to one binary plus read-only access to /home.
Example 12: passes HOME, PATH and a custom variable into the sandbox, since no environment is passed by default.
Example 8, a DNS-capable client allowed to connect only to port 443 (the README's example also includes --ro /etc,/usr and --log-level debug).
Example 9: a web server allowed to bind only ports 80 and 443 with selected read and write paths.
Example 10: with no paths or network rules, landrun applies maximum restrictions, so this runs in a maximum-security jail.
Example 11: suggested debugging step when permission denied errors are unclear.
Example 15: --ldd adds required shared libraries to --rox, and --add-exec adds the target binary.
Example 16: allows connecting to one pathname UNIX socket on ABI v9+ kernels.
Troubleshooting step to check that Landlock is enabled in the kernel config; the output should include CONFIG_SECURITY_LANDLOCK=y and lsm=landlock,...

brief.install_notes: Requires Linux kernel 5.13 or later with Landlock enabled. TCP restrictions need kernel 6.7 or later, and UDP restrictions need 7.2 or later (ABI v10). Building from source needs Go 1.24 or later: clone the repo, run `go build -o landrun cmd/landrun/main.go`, then copy the binary to /usr/local/bin. Distro packages are listed: Arch AUR (landrun and landrun-git), Slackware via SlackBuilds, and `sudo apt install landrun` on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Debian forky. No root is needed to run the sandbox itself. Systems without Landlock enabled will need the kernel config checked. Most real use will need --best-effort on older kernels, and paths such as /usr, /usr/lib, and /lib64 usually have to be granted explicitly. There is no first-run configuration. A systemd unit example is included in the README.
brief.standout: Landrun brings Landlock, a kernel feature most people never touch, to a simple command-line wrapper. Users get path- and port-level restrictions with no root, no container, and no policy language to write. The README also documents Landlock's newer features, including UDP port control, IPC scoping, and pathname UNIX socket control, with a kernel-version table to match.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release dates, changelog, or last-commit information, and I did not open the repository's releases or commit history. Signs of ongoing packaging are that it is in Ubuntu 26.04 and Debian forky and has several AUR and SlackBuild maintainers. It targets recent kernel features such as ABI v10 and Linux 7.2 UDP restrictions. The README has a Contributing section that invites pull requests.
brief.caveats: Strict mode fails on kernels below the requested ABI, so most users will need --best-effort. TCP restrictions do not apply to Multipath TCP, and since Go 1.24 net.Listen defaults to MPTCP, so Go servers may not be restrictable (kernel bug landlock-lsm/linux#54). Files opened before sandboxing are not restricted. Shared libraries need exec permission, so the rules are not always as minimal as they look. Linux only. The README does not state a license in what I read. It also links an article titled "Binaries are not trustworthy", which suggests building from source.
quotes: Think firejail, but with kernel-level security and minimal overhead.
No root. No containers. No SELinux/AppArmor configs.
Landlock is an access-control system that enables processes to securely restrict themselves and their future children.

name: ksh93
desc: KornShell, ksh93
why: KornShell is an old-school shell with rich history and quirks worth an afternoon of exploring.

brief.what_it_is: KornShell 93u+m (ksh93) is a Unix command-line shell and scripting language, maintained as a fork of the last stable AT&T ksh93 release (93u+ 2012-08-01). It takes shell scripts and interactive commands and runs them, with built-in utilities, arrays, arithmetic, job control and line editing. The Homebrew package installs the executables ksh, ksh93, rksh, rksh93 and shcomp. The README covers building from source, not the brew package itself.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that an attempt to refactor ksh93 into ksh2020 (2017 to 2020) was abandoned with many critical bugs, but its AST issue tracker held documentation on fixing bugs. This reboot backports those fixes to the last stable release and adds patches from OpenSUSE, Red Hat, Solaris and the community, with the aim of being 'the least buggy version of ksh93 ever released'.
brief.how_it_works: The build is driven by a POSIX shell script, bin/package, which compiles everything into an arch directory named for your architecture, with dynamically linked binaries in dyn/bin and dyn/lib when supported. Features are chosen at compile time by editing src/cmd/ksh93/SHOPT.sh. Regression tests run through bin/shtests, and bin/package use lets you try the shell without installing it.

commands_seen.context: Builds ksh from the top of the source tree, run from the repository's top directory.
Alternative to 'bin/package make' that suppresses compiler output.
Parallel build using up to four concurrent jobs.

Builds with flags and an alternative build-script shell passed on the command line for that one command.

Lets you hand-test ksh, its utilities and autoloadable functions without installing.
Usage is 'bin/package install install_root_directory [command ...]'; with no command it installs ksh and shcomp.

brief.install_notes: The README covers building from source, not the Homebrew formula. The build needs a basic POSIX shell, utilities and a compiler, with cc, ar and getconf required at build time and tput optional at runtime for multiline editing. On macOS, install the Xcode Command Line Tools with xcode-select --install. On Android/Termux, install build dependencies with pkg install (clang, binutils, getconf). On NetBSD and OpenBSD, disable SHOPT_SYSRC if the system /etc/ksh.kshrc is incompatible. Set DESTDIR for packager-style staged installs, and export AST_NO_DYLIB to skip the dynamic build. No accounts or hardware are needed.
brief.standout: It is a historical revival: the project backports fixes from an abandoned rewrite and from distro patch sets into the last stable ksh93, and the README is explicit that it is willing to break undocumented behaviour rather than keep bug-for-bug compatibility. Its policy of squashing each pull request into one self-documenting commit is also unusual.
brief.status: Described as active in the README ('where the KornShell is under active development') and its policy sections describe ongoing maintenance on dev and 1.0 branches. The fetched README shows no release date or last-commit date, so I could not confirm recency beyond that statement.
brief.caveats: The README lists supported systems (Android/Termux, Cygwin, BSDs, Haiku, illumos, Linux with glibc or musl, macOS, QNX, Solaris) and says AIX, HP-UX and UnixWare may work but are untested. EBCDIC and z/OS support were removed. The prepare section ends with a '(to be completed)' placeholder. Compiler flags that emit colour codes or -ffast-math break the build or cause arithmetic bugs. The brew description calls it 'KornShell, ksh93' while the project calls itself 93u+m. Its test and install commands live in bin/package rather than a standard make target. The README does not state a licence.

we are confident at this point that 93u+m is already the least buggy version of ksh93 ever released.
No 100% bug compatibility. Broken and undocumented behaviour gets fixed.
No bureaucracy, no formalities. Just fix it, or report it: create issues, send pull requests.

name: latexml
desc: LaTeX to XML/HTML/MathML Converter
why: Converting LaTeX into structured XML and MathML is a fascinating transform, though it is document tooling at heart.

brief.what_it_is: LaTeXML is a converter that takes LaTeX (or TeX) source documents and turns them into LaTeXML's own XML format. From that XML it can produce HTML in several flavors with MathML and SVG, or other formats such as JATS and ePub. Its distinctive output is mathematics rendered as both content and presentation MathML. The homepage names the executables latexml, latexmlc, latexmlfind, latexmlmath and latexmlpost, but it does not explain what each one does.
brief.why_it_exists: It was started during development of the Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF), which needed LaTeX sources transformed into XML for further manipulation and for building the web site. The authors wanted a digital library to focus on the semantics of the material, and found no existing software suitable, so they built it in-house.
brief.how_it_works: LaTeXML emulates TeX as far as possible, implemented in Perl, and converts the TeX or LaTeX document into its XML format. That XML is modelled on typical LaTeX document structure and is inspired by HTML, MathML, OpenMath and others. The abstract document is then transformed further into the target output such as HTML, MathML, SVG, JATS or ePub.
brief.install_notes: The fetched pages say nothing about installation, runtimes, or configuration beyond the Perl-based design. The brew package lists five executables: latexml, latexmlc, latexmlfind, latexmlmath and latexmlpost. No commands were shown on the pages I read.
brief.standout: Rather than translating LaTeX markup directly, it emulates TeX's processing and produces a semantic XML intermediate, so the same document can feed HTML, MathML and other outputs. It emits both content and presentation MathML for math, and arXiv has offered experimental HTML preprints built with it.
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage announces 'Now available: LaTeXML 0.8.8!' but gives no release date, and I did not check a repository or commit history. The homepage and the DLMF-hosted copy of the manual both loaded with the same content.
brief.caveats: The homepage itself says 'emulating TeX is kinda hard' and that 'there are gaps in fidelity and coverage', so some LaTeX packages and documents will not convert faithfully. The brew caveats field is empty. I found no platform, licence or build notes on the pages I read.
quotes: The approach is to emulate TeX as far as possible (in Perl), converting the TeX or (LaTeX) document into LaTeXML's XML format.
Of course, emulating TeX is kinda hard, there are many clever LaTeX package developers, and the Web moves quickly, so there are gaps in fidelity and coverage.
At the time, we found no software suitable to our needs, so we began development of LaTeXML in-house.

name: ladspa-sdk
desc: Linux Audio Developer's Simple Plugin
why: LADSPA is a fascinating old plugin standard, but the SDK itself is mostly headers and tooling for developers.

brief.what_it_is: LADSPA (Linux Audio Developer's Simple Plugin API) is a standard for audio processors and effects, the plugins that sit inside audio software. A developer writes an effect such as a reverb, bundles it into a plugin library, and any LADSPA-friendly host application can load and use it. The API is captured in a C header file, and the SDK adds terse documentation, three small command-line hosts (analyseplugin, applyplugin, listplugins), and ten example plugins. The homepage lists hosts such as Ardour, Audacity, LMMS, Rosegarden, Csound and Pd, and many plugin libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a deliberately small compromise: the API aims to be 'a good compromise between functionality, intuition and compatibility but is simple. The "S" in "LADSPA" is meant seriously.' It was proposed on the Linux Audio Developer mailing list and version 1 was finalised on 2 April 2000.
brief.how_it_works: Plugins are compiled into shared libraries that contain one or more individual plugins, each identified by a unique ID. The host discovers libraries by searching the directories in the LADSPA_PATH environment variable (a colon-separated list), or the locations the distribution manages. The API handles only 32-bit floating point data by design, and the host decides how to wire plugins into its own processing, since LADSPA does not impose an architecture. The homepage does not describe the exact function-call sequence; that lives in the header and SDK docs.

commands_seen.context: Named on the homepage as a trivial LADSPA host included in the SDK; if LADSPA_PATH is set correctly it should list all your plugins. No command line is shown on the page.
Named on the homepage as one of three trivial LADSPA hosts in the SDK. No usage shown.
Named on the homepage as one of three trivial LADSPA hosts in the SDK. No usage shown.

brief.install_notes: Many Linux distributions install LADSPA plugin libraries into a central location for you. If a host cannot find your plugins, set the LADSPA_PATH environment variable manually to a colon-separated list of directories. The SDK is a separate download from the homepage and contains the docs, hosts and example plugins. name: launch_socket_server
desc: Bind to privileged ports without running a server as root
why: Uses launchd socket activation to bind privileged ports, a small door into how macOS hands out sockets.

brief.what_it_is: launch_socket_server is a small Go program for macOS (OS X) that sits between launchd and your server. launchd opens a privileged port (under 1024), and the proxy forwards incoming connections from that port to your unprivileged program over a Unix domain socket or a local TCP port. Your server takes its connections from the proxy and never needs to run as root. By default the proxy creates the socket path and passes it to your program in the LAUNCH_PROGRAM_SOCKET_PATH environment variable. The README describes it as an MIT-licensed fork maintained by Misty De Méo, with the original by Sam Stephenson in 2014.
brief.why_it_exists: The README states the problem: you want to accept connections on a port number under 1024 on OS X, but you don't want your server to run as root. The solution it offers is to run your server with launch_socket_server.
brief.how_it_works: launchd holds the privileged socket and uses the launch_activate_socket API (available on OS X 10.9 and higher) to hand it to launch_socket_server, which then proxies each connection to your program. Your server reads LAUNCH_PROGRAM_SOCKET_PATH, unlinks any existing socket file, binds to that path, and runs in the foreground. Setup is a launchd plist in /Library/LaunchDaemons whose Sockets key names the port (for example 80) and whose ProgramArguments begin with the launch_socket_server path.

commands_seen.context: Registers and loads the launch daemon plist as root. This is how you start the daemon.
Unloads the launch daemon as root.
Installs Go, which is required to build launch_socket_server from source (the README suggests Homebrew).
Run inside a copy of the source tree to build launch_socket_server.
Installs launch_socket_server into /usr/local by default. Set the PREFIX environment variable to install elsewhere.

brief.install_notes: There is no binary install described in the README. You build from source: install Go (the README suggests brew install go), run make, then make install, which targets /usr/local unless PREFIX is set. Setup also needs a launch daemon plist at /Library/LaunchDaemons/<identifier>.plist, loaded as root with launchctl. The plist sets Label, RunAtLoad, KeepAlive, UserName, GroupName, optional log paths, ProgramArguments, and a Sockets entry (SockNodeName 0.0.0.0, SockServiceName 80 or a service name from /etc/services). Optional EnvironmentVariables set LAUNCH_PROGRAM_SOCKET_PATH or LAUNCH_PROGRAM_TCP_ADDRESS (for example 127.0.0.1:8000). Passing login_wrapper gives your program the user's login-shell environment.
brief.standout: It uses launchd's own socket activation, so the privileged bind is done by the system and your program never runs as root. It can also run as a pure proxy with no child program (use '-' in place of the server path), or proxy to a TCP address instead of a Unix socket.
brief.status: unknown. The README mentions that this is a current fork maintained by Misty De Méo, but it shows no release date, version number, or recent commit, and I did not check the repository's commit or release history.
brief.caveats: macOS only. The README describes OS X and requires OS X 10.9 or later for launch_activate_socket. Building needs Go. Your server must read LAUNCH_PROGRAM_SOCKET_PATH, unlink the socket before binding, and should unlink it on exit. Your server must stay in the foreground and must not fork into the background. Launch daemons are loaded with sudo. The program runs with a minimal environment unless you use login_wrapper. The README's example image points to a sstephenson/launch_socket_server URL rather than this fork.

name: lastz
desc: Pairwise aligner for DNA sequences
why: A real DNA pairwise aligner you can run on genomes at home, a legitimate bioinformatics rabbit hole.

brief.what_it_is: LASTZ is a command-line pairwise aligner for DNA sequences, written in C. You give it a target sequence file and a query sequence file (FASTA, Nib, or 2Bit, with optional FASTQ and other inputs), and it writes alignments to stdout in formats such as MAF, LAV, AXT, SAM, PAF, BLASTN-style, or a general tab-delimited format. It can also infer scoring parameters from the sequences. It is a drop-in replacement for BLASTZ and accepts BLASTZ's command-line syntax, plus many extra options.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a more capable, backward-compatible successor to BLASTZ, offering extra options and different results from BLASTZ for DNA-to-DNA alignment of whole chromosomes, short reads, and self-alignments. The author is Bob Harris of the Miller Lab at Penn State.
brief.how_it_works: LASTZ runs a staged pipeline. It indexes the target's seed words in a position table, then for each query finds seeds (short near-matches), extends them gap-free into HSPs, chains HSPs into syntenic anchors, extends those with gapped alignment, filters by score and user criteria, and interpolates in the gaps at higher sensitivity. The query's reverse complement is processed as well. Sensitivity is tuned with options such as --step, --seed, --notransition, --nogapped, and --chain.

brief.what_it_is: LCDF Typetools is a set of eleven command-line programs for reading and rewriting the internals of PostScript Type 1, Type 1 Multiple Master, OpenType (CFF and TrueType flavored) and TrueType fonts. Inputs are font files (PFA/PFB, OTF/TTF, AMFM and AFM for multiple masters). Outputs vary by tool: Type 1 fonts converted from CFF (cfftot1), AFM metrics files (mmafm, t1rawafm), single-master instances of multiple-master fonts (mmpfb), TeX TFM metrics and encodings (otftotfm), Type 42 wrappers (ttftotype42), PostScript test pages (t1testpage), and plain-text feature or codepoint reports (otfinfo). Some tools also check (t1lint) or modify (t1reencode, t1dotlessj) existing Type 1 fonts.

Otftotfm interprets OpenType glyph positioning, substitution and ligature tables as far as it can and writes TeX metrics and encoding files, optionally activating features you name. name: lci
desc: Interpreter for the lambda calculus
why: An interpreter for the untyped lambda calculus, a minimal language where all computation reduces to functions.

brief.what_it_is: LCI is a command-line interpreter for the untyped lambda calculus, written in C and distributed as free software under the GPL. You give it lambda terms, aliases, and user-defined operators, usually in a file or interactively, and it reduces them and prints the result. Results are displayed in readable form, so Church numerals appear as numbers and lists as [a,b,c]. The homepage also says it can run in a browser via WebAssembly.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents LCI as a way to explore the pure lambda calculus, where all computation reduces to functions, and as a small but capable functional programming language built on that base. It includes an N-Queens example (queens.lci) written in a Haskell-like style to show what the calculus can do.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes reduction under two evaluation strategies, call-by-name and call-by-value, which can coexist in one program. Integers are encoded in Church by default (set in .lcirc), with Scott encoding available. Recursion works by expanding self-referencing aliases at run time, or by converting recursive terms to non-recursive ones with a fixed-point combinator. A let x = M in N form is parsed as (\x.N) M, and tracing of execution is supported.

name: leela-zero
desc: Neural Network Go engine with no human-provided knowledge
why: A neural network Go engine that learned without human knowledge is a fascinating, runnable piece of AI history.

brief.what_it_is: Leela Zero is an open-source Go-playing engine, a reimplementation of the AlphaGo Zero design that learns from self-play with no human game knowledge. It is a Monte Carlo tree search guided by a deep residual convolutional neural network. It takes a board position and a weights file (the trained network) and outputs move choices and evaluations over the GTP protocol. It is not meant to be used directly: you pair it with a Go GUI such as Lizzie or Sabaki. The homepage says the distributed training effort has finished and its server is closed.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a faithful reimplementation of the 'Mastering the Game of Go without Human Knowledge' system, which the author says amounts to 'an open source AlphaGo Zero.' The project also ran a public distributed effort to repeat the training work, since the README says recomputing the weights would take about 1700 years on commodity hardware.
brief.how_it_works: The engine runs MCTS without Monte Carlo playouts, using a deep residual convolutional network to supply move priors and position evaluations, as in the AlphaGo Zero paper. The network is loaded from a plain-text weights file, and the program autodetects the number of residual blocks and filters at startup. Self-play games produce training data (search probabilities plus game outcome) that can be fed to a deep learning framework to train new networks.

name: lfe
desc: Concurrent Lisp for the Erlang VM
why: A Lisp dialect running on the Erlang VM, a genuinely unusual pairing worth an afternoon of exploring.

brief.what_it_is: LFE (Lisp Flavoured Erlang) is a Lisp-syntax front-end to the Erlang compiler, so LFE code runs on the BEAM virtual machine. You give it LFE source, either typed into its REPL, saved as a script, or compiled as a module, and it produces ordinary Erlang-compatible code that can call and be called by normal Erlang modules. It includes a REPL and evaluator for interactive work, plus lfescript for one-off scripts. Its data types are Erlang's: lists, tuples, maps, atoms, and binaries, with strings being lists of integers.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage tagline is "Taking the syntax out of distributed systems programming", and the README says LFE is a lisp syntax front-end to the Erlang compiler, so the idea is to give Erlang/OTP's concurrency, distribution, and fault-tolerance machinery a Lisp surface syntax.
brief.how_it_works: LFE source is read by an LFE reader and compiled through the Erlang compiler toolchain into BEAM bytecode, so it is interchangeable with Erlang modules at runtime. Macros are compile-time only, except in the REPL, and they are unhygienic but scoped, with no gensym, because the author says that would be unsafe for code shared with remote nodes. The homepage also describes OTP behaviours (gen_server, supervisors) being used directly from LFE syntax.

The author's choice to drop gensym and accept unhygienic macros, because code is shared with remote nodes, is an unusual trade-off, stated plainly in the homepage text.

name: lensfun
desc: Remove defects from digital images
why: A lens database and correction library that undoes optical distortion, with a surprising amount of real optics behind it.

brief.what_it_is: Lensfun is an open source C/C++ library with a database of photographic lenses and their characteristics. It reads that database, lets you search it, and applies correction algorithms to images based on known lens properties. It currently corrects three defects: geometric distortion, transversal (lateral) chromatic aberration, and vignetting. Its C interface is a wrapper around the C++ classes. The package also ships helper executables, including lenstool, which the build options describe as the Lensfun reference implementation.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to fix the imperfections every camera and lens has, so that shots come out closer to ideal: "rectifying the defects introduced by your photographic equipment." The README adds that an earlier free lens database, PTLens, had frozen when its author went commercial, and Lensfun was built to continue an open version of that database.
brief.how_it_works: The library stores lens characteristics in an XML-based database, which it parses with GLib. Client code searches that database for a given lens and then uses the stored lens model to correct distortion, lateral chromatic aberration, and vignetting in an image. The README does not describe the correction math in detail beyond saying the algorithms rely on detailed knowledge of lens properties.

brief.how_it_works: The loaders parse each format's escape sequences, font data and palettes (including SAUCE metadata) and draw the characters onto a canvas. The canvas is then output as a PNG through GD. The project's changelog shows the loaders moved to state machines and got extensive format validation and fuzzing, which matters because these are untrusted input files.

name: libaribcaption
desc: Portable ARIB STD-B24 Caption Decoder/Renderer
why: Decodes ARIB Japanese broadcast captions from transport streams, a real door into obscure broadcast standards.

brief.what_it_is: libaribcaption is a portable C++17 library, with a C API, that decodes and renders ARIB STD-B24 captions, the closed-caption system used in Japanese ISDB TV broadcasting. It is meant to be embedded in video players. The README does not name its input format explicitly. It points to a sample with ffmpeg, which suggests caption data is taken from a demuxed broadcast stream. Output is rendered caption graphics, and the README says the goal is to match or beat how a television displays these captions. It supports Japanese (ARIB JIS), Latin (ABNT NBR 15606-1) and Philippine UTF-8 caption variants.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says ARIB captions are still poorly supported by general video players even though ISDB broadcasting has run for about 20 years. The library aims to let those players render ARIB captions with the same effect as a TV, or better.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the internal pipeline in detail. It says the library provides a decoder and a renderer, with pluggable text backends: DirectWrite on Windows, CoreText on macOS and iOS, and FreeType or Fontconfig elsewhere. It also includes built-in font fallback, support for ARIB gaiji (additional symbols) and DRCS characters, and a built-in table that maps known DRCS characters to alternative Unicode. Graphics rendering is SSE2-optimised on x86/x64.

name: libbladerf
desc: USB 3.0 Superspeed Software Defined Radio Source
why: Driver library for the bladeRF software defined radio, a doorway into transceiver hardware and raw RF streams you can actually play with.

brief.what_it_is: libbladeRF is the host-side C driver library for the bladeRF software defined radio, a USB 3.0 SuperSpeed SDR board from Nuand. Software on a computer talks to the board over USB and gets back raw RF sample streams, or sends samples out to be transmitted, across the radio's tuning range of about 47 MHz to 6 GHz with 2x2 MIMO channels and up to 61.44 MHz sampling. The Homebrew package adds four command-line tools on top of the library: bladeRF-cli, bladeRF-fsk, bladeRF-power and bladeRF-update. The repository also contains the FX3 USB controller firmware and the Cyclone IV FPGA HDL that the hardware needs. Without the physical bladeRF board the library has nothing to talk to.
brief.why_it_exists: The repository's own framing is that by providing source code, thorough documentation, easy to grasp tutorials, and a place for open discussion, modern radio systems will be demystified. The brew scout note describes it as a doorway into transceiver hardware and raw RF streams you can actually play with.
brief.how_it_works: The host library talks to the bladeRF board over USB through a libusb backend (a Cypress FX3 SDK backend is available on Windows only). The FX3 controller firmware handles the USB side and the Cyclone IV FPGA carries the radio's signal-processing logic. Tools such as bladeRF-cli load the FPGA, query the device, and drive it from the command line.

name: libbs2b
desc: Bauer stereophonic-to-binaural DSP
why: Crossfeed DSP that turns stereo into a more natural headphone soundstage, a neat audio idea nobody knows about.

brief.what_it_is: libbs2b is a C library and set of plugins implementing the Bauer stereophonic-to-binaural DSP (bs2b), a crossfeed filter for headphone listening. It takes a stereo audio signal and mixes a filtered, delayed copy of each channel into the opposite channel, with a low-pass filter and a high-boost filter, so the sound seems less like it is inside the head. The homepage describes single-pole recursive digital filters with a fixed time delay to the far ear. The Brew formula installs two command-line tools, bs2bconvert and bs2bstream, but the homepage does not document them. The SourceForge page lists Windows, Mac, Linux, BSD and ChromeOS, and mentions Winamp and foobar2000 plugins in user reviews.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's preface argues that stereo records are mixed for loudspeakers, so long headphone listening causes fatigue from a 'superstereo' effect. What headphones lack is the sound from each channel reaching the opposite ear a little later and with some high-frequency roll-off from head shadowing. bs2b is meant to supply that missing crossfeed cheaply in digital form.
brief.how_it_works: The DSP is built from single-pole recursive filters, with the recursion O[n] = a0 * I[n] + a1 * I[n-1] + b1 * O[n-1]. The author says these behave like RC analog filters, which avoids the comb-filter artifacts he associates with FFT-based crossfeed. The low-pass and high-boost cutoffs are chosen so the crossfeed delay and frequency response come out smooth. The page says it does not simulate ambience and does not apply an HRTF at high frequencies.

commands_seen.context: Example from the Theory section's Perl script comments, labelled 'Default preset (700Hz, 4.5dB)'. It prints the filter's frequency and delay response for the given low-pass cutoff, low-pass gain in dB, and high-boost gain in dB.

The SourceForge page offers downloads per platform and a Winamp plugin file, and user reviews describe placing the Winamp DSP in AIMP's plugins folder. brief.standout: It is a small, documented DSP built on a few one-pole filters with presets tied to named crossfeed designs from Bauer, Chu Moy and Jan Meier. The homepage includes the Perl script that computes the response, so the filter math can be checked directly.
brief.status: Maintained, with weak evidence. The SourceForge project page shows Last Update 2024-10-23 and registration in 2005. I did not check a commit history or a changelog, and the homepage itself has no release notes or date.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not document the bs2bconvert or bs2bstream command-line usage, so the entry should not describe their options. The homepage has no build instructions and no licence statement. The SourceForge page lists GPLv2 and MIT, so check the licence in the source before relying on it. name: libcec
desc: Control devices with TV remote control and HDMI cabling
why: Drives TVs over HDMI-CEC, a hidden control channel in every living room you can talk to from a terminal.

brief.what_it_is: libCEC is a C/C++ library, with Python, Node.js, .NET and Rust bindings, for talking to HDMI-CEC, the control channel built into HDMI cabling. It lets a computer send and receive CEC messages, so a TV remote can drive a media centre and the software can command other HDMI devices. It needs suitable hardware: Pulse-Eight's USB-CEC adapter, certain NUC adapters, a Raspberry Pi, or a few other SoCs. The executables it installs are cec-client (plus cecc-client, and versioned copies named 8.1.6), which are the command-line front ends to the library.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it is an enabling platform for the CEC bus in HDMI, so developers can talk to other HDMI devices without dealing with the communication overhead, handshaking, and vendor-specific ways of sending each message.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes libCEC as a layer over the CEC bus that handles the messaging details and per-vendor quirks, so callers work with higher-level operations. It supports several adapter backends, selected at build time with cmake flags such as HAVE_LINUX_API for the Linux CEC framework (v4.10+), HAVE_EXYNOS_API, HAVE_AOCEC_API and HAVE_TDA995X_API. The homepage also notes that not every TV implements CEC the same way, so libCEC works around limits where it can.

name: libcaption
desc: Free open-source CEA608 / CEA708 closed-caption encoder/decoder
why: Encodes and decodes CEA-608 and CEA-708 closed captions, a hidden data channel inside broadcast video.

brief.what_it_is: libcaption is a C library for creating and parsing closed-caption data, using the CEA-608 and CEA-708 standards. For CEA-608 it encodes and decodes the control and preamble codes and the Basic North American, Special North American, and Extended Western European character sets. For CEA-708 it only encodes, by placing 608 data in an NTSC field 1 user data structure. It also provides utilities that wrap a 708 payload into an H.264 SEI NAL unit and reverse that wrapping.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says libcaption is meant to help community-developed broadcast tools handle closed captions consistently across platforms, and it aims to implement a subset of EIA-608 and CEA-708 as supported by Apple iOS.
brief.how_it_works: For H.264, the 708 payload is prefixed with three bytes (nal_unit_type = 6, payloadType = 4, and a variable PayloadSize) and ends with a stop bit in a full byte (value 127). If the payload contains an emulated start code (0,0,1), an emulation prevention byte (3) is inserted. Functions to reverse this are also provided.

commands_seen.context: Build on Mac OS or Linux with re2c enabled (the default).
Build on Mac OS or Linux without re2c.
Install the built library on Mac OS or Linux.

brief.install_notes: Build dependencies on Mac OS and Linux are git, cmake, a compiler (Xcode, gcc, or clang), and optionally re2c and ffmpeg. The build is cmake followed by make, then sudo make install. Windows is untested by the author, who says it is pure C with no dependencies, so it should work there. No accounts or runtime setup are mentioned.
brief.standout: It targets a deliberately narrow subset of 608/708 chosen to match Apple iOS, so output is consistent across platforms. It also includes a helper for embedding captions in an H.264 elementary stream as SEI NAL units, which is the step most caption tooling has to handle separately.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows version v0.8 and the author's contact details, but it has no release date or changelog, and I did not check the commit history or releases page, so I can't say when it was last updated.
brief.caveats: The scout note says it both encodes and decodes 608 and 708, but the README limits 708 to encoding only, wrapped in NTSC field 1 user data. Support is partial for 608 as well: only the listed control codes and character sets are covered. B-frame support for caption creation is minimal, and the README says no caption reordering is needed on playback. Windows has never been tested by the author. The README contains no license file link, but the text says the project is MIT-licensed.

It is written in pure C with no dependencies, so there is no reason it would not work.
I have never tested libcaption in windows.

name: libcello
desc: Higher-level programming in C
why: A library bringing higher-level features like generics and classes to C, a fascinating look at pushing C into new shapes.

brief.what_it_is: Cello is a C library that adds higher-level programming features to ordinary C: generic data structures, polymorphic functions, interfaces or type classes, constructors and destructors, optional garbage collection, exceptions, and reflection. A program includes Cello.h, creates objects on the stack with $(Type, value) or on the heap with new(Type, ...), and loops over collections with foreach. The output is a normal C program that links against libCello.a. The example programs print typed values and walk arrays and tables.
brief.why_it_exists: Daniel Holden made it as a fun experiment to see what C looks like hacked to its limits, and says it should interest anyone who wants to explore what is possible in C.
brief.how_it_works: The README itself does not explain the mechanism. It points readers to the article 'A Fat Pointer Library' for an overview of how Cello works, and says the source code is fairly readable. Cello is described as a runtime system layered on standard C.

brief.install_notes: Cello is a plain C library, so you download the source tarball from the download link on libcello.org, unpack it, and build it. It needs a gnu99-compatible C compiler: gcc on Linux, Xcode with command line tools on Mac (clang), and MinGW64 or Cygwin on Windows. Build with make, check with make check, then optionally make install. No accounts, runtimes or hardware are mentioned. The installation page says installing a C library is not always trivial and suggests searching general C help if you get stuck.
brief.standout: It is a runtime library that makes C feel like a higher-level language without a new compiler or syntax: the code is ordinary C that includes one header. The author openly calls it a hack and presents it as an exploration of how far C can be pushed.
brief.status: unknown. The README and installation page mention a 'latest release' and a download link but show no release date, version number or last-commit date. The author's FAQ says Cello 'does aim to be production ready'. The homepage and GitHub README were both reachable.
brief.caveats: Written in C with a gnu99-compatible compiler required. Windows needs MinGW64 or Cygwin. Make install may fail, in which case manual installation is needed. The license is in LICENSE.md, but the README does not name it.

name: libcoap
desc: Lightweight application-protocol for resource-constrained devices
why: A reference CoAP implementation, a door into the constrained-device protocol running in sensors and IoT gear.

brief.what_it_is: libcoap is a C library implementing CoAP, the Constrained Application Protocol standardized as RFC 7252, for devices with limited computing power, memory, bandwidth, or packet sizes. It provides a protocol parser and basic networking on platforms with malloc() and BSD-style sockets, and also supports Contiki-NG, ESP-IDF, LwIP and RIOT-OS. The repository's examples directory contains a CoAP client, a CoAP Resource Directory server and a CoAP server. The Homebrew formula installs six executables: coap-client, coap-client-openssl, coap-rd, coap-rd-openssl, coap-server and coap-server-openssl. The README does not describe their command-line usage.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames CoAP as a lightweight application protocol for resource-constrained devices, and libcoap is a C reference implementation of it. The README also points to libcoap-minimal for usage examples.

name: libchaos
desc: Advanced library for randomization, hashing and statistical analysis
why: Chaos, randomness and statistics library with an ambitious scope, though obscure and possibly unmaintained.

brief.what_it_is: Libchaos is a C++ library (C++11) for randomization, hashing and statistical analysis. It offers two families of algorithms: "chaos machines", which act as a pseudo-random oracle that you feed data with push and read from with pull, and pseudo-random number generators such as xoroshiro and KISS. Its main entry point is chaos::password, which takes a password and a salt plus time, space and output-size parameters and returns a hex string. The README also describes a planned statistical-tests module and a chaosdeep fork of Hashdeep, but those are listed as in progress or TODO.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants a general, modern, easy-to-use C++ toolkit for scientific research that implements and analyzes randomization and hashing algorithms. The README says TestU01, Dieharder and Hashdeep are obsolete or stopped in development, and that libchaos aims to replace them.
brief.how_it_works: A chaos machine is built from a pseudo-random function combined with a chaotic system, and is controlled by three parameters: time (execution time), space (memory or period length) and an initial secret key. You push data in with push or <<, pull blocks out with pull, and set the parameters with set_time, set_space and set_key. The PRNG side uses seed and next in the same style.

name: libdsk
desc: Library for accessing discs and disc image files
why: Reads and writes raw disc images across obscure floppy formats, a good door into old disk layouts.

brief.what_it_is: LIBDSK is a C library for reading and writing floppy discs and disc image files through one common interface. Its drivers cover raw image files, many emulator formats (.DSK, IMD, CopyQM, TeleDisk, Compaq QRST, APRIDISK, JV3, D88, SAP, CP2, D64, dc42 and others), and real floppy drives on Linux, DOS and Windows. The page also lists utilities built on it (dskdump, dskform, dskid, dsktrans, dskconv, dsklabel and others) and a Gotek USB-stick backend. Input is a disc image or a physical drive, and output is the same data in another image format or on another medium.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says it is meant for converting between real floppy discs and disc images, as CPCTRANS and PCWTRANS did under DOS. It also lets CPMTOOLS and emulator floppy controllers read .DSK files and real discs without format-specific code.
brief.how_it_works: Drivers sit behind one API, and the page says newer versions (1.5.x) store intermediate data in a common format called LDBS, which the DSK, EDSK, ApriDisk, CFI, IMD, JV3, CopyQM and TeleDisk drivers now use. The rcpmfs driver presents a Unix or Windows directory as a CP/M disc image. Lib765, a separate package, runs the other way: it turns uPD765A floppy controller commands into LIBDSK API calls.

commands_seen.context: Build CPMTOOLS against an installed LIBDSK so it can read emulator .DSK images (the page's example for CPMTOOLS integration).

brief.install_notes: The page offers source tarballs (libdsk-1.4.2.tar.gz stable, libdsk-1.5.22.tar.gz development), Windows and DOS executable builds, and Debian, Fedora/Redhat and Gentoo packages from third parties. Using real floppy drives under Linux needs a kernel with FDRAWCMD support, which the page says is deprecated since 5.18 and slated for removal. So you need a custom kernel or an older one that still has it. Nothing in the page mentions Homebrew specifically.
brief.standout: It is a long-running, format-heavy library that treats old and obscure disc formats (CP/M, Amstrad, Commodore 64, TRS-80, Compaq, Gotek sticks) as first-class citizens, and it doubles as a bridge between emulators and real hardware. Its disc-format coverage is much wider than most floppy tools.
brief.status: Maintained, with evidence from the page itself: the page was last updated 2024-11-11 by John Elliott, and the development version is 1.5.22, with changelog entries running through 1.5.x. I did not check a repository commit history or release dates.
brief.caveats: Real-drive access on modern Linux needs FDRAWCMD, which the kernel is dropping. The README warns that rcpmfs users with files over 16k that are not a multiple of 128 bytes must use LibDsk 1.5.18 or later, since earlier versions could corrupt them. The GUI front-end (Diskette Tools) needs wxWidgets to build from source. Licensing was not stated on the page. The page is the author's own site, not a repository, so I could not check issue trackers or a README.

Lib765 is the floppy controller emulation from JOYCE, separately packaged. It is (in some sense) the reverse of LibDsk; it converts uPD765a commands into LibDsk API calls.

name: libeatmydata
desc: LD_PRELOAD library and wrapper to transparently disable fsync and related calls
why: An LD_PRELOAD trick that quietly lies about fsync, a delightful look at how programs assume durability.

brief.what_it_is: libeatmydata is a small LD_PRELOAD shared library, plus an eatmydata wrapper script, that transparently turns off fsync and related calls such as open(O_SYNC) for whatever program you run under it. You run a program through the wrapper (eatmydata foo), and that program's flushes to disk become no-ops. The result is faster writes for software that insists on durable storage, at the cost of no longer being crash-safe. It takes a normal command and its data as input and outputs the same program's behavior, minus the durability guarantees.
brief.why_it_exists: The author built it to speed up database test runs and similar workloads where safe, synchronous disk writes dominate the runtime. The homepage's framing is that it makes software that writes data safely to disk much quicker while making that software no longer crash safe, and it warns: "DO NOT use libeatmydata on software where you care about what it stores."
brief.how_it_works: It is an LD_PRELOAD library, so it is loaded ahead of the C library and intercepts the fsync-family system calls for the process it wraps, letting them return without actually flushing. The eatmydata wrapper script sets this up so you do not have to set LD_PRELOAD by hand. The homepage does not go into further internals.

name: libewf
desc: Library for support of the Expert Witness Compression Format
why: Reads Expert Witness forensic disk images, a rare look at how evidence files are structured internally, though it is mainly a library.

brief.what_it_is: libewf is a C library for reading and writing Expert Witness Compression Format (EWF) files, the container format used for forensic disk images, and it ships a set of command-line tools built on that library. It reads SMART .s01, EnCase .E01 and .Ex01 images, and reads (but does not write) Logical Evidence Files .L01 and .Lx01. Its tools take storage media data from devices, files or stdin and write EWF files (ewfacquire, ewfacquirestream), export to split RAW or another EWF version (ewfexport), print metadata (ewfinfo), verify stored data (ewfverify), mount EWF files through FUSE (ewfmount), and rebuild a new EWF set from a corrupt one (ewfrecover). The scout note calls it mainly a library, which the README supports: the tools are thin front ends to the library.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit problem statement. It describes the project as a library to access the Expert Witness Compression Format, and its purpose is to let other software and people read and write those forensic evidence files without depending on a proprietary tool.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. It lists supported variants (EWF-S01, EWF-E01, EWF2-Ex01, EWF-L01, EWF2-Lx01) and features such as empty-block compression, delta or shadow files for read/write access, and write resume. The tools are described as wrappers, for example ewfrecover is a special variant of ewfexport.

name: libfaketime
desc: Report faked system time to programs
why: Lies to programs about the time, a sharp little hack that opens a door into how software depends on the clock.

brief.what_it_is: libfaketime is a C shared library that intercepts the system calls programs use to read the clock, then reports a faked date and time to those programs while the real system clock stays unchanged. You supply the fake time through environment variables or a config file (FAKETIME, .faketimerc, /etc/faketimerc, or a timestamp file), either as an absolute date, a start-at date, or a relative offset such as -15d. It ships with a 'faketime' wrapper script that accepts natural-language dates and is installed alongside the libraries. Output is the same program behaving as if it were running on a different day.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is for use cases such as deterministic build processes, debugging time-related issues like expired SSL certificates, and testing software for year-2038 compliance. It lets you change the time one program sees without changing the time system-wide.
brief.how_it_works: On Linux it is loaded through LD_PRELOAD (on macOS through DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES with DYLD_FORCE_FLAT_NAMESPACE), so its versions of time-reading functions override the libc ones for that process. Relative offsets are computed from real time plus the offset, so the faked clock keeps ticking; absolute dates freeze the clock. Optional modes add clock speed multipliers (x2, x0,5), a fixed per-call step (i2,0), file-based timestamps, record and replay of timestamps, and deterministic getrandom() output.

brief.install_notes: The README says 'make' compiles both library versions (libfaketime.so.1 and libfaketimeMT.so.1) and runs a test program. Root is not required for a local copy; you can copy the libraries anywhere and set PREFIX in the Makefiles. For 32-bit builds on a 64-bit host, see CFLAGS and LDFLAGS in src/Makefile. On macOS, use Makefile.OSX to build libfaketime.1.dylib, set DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES and DYLD_FORCE_FLAT_NAMESPACE, and read README.OSX. On Linux, you can register the library in /etc/ld.so.conf.d and run ldconfig so LD_PRELOAD can use a bare filename. Optional -D flags such as FORCE_MONOTONIC_FIX, FAKE_SETTIME, and FAKE_RANDOM are set at compile time. I did not see brew-specific instructions in the README.
brief.standout: Instead of a fixed fake time, it can make the clock run at a chosen speed or step a fixed amount per call, which gives programs a repeatable, deterministic clock. Its documented file-timestamp mode lets an outside process pause and resume the fake clock by touching a file.
brief.status: Looks maintained. The README header reads 'libfaketime, version 0.9.13 (August 2026)' and describes a CI matrix covering macOS, many Linux distributions, and sanitizers. I did not check commit history or release dates beyond what the README states.
brief.caveats: Works only on Linux and macOS, with other Unix-like systems reported to work. It cannot intercept statically linked binaries or setuid programs such as ping or passwd. Go, Python, .NET, JVM, and some other runtimes may bypass the preload through vDSO, direct syscalls, or late library loading; the README says this is a compatibility limit, not a bug. Absolute dates freeze the clock, which breaks programs that measure elapsed time. Config files are cached for 10 seconds by default. Some hangs in CLOCK_MONOTONIC tests need compile-time FORCE_MONOTONIC_FIX or FORCE_PTHREAD_NONVER flags. FAKETIME_SPAWN_TARGET is passed to a shell and is unsafe with untrusted input or privileged processes. FAKE_RANDOM is Linux-only and explicitly insecure, so it must not be used for cryptography. FAKE_PID and FAKE_RANDOM are Linux-only, and macOS builds can abort if they are enabled. FAKETIME_XRESET is labelled experimental. Stale shared memory under /dev/shm can cause errors after killed processes. The README is licensed under GPL, per its License section.
quotes: libfaketime intercepts various system calls that programs use to retrieve the current date and time.
This means you can modify the system time a program sees without having to change the time system-wide.
Whenever possible, you should use relative offsets or 'start at' dates, and not use absolute dates.

name: libfreenect
desc: Drivers and libraries for the Xbox Kinect device
why: Drivers for the Xbox Kinect, letting you read depth and IR streams from a cheap sensor over USB.

brief.what_it_is: libfreenect is a userspace driver library for the Microsoft Kinect (the original Xbox 360 model, per the firmware note about model 1414). It takes data from the sensor over USB and exposes RGB and depth images, motor tilt, accelerometer, LED, and audio. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows, and ships C, C++, C#, Python, Ruby, ActionScript, and Java (JNA) wrappers plus a set of demo viewers such as freenect-glview and freenect-wavrecord. The README does not mention infrared streams, although the scout note says it does.

brief.how_it_works: The library talks to the device over libusb (1.0.18 or later; 1.0.22 or later on Windows) and is built with CMake. The fakenect component can record a live session to a directory and later replay it by preloading libfakenect.so with LD_PRELOAD and pointing FAKENECT_PATH at the recording, so programs can run without the hardware attached.

name: libforensic1394
desc: Live memory forensics over IEEE 1394 ("FireWire") interface
why: Reads live machine memory over FireWire DMA, a striking door into hardware-level memory access with a real huh.

brief.what_it_is: An open source C library, with Python bindings, for live memory forensics over the IEEE 1394 (FireWire) interface. It uses the direct memory access that FireWire offers to read a running machine's physical memory. The homepage says it runs on GNU/Linux and Mac OS X, and it exposes a simple C API for this. Its input is a 1394 connection to the target machine, and its output is the memory contents read over that link.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a modern alternative to pythonraw1394 (a Python wrapper around libraw1394), with native support for the newer "Juju" stack used by many GNU/Linux distributions. The homepage says it improves on existing libraries by offering a simple and clean interface to FireWire direct memory access.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage gives only a high-level account. The library presents an SBP-2 unit directory to a remote device so it can acquire physical memory access. It uses a vectorised API that exploits the asynchronous capabilities of 1394 controllers, and on Linux it works through the Juju stack, on Mac OS X through IOKit.
brief.install_notes: The homepage lists a git repository for the latest version and source tarballs for release 0.2 (libforensic1394-0.2.tar.gz and .zip). The build uses CMake and CPack. Hardware is implied to be a 1394 (FireWire) controller on the target and analysis side, but the homepage does not state requirements. Windows and FreeBSD are not supported. The homepage does not describe first-run steps or configuration.
brief.standout: It reads live physical memory through FireWire's DMA path, so the target machine needs no installed agent or software running on it. The page notes the author's own paper on the technique, which is the main source for the method.
brief.status: Quiet. The latest release, 0.2, was tagged 2010-10-05. A developer preview came out 2010-08-03. The page was last updated 2015-02-07, and the copyright line says 2015. The homepage describes the project as feature complete, with the Windows port postponed. I found no newer release or commit information on the page.
brief.caveats: Supported only on GNU/Linux and Mac OS X. FreeBSD and Windows support are listed as future work, and the Windows driver is described as requiring a prohibitively expensive cross-signing certificate. The known bugs and limitations are in a BUGS file in the source distribution, which I did not fetch. The release is from 2010 and the page was last updated in 2015, so current kernel and OS versions are untested as far as the page shows. The library is LGPLv3+. The Doxygen docs and the paper are referenced, but the page gives no direct URLs for them.
quotes: An open source (GNU LGPLv3+) library for performing live memory forensics over the IEEE 1394 ("FireWire") interface.
libforensic1394 improves upon existing libraries by providing a simple and clean interface to the the direct memory access functionality available over FireWire.
Available through git libforensic1394 is currently feature complete and undergoing extensive field testing.

name: libimobiledevice
desc: Library to communicate with iOS devices natively
why: Talks to iOS devices over the native protocols without Apple's tools, a real door into a closed ecosystem.

brief.what_it_is: libimobiledevice is a cross-platform, free C library, plus a set of command-line tools, for talking to iOS devices such as iPhones and iPads over Apple's native protocols. It takes a device connection, either USB through usbmuxd or wireless if Wi-Fi sync is enabled on iOS 11 and later, and exposes device services for apps, backup, filesystem, debugging, activation, provisioning, SpringBoard, syslog, and firmware updates. Output is device data returned through the C API or printed by the bundled utilities, such as ideviceinfo printing device key/value details. The bundled tools are ideviceinfo, ideviceactivation, idevicediagnostics, idevicebackup2, idevicescreenshot, idevicesyslog, ideviceinstaller and others, 22 executables in the Homebrew listing.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Linux enthusiasts were not amused by hardware like the iPhone 2G, and because iTunes was not available for Linux, libiphone was born, which became libimobiledevice with the goal to "bring freedom and 'allow penguins to talk to fruits'".
brief.how_it_works: The library reimplements the native protocols itself and, per the homepage, does not depend on or bundle any existing libraries from Apple. Connections go through usbmuxd, which the release notes describe as a socket daemon that multiplexes connections from and to iOS devices. The C API opens a device with idevice_new_with_options, then performs a lockdown handshake (lockdownd_client_new_with_handshake) before reading values such as DeviceColor.

brief.what_it_is: libgphoto2 is a C library that lets other programs talk to digital cameras over USB and similar links. It takes in camera requests from a calling application (list files, fetch images, change settings) and sends them to the camera using protocols it understands, mainly PTP, with MTP also covered. It has no window of its own. The project describes it as a backend that frontends such as the gphoto2 command-line tool, digiKam, gThumb and Darktable build on.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as the core library designed to allow access to digital cameras by external programs. The README frames it as the successor to the original gphoto, with more features and additional camera drivers.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says it abstracts communication ports from camera protocol, so a new physical link can be added as a port in libgphoto2_port and a new camera family as a camlib with the required callbacks. Client programs stay unaware of these details. The README adds that cameras using USB Mass Storage need no libgphoto2 because the OS already mounts them, while PTP cameras unknown to the library fall back to a generic PTP driver that usually works without configuration.

name: libirecovery
desc: Library and utility to talk to iBoot/iBSS via USB
why: Talks to Apple devices in recovery mode over raw USB, a door into iBoot and DFU low-level behaviour.

brief.what_it_is: libirecovery is a cross-platform C library and command-line tool that talks to iBoot/iBSS on Apple iOS devices over USB. The bundled utility is named irecovery, and its documented entry point is irecovery --shell, which opens an interactive shell on a device in recovery mode. From that shell you can run iBoot commands such as setenv and saveenv, or reboot the device. Input is a device attached over USB in recovery mode; output is terminal text and the library's API for other programs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is a fork of an older version from openjailbreak.org and is meant to be used with idevicerestore from the libimobiledevice project. The libimobiledevice homepage frames the wider effort as bringing Linux users access to iPhones, which were originally unavailable on that platform.
brief.how_it_works: It implements the USB communication to iBoot/iBSS, the low-level bootloader code that runs when a device is in recovery mode, rather than talking to services on a booted OS. It depends on libimobiledevice-glue and uses libusb on Linux and an IOKit USB backend on macOS, as shown in the configure output in the README.

name: libklvanc
desc: VANC Processing Framework
why: Decodes VANC ancillary data hidden in broadcast video streams, a rarely seen door into SDI broadcast plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: Libklvanc is a C library for parsing and generating Vertical Ancillary Data (VANC) found in the Serial Digital Interface (SDI) video wire protocol. It takes VANC line data from captured SDI video and decodes it into structured packets, and it can also encode packets back into VANC lines for an SDI output. Protocols listed in the README include CEA-708 closed captions (SMPTE ST 334), AFD and Bar Data (ST 2016), SCTE-104 ad triggers, ST 2038 arbitrary VANC encapsulation, ST 12-2 timecodes, RDD 8 subtitle packets, and ST 2108-1 HDR/WCG metadata. It also includes utility functions for colour representations such as the V210 format used by Blackmagic DeckLink cards.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a general parser/decoder and encoder for VANC, so that capture and output applications can both work with the ancillary data SDI carries alongside video. It is meant to be the library underneath real capture tools, with the separate klvanc-tools project using it with Blackmagic cards to capture live SDI signals.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the library provides a general parser/decoder and an encoder for VANC lines, with per-protocol support for each SMPTE or SCTE format it lists. It computes and validates checksums at several levels and handles line-formatting edge cases such as keeping packets contiguous. API documentation is generated with Doxygen, and the tools subdirectory holds test programs that call the library.

brief.why_it_exists: liblcf is part of the EasyRPG Project, a community effort to create a free, open source role playing game creation tool compatible with RPG Maker 2000/2003 games. The README describes the library as a way to handle RPG Maker 2000 and 2003 game data.
