name: liblouis
desc: Open-source braille translator and back-translator
why: Braille translation and back-translation is a fascinating transform between text and tactile code, with a rich table-driven design behind it.

brief.what_it_is: Liblouis is an open-source braille translator and back-translator, a C library that converts text into braille and braille back into text. It supports computer and literary braille, contracted and uncontracted translation for many languages, hyphenation, and math braille (Nemeth and Marburg). Translation rules live in table files, and the library is distributed as a shared library on Linux and macOS and as a DLL on Windows. The package also includes command-line tools (lou_allround, lou_checkhyphens, lou_checktable, lou_debug, lou_translate, lou_trace) for testing and debugging translation tables. A companion project, Liblouisutdml, adds a formatter that turns XML or plain text into embosser-ready braille.
brief.why_it_exists: The project is named in honor of Louis Braille and aims to provide braille translation for many languages and braille codes as a free library that applications can embed. The README says it is based on the translation routines in the BRLTTY screenreader and has 'gone far beyond these routines'. Its screen-reader support is a stated purpose: it is used by NVDA and Orca and in commercial products such as ViewPlus.
brief.how_it_works: Translation is table-driven: new languages are added through tables that support rule-based or dictionary-based approaches, and the repository ships tables for many languages (en-us-g2.ctb and en-us-g1.ctb are named as examples). The library is written in C so it needs no runtime and can be called from Python, Java, and JavaScript bindings. Back-translation uses the same tables in reverse, and the included tools test and trace those translations.

brief.what_it_is: Liquid Rescale Library (liblqr) is a free, open source C/C++ seam carving library. It implements the content-aware resizing algorithm from a paper by Shai Avidan and Ariel Shamir. Per the wiki, you give it a picture and a target size, and it resizes the image non-uniformly while trying to keep the important parts from distorting. The homepage says it also supports saving and loading carving information, real-time scaling, manual feature selection, and customizable progress reporting. The library requires glib-2.0 version 2.8 or later. The README-equivalent here is a Wikidot wiki, not a repository README, and it does not show input or output formats beyond that.
brief.why_it_exists: The wiki says the goal is to resize pictures non-uniformly while preserving their features, avoiding distortion of the important parts. It also says the API is meant to be 'powerful, yet fast and easy to use'.
brief.how_it_works: The wiki does not explain the mechanism beyond naming the Avidan and Shamir seam carving paper. It only says the library implements that algorithm.
brief.install_notes: The homepage requires glib-2.0 version 2.8. Windows users who only want the GIMP Liquid Rescale plug-in do not need the library, since the plug-in ships with it. The Download and Installation pages are linked from the wiki, but my guessed Installation and Features URLs returned 404, so I have no install steps beyond the glib requirement. The wiki says code hosting moved to GitHub in July 2014, but the page gives no URL for it, so I did not fetch the repository.

name: libltc
desc: POSIX-C Library for handling Linear/Logitudinal Time Code (LTC)
why: A C library for decoding and encoding SMPTE timecode carried as audio, a niche transform from sound into time data with a bit of mystery.

brief.what_it_is: libltc is a POSIX C library for encoding and decoding Linear (Longitudinal) Timecode, which is SMPTE or EBU timecode stored as a Manchester-biphase audio signal. On the decode side it takes 8-bit unsigned audio samples and returns decoded LTC frames tagged with the audio sample numbers where each frame starts and ends. On the encode side it takes timecode values and produces the audio samples for an LTC signal. It is a library, not an application, so it ships no command-line tools of its own.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as the successor to libltcsmpte, which had API and ABI problems from early design choices such as naming conventions and compile-time sample-format options. libltc is meant to operate on LTC frames only and to stay ignorant of framerate and timecode semantics, which the author says belong to the application or to the separate libtimecode project.
brief.how_it_works: The library runs a signal tracker over the audio samples, recovers the Manchester-biphase bit stream, and maps the 80 LTC bits to HH:MM:SS:FF timecode, including SMPTE date support. It follows speed variations (vari-speed) and reverse-played tape, and each decoded frame carries its audio sample position. The encoder accepts a per-byte speed parameter and can increment or decrement timecode.

name: libmapper
desc: Distributed system for media control mapping
why: A distributed mapping system linking control signals across instruments and software, a fascinating model of live performance wiring.

brief.what_it_is: libmapper is an open-source, cross-platform C library for declaring data signals on a shared network and creating arbitrary connections, called mappings, between them. A mapping streams data from one or more source signals to a destination signal, over shared memory or Open Sound Control (OSC) across a network. The library handles address and datatype translation and lets you write mathematical expressions to condition, combine and transform source values. Its README gives the example of connecting a set of sensors to a synthesizer's input parameters.
brief.why_it_exists: It began as a tool for composers and performers to connect custom-built instruments, such as Arduino-based controllers, to sound synthesizers, and it was first written in Max/MSP before being re-implemented in C. The author wanted to change OSC mappings at runtime, including scaling, derivatives, integration, filtering and smoothing, and the project was built to avoid any master node or central device database.
brief.how_it_works: Devices announce their signals over a multicast UDP port that all nodes listen on, and a collision-handling protocol on that port assigns each device a unique ID. Signal data then travels directly peer-to-peer from sender to receiver over UDP or TCP, with the transport configurable at runtime. Convergent (many-to-one) mappings and signal instancing are supported, and the README says the peer-to-peer design may be redundant when many nodes subscribe to one signal.
brief.install_notes: Install via Homebrew, PyPI, NuGet or crates.io, or download source and binaries from libmapper.org or idmil.org. Building from source uses autogen.sh and configure.ac or CMakeLists.txt, and there is a windows_build.ps1 for Windows. The only required dependency is liblo (LGPL). Python, Java (openjdk), and C# (.NET) bindings are optional and need their own toolchains. Separate documentation in the doc folder covers building and the API tutorials, which I did not open.
brief.standout: Mappings are first-class and can be rewired at runtime, with a built-in expression language for signal conditioning, and there is no central broker. It is positioned as an open-source alternative to commercial tools like Osculator, and it has been built into hardware instruments such as the T-Stick and the Maplet Eurorack module.
brief.status: Probably maintained. The GitHub repo shows about 3,617 commits, CI workflows under .github/workflows, and a current-looking package set across several registries. I could not see a last-release date or last-commit date in the fetched pages, so I can't confirm recency more precisely.
brief.caveats: The library is LGPL-2.1 (the homepage says 2.1 or later). The README says commercial use is allowed only if the library stays dynamically linked, and other uses need an agreement with the authors. Data types are limited to homogeneous numeric vectors (integer, float, double), so structured data and images are not supported directly. The README says the time-based history syntax in expressions is not yet usable. Peer-to-peer delivery can duplicate traffic when many nodes subscribe to a signal. The homepage is a short plain-HTML page, so most of the detail above comes from the GitHub README.
quotes: A library for connecting things.
This library is a system for representing input and output signals on a network and allowing arbitrary "mappings" to be dynamically created between them.
We specifically wanted to avoid keeping a "master" node which is responsible for arbitrating connections or republishing data

brief.what_it_is: The Memory Pool System (MPS) is a C memory management library from Ravenbrook Limited, distributed as the MPS Kit: source code, manuals, and design documentation. You compile mps.c into an object file and link it into your own program, which then asks the MPS for memory through its allocation interfaces. It ships with a library of memory pool classes, each implementing a different memory management policy. The brew package is named libmps and installs no executables, so it is a library for developers, not a command-line tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the MPS exists to be a very general, adaptable, flexible, reliable, and efficient memory management system that lets you combine memory management techniques flexibly. It is meant to support both manual and automatic memory management in one framework. The project has been in development since 1994 and in commercial products since 1997.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. It lists the features the MPS supports: in-line allocation, finalization, weakness, and multiple concurrent cooperating incremental generational garbage collections. Its pool classes provide specialized policies, and the design details live in the manual and design documents that the README points to.

name: libnatpmp
desc: NAT port mapping protocol library
why: A door into NAT-PMP, the router port mapping protocol quietly running in most homes, with a small client to explore.

brief.what_it_is: libnatpmp is a C client-side library for NAT-PMP, the NAT Port Mapping Protocol, which lets a program ask a router for its public address and for a port mapping from a private port to a public one. The author describes it as an attempt at a portable, fully compliant client implementation. The API is declared in natpmp.h and is driven by request calls (sendpublicaddressrequest, sendnewportmappingrequest) followed by polling readnatpmpresponseorretry until it stops returning NATPMP_TRYAGAIN. The Homebrew formula also installs an executable called natpmpc, but the pages I read say nothing about its options or output.
brief.why_it_exists: NAT-PMP is described on the homepage as the direct competitor to the UPnP IGD specification, offering a way to do NAT traversal. The homepage says it was mainly supported by Apple software and hardware at the time.
brief.how_it_works: The library uses non-blocking sockets and every API call is asynchronous, so it can be folded into an event-driven loop. A caller sends a request, then waits on the socket with select() or poll() using getnatpmprequesttimeout() as the timeout, and calls readnatpmpresponseorretry() repeatedly until the response arrives. The sample code in the homepage shows this pattern for a TCP port redirect with a 3600-second lifetime.

name: libmysofa
desc: Reader for AES SOFA files to get better HRTFs
why: Reads SOFA head-related transfer function files, a real door into binaural spatial audio and how ears localise sound.

brief.what_it_is: libmysofa is a small C library for reading AES SOFA files that contain head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) in the AES69-2015 standard. It takes a .sofa file (or a buffer already in memory) and a target sample rate, then gives you the HRTF filter for any requested [x,y,z] position as left and right impulse responses plus left and right delays in samples or seconds. Filters can be linearly interpolated from nearest neighbours or taken exactly as stored. The README also documents spherical-to-Cartesian coordinate helpers. The brew formula lists an executable called mysofa2json, but the README does not describe it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a simple reader so that software can use HRTF data stored in AES SOFA files, which the author's MySofa work relies on for personal HRTF design and better binaural audio.
brief.how_it_works: mysofa_open (or the normalising, advanced, in-memory or cached variants) parses the SOFA HDF5 data and builds a nearest-neighbour search structure over the measurement grid, with optional normalisation. mysofa_getfilter_float or mysofa_getfilter_short then returns a weighted sum of the nearest neighbours' filters for a position, or the exact stored filter via the _nointerp variant. The caller applies the returned delays and convolves audio with the impulse responses using FIR filtering.

brief.what_it_is: libnetfilter_queue is a userspace C library that gives programs an API to packets the Linux kernel packet filter has queued for them. A program receives queued packets from the kernel's nfnetlink_queue subsystem, inspects them, and sends back a verdict or reinjects an altered packet. brief.how_it_works: The kernel's nfnetlink_queue subsystem holds packets that firewall rules send to a queue, and the library passes them to userspace over netlink. The program then issues a verdict on each packet or reinjects a changed version back into the kernel. The homepage names the two main features as receiving queued packets and issuing verdicts and/or reinjecting altered packets, but does not go into further detail.

name: libngspice
desc: Spice circuit simulator as shared library
why: The ngspice circuit simulator as a library; real electronics simulation, but packaged as a shared library rather than a playground.

brief.what_it_is: ngspice is an open source SPICE circuit simulator for electric and electronic circuits. Per its homepage, a circuit is written as a netlist that can include JFETs, bipolar and MOS transistors, passive R/L/C elements, diodes, transmission lines, and digital gates, including mixed-signal circuits. Input is command-line or file based, with no schematic entry. Output is one or more graphs of currents, voltages and other quantities, or a data file. The brew entry libngspice is the shared-library form of this simulator; the pages I read describe the simulator itself and do not describe the library interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents ngspice as an open source alternative for simulating electric and electronic circuits in the SPICE tradition, and says it aims to be SPICE compatible so existing PSPICE, LTSPICE and HSPICE (foundry PDK) models and netlists can be used. The README frames it as a successor built from Spice3f5, Cider1b1 and Xspice, with many contributors beyond those packages.
brief.how_it_works: The README says ngspice is a mixed-level/mixed-signal simulator combining Spice3f5 (analog circuit simulation), Cider1b1 (coupling to the DSIM device simulator for device-structure-level accuracy), and Xspice (code-model support and event-driven digital simulation). The homepage says digital parts are event driven. I did not find any description of how the shared library exposes this to other programs.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says Windows source and binaries are on the SourceForge download page, that popular Linux distributions, Cygwin and FreeBSD packages exist, and that Homebrew covers macOS. Beyond brew install, I saw nothing about libraries, headers, runtimes, accounts or first-run configuration; the pages I reached do not cover the shared-library build or linking.
brief.standout: Unlike most circuit simulators with a GUI, ngspice is a plain-text netlist engine that reads both PSPICE/LTSPICE and HSPICE foundry model libraries and mixes analog and event-driven digital in one circuit. Packaging it as a shared library, as libngspice does, makes that engine embeddable in other programs, which is the part the scout notes highlight.
brief.status: Apparently maintained, though I found no release date or last-commit date. The homepage lists introductory FOSDEM talks on ngspice status and updates through FOSDEM'25, and the GitHub repository ngspice/ngspice exists with a README pointing to active mailing lists. The libngspice formula's own date was not checked.
brief.caveats: No schematic entry; users need third-party front ends for schematics. The shared-library interface is not documented on any page I reached, so the entry should not describe its API. Two guessed sub-pages (development.html and features.html) returned 404, so the homepage was the only documentation source that loaded. The homepage's FOSDEM and manual links were not followed, so the detailed manual was not read.

name: libplctag
desc: Portable and simple API for accessing AB PLC data over Ethernet
why: A door into Allen-Bradley PLC protocols over Ethernet, letting you talk to real industrial controllers.

brief.what_it_is: libplctag is an open source C library for Linux, Windows and macOS that talks to PLCs over EtherNet/IP or Modbus TCP to read and write tags. Your program passes it a tag name and a PLC address, and it returns the tag's values as integers, floats, bits or arrays of those. The README says it has been in production since early 2012 and supports Rockwell/Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, Micro850, PLC-5, SLC 500 and MicroLogix, plus Omron NX/NJ series. The Homebrew entry lists two executables, modbus_server and tag_rw2, but the README does not describe either one.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a portable, simple API for reading and writing PLC data without tying the user to vendor tooling. It also says the library has very stable API with almost no changes other than feature additions since 2012, and that it is designed for easy wrapping in other languages. The History link points to a wiki page on why it was built, which I did not fetch.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals beyond saying it is a pure C library with no dependencies apart from libc or musl and pthreads on some platforms. It says it uses protocol-specific features for performance and supports multiple requests per packet and packet size negotiation with newer ControlLogix firmware. The API is described as mostly data access, covering single bits and 8 to 64-bit integers and floats.
brief.install_notes: The README does not mention brew. It says to get pre-built ZIP binaries from the GitHub releases page for your system, and it lists 32 and 64-bit builds for x86 Linux and Windows and 64-bit for x86-64 macOS. For a source build it points to a CMake build system and says native CMake support is in recent Visual Studio. Raspberry Pi is supported on Linux and Windows IoT, and the README says some effort is needed to configure Visual Studio for the Windows IoT build. Using it for real work requires a reachable PLC on the network, since the examples read a tag named TestBigArray from a Logix-class Allen-Bradley controller. No PLC is needed to build or run the library itself.
brief.standout: It has been in production for over a decade with an API that has barely changed, and it is the base for several language wrappers, including the popular libplctag.NET, plus Go, Java and Julia. It is dual licensed under MPL 2.0 or LGPL 2+, so it can be embedded in both open and closed projects.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I could not confirm a date. The README shows CI badges on the release branch and tested toolchains such as GCC 15.2.0, Alpine 3.23 and MSVC 19.44, which suggests recent activity. It has a release badge and a releases page, but I did not see a release date or last commit date on the fetched page.
brief.caveats: The README carries a safety warning: PLCs control equipment, and loss of property, production or life can happen if mistakes are made. The authors say they make no claims about suitability for any purpose. Testing is limited because they do not own all the hardware, and they ask for bug reports from users who have it. Tier One platforms are a fixed list of OS and compiler combinations, and the README notes that Windows IoT needs extra Visual Studio setup. Some features are marked as partial: SLC 500 arrays were not tested, and user-defined structures must be read piece by piece. Wrappers in other languages may carry different licenses. The homepage fetch gave the README only, so I did not check the wiki API page or the examples README.

name: libpointing
desc: Provides direct access to HID pointing devices
why: Direct access to HID pointing devices is a real hardware door, though it reads more like a library than a toy.

brief.what_it_is: Libpointing is an open-source C++ library, cross-platform across Windows, Mac OS X and Linux, that gives programs direct access to HID pointing devices such as mice. It delivers raw input events (displacements in x and y, button state, timestamps) and can bypass the operating system's own pointer acceleration. It also supports writing and applying pointer transfer functions, and it can replicate the ones used by Windows, OS X and Xorg. Bindings exist for Java, Python and Node.js.
brief.why_it_exists: The citation frames it as "No more bricolage! Methods and tools to characterize, replicate and compare pointing transfer functions" (Casiez and Roussel, UIST'11). The README says it is meant to help characterize, replicate and compare pointer acceleration curves.
brief.how_it_works: A program creates a PointingDevice and a DisplayDevice from URI-style strings such as "any:?debugLevel=1", then creates a TransferFunction (for example "sigmoid:?debugLevel=2") linking them. It registers a callback that receives the timestamp, raw dx and dy, and button bits for each event, and calls the function's applyi method to get pixel displacements. The main loop calls PointingDevice::idle(100) to pump events.

name: libpostal
desc: Library for parsing/normalizing street addresses around the world
why: Statistical street-address parsing trained on OpenStreetMap data is a clever library, though still a library at heart.

brief.what_it_is: libpostal is a C library that parses and normalizes street addresses from around the world. It takes a free-form address string and returns labeled components such as house_number, road, city, and postcode, or it returns a set of normalized expansions of the address (for example, abbreviations spelled out and numbers written as digits) for search indexing and comparison. Bindings exist for Python, Ruby, Go, Java, PHP, and NodeJS. The README says it is not a geocoder: it does not turn addresses into lat/lon.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it was created inside the OpenVenues project to dedupe venues drawn from millions of Common Crawl-derived places, where conventional abbreviations (Road/Rd, California/CA, New York City/NYC) defeat simple string and MinHash matching. It also says the goal is to 'understand location-based strings in every language, everywhere.'
brief.how_it_works: The address parser is a Conditional Random Field trained on about a billion synthetic and real addresses built from OpenStreetMap, OpenAddresses, and GeoPlanet, using OpenCage address-format templates, with random abbreviations and dropped components added for robustness. A separate language classifier (multinomial logistic regression trained with FTRL-Proximal) detects which language(s) an address uses so the right abbreviation dictionaries apply. Expansion works from per-language dictionaries, and transliteration uses CLDR transforms without requiring ICU.

name: libprotoident
desc: Performs application layer protocol identification for flows
why: Identifies application protocols from flow data, a fascinating door into how traffic reveals its own identity.

brief.what_it_is: Libprotoident is a C library that labels each network flow with the application protocol it most likely carries, such as BitTorrent, SMTP, or POP3. It works from the first four bytes of application payload sent in each direction, not from full packet contents. It ships three command-line tools (lpi_protoident, lpi_find_unknown, and lpi_arff) that read a libtrace URI, which can be a trace file or a live network interface. lpi_protoident prints one line per flow to stdout, with the protocol label, endpoints, ports, transport protocol, timestamps, byte counts, and the first four payload bytes per direction.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a library for application protocol identification, built so that programmers can write their own tools that use protocol information. It also notes that some traffic patterns in the WAND group's trace sets cannot be tied to any known protocol, and asks readers for help naming them.
brief.how_it_works: The library matches patterns in the first four bytes of application payload sent from each endpoint. The tools use libflowmanager to track flows, and identification happens only when a flow concludes or expires. Flows can also be grouped into categories, so BitTorrent, Gnutella, and eMule all fall under P2P, and SMTP, POP3, and IMAP fall under Mail.

name: libquantum
desc: C library for the simulation of quantum mechanics
why: Simulates quantum registers and algorithms like Shor's on a classical machine, a real door into quantum computation.

brief.what_it_is: libquantum is a C library for simulating quantum mechanics, with its main focus on quantum computing. It provides a quantum register with basic gates such as Hadamard and Controlled-NOT, and measurements on single qubits or the whole register. It can also compute the time evolution of arbitrary Hamiltonians, including time-dependent ones, by numerical integration of the Schrödinger equation or by exact diagonalization. The homepage says it includes implementations of Shor's factoring algorithm and Grover's search algorithm. It is a library, not a command-line tool: brew reports no executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it started as a pure quantum computer simulator and that support for general quantum simulation was added later. name: librsync
desc: Library that implements the rsync remote-delta algorithm
why: Implements rsync's rolling-checksum delta algorithm as a library, a clever idea hidden under a lot of everyday plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: librsync is a C library for calculating and applying network deltas, the rsync remote-delta algorithm packaged as an API for other programs. To compute a delta you need only a signature (per-block checksums) of the old file plus the new file, not both files together. The tree also builds an rdiff command-line tool that exposes the key operations: generating a file signature, generating a delta from a signature to a new file, and applying the delta to rebuild the new file from the old one. It works on byte streams only.
brief.why_it_exists: It is meant for building other programs that transfer files as efficiently as rsync, such as backup tools, binary patch distribution, or directory sync to a server or between peers. It was originally written for the rproxy experiment in delta-compression for HTTP. The README says Dropbox, rdiff-backup and Duplicity use it.
brief.how_it_works: The receiver computes a signature: a set of checksums over each block of one file. The sender then scans the other file, and blocks at any position whose checksum matches are likely identical, while the remaining bytes are the difference. The README says this lets differences be transferred without both files being on the same system. It uses BLAKE2 for hashing, which the README says is included in the tree.

commands_seen.context: Named in the README as the command-line tool that exposes librsync's signature, delta, and patch operations. The README gives no concrete invocation, and I saw no example command lines.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the package manager was described on the homepage. The README's Installing section is only linked, not reproduced, so I could not confirm build dependencies or steps. No accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration were mentioned.
brief.standout: The rsync algorithm needs only checksums of one file, not the file itself, so the two sides never have to share a filesystem. The project also makes the point that it is a library: it deliberately leaves out the rsync wire protocol, SSH, and file metadata, so it fits into other programs rather than replacing rsync.

brief.caveats: It does not talk to an rsync server; you have to shell out to rsync for that. It does not handle filenames, permissions, or directories, and it has no network code of its own. Licensing is LGPL v2.1: you can link it dynamically into non-GPL programs, but you must redistribute librsync source with any modifications. The BLAKE2 code in the tree is CC0.

brief.what_it_is: libsixel is an encoder and decoder library for DEC SIXEL graphics, a terminal-friendly image format, plus command-line converters. img2sixel takes image files (the README mentions JPEG, PNG and animated GIF, via libjpeg, libpng and related build options) from file arguments or stdin and writes a SIXEL escape-sequence stream to stdout or a named file. sixel2png goes the other way, turning a SIXEL file into a PNG. Because the output is plain escape sequences, you can cat it to a SIXEL-capable terminal to display the picture. The package also ships C APIs and bindings for Python, Perl, PHP and Ruby.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says SIXEL was built for 1980s DEC printers and terminals, where drawing images was painfully slow, and that modern CPUs and networks make the format practical again. It also says the author's encoder was redesigned for terminal emulators rather than dot-matrix printers, to reduce the transport overhead while staying compatible with older SIXEL terminals.
brief.how_it_works: SIXEL data is an escape sequence (DCS) stream, so any program that can write bytes to a terminal can show an image. The encoder quantizes colours (median-cut, with selectable dithering such as Floyd-Steinberg, Atkinson and Stucki) and emits the bands of six pixel rows that SIXEL uses, with an encoding policy aimed at terminal display speed rather than printer head movement. The decoder reverses this into an indexed bitmap plus palette.

name: libtpms
desc: Library for software emulation of a Trusted Platform Module
why: Software TPM emulation is a real door into trusted computing and the TPM command protocol, though it is a library first.

brief.what_it_is: libtpms is a C library that emulates a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) in software. It takes TPM command bytes from a caller and returns the TPM's response bytes, so a program can talk to a virtual TPM without hardware. It ships as a shared library (libtpms.so) with a small public header set (tpm_library.h and related files) and man pages for each API call. The README says the user must already know how to build valid TPM commands and parse their results, since the library does not teach TPM concepts.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says libtpms exists to integrate TPM functionality into hypervisors, primarily QEMU, and it deliberately keeps the public API very narrow so that this integration is possible.
brief.how_it_works: The caller initializes the library with TPMLIB_MainInit, registers callbacks with TPMLIB_RegisterCallbacks, and sends TPM commands through TPMLIB_Process. Its API list also includes TPMLIB_VolatileAll_Store, TPMLIB_DecodeBlob, and TPMLIB_GetTPMProperty. The README gives no deeper explanation of the internals beyond this list of API calls and man pages.

name: libusbmuxd
desc: USB multiplexor library for iOS devices
why: The usbmuxd multiplexing protocol that quietly connects iPhones to Macs is a door worth opening, though the library is plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: libusbmuxd is a C client library that lets applications speak the usbmux protocol, which multiplexes connections to iOS devices over USB. It does not talk to the device directly. It connects to a socket served by a usbmuxd daemon, which owns the USB link. The package also ships two command-line tools: iproxy, which binds local TCP ports and forwards them to ports on the device, and inetcat, a netcat-like tool that exposes a raw TCP connection to the device on stdin and stdout.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the library is primarily used by applications built on libimobiledevice to reach services on iOS devices. The homepage explains that the usbmuxd daemon ships with iTunes on Windows and Mac OS X, and that the libimobiledevice project reimplemented it as open source for Linux and for people who do not want iTunes.
brief.how_it_works: Applications link against libusbmuxd and connect to the usbmuxd socket instead of opening USB themselves. The USBMUXD_SOCKET_ADDRESS environment variable can point the client at a socket on another host, such as a remote machine's usbmuxd. iproxy and inetcat use this same client interface to open TCP connections to ports on the device.

name: libusrsctp
desc: Portable SCTP userland stack
why: A userland SCTP stack, a door into a transport protocol almost nobody has seen running, used in WebRTC data channels.

brief.what_it_is: libusrsctp is a C library that implements SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) in userland, so an application can run SCTP without kernel support. It is built from the sctplab/usrsctp repository and the README says it supports FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Linux, Mac OS X and Windows. Applications start it with usrsctp_init(), create sockets with usrsctp_socket(), and exchange messages with usrsctp_sendv() and usrsctp_recvv(). Its API is modelled on RFC 6458, the Sockets API Extensions for SCTP, with differences listed in the Manual. Data can go straight over SCTP or be encapsulated in UDP, and the Manual describes a set of sysctl-style tunables exposed as usrsctp_sysctl_set_* and usrsctp_sysctl_get_* functions.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says SCTP is a message-oriented, reliable transport with multihoming and multi-streaming that runs on top of IP or UDP, and it is an alternative to TCP for those features. The userland port lets programs use it on operating systems where it is not built into the kernel. The Manual also notes that some NAT boxes cannot pass SCTP packets, which is why UDP encapsulation exists.
brief.how_it_works: Each application calls usrsctp_init() with a UDP encapsulation port (default 9899, or 0 to disable encapsulation) and then creates sockets with the RFC 6458 style calls. Sends and receives go through usrsctp_sendv() and usrsctp_recvv(), which pass data as a plain buffer and carry per-message info such as sndinfo and prinfo. Direct SCTP mode uses raw sockets, which is why it needs root, while UDP mode wraps SCTP packets in UDP datagrams for NAT traversal.

brief.install_notes: Unix-like systems: run ./bootstrap, ./configure and make in the usrsctp folder, then optionally sudo make install. Windows needs a compiler such as Microsoft Visual Studio and is built with nmake or CMake. CMake builds default to DEBUG. Sending data directly over SCTP uses raw sockets, so it needs sudo on Unix or an administrator console on Windows; UDP encapsulation avoids this. The README and Manual do not mention any Homebrew-specific steps beyond the formula itself.
brief.standout: Instead of a fixed set of kernel parameters, it exposes the kernel's SCTP tunables (send and receive buffer sizes, RTO timers, SACK frequency, congestion control module choice, CMT, and others) as usrsctp_sysctl_set_* functions the application calls at runtime. It also ships a discard server and client as runnable test programs, which makes it easy to watch SCTP move data end to end.

name: libxmi
desc: C/C++ function library for rasterizing 2D vector graphics
why: GNU vector graphics rasterizer library with a rare pedigree, a close call that could yield pictures from code.

brief.what_it_is: GNU libxmi is a C/C++ function library that rasterizes 2-D vector graphics. Its input is 2-D graphical primitives, including wide polygonal lines, circular and elliptical arcs, and polygons to fill or texture, along with line styles such as multicolored dashing patterns. Its output is pixels drawn into a user-supplied matrix of pixels. The page calls it a drop-in rendering module for any application that needs to scan-convert 2-D vector graphics. The page does not describe a file format or a standalone program that produces images.
brief.why_it_exists: The page presents it as a rendering module split out of the GNU plotting utilities package, so other applications can reuse the scan-conversion code. The author says it was distributed separately under the name libxmi.
brief.how_it_works: The page says libxmi uses a two-stage graphics pipeline, where the second stage is pixel-merging. The default merge is the Painter's Algorithm, in which a new pixel value replaces the old one. The page says the pixel datatype and the compositing algorithm can be redefined, and that switching to alpha compositing would be trivial.
brief.install_notes: The page says it can be installed on GNU/Linux, FreeBSD, and Unix systems. It is written in ANSI C, so any system with a C compiler should be able to build it. The page does not give build steps, dependencies, or a source download URL. It links to a 'obtaining the source code' page, but the link target was not in the text I received, so I did not follow it. The brew description and the fact that no executables are listed suggest this is a library to link against, not a command-line tool.
brief.standout: The scan-conversion code descends from the X11 sample server, written in the late 1980s by people associated with the X Consortium. It keeps pixel-level compatibility with X11 drawing functions but no longer needs an X display. The pixel type and compositing rule can be changed at compile time, so it is unusually customizable for a small rasterizer.

name: libxmp
desc: C library for playback of module music (MOD, S3M, IT, etc)
why: Plays decades-old tracker module formats like MOD and S3M, a window into a vanishing music culture.

brief.what_it_is: Libxmp is a C library that renders tracker module music files (MOD, S3M, XM, IT and many others) into linear PCM audio buffers at a sample rate and format the calling application chooses. It takes a module file and outputs PCM samples; it is not a player by itself. The separate xmp command-line player, built on libxmp, is what a person would run to hear a module. The library also reads compressed modules, using built-in decompressors for formats like gzip, bzip2, zip, and LZX, and external helpers for MO3 and RAR. The README says it supports over 90 formats.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes libxmp as a way to play many mainstream and obscure module formats, and says applications for it include players, module information extractors, module-to-mp3 renderers, and game music. The project keeps decades of tracker music playable, including formats like Amiga Protracker MOD and PC Scream Tracker 3 S3M, and the site's own voice treats the work as preservation of classic and rare modules.
brief.how_it_works: Libxmp loads the module file and renders its sound as PCM samples into a buffer, at the rate and format the user specifies. The README says that by default Protracker MODs are played with a mix of Protracker 2/3 quirks, other Amiga 4-channel MODs use a generic Noisetracker/Protracker-style replayer, Scream Tracker III MODs use a Scream Tracker style replayer, and multichannel MODs use a Fasttracker II style replayer. Multi-file formats such as Startrekker AM and Magnetic Fields need all their files in the same directory.

name: libwbxml
desc: Library and tools to parse and encode WBXML documents
why: Parses WAP Binary XML, a door into the old mobile protocol world of compact encoded XML used by phones for sync.

brief.what_it_is: libwbxml is a C library and two command-line tools for working with WBXML, the WAP Binary XML format. The library parses WBXML documents, builds an internal tree, and encodes that tree back out. The tools are wbxml2xml, which takes a WBXML file and writes readable XML, and xml2wbxml, which takes an XML file and writes WBXML. The README describes the library as a SAX-like parser, so it works like Expat but for WBXML.

name: lief
desc: Library to Instrument Executable Formats
why: A library for parsing and modifying ELF, PE and Mach-O binaries, a real door into instrumenting executables.

brief.what_it_is: LIEF is a cross-platform library that parses, inspects, modifies, and rebuilds executable files in ELF, PE, and Mach-O formats (and also COFF, DEX, and others, per the README). You feed it a binary file or an in-memory buffer and get back a structured object model with sections, symbols, relocations, and entry points, plus a shared abstraction across formats. You can change parts of that model, such as adding a section or renaming a symbol, and write a valid binary back to disk. The API is available in C++, Python, and Rust. The optional LIEF Extended tier adds disassembly, assembly, DWARF and PDB debug info, and Objective-C metadata.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a way to move from raw executable file formats to a high-level representation, make precise changes, and write a valid binary back, without booting a heavyweight reverse-engineering stack. The README frames the purpose as providing a cross-platform library to parse, modify and abstract ELF, PE and MachO formats.
brief.how_it_works: LIEF parses the file into a format-specific object model, and for ELF, PE, and Mach-O it also offers a common abstraction layer over shared concepts like sections, symbols, and entry points. Changes are made on that model, and format-aware builders serialize the result back to a file. The Extended tier layers disassembly and assembly (AArch64, x86/x86-64, ARM, RISC-V and others) on top of the same model.

name: limine

why: A multiprotocol bootloader that is a readable route into how machines hand off to a kernel, though boot tooling is plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: Limine is a bootloader and boot manager, the program that runs at power-on and loads an operating system kernel. You give it a limine.conf configuration file plus its boot files, which are copied onto a FAT EFI system partition for UEFI, written into an MBR or GPT BIOS boot partition for BIOS, or placed in a hybrid ISO or on a PXE server. It supports IA-32, x86-64, aarch64, riscv64 and loongarch64, and can start Linux, Multiboot 1 and 2, the Limine boot protocol, or chainload other loaders. A small host tool called 'limine' does installation work, such as 'limine bios-install'. The README also says it is the reference implementation of the Limine boot protocol.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as a 'modern, secure, portable, multiprotocol bootloader and boot manager'. Its stated purpose is to be the reference implementation of the Limine boot protocol, a handoff interface for kernels. No further problem statement appears in the fetched pages.

USAGE.md describes the flow: on UEFI, the BOOT*.EFI files are copied to /EFI/BOOT on a FAT EFI system partition alongside a config file; on BIOS, 'limine bios-install' is run against a disk or image, and limine-bios.sys and limine.conf must sit on a supported filesystem. USAGE.md also documents opt-in Secure Boot enforcement (config hash enrollment, hashed file paths) and Measured Boot that extends TPM PCRs 8 and 9 with the loaded artifacts.

name: link-grammar
desc: Carnegie Mellon University's link grammar parser
why: A link grammar parser that diagrams English sentences as linked word pairs; a real window into computational linguistics.

brief.what_it_is: Link Grammar Parser is a natural-language parser from the OpenCog project, based on the Carnegie Mellon link grammar theory. It takes a plain-text sentence and produces a graph of typed links between the words, drawn as ASCII diagrams with per-word disjunct lists and costs. The README says it covers English, Thai, Russian, Arabic, Persian and limited subsets of several other languages. It ships a command-line tool, link-parser, plus C, Python, Java, Node.js and other bindings. The README says it is at version 5.13.0 and that the package also includes an experimental link-generator for filling blanks in sentences.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as going a bit deeper than conventional parsers: it gives finer-grained syntactico-semantic structure, and HPSG-style constituent or dependency trees can be derived from it by conversion rules. It is the reference implementation of a theory first published in 1991 by Temperley, Lafferty and Sleator.
brief.how_it_works: Each word has a dictionary entry of connectors, and a parse is a set of links that pair compatible connectors between words, with the links forming a planar graph. Each word's chosen connector set is its disjunct, and disjunct costs roughly reflect how likely that grammatical usage is. The README also describes morphology handling through a tokenizer that can offer alternative splittings, and dictionaries that can be updated at run time while parsing continues safely across threads.

name: liquidsoap
desc: Audio and video streaming language
why: A domain-specific language for composing audio and video streams, a genuinely odd tool that treats radio stations as code.

brief.what_it_is: Liquidsoap is an open-source audio and video streaming language. You write a short script (.liq file) that describes streams: sources such as a folder of music files, a playlist, or a live RTMP feed from OBS, combined with operators such as rotate, crossfade and fallback, then sent to an output such as an Icecast server, YouTube Live over RTMP, SRT or HLS. Inputs are files, network feeds and request backends; outputs are live streams, and FFmpeg encoders and filters are available from inside the language for transcoding. It is aimed at internet radio and web TV.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a way to build audio and video streams from a few lines of code, covering internet radio, live shows, RTMP to YouTube, and transcoding. The README calls it a swiss-army knife for multimedia streaming, notably used for netradios and webtvs, and describes it as a language for describing your streams rather than a fixed configuration file.
brief.how_it_works: A script declares sources and combines them with operators, and the liquidsoap binary runs that graph as a long-running process. The homepage's example builds a playlist, weights it with rotate, applies crossfade, and then calls output.icecast to send the result out. FFmpeg is wired in, so the same language can re-encode a stream or pass it through untouched when no re-encoding is needed.

name: liquidctl
desc: Cross-platform tool and drivers for liquid coolers and other devices
why: Talks to USB HID liquid coolers and fans by poking at their undocumented protocols, a real door into hardware.

brief.what_it_is: liquidctl is a cross-platform command-line tool and Python library for monitoring and controlling liquid coolers and other PC hardware. You point it at a supported device and it reads status (fan speeds, pump speed, liquid temperature, noise level, DIMM temperature) or sets fan and pump speed curves, LED colours and lighting modes. Output is human-readable text, or JSON with --json for the list, initialize and status commands. The README lists supported AIO coolers, fan and LED controllers, PSUs, motherboard RGB, GPU RGB and DDR4 memory from Corsair, NZXT, ASUS, Aquacomputer, Gigabyte, Lian Li, MSI and others.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a single cross-platform tool and set of drivers for liquid coolers and other devices, so vendor control software is not needed on every operating system. It also points to Linux hwmon drivers and a GUI as sibling or related projects.
brief.how_it_works: Each supported device has a driver module that talks to it over USB HID (via hidapi), raw USB (via PyUSB and libusb 1.0), or SMBus on Linux for some memory and motherboard RGB parts. Some devices can also use the Linux hwmon driver, which the README marks with an 'h' note. Devices usually need an initialize step after each boot, and the README says so explicitly. Per-device details are in the docs/ directory, and the driver APIs are documented for use from Python.

name: lldpd
desc: Implementation of IEEE 802.1ab (LLDP)
why: A door into LLDP, the neighbour-discovery protocol your switches chatter over constantly, and almost nobody looks at it.

brief.what_it_is: lldpd is a Unix daemon and command-line tool that implements IEEE 802.1AB, the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP). It sends LLDP frames out of each network interface and listens for frames from neighbouring devices, so a server or host can learn which switch port it is plugged into. The collected neighbour data is queried with the lldpcli command, as text or XML, or through SNMP. It runs on FreeBSD, GNU/Linux, macOS, NetBSD, OpenBSD and Solaris. It also partially supports LLDP-MED and some vendor protocols (CDP, FDP, SONMP, EDP).
brief.why_it_exists: LLDP is an industry-standard, inter-vendor mechanism for link-layer notifications, meant to replace proprietary protocols such as Cisco's CDP and Extreme's EDP. The homepage frames the goal as: "LLDP allows you to know exactly on which port is a server (and reciprocally)."
brief.how_it_works: The lldpd daemon uses privilege separation: a small root process handles the privileged work, and a second unprivileged process in a chroot does most of the work. The daemon both receives and transmits LLDP frames on each interface, and it can also answer with CDP, FDP, SONMP or EDP when it sees those frames. Linux kernel version affects which VLAN, bond and bridge information it can read through Netlink.

Privilege separation needs a system user and group both named _lldpd (configurable at configure time) and an empty root-owned directory /usr/local/var/run/lldpd. lldpcli can run unprivileged if installed setuid or setgid _lldpd. The macOS route can also build an installer package with make -C osx pkg. Android requires the NDK version 22 or later, a hand-written compile.sh, and manual copying of files to /system, so it is a substantial job. Docker needs --net=host, --uts=host, NET_RAW and NET_ADMIN capabilities. The official website has the full installation guide, which the README recommends over its own text.
brief.standout: It is a small, widely deployed, open-source daemon for a protocol most people never see, and it includes an LLDP sender and receiver that also speak vendor protocols. Intel X710 and ice cards may need their firmware LLDP agent stopped. lldpcli links GNU Readline (GPL) when available, unless you configure --without-readline. Building for Android is involved. The core code is ISC-licensed.

name: lisette
desc: Language inspired by Rust that compiles to Go
why: A Rust-inspired language that compiles to Go, an interesting transpiler design choice worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Lisette is a small programming language with Rust-like syntax that compiles to Go source code, so its output runs on Go's runtime and can use Go packages. You write .lis files and run the `lis` compiler, which emits readable Go. The language adds algebraic data types, pattern matching, Option and Result in place of nil and bare errors, immutability by default, a |> pipeline operator, and try blocks. The homepage also presents a set of compile-time checks that flag Go pitfalls, such as unchecked Results, non-exhaustive matches, and a defer skipped by os.Exit.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as "A love letter to Go written in Rust" and says it combines compile-time safety, expressive syntax and Go's ecosystem. The README calls it a "Little language inspired by Rust that compiles to Go."
brief.how_it_works: The `lis` compiler translates Lisette source into Go, and the README describes the output as readable Go. Go packages are imported with `import "go:..."`, and Go types and functions are called directly, with Go stdlib signatures described in `.d.lis` declaration files (the homepage shows an os.d.lis example). Structs can carry Go-style tags, and `#[json(...)]` attributes generate tagged Go structs, as the homepage's UserProfile example shows.

name: logtalk
desc: Declarative object-oriented logic programming language
why: A logic-programming language that fuses Prolog with object-oriented ideas, rarely encountered and genuinely odd to play with.

brief.what_it_is: Logtalk is a declarative object-oriented logic programming language that extends Prolog with modules, prototypes, classes, protocols (interfaces), and categories (components with hot patching). It is implemented as a transcompiler, so you write Logtalk source and it is compiled down to code for an existing Prolog system, which serves as the backend. The distribution also bundles libraries, developer tools, a handbook, API docs, and examples. The brew caveats show that the install is configured through the LOGTALKHOME and LOGTALKUSER environment variables. The executables it ships include per-backend launchers such as swilgt, gplgt, and yaplgt, plus lgt2html, lgt2md, lgt2pdf and similar documentation generators, and logtalk_tester.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to bring Prolog up to 'programming in the large' by adding code encapsulation and code reuse mechanisms while preserving Prolog's declarative features. The homepage pitches it as 'Logic Programming meets Software Engineering'.
brief.how_it_works: Logtalk source is compiled by a transcompiler into code for a standards-compliant Prolog system, which the README says can be most modern ones. It uses standard Prolog syntax plus some added operators and directives to ease the learning path. Multi-threading is available on selected backends only.

commands_seen.context: Mentioned in the README as a way to generate a list of the POSIX man pages for Logtalk's shell scripts. It appears in prose, not as a code block.

brief.install_notes: Install from sources by running a couple of shell scripts, or use an OS-specific installer from logtalk.org/download.html. Manual steps are in INSTALL.md, quick-start instructions are in QUICK_START.md, and customization is in CUSTOMIZE.md. You need a supported Prolog compiler installed first. Upgrading from Logtalk 2.x requires reading UPGRADING.md. Registration at logtalk.org/regform.html is optional. Homebrew sets LOGTALKHOME=$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/share/logtalk and LOGTALKUSER=$HOME/logtalk.
brief.standout: It is a layer over existing Prolog systems rather than a new Prolog, so you keep your backend and gain objects, protocols, and categories on top. The tool suite is unusually large for a niche language and is portable across backends.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage shows v3.102.0 dated September 14, 2026. The GitHub README carries a 1998-2026 copyright notice and links to active release notes, a discussions forum, and a Gitter chat.
brief.caveats: Requires a separately installed Prolog backend, and some features such as high-level multi-threading work only on selected backends. Going from Logtalk 2.x to 3.x needs manual porting per UPGRADING.md. The language is niche, so community size is small compared with mainstream languages. The fetched README did not show any build warnings.

Logtalk is a declarative object-oriented logic programming language that extends and leverages the Prolog language with a feature set suitable for programming in the large.

Distributed under a commercial-friendly license, it includes full documentation, extensive portable libraries, a comprehensive set of portable developer tools, and a large number of programming examples to help get you started.

name: logstalgia
desc: Web server access log visualizer with retro style
why: Turning web server access logs into a Pong-like animated stream of requests is a strange and satisfying way to watch traffic.

brief.what_it_is: Logstalgia is a website traffic visualizer that replays or streams web-server access logs as a Pong-like animation. Each request is drawn as a colored ball, colored to match the requesting host, that travels across the screen to the requested location. It reads standard Apache and Nginx access log formats (NCSA Common, Combined, and virtual-host variants), a pipe-delimited custom format, or live input on STDIN. The output is an on-screen animation rather than a file or report.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a way to watch a busy website's traffic as a never-ending torrent of requests, a pong-like battle between the web server and its visitors. It is pitched as a dashboard for work use, and the author invites contact about bespoke visualization work.
brief.how_it_works: Successful requests are hit by the paddle, while unsuccessful ones such as 404 File Not Found are missed and pass through. Paths are summarized by finding common path prefixes, and related paths are grouped under headings; by default, paths ending in png, gif or jpg fall under 'Images', and everything else goes to 'Miscellaneous'. Logs can be replayed from a file or followed live, for example by piping tail -f into it.

name: lolcode
desc: Esoteric programming language
why: A lolspeak esoteric language with a real interpreter, a delightful and strange thing to run for a minute.

brief.what_it_is: LOLCODE is an esoteric programming language written in lolspeak. The reference interpreter, lci, is a C program that takes a .lol source file and runs it. The homepage's hello-world program is HAI 1.3 / CAN HAS STDIO? / VISIBLE "HAI WORLD!!!1!" / KTHXBYE, which prints a line of text. Beyond core language, lci provides standard libraries you load with CAN HAS, covering file I/O (STDIO), TCP sockets (SOCKS), string helpers (STRING), random numbers (STDLIB), and a character-level transformer language model (BRAINZ).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as an esoteric programming language, and the README's framing is that lci is meant to be correct, portable, fast, and precisely documented. The joke is the lolspeak syntax; the engineering is a real implementation of the spec.
brief.how_it_works: lci runs programs in up to three stages and falls back a stage when the next cannot handle a construct. Stage 1 is a tree-walking interpreter that defines the semantics. Stage 2 is a register machine that compiles the parse tree to bytecode. Stage 3 is a JIT that emits AArch64 or x86-64 machine code, but only when a dataflow pass proves every value in a procedure is an integer or boolean. The README also says LOLCODE is dynamically scoped, so a whole-program analysis decides which names can become registers.

name: lrzsz
desc: Tools for zmodem/xmodem/ymodem file transfer

brief.what_it_is: lrzsz is a Unix command-line package that implements the XMODEM, YMODEM and ZMODEM file transfer protocols. The installed programs (lrb, lrx, lrz, lsb, lsx, lsz, rz, sz) send or receive files over a communication link, typically a serial line or a terminal session, rather than over a network protocol of their own. The sender reads files and the receiver writes them, with error checking and block-size handling along the way. The page describes it as free x/y/zmodem software released under the GNU General Public Licence.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Uwe Ohse, says lrzsz is a reworked version of the last public domain release of Omen Technologies' rzsz package, and that he took the work up again after security flaws were reported. The changelog frames the older ZMODEM design as proprietary and insecure, noting that the receiver could be made to run commands the sender chose.
brief.how_it_works: The page gives little mechanism detail. It says ZMODEM supports crash recovery, block sizes up to 8KB (ZMODEM8K), and automatic block-size tuning based on the number of errors seen. The 0.13.0 release notes say the package includes ZMODEM documentation and a work-in-progress specification.

name: lucky-commit
desc: Customize your git commit hashes!
why: Brute-forces git commit hashes to match a pattern, a fun hash-collision toy that shows how hashes can be steered.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line tool called lucky_commit that rewrites the most recent git commit so its hash starts with a prefix you choose. It takes a hex prefix as an argument (default 0000000) and may include _ placeholders that match any hex character. It works by adding whitespace characters to the commit message and retrying until the resulting SHA1 hash matches. The output is the same commit with a new message and a hash beginning with the requested prefix.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives the framing as 'Make your git commits lucky!' and 'With this simple tool, you can change the start of your git commit hashes to whatever you want.' It offers no deeper rationale; its Why section is just the shrug emoticon.
brief.how_it_works: lucky-commit amends the commit message by inserting a few characters of different whitespace types, then keeps trying new variants until the hash matches. Hashing runs on a GPU through OpenCL by default, with a multithreaded CPU fallback. For non-GPG-signed commits it caches the SHA1 buffer state so each attempt hashes only one 64-byte block; for GPG-signed commits the whitespace goes at the end of the signature, which makes each attempt slower.

The _ placeholder means that slot may be any hex character, so the hash must start 00 then any character then 111.

brief.standout: Instead of changing the commit's content, it searches over invisible whitespace in the message, so the hash changes while the visible text stays the same. The README also explains the speedup from caching SHA1 state over the 64-byte-aligned tail of the message, and gives a benchmark for estimating time on your machine.

name: luajit
desc: Just-In-Time Compiler (JIT) for the Lua programming language
why: A famously fast JIT for Lua with a fascinating internals story, but widely used and somewhat familiar.

brief.what_it_is: LuaJIT is a just-in-time compiler for the Lua programming language, and it ships as a standalone interpreter/runtime. You give it Lua source or bytecode and it runs the program, compiling hot code paths to machine code while it runs. The Homebrew formula installs two executables, luajit and luajit-2.1.1791890110. The project is API-compatible with Lua 5.1, so existing Lua 5.1 embeddings can usually switch to it by relinking.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a fast, low-footprint way to run Lua, pitched at embedding in games, appliances, network and graphics apps, numerical simulations and trading platforms, and says it has been in continuous development since 2005. The page presents LuaJIT as a rewrite of the whole VM for LuaJIT 2.0 aimed at closing the performance gap between dynamic languages and offline static compilers.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says the VM has a high-speed interpreter written in assembler plus a trace compiler with SSA-based optimizations and tuned code generation backends. name: lziprecover
desc: Data recovery tool and decompressor for files in the lzip compressed data format
why: Recovers damaged lzip archives by exploiting redundancy in the format, a fine door into how compressed files fail.

brief.what_it_is: Lziprecover is a command-line tool that decompresses and tests files in the lzip (.lz) compressed format, and tries to recover data from damaged ones. It takes damaged or intact .lz files, plus optional reference copies or FEC files, and writes recovered or decompressed output, or .fec files. It can also append a recovery record to a tar.lz archive, and it can remove damaged members from multimember files. Its FEC files can protect any kind of file, not only lzip files, and they are offered as an alternative to par2.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as a last line of defense for when backups are also damaged, and argues that lzip's format makes automatic repair practical in a way it is not for gzip. The page also says compressed copies can be more useful redundancy than uncompressed ones, because lziprecover can combine the good parts of several damaged copies.
brief.how_it_works: Lzip's LZMA stream treats any match distance larger than the dictionary size as a forbidden symbol, so the decoder can locate roughly where a bit flip occurred, and the CRC and sizes handle the rest. Byte-repair mode can fix up to one single-byte error per member, merge mode rebuilds a correct file from the good parts of several damaged copies, and reproduce mode regenerates a zeroed sector from a reference file using the same lzip version that made the file. FEC data uses Galois fields GF(2^8) or GF(2^16) and is applied as recovery blocks alongside the file.

name: lzsa
desc: Lossless packer that is optimized for fast decompression on 8-bit micros
why: A packer built for 8-bit machines, a fun window into retro compression tradeoffs and decompression constraints.

brief.what_it_is: LZSA is a set of byte-aligned lossless compression formats, with a packer that encodes files into them, aimed at very fast decompression on 8-bit CPUs. It takes a file of any size, splits it into blocks of up to 64 KB, and emits a packed file that decompresses back to the original. Matches can reach back up to 64 KB. The README points to decompressors for Z80, 6502, 6809, 8088, i8080, PDP-11, MC68000 and Game Boy, written by various contributors. The packer's executable is named lzsa.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a compression format for retro machines where decompression speed and decompressor size matter most, offering alternatives to LZ4 and ZX7 in 8-bit scenarios. LZSA1 is meant to replace LZ4 and LZSA2 to replace ZX7.
brief.how_it_works: The optimizer searches for the sequence of commands that gives the smallest output while keeping decompression as fast as possible, and the match-finder and optimizer cooperate to prefer 8-bit match offsets. LZSA2 uses 5-, 9-, 13- and 16-bit offsets encoded with nibbles, plus rep-matches, and avoids slow bit-packing in favour of byte alignment and nibbles. The encoding avoids 16-bit arithmetic on the decoder side.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no build, install or usage steps and shows no command lines. The brew formula supplies the lzsa executable. Packing needs nothing special; the decompressors are assembly routines meant for the target 8-bit machines.
brief.standout: The packer's optimizer deliberately spends effort to keep decompression fast on 8-bit CPUs, not just to shrink output, and the authors cite a 67-byte size-optimized Z80 decompressor for LZSA1. Many retro projects have adopted it, including demos, a game port and an assembler.

Licensing is split: the LZSA code is zlib, and matchfinder.c is CC0 because it reuses parts of Wimlib. Several decompressors are third-party ports with their own origins.

name: m4rie
desc: Library for fast arithmetic with dense matrices over GF(2^e), 2<=e<=16
why: Fast GF(2^e) dense matrix arithmetic is real algebra underneath coding theory, but it is a library needing context to enjoy.

brief.what_it_is: M4RIE is a C library for fast arithmetic with dense matrices over finite fields GF(2^e) for 2 ≤ e ≤ 16. It supports basic matrix operations such as addition, equality testing, stacking, augmenting and sub-matrices, plus multiplication, row echelon form, inversion and triangular solving over those fields. Matrices go in as its own mzd/mzed data types, and results come back as matrices or echelon forms; it is a building block, not a standalone tool. It is part of the Sage mathematics software and depends on the companion library M4RI.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the name stems from the fact that the library relies heavily on M4RI, and it is aimed at dense linear algebra over small fields of even characteristic. The 2011 technical report frames it as improving on the state of the art for dense linear algebra over GF(2^e) with small e.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes a Karatsuba-style reduction, due to Boothby and Bradshaw, that turns multiplication over GF(p^k) into a series of multiplications over GF(p), giving O(n^log2 7) matrix multiplication. It also uses 'Newton-John tables', a caching technique inspired by Kronrod's M4RM method, to avoid repeated field multiplications, which gives fast row echelon form and inversion using PLE decomposition. The docs say large matrices should use the mzd_slice_t type and smaller ones the mzed_t type.

name: magic-wormhole
desc: Securely transfers data between computers
why: Its PAKE handshake over a short spoken code is a neat door into password-authenticated key exchange, though the tool is fairly well known.

brief.what_it_is: Magic Wormhole is a Python library plus a command-line tool, `wormhole`, for moving files, directories, short pieces of text, or other network streams from one computer to another. The sender runs a command that prints a short code, such as 7-crossover-clockwork, and the receiver types that code into a second command. The code is single-use and does not need to be memorized. Once the two peers have authenticated each other with the code, the data travels over an end-to-end encrypted connection, either direct or through a relay.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs frame it as a way to get things between two people's machines when the humans can talk to each other but the computers cannot. They contrast it with USB sticks, scp/ssh (which needs prior accounts), email, and Dropbox links, and say that secrets like passwords or SSH keys are the main use case. The name comes from the image of two wizards speaking the same phrase to open a connection between them.
brief.how_it_works: The two peers run SPAKE2, a password-authenticated key exchange, using the short code as the low-entropy password. The code's words also let the receiver tab-complete, and a mailbox server (a WebSocket relay) carries the initial messages so the codes do not need IP addresses. Peers exchange network hints and first try a direct connection on the LAN or public IP; if that fails, a Transit Relay glues the two TCP connections together, and all traffic is encrypted with keys derived from the PAKE secret.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew, apt, dnf (Fedora 36 and earlier only), zypper, snap (third-party 'snapcrafters' package), winget, and Chocolatey packages exist. Windows binaries come from a separate community project. Installing from source needs Python (3.10 to 3.13 are supported) and a virtualenv or a per-user pip install; avoid sudo with pip. On macOS you may need Xcode command line tools to compile libsodium. On Linux, a libsodium headers error can be worked around with SODIUM_INSTALL=bundled pip install magic-wormhole or by installing libsodium-dev. No account or server setup is needed: a public mailbox server and transit relay are built in. Both peers must use the same mailbox server, and the --relay-url option overrides the default.
brief.standout: The code is short and human-speakable, but PAKE means each code is single-use and a man-in-the-middle gets only one guess, so failed guesses show up as errors on the other side. Unlike most file-transfer tools, it needs no accounts, keys, or shared server, and it works as a PAKE building block for other apps. The docs also list Fowl, which uses a dilation feature to stream data, and the ecosystem page lists more clients.
brief.status: Unknown from the pages I read; leaning maintained. The docs show version 0.24.0+48 (48 commits past a tag), tests run on Python 3.10 to 3.13, and the Fedora packaging was removed in 37. I did not find a release date or last-commit date on these pages.
brief.caveats: The README says there are no built-in timeouts, and both clients must be run within about an hour of each other and left running until the transfer finishes. Peers must be online at the same time, so it does not do asynchronous delivery. The public mailbox and transit relay are provided on a best-effort basis and may be withdrawn if abused. Source installs can fail on libsodium or other compiled dependencies, and Windows install guidance mentions python2 and Visual C++. The docs describe the library's blocking/synchronous API as future work, with Twisted support available now. The page's asciinema demo is not screen-reader friendly. Licence is MIT. The cli.html page I tried returned 404, so I got CLI option details from the Welcome page instead.
quotes: Get things from one computer to another, safely.
Each code is one-time use only, so attackers (e.g. a malicious Mailbox server) get only a single guess when attempting to subvert a connection.
The notion of a "magic wormhole" comes from the image of two distant wizards speaking the same enchanted phrase at the same time, and causing a mystical connection to pop into existence between them.

name: magika
desc: Fast and accurate AI powered file content types detection
why: Google's AI file type detector, a neat way to see how content sniffing works beyond magic bytes.

brief.what_it_is: Magika is a command-line tool, with Python, Rust, and JavaScript/TypeScript bindings, that identifies what kind of content a file holds using a small deep-learning model. You give it file paths, a directory with -r, or data on standard input, and it prints a content-type label and description for each file, such as 'Python source' or 'Microsoft Word 2007+ document'. Output can be plain text, JSON, JSONL, MIME type, a simple label, or a custom format. The model is a few MB and reads only a limited part of each file, so inference time stays near-constant regardless of file size. The README says it covers 200+ content types, both binary and textual.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a more accurate alternative to traditional file type detection, saying it 'relies on the recent advance of deep learning to provide accurate detection' and outperforms existing approaches 'especially on textual content types'. The homepage says Google uses it at scale to route Gmail, Drive, and Safe Browsing files to the right security and content-policy scanners.
brief.how_it_works: A custom, highly optimized model (a few MBs) is trained on about 100M samples and predicts a content type from a limited subset of each file's bytes. A pre-tuned, per-content-type threshold decides whether to trust the prediction or fall back to a generic label such as 'Generic text document' or 'Unknown binary data'. Prediction modes named high-confidence, medium-confidence, and best-guess control how tolerant it is of errors. Each result includes a score; the JSON output shows both the raw model output and the final output when it is overruled.

name: manifold
desc: Geometry library for topological robustness
why: A robust geometry kernel for manifold meshes, close to the mathematics of solids and worth a deeper look.

brief.what_it_is: Manifold is a C++ geometry library for creating and operating on manifold triangle meshes, meaning meshes that represent closed solid objects. It takes in manifold meshes, which it can build with OpenSCAD-style constructors or from signed-distance functions via a level-set function, or external mesh data, which it rejects with an error status if the mesh is not manifold. It outputs manifold meshes from Boolean operations (union, difference and similar), smoothing and refinement, and file I/O. It has bindings for C, JS/TS via WASM, Python, and several other languages.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the primary goal is reliability: "guaranteed manifold output without caveats or edge cases." The secondary goal is performance through parallelization. The README calls a robust mesh Boolean algorithm "an open problem for many years" and claims the guaranteed-manifold Boolean is possibly the first of its kind.
brief.how_it_works: The core is a guaranteed-manifold mesh Boolean algorithm, which the README describes as the library's most significant contribution and as the basis for a CAD kernel. It uses vertex properties and IDs to track materials and which input object or face each surface came from. Parallelism comes through TBB when enabled, with a serial fallback for small problems and a serial-only WASM build. The README gives no deeper algorithm detail beyond links to the wiki.

name: masscan
desc: TCP port scanner, scans entire Internet in under 5 minutes
why: Famous among security people for its scanning speed, but it is a well-known tool and mostly a fast port scanner.

brief.what_it_is: Masscan is a command-line TCP port scanner written in C, aimed at scanning very large address ranges, up to the whole IPv4 Internet. You give it target IPv4 or IPv6 addresses or ranges and a list of ports, and it prints the open host and port pairs to stdout or to a file. Output can be XML, binary, grepable, JSON, or a simple list. It can also complete TCP connections to grab banners from services such as SSH, HTTP, SMB, RDP and VNC. Its option syntax is modelled on nmap's.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames it as an Internet-scale port scanner that can scan the entire Internet in under 5 minutes, transmitting 10 million packets per second from a single machine. He says its usage is similar to nmap, the most famous port scanner, but it is built for wide scanning of many machines rather than in-depth scanning of one.
brief.how_it_works: It is asynchronous, with separate transmit and receive threads, similar in design to ZMap, scanrand and unicornscan. It walks a single index from zero and passes each index through an encryption function, so the probe order is random yet covers every target exactly once. Masscan uses its own user-mode TCP/IP stack, which is why the local OS can interfere, and why source-IP or firewall setup is needed for banner grabbing.

The output lands in bin/masscan, and make install works on Linux. The only dependency is a C compiler such as gcc or clang. Other platforms: Windows with Visual Studio uses the VS10 project, Windows with MinGW uses make, macOS uses make or the XCode4 project, FreeBSD uses gmake, and cygwin is said not to work. make -j needs more than 2 GB of RAM on a Raspberry Pi, so use something like -j4 there. brief.standout: Scan order is produced by encrypting a linear index, so probes are random across the target space without repeats, and a scan can be paused with ctrl-c and resumed from the saved index. It also makes nmap-style options and output work at very high packet rates, which is the unusual combination here.

It is licensed under AGPL v3. Scanning the whole Internet is discouraged, because networks may react badly and ban your IP, and the default rate is 100 packets per second. Only SYN scanning is supported, and there is no DNS name resolution and no default port list. IPv6 scans at high rates can overwhelm target networks. Windows and macOS reach about 300,000 packets per second, and PF_RING mode needs special drivers. The README also asks for donations to a Bitcoin address.
