name: mat2
desc: Metadata anonymization toolkit
why: Stripping metadata means looking hard at file internals, and seeing what hides in your own files is a genuine eye-opener.

brief.what_it_is: mat2 is a metadata anonymization toolkit that strips hidden metadata from files such as images, PDFs, Office documents, audio, video, archives and SVGs. It ships as a Python library called libmat2, a command line tool called mat2, and a service menu for the Dolphin file manager. You give it files; it writes cleaned copies alongside the originals, and with --show it lists the metadata it can detect without removing it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says files carry metadata that can reveal who made them and when: cameras record when and with what a picture was taken, and Office and PDF tools add author and company information. The stated job is 'getting rid, as much as possible, of metadata.'
brief.how_it_works: mat2 dispatches each file to a format-specific cleaner, relying on helpers such as ExifTool, FFmpeg, mutagen and GObject-introspection bindings for Poppler, GdkPixbuf and librsvg, depending on the format. By default it may re-encode or alter content to strip more metadata. The -L (lightweight) flag removes only some metadata and promises not to modify the file's data.

name: marisa
desc: Matching Algorithm with Recursively Implemented StorAge
why: A compact recursive trie library with a neat data structure idea, though it is mostly a linkable library.

brief.what_it_is: MARISA (Matching Algorithm with Recursively Implemented StorAge) is a static, space-efficient trie data structure, implemented as the C++ library libmarisa. The package also ships command-line tools for building and querying a MARISA-based dictionary: marisa-build, marisa-lookup, marisa-reverse-lookup, marisa-common-prefix-search, marisa-predictive-search, marisa-dump and marisa-benchmark. A dictionary supports lookup (is this string a key?), reverse lookup (restore a key from its ID), common prefix search (find keys that are prefixes of a given string) and predictive search (find keys starting with a given string). The README does not spell out the exact input and output formats of each tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's stated advantage is size: libmarisa's dictionary is considerably more compact than other implementations. Its benchmark uses all English Wikipedia page titles (about 9.8 million keys, 200 MB plain) and reports 50.8 MB for marisa-trie against 376.6 MB for darts-clone and 127.7 MB for tx-trie.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives little mechanism detail beyond the name, which spells out Matching Algorithm with Recursively Implemented StorAge. It calls the structure a static trie, meaning the dictionary is built once from a key set and then queried. The deeper internals are in the linked docs, which I did not fetch.

name: mcap
desc: Serialization-agnostic container file format for pub/sub messages
why: Robotics log container format with a neat self-describing design, but it is a file format more than a door into something alive.

brief.what_it_is: MCAP (pronounced "em-cap") is an open source container file format and logging library for multimodal, timestamped log data. It stores multiple channels of pre-serialized messages in one file, and the README says it is commonly used in robotics. Input is messages from pub/sub or sensor streams in any binary encoding; output is a single MCAP file that can be read back with the language libraries or the mcap CLI, which can inspect, merge, and split files.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches MCAP as a way to record and replay pub/sub and multimodal sensor logs regardless of serialization format, and says it is designed for robotics and pub/sub use. The GitHub README describes it as a logging library and file format that works under various workloads, resource constraints, and durability requirements.
brief.how_it_works: Files are row-oriented and append-only, which the homepage says minimizes disk I/O and reduces corruption risk on unclean shutdowns. Message schemas are stored alongside the data so files stay readable as code changes. Optional features include an index for fast seeking, chunk-based compression with LZ4 or Zstandard, and CRC checksums, which the homepage says can be configured per application. The format is specified at mcap.dev/spec and has a Kaitai Struct definition in the repo.

commands_seen.context: Install command given in the GitHub README for the MCAP CLI, used to inspect, merge, and split MCAP files.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install mcap, the README points to the GitHub releases page (github.com/foxglove/mcap/releases?q=cli) for downloading the CLI directly. Libraries are installed through each language's package manager: pip package mcap for Python, npm @mcap/core for TypeScript, crates.io mcap for Rust, Conan mcap for C++, and Go and Swift via releases. The CLI guide at mcap.dev/guides/cli covers installation and usage, but I did not fetch it. No hardware, accounts, or first-run configuration were mentioned.
brief.standout: The file is self-describing: schemas live inside the file, so it stays readable without the original code, and the serialization is left to the user. The homepage also says MCAP is the default log format in ROS 2, which is a notable adoption claim for a file format.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage and README are current in tone and link to a maintained-looking docs set, and the homepage says it is used in production. I did not see a last release date or last commit date in the pages I fetched, so I cannot confirm activity. The project is a Foxglove project.
brief.caveats: This is a file format and libraries, not a service or app, so there is little to try interactively beyond the CLI. The README's CLI section is brief and I did not check the CLI guide for supported platforms. The homepage's 'Trusted by leading robotics teams' section lists logos only in text form, so company claims are unverified. Licensed MIT per the README.

Record and replay binary messages in any format – like Protobuf, DDS (CDR), ROS, JSON, and more.
MCAP stores message schemas alongside data, so your files remain readable in the future even as your codebase evolves.

name: mbpoll
desc: Command-line utility to communicate with ModBus slave (RTU or TCP)
why: A Modbus client for talking to industrial PLCs and sensors, a real door into factory protocols.

brief.what_it_is: mbpoll is a command-line Modbus master, a tool that polls and writes registers on Modbus slave devices over serial (RTU) or Ethernet (TCP). You give it a serial port or host name, a slave address, a data table type and a start register, and it prints the values it reads or writes them from the arguments. It can read discrete inputs, read and write coils, read input registers, and read and write holding registers, shown as decimal, hex, or 32-bit int/float. Its output format and option syntax are modelled on the proprietary modpoll tool, but the README says mbpoll is an independent GPL project with its own source.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a motivation in its own words. It presents mbpoll as a command-line way to 'communicate with ModBus slave (RTU or TCP)', and it is positioned as a Modbus master simulator for testing and polling field devices from a shell.
brief.how_it_works: Each run opens a connection (serial port for RTU, host and port for TCP), sends Modbus requests for the chosen table and address range, and prints the replies. With no write values it reads; with values listed after the device it writes them. Without -1 it keeps polling at the poll rate (-l) until Ctrl-C, and it prints per-run frame statistics. RS-485 direction control can use the RTS line, optionally driven from a GPIO pin via piduino.

name: mcpsnoop
desc: Transparent proxy and TUI for debugging MCP traffic
why: A transparent proxy for watching MCP traffic opens a fresh, little-examined protocol to inspection.

brief.what_it_is: mcpsnoop is a transparent proxy and terminal UI for watching Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic. You wrap your MCP server command with it, and it sits between your real AI client (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Claude Desktop) and the server, copying every JSON-RPC frame they exchange without changing either side. Captured frames can be watched live in a TUI, saved as session logs, checked in CI, or exported as json, html, text, har, or OpenTelemetry spans. It is written in Go and ships as a single binary, also available through npm and Homebrew.
brief.why_it_exists: The README argues that the official MCP Inspector connects as its own client, so it never sees what your client actually sends your server. Calls the model never made, or made with wrong arguments, and capability mismatches are invisible to it. mcpsnoop is meant to sit in the real data path so you can see what your real client and server actually say to each other.
brief.how_it_works: mcpsnoop runs as two roles in one binary. 'mcpsnoop -- <server>' is a transparent shim that your client spawns; it forwards bytes verbatim and ships a copy of every frame to a hub. Running 'mcpsnoop' with no arguments starts the hub and live TUI. The two find each other through a well-known socket and on-disk logs, so neither has to start first. For Streamable HTTP servers, 'mcpsnoop http' runs as a reverse proxy instead, and it records the HTTP status of every response, including 401, 403, 202 and 502 responses that carry no JSON-RPC message.

brief.install_notes: Four routes are documented: npx mcpsnoop (no Go needed; the npm package ships six platform packages and installs only the one matching your machine, so nothing downloads at install time), npm i -g mcpsnoop, brew install mcpsnoop, or go install. Prebuilt binaries for every platform are on the Releases page. Shell completions exist for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell, via 'mcpsnoop completion <shell> --help'. Wrapping a client requires editing its MCP config to put 'mcpsnoop' as the command with args ['--', <original command>], or using 'mcpsnoop wrap' for Claude Desktop, then restarting the client. For remote machines, 'mcpsnoop remote <user@host>' prints an SSH tunnel command. For CI, the GitHub Action needs 'security-events: write' permission to upload SARIF to code scanning. No accounts or API keys are mentioned; the README says no model or API key runs in CI.
brief.standout: It is positioned as Wireshark for MCP, sitting on the wire rather than being a client of its own. Two features stand out: it can replay a real client's recorded session against each new build of a server in CI, without calling a model, and it exports MCP traffic as OpenTelemetry spans following the MCP semantic conventions. Its 'wrap' command also edits Claude Desktop's config while keeping a backup and leaving other servers untouched.

name: mdk
desc: GNU MIX development kit
why: GNU MIX development kit for Knuth's hypothetical 1960s machine, a delightful way to watch an imaginary computer execute.

brief.what_it_is: GNU MDK (MIX Development Kit) is an emulator toolkit for Donald Knuth's MIX, the imaginary computer from The Art of Computer Programming, and its assembly language MIXAL. It takes MIXAL source files, which mixasm compiles into binary files that the MIX virtual machines run. The toolkit has two VM front ends: mixvm, a command-line debugger built on readline, and gmixvm, a GTK+ graphical one. It also includes mixguile, a Guile interpreter with an embedded MIX VM that can be scripted in Scheme, plus Emacs integration (mixal-mode.el and mixvm.el). Version 1.3.1 is the current release.
brief.why_it_exists: The page presents MIX as a teaching tool: MIX is a simplified version of real CISC computers, and its assembly language closely resembles real ones, so it can be used to learn computer architecture and assembly programming.
brief.how_it_works: MDK emulates MIX's registers, memory cells, overflow toggle, comparison flags, I/O devices and binary instruction set. mixasm translates MIXAL source into binaries that the VMs execute. The VMs support breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, step execution, timing statistics, instruction tracing, and inspection or modification of registers, flags and memory at any step, with I/O simulated through standard output and the file system.

name: mediaconch
desc: Conformance checker and technical metadata reporter
why: Checks media files against archival conformance policies, a real look into file format internals if you dig in.

brief.what_it_is: MediaConch is an open source toolset that checks preservation-level audiovisual files against conformance policies. Its parts are an implementation checker, a policy checker, a reporter, and a fixer. It targets Matroska, LPCM and FFV1 files, and it can be run from the command line, a graphical user interface, or a web interface. The homepage describes an adaptable application program interface for detailed individual and batch-level conformance checking. The input is media files, and the output is conformance and technical reports.
brief.why_it_exists: It exists to improve standardization and validation of preservation-level audiovisual files in memory institutions, and to help keep Matroska, LPCM and FFV1 viable as recommended digital preservation formats. The README frames it as a way to validate, assess and find solutions to repair files in collections.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the implementation checker, policy checker, reporter and fixer work together to validate files. The repository list says the analysis engine is MediaInfoLib, extended with Matroska and FFV1 tests, and that XSD schemas for MediaConch, MediaInfo and MediaTrace live in a separate repository. The README does not describe the internals beyond this.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are offered for Windows, macOS, Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Raspbian, RedHat Enterprise Linux, CentOS, Fedora, openSUSE, ArchLinux, Flatpak, Snap, AppImage, AWS Lambda, and JavaScript, plus other systems. The homepage lists Version 25.04 and says other versions are available. Monthly releases and nightly builds are on the project's download page. name: mdxmini
desc: Plays music in X68000 MDX chiptune format
why: Plays X68000 MDX chiptune files, a door into a obscure Japanese retro sound format and its hardware era.

brief.what_it_is: mdxmini is a C library with a small API for playing back MDX chiptune files made for the X68000 home computer. A caller opens an MDX file (plus an optional directory of .pdx sample files), reads metadata such as title, length in seconds, and track count, then calls mdx_calc_sample repeatedly to render raw PCM audio into a buffer at a chosen sample rate. Each call can also report the note or sample index active on each channel, which is useful for visualizations. The README's Shift-JIS note means titles come back in that encoding.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a way to play the large MDX archive of FM-sound-era music from the X68000, whose 8-channel YM2151 and PCM chip gave it strong music support. The Credits section traces it from the original X68000 MXDRV player through Daisuke Nagano's Unix mdxplay to BouKiCHi's library.
brief.how_it_works: The caller initialises a t_mdxmini struct with mdx_open, sets the output rate with mdx_set_rate, and then loops on mdx_calc_sample to fill a 16-bit buffer. mdx_calc_sample returns 0 at the final frame of the song. mdx_get_current_notes fills an array with per-channel values: channels 0 to 7 are FM notes (0 is the lowest C), and channels 8 to 15 are PCM sample indices. The README does not say how the chip output is generated internally.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no build, install, or dependency steps. The API is documented in the mdxmini.h header, and the README's C sample shows the call sequence. The Homebrew formula provides an executable named mdxplay, but the README does not describe how that binary works or how to run it. Some songs need a directory of .pdx sample files passed as path_to_samples, which can be NULL.
brief.standout: It is a reusable playback library rather than only a player, and it exposes live per-channel note data for visualizations. Its downstream uses include an Android player and the Modizer music-module player, so the same core runs on mobile and desktop.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no dates or version notes. The GitHub releases page has no releases. The README names Misty De Meo as current maintainer, but I could not check recent commits.

name: mdsh
desc: Markdown shell pre-processor
why: Runs shell code embedded in markdown, a neat quirky idea that is still fairly shallow.

brief.what_it_is: mdsh is a command-line preprocessor for Markdown files, written in Rust. It reads a Markdown file (README.md by default, or stdin with -i -) and finds special mdsh blocks, HTML comments, or links inside it. It then runs shell commands, reads files, or sets shell variables, and writes the results back into the same Markdown, updating the file in place. Output goes to a different file or stdout if you pass -o.
brief.why_it_exists: The author often needs to embed a snippet from another file or show the output of a command in a README, and keeping those pasted results current by hand gets out of sync. The author wants the Markdown syntax to stay natural and the update to be idempotent, so running mdsh again refreshes the generated blocks in place.
brief.how_it_works: Commands use the form [langname] <out_cmd> <in_cmd> [data_line] followed by optional data. The in_cmd sources the data: < reads a file, $ runs a shell command, and an empty in_cmd uses the data as-is. The out_cmd decides the result: a language name produces a fenced code block, > produces raw Markdown wrapped in comment tags, and ! expands the data into shell variables. The commands can sit in inline code, fenced code blocks, single-line or multi-line HTML comments, or link syntax. The README says mdsh finds these blocks with regular expressions rather than parsing the Markdown.

name: mergiraf
desc: Syntax-aware git merge driver
why: A syntax-aware merge driver that parses code into trees, a neat idea hiding in plumbing most developers never inspect.

brief.what_it_is: Mergiraf is a command-line merge driver for Git that merges files by parsing them into syntax trees rather than only comparing lines of text. It takes the base, left and right versions of a conflicted file and outputs a merged file, which it reports as solved or leaves with conflict markers where it cannot be sure. It is aimed at source code and structured formats, and the project describes support as a growing collection of programming languages and file formats. It can also be run by hand on a conflicted file after a merge, or used as a merge tool with Jujutsu.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to solve a wide range of Git merge conflicts by understanding the trees in your files, so that it can often reconcile the needs of both sides. Its stated aspirations are not to sweep conflicts under the rug, to stay fast enough for interactive use, and to stay open to other methods, falling back to line-based merging when that is conflict-free.
brief.how_it_works: Mergiraf first runs a normal line-based merge, and if that is conflict-free it returns the result immediately. Otherwise it parses the files with a language-specific grammar, reconstructs the base, left and right revisions, and resolves conflicts using syntax-aware heuristics. When it cannot parse a file it falls back to line-based merging, and it leaves conflict markers behind where it judges a resolution suspicious. The usage page says a diff3 conflict style is needed because Mergiraf reconstructs the base revision from the markers.

It also lists package repositories, but the names were not captured in the page text. From source, you need Rust: clone the repository and run cargo install --path . or cargo install --locked mergiraf. Afterwards, configure Git: set merge.conflictStyle to diff3 (the usage page calls this required for every workflow), register the mergiraf merge driver, and add merge=mergiraf to a gitattributes file. The docs recommend Git v2.44.0 or newer. The page also suggests installing Difftastic, a structural diff tool that works well alongside Mergiraf. No accounts or runtimes beyond Rust are mentioned.
brief.standout: Mergiraf is a merge driver that uses real syntax trees, not only line diffs, and it deliberately prefers to leave conflict markers rather than guess. It can be wired into Git's own merge, rebase, cherry-pick and revert, so the resolution happens without a separate step. Languages are added declaratively, which the homepage presents as the nonviolent option.

name: metalang99
desc: C99 preprocessor-based metaprogramming language
why: A metaprogramming language built entirely out of C99 preprocessor macros, a strange and fun exercise in what the preprocessor can do.

brief.what_it_is: Metalang99 is a header-only library for C99 (and C++11 onward) that runs a small functional language inside the C preprocessor. You include metalang99.h and write metaprograms as ML99_EVAL or ML99_call expressions, with ML99_ naming throughout. The interpreter takes those expressions at compile time and expands them into plain C text, such as static arrays, struct initializers, or overloaded macros. The standard library, documented on the readthedocs site, supplies lists, tuples, choice types, naturals, booleans, and assertions. The README says it offers algebraic data types, pattern matching, recursion, currying, and collections.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Hirrolot, says C metaprogramming is crippled: the preprocessor cannot do control flow, integers, unbounded sequences, or compound data, and Boost/Preprocessor's recursion limits made his Poica project unmaintainable. Metalang99 was built to give pure C a proper paradigm for metaprograms. It also underpins Datatype99 and Interface99, and the README says it is used at OpenIPC as an indirect dependency.
brief.how_it_works: The README says preprocessor macro recursion is prohibited, so Metalang99 uses an ad-hoc recursion engine that defers expansions and passes continuations. On top of that, a continuation-passing-style interpreter reduces language expressions to final results. The standard library is ordinary metafunctions written in the core metalanguage and evaluated by that interpreter. The README also says a fixed number of reduction steps bounds each metaprogram, so it is not Turing-complete in practice.

commands_seen.context: FAQ example compiling a file of ML99_EVAL lines to show the built-in syntax checker's error messages. The flag disables GCC's macro expansion backtraces.
FAQ answer on compilation times: run from the repository root to execute the benchmarks.

brief.install_notes: No package manager or account is needed. Metalang99 is just header files: add metalang99/include to your include directories. Add -ftrack-macro-expansion=0 for GCC or -fmacro-backtrace-limit=1 for Clang to avoid useless macro-expansion errors. With CMake, the recommended route is FetchContent, pulling the release tarball from GitHub, then linking target metalang99 and setting the same flag per compiler. Precompiled headers are optional and speed up builds. The README lists GCC, Clang, MSVC, and TCC as tested compilers. The brew formula's executables list is empty, which fits a header-only library.
brief.standout: It treats the preprocessor as an interpreted FP language, with a real recursion engine, partial application, and ML99_abort/ML99_fatal for debugging macros. Most macro libraries like Boost/Preprocessor copy-paste recursive definitions up to a fixed depth. The built-in syntax checker turns many macro mistakes into readable static assertion messages, which is unusual for this kind of code.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I could not confirm a date. The docs show version 1.13.5, the GitHub README has a CI badge and a documented release procedure, and it links to a book and a spec PDF. I saw no last-commit or release date in what I fetched.
brief.caveats: The README says it is for syntax transformation only and not CPU-bound work, since the preprocessor is slow and limited. Recursion is bounded by a reduction-step limit. Compile-time errors can still be obscure when code is awkward; the README shows one example. The flags -ftrack-macro-expansion=0 or -fmacro-backtrace-limit=1 are required for good diagnostics. IDEs show macro-generated code but do not highlight macro syntax. The license was not in the README text I fetched, so I could not confirm it. The homepage I first fetched is only the standard library reference, not the overview.
quotes: Metalang99 is a firm foundation for writing reliable and maintainable metaprograms in pure C99.
Metalang99 is only about syntax transformations and not about CPU-bound tasks; the preprocessor is just too slow and limited for such kind of abuse.
Metalang99 is built for humans, not for macro monsters.

name: metaproxy
desc: Z39.50 proxy and router utilizing Yaz toolkit
why: A Z39.50 proxy and router, a door into a library-world search protocol almost nobody outside libraries has met.

brief.what_it_is: Metaproxy is server software, with no user interface, that sits in front of several Z39.50, SRU, SRW, and Solr back-end search servers and presents them as one searchable endpoint. It takes incoming Z39.50 or SRU/SRW requests from a client, runs them through a configurable chain of filters (for example query rewriting, load balancing, caching, filtering, and routing to a virtual database), and returns a single merged result set. Its configuration is an XML file that defines the routes requests take. The package installs two executables: metaproxy, the server, and metaproxy-config, a script that reports on the installation. The homepage calls it a 'metasearch server in-a-box.'
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it exists to integrate multiple back-end databases, within one organization or across several, into what looks to the user like a single searchable resource. The manual describes it as a universal router, proxy and encapsulated metasearcher for information retrieval protocols.
brief.how_it_works: Metaproxy is configured by an XML file that defines routes that request packets take through the proxy, with each step on a route being an instance of a filter. Filter types cover operations such as accepting Z39.50 packets, logging, query transformation, and multiplexing, and new filter types can be added as loadable modules through a filter API. The manual's filter list includes sru_z3950 (SRU requests translated to Z39.50), z3950_client (Z39.50 back-end client), virt_db and multi (virtual databases and multi-database search), load_balance, and cql_rpn (CQL to RPN query conversion).
brief.install_notes: The manual's installation chapters cover building from source (libxml2 and libxslt, optional USEMARC ON, YAZ and YAZ++, Boost, then Metaproxy itself), Debian and RPM-based Linux packages, and Windows (separate steps for Boost, libxslt, YAZ, YAZ++, and Metaproxy). Behaviour is set up through an XML config file, and the manual has a section on config syntax checking. The homepage also describes Index Data's hosted MasterKey Connect service as an option for remote resources that are not directly accessible. The brew formula is not covered by the pages I read.
brief.standout: Metaproxy is a router rather than a search front end: it has no UI, and everything is wired together as a chain of filters in an XML file, so one endpoint can fan out to many Z39.50 and SRU back ends. Most people outside libraries have never encountered Z39.50 at all, so it is an unusual entry point into that world.

name: micropython

brief.what_it_is: MicroPython is an implementation of the Python 3 language built to run on microcontrollers and other constrained systems. It includes an interactive prompt (the REPL) and can run and import scripts from an on-device filesystem. It ships a subset of the standard library plus a 'machine' module and other MicroPython-specific modules for GPIO, timers, ADC, DAC, PWM, SPI, I2C, CAN, Bluetooth and USB. Source code goes in and a firmware image or Unix/Windows executable comes out; the Homebrew formula installs a 'micropython' executable and an 'mpy-cross' cross-compiler.

The README adds that the design values are minimalism, efficiency and consistency, and that the goal is a 'bare-metal feeling' where 'very little [is] between the programmer and the physical world'.
brief.how_it_works: The core is a compiler and runtime written in C99 with no external dependencies. Scripts can run as source (.py) or as precompiled bytecode (.mpy), and the mpy-cross tool produces the .mpy files, which can also be frozen into the firmware so they take no RAM. Ports for each target (ESP32, RP2040/RP2350, STM32, nRF, SAMD and others, plus Unix and Windows) supply the hardware-specific code.

Those outlines are then assembled into a Type 1 font, with the encoding read from the TFM file or given by an encoding file. Optional steps run through FontForge for rounding, simplifying, and autohinting.

name: midicsv
desc: Convert MIDI audio files to human-readable CSV format
why: Turning MIDI binaries into readable CSV is a clear way to see how a music file is structured.

brief.what_it_is: midicsv is a pair of command-line programs by John Walker (Fourmilab). midicsv reads a standard MIDI file and writes a CSV text file that records every event in it, one event per line, with track number, absolute time, and event type as the first fields. csvmidi reads a CSV file in that same format and writes an equivalent MIDI file. Both read standard input and write standard output, so they can sit in a Unix pipeline between text tools.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that MIDI files are compact binary files that are hard to read and write without a special-purpose library, while Perl and Python are well suited to the transformations musicians want. The programs are meant to let text-processing tools transform MIDI files, or generate them from scratch, in bulk.
brief.how_it_works: midicsv decodes the binary MIDI file into records such as 'Track, Time, Note_on_c, Channel, Note, Velocity', with each event type given a readable name and a '_c' suffix for channel events or '_t' suffix for text meta-events. Records are sorted by track, then time, and the file opens with a Header record and closes with End_of_file. csvmidi parses those records back into binary MIDI and reports errors as warnings on standard error, skipping bad records. The README includes Perl examples (transpose, chorus, channel extraction, a drum machine, and a random guitar composer) that edit or generate the CSV.

Pipeline from the Extract Channel example: keeps only events on the chosen channel (set to 9 for the General MIDI percussion track) and writes the result as MIDI.
Dumbest Drummer example: the Perl script prints CSV for a simple repeating drum pattern with no source MIDI file, and csvmidi turns it into drumtrack.mid.
Stoned Guitarist example: the Perl script writes CSV for a randomly generated guitar line with cymbal accompaniment and a closing applause effect, and csvmidi writes performance.mid.

brief.caveats: midicsv assumes its input is a well-formed MIDI file. brief.what_it_is: mfterm is a terminal interface for working with Mifare Classic tags, the 1k to 4k MIFARE RFID cards. It takes in a physical tag, a tag dump file, a key file, a key dictionary file, or a spec file, and it writes out tag data to a file or to a physical tag. The README does not say what hardware reader is needed for physical reads and writes.

Reading a physical tag needs the 'current keys' set to that tag's keys, and writing needs the 'current keys' set to values the card accepts. The 'dict attack' command tries keys from a loaded dictionary against a tag's sectors, and 'mac compute' computes a DES MAC over the UID plus 14 bytes of a block. A spec file names parts of the tag data so you can reach them with dotted paths such as '.sector_0.block_0.atqa'.

name: min-lang
desc: Small but practical concatenative programming language and shell
why: A small concatenative language that doubles as a shell, a delightfully odd corner with a real idea behind it.

brief.what_it_is: min is a functional, concatenative programming language with minimalist syntax, a small standard library, and a REPL, all packed into a single file. Programs are written as sequences of values and quotations that operate on a stack, and the language has a few data types: integers, floats, strings, booleans, dictionaries, and quotations (lists). The project's repo describes it as a language and shell. The homepage example shows it listing files modified in the last hour, so it is used for practical scripting as well as pure stack puzzles. The input is min source code or REPL input, and the output is computed values or side effects such as printed results or files.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames min as a small but practical language that stays minimal in syntax and size while still being useful for everyday tasks. Its sibling mn is pitched as the even more bare-bones option for people who do not need all of min's features.
brief.how_it_works: Code is a sequence of words that push values or quotations onto a stack, and combinators such as filter and linrec consume and produce stack values. Quotations are parenthesised blocks of code, and the language is homoiconic, so code can be accessed as data. Sigils provide syntactic sugar for environment variables, quoting, and defining or binding data, and sys.pwd and fs.mtime show the namespaced standard library in use. The implementation is written in Nim and statically compiled into one file, so it can also be embedded in other Nim programs.

name: miniprot
desc: Align proteins to genomes with splicing and frameshift
why: Aligns proteins to genomes across introns and frameshifts, a real bioinformatics tool that reveals how genes are spliced.

brief.what_it_is: miniprot is a command-line tool that aligns protein sequences against a genome, allowing for introns (splicing) and frameshifts. You give it a genome FASTA (optionally gzipped, or a prebuilt index) and a protein FASTA. It writes protein-style PAF alignments by default, or GFF3 with --gff, and GFF3 embeds the PAF lines. Its stated main use is annotating protein-coding genes in a new species using known proteins from other species.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says miniprot is primarily intended for annotating protein-coding genes in a new species using known genes from other species. It positions itself against GeneWise and Exonerate: similar in function, but able to map proteins to whole genomes and much faster at the residue alignment step.
brief.how_it_works: Per the README's algorithm overview: the genome is translated in six frames and ORFs under 45bp are dropped; amino acids are reduced to 13 classes and open syncmers of 6 amino acids are indexed in a dense hash table. For a query protein, seed matches are found and chained minimap2-style, then a second round of chaining uses reduced 5-mers within each chain. The top 100 chains (see -N) are kept, anchors around potential introns or long gaps are filtered, and striped dynamic programming between the remaining anchors gives the final alignment. Optional minisplice splice scores can be fed in with --spsc.

name: miniupnpc
desc: UPnP IGD client library and daemon
why: The key to UPnP on your router; a perfect door into how devices quietly open ports.

brief.what_it_is: MiniUPnP is a pair of small C libraries and daemons for UPnP Internet Gateway Device (IGD) support, the protocol that lets a machine on a home network ask its router to open a port. MiniUPnPc is the client side: a control point that discovers a gateway on the LAN and sends it port-mapping requests. MiniUPnPd is the server side: a daemon that runs on a Linux or BSD box acting as the gateway and answers those requests by writing firewall rules (pf, ipfw, ipf, netfilter or nftables). MiniSSDPd is a companion SSDP daemon that listens for discovery traffic so several UPnP services can share one machine. The README's commands section is empty, so the tools are described here only by their roles.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted a free, minimal UPnP IGD implementation because libupnp was 'too heavy' for him, and he wanted 'the simplest library possible, with the smallest footprint and no dependencies to other libraries such as XML parsers or HTTP implementations.' The stated goal is to let applications that must accept incoming connections, such as P2P clients, games and servers, open ports on a NAT router automatically.
brief.how_it_works: The client discovers the router with SSDP, either by its own multicast search or by asking MiniSSDPd, which listens for SSDP traffic so clients can skip discovery and set up a redirection faster. The client then talks to the gateway's UPnP SOAP/HTTP services to add or remove port mappings. The daemon is described as a single process with no extra threads, and it does not call system() or exec(), which the author presents as a reason it is light enough for low-memory routers.
brief.install_notes: The README and homepage give no build or install commands. Homebrew reports the executables external-ip, upnp-listdevices and upnpc, but I did not see their usage in the pages I read. Building the daemon requires a supported firewall backend (pf, ipfw, ipf, netfilter or nftables), and the README says MiniUPnPc and MiniSSDPd are portable to any POSIX system and also work on MS Windows and AmigaOS. The README points to the Forum and to a compatibility list for router testing, but I did not open either.
brief.standout: It is a tiny, dependency-free C implementation, with the client library described as under 50KB of x86 code. It pairs the client with a daemon for the gateway side, and it doubles as a readable example of how the UPnP IGD protocol works on both sides of the connection. The homepage calls out the security risk directly: SSDP and HTTP/SOAP ports should be reachable only from the LAN.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I could not confirm it. The homepage says 'Last modified on August 30th 2024', and the GitHub repository README is live and lists active subprojects. I did not see a release date or recent commit timestamps, so the exact maintenance cadence is unknown.
brief.caveats: The homepage notes that the ipf implementation is 'not maintained' and that the ipfw port for FreeBSD has had no feedback. The README warns that 'In the past, several vulnerabilities have been found in MiniUPnPd, so it is very important to update your code to the last version.' The author also says that for some uses 'it may be not the good solution for you to use the code from the MiniUPnP project directly.' Console compatibility 'may need a fine configuration tuning.' The README does not cover licensing, so I did not verify it.

name: minizinc
desc: Medium-level constraint modeling language
why: A constraint modeling language with real solver behind it, a genuine door into combinatorial optimisation.

brief.what_it_is: MiniZinc is a high-level, solver-independent constraint modelling language for constraint satisfaction and optimisation (discrete optimisation) problems. You write a model in its own readable language, using a large library of predefined constraints. The MiniZinc compiler translates the model into FlatZinc, a solver input language, and a wide range of solvers can then run it. The homepage also describes an IDE, Python and JavaScript embedding, and in-browser use. The brew package installs the minizinc and mzn2doc executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to model constraint problems at a high level without being locked into one solver: "MiniZinc is a free and open-source constraint modeling language." The homepage stresses being able to "express and solve discrete optimisation problems" in readable, type-safe form.
brief.how_it_works: A model is compiled into FlatZinc, a lower-level solver input language, which is then handed to whichever solver you choose. Because the model and the solver are separate, the same model can run on different solver technologies. The compiler is the part in the libminizinc repository; the IDE and the solvers such as Gecode and Chuffed live in their own repositories.

Gecode, Coin-OR CBC and proprietary solver headers (CPLEX, Gurobi, SCIP, Xpress) are optional build inputs, and CPLEX can be loaded at runtime. name: minuit2
desc: Physics analysis tool for function minimization
why: CERN's function minimizer from particle physics is real scientific software you can run at home, though it is a library.

brief.what_it_is: Minuit2 is a C++ library for function minimization, a C++ rewrite of the long-standing MINUIT package from CERN. You supply a function (the FCN, usually a chi-square or log-likelihood) and starting parameter values with uncertainties. It searches for the parameter values that minimize the function, then reports the best-fit values, parameter errors, and correlations, and can compute MINOS asymmetric errors and CONTOURS. Results come back as objects you print or query, and CONTOURS returns (x,y) points. It does no histogramming, data handling, or graphics.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames M as a tool to find the minimum of a multi-parameter function and analyze its shape around the minimum, mainly for statistical analysis of chi-square or log-likelihood fits, and especially for difficult problems that may need guidance to find the right solution. It was written at CERN for experimental data analysis, and is also used outside high-energy physics.
brief.how_it_works: The user implements a derived class of FCNBase that computes the function value, and the minimizers (MnMigrad, MnHesse, MnMinos, MnContours) search the parameter space. Parameters with limits are mapped to an unbounded internal space with a non-linear transform (sine-based for double-sided limits), and the error matrix is twice the inverse of the second-derivative matrix multiplied by FCNBase::up(). Error definition up is 1.0 for chi-square and 0.5 for negative log-likelihood by default.

brief.standout: It is a real CERN statistics tool with a long pedigree: the README describes the original Fortran MINUIT written at CERN around 1975-1980 by Fred James and M. Winkler, and this C++ version keeps the numerical behavior while adding single-sided parameter limits and the FUMILI least-squares algorithm. The MINOS method, which computes asymmetric errors that include parameter correlations and non-linearity, is described as probably the first generally available program to do so.

name: mlkit
desc: Compiler for the Standard ML programming language
why: A Standard ML compiler is a rare, academic language implementation with a strong old-school flavour worth a detour.

brief.what_it_is: MLKit is a compiler toolkit for Standard ML. Its native backend (x64 on Linux, arm64 on Apple Silicon macOS) takes SML source and produces native executables, using region inference to decide where memory is allocated and freed, with optional reference-tracing garbage collection. It also ships an interactive REPL (run mlkit with no arguments), a region profiler, and ReML, a variant that adds explicit regions and effects to SML. A sibling backend, SMLtoJs, compiles SML to JavaScript for browsers, and the repo includes Barry, a source-to-source tool that eliminates modules.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a way to compile Standard ML to native code with region-based memory management and to give programmers more control over allocation and memory use (via ReML's explicit regions). The README describes it as covering all of Standard ML as defined in the 1997 Definition, plus most of the Standard ML Basis Library.
brief.how_it_works: Memory allocation and deallocation directives are inferred by the compiler from program analyses about lifetimes and storage layout, which is the region-inference scheme. Region inference can be combined with reference-tracing garbage collection for better memory behaviour, or the GC can be disabled to avoid unbounded pauses for real-time work. Modules are removed at compile time by a scheme called Static Interpretation.

brief.standout: Few production-quality compilers for a functional language can point to inferred region-based memory management alongside an optional tracing GC, and ReML lets programmers write regions and effects by hand. name: mmseqs2
desc: Software suite for very fast sequence search and clustering
why: Real bioinformatics sequence search and clustering at scale, a genuine science tool you can run on your own data.

brief.what_it_is: MMseqs2 is a free, open-source C++ software suite for searching and clustering very large protein and nucleotide sequence sets. You give it FASTA/FASTQ files, or its own database format, and it returns search hits (alignments in a tab-separated format by default), sequence clusters, or taxonomic labels. It runs on multiple cores and across servers, and the README says it is available for Linux and macOS, with Windows only as a beta via cygwin. The README also describes a GPU-accelerated search path and prebuilt workflows that download public reference databases such as UniProt/Swiss-Prot, UniRef, NR, NT and Pfam.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a fast, sensitive alternative to BLAST and PSI-BLAST for massive data sets: "MMseqs2 can run 10000 times faster than BLAST. At 100 times its speed it achieves almost the same sensitivity." The stated goal is searching and clustering "huge" sequence collections, where classic tools are too slow.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the algorithm in detail. It describes easy-cluster (a cascaded clustering algorithm), easy-linclust (runtime that scales linearly with input size, recommended for huge data), and search modes including iterative profile searches like PSI-BLAST, translated searches, and ungapped prefilter searches. Memory use is stated as about 1 byte per residue for clustering and per target residue for search, and the software splits the target database into parts that fit in available RAM.

name: mmix
desc: 64-bit RISC architecture designed by Donald Knuth
why: Knuth's 64-bit RISC teaching machine with its own assembler and simulator, a delightful door into how computers really execute.

brief.what_it_is: MMIX is a 64-bit RISC machine designed by Donald Knuth, described on this site as a teaching architecture that is easy to learn yet representative of modern machines. MMIXware is the software package around it: an assembler (mmixal) and a simulator (mmix), plus related tools. You feed it MMIX assembly source and run it on the simulator, which executes the program on the emulated machine. The homepage names the assembler and simulator but does not describe the other installed executables (mmmix, mmotype) in any detail.
brief.why_it_exists: Knuth designed MMIX to replace the MIX machine in the published volumes 1 to 3 of The Art of Computer Programming and to use it in later volumes, starting with volume 4. The MMIX Supplement provides MMIX versions of every MIX program in those volumes.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal mechanism of the simulator or assembler beyond saying that MMIXware, as described in Volume 1 Fascicle 1 of TAOCP, was frozen in September 2011. The MMIXware book, a Lecture Notes in Computer Science volume, documents Version 1 of the architecture and corresponds to the mmix-20131017.tgz release.
brief.install_notes: The homepage lists prebuilt executables for Win32, Linux 32-bit and Mac OS X, and says the sources are in a git repository at https://gitlab.lrz.de/mmix. It also mentions MMIXVD, a Windows-only visual debugger and IDE that bundles an editor, mmixal and mmix. A Java IDE by Anselm Binninger (BWK-Technik) is linked. No accounts, runtimes or configuration steps are mentioned on the homepage. The Homebrew formula supplies the four executables directly.
brief.standout: Knuth designed a whole machine, instruction set and toolchain for teaching, and the software is a frozen, bug-free-by-definition reference rather than a moving project. The software is tied to a published book and to the TAOCP series, so it reads as a companion to Knuth's text rather than a standalone tool.
brief.status: Mixed. The homepage says MMIXware Version 1 was frozen in September 2011 and is 'permanently frozen', with the last named tarball dated 2013 (mmix-20131017.tgz). The site says it 'coordinates the future development of MMIXware' and mentions a new MMIXVD 1.1 release, but gives no dates for it. Overall: the core is frozen and the site is maintained as a reference hub; recent software activity is unknown.
brief.caveats: Version 1 of the architecture is frozen, so no new features are expected in the core. The Linux binaries are 32-bit only. MMIXVD is Windows-only. Much of the documentation is in PDF. The homepage itself lists no commands and no quick-start steps; those are on the Getting Started page, which I did not reach because the homepage did not expose its link targets to me.

A RISC computer for the new millennium

name: mlton
desc: Whole-program, optimizing compiler for Standard ML
why: Whole-program optimising compiler for Standard ML, an old-school functional language with a distinctive compilation approach.

brief.what_it_is: MLton is a whole-program optimizing compiler for Standard ML. You give it SML source (and ML Basis files for libraries), and it produces standalone native executables that the homepage describes as small and fast. It also ships a Standard ML environment with the Basis Library and tools: the mllex lexer generator, the mlyacc parser generator, the mlprof source-level profiler, and the mlnlffigen foreign-function-interface generator.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames MLton as a compiler that generates small executables with excellent runtime performance, and as a feature-rich Standard ML programming environment with full SML97 support.
brief.how_it_works: Because it is whole-program, MLton compiles the entire program together so it can optimize across module boundaries. The README credits untagged and unboxed native integers, reals and words, unboxed native arrays, GMP-based arbitrary-precision arithmetic, and several selectable code generation and garbage collection strategies. The README does not go into more detail on the optimization pipeline.

Pre-built binaries come from OS package managers or from mlton.org for some platforms. A binary .tgz or .tbz package can be extracted anywhere and run in place (./bin/mlton), after make update. Default install goes to /usr/local, and PREFIX changes that.

name: modflow6
desc: USGS modular hydrologic model
why: USGS groundwater flow simulator, real hydrology you can run at home, though niche and obscure.

brief.what_it_is: MODFLOW 6 is the USGS's sixth core release of its modular groundwater simulation program, and it models three-dimensional, transient groundwater flow. The user supplies a model description as input files covering the grid, aquifer properties, and stresses such as wells, rivers, recharge, and boundary conditions. It outputs simulated heads, flows, and budgets. The homepage also lists groundwater transport, energy transport, and particle tracking models, while the GitHub README mentions only flow and transport. The brew-installed executable is mf6.
brief.why_it_exists: The USGS says MODFLOW has spawned many incompatible variants for surface-water interaction, nested and unstructured grids, karst, solute transport, and saltwater intrusion, because the old program was built to run one model on a regular layer-row-column grid. MODFLOW 6 is a new object-oriented framework meant to run multiple models and multiple model types in one simulation, so those capabilities can live in one program.
brief.how_it_works: Each model is divided into packages, and each package handles one aspect of the simulation, such as flow, wells, rivers, lakes, or streamflow routing. Any number of models can run in one simulation, either independently, exchanging information through exchange objects, or tightly coupled in a single matrix solution. The Water Mover package moves water from provider packages to receiver packages, for example routing pumped groundwater into a lake.
brief.install_notes: Nothing I read covers installation beyond the brew formula, which provides mf6. The GitHub README says pre-built Linux, macOS, and Windows binaries from the develop branch are posted nightly in a separate MODFLOW-ORG/modflow6-nightly-build repository, and that building from source requires following DEVELOPER.md, which I did not open. The official distribution and past releases are on the USGS release page and on code.usgs.gov. Running it means preparing input files, or using a Python package such as FloPy or a GUI such as ModelMuse, which the USGS lists as related tools.
brief.standout: One program absorbs the features of MODFLOW-2005, MODFLOW-NWT, MODFLOW-USG, MODFLOW-LGR, SEAWAT's buoyancy, MT3D-USGS, and MODPATH 7 functionality. It also ships the ZONEBUDGET and Mf5to6 converter tools with the release, so older models can be converted rather than rebuilt.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage is dated September 23, 2026, and its software citation gives version 6.8.1 with a release date of 23 September 2026. The GitHub README says the develop branch is under active, frequent updates and that nightly builds are produced, with the version string at 6.9.0.dev0. I did not check commit dates directly.
brief.caveats: The README includes a disclaimer that the software is preliminary or provisional, has not received final USGS approval, and comes with no warranty. The GitHub README and the homepage disagree: the README says 30 years and lists only the GWF and GWT models, while the homepage says 40 years and also lists GWE and PRT, so the README may lag. The particle tracking model does not support DISU grids or tracking through lake and stream features. The scout notes call it niche, and the documentation assumes hydrogeology background. I did not find any licensing statement beyond the USGS public-domain framing, and I did not check the brew formula version.

name: mlt

Its parts are ready-to-use tools (the melt command-line player and renderer), XML authoring components, and a plug-in API. Media clips, XML composition files, and filter or transition plug-ins go in; rendered or played audio and video come out. The executables installed by the Homebrew formula are melt and melt-7.

The README does not explain the internal pipeline in detail. The README's melt example uses an SDL audio consumer, and the news items mention producers, consumers, filters, transitions, and tractors. I did not open the docs to confirm the mechanism.

name: mobiledevice

brief.what_it_is: mobiledevice is a command-line utility for macOS that talks to iPhones and iPads connected over USB, using Apple's private MobileDevice framework. It can list connected devices by UDID, read device and app properties, install and uninstall .app folders, look up an app's bundle identifier from a local .app, and forward local TCP ports to a port on the device. Input is a device UDID or a bundle ID or .app path, and output is plain text on stdout, with errors on stderr and a non-zero exit status on failure.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it automates tasks such as installing and uninstalling apps on an iPhone or iPad without doing it by hand in Xcode or iTunes. It also says 'You don't need a jailbroken device!'
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals beyond saying the tool interacts with Apple's Private Mobile Device Framework. The tunnel command listens on a local port on the Mac and forwards each connection over USB to the given port on the device. Commands take an optional -t timeout and -u UDID, and default to the first detected device.

name: monocle
desc: See through all BGP data with a monocle
why: A BGP data explorer that lets you watch the internet's routing tables, a real window into a protocol almost nobody looks at.

brief.what_it_is: Monocle is a command-line tool, written in Rust and also usable as a library, for searching and inspecting BGP routing data. It takes public BGP sources (MRT archives from RIPE RIS and Route Views found through the BGPKit Broker, local or remote MRT files, and the live RIPE RIS Live stream) plus supporting datasets such as RPKI, prefix-to-AS mappings, AS relationships, and AS registration info. It outputs filtered BGP messages or reconstructed routing tables as table, markdown, JSON, JSON lines, PSV, or SQLite. It also has an HTTP/SSE server mode.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is a way to "See through all Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) data with a monocle." It is aimed at turning the large, scattered public BGP archives into something you can query from a shell, with one filter syntax shared across parse, search, and watch.
brief.how_it_works: Subcommands read MRT files (parse), query the BGPKit Broker for matching public archive files (search), subscribe to RIS Live (watch), or load a RIB at or before a timestamp and replay updates up to the requested time (rib). Filters such as origin ASN, prefix, peer, community, and AS-path regex apply to each BGP element. For watch, host, prefix, peer IP, and elem type are pushed down to the RIS Live subscription, and the rest are checked client-side. Results go to the chosen formatter, or to SQLite or MRT files.

The Docker image defaults to server mode; docker compose up -d starts the server, and the README shows a health check at http://localhost:8080/health. Config defaults to $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/monocle/monocle.toml, with environment variables prefixed MONOCLE_ and an optional --config flag. Data and cache paths follow XDG as well. Automatic database updates run unless --no-update is given. No accounts or special hardware are mentioned in the README. Server auth is optional, using a token.
brief.standout: Watch and parse share one filter vocabulary, and a live watch can be recorded as an MRT file and then replayed offline through parse with the same filters. The rib command rebuilds the routing table at an arbitrary timestamp from the nearest earlier RIB plus updates, instead of only offering raw archive files.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub releases page lists v1.6.0 as Latest, dated 11 Sep (the year is not shown in the fetched text; the README's example dates suggest 2025). name: montage
desc: Toolkit for assembling FITS images into custom mosaics
why: Real astronomy mosaicking software from Caltech, a genuine science tool, though its appeal depends on whether you work with FITS images.

brief.what_it_is: Montage is a toolkit for assembling FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) astronomy images into custom mosaics. You give it input FITS images and specify the target coordinates, projection, spatial sampling, rotation and background matching, and it reprojects, background-matches and co-adds them into a FITS mosaic. It also includes tools for reading and tabulating image metadata, examining images, and visualizing results with three-colour displays and catalogue overlays. The tools are ANSI-C stand-alone executables with names beginning in m (such as mAdd), also available as a library, and since version 6 as a Python package called MontagePy.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as an accurate, open-source way to build custom sky mosaics from FITS images while preserving spatial and calibration fidelity, and as a tool that runs from a desktop up to clusters and computational grids.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes separate engines for analysing the geometry of images on the sky, re-projecting images, rectifying background emission to a common level, and co-adding images. The 7.0 README adds HiPS tooling that builds large mosaics with the existing reprojection, background matching and co-addition modules, using a HPX projection, then repeatedly shrinks by factors of two to form a tile hierarchy and cuts 512x512 tiles.

commands_seen.context: Installs the Python binary-extension version of Montage from PyPI, offered as an alternative to building from source.
The README says the distribution contains all libraries needed to build the toolkit from a single simple make command; it bundles CFITSIO and the WCS library.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs only a C toolchain and make, since CFITSIO and the WCS library are bundled. For Python, MontagePy needs Python 3.x (3.6+ recommended) and is distributed as binary wheels for Linux and Mac via PyPI. Native Windows executables are cross-compiled, and Cygwin is listed as a Windows option. No accounts or service sign-up are mentioned. The Homebrew caveat points to a licence download page that the user should read before use.
brief.standout: Montage has a long academic pedigree, is written in portable C, and is used as an example application in workflow and cloud research. Version 7.0 adds tools for building HiPS tile sets on a single desktop at arcminute scale, with cloud job generation for arcsecond scale. The Python wheels are built from the C code through Cython, so the same algorithms run at compiled speed.
brief.status: Maintained, with some evidence of recent activity. The homepage was rebuilt on a new VM in April 2022 and still has active news. name: moreutils
desc: Collection of tools that nobody wrote when UNIX was young
why: A collection of forgotten Unix tools like sponge and ifdata; widely installed but the odd corners still reward exploring.

brief.what_it_is: moreutils is a collection of small general-purpose Unix command-line tools, fifteen in all: chronic, combine, errno, ifdata, ifne, isutf8, lckdo, mispipe, parallel, pee, sponge, ts, vidir, vipe, and zrun. Each takes ordinary text or arguments from the shell and does one narrow job, such as soaking up stdin into a file, timestamping lines, or opening a directory listing in your editor for renaming. The page describes them as the basic tools that were never written. The tools are installed as separate executables, so they slot into existing pipelines.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's view is that the most basic tools fall through the cracks and are never noticed by people who could benefit from them, so the collection was born to stop these programs from falling through the cracks.

name: mp4ff
desc: Tools for parsing and manipulating MP4/ISOBMFF files
why: A Go library and toolset for poking inside MP4 box structure, a useful way to see how the container is built.

brief.what_it_is: mp4ff is a Go module and a set of nine command-line tools for reading, writing and changing MP4 (ISOBMFF) files. It parses AVC and HEVC video, AAC and AC-3 audio, stpp and wvtt subtitles, and timed metadata, and it focuses on fragmented files used for MPEG-DASH, MSS and HLS fMP4, though it also handles progressive MP4. The CLI tools take an MP4 file in and print information about it (mp4ff-info, mp4ff-pslister, mp4ff-nallister, mp4ff-subslister) or write a new file out (mp4ff-crop, mp4ff-encrypt, mp4ff-decrypt, mp4ff-defragment, mp4ff-mvhevc). The README does not say what the output format of the listers is.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the module 'implements MP4 media file parsing and writing' for streaming-oriented formats, and that the repo is 'focused on the file format' while also covering codec-specific boxes. It does not state a separate motivation beyond that.
brief.how_it_works: The top-level type is mp4.File. For progressive files it exposes Ftyp, Moov and Mdat. For fragmented files it exposes Init, Segments and Fragments, and it can run in a lazy mode that reads only metadata and defers media data, using ReadData or CopyData with a byte range. Boxes are dispatched by name from decoder tables (decodersSR and decoders), and unknown boxes become UnknownBox. Newer SliceReader and SliceWriter paths were added in version 0.27 to cut allocations.

name: mrbayes
desc: Bayesian inference of phylogenies and evolutionary models
why: Real Bayesian phylogenetic inference you can run on sequence data at home, a genuine door into how evolutionary trees are estimated.

brief.what_it_is: MrBayes is a command-line program for Bayesian inference of phylogenies and evolutionary models. It takes sequence or character data (nucleotide, amino acid, restriction site, and morphological characters, alone or mixed in one analysis) and uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to estimate the posterior distribution of model parameters and trees. Output includes posterior samples and majority-rule consensus trees in FigTree format, with branch and node summaries. It also supports model choice via Bayes factors using the stepping-stone method.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a general-purpose program for Bayesian model choice and inference across a wide range of phylogenetic and evolutionary models, with one common command-line interface across Macintosh, Windows, and UNIX.
brief.how_it_works: It runs MCMC sampling over the posterior of the chosen model's parameters and tree topologies, with convergence monitoring during the run and diagnostics afterward. Checkpointing lets a run be extended or recovered after a crash. Optional MPI spreads jobs across a cluster on macOS and UNIX, and optional BEAGLE support speeds up codon and amino acid models on compatible NVIDIA GPUs.

name: mpremote
desc: Tool for interacting remotely with MicroPython devices
why: Remote control of MicroPython boards over serial is a practical door into talking to physical devices, though fairly standard tooling.

brief.what_it_is: mpremote is a command-line tool for talking to a MicroPython board over its serial connection. With no arguments it finds the first USB serial device and opens an interactive REPL, which is the device's Python prompt and program output. It also takes a sequence of subcommands that copy, list, edit, and delete files on the device, run or evaluate Python code, mount a host folder onto the device, install packages with mip, deploy ROMFS images, and reset the board. Output is terminal text, plus any files you ask it to pull back from the device.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs describe it as an integrated set of utilities to remotely interact with, manage the filesystem on, and automate a MicroPython device over a serial connection. It gathers into one tool the serial-terminal, file-transfer, and reset steps that MicroPython developers otherwise handle separately.
brief.how_it_works: Each command has the form <command name> [--options] [args...], and several commands can be chained in one invocation and run in order. Any command that needs the device connects implicitly, and actions stop a running program without clearing interpreter state, so variables persist until a soft-reset. The run command sends a local script to the device and executes it from RAM without writing it to the filesystem. The mount command installs a filesystem driver on the device that uses the serial link as a side channel, exposing the host directory at /remote.

commands_seen.context: Installs mpremote with pip for the current user; the docs also offer pipx install mpremote.
Run with no arguments: connects to the first USB serial device and opens the REPL.
Copies main.py from the host to the device (the colon marks the remote path), then enters the REPL; the + ends the file argument list.
Executes a local script directly from device RAM without copying it to the device filesystem.
Mounts the current local directory on the device as /remote and opens a REPL with /remote as the working directory.
Builds a ROMFS image from the host directory myapp/, compiling .py files to .mpy when mpy_cross is installed.
Installs the aioble package from micropython-lib onto the device.
Hard-resets the device, waits 500 ms, then puts it into its bootloader.
Updates one file on the device, then runs the local test.py from RAM, which is never copied to the device.
Runs the given Python code on the device and prints its output, the same as typing it at the REPL.

brief.install_notes: Install with pip install --user mpremote or pipx install mpremote; pipx run mpremote ...args runs it without a permanent install. The device needs to be a MicroPython board reachable over a serial port; auto-detection only finds USB serial ports (CDC/ACM or FTDI-style), and rfc2217://host:port reaches a networked serial port. Optional: pip install mpy_cross enables .py to .mpy compilation for romfs. Optional user config lives at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mpremote/config.py (or $HOME/.config/mpremote/config.py, or %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows) for custom shortcuts and auto_soft_reset. The edit command needs $EDITOR set.
brief.standout: mount exposes a host folder to the device as its filesystem over the existing serial link, so you can iterate on code without copying files. Its cp command follows the scp colon convention and skips files whose SHA256 already matches, and run executes a script without writing anything to the device.
brief.status: unknown for an exact date: the docs page lists releases from v1.4.4 through v1.29.0 plus a latest development branch, which suggests ongoing releases, but the page shows no release or commit date. The docs say they describe the latest development branch.
brief.caveats: The docs warn that there is no supported way to undelete files removed by mpremote rm -r :, and that rm -rv :/ removes everything including mounted filesystems. Only USB serial ports are auto-detected. On some devices, such as those using a dynamic USBDevice or WebREPL, soft-reset drops the connection. If the device runs main.py at startup, remount after a Ctrl-D soft reset may fail, so a raw-mode reboot (Ctrl-A Ctrl-D, then Ctrl-B) is needed. Shortcut aliases are platform-specific (a0 for /dev/ttyACM0 on Linux, c1 for COM1 on Windows). Serial ports open in exclusive mode. The docs describe the development branch, which may differ from released versions. License not stated on the page.

name: msdfgen
desc: Multi-channel signed distance field generator
why: Turns vector glyphs into multi-channel distance fields, a neat transform with a real trick, though mostly used as a library.

brief.what_it_is: A C++ command-line tool and library that turns vector shapes and font glyphs into distance field textures. The console program takes a font glyph (-font file.ttf 'M'), an SVG file (-svg), or a text shape description (-shapedesc, -defineshape, -stdin) and writes an image such as PNG, BMP, TIFF, or raw float formats. Its default mode, msdf, produces a multi-channel signed distance field, and it can also write monochrome sdf, perpendicular psdf, or mtsdf, which puts a true distance field in the alpha channel. The output is meant to be sampled in a fragment shader for resolution-independent text and shape rendering.
brief.why_it_exists: Monochrome distance fields lose sharp corners when magnified, and the author's stated purpose is to generate multi-channel distance fields, using a method he developed, that reproduce corners almost perfectly by using all three colour channels. The README also notes that conventional and perpendicular distance fields are supported.
brief.how_it_works: Each edge of the shape is assigned a colour (c, m, y or w) so that neighbouring edges meeting at a sharp corner are encoded in different channels. The shader takes the median of the three channels to recover a signed distance, which is then used like an ordinary SDF to get anti-aliased edges. The README gives the GLSL for this, and the method is described in the author's master's thesis, linked below.

Sets the output file. The format is deduced from the extension (png, bmp, tiff, rgba, fl32, txt, bin), or set with -format.

brief.install_notes: The core module needs only bare C++. The extensions for loading fonts and SVG and saving PNG use FreeType, TinyXML2 and libpng, with Skia optional. The README says a Windows binary is in the GitHub Releases section. To build from source, use the included CMake script. By default this needs vcpkg, so set the VCPKG_ROOT environment variable to the vcpkg directory and CMake will fetch the dependencies from it. Using it as a library means the Shape, edgeColoringSimple and generateMSDF API from msdfgen.h and msdfgen-ext.h.
brief.standout: The colour-channel trick is the main idea. Three channels encode sharp corners that a single-channel distance field smooths over, and the same texture still works with a simple median in the shader. The tool also includes testrender and exportshape options to check the result.

name: msdf-atlas-gen
desc: Generator of multi-channel signed distance field atlases from fonts
why: Turning font glyphs into multi-channel distance fields is a neat transform from outlines to sharp-corner textures, though it is mainly a graphics tool.

brief.what_it_is: msdf-atlas-gen is a C++ utility that turns a TTF or OTF font into a texture atlas of multi-channel signed distance fields. It loads a chosen set of glyphs (by character set, glyph index, or all glyphs), generates a distance field for each, and packs them tightly into one bitmap. The output is the atlas image and/or its layout metadata, exported as an Artery Font file, a plain image, a CSV sheet, or a JSON file. It runs as a standalone console program or as a library that is linked into other code.
brief.why_it_exists: A font atlas is typically stored in texture memory and used to draw text in real-time rendering contexts such as video games. The README describes it as a utility for generating compact font atlases using MSDFgen, the author's distance-field library.
brief.how_it_works: Glyph outlines are loaded through FreeType and each glyph gets a distance field. In the MSDF mode, edges are colored across three channels so that sharp corners survive when the texture is upscaled. The packer then bin-packs the glyph boxes into an atlas, or places them in a uniform grid if -uniformgrid is set. The README does not describe the internals beyond this.

name: msieve
desc: C library for factoring large integers
why: Runnable number field sieve for factoring large integers, a real piece of computational number theory you can drive from the shell.

brief.what_it_is: Msieve is a C library, with a small demo command-line program also called msieve, for factoring large integers. You give it an integer (or a text file of integers, one per line, or an arithmetic expression such as (10^53 - 1) / 9) and it returns the prime factors. Internally it runs trial division and Pollard rho, then P-1, P+1 and ECM through GMP-ECM if that is installed, then the self-initializing quadratic sieve by default. The number field sieve is also included for much larger inputs, but the README says it is for users who know what they are doing. Output goes to a logfile, with a summary on screen.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Jason Papadopoulos, says it is the result of his efforts to understand and optimize how integers are factored using the most powerful modern algorithms. It is a learning and optimization project, and it is released as a public-domain 'hobby' effort.
brief.how_it_works: The library runs cheap methods first and escalates. Trial division and Pollard rho run on every input, and inputs under about 25 digits use small custom routines. Larger inputs go to GMP-ECM's P-1, P+1 and ECM with user-set effort. If those fail, the self-initializing quadratic sieve runs, and the README says failure there would indicate a library bug. Savefiles let an interrupted factorization restart. The README notes that the sieving stage is the expensive part and that its own multiple-precision library replaces GMP.

commands_seen.context: Shows the full list of command-line options for the demo application, according to the README.
Example of an arithmetic expression the demo accepts as input (from v1.08 on). It evaluates to 11111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111. This is an input example, not a shell command.

brief.install_notes: Build from source with the included unix Makefile, which produces a static library libmsieve.a and a msieve demo binary. Precompiled Windows binaries are on the author's web page (www.boo.net/~jasonp). Visual Studio 2007 build files (from Brian Gladman) are included, and there are also build.vc9 and build.cuda.vc9 folders. The README says the only requirement is a compiler with a native 64-bit integer type. ECM support needs the external GMP-ECM library. Memory use grows with input size: a 100-digit quadratic sieve job needs roughly 55-130 MB, while completing a 512-bit RSA-sized number by NFS needs 2-3 GB. The README does not mention Homebrew specifically; the brew install is the one listed in the catalogue data.
brief.standout: It is a complete factoring pipeline in one small, self-contained C library with no required dependencies, and it is public domain. The author's FAQ says large jobs should use GGNFS for the first stage and msieve for the last part. The scout note calls it a runnable number field sieve, but the README says the default path is the quadratic sieve and the NFS code is for advanced use.
brief.status: Unknown, with mixed evidence. The SourceForge page shows 'Last Update: 2026-10-12', 127 downloads this week, and a 5.0 rating from 4 reviews, with the project registered in 2009. The GitHub mirror (radii/msieve) shows 163 commits, 282 stars and 57 forks, but I did not see a release date or last-commit date. The README documents version 1.46 and reads like a finished, long-stable project, so it is probably low-activity rather than actively developed, but I could not confirm this.
brief.caveats: The README says the code can take numbers up to 275 digits, but the author does not expect it to complete factorizations above about 120 digits on its own. Above roughly 110 digits, the README says the quadratic sieve is 'not appropriate' and the NFS implementation 'isn't even close to done' (its wording). Multithreading only covers the linear-algebra and final stages, not sieving. The multiple-precision library is described by the author as one that 'sucks', and GMP is not used. The license is public domain (SourceForge lists 'Public Domain'). The scout note's description of 'runnable number field sieve' overstates how the tool defaults. The SourceForge page's 'Last Update' date is in the future relative to typical catalogue dates, so treat it cautiously.
