name: msolve
desc: Library for Polynomial System Solving through Algebraic Methods
why: A serious computer algebra solver for polynomial systems that you can run at home on real math problems.

brief.what_it_is: msolve is an open-source C library and command-line program for solving multivariate polynomial systems exactly. You give it a text file listing variables, a field characteristic (0 for rationals, or a prime), and the polynomials. It can compute Groebner bases, decide whether the system has finitely many complex solutions, and isolate the real solutions as rational boxes. It writes its results to an output file.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a library for exact, algebraic solving of polynomial systems, built on computer algebra (symbolic computation) rather than floating-point numerics. The README says it is meant to be usable from other computer algebra systems as well as directly.
brief.how_it_works: It uses Groebner basis algorithms, including F4 and changes of monomial ordering, as its core. For systems with finitely many complex solutions and rational coefficients, it computes real root isolation. Over prime fields it computes a parametrization of the solutions. The README says multi-threading is applied to the linear algebra for prime-field Groebner bases, to multi-modular real solving, and to real root isolation.

commands_seen.context: Basic run: reads the input system from in.ms and writes results to out.ms. Detects dimension zero, then isolates real roots (rational coefficients) or computes a parametrization (prime field).
Same basic run with verbosity set to 2 so you can see what msolve is doing.
Computes only the leading monomials of the reduced Groebner basis in graded reverse lexicographic order, from which dimension and degree of the ideal can be read.
Returns the full reduced Groebner basis in graded reverse lexicographic order.
Groebner basis with one-block elimination order, eliminating the first variable. Using -e k eliminates the first k variables.
Runs with 4 threads.

brief.install_notes: The README points to an INSTALL file in the repository for build steps; I did not read it. It does not support 32-bit architectures. Beyond the Homebrew formula, there are no accounts or hardware requirements mentioned. Input format: first line is comma-separated variables, second line is the field characteristic (e.g. 0), then polynomials, each ending in a comma except the last. Rational coefficients use /, e.g. -2/3*x2*y1^2. Each monomial should appear only once per polynomial. Prime-field Groebner computation requires characteristic below 2^31.
brief.standout: Unlike many solvers that return approximate numerical roots, msolve returns exact encodings: rational isolating boxes for real roots and rational parametrizations. It is also embedded in Oscar, SageMath (via Variety) and Macaulay2, so it can be used without learning its file format directly.
brief.status: Unknown, leaning active. The homepage lists release v0.11.0 but gives no date. I did not see a last-commit date or release date in the README I read. Signs of ongoing work: it is wired into Oscar, SageMath and Macaulay2, the README cites a 2021 ISSAC paper, and it lists current funding from the RPTU research initiative and ANR.
brief.caveats: Licensed GPLv2+, which matters if you want to embed it in closed-source software. No 32-bit support. Groebner computations over prime fields are limited to characteristic below 2^31. Real root isolation applies only when the system has finitely many complex solutions and rational coefficients. The input parser's behaviour is undefined if a monomial repeats, so you must avoid that. The brew description calls it a library, but the Homebrew formula installs an msolve executable.
quotes: msolve is a library, written in plain C, for solving multivariate polynomial systems.
msolve is distributed under the license GPLv2+
open source C library implementing computer algebra algorithms for solving polynomial systems (with rational coefficients or coefficients in a prime field).

name: msitools
desc: Windows installer (.MSI) tool
why: Lets you inspect and extract Windows MSI installer databases on a Mac, a real file-format door.

brief.what_it_is: msitools is a set of command-line programs for inspecting and building Windows Installer (.MSI) packages. The inspection tools (msiinfo, msidump, msiextract, msidiff) take an existing MSI file and show its tables, streams, and embedded files, or extract the files, or diff two packages. The build tools (msibuild, a low-level builder, and wixl, a WiX-like builder) take MSI tables or an XML description and produce an MSI file. wixl-heat builds XML fragments from a list of files and directories. The wiki also notes that osslsigncode 1.5.1 or later can sign the resulting MSI files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says msitools is meant to be a solution for packaging and deploying cross-compiled Windows applications. It is built on libmsi, a portable library for reading and writing MSI files, which is itself a port of a subset of Wine's Windows Installer implementation.
brief.how_it_works: libmsi does the reading and writing of MSI files, and the command-line tools sit on top of it. The README says MSI files are OLE Structured Storage files, and msitools uses libgsf to read that container format. wixl parses an XML document and tries to use the same syntax as the WiX toolset.
brief.install_notes: The brew formula is the only install path the README mentions. The wiki says release tarballs are at https://download.gnome.org/sources/msitools/. Nothing beyond the normal build dependencies (libgsf is one) is mentioned, and I saw no first-run configuration.
brief.standout: wixl tries to accept the same XML syntax as Microsoft's WiX toolset, so you can build Windows installers on macOS or Linux without the Windows toolchain. The inspection tools also let you open and extract MSI files, which is a file-format look that most people never get.

The README is from the GitLab project and I saw no release date or last-commit date in either page, so I cannot confirm current maintenance.

The README and wiki both say wixl lacks many features compared with WiX. The homepage in the brew formula is a retired wiki, so some links may be stale. Signing needs a separate tool, osslsigncode. name: mt32emu
desc: Multi-platform software synthesiser
why: An emulator of the Roland MT-32 synth, a 1987 machine with a distinctive sound and a window into vintage hardware synthesis.

brief.what_it_is: Munt is a monorepo of related subprojects built around mt32emu, a C/C++ library that approximates the Roland MT-32, CM-32L and LAPC-I synthesiser modules in software. The main end-user application is mt32emu_qt, a Qt GUI that takes MIDI input from virtual or real MIDI ports (or from Standard MIDI files) and outputs audio, and can also render SMF files to WAV or RAW. Other parts include a Linux ALSA driver, an SMF-to-WAV converter, a Windows MME driver, and a DOSBox patch. The README does not give a release year for the hardware, although the scout note calls it a 1987 machine.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the project as an approximate emulation of Roland's MT-32, CM-32L and LAPC-I modules, for developers who want to embed one in a driver or application, and for users who want to play MIDI through it on a computer. The mt32emu_qt README also notes that the app 'Emulates the funny MT-32 LCD' and shows the synth's internal state in real time.
brief.how_it_works: mt32emu is the emulation engine, exposed as a C++ library with an optional C-compatible API. Front ends feed it MIDI messages through platform MIDI systems (Windows Multimedia, CoreMIDI, ALSA sequencer, raw ALSA/OSS4 ports, or JACK MIDI) and receive rendered audio, which is sent to the host audio system (PulseAudio, JACK, ALSA, OSS, or Windows multimedia). The README says the library's emulation 'requires enough processing power from CPU to perform in real-time', and an optional external resampler (libsoxr or libsamplerate) can replace the built-in one.

commands_seen.context: Configure an in-tree POSIX build with optimisations on; the README says compiler optimisations are off by default otherwise. Appears in both the mt32emu and mt32emu_qt READMEs.
Compile after the CMake configure step. Same in both READMEs.

From the ALSA & OSS4 raw MIDI section of mt32emu_qt: creates a FIFO to act as a virtual MIDI port when no native virtual port is available. Described as the simplest approach.
Links the FIFO into /dev so applications expecting an OSS sequencer device can find it. Paired with the mkfifo line above.
Loads the Linux kernel module that creates virtual raw MIDI ports; the README says it creates 4 by default, bound to ALSA sequencer ports.

brief.install_notes: Building needs CMake and the Qt framework (the README says Qt major versions 4 to 6 are supported, selectable with mt32emu-qt_WITH_QT_VERSION), plus the mt32emu library, which mt32emu_qt can be built within the monorepo. Other dependencies depend on platform: PortAudio, the DirectX SDK (Windows, for DirectSound and WDMKS), PulseAudio, and JACK. Build options such as mt32emu-qt_USE_JACK_DYNAMIC_LOADING, mt32emu-qt_WITH_ALSA_MIDI_SEQUENCER and CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE are set on the cmake command line, in CMakeCache.txt, or via the CMake GUI. On Windows, the README suggests the CMake GUI. The READMEs I read do not say where the Roland control and PCM ROM images come from, though mt32emu_qt has a GUI to 'manage ROMs'. Expect to supply them yourself. Virtual MIDI setup varies by OS: CoreMIDI and ALSA create ports automatically on startup, while Windows needs the bundled MME driver installed.
brief.standout: The MT-32 LCD is emulated, and mt32emu_qt shows the synth's internal state live. Its MIDI support is broad: several MIDI systems, including a JACK mode where one client acts as a full synth with no added latency. The core is a library that others can embed, not only a standalone app.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as I can tell. The README copyright lines run to 2011-2026, and the project has a Windows driver, a FreeBSD port directory and a Qt 6 target. I could not see a release date or last-commit date on the pages I fetched, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: The README says the emulation is approximate. It needs a real-time-capable CPU; its suggested minimum is an 800 MHz Pentium III with 8 MB RAM for one synth. Compiler optimisations are off unless you set Release. The ALSA/OSS raw MIDI support is described as very basic, and the Linux ALSA GUI (mt32emu_alsadrv) is called mostly obsolete in favour of mt32emu_qt. The JACK exclusive-mode synth cannot be pinned, so no extra MIDI sessions can be routed into it. The DOSBox patch targets DOSBox 0.74 and is aimed at developers. Roland is a trademark, and the README includes a trademark disclaimer. The project is GPL-3.0 for the application and LGPL-2.1 for the library.

name: mummer
desc: Genome alignment tool
why: Genome alignment suite using suffix trees, real bioinformatics you can run on sequences at home.

brief.what_it_is: MUMmer is a command-line suite for aligning whole genomes and other DNA or protein sequence sets. Its core program, mummer, finds exact maximal matches between a reference FASTA file and one or more query FASTA files. The main entry points, nucmer and promer, build alignments on top of those matches and write a .delta file. A set of show-* tools (show-coords, show-snps, show-aligns, show-tiling, show-diff) and helpers (delta-filter, dnadiff, mummerplot) then parse that output into coordinates, SNP lists, breakpoint classifications, statistics, or plots. Inputs are FASTA; outputs are plain text tables, delta files, and optionally gnuplot or PNG images.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames MUMmer as a system for rapidly aligning entire genomes, noting that version 4 finds all 20 bp maximal exact matches between two bacterial genomes of about 5 Mbp each in 20 seconds using 90 MB of memory. It also positions the tool for draft assemblies, which may contain hundreds or thousands of contigs, and for comparing divergent genomes at the protein level via promer.
brief.how_it_works: mummer uses a suffix-tree based match-finding routine to find maximal matches. nucmer aligns nucleotide sequences all-vs-all and by default keeps only matches unique in the reference, with --mum or --maxmatch to change that. promer translates both inputs in all six reading frames and aligns them the same way, with delta integers measured in amino acids (1 delta int = 3 nucleotides). delta-filter applies a longest-increasing-subset calculation to keep a 1-to-1 or mutually consistent set of alignments.

commands_seen.context: Basic nucmer run from the README 'Simple use case'; writes <prefix>.delta with alignments between the reference and query.
Lists nucmer's options; the README points here for parameter details.

Usage for finding exact tandem repeats in a single FASTA sequence; post-processes repeat-match output.

Usage line for the filter that keeps the best alignments from a nucmer or promer delta file; -1 and -m are the recommended modes depending on the task.

Upstream recommends a release tarball; building from the git tree also needs autoconf, automake, libtool, gettext, and yaggo. Only GCC is supported. On macOS, the README says not to use Clang or Apple's gcc, and to compile with gcc-14 (CC=gcc-14 CXX=g++-14). On FreeBSD, use gmake and gcc14. Ubuntu needs build-essential. name: nak
desc: CLI for doing all things nostr
why: A nostr swiss army knife that lets you poke at relays and events, a door into a decentralized protocol few have touched.

brief.what_it_is: nak is a command-line tool, written in Go, that does a wide range of things with the Nostr protocol. It takes Nostr keys, event JSON, NIP-19 codes like npub, note1, nevent1 and naddr1, and relay URLs as input, and prints JSON events, decoded or encoded identifiers, profile details, verification results, and relay responses to stdout. Many subcommands also publish events to relays, serve a local relay, run a remote-signing bunker, mount a FUSE filesystem, or move files through Blossom servers.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a 'nostr army knife' for 'doing all things nostr' from the terminal, and says to read the built-in help text to discover everything it can do. The README gives no longer statement of motive.
brief.how_it_works: Each subcommand is a verb (event, req, fetch, decode, encode, key, profile, verify, bunker, serve, fs, blossom, gift, sync, admin). Output is line-delimited JSON, so it pipes into jq and into other nak subcommands; the README chains them, for example nak req ... | nak event relay1 relay2 to republish an event. Built-in jq helpers are available via --jq and a ~/.jq file, and the README points to jq.go for the function definitions.

The input is a graph or digraph, and the output is its automorphism group or a canonical form. The package bundles gtools, a suite of about fifty command-line tools (listed in the executables field) for generating graphs (geng, genbg, gentreeg and others), manipulating them (addedgeg, deledgeg, complg, linegraphg), and converting between formats. name: nacl
desc: Network communication, encryption, decryption, signatures library
why: The NaCl crypto library is the basis of many modern protocols and a good door into how modern public-key primitives are assembled.

brief.what_it_is: NaCl (pronounced "salt") is a C and C++ software library for network communication, encryption, decryption, signatures and related core cryptographic operations. The caller hands it plaintext or messages plus keys, in the form of byte strings, and gets back ciphertext, authentication tags, signatures or hashes, also as byte strings. Its public-key section covers authenticated encryption, scalar multiplication and signatures. Its secret-key section covers authenticated encryption, encryption, authentication and one-time authentication. Its low-level section covers hashing and string comparison. The homepage describes the Python wrappers as prototypes and the Python API as a future priority, not a shipped feature.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the goal is "to provide all of the core operations needed to build higher-level cryptographic tools" and that it improves on existing libraries "by improving security, by improving usability, and by improving speed." The features page argues that typical libraries force programmers to pick primitives and modes, and that NaCl lets the programmer "simply say 'sign this message.'"
brief.how_it_works: NaCl ships a preselected set of modern primitives, so callers do not choose algorithms. A single crypto_box call handles the whole sequence of key handling, encryption and authentication, which the features page contrasts with a multi-step RSA/AES/SHA-256 pipeline. The library compiles every implementation of each function with each compiler option, then times them on the build machine and picks the fastest for that CPU. The docs also say the code avoids secret-dependent branches and secret-dependent array indices, to resist timing and cache attacks.

commands_seen.context: Download step from the installation page, using the 2011 release tarball.
Unpacks the downloaded tarball from stdin.
Changes into the unpacked source directory.
The build script. It compiles NaCl for every ABI and compiler it detects and writes the libraries and headers into a host-specific build/ subdirectory.

brief.install_notes: The installation page says NaCl works on a wide variety of UNIX-like systems, including Linux, BSD and Solaris. It is built from source rather than a package, using the wget, unpack and ./do steps above. The build writes to build/<hostname>, so several machines can share one filesystem and build at once. On multi-ABI machines it produces both 32-bit and 64-bit libraries, plus helper programs bin/okabi and bin/okc-amd64 that list supported ABIs and compilers. The page says system-wide install (headers and -lnacl) is still a TO DO. The recommended route is to copy the NaCl source into your application and let it choose the fastest ABI and compiler itself. Homebrew's 'nacl' formula is not mentioned in the sources I read, and the Homebrew metadata lists no executables.
brief.standout: Instead of hard-coding CPU detection, NaCl builds every implementation and picks the fastest by measuring on the target machine, so new CPUs get the best code without a library update. The one-call crypto_box API, which fixes the primitives and the wire format, is also distinctive compared with the usual pick-your-algorithm libraries.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage is stamped 'version 2016.03.15' and its 'Upcoming features' section lists PIC support, Ed25519 and NEON optimizations as next-release items. The features page is stamped 2011.02.20 and the example tarball is nacl-20110221. I did not see a release log or commit history, so I cannot give a last-release date beyond these page stamps.
brief.caveats: The site's own text says the current version supports C and C++ and that Python support is a 'high priority,' so there is no mature Python binding from the project itself. Multi-ABI system installation is still a TO DO in the installation docs. C NaCl functions return error codes that callers must check, and the docs warn that a caller who ignores them will 'blithely proceed as if the signatures were valid.' The no-malloc guarantee applies only to C NaCl, not Python. The project is in the public domain, so no licence restrictions apply. The homepage and install pages are old and the Ed25519 and PIC items listed as upcoming are from 2016, so check the current state before relying on any of it.
quotes: NaCl (pronounced "salt") is a new easy-to-use high-speed software library for network communication, encryption, decryption, signatures, etc.

name: ndpi
desc: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) library
why: Deep packet inspection library that identifies protocols from raw traffic, a useful door into how networks get classified.

brief.what_it_is: nDPI is an open source C library for deep packet inspection that identifies the application-layer protocol behind network traffic. It takes raw packets or flows and reports the protocol (the README cites 450+ protocols), a traffic category, flow risks, and metadata such as URLs, TLS certificates, and operating system. It is built as a library to embed in other tools, and it ships a C API. The README also says it is used in ntop's own tools (ntopng, nProbe, nProbe Cento) and in third-party applications.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says nDPI extends the original OpenDPI library by adding protocols that were otherwise available only in OpenDPI's paid version, under the LGPL. It also says the port-to-application mapping no longer holds, so detection has to look at the traffic itself.
brief.how_it_works: nDPI inspects packet payloads and flow behaviour to decide which application protocol a flow belongs to, regardless of the port used. Dissectors are added per protocol under src/lib/protocols/, and the README says configuration files can extend detection by host, BPF, protocol, or port. The homepage also describes ETA (Encrypted Traffic Analysis) for classifying TLS and QUIC traffic, and FPC (First Packet Classification).

brief.install_notes: Build from source: the README gives ./autogen.sh && ./configure then make. Required GNU tools are autoconf, automake, libtool, pkg-config, gettext, flex, and bison, plus gcc or clang. On Windows there are three routes: MSYS2, Mingw-w64, or Visual Studio (windows/nDPI.sln), and all need npcap with WinPcap compatibility mode enabled. Unit tests need nBPF from PF_RING plus PCRE2 for full coverage. The README does not describe what ndpiReader or ndpiSimpleIntegration do; I did not find them documented in the pages I read.
brief.standout: Unlike most DPI tools, nDPI is meant to be embedded: it is a library, not a sniffer, and the README says ntop removed features that slow the engine down for monitoring use. It also goes beyond naming the protocol: it extracts metadata, detects flow risks, and classifies encrypted TLS and QUIC traffic through ETA.

Connectivity is stored as an adjacency list rather than a weight matrix, so any two neurons can have several connections with different properties. You can inspect and modify the state of each neuron and connection during a run, and devices write their data to memory or to file.

brief.what_it_is: Net-SNMP is a suite of command-line tools, a graphical MIB browser, a trap receiver daemon, an extensible SNMP agent daemon, and a C and Perl library for building SNMP applications. name: netcode
desc: Secure client/server protocol for multiplayer games built on top of UDP
why: A secure UDP protocol for multiplayer games, an interesting look at connection handshakes and encryption design.

brief.what_it_is: netcode is a C library implementing a secure client/server connection protocol that runs on top of UDP. Your game code hands it a 32 byte private key and a server address, creates a server with a fixed number of client slots, and then your backend issues connect tokens that clients present to connect. Once connected, clients and server exchange unreliable, unordered packets that are encrypted and signed. The README lists it as a library with no executables, so nothing is installed as a command.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says real-time multiplayer games use UDP instead of TCP because TCP's head-of-line blocking delays newer packets while older dropped packets are resent, but UDP has no notion of a connection, so developers must build connection handling themselves, which the author calls 'a lot of work!'. netcode provides a minimal, secure, connection-oriented layer so developers can start exchanging packets sooner.
brief.how_it_works: A backend (for example a web matchmaker) issues a connect token to each authorized client, and only clients holding a valid token can connect. The server is created with the shared private key and a max_connect_token_lifetime, which it uses to refuse tokens that could have been issued before it started. Packets are encrypted and signed using libsodium, and the server assigns each connected client to one of its n slots, denying new clients quickly when all slots are full.

commands_seen.context: A test private key shown in the README as a C array of 32 bytes. The README warns to generate a random key and never ship the private key inside a client executable.

Sets the longest connect token lifetime in seconds, which must match what the backend issues.

Starts the server with 16 client slots.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no package-manager or build instructions. It is a C codebase and you use it from source; the code is in client.c and server.c, which the README links to. Cryptography depends on the libsodium library, which the README links to but does not explicitly describe as a build dependency. Using it in a real game also needs a backend that issues connect tokens; the README points to an example matchmaker written in Go in the yojimbo repo. You must generate your own random 32 byte private key, and keep it off the client.
brief.standout: The connection design puts trust in the backend: a server accepts only clients holding tokens the backend issued with the shared key, so matchmaking and access control live in a web service rather than in the game server. The README also documents a replay-protection overflow and errata in IMPLEMENTERS.md, and many ports exist in other languages (C#, Go, Rust, Unity, UE4, TypeScript).
brief.status: unknown. The README has a CI badge pointing at a GitHub Actions workflow on main, but it shows no release dates, version numbers, last commit, or maintenance notes. It does reference a 'netcode 1.02 standard' document and multiple third-party implementations.
brief.caveats: The README does not state supported platforms, build steps, or a version. The test private key is for testing only. The BSD 3-Clause license asks for credit in product credits ('netcode - Glenn Fiedler and Rowan Claude'), and the README says this is a request, not a license requirement. The README pushes support via a Patreon page.

name: netpbm
desc: Image manipulation
why: Old-school Unix image filters that treat pictures as plain text pipelines, a classic toolkit well worth knowing.

brief.what_it_is: Netpbm is a toolkit of command-line image tools, with over 350 separate programs, including converters for about 100 graphics formats. Its homepage gives examples such as shrinking an image by 10%, cutting the top half off an image, making a mirror image, and creating a sequence of images that fade from one image to another. The homepage does not describe the tools as shell pipelines, though the programs are small single-purpose filters.
brief.why_it_exists: The stated goal is to be a single source for all the primitive graphics utilities, especially converters, one might need. The history section says Netpbm replaced the widely spread Pbmplus package (last released December 10, 1991) and collected the many filters that circulated on the net after it, hence the name.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal mechanism in detail. It does say the programs are useful from a typed shell command but are mostly oriented toward being used internally by other programs. It also says the -version option on most programs reports the release in use.

Building needs about 9 MiB of disk space, plus 4 MiB for documentation, which is optional because a public copy is online. Build steps are in doc/INSTALL in the source tree. name: nexttrace
desc: Open source visual route tracking CLI tool
why: Visual traceroute with rich route mapping; a close call since traceroute itself is a known door but this one adds geography.

brief.what_it_is: NextTrace is an open source, Go-based command-line route tracer. You give it an IP address, hostname, or URL, and it sends ICMP probes by default (TCP or UDP optional) and lists each hop along the path. Each hop is annotated with geographic and network-owner information, and a map of the route can be drawn from the per-hop coordinates; the README prints a MapTrace link for this. Output can be terminal text, a table, pipe-delimited RAW lines, or JSON. The full build also bundles MTR-style continuous probing, path-MTU discovery, a standalone DNS client, a CDN speed test, and IP annotation for text streams.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a light-weight, visual routing tool: "An open source visual routing tool that pursues light weight, developed using Golang." The visual, geography-aware view of a traceroute is the main idea, and the project is run by the nxtrace organisation, which also provides its API and the network infrastructure it runs on.
brief.how_it_works: By default it runs a normal traceroute over ICMP, supporting IPv4 and IPv6, and reports why the trace stopped. Geographic data for each hop comes from the NextTrace API, IPInfo, or IP-API.com, and the map is a separate component at nxtrace/traceMap. On Linux, the README says route queries use netlink, macOS uses routing sockets, and Windows uses GetBestRoute2. Three build flavors exist (nexttrace full, nexttrace-tiny, ntr MTR-only) that use compile-time build tags to exclude modules.

name: ngspice
desc: Spice circuit simulator
why: A real SPICE circuit simulator lets you build and watch analog circuits run on your own machine.

brief.what_it_is: ngspice is an open source SPICE circuit simulator for electric and electronic circuits. You describe a circuit as a netlist, either as a text file or typed on the command line, and it simulates analog circuits built from transistors (JFET, bipolar, MOS), passive R, L, C elements, diodes, and transmission lines. It also simulates digital circuits, from single gates up to complex ones, and mixed analog/digital circuits. The output is one or more graphs of currents, voltages and other quantities, or a data file.
brief.why_it_exists: The site presents it as a free, SPICE-compatible simulator: newcomers are invited to try it, and professionals are promised robustness and flexibility. It can read PSPICE and LTSPICE model parameters and netlists, and HSPICE libraries from semiconductor foundry PDKs.
brief.how_it_works: The user writes a netlist of circuit elements and device models, and ngspice reads it, preprocesses it (compatibility, subcircuits, parameters), builds the circuit structure, sets up and solves the matrix, and runs the simulation. Device models come from its own collections, from semiconductor manufacturers, or from foundries. The homepage explicitly does not offer schematic entry; input is command line or file based, and third-party interfaces exist.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says ngspice builds on many operating systems: Windows source and binaries are on the SourceForge download page, and Linux distributions, Cygwin, FreeBSD and Homebrew for macOS also offer it. From the Homebrew metadata supplied with the request (not from the fetched pages): if you need the graphical plotting functions, install X11 with brew install --cask xquartz. No runtime or account is mentioned on the pages I fetched.
brief.standout: It is a long-running open source SPICE that accepts PSPICE, LTSPICE and HSPICE model files, including foundry PDK libraries, so it can run circuits written for commercial tools. Its digital and mixed-signal event-driven simulation is also built in, which is less common in free SPICE tools.

name: ngrep
desc: Network grep
why: Greps live network traffic by pattern, a direct window into the packets your machine sends and receives all day.

brief.what_it_is: ngrep is a command-line packet sniffer that works like GNU grep applied to network traffic. You give it a regular expression (or a hexadecimal pattern with -X) and an optional BPF filter, and it captures live packets through libpcap or reads a saved pcap file. It prints the packets whose payloads match, with source and destination addresses, and it can also write matched traffic to a dump file with -O. It understands IPv4/6, TCP, UDP, ICMPv4/6, IGMP and raw packets.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says ngrep was originally built to debug plaintext protocols such as HTTP, IMAP, DNS and SIP, to analyze suspicious traffic such as malware communications, and to search and reprocess pcap dump files for specific data patterns. The README also notes it could be used to collect plaintext credentials, and adds that 'Like all useful tools, it can be used for good and for bad.'
brief.how_it_works: It uses libpcap to capture packets from one or more interfaces, and BPF filter syntax (the same kind tcpdump uses) to limit what is captured. Each packet payload is then matched against the given extended regex or hex expression, and matches are printed with addresses and flags. The README says PCRE2 is the default on macOS/Homebrew and Windows builds, while GNU regex is the other option.

name: nickel
desc: Better configuration for less
why: A configuration language with contracts and lazy evaluation, a genuinely different take on generating config.

brief.what_it_is: Nickel is a configuration language, described by its authors as "the universal configuration language." It is a small programming language meant to generate static configuration files such as JSON, YAML, or TOML, which another system then consumes. You write modular blocks of records and functions, merge them into one configuration, and export the result with the nickel export command. The README describes the core as "in essence JSON with functions." It is lazily evaluated, has optional gradual static typing, and uses contracts as schemas for validation.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the purpose is to automate generation of static configuration files, "configuration templating, but done right." It positions Nickel as an evolution of the Nix language that overcomes some of Nix's limitations, aimed at complex config for apps, machines, infrastructure, and build systems.
brief.how_it_works: Records (JSON objects) are composed with a merge operator, which also combines metadata such as docs, defaults, and type contracts. Functions are first-class. Static types are opt-in via a sound gradual type system, so you can statically check functions but use runtime validation for data. Contracts act as schemas; you enforce correctness by adding type-like annotations to data.

Without Nix, building from source needs Rust and Cargo, via cargo build -p nickel-lang-cli --release. Nix users can enter a dev shell with nix-shell or nix develop, and a Tweag Cachix binary cache (tweag-nickel.cachix.org) avoids rebuilding packages. Editor support is optional: Vim/Neovim, Emacs, and VSCode plugins exist, plus a Nickel Language Server (NLS) for diagnostics, type hints, completion, and formatting, set up via the LSP guide in the repo.
brief.standout: Its pitch is a middle path: lazy, Turing-complete, and functional like Nix, but with optional static typing and contracts for schemas, so you only annotate what needs checking. The README's comparison table lays this out against CUE, Dhall, Jsonnet, KCL, and Starlark, and it is explicitly built to be embeddable in other languages.

name: nickle
desc: Desk calculator language
why: A C-like desk calculator language with arbitrary precision and a real interpreter is a delightful, underused little language.

brief.what_it_is: Nickle is a programming language and prototyping environment that vaguely resembles C. It handles arbitrary precision integers, arbitrary precision rationals, and unbounded floating-point reals with specifiable precision, alongside arrays, strings, structures, tagged unions, and pointers. The homepage says it provides the functionality of UNIX bc, dc and expr in improved form, and can serve as a scripting tool or a replacement for spreadsheets in some uses. The homepage does not say what the input and output formats are beyond this.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Nickle as a language-based prototyping environment for numeric work, meant to go beyond bc, dc and expr and to complement the limited numeric support of AWK and Perl.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes optional static type checking backed by full run-time type checking, and a simple thread model with semaphores and mutexes. It also mentions typed exceptions, first-class functions, and continuations, drawn from Modula 3, ML and Java. It does not explain the interpreter's internals on this page.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says the current version is normally in Debian unstable: run 'apt-get update' then 'apt-get install nickle'. Release builds are also offered as .deb, .rpm and .tar.gz from a release directory, and the git master is described as canonical. Nightly snapshots are built each morning when git has changed. The homepage gives no Homebrew-specific notes, and it does not describe first-run configuration.

It can load workspaces saved by its predecessor nip2, and it has a batch mode that runs an image processing system from the command line without the GUI. brief.how_it_works: nip4 is purely functional, so there is no assignment and no side effects. It is fully lazy, which means all computation is driven by the user interface, down to the pixel level. Recalculation happens when a connected input changes.

name: nmrpflash
desc: Netgear Unbrick Utility
why: Talks the NMRP recovery protocol to rescue bricked Netgear routers, a hidden bootloader door you can actually walk through.

brief.what_it_is: nmrpflash is a command-line utility that pushes a firmware image onto a Netgear router over Ethernet using Netgear's NMRP recovery protocol, which the device's bootloader listens for. You give it a network interface connected directly to the router and a firmware file (typically .chk, .bin, .trx or .img, extracted from the Netgear download zip). It advertises an NMRP server, assigns the router a temporary IP, uploads the image via TFTP, and then reports when it is safe to reboot. It runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, the BSDs and other POSIX systems.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to recover Netgear devices that have been bricked, using Netgear's NMRP protocol to flash a new firmware image to a compatible device. Its title is 'Netgear Unbrick Utility'.
brief.how_it_works: After you start nmrpflash on a chosen interface and then power on the router, the tool advertises an NMRP server on that link and answers the router's configuration request by assigning it an IP (default 10.164.183.252, with the host side at 10.164.183.253). It then receives the router's upload request and sends the firmware over TFTP, printing progress and keep-alive messages. Once the transfer finishes, the router may spend many minutes writing to flash, and the tool prints 'Reboot your device now.' only when the process is done.

commands_seen.context: Lists the network interfaces on the machine so you can find the one wired to the router.

Example invocation: waits on interface eth2 for the router to appear, then uploads the given firmware file. Turn the router off first, then power it on when the 'Waiting for Ethernet connection' message appears.
Installs the runtime libraries on Debian-based distros (such as Ubuntu) so the Linux binary will start.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the README's preferred route on Linux and macOS. On Windows you need Npcap installed with the 'WinPcap Compatibility' option enabled, and prebuilt binaries are on the GitHub releases page. A FreeBSD package exists in the ports tree. On Linux you need libpcap and libnl-3 at runtime. Building from source on Windows uses the included CodeBlocks project file (nmrpflash.cbp) and requires the Npcap SDK extracted into an Npcap folder in the source root. Before flashing, you extract the firmware from the Netgear zip, and you connect the router to the computer with an Ethernet cable on the LAN port labeled 1 (often blue).
brief.standout: It turns a router's built-in recovery mode into a scripted, cross-platform push: the tool impersonates the recovery server, assigns addresses on both ends, and walks you through the power-on timing. The README is unusually practical, with a long troubleshooting section that explains each error message and what to do about it.
brief.status: maintained. The GitHub releases page shows nmrpflash 0.9.27 as Latest, dated '05 Mar' (the year was not visible in the fetched text), and reports 4 commits to master since that release. The README also lists a FreeBSD port and a Homebrew formula.
brief.caveats: Tested on a specific list of models (D7000, DC112A, DNG3700v2, EX2700, R7000, RAX75, WNDR3800 and others), and the README says other Netgear devices are only 'likely' to work. Some devices need the reset button held while powering on. Flashing can take 15 minutes or more, and the router must not be rebooted until the tool says so. TFTP uploads are limited to about 32 MiB, so larger images may fail. Windows needs Npcap, and version 0.9.13 was the last to support Windows XP. macOS Gatekeeper may block the binary. The README notes that the bootloader itself may be bricked or the device may not support NMRP at all. The README says nothing about risks from flashing the wrong image.

name: norm
desc: NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast
why: NACK-oriented reliable multicast is an obscure transport protocol, and this is a real implementation to explore.

brief.what_it_is: NORM (NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast) is a reliable multicast transport protocol from the US Naval Research Laboratory, shipped as a source release. The repo builds libnorm, a static C library with a NORM API (normApi.h) for Unix and a Norm.lib for Win32, plus a command-line demo app called norm, a simple normTest playground, and API examples. The norm demo is for file transfers, and for streaming on Unix. The README also describes a NORP proxy in a norp directory, and two NRL apps built on NORM: a GUI multicast chat with file and image sharing, and a tunnel for real-time UDP streams such as RTP. The README does not spell out the input and output formats in detail.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a problem statement. It presents NORM as a reliable multicast protocol and the NRL source release that goes with it. The name says the design is NACK-oriented, meaning receivers ask for missing data rather than the sender acknowledging every packet, but the README does not expand on the reasoning.

The build depends on the protolib library, a separate NRL repo at github.com/USNavalResearchLaboratory/protolib, which is a git submodule, so the clone needs --recurse-submodules or a later git submodule update --init. Docker is an option: the Dockerfile defaults to the ubuntu base image, latest tag, and version v1.5.9. No accounts or hardware are mentioned. The README gives no more first-run steps.
brief.standout: It is an NRL-built transport protocol with a real C API, a demo CLI, and a Docker path, and the README mentions a chat app that needs no server, like IRC but for multicast. The NACK-oriented name points to a different design from the usual acknowledgment-based reliable transports.

name: notcurses
desc: Blingful character graphics/TUI library
why: A character graphics library that pushes terminals to render images, video, and effects far beyond normal expectations.

brief.what_it_is: Notcurses is a C library, with C++-safe headers and Rust, C++, and Python wrappers, for building text user interfaces on modern terminal emulators. Programs draw into stacked rectangular planes (ncplane objects) using 24-bit color, Unicode, and transparency, and the library renders the composed result to the terminal, quantizing color for limited terminals. It can show still images and video, decoded through ffmpeg or OpenImageIO, using character blitters or pixel protocols such as Sixel and Kitty. It installs nine small tools, including ncls (an ls that displays media), ncplayer, notcurses-demo, and nctetris. It is not an X/Open Curses implementation and not a drop-in ncurses replacement.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says Curses assumes the minimum and lets you step up with effort, whereas Notcurses assumes the maximum and steps down by itself when necessary. The stated goal is vivid color, multimedia, thread safety, and full Unicode in terminal apps that ncurses was not designed for.
brief.how_it_works: Each screen cell is resolved by descending the plane stack from the topmost plane until a glyph and foreground/background colors are locked in, then the resulting frame is blitted to the terminal as UTF-8 characters and escape codes. Each plane cell has two alpha bits per color channel (opaque, blend, transparent, or high-contrast) that control how lower planes show through, and glyph choice is independent of alpha. Terminal capabilities come from terminfo plus queries the library sends to the terminal at startup.

commands_seen.context: Runs the demo program, which the README says covers most of the library's functionality. From a source checkout it needs the data directory passed with -p, and -d scales the delay.
From the dankwiki performance section: a benchmark run of ncplayer with the pixel blitter on a sample video, used to time different terminal emulators.
Runs the test suite from a source checkout, which runs notcurses-tester; that needs the data directory via -p.
Diagnostic tool that prints terminal capabilities and lets you inspect how your font renders the drawing characters.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the path in this brief. Building from source needs CMake 3.21+ and a C17 compiler, plus terminfo 6.1+ from NCURSES and GNU libunistring 0.9.10+. Optional extras are libgpm, libqrcodegen, FFmpeg libraries, OpenImageIO 2.15+ (requires C++), doctest, and pandoc. Supported runtimes are Linux 2.6+, FreeBSD 11+, DragonFly BSD 5.9+, Windows 10 1093+, and macOS 11.4+. At runtime, TERM must match your terminal and have an up-to-date terminfo entry, or Notcurses refuses to start. LANG should be a generated UTF-8 locale. Optionally set COLORTERM to truecolor or 24bit when the terminal supports 24-bit color but does not advertise it. Docker users are directed to the README's Environment notes section.
brief.standout: It treats pixel graphics as a first-class part of a text UI: one API covers Sixel, the Kitty graphics protocol, and the Linux framebuffer, with several cell-based blitters as fallbacks. Its plane model adds z-order, per-channel alpha, and sprites to a character grid, which is unusual for terminal libraries.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub README I fetched has no release date or commit date. I did not check the releases or commit history, so I cannot confirm recent activity. The repository has CI badges for Linux, macOS, and Windows.
brief.caveats: Not a drop-in replacement for ncurses, and it expects a current terminfo database and UTF-8 locale. Output quality depends on the terminal and font: the README says Windows Terminal needs particular fonts and settings, and screen and mosh render poorly. The Linux console supports only a limited glyph set. Some features need optional dependencies, and the full multimedia stack is heavy. Direct Mode is substantially slower and less capable than rendered mode. The dankwiki benchmarks date from 2019 and 2021. The README says the tool list includes notcurses-tester, which the Homebrew executables list omits. Source is Apache-2.0.

name: nkf
desc: Network Kanji code conversion Filter (NKF)
why: Network Kanji filter converts between Japanese encodings like ISO-2022-JP and Shift_JIS, a sliver of computing history worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: nkf (Network Kanji Filter) is a command-line filter that converts Japanese text between character encodings. It reads text from files or standard input and writes it out in a designated encoding such as ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32. It can also convert line endings, convert half-width and full-width kana and alphabet forms, and decode or encode MIME, base64, quoted-printable, URL, hex and HTML numeric character references. The README's own description is: "Nkf is a yet another kanji code converter among networks, hosts and terminals."
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a converter for moving Japanese text between networks, hosts and terminals that each use different kanji codes. Its distinguishing idea is that users do not have to say what the input encoding is.
brief.how_it_works: Input encoding is guessed automatically. The README says it recognizes ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32, so users needn't set the input kanji code explicitly. By default half-width (X0201) katakana is converted to full-width (X0208) kana, and for automatic detection nkf assumes there is no X0201 kana in Shift_JIS. Options such as -X, -x or -S change that assumption.

brief.standout: Automatic input-encoding detection across several Japanese encodings and Unicode forms means the caller never has to declare the source. It is a small, single-purpose filter in the Unix tradition, and the README's history (a 1987 Fujitsu original, later extended by The nkf Project) is part of its appeal.
brief.status: unknown. The README is a man-page-style document with no release date, version number, or recent-change note. The copyright line runs to 1996-2012, which suggests the text has not been revised for a long time. I did not check the commit history or releases page.

name: nqp
desc: Lightweight Raku-like environment for virtual machines
why: A stripped-down Raku-flavoured language built to target virtual machines, a rare and interesting language-implementation artifact.

brief.what_it_is: NQP ("Not Quite Perl") is a small, Raku-flavoured language and runtime environment for building compilers and libraries on virtual machines. It takes NQP source files (such as hello.nqp) and runs them on one of three backends: MoarVM, the JVM, or JavaScript (the JVM and JavaScript backends are experimental). It is not a general-purpose Raku implementation. It provides a Raku object model and a regular expression engine with as small a runtime footprint as possible. Running `nqp` with no script starts a small interactive mode.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says NQP is designed to be a very small environment compared with Raku or Rakudo, focused on being a high-level way to create compilers and libraries for virtual machines like MoarVM and the JVM. It is a tool for writing Raku compilers, not a low-level module for Raku programmers.
brief.how_it_works: NQP is built with a Perl Configure.pl script followed by make, which produces an nqp executable. Configure.pl takes --backends to choose targets and either --with-moar to point at an existing MoarVM or --gen-moar to have MoarVM downloaded and built. The README gives no further internal detail on how the compiler or object model is implemented.

brief.install_notes: Needs a make utility and Perl 5.8 or newer. A git client is needed if MoarVM is to be fetched automatically. The JVM backend requires JDK 9 or higher. The JavaScript backend requires node.js 10.10.0 or newer and a build of the moar backend. The README says make install puts NQP into the same location as the MoarVM installation used to build it, and that the executable only runs reliably from the build root until that step is done. Default MoarVM lookup and install goes to ./install unless --prefix is given. The README mentions an OS X workaround for a missing mach/mach.h header during configuration. The README does not mention an nqp-m executable, which Homebrew lists alongside nqp.
brief.standout: It is a deliberately tiny language runtime whose purpose is to build other language implementations. It carries a Raku object model and regex engine without the weight of Rakudo, and it targets several VMs from one source language.
brief.status: maintained. The repository has about 13,060 commits, GitHub Actions workflows and an azure-pipelines.yml, and the README copyright runs to 2026. I did not check the VERSION file or the release dates, so the most recent release date is unknown.
brief.caveats: The README says there is no end-user support and that behaviour can change without notice. The JVM and JavaScript backends are experimental. Configuration on OS X can fail with a missing mach/mach.h header. The JVM may report it cannot reserve enough memory. The JavaScript backend has few docs, and the README points users to the pmurias contact on IRC. The Homebrew executable nqp-m is not described in the README. The README does not state a licence, but it says the LICENSE file governs and the copyright belongs to The Raku Foundation.

The key feature of NQP is that it's designed to be a very small environment (as compared with, say, raku or Rakudo)

name: noweb
desc: WEB-like literate-programming tool
why: Norman Ramsey's literate-programming tool is a small, old, language-agnostic weave-and-tangle design worth an afternoon of curiosity.

brief.what_it_is: noweb is a literate-programming tool in the WEB family: you write one source file that mixes prose and named code chunks, and it produces two outputs. The weave side formats the document for reading (TeX, LaTeX, HTML, or troff back ends). The tangle side extracts the code in compilable order. The homepage says it works with any programming language and uses only 5 control sequences, against WEB's 27. The brew package installs a set of small command-line executables (notangle, noweave, noroots, noindex and others) for these jobs.
brief.why_it_exists: Norman Ramsey built noweb to keep literate programming simple and extensible, and largely language-independent. He says WEB's pretty-printing is the main thing he dropped on purpose, because he finds it distracting while editing and too costly to build per language.
brief.how_it_works: Code is organised into named chunks, written as <<name>> references, and the tangle step expands them into source code. The weave step produces formatted documentation from the same file. The homepage says the design is extensible: new back ends are small (a simpler one can be written in 40 lines of awk, a fuller one in about 250 lines), and customisation can happen without recompiling. Prettyprinting is done by optional filters rather than by the core tool.
brief.install_notes: The brew caveat says TeX support files are installed under $HOMEBREW_CELLAR/noweb/2.13/tex/generic/noweb and may need to be added to TEXINPUTS before noweb's LaTeX output will run. The homepage gives no other setup steps. It mentions Debian packages, CTAN, an RPM attempt, and Jim Pettigrew's Windows 7 instructions using mingw, but none of these is needed on macOS with brew.
brief.standout: The design is deliberately minimal and language-agnostic, and the project makes the case for that in print: the homepage argues for plain-ASCII source over prettyprinted fonts. It has been in use for about thirty-five years and is noted as having been used for tens of thousands of lines across many languages.
brief.status: Maintained, with some caveats. The homepage says the current supported version is 2.12 (28 June 2018), that it moved to GitHub in 2018, and that the copyright runs to 2024. Brew installs 2.13, which is newer than the version the page names, so the homepage may be somewhat behind. The author says Noweb 3 is effectively stuck in alpha and he doubts it will leave that stage, and he advises newcomers to use the 2.x line. I could not see a last-commit date from the homepage.
brief.caveats: The author recommends 2.x over the Noweb 3 alpha. Code is seldom prettyprinted by default. The homepage says no working Emacs mode for noweb existed for Emacs 23 or 24 as of 2012, though the distribution has shipped Thorsten Ohl's noweb-mode since 2.8a. Modified versions may not be called noweb without the author's consent. The TEXINPUTS step is needed for LaTeX output. The homepage describes Lua porting as something it deserves but that will not happen soon.
quotes: Literate programming is the art of preparing programs for human readers.
noweb uses 5 control sequences to WEB's 27.
noweb works "out of the box" with any programming language, and supports TeX, latex, HTML, and troff back ends.

name: ntfs2btrfs
desc: In-place conversion of NTFS filesystem to Btrfs
why: Converts a filesystem in place by reshaping its on-disk structures, a real and risky look inside storage formats.

brief.what_it_is: Ntfs2btrfs is a command-line tool that converts an NTFS filesystem to Btrfs in place, so the data is reshaped on the same disk rather than copied elsewhere. It takes an NTFS volume (a drive letter on Windows, or a device such as /dev/sda1 on Linux) and leaves a Btrfs filesystem in its place. The original image is kept as a reflink copy at image/ntfs.img, and you can delete it once you are happy with the conversion to free the space. The README says it is modelled on btrfs-convert, which does the same job for ext2.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as the NTFS counterpart to btrfs-convert for ext2, letting someone move a Windows-formatted disk to Btrfs without a full backup-and-restore cycle. It also points to the author's WinBtrfs driver for Windows as a related project.
brief.how_it_works: The tool rewrites NTFS on-disk structures into Btrfs structures in place, and the original image is preserved as a reflink copy at image/ntfs.img so the change can be rolled back to NTFS. The README credits Eric Biggers's reverse-engineering of Windows 10 'WOF compressed data' and says his code is reused here for that part. The README does not go into further detail on the mechanism.

commands_seen.context: Windows usage from an Administrator command prompt, converting the D: drive.
Linux usage run as root, converting the partition /dev/sda1.
Linux compilation step: create a build directory.
Linux compilation step: enter the build directory.
Linux compilation step: configure the build from the parent source directory.
Linux compilation step: build the ntfs2btrfs binary.

brief.install_notes: On Windows, download the latest Zip from the GitHub Releases page, or install via Winget or Scoop. On Linux, packages exist for Arch (AUR), Fedora, Gentoo (sys-fs/ntfs2btrfs in the guru repository), Debian, Ubuntu, and openSUSE; other systems need to compile it. Source build on Linux uses CMake, and the README says libfmt must be installed. However, the 20260810 changelog entry says the code now uses std::format and no longer needs libfmt, so the README's libfmt note may be out of date. The same entry says the code uses C++ modules and needs GCC 15, possibly 16. Compression support needs zlib, lzo, and/or zstd, and can be turned off with the CMake options WITH_ZLIB, WITH_LZO, and WITH_ZSTD. On Windows, build with MSVC by opening the source directory and compiling CMakeLists.txt. Running it requires root on Linux or an Administrator prompt on Windows.
brief.standout: It converts a live NTFS volume into Btrfs in place, keeps the original as a reflink so the conversion can be rolled back, and reuses reverse-engineered Windows WOF compression code. The README also says it can make a Windows boot drive run from Btrfs when paired with the separate Quibble project.
brief.status: Maintained, based on the changelog. The newest entry is dated 20260810 and the earlier ones run through 2025 and 2024, showing regular updates. I did not see commit or release-page dates, so this rests on the changelog alone.
brief.caveats: The author says 'I take no responsibility if something goes awry!' It will not work on a boot drive or on a drive with an active pagefile. Cluster sizes over 1MB are unsupported, encrypted files are unsupported, large ADSes over 16KB are unsupported, and the case-sensitivity flag is not preserved. name: numbat
desc: Statically typed programming language for scientific computations
why: A statically typed language with unit-checked scientific computation, a genuinely useful door into dimensional analysis as a type system.

brief.what_it_is: Numbat is a statically typed programming language and interactive calculator for scientific work, with physical dimensions and units built into its type system. You type expressions or small programs, and it checks that the units make sense, converts between compatible units with the -> operator, and prints the result. Running numbat with no arguments opens a REPL with history, Ctrl-R search and tab completion. The homepage describes it as a high precision scientific calculator with full support for physical units. The homepage itself is a JavaScript and WebAssembly shell, so the description here comes mainly from the GitHub README.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a language for scientific computations with first class support for physical dimensions and units, designed for quick one-off calculations. It explicitly positions itself as a calculator rather than a computer algebra system.
brief.how_it_works: Physical dimensions such as Length and Time act as static types, so annotated functions and constants are checked at compile time, and unannotated ones are inferred. The whole unit and dimension system lives in a standard library written in the Numbat language itself, so a single line such as unit bathtub = 150 L adds a new unit. Users can add their own definitions through an init.nbt file, or replace the prelude module entirely.

Nothing in the README suggests accounts, hardware or a runtime beyond that.
brief.standout: Units are first-class values, not strings: you can enter them many ways (km/h, kilometer/hour, m^2, m²), define new ones inline, and convert between compatible ones with ->. Because the standard library is itself written in Numbat, the unit system is ordinary editable code, and the static dimension checks happen before any calculation runs. That makes it a practical entry point into dimensional analysis as a type system.

name: nut
desc: Network UPS Tools: Support for various power devices
why: Network UPS Tools speaks to a surprising zoo of power hardware over serial and USB, a close call worth a second look.

brief.what_it_is: Network UPS Tools (NUT) is an open-source suite of programs for monitoring and managing power hardware: uninterruptible power supplies, power distribution units, automatic transfer switches, power supply units and solar controllers. Drivers read data from the attached device over serial, USB and other media, and a network server (upsd) publishes that data under one common set of variable names. Clients such as upsc query it, and upsmon watches it and can trigger a shutdown. The brew executables list names about 90 binaries, which is consistent with this split into drivers, server, and client tools, but I took that from the metadata, not from the site.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the primary goal is to provide support for power devices and to offer 'a common protocol and set of tools to monitor and manage such devices, and to consistently name equivalent features and data points, across a vast range of vendor-specific protocols and connection media types.'
brief.how_it_works: Per-device drivers (the executables list includes names such as usbhid-ups, dummy-ups and many vendor-specific ones) talk to the hardware and map its data onto NUT's standard variable names. The upsd network server serves that data to clients over TCP; the homepage's news links the IANA service registry entry for port 3493 and RFC 9271, the 'UPS management protocol' that the IETF published in 2022. The user manual's table of contents describes a layered, modular design with multiple processes, and upssched for scheduled actions.
brief.install_notes: The brew formula is the simplest route. The site's Download section and user manual also cover building from source (chapters 4.1 and 5.1), binary packages (4.3), and in-place upgrades. Configuration has a basic-setup chapter (6.2), a chapter on automatic shutdowns for low battery (6.3), and a securing-NUT chapter (10) that covers verifying source signatures and checksums. Hardware matters: the manual has a cable-reference appendix (G) for specific UPS models, so you need to know which driver and cable match your unit. I did not see any runtime or account requirements beyond that.
brief.standout: One project claims support for at least 201 manufacturers and 1441 device models under one naming scheme, far wider than most UPS tools. The IETF published its management protocol as an informational RFC (RFC 9271) in 2022, though the RFC is not formally an Internet Standard.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists NUT v2.8.5 released Apr 07, 2026, and a jNut 1.0 release on Apr 9, 2026 (followed by jNut 1.1 on Apr 10). The footer says the site was last updated 2026-10-18, and the news shows steady releases and CI work through 2025 and 2026.
brief.caveats: The homepage says the APC Modbus driver (apc_modbus) needs a libmodbus build with USB support, and that the upstream libmodbus lacks it, so a fork is in use. The Windows port was merged into main in 2022, but the site says more community work is needed for some drivers and the MSI packaging. A 2026 errata note says an early Windows archive was missing DLLs, so upsmon would not start. A 2025 errata says usbhid-ups ignored instant commands without arguments, which could break default shutdown. The homepage is a long news-heavy site, so the useful docs sit in the user manual. The license is GPL, as the homepage states.

name: nvc

brief.what_it_is: NVC is a free, open-source VHDL compiler and simulator that implements almost all of VHDL-2008 (IEEE 1076-2008). You give it VHDL source files and a top-level testbench entity name, and it analyses, elaborates and runs the simulation from the terminal. It uses LLVM to compile the design to native machine code. It is a simulator only and does not synthesize anything for an FPGA or ASIC. Waveforms can be viewed in GTKWave or Surfer.

brief.how_it_works: Simulation runs in three steps, which the README compares to compiling, linking and executing a software program: analysing the source files (-a), elaborating the design (-e), and running the simulation (-r). Because NVC uses LLVM to compile VHDL to native code, the simulated design runs as machine code. Vendor and verification libraries such as OSVVM, UVVM, Vivado and Quartus are installed with nvc --install <name>, into ~/.nvc/lib.

brief.how_it_works: Every IR instruction operates on a single memory tape of double-precision floats that serves as both stack and heap. Variables get fixed offsets relative to a per-function base pointer, and the compiler rewrites variable references into those addresses. The compiler flattens struct methods into plain functions that take a pointer to the struct, then lowers expressions into IR, and a backend implements the IR's instructions through a `Target` trait so new languages can be targeted.

name: oclgrind
desc: OpenCL device simulator and debugger
why: An OpenCL device simulator lets you watch GPU kernels execute instruction by instruction, a real window into program execution.

brief.what_it_is: Oclgrind is a virtual OpenCL device simulator. It presents itself to an application as an OpenCL platform and device, but the kernels run on an interpreter for LLVM IR, not on a GPU or CPU driver. The input is an OpenCL application run through the oclgrind command, or a kernel file run through the standalone oclgrind-kernel executable. The output is the program's normal results plus diagnostics on stderr, such as invalid memory accesses, and an optional interactive GDB-style debugging session. The README also lists data-race and barrier-divergence detection and instruction histograms.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the goal is 'to provide a platform for creating tools to aid OpenCL development', and that the project was originally created by James Price and Simon McIntosh-Smith at the University of Bristol. The tools it currently ships target memory access errors, data races, barrier divergence, instruction counts, and interactive kernel debugging.
brief.how_it_works: Kernels are compiled to LLVM IR and then interpreted, with every memory access bounds-checked. That is why it is slow: the README says it is 'typically a couple of orders of magnitude slower than a regular CPU implementation'. Errors are reported with the kernel name, work-item entity (Global/Local/Group IDs), the offending IR instruction, and the source line. With -i or OCLGRIND_INTERACTIVE=1, execution breaks at the start of each kernel invocation and at any invalid access, and the user gets a prompt where 'help' lists commands.

On Windows you need Visual Studio 2017 or newer, and the ICD is registered by adding a REG_DWORD under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Khronos\OpenCL\Vendors (or the Wow6432Node variant for 32-bit apps), with the name set to the full path of oclgrind-rt-icd.dll and the value 0. name: ocproxy
desc: User-level SOCKS and port forwarding proxy
why: Userspace TCP/IP stack that tunnels through OpenConnect VPNs without root, a clever way to take a network stack apart.

brief.what_it_is: ocproxy is a user-level SOCKS5 and port-forwarding proxy for OpenConnect VPNs, built on the lwIP TCP/IP stack. OpenConnect runs it as a script, passing it the tunnel file descriptor, and ocproxy turns that tunnel into a local SOCKS5 server (-D) and local ports that forward over the VPN (-L). Only the connections a user explicitly sends through it go over the VPN, so the VPN no longer captures all host traffic. The optional vpnns companion tool, which is Linux-only and marked experimental, instead runs an application in a separate network namespace attached to the VPN.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that when using ocproxy, OpenConnect only handles network activity the user specifically asks to proxy, so the VPN interface no longer "hijacks" all network traffic on the host. It also aims at situations where root is unavailable or undesirable, such as multiuser systems, and at connecting to several VPNs at once even when their IP ranges overlap.
brief.how_it_works: OpenConnect is started with --script-tun and --script pointing at ocproxy, which reads its network settings from environment variables set by OpenConnect (INTERNAL_IP4_ADDRESS, INTERNAL_IP4_MTU, INTERNAL_IP4_DNS, CISCO_DEF_DOMAIN) and receives the tunneled traffic on the file descriptor named by VPNFD. Inside the process, lwIP handles the TCP/IP, and the SOCKS5 server and -L forwards open connections over the VPN. The separate vpnns approach creates a fresh user/net/uts/mount namespace with only loopback, then uses --attach to give it a tunnel device, default route and resolv.conf, so no proxy configuration is needed.

name: octomap
desc: Efficient probabilistic 3D mapping framework based on octrees
why: Probabilistic 3D occupancy mapping with octrees is a genuinely neat data structure you can run and visualise.

brief.what_it_is: OctoMap is a C++ library for building 3D occupancy maps of an environment, stored in an octree. It takes in sensor readings from robots, such as laser scans, and folds them into a probabilistic model in which each region is marked occupied, free, or unknown. The map grows as needed and can be saved in a compact form for later use or exchange between robots. The repository also includes octovis, a visualisation library and set of tools. The metadata lists eight executables (binvox2bt, bt2vrml, compare_octrees, convert_octree, edit_octree, eval_octree_accuracy, graph2tree, log2graph), but the README I read does not describe any of them.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the library is for robotics and aims at a full 3D model with no prior assumptions about the environment. It needs to represent unknown space as well as free and occupied space, because unknown areas matter for autonomous exploration. It is developed at University of Freiburg and cited as Hornung et al., Autonomous Robots, 2013.
brief.how_it_works: The map is an octree, and each node holds a probability of occupancy that is updated from new sensor readings, which handles noise and dynamic objects. Nodes can be at different resolutions, so a coarse map can serve a high-level planner while a fine map serves a local planner. Unexplored regions are simply absent from the tree, which is how unknown space is encoded.

name: odin
desc: Programming language with focus on simplicity, performance and modern systems
why: A systems language with a distinctive design philosophy that is worth an afternoon for anyone who has not tried it.

brief.what_it_is: Odin is a general-purpose, open source compiled programming language with distinct typing, aimed at high performance and modern systems. The source code you write goes to the Odin compiler, which produces native programs. The language ships with a core library of packages (fmt, simd and others) and a vendor library of official bindings for graphics APIs and libraries such as SDL2, GLFW, raylib, microui and miniaudio. The homepage's showcase lists many programs and Steam games written in it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls Odin 'the C alternative for the joy of programming' and 'The Data-Oriented Language for Sane Software Development'. The homepage's stated principles are simplicity ('clear is better than clever'), high performance through low-level control of memory layout and custom allocators, and built-in support for modern hardware such as SOA data types and array programming.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage examples show the language's built-in features rather than a single mechanism: fixed and slice arrays with component-wise array math and swizzles, bit_set and enumerated arrays, defer for cleanup at scope exit, multiple return values, labelled control flow, SIMD vectors and inline assembly. The README does not describe the compiler's internals.
brief.install_notes: The homepage links to a Getting Started install page (https://odin-lang.org/docs/install) and a nightly builds page, which I did not fetch, so I cannot give the exact steps beyond the brew formula. The README and homepage mention no accounts, runtimes or hardware requirements. Programs are written in .odin files with a 'package main' and a 'main :: proc()' entry point, and the homepage examples import 'core:fmt'. The brew formula installs the 'odin' executable.
brief.standout: Odin takes a data-oriented route: bit sets, enumerated arrays, SOA layout, SIMD and built-in array programming are part of the language, not libraries. Its batteries-included approach (official graphics bindings for Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D and WebGL, plus raylib and SDL bindings) is unusual for a young language, and the homepage shows a long list of games shipped on Steam built with it.

brief.what_it_is: Oggz is a command-line tool, with a C library underneath, for inspecting, editing and validating Ogg files. It reads Ogg multiplexed files conforming to RFC3533 and can parse headers for CELT, CMML, FLAC, Kate, PCM, Speex, Theora and Vorbis, plus Ogg Skeleton logical bitstreams. brief.how_it_works: Oggz reads the Ogg page framing and the codec headers of each logical bitstream, then either reports on them or rewrites the pages. The oggz-chop binary also detects when it is run as a CGI script by checking environment variables and then reads a t= query parameter, so a web server can serve time ranges over HTTP.

name: one-ml

brief.what_it_is: 1ML is an experimental reboot of the ML functional language in which modules are first-class values and the core language and the module layer are merged into one small language. The homepage describes it as a language where functions, functors, and type constructors are one construct, and structures, records, and tuples are not distinguished. The homepage links a simple prototype interpreter, version 0.1, which runs small examples. It is a research artifact rather than a production tool. The homepage does not say what input or output format the interpreter uses beyond running ML-style programs.
brief.why_it_exists: ML splits into a core language of types and expressions and a separate higher-order module language, which duplicates syntax and semantics and limits expressiveness, for example by preventing a module from being selected by a dynamic decision. The author's framing is that 1ML is a redesign that makes modules truly first-class and unifies the two layers into one language.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage gives the design at a high level: 1ML does not require dependent types, and its type structure can be expressed in plain System Fω (a variant of the F-ing modules approach). The author describes it either as one language where everything is a mode of use of modules, or as a user-friendly surface syntax for System Fω. The homepage does not explain the interpreter's internals.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says you need OCaml 4.02 and Make to build the prototype, and that the README in the GitHub repository has basic documentation. I did not fetch the repository, so I have no build or run commands. The Homebrew formula lists an executable named 1ml, which suggests the interpreter is installed under that name.
brief.standout: It is a design-research language arguing that the core/module split in ML is unnecessary, and that functions, functors, type constructors, structures, and records can be one construct. It also claims the type system fits in plain System Fω without dependent types, and that it can be presented with Damas/Milner-style implicit quantification.
brief.status: Unknown from the homepage alone. The page has a copyright line of 2015-2017, and the prototype is listed as Version 0.1, with no release date or last-commit date shown. The papers are from 2015 to 2018. The page does not mention recent activity, and the GitHub repository was not fetched.
brief.caveats: The prototype is a simple interpreter that does not yet implement the effect polymorphism extension from the latest paper. The author states that type inference for the implicitly typed version is not complete, though he argues it is not substantially worse than Standard ML's. It needs OCaml 4.02 and Make to build, which is an old OCaml version. The homepage describes the project as research, and the scout notes call it obscure.
