name: onioncat
desc: VPN-adapter that provides location privacy using Tor or I2P
why: Turning Tor or I2P into a VPN adapter with IPv6-derived addresses is a clever door into how overlay networks route traffic.

brief.what_it_is: OnionCat (command ocat) is a userland program that creates a transparent IPv6 layer on top of Tor's hidden services or I2P's tunnels. It opens a TUN device and assigns it an IPv6 address derived from the local .onion or I2P identifier. Packets the kernel sends to that device are carried over Tor or I2P to other OnionCat instances, and any IP-based protocol can pass through, with TCP and UDP the main use. The source README is actually the ocat(1) man page, dated 2023-10-25.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a peer-to-peer VPN between hidden services: 'You can think of it as a peer-to-peer VPN between hidden services.' Its stated goal is location-hidden transport of IP traffic over Tor or I2P.
brief.how_it_works: ocat opens a TUN device and gives it an IPv6 address whose prefix is fd87:d87e:eb43:: in Tor mode and fd60:db4d:ddb5:: in I2P (GarliCat) mode. The address comes from the onion_id or i2p_id, so the hidden-service name determines the IPv6 address. Kernel packets for that address are relayed through the local Tor SOCKS proxy (default 127.0.0.1:9050) to the peer's hidden service port. Because Tor v3 addresses are too long for IPv6, v3 peers need manual entries in a hosts file, with the -H option set on the client side.

commands_seen.context: Synopsis form 1: converts an onion_id to an IPv6 address and exits.
Synopsis form 2: converts an IPv6 address back to an onion_id and exits.
Synopsis form 3: the normal way to run ocat with your own .onion hostname and options.
Synopsis form 4: generates a random local onion_id instead of using a configured hidden service. The man page says outgoing use only, and it warns that you usually should not use it.
Synopsis form 5: runs in GarliCat (I2P) mode with an I2P identifier.
From the example ifup script run via -e: assigns the IPv6 address and prefix length to the new tunnel interface.
From the same example ifup script: brings the tunnel interface up.

brief.install_notes: The README mentions no install steps beyond the ./configure options. Two build-time items appear: --enable-debug turns on debug output, and the man page cites packaged source releases on abenteuerland.at. Running needs a Tor (or I2P) instance with a configured hidden service whose hostname is supplied to ocat. The TUN device setup needs root, and ocat drops to a 'tor' user (or uid 65534) afterward. An optional -e ifup script runs as root at startup to configure the interface.
brief.standout: It maps a Tor hidden-service name directly to an IPv6 address, so ordinary IP tools and sockets work over the onion network without per-app proxying. The README also includes a diagnostic trick: pinging fd87:d87e:eb43::dead:beef tests the kernel-to-ocat link, and pinging fd87:d87e:eb43::feed:beef tests the Tor side.
brief.status: The README is a man page dated 2023-10-25 with copyright 2008-2023, which suggests active work through late 2023. I did not check the commit history or release tags, so I cannot confirm recent activity. Treat it as maintained but unverified.
brief.caveats: The README says plainly that OnionCat does not implement encryption: 'OnionCat does not implement any encryption technique! It is a plain tunneling through TCP sessions.' Tor v3 hidden-service addresses are too long to map to IPv6, so v3 peers need manually maintained hosts entries, and the man page says it 'does not work out of the box any more.' The -R random-id mode cannot receive incoming connections unless the remote side is bidirectional. The local controller on 127.0.0.1:8066 is unauthenticated and not thread-safe, and the README says it should not be used in production. The direct (-5 direct) mode is marked experimental and skips hostname validation. Debug output needs a build with --enable-debug. The license is GPLv3.

name: open-ocd
desc: On-chip debugging, in-system programming and boundary-scan testing
why: JTAG and boundary-scan access to chips is a real door into hardware debugging, though the tool itself is well-established in embedded circles.

brief.what_it_is: OpenOCD (Open On-Chip Debugger) is an open-source tool for on-chip debugging, in-system programming and boundary-scan testing of embedded chips. It drives a hardware debug adapter (dongles such as FT2232, J-Link, ST-LINK, CMSIS-DAP and others) that connects a computer to a target board over JTAG or SWD. It is configured with interface, board and target config scripts, and it can be driven from a telnet/Tcl interface or a GDB server. Its output is flash programming, memory access, breakpoints, trace and debugging sessions against the chip. The homepage presents version 0.12.0 as the current release.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage does not state a problem-statement or mission in its own words. The release notes and user guide describe it as a debugger for embedded targets that works through on-chip debug ports, and the scout notes describe JTAG and boundary-scan access to chips as the door it opens.
brief.how_it_works: The user guide's table of contents describes a layered design: a debug adapter is selected and configured, a JTAG or SWD transport is set up, and TAP declarations describe the scan chain of the target. Target CPU objects are then defined, and a server stage exposes GDB, telnet and a Tcl RPC interface. Boundary-scan support includes SVF and XSVF file playback, and IPDBG JTAG-host server functionality, per the guide's section list.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says Homebrew packages OpenOCD 0.12.0 for macOS, alongside Debian, Fedora, Gentoo, OpenWrt and MSYS2. Beyond the package, you need a supported debug adapter dongle and the matching interface and board or target config files (the guide has sections on 'Choosing a Dongle', 'Hooking up the JTAG Adapter' and 'Configuration Basics'). I did not read those sections' contents, only their headings, so I have no exact invocation or first-run steps.
brief.standout: Board and target support is enormous and is delivered as Tcl config scripts; the 0.12.0 notes list dozens of new board, target and adapter configs, including Raspberry Pi, ESP32 and STM32 parts. It is also used for boundary-scan work through SVF and XSVF, not only for debugging.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage announces OpenOCD 0.12.0 as released, with an 0.12.0-rc1 post before it and an 0.11.0 release before that. The 0.11.0 post says it came four years after the previous release. The homepage does not give a date for 0.12.0 itself, and I did not check the git log.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a news feed and contains no usage examples or commands. I read only the user guide's table of contents, not its body, so I could not verify the command syntax. Hardware is required: you need a compatible debug adapter and a board. Licensing of the code was not confirmed; the guide itself is under GFDL 1.2. The guide header states 'release 0.12.0+dev, dated 19 October 2026', which does not match the homepage's account of a released 0.12.0, so treat its version and date as unreliable.
quotes: I'm happy to announce the availability of OpenOCD version 0.12.0.
Some major GNU/Linux distros (Debian, Fedora, Gentoo, OpenWrt), Homebrew for macOS and MSYS2 for Windows have already picked the release up.
Finally! Final.
Hooray for the developers!

name: open-simh

why: Boot real PDP, VAX, and other vintage machines in software and poke at operating systems from the era.

brief.what_it_is: Open SIMH is a family of software simulators of historic computers, built as one framework (SCP) with many machine-specific simulator programs. The brew package ships 24 executables, including altair, pdp1, pdp8, pdp10, pdp11, vax, vax780, sigma, i7094 and b5500-era families, though the list of machines is not all covered in the README. Each simulator emulates the hardware of one machine so that its original operating system and software can run unchanged; the homepage cites Version 7 Unix (1979) running on it. Per the status document, disk and tape images (raw disks, virtual disk containers, AWS and TAR tapes) are attached to the simulated devices, and console I/O goes to your terminal or a TELNET port, with optional SDL2 video windows.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the goal as preserving knowledge held in old software by providing the ability to execute and experience it through simulation of the original hardware. The README describes SIMH as created by Bob Supnik, originally at Digital Equipment Corporation, and extended by many contributors.
brief.how_it_works: Each simulator emulates a specific machine's CPU and devices in software and runs the period operating system from disk or tape images. The shared SCP command layer provides the console prompt, ATTACH/DETACH of media, BOOT and breakpoint handling, and scripting through DO files, EXPECT and SEND. The README does not spell out the emulation internals beyond this.

Windows builds use Visual Studio 2008 through 2019 or MinGW32, with steps in a Visual Studio Projects readme. The homepage has Download links for tar, zip and source, and the TOC mentions prebuilt Windows simulators, but I did not read those pages.

name: opencbm
desc: Provides access to various floppy drive formats
why: Lets a PC talk to Commodore 1541 floppy drives via a parallel cable, a door into old serial bus protocols and vintage hardware.

brief.what_it_is: OpenCBM is a kernel driver and development library, plus command-line tools, for talking to Commodore 8-bit floppy drives such as the VIC-1541 over the IEC serial bus. The PC connects to the drives through a parallel-port cable (XM1541 or XA1541, optionally with an XP1541 or XP1571 add-on) or through a USB adapter (XU1541 or XUM1541, also called ZoomFloppy). Commands such as cbmctrl, cbmcopy, d64copy and cbmformat take drive commands and disk images or files as input and read or write files, D64 images and drive status on the PC. The package also includes imgcopy, a fast disk copier, and supports other CBM IEC devices, some IEEE drives through a converter, and the VIC-1530/1531 tape units through ZoomTape.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the Commodore serial bus protocol is proprietary and not natively supported by modern hardware or software, and OpenCBM provides an interface to it at the level of simple TALK and LISTEN commands, similar to the C64 kernel routines, with lower-level bus control available as well. It is the Windows port (cbm4win) and successor to cbm4linux.
brief.how_it_works: Each supported cable is driven by a plugin selected in opencbm.conf or with the -@ adapter option. The homepage FAQ explains that the parallel-port cables need the drive's DATA line to raise a parallel-port interrupt, so the driver can answer CLK without busy-waiting the whole CPU. That is why the XM1541 cable swaps the RESET and DATA lines relative to the XE1541 design. USB cables go through libusb-1.0, or libusb-0.1 for compatibility.

commands_seen.context: Lists the parameters and subcommands for cbmctrl (the homepage FAQ says to run it from a DOS console on Windows). Also referenced for the other tools, which each accept --help.
Windows Run-dialog entry the FAQ recommends to open a console window before running the tools, because the Start-Run route closes the window immediately.
Option text from the 0.4.0.60 notes: selects the xu1541 plugin on cbmctrl, cbmcopy, d64copy, cbmformat, cbmforng and cbmrpm41. The adapter name must appear in opencbm.conf.
Option text from the 0.4.0.60 notes: selects the xa1541 plugin on LPT1. Use xa1541:2 for LPT2.
Option mentioned in a FAQ entry for d64copy and cbmcopy. The FAQ says it needs an XP1541 companion cable and otherwise hangs.

brief.install_notes: On Windows, the project ships a zip (opencbm-0.4.99.104.zip, i386 and AMD64), and an install.cmd script installs OpenCBM, the plugin and the drivers together. The manual covers installation and uninstallation, and the Windows installer is not a simple package. Parallel-port cables need a working LPT port; the FAQ notes one Windows 2000 laptop needed 'Legacy Plug+Play Detection' enabled on the LPT port. Linux and BSD builds compile from source; the README points to the manual at opencbm.trikaliotis.net for the steps. Configuration lives in /etc/opencbm.conf (or under the OPENCBM_HOME path). Plugins are built only when libusb or the matching sources are present. Hardware: a real drive and a supported cable.
brief.standout: Unlike a typical emulator bridge, this talks to real 1541-era hardware through a parallel port and gives a low-level IEC bus interface, so the PC can act as a controller for vintage drives. The project has moved from parallel cables to USB adapters, and the homepage argues about interrupt timing in some detail.
brief.status: Quiet but not abandoned, as far as I can tell. The homepage's changelog has a dated entry for version 0.4.99.104 (Jan 23rd, 2022), which is labelled an RC on the download line. The GitHub README shows no date, and I could not see a later release or commit date from the pages I read, so the current state is unknown beyond January 2022. The README names two maintainers (spiro-trikaliotis and go4retro).
brief.caveats: The homepage is an older personal site, and parts of its history section describe cbm4win from 2004-2006. Its FAQ says the XE1541 cable will very likely never be supported. The version history is full of 'ALPHA STAGE' and 'BETA STAGE' labels from 2009-2016. The README says XUM1541 PROMICRO and TEENSY2 firmware is UNSUPPORTED, and Itanium Windows is no longer supported. Native USB support also covers FreeBSD and macOS. The README says libusb-0.1 support will be dropped in some future version. Compiling on Linux can be fiddly, and the 2014 source packages needed fixes to build. The homepage has been updated only sporadically. The scout note's 'parallel cable' framing is incomplete, because USB adapters are also supported. License: GPLv2.
quotes: Win NT/2K/XP/7/8/10/11, Linux/i386/AMD64/ARM, FreeBSD and MacOS X kernel driver and development library to control serial CBM devices, such as the Commodore 1541 disk drive, connected to the PC's parallel port via a XM1541 or XA1541 cable.
OpenCBM provides an interface to this so-called IEC bus at the level of simple TALK and LISTEN commands, similar to the one provided by the Commodore kernel routines.
It is very unlikely that an XE cable will ever be supported.

name: open62541
desc: Open source implementation of OPC UA
why: An open implementation of OPC UA, the industrial protocol behind factory floors, a real door into a protocol nobody outside automation sees.

brief.what_it_is: open62541 is an open source implementation of OPC UA (OPC Unified Architecture, also IEC 62541), written in C99. It provides the building blocks for dedicated OPC UA clients and servers, or for adding OPC UA communication to an existing application. The homepage calls it an open source OPC UA stack in C99. The library is platform independent, with platform-specific code moved into exchangeable plugins. It also ships as a single-file distribution, a pair of open62541.c and open62541.h files that can be dropped into an existing project.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a free, portable way to implement OPC UA without proprietary licensing: the homepage says the stack is free of charge, even for commercial use, and that it targets everything from embedded systems to cloud servers.
brief.how_it_works: The core library in /src depends only on C99 standard headers. Architecture support sits behind an EventLoop plugin in /arch, and other backends such as crypto, information-model storage and so on are plugin interfaces in /plugins with default implementations. Some code is generated from the OPC UA standard's XML definitions by Python scripts during the build. Encryption can pull in mbedTLS or OpenSSL depending on the build configuration.

commands_seen.context: On Debian/Ubuntu, installs the library and development headers from the distribution package.
Compiles an example server source file against the installed library using GCC.
Run after cloning the repository to initialize all submodules before configuring the build with CMake.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew: on Debian/Ubuntu, apt install libopen62541-1.4-dev, then compile with gcc -std=c99 and -lopen62541. For a source build, clone the repository, run git submodule update --init --recursive, then configure with CMake. The full build steps are in the docs at open62541.org/doc/master. The README says a bare-bones build needs only the C standard library, but some configurations need mbedTLS or OpenSSL for encryption. The example server listens on port 4840 by default. Its code uses UA_Server_new, UA_Server_addVariableNode and UA_Server_runUntilInterrupt, and the client connects to opc.tcp://localhost:4840 and reads a node with UA_Client_readValueAttribute. Nothing in the README mentions a runtime, account, or hardware requirement.
brief.standout: It is a small, portable C99 stack under MPLv2, so it can be linked into proprietary software without relicensing that code. Contributors keep their own copyright, which the README says prevents future relicensing. The project also publishes a long list of quality gates: zero OPC Foundation CTT errors, zero warnings under strict flags, fuzzing through oss-fuzz, and Valgrind and sanitizer runs. OPC UA is mostly invisible outside automation, and this is a readable C entry point into it.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage calls it an active community project with 'Active community development', lists a Stable Release 1.5 and a Development Branch, names o6 Automation GmbH as official maintainer, and advertises a training course for 10.11.26 to 12.11.26 in Karlsruhe. The README links a live issue tracker and mailing list. I could not see a last-commit or release date on either page, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: The 'OPC UA Certified' claim applies to an example server built with v1.4 and checked against the Standard UA Server Profile 2017, not to every use of the library. A source build needs CMake and git submodules. Encryption adds a dependency on mbedTLS or OpenSSL. The homepage pushes paid support and training, and o6 Automation employs the core contributors. The homepage did not show a Homebrew-specific install path, and the brew formula notes were empty. The brief's scout notes frame it as a window into factory-floor protocols; the README itself does not say that.
quotes: Open Source OPC UA licensed under the MPL v2.0
Written in C99 with minimal dependencies. Runs everywhere from embedded systems to cloud servers.
contributors retain their individual copyright. This prevents future relicensing under different license conditions.

name: openfast

why: NREL's whole-turbine simulator lets you model wind turbine dynamics in software, real engineering you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: OpenFAST is an open-source wind turbine simulation tool, a multi-physics, multi-fidelity framework that couples aerodynamics, hydrodynamics for offshore structures, control and electrical (servo) dynamics, and structural dynamics. You give it a turbine description (input files covering the rotor, tower, substructure, controller and so on) plus inflow and wave conditions, and it runs nonlinear, coupled aero-hydro-servo-elastic simulations in the time domain. The README does not spell out the output files in the pages I read, but the docs describe running time-series simulations and linearization about operating points to get natural frequencies, damping and mode shapes. It is a simulator with no GUI described in these pages.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs present it as a community model for research labs, academia and industry, built to be well tested, well documented and self-sustaining, and it is the successor to FAST v8. The brew description calls it NREL-supported; the README now credits the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), with support from the US Department of Energy's Wind Energy Technology Office.
brief.how_it_works: The glue code (the coupler) connects separate modules for aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, control and electrical systems, and structural dynamics through a modular interface, and advances them together in time. The glue code and most modules are Fortran 2003, and modules can also be written in C or C++. The FAST.Farm extension runs one OpenFAST model per turbine to simulate multi-turbine wind farms.

name: openfst
desc: Library for weighted finite-state transducers
why: Weighted finite-state transducers are a fascinating formal-language idea, though it is a library first.

brief.what_it_is: OpenFst is an open-source C++ template library for building, combining, optimizing, and searching weighted finite-state transducers (FSTs). Each transition in these automata has an input label, an output label, and a weight, and the finite-state acceptor is the special case where input and output labels match. The library takes FSTs as input, whether built in code or from AT&T-format text files, and produces new FSTs or search results such as shortest paths. It also ships about 60 shell commands (fstcompile, fstcompose, fstshortestpath, and others, plus far* and pdt/mpdt tools) that read and write binary FST files.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes FSTs as a way to represent sets of strings (acceptors) and binary relations between strings (transducers), with key uses in speech recognition and synthesis, machine translation, OCR, pattern matching, and information extraction. The library was developed by contributors from Google Research and NYU's Courant Institute and is meant to be comprehensive, reliable, flexible, efficient, and to scale well.
brief.how_it_works: Weights form a semiring: one operation (Plus) combines alternative paths with the same labels, and another (Times) combines weights along a path. Predefined weight types include Tropical and Log, which suit shortest-path and probabilistic models. Operations such as determinization, minimization, composition, and shortest path are applied to FSTs, which can be chained together. The shell commands read binary FST files, run the matching C++ operation, and write an output file, using standard input and output when file names are omitted.

commands_seen.context: Install route given on the homepage for Linux (x86) and Mac OS X users who already have conda.

Prints a binary FST in text form using the symbol tables.
Writes a Graphviz dot drawing of an FST; the quick tour then renders it with dot -Tps.
Sorts arcs by output label, which composition needs on one of its two inputs.
Computes the relational composition of two transducers, here applying a model to an input.
Keeps only the output labels of a transducer, yielding an acceptor of output strings.

brief.install_notes: Installing from source is not covered on the pages I read; the homepage only gives the conda-forge command for Linux (x86) and Mac OS X. To use the C++ API, include <fst/fstlib.h> from the installation include directory and link against libfst.so in the library directory. The shell tools are in the installation bin directory, and --help gives usage for each. No accounts, hardware, or first-run configuration were mentioned.
brief.standout: Weighted transducers unify acceptors, transducers, and probabilistic models behind one semiring framework, so composition, determinization, and shortest path work the same way across speech, translation, and string-processing uses. The shell commands are small Unix-style filters that can be piped together, as the quick tour's one-line composition example shows.

name: opendht
desc: C++17 Distributed Hash Table implementation
why: A C++ distributed hash table with a bundled tool, a real peer-to-peer door into how DHTs route and store data.

brief.what_it_is: OpenDHT is a lightweight C++17 distributed hash table library. Every node in the network can read and write values to a shared, distributed in-memory store, and values are spread across the network with redundancy. Programs use it through a C++17 map-style API, with bindings for C, Rust and Python 3, or through an optional REST API with HTTP client and server support and push notifications. It takes keys and values from the calling program and returns stored values to it through get/put calls. The package also ships dhtnode, a command-line tool that runs a DHT node and performs get and put operations on text values, and dhtchat, a simple chat client that runs over the DHT.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as an easy-to-use distributed in-memory data store designed for large networks and small devices, with high resilience to network disruption. It was originally based on jech/dht by Juliusz Chroboczek, and the README credits that origin in its acknowledgements.
brief.how_it_works: A program starts a node with a generated RSA identity on a chosen port, then joins the network through a known bootstrap node. Data is stored under hashed keys and distributed over the network with redundancy. An optional public-key layer, built on GnuTLS, adds data signing and encryption, as the putSigned call in the example shows. The README does not describe the routing internals in detail.

name: openfpgaloader
desc: Universal utility for programming FPGA
why: A universal FPGA programmer that talks to many boards over USB, a real door into hardware bitstream loading.

brief.what_it_is: openFPGALoader is a command-line utility that loads bitstreams onto FPGAs. You give it a bitstream file and either a board name (-b) or a JTAG cable model (-c), and it writes the design either straight into the FPGA's SRAM or into an attached flash chip (-f). It covers FPGAs from Xilinx, Altera/Intel, Lattice, Gowin, Efinix, Anlogic and Cologne Chip, across many boards and USB cables. The README says it runs on Linux, Windows, macOS and OpenBSD. Its own scout note calls it a universal FPGA programmer that talks to many boards over USB.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a universal utility for programming FPGAs, so one tool replaces the separate vendor programmers for each FPGA family and cable. The homepage adds a compatibility-list approach: check whether your specific hardware is supported before you start.
brief.how_it_works: Cable or board selection picks a driver for the JTAG interface, such as FTDI MPSSE, CMSIS-DAP, USB-Blaster or Xilinx cables, and the bitstream parser matches the file type. With -m (default) the bitstream goes into SRAM. With -f it goes into external flash, and for flash-attached boards the tool can first load a small helper bitstream called spiOverJtag, so it can reach a SPI flash through the JTAG port. The README says spiOverJtag bitstreams are looked up in /usr/local/share/ by default and can be redirected with the OPENFPGALOADER_SOJ_DIR environment variable.

commands_seen.cmd: openFPGALoader -b arty arty_bitstream.bit # Loading in SRAM
commands_seen.context: Quick usage: loads a bitstream into SRAM for the named board (arty is one of the board names on the compatibility list).

commands_seen.cmd: openFPGALoader -b arty -f arty_bitstream.bit # Writing in flash
commands_seen.context: Quick usage: same board, but -f writes the bitstream into the board's flash so it persists across power cycles.
Selects a JTAG cable model directly with -c instead of a board name; here a CMSIS-DAP probe.
Sets the directory where spiOverJtag bitstreams are searched, replacing the /usr/local/share/ default.
Same spiOverJtag directory override, applied to a single invocation instead of the whole shell session.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no install steps beyond a documentation link, and I did not open the install page. It does say the build uses CMake with ENABLE_xxx options to switch individual cables and vendor drivers on or off. The v1.1.0 and v1.1.1 release notes mention libFTDI detection through find_package with pkg-config as a fallback, a plugdev/dialout group note, and a 70-openfpgaloader.rules udev file for Linux USB access. The v1.2.0 notes mention a hidapi dependency for macOS CI builds. The release notes also list a MinGW-w64 Windows cross-compile path. I did not see any Homebrew-specific steps.
brief.standout: One tool covers many vendors' FPGAs and many boards and cables, with a single command-line grammar. The spiOverJtag approach, which loads a helper bitstream so the tool can reach a SPI flash through JTAG, is a clever way to program flash on boards that have no dedicated flash interface.
brief.status: Maintained. The latest release, v1.2.0, is dated 18 Oct in the fetched GitHub releases page; the year is not shown in the extracted text. A nightly pre-release is dated 30 Dec and v1.1.1 is dated 11 Mar, so releases recur roughly every few months. The release notes list recent hardware additions such as Agilex and Xilinx Kria parts and Vivado 2025.2.1 compatibility, which points to 2025. The GitHub release page was cut off at about 40,000 characters, so I did not read the full list.
brief.caveats: Support depends on the exact board, cable and FPGA, so you have to check the compatibility lists before buying hardware. Some boards need specific jumper settings or only partly work; for example, one older release notes that a board's SPI flashing does not boot. The default build is a CMake build with native library dependencies, and the install page was not checked. Vendor-specific behaviour is documented separately for each vendor. The homepage footer shows a 2019-2022 copyright, which does not match the 2025-era release notes; I read this as an old footer not a sign of abandonment. The README is terse, so the usage guide holds the detail.

Compatible with many boards, cables and FPGA from major manufacturers (Xilinx, Altera/Intel, Lattice, Gowin, Efinix, Anlogic, Cologne Chip).

name: openhmd
desc: Free and open source API and drivers for immersive technology
why: Drivers for VR headsets over USB HID; a real door into talking to immersive hardware, though the library itself is plumbing-adjacent.

brief.what_it_is: OpenHMD is a C library, with drivers, that lets applications read head tracking and related data from immersive hardware such as VR headsets (Oculus Rift, HTC Vive, PlayStation VR, Windows Mixed Reality, and others) and some VR controllers. It takes in raw USB/HID reports from those devices and presents them through one cross-platform C API that applications can enumerate, open and read from. The homepage says it also ships a Generic Android driver and an External Sensor driver, so you can feed in your own sensor data and still use its sensor fusion. Language bindings exist for Go, Java, .NET, Perl, Python and Rust.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the aim is to provide a Free and Open Source API and drivers for immersive technology, implementing support for as many devices as possible in a portable, cross-platform package. The blog credits years of reverse engineering, hacking and testing for each device's driver.
brief.how_it_works: Drivers talk to headsets and controllers over USB HID, using HIDAPI (hidraw on Linux). Each device has its own driver, and you choose which drivers to compile in at build time. Applications link the library and read tracking data through the public API, which is documented with Doxygen.

brief.install_notes: You need HIDAPI, and either Meson with Ninja, GNU Autotools (only if building from the git repository), or CMake. On Linux, add a udev rule so you can open USB devices without root, then unplug and replug the device; the README points to a wiki list of udev rules. On Windows with CMake, a Visual Studio generator works; if you link statically with MinGW or MSVC, define OHMD_STATIC before including openhmd.h, but do not define it when using the DLL. By default all drivers except android are enabled. The homepage says v0.3 is the last release to support Autotools.
brief.standout: Instead of being one vendor's SDK, it is one open C API that reverse-engineered drivers for many competing headsets share, with a Boost license that lets it be linked into proprietary software. Its own project history is part of the appeal: the blog describes device support arriving through hackathons and reverse engineering.
brief.status: Unmaintained. The GitHub README opens with 'UNMAINTAINED' and says OpenHMD is 'currently NOT ACTIVELY MAINTAINED', asking people to open an issue if they want to maintain it. It also says driver development has largely moved to Monado. The latest release on the homepage is v0.3.0, dated 2019-07-12, and the homepage's newest blog post is from that date. I did not check commit history.
brief.caveats: The README says the project is not actively maintained, and development has largely moved to Monado. The 0.3.0 release notes say PSVR was disabled because of Windows and modern macOS issues, and that NOLO firmware versions were not all tested. Some peripherals (WMR controllers, PS Move, DualShock 4) work on Linux only through hidapi-hidraw. Oculus Rift CV1 positional tracking lives in a fork, not in this repository. The Unity plugin is labelled alpha, tested only on Unity 5.6 for Windows and Linux 64-bit, with no lens-correction shader. The homepage device table is not a full support list; the README sends you to a GitHub wiki for that. Several links on the homepage are to the old site and may be stale.

name: openkermit

why: Kermit is a forgotten serial and network file transfer protocol, and a scriptable implementation is a real door into retro comms.

brief.what_it_is: Open Kermit is the home of ongoing development of C-Kermit, a communications package with a text UI. Its parts include a portable scripting language that works like a shell but has built-in screen-scraping automation (similar in concept to expect) and built-in file transfer, an implementation of the Kermit file transfer protocol, a network client and server, a serial port interface, and a BBS client. The homepage says it runs on hundreds of platforms, from 1970s computers and 1990s pocket calculators to modern desktop and mobile OSes. The homepage text does not describe the inputs and outputs in detail.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Kermit as a long-running communications tool that has been carried forward since 1981, starting at Columbia University, passing through the Kermit Project, and now continued by Open Kermit after one of Kermit's founders retired following 44 years. The site also says the earlier project websites remain online as a historical snapshot.

It points to a 'Getting Kermit and Downloads' page with links to GitHub source and binaries, covering modern and historical platforms. The Homebrew formula lists the executables as ckermit.ini, kermit, and kermit-sshsub, but I did not confirm those names from the homepage text.
brief.standout: Kermit is a serial and network file transfer tool with a scripting language built in, and it has been continuously developed since 1981 across three successive projects. The homepage says the earlier project sites are still online, which makes the history itself browsable.
brief.status: Active as far as the homepage shows: it describes Open Kermit as currently carrying the project forward and invites contributions, and it is managed by John Goerzen. I found no release date or last commit date because I did not reach the GitHub repository or the downloads page.

name: openmsx
desc: MSX emulator
why: A thorough MSX emulator with debugger and tooling, a window into 1980s home computing and its odd hardware.

brief.what_it_is: openMSX is an open-source emulator for MSX, the 1980s home computer standard, and related machines. The homepage describes it as 'the MSX emulator that aims for perfection'. It runs MSX software and games from emulated cartridges, disk images, tapes and other media, and it emulates many MSX hardware variants and extensions. Its release history also includes the Spectravideo SVI-318/328, ColecoVision and Sega SG-1000 support. The homepage does not spell out exact inputs and outputs, so the brief keeps this high level.
brief.why_it_exists: The project's stated aim is accuracy: the homepage tagline is 'the MSX emulator that aims for perfection', and the release notes describe work on cycle-accurate VDP timing, floppy (DMK) accuracy and chip-level details. The README is a plain notice that the code is GPL with some files under their own licences, and it is not framed around a problem statement.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage news describes a built-in debugger and a graphical user interface (introduced in 20.0, replacing the OSD menu) for configuring the machine. In 21.0 it added 'setups', which save and load a complete MSX configuration (for example a Philips VG 8020 with an external disk drive, joystick, data recorder and printer) that can be started automatically. Tcl scripting is mentioned in the 0.7.1 and 0.8.1 notes, and reverse/rewind and TAS scripts appear in the 0.8.0 and 0.8.1 notes. The README does not explain the emulation mechanism itself.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are on the homepage: 21.0 for Windows 64-bit (installer or zip), 21.0 for macOS Intel and Apple Silicon, 21.0 for Linux x86 64-bit, 0.15.0 for Android 4.1+ ARM (apk), 19.1 for OpenDingux (opk), and 21.0 source code. The homepage also lists deprecated Catapult and Debugger downloads, and GitHub nightly and Windows community builds. The homepage news says a system with OpenGL 2 support is required. The README points to HTML manuals in doc/manual and release notes in doc/release-notes.txt inside the source tree. I did not see step-by-step build instructions.
brief.standout: It is one of the few MSX emulators approved as a tool-assisted speedrun (TAS) emulator on tasvideos.org (approved 2010), and it has reverse/rewind and TAS scripting built in. Its accuracy claims cover things like VDP access timing and floppy copy protection, not just running software.

name: openslide
desc: C library to read whole-slide images (a.k.a. virtual slides)
why: Reads gigapixel pathology whole-slide images, a real scientific format door into digital microscopy.

brief.what_it_is: OpenSlide is a C library that gives programmers one simple interface for reading whole-slide images, also called virtual slides, which are very large high-resolution pathology scans. It takes in vendor files in a range of formats (Aperio .svs, Hamamatsu .ndpi, Leica .scn, MIRAX .mrxs, Zeiss .czi, DICOM, generic tiled TIFF, and others) and lets callers read tiles and regions at chosen resolutions without loading the whole image into RAM. It also exposes ICC profiles, textual metadata, and associated images such as a label and thumbnail. Python and Java bindings are published separately; the Python binding includes a Deep Zoom generator and a simple web viewer, and the Java binding includes a simple image viewer.
brief.why_it_exists: Whole-slide images routinely exceed RAM and are stored in vendor-specific formats that are often undocumented and usually readable only with a vendor's own Windows tools. The homepage frames OpenSlide as a vendor-neutral foundation so doctors and researchers are not tied to one vendor's viewer, and so non-Windows platforms can read these files.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals in detail. It describes a C API with a consistent interface over the many vendor formats, and points to the API reference and per-format pages on the website for specifics. The 2013 Journal of Pathology Informatics paper linked from the homepage describes the design and implementation.

commands_seen.context: Configures a build directory for compiling OpenSlide from source; first step of the README's build instructions.

The homepage also links a Windows usage guide and offers binary builds (version 4.0.1.2 is the latest listed). No accounts or hardware are needed. The Homebrew entry lists four executables (openslide-quickhash1sum, openslide-show-properties, openslide-write-png, slidetool), but neither fetched page documents them, so their usage is unverified.
brief.standout: It is a real scientific-format door into digital microscopy: it reads gigapixel pathology scans that most image libraries cannot open, and it was built by reverse-engineering vendor formats that were never documented. It comes from Satyanarayanan's group at Carnegie Mellon, and the website also hosts a web-based demo that renders several slide formats.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists OpenSlide 4.0.1 released 2026-06-07, with binary build 4.0.1.2 dated 2026-06-19, plus Python 1.4.6 and Java 0.13.3 releases on 2026-06-07. name: opentimestamps-client
desc: Create and verify OpenTimestamps proofs
why: Anchors proofs in Bitcoin's blockchain via Merkle trees; a real door into timestamping and a protocol few have examined.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line tool, written in Python, that creates and verifies OpenTimestamps proofs. You give it a file; it hashes the file and sends only the digest to remote calendar servers, which batch digests into Bitcoin transactions. The output is a .ots proof file that can be checked later against the Bitcoin blockchain. The same package can also timestamp PGP-signed Git commits and verify timestamps on whole commits or individual files in a Git repository. The installed commands are ots and ots-git-gpg-wrapper.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to use the Bitcoin blockchain as a timestamp notary, so anyone can prove that data existed at a given time without a trusted third party. The homepage says the project 'aims to be a standard format for blockchain timestamping.'
brief.how_it_works: Stamping hashes the file and submits the digest to one or more remote calendars, which return a pending proof, and the digest is committed to Bitcoin in a batched transaction. The README says the calendar only ever receives an opaque digest, with a per-file nonce protecting the contents. Verification needs the Bitcoin block header: until a calendar upgrades the proof with the path to that header, the proof reads as pending, and a local Bitcoin node can check it directly. The README does not use the phrase Merkle tree; the ots info output shows a chain of append, prepend and sha256 operations that the proof replays to reach the block.

Creates README.md.ots by submitting the file's digest to three remote calendars; the README shows the calendar URLs printed during submission.
Right after stamping, reports each calendar as 'Pending confirmation in Bitcoin blockchain'; confirmation takes a few hours.
Verifies a bundled example locally with no waiting; the README says it succeeds against Bitcoin block 358391, dated 2015-05-28.

Adds the Bitcoin path to the proof itself so it no longer needs the calendar.

Installs from a source checkout instead of PyPI.

brief.install_notes: Needs Python 3. Install with pip3 install opentimestamps-client, or from source with python3 setup.py install. On Debian Stretch the README lists system packages: python3 python3-dev python3-pip python3-setuptools python3-wheel. Creating timestamps needs no Bitcoin node and no account or API key, since the default calendars are free. Verifying needs a local Bitcoin Core node (a pruned node is fine), or the calendars can complete proofs for you. The --bitcoin-node flag takes an RPC URL with credentials. The README warns that a conflicting 'bitcoin' pip package can break ots, and gives a fix: uninstall both bitcoin and python-bitcoinlib, delete the leftover bitcoin directory from dist-packages, then reinstall python-bitcoinlib.
brief.standout: Stamping needs no blockchain node or fees: the client sends a digest to free calendar servers, which batch many digests into one Bitcoin transaction, and the proof file carries its own path to the block. The README's Privacy section is unusually candid about metadata leaks, such as timestamps created close together, or several files stamped in one command, which share most of their proof operations.
brief.status: Unknown from the fetched pages. The GitHub page shows no release date, last commit, or version number. The README calls it 'production software that has been in use for many years' and promises the timestamp format will stay verifiable. It lists open issues with no fixes shown, including 'Need unit tests for the client.' The homepage says the default calendars depend on donations.
brief.caveats: Verification needs a local Bitcoin Core node or a calendar's help, and proofs can sit pending for hours. The README says the REST protocol to calendars may change in incompatible ways, so clients must be upgraded. Known issues include: no unit tests; Git re-hashing fails on filenames with invalid Unicode; Git annex works only with the SHA256 and SHA256E backends; Bitcoin RPC errors are not user-friendly; some Python platforms do not check SSL certificates, so calendar connections could be intercepted (though only to produce a proof that fails validation); and ots-git-gpg-wrapper does not check whether the commit timestamp makes sense. Its requirements are Python 3 and Bitcoin Core; the README does not mention Windows. The brew entry had no caveats. The scout notes mention Merkle trees, which the README does not name.
quotes: Command-line tool to create and validate timestamp proofs with the OpenTimestamps protocol, using the Bitcoin blockchain as a timestamp notary.
File contents *are* protected with nonces: a remote calendar learns nothing about the contents of anything you timestamp as it only ever receives an opaque and meaningless digest.
OpenTimestamps is production software that has been in use for many years.

name: opensc

brief.what_it_is: OpenSC is a set of libraries and command-line utilities for working with smart cards, with its main focus on cards that support cryptographic operations. The wiki says it implements the standard smart card APIs (PKCS#11, Windows Smart Card Minidriver, and macOS CryptoTokenKit) so applications can use those cards. The brew formula installs about two dozen tools, including pkcs11-tool, pkcs15-tool, opensc-tool, opensc-explorer, and piv-tool. The fetched pages did not show the exact inputs and outputs of each tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The wiki frames it as serving security applications such as authentication, mail encryption and digital signatures, by making smart cards usable through standard APIs. It is written by an international team of volunteers and licensed as open source.
brief.how_it_works: Neither the wiki nor the README explains the internals in detail. The wiki says OpenSC implements the standard APIs so that applications can reach cards through them. Related sub-projects such as libp11 and pkcs11-helper are wrapper libraries for PKCS#11 modules, and they can be used without OpenSC.
brief.install_notes: The brew caveat says the OpenSSH PKCS11 smartcard integration will not work with this formula. To get that functionality, unlink this formula and install the OpenSC cask instead. The README lists official downloads: Windows MSI installers for x64, x86 and arm64, a macOS DMG, and a source tarball for Unix. Unix build steps are on the wiki page 'Compiling and Installing on Unix flavors', and there are Windows and macOS Quick Start pages. Nightly builds are available by git hash from the OpenSC/Nightly repo. The wiki says download links should come from the README or the GitHub main page, not the wiki. I did not see reader hardware or first-run configuration requirements in the pages I read.
brief.standout: OpenSC is a family rather than one tool. It implements several platform smart-card APIs at once and ships sub-projects (libp11, pkcs11-helper, PAM-PKCS#11, pam_p11, OpenCT, OpenSC-Java) that can be used independently. The README also lists a card support matrix covering CAC, SmartCard-HSM, PIV, OpenPGP, GIDS, and Pico HSM applets, with CI, Coverity, CodeQL, and OSS-Fuzz badges. The security history is tied to APDU and response data handling, which fits the scout note about APDU traffic and card file structures.

name: opkssh
desc: Enables SSH to be used with OpenID Connect
why: Uses OpenID Connect identities in SSH certificates, a door into how SSH authentication can be reinvented.

brief.what_it_is: opkssh is a command-line tool that lets people use OpenID Connect identities, such as alice@example.com, to log in over SSH instead of managing long-lived SSH keys. It does not replace SSH. Running `opkssh login` opens a browser so you can sign in with an OpenID Provider such as Google, Microsoft, GitLab, or Keycloak, then generates an SSH key at ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa that carries your PK Token (an OpenID Connect ID Token bound to a public key). On the server, opkssh works with sshd to check that token against an allow-list of identities and Linux accounts. Input is a browser login plus a policy file; output is an SSH key that ssh and sftp use as normal.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as making SSH access manageable through identities like alice@example.com instead of long-lived SSH keys. It builds on OpenPubkey, which the README describes as adding user public keys to OpenID Connect without breaking compatibility with existing OpenID Providers.
brief.how_it_works: It uses two SSH features. First, SSH certificates can carry arbitrary extensions, so the PK Token (which includes the ID Token) is placed in an extension field of the SSH certificate. Second, sshd's AuthorizedKeysCommand sends the certificate to the installed opkssh program (configured as `opkssh verify %u %k %t`), which verifies the PK Token before the login is allowed.

Installs the opkssh binary via Homebrew on macOS.
Opens a browser to authenticate with your OpenID Provider and writes an SSH key at ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa containing your PK Token. Keys expire after 24 hours by default.

Logs in against a custom OpenID Provider such as Authentik, Authelia, Keycloak, or Zitadel.
Shows the details of an opkssh-generated SSH key or certificate.
Developer build from source using Go, as given in the README's Building section.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew: Windows users can use `winget install openpubkey.opkssh` or `choco install opkssh -y`; Nix users can run `nix-shell -p opkssh`; or download a binary from the GitHub releases page and chmod +x it on Linux/macOS. Logging in needs a browser on the client. Servers need root: the Linux installer creates a low-privilege opksshuser, adds AuthorizedKeysCommand and AuthorizedKeysCommandUser to /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and writes config under /etc/opk/. Windows servers use an elevated PowerShell script (Install-OpksshServer.ps1) and config under %ProgramData%\opk\. NixOS has a services.opkssh module. Custom providers can be set with a flag, a ~/.opk/config.yml file (created by `opkssh login --create-config`), or the OPKSSH_PROVIDERS environment variable. For production, the README says to register your own OpenID Connect client ID rather than the shipped defaults.
brief.standout: Rather than changing SSH's key format or running a new daemon, it hides the identity token inside a standard SSH certificate extension and lets sshd call a small verifier, so users keep using ssh and sftp unchanged. The README also says it works with existing identity providers without asking them to change anything.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release date or changelog, and the fetched page did not show a last-commit date. It does show current-looking activity: a Go coverage badge, a mailing list, and support notes for Windows Server 2025, openSUSE Leap 16, and Forgejo v15.0+. The homepage's paper history (last revision 2025-03-29) refers to the paper, not the code.
brief.caveats: The homepage given in the request is the OpenPubkey research paper on eprint.iacr.org, not a project site; the code and docs live on GitHub. Client support: Linux, macOS, and Windows 11 are supported; Android is experimental (Termux). Server support: Linux and Windows Server; macOS servers are not supported yet. The shipped default client IDs are for testing and development only. The README warns not to reuse a client ID between opkssh and other OIDC services, because a server could replay the token elsewhere. The README's example config contains a Google client secret, which should not be reused. The Linux install is a curl-or-wget piped straight into sudo bash. Some providers need specific setup, such as public client mode for PocketID and not using confidential/secret mode. License was not checked.

name: orbuculum
desc: Arm Cortex-M SWO/SWV Demux and Postprocess
why: Demuxes ARM SWO trace streams from a live microcontroller, a genuine window into watching firmware think.

brief.what_it_is: Orbuculum is a set of command-line tools that decode and present the trace output pins of an Arm Cortex-M CPU, either SWO (UART or Manchester encoded) or parallel TRACE pins via ORBTrace hardware. Input comes from a debug probe (Black Magic Probe, SEGGER J-Link, USB or FTDI serial, OpenOCD or PyOCD SWO, ORBTrace Mini) or from a saved raw file. Output is a network feed (orbflow on TCP 3402, legacy frames on 3443) that clients such as orbcat, orbtop, orbstat, orbmortem and orbzmq read to show printf-style text channels, program counter samples, statistics and, with ETM, instruction trace.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls an Orbuculum a crystal ball, 'used for seeing things that would be otherwise invisible', with a nodding reference to the Black Magic Probe (BMP). It exists so that data a running microcontroller pushes out its trace pins can be read by ordinary host tools while the firmware runs.
brief.how_it_works: The orbuculum mux talks to the probe and exposes a network interface to which any number of clients can connect. Since 2.2.0 it speaks orbflow, a COBS-framed, sequenced packet protocol, and an ORBTrace Mini 1.4.0+ probe can strip TPIU framing itself, with clients falling back to legacy protocol when needed. The -T and -t options control TPIU stripping and which streams are routed.

name: ophcrack
desc: Microsoft Windows password cracker using rainbow tables
why: Rainbow table password cracker that shows how Windows LM and NTLM hashes actually get attacked; a clear window into authentication weakness.

brief.what_it_is: Ophcrack is a free, GPL-licensed Windows password cracker that uses rainbow tables. It takes password hashes (LM and NTLM) and looks them up against precomputed tables to recover the original passwords. It ships with a graphical interface and runs on Windows, Linux/Unix and Mac OS X. The site also offers free tables for Windows XP and Vista/7, plus a LiveCD that boots and cracks without installation. Its feature list includes a brute-force module for simple passwords, an audit mode with CSV export, real-time graphs, and the ability to load hashes from an encrypted SAM recovered from a Windows partition.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a very efficient implementation of rainbow tables, built by the inventors of the method. Its purpose is to demonstrate and exploit how weak Windows password hashing is in practice.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the mechanism in detail. It says the tool is based on rainbow tables and that the tables cover specific charsets and password patterns, such as dictionary-plus-suffix sets, length-limited full charsets, and numeric-only sets. The tables are precomputed and downloaded separately, and the XP tables target LM hashes while the Vista/7 tables target NT hashes.
brief.install_notes: The brief's install path is brew install ophcrack. Beyond that, the site offers a Windows portable zip (ophcrack-3.8.0-bin.zip, supports Windows 2000 through 10), a source tarball (ophcrack-3.8.0.tar.bz2), and a LiveCD ISO that needs no installation. Three LiveCD variants exist: XP (LM hashes), Vista/7 (NT hashes), and a no-tables build. Rainbow tables are a separate download: the free XP set totals 17.0GB, the free Vista set 11.9GB, and the professional Vista set 2.3TB, all distributed largely via torrent. The site lists md5sums for every file.
brief.standout: Ophcrack is a long-lived, open reference for attacking the LM and NTLM hashes that Windows has used for decades, so it is a concrete demonstration of authentication weakness. Its tables are published openly with stated success rates and charset details, which makes it easy to see exactly what coverage each set provides.
brief.status: The download page says the latest version is 3.8.0 and the LiveCD is at 3.6.0, so the project is still being published. I found no release date or commit history on the pages I read, so I cannot give a firm last-release date. Treat it as maintained by the site's own account, but unverified beyond that.
brief.caveats: The XP tables cannot crack Vista or 7 passwords, and the Vista tables cannot crack XP (LM) passwords. The table downloads are very large, and the professional Vista set is 2.3TB, offered only as a torrent. The brute-force module is described only for simple passwords. The site's table success rates are as stated by the authors and I did not verify them. The site does not state platform-specific install steps for macOS or Linux. Mac OS X is listed under platforms, but I saw no Mac build on the download page, only Windows and source.

name: osmcoastline
desc: Extracts coastline data from OpenStreetMap planet file
why: Extracting coastlines from the full planet file is a real geospatial job, though a niche one worth a closer look.

brief.what_it_is: OSMCoastline is a command-line tool that reads an OpenStreetMap planet file (PBF or XML) and pulls out the ways tagged natural=coastline. It joins those ways into rings and assembles them into land and water polygons, plus error tables. By default the output is a SpatiaLite database, and GDAL can write other formats such as shapefiles or GPKG. Output is in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) by default, or Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) with --srs=3857.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it exists to extract the coastline from an OSM planet file and assemble all the pieces into polygons for use in map renderers and similar tools.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes five steps: filter out coastline ways and their nodes; assemble the ways into rings, closing gaps smaller than --close-distance; build land polygons from the rings, with holes for water; split large polygons using --max-points and --bbox-overlap; and create water polygons as the inverse of the land polygons. Problems found in each step are written to the error_points and error_lines tables. osmcoastline_filter can pre-filter a planet file to under 1% of its size so the main tool can be rerun quickly.

brief.install_notes: Installing via brew install osmcoastline is the simple path. Building from source needs CMake and a C++ toolchain, plus libosmium (at least 2.16.0), protozero (at least 1.6.1), zlib, GDAL 2 or newer built with Spatialite and GEOS support, GEOS, and SpatiaLite. LZ4 and pandoc are optional; pandoc enables building the man pages. The README gives Debian/Ubuntu package names for these. No accounts or runtime services are mentioned. You need a planet or regional OSM extract as input, and the README warns that the full planet file is large.
brief.standout: The Antarctica handling is unusual: the coastline there is the only one allowed to stay open, so the tool finds the open ends near 180° and joins them into a polygon that runs to the South Pole (EPSG:4326) or to the 85.0511° line (EPSG:3857). The tool also deliberately separates warnings (fixed or small geometry problems) from errors (larger problems), and the README tells you to fix the OSM data if any errors remain.

Output geometry is never simplified, so you need the separate simplify_and_split scripts for PostGIS or SpatiaLite. Only EPSG:4326 and EPSG:3857 are supported. The dependency list is long, and the README's Debian package names include libgdal1-dev, which is an old GDAL name. The README says the tool produces errors and warnings on its own test data by design. Licensed under GPL v3 or later.

name: ott
desc: Tool for writing definitions of programming languages and calculi
why: A tool for writing formal semantics of programming languages and calculi, a genuine door into programming language theory.

brief.what_it_is: Ott is a command-line tool for writing definitions of programming languages and calculi. You write a language's syntax and semantics in a concise ASCII notation that looks like informal mathematics. From that one source file it can generate a LaTeX file for typeset output, plus Coq, HOL, Isabelle/HOL and Lem versions of the definition, and an OCaml syntax module. It can also run as a filter over LaTeX or proof-assistant files, parsing embedded terms and replacing them with typeset versions. Parsing the input also sort-checks it, so simple errors such as inconsistent judgement forms or metavariable naming are caught early.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to ease the move from informal to formal mathematics: write the definition once in a clear, editable ASCII notation without LaTeX noise, typeset it for papers, and generate formal definitions for proof assistants from the same source.
brief.how_it_works: Ott reads a grammar-and-rules source file in its ASCII notation and parses and sort-checks it. Annotations in the source control what gets generated. It then emits the chosen backend output, such as LaTeX, Coq, HOL, Isabelle or Lem. It can also generate helper functions automatically, including free variables, single and multiple substitutions, subgrammar checks and binding auxiliaries. The README says only a fully concrete representation of binding, without quotienting by alpha-equivalence, is fully supported.

commands_seen.context: Runs Ott on the bundled test file tests/test10.ott and writes LaTeX to test10.tex and Coq to test10.v. The README says Isabelle, HOL and Lem outputs use -o test10.thy, -o test10Script.sml and -o test10.lem.
Installs the latest released Ott from the opam package repository. The README says the Emacs mode and documentation then land under the opam prefix.
Adds the Coq released opam repository. Needed before installing the Coq auxiliary files.

Builds with ocamlc instead of ocamlopt. The README says this may run Ott significantly slower.
Run in the coq/ subdirectory after make, to install the Coq auxiliary files into Coq's user-contrib.

brief.install_notes: Easiest route is opam 2.0 or later (the README says opam 1 versions are no longer supported): opam install ott. Optional Coq support needs the coq-released opam repository added first, then opam install coq-ott. Building from source needs OCaml 4.07.0 or later plus the ocamlgraph package; the README says it builds with OCaml 4.07.0 and 4.14.0 and ocamlgraph 1.8.8. Without opam, run make in the checkout, and run make inside coq/ then make install for the Coq files. An Emacs mode (emacs/ott-mode.el) and a VS Code extension are also available.
brief.standout: It is a single ASCII source that feeds both a typeset paper appendix and formal proof-assistant definitions, and it checks the sorts and judgement forms as it parses. The filter mode, which typesets Ott terms embedded in existing LaTeX or proof files, is a practical touch. The README lists real systems built with it, including TAPL-style calculi, POPLmark Fsub, the Leroy JFP96 ML module system, Lightweight Java and an OCaml-light semantics.
brief.status: Maintained, though thinly. The README says As of 2024, Ott remains in continuous use, and the GitHub repo shows a Docker CI badge on master. The README also says the issue tracker is now GitHub's, though resources for fixing issues are very limited. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in what I fetched.
brief.caveats: The README warns that resources for fixing issues are very limited. Only the fully concrete binding representation is fully supported; the locally-nameless backend is experimental, and the menhir parser and pretty printer are marked experimental. Some POPLmark examples would need explicit alpha-conversion to capture the intended semantics, per the README footnote. Building from source needs a fairly specific OCaml setup. The Coq and HOL outputs are generated definitions, so proof scripts are separate. The licence is BSD-style, per the README. I did not check platform support beyond the opam route.

name: p0f
desc: Versatile passive OS fingerprinting, masquerade detection tool
why: Passive OS fingerprinting reads TCP/IP handshake quirks to identify machines you never talk to, a delightful door into how the network leaks identity.

brief.what_it_is: p0f is a passive OS and software fingerprinting tool. It watches TCP/IP traffic, often from as little as one normal SYN packet, and infers the operating system and software on both ends of a connection without sending any probes. It also reasons about application-level payloads such as HTTP requests, and reports things like uptime, network link type, distance, language preference, and NAT or proxy setups. Output is printed as text blocks per detection (for example os, dist, params, raw_sig, mtu, uptime, and http request), and it can run in the foreground or as a daemon with a real-time API for third-party components.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that p0f identifies the players behind incidental TCP/IP communications without interfering in any way, as an alternative to active tools like NMap that can be blocked, slow, unreliable, or set off alarms. The page lists uses such as penetration-test reconnaissance, routine network monitoring, detecting unauthorized network interconnects, abuse prevention, and forensics.
brief.how_it_works: According to the page, p0f uses an array of passive fingerprinting mechanisms and matches observed traits against a signature database. Its TCP-level checks rely on handshake quirks, such as the relationship between window size and MTU, and it reads HTTP request and response headers for application-level signatures. Version 3 is described as a complete rewrite with a new signature database, and the page notes that earlier p0f versions are reused in projects such as pfSense, Ettercap, PRADS, and the OpenBSD firewall.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers the current release (3.09b) for download, with older 2.0.x and 1.8.x releases available. The README was not fetched, so compile and configuration steps are unverified. The page says the p0f-sendsyn tool must be compiled from the supplied source to collect SYN+ACK signatures, and that a README covers it. It also says p0f can run in the foreground or as a daemon.
brief.standout: Passive fingerprinting from a single SYN is a clever way to learn about machines you never talk to. The author says many other tools either reuse p0f's TCP checks or use weaker methods, which makes p0f something of a reference point in the field.
brief.status: Quiet, with evidence of some age. The latest version named on the page is 3.09b, and the copyright line reads 2000-2014. The page also says the public demo no longer works because the server now sits behind a load balancer. I found no release date or commit history, so I cannot confirm current activity.
brief.caveats: The public demo is broken, according to the homepage. The page asks for new signatures, especially for SYN+ACK and older platforms, and says the database is minimal for some categories, so detection coverage is uneven. Neither the license nor platform support was stated on the page. The README and design document were not fetched, so details on build dependencies and supported operating systems are missing.
quotes: P0f is a tool that utilizes an array of sophisticated, purely passive traffic fingerprinting mechanisms to identify the players behind any incidental TCP/IP communications (often as little as a single normal SYN) without interfering in any way.

Common uses for p0f include reconnaissance during penetration tests; routine network monitoring; detection of unauthorized network interconnects in corporate environments; providing signals for abuse-prevention tools; and miscellanous forensics.

name: packetq

It was formerly called DNS2db and was renamed in 2011 when it was rebuilt to handle protocols beyond DNS.

brief.what_it_is: Pachi is a free, open-source Go (Weiqi/Baduk) playing engine, plus a modular framework for building Go-playing programs. It has no board or user interface of its own. It runs as a GTP client: a Go frontend such as GoGui, Sabaki, or Lizzie sends it moves and time settings over the GTP protocol, and it replies with its own moves. name: packmol
desc: Packing optimization for molecular dynamics simulations
why: Packs molecules into boxes for molecular dynamics setups, real science, though a niche preprocessing step.

brief.what_it_is: Packmol is a command-line program that builds starting coordinates for molecular dynamics simulations by placing copies of molecules into a region of space without overlaps. You supply a coordinate file for one molecule of each type (PDB, TINKER, or XYZ), the number of copies of each, and spatial constraints such as being inside a box, sphere, cylinder, or above a plane. It writes a coordinate file of the packed system. The user guide's example packs 2000 water molecules into a 40 Å cube from a short text input file.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says PACKMOL "creates an initial point for molecular dynamics simulations by packing molecules in defined regions of space" so that short-range repulsive interactions do not disrupt the simulation. It also says that the variety of constraints makes it easy to build ordered systems such as lamellar, spherical, or tubular lipid layers.
brief.how_it_works: The input file lists each molecule type with a number of copies and constraint keywords (inside/outside box, sphere, ellipsoid, cylinder, plane, and others). The tolerance keyword sets the minimum atom-atom distance, which is 2.0 Å for typical all-atom systems. The program optimizes the positions and rotations of the molecules to satisfy the distance and region constraints, and it reports a final objective value and maximum violations when it succeeds. The guide says it is a first-pass coordinate generator and that the output should go through minimization and equilibration afterward.

name: paperkey
desc: Extract just secret information out of OpenPGP secret keys
why: Strips an OpenPGP secret key down to its raw secret bytes for paper backup, a neat dissection of a file format.

brief.what_it_is: Paperkey is a command-line tool that takes an OpenPGP secret key (GnuPG, PGP, etc.) and strips it down to just the secret bytes, printing them as text or raw output for a paper backup. Going the other way, it takes those printed or re-entered bytes plus the matching public key and rebuilds the full secret key file. It is a single C program distributed as a tarball, with a Win32 binary also offered.
brief.why_it_exists: David Shaw's framing is that paper is a durable 'if-all-else-fails' backup for keys, since CD-Rs, tapes and drives often lose data within years. A full secret key file is much larger than its secret parts because it includes a complete copy of the public key, and the public key is widely available on keyservers, so only the secret portion needs archiving.
brief.how_it_works: Paperkey parses the OpenPGP packet structure and keeps only the secret key material plus minor packet structure, which the author says is about 149 bytes for a DSA+Elgamal key that was 1281 bytes whole. Restoring requires the public key file; paperkey combines it with the pasted-in secret bytes to produce a secret key. It does no cryptography itself, and any passphrase on the original key carries over unchanged. Output can be base16 (human-readable, default width 78) or raw, and it includes a CRC check that can be overridden with --ignore-crc-error.

commands_seen.context: Extracts the secret data from the key file into a text file meant for printing.
Restore: combines the public keyring with the printed secret data to rebuild the secret key file.
Pipes an exported secret key through paperkey straight to the printer, since stdin is used when --secret-key is absent.

brief.install_notes: Not covered by the homepage beyond the tarball and Win32 zip downloads, each with a detached OpenPGP signature from the author's key 0x99242560. Building from the POSIX tarball is the standard route. A RPM spec file is included; the README-style instructions say to build with rpmbuild -ta /path/to/the/paperkey/tarball.tar.gz. No account or runtime is needed beyond the binary. The author recommends test-restoring the key before filing the paper away.
brief.standout: The project's clever observation is that the secret part of a key is tiny compared to the whole file, so a key can be reduced to a few hundred bytes of text you can retype, which makes a paper backup practical. Its honest framing that paper is not a secure store and that it adds no crypto is also unusual for a security-adjacent tool.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage shows version 1.6 with a copyright range of 2007-2018, and says earlier releases and 'the usual GitHub stuff' are on GitHub, but the page gives no release date or recent-activity signal and I did not check GitHub. Treat as unknown beyond 'not recently announced'.
brief.caveats: Output is a paper backup, not secure storage; the page stresses it is for last-resort restore only. Any passphrase on the original key carries over unchanged. Reconstruction needs the public key as well. Restored text must be re-entered accurately, by hand, OCR or QR, and a CRC error stops restore unless you pass --ignore-crc-error. Build and install details beyond the tarball are thin on this page. The Win32 binary is a precompiled download. The licence is not stated on the homepage.
quotes: The goal with paper is not secure storage.
In fact, paperkey doesn't do any crypto at all, but just saves and restores the original secret key, whether it is encrypted or not.
It's a lot easier to re-enter 149 bytes correctly.

name: pacparser
desc: Library to parse proxy auto-config (PAC) files
why: A door into proxy auto-config PAC files, a protocol-adjacent mechanism most people never see running.

brief.what_it_is: Pacparser is a library for parsing proxy auto-config (PAC) files, which are JavaScript files that tell a browser or program which proxy to use for a given URL. You give it a PAC file path, a URL and a host name, and it returns the proxy string, such as 'DIRECT' or 'PROXY proxy1.manugarg.com:3128; PROXY proxy2.manugarg.com:3128; DIRECT'. It ships as a shared C library (libpacparser.so, libpacparser.dylib or pacparser.dll) and as a Python module. The Homebrew formula also installs a pactester executable, which the README does not document.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says PAC files are widely used for proxy configuration and can return different proxies based on URL, source IP, protocol or time of day. Its stated goal is to 'make it easy to add PAC-file parsing capability to any program (C and python supported right now)'.
brief.how_it_works: Pacparser runs the PAC file's JavaScript with the QuickJS engine. The README says the standard's helper functions, which are not part of plain JavaScript, come from Mozilla's PAC implementation, except for a couple of DNS functions that pacparser defines itself. The author describes the result as 'as close to standard as it gets :)'.

commands_seen.context: Installs the Python module from PyPI with pip; prebuilt wheels are listed for 64-bit Linux, Windows, MacOS-Intel and MacOS-ARM.
Installs a specific pacparser version (1.5.0) from PyPI, per the README's inline note.

Python: sets the client IP address that the PAC script sees, which changes the result of later find_proxy calls.
C: compiles the README's example program against the pacparser shared library (the README's prompt prefix is omitted here).
C: runs the compiled example with a PAC file, a URL and a host, and prints the proxy string.

brief.install_notes: For Python, pip install pacparser works with prebuilt modules for 64-bit Linux, Windows, MacOS-Intel and MacOS-ARM, on Python 3.8 through 3.14. Other prebuilt binaries are on the GitHub releases page, and the latest builds are on GitHub Actions artifacts. Building from source is described in an INSTALL file in the repo. C programs link with -lpacparser. The README shows no accounts, licence keys or runtime configuration beyond calling init, parse_pac and cleanup in order.
brief.standout: It is a small embeddable parser for a mechanism most people never see running: browsers run a PAC script to pick a proxy and the script can branch on URL, source IP and time. It runs that JavaScript in an embedded QuickJS engine, so any C or Python program can make the same proxy decision.
brief.status: Unknown as to date. The README has a GitHub Actions build badge, a PyPI version badge and a Repology badge, and it lists Python wheels up to 3.14 and a pinned version of 1.5.0. The fetched page showed no release date or last-commit date, so I could not confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The API is not thread-safe. Tested platforms are Linux (all Debian architectures), FreeBSD, Mac OS X and Win32. name: patchelf
desc: Modify dynamic ELF executables
why: Edits dynamic ELF executables in place; a useful door into how binaries link, though widely used.

brief.what_it_is: PatchELF is a command-line utility that edits existing dynamic ELF executables and shared libraries in place. You give it a binary and one or more flags, and it rewrites the binary's header metadata: the dynamic loader (ELF interpreter), the RPATH/RUNPATH search directories, the DT_NEEDED dependency list, and a library's SONAME. name: patchutils
desc: Small collection of programs that operate on patch files
why: Operates on patch files as data, letting you split, filter and rewrite diffs, a neat look at what patches really are.

brief.what_it_is: Patchutils is a collection of about two dozen command-line programs that read, transform and rewrite patch (diff) files as data. Inputs are existing patch files; outputs are new patch files or listings. Tools cover combining two incremental patches into one (combinediff), generating an incremental patch between two patches (interdiff), filtering a patch by file wildcard (filterdiff), splitting a patch into one-file-per-patch pieces (splitdiff), and listing affected files (lsdiff). The executables list also includes gitdiff, gitshow, svndiff, patchview, move-to-front, and others.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no separate mission statement. It describes the tools as fixing up real-world patches: correcting output from 'cvs diff', repairing hand-edited patches, and reviewing or merging pre-patches against the same source tree.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain internals. It describes each tool by its job: interdiff compares two patches against a common source, combinediff merges two incremental patches so each file is altered only once, and rediff compares an original patch with a hand-edited one to fix offsets and counts.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no install steps beyond the signed release tarballs at https://cyberelk.net/tim/data/patchutils/stable/ and a git repository on GitHub. No runtime, account, or configuration requirements are mentioned.
