name: payload-dumper-go
desc: Android OTA payload dumper written in Go
why: Extracts partitions from Android OTA update payloads, a practical way to take firmware apart and see what is inside.

brief.what_it_is: payload-dumper-go is a command-line tool that unpacks Android OTA update packages. It takes a raw payload.bin file or an OTA zip (detected by content) and writes out each partition as an image file, such as boot, system, vendor, and so on. It can list the partitions with -l, dump selected ones with -p, and rebuild full images from incremental (delta) OTAs when given a directory of base images with -old. It is written in Go and also usable as a library via the github.com/ssut/payload-dumper-go/payload package.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a single motivating problem. Its framing is practical: it is a fast, verifying Android OTA payload dumper, and it stresses speed, bit-exact output, and verification that fails loudly.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes parallel decompression of partition operations, with a worker count set by -c (default: number of CPUs). It shells out to the system xz library through CGO rather than the pure Go xz implementation, which the author found about 6 times slower. For delta OTAs it regenerates the dm-verity hash tree and FEC parity that the payload omits, and it checks operation data, source images, and final images with sha256. The payload format is defined by update_engine's update_metadata.proto, linked in the README.

name: pbc
desc: Pairing-based cryptography
why: A pairing-based cryptography library from Stanford, a glimpse into bilinear maps, though it is a library at heart.

brief.what_it_is: PBC (Pairing-Based Cryptography) is a free C library, built on GMP, that performs the mathematical operations underlying pairing-based cryptosystems. It provides routines for elliptic curve generation, elliptic curve arithmetic, and pairing computation. The homepage describes it as meant to be the backbone for implementations of pairing-based cryptosystems, and it ships example programs for several such systems. The fetched pages do not describe the exact inputs and outputs at the API level.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Ben Lynn, wrote it as a library so that pairing-based cryptosystems could be built on a common base, with speed and portability as goals. He says the API is abstract enough that a programmer needs only an elementary understanding of pairings, without much elliptic curve or number theory.
brief.how_it_works: PBC sits on top of GMP for big-integer arithmetic and implements curve generation, group arithmetic and the pairing itself in C. The homepage says that thanks to GMP, pairing times are reasonable despite the code being C. The pages I read do not go into deeper mechanism detail; the manual's internals chapter covers Type A through Type I curve internals but I did not open it.
brief.install_notes: PBC requires the GMP library. The download page lists the pbc-1.0.0.tar.gz source tarball, a Windows binary zip compiled with MinGW, and a Visual C++ conversion zip (pbc-0.4.7-vc.zip). It also lists third-party packaging: a Homebrew entry, Ubuntu packages, and a Gentoo overlay. The manual's Installing chapter covers a Simple Makefile and a Quick start, which I did not read. No accounts or hardware are needed.
brief.standout: The author writes his own retrospective on the page and tells readers to use something else today: he recommends MIRACL Core, which he says he used himself, and he contrasts its RFC 9380 hash-to-curve against the ad hoc rejection sampling in his own library. Few libraries openly point users to a successor like this.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage says the library is 'almost frozen in amber' and is kept alive by volunteer patches. The current release on the download page is pbc-1.0.0, and the manual is revision 1.0.0 dated 2006. I did not see a last-commit date for the git repository, so I cannot say more precisely.
brief.caveats: The author's own homepage recommends a newer library, MIRACL Core, for new work. Hash-to-point uses a rejection sampling routine that the author does not present as standard. The benchmark figures (11ms fastest pairing, 31ms short pairing) are from a 1GHz Pentium III and are historical. The homepage describes the library as free but I did not find an explicit license statement in the pages I read. The examples are demonstrations and the author says more work would be needed before any were practical applications. The manual has a Security issues chapter that I did not read.
quotes: The PBC library is designed to be the backbone of implementations of pairing-based cryptosystems, thus speed and portability are important goals.
I started the PBC library decades ago, for a degree. I also graduated decades ago, and as a result, the library is almost frozen in amber.
Today, I would recommend using a newer library instead, such as MIRACL Core, which I used myself when I last played with pairings.

name: pcsc-lite
desc: Middleware to access a smart card using SCard API
why: Middleware for smart card readers, a door into APDU and smartcard protocols most developers never touch.

brief.what_it_is: pcsc-lite is a middleware library and daemon that gives applications access to smart card readers through the PC/SC API (SCard API). Client programs call the standard SCard functions, and the pcscd daemon talks to the physical reader and its driver, typically via USB. Its executables include pcscd, the daemon, and pcsc-spy, a debugging tool that spies on API calls. The project site describes it as 'Middleware to access a smart card using SCard API (PC/SC).' Input is smart card reader hardware with cards inserted, and output is card responses to APDU commands, returned to the calling application.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a free, portable implementation of the PC/SC standard for smart card access. The project was started by David Corcoran in 1999, and Ludovic Rousseau has been the main author since 2001.
brief.how_it_works: The site does not describe the internal architecture in detail. It mentions a card movement notification mechanism, card auto power on and off, and pcscd auto start through systemd. Its debug section describes an API spy built on the LIBPCSCLITE_DELEGATE mechanism. The homepage also notes that PC/SC clients and the server can run on two different hosts.

name: pdfalyzer
desc: PDF analysis toolkit
why: Builds a tree and graph view of PDF internals for forensic poking; a decent way to see a file format's structure.

brief.what_it_is: A Python command-line tool, with a library API, for analysing the internal structure of a PDF file. It takes a PDF and produces Rich-rendered tree and graph views of its object structure (exportable as HTML, ANSI text, PNG or SVG), font details with character maps, and YARA-based scans of the embedded binary streams for suspicious byte patterns. It also ships three helper commands for combining PDFs, extracting page ranges, and extracting text with OCR on embedded images. It does not render or execute PDF content.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted a tool that combined visualisation and a usable data model with binary analysis. He found Didier Stevens's pdfid.py and pdf-parser.py strong but lacking in visualisation and in a data model for writing your own code, and found Peepdf buggy and out of date.
brief.how_it_works: The Pdfalyzer class wraps PyPDF's internal objects in AnyTree NodeMixin nodes to build a logical tree, with non-tree references drawn as symlink nodes. Font information is pulled together across several objects into FontInfo, and the BinaryScanner class searches embedded streams using YARA rules (via The Yaralyzer). Output is rendered with Rich.

name: peg
desc: Program to perform pattern matching on text
why: Piumarta's PEG pattern matcher, a compact tool tied to parsing expression grammars with an old-school feel.

brief.what_it_is: peg and leg are command-line tools that read a Parsing Expression Grammar (PEG) from files or standard input and write C source for a recursive-descent parser. The generated C file defines a function yyparse() that returns non-zero when the input matches the grammar and zero when it does not. peg reads the original Ford-style PEG syntax, and leg reads a variant with lex/yacc-style conventions. Grammar rules can carry C actions that run after a successful match, with the matched text available as yytext.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents leg as an attractive replacement for parsers built with lex and yacc. The stated advantages are unlimited backtracking, ordered choice for disambiguation, and combining scanning and parsing in one activity.
brief.how_it_works: The grammar is a set of named rules whose patterns are matched left to right, descending into named sub-rules and backtracking on failure, so the parser performs a depth-first search for the first successful path. Predicates (& and !) are evaluated during the search, while actions run only after a complete match, in left-to-right order along the successful path. The output is plain C with a yy/YY prefix on external symbols, which the manual says is meant to avoid namespace pollution in client programs.

commands_seen.context: From the manual's simple example: writes the generated parser for the grammar in username.peg into username.c.

The manual's SYNOPSIS line; leg takes the same form. -h prints options, -o writes output to a file instead of stdout, -P suppresses #line directives, -v is verbose to stderr, -V prints version to stderr.
Quoted from the BUGS section, which notes that leg's manual page is read via 'man peg'.

brief.install_notes: The page documents no installer beyond the source tarball (peg-0.1.19.tar.gz) and the Brew formula. Building from source needs a C compiler, and the version history mentions Win32 and MacOS build files added in 0.1.11. The generated parser needs no runtime and carries no license burden. A leg-mode.el Emacs mode is also distributed. A C program using the output calls yyparse() in a loop, and the manual's example adds a main() for that.
brief.standout: It is a small, old-school PEG-to-C generator that predates and sits outside the usual modern PEG toolchains, with a leg dialect designed as a drop-in conceptual replacement for lex and yacc. Its design choices (ordered choice, unlimited backtracking, a single pass that does both scanning and parsing, and the author's own quirky operator names) are documented openly in the manual's BUGS section.
brief.status: quiet. The latest stable release is 0.1.19, dated 2023-03-06. A development version 0.1.20 is dated 2023-11-19 and described as 'updated periodically'. The page gives no later date and I saw no repository activity to check against.
brief.caveats: Left recursion is detected in the grammar but not handled correctly in the generated parser; the manual suggests rewriting it as a repeatable suffix. A grammar that accepts empty input will loop forever, so the manual recommends using + or adding !. at the end. The manual lists missing lex features such as yywrap() and yyin, says diagnostics are obscure, and says the generated code lacks #line directives to point C errors back to the grammar. The manual also states that the operators ! and ~ 'should really be named the other way around'. The output targets C only. Named Windows and MacOS build files exist, but the page does not describe platform testing.
quotes: Unlike lex and yacc, peg and leg support unlimited backtracking, provide ordered choice as a means for disambiguation, and can combine scanning (lexical analysis) and parsing (syntactic analysis) into a single activity.
peg is distributed under the MIT license. It will not infect your project with a contagious disease license if you decide to modify it for your own use.
The parsers that peg and leg create are unencumbered and you are free to use and/or distribute them any way you like.

name: pgpdump
desc: PGP packet visualizer
why: Dumps the packet structure of PGP messages, a good way to see how OpenPGP data is actually laid out.

brief.what_it_is: pgpdump is a command-line PGP packet visualizer written by Kazu Yamamoto. You give it a PGP file, either binary or ASCII-armored, and it prints the packet structure: each packet's tag, length, and version, plus its fields such as signature type, hash and public-key algorithms, creation times, salts, fingerprints, and signature bytes. It covers OpenPGP (RFC 9580 and RFC 4880), the post-quantum algorithms of RFC 9980, PGP version 2 (RFC 1991), and the LibrePGP extensions generated by GnuPG. The homepage's example takes the RFC 9580 Appendix A.7 signed message and prints each packet with its fields.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it is very hard to understand the data structure inside a PGP file by looking at it, so pgpdump shows the packet layout in readable form.
brief.how_it_works: PGP output is binary or ASCII armor (Base64-like text between BEGIN and END lines). pgpdump decodes the armor, walks the packet sequence, and prints a labelled line for each packet and each field. The homepage shows this with a sample where the one-pass signature, literal data, and signature packets are listed in order with their algorithms and byte counts.

commands_seen.context: Shows the ASCII-armored sample file (the RFC 9580 Appendix A.7 signed message) before it is dumped.

name: picat
desc: Simple, and yet powerful, logic-based multi-paradigm programming language
why: A logic-based multi-paradigm language blending Prolog-style search with imperative features, unusual and worth an evening.

brief.what_it_is: Picat is a logic-based, multi-paradigm programming language for general-purpose work, built on pattern-matching rules that define predicates, functions, and actors. It takes Picat source programs, including scripts that read files, and runs them on its own virtual machine. It also supports constraint modeling through solver modules (cp, sat, mip, smt) and planning built on tabling. The homepage says it can be used for symbolic computation, scripting, and modeling tasks.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Picat as a simple yet powerful language that mixes declarative features (explicit non-determinism, unification, functions, list comprehensions, constraints, tabling) with imperative ones (assignments, loops) so everyday programming stays practical. It claims to be more expressive and scalable than Prolog, and to suit problems that would otherwise need an imperative algorithm.
brief.how_it_works: Programs are sets of rules with pattern matching, which the homepage says lets the implementation index rules and run faster than Prolog. Tabling memoizes calls and answers, and mode declarations such as max on an argument let tabled search keep only the best answer; the homepage's Euler #67 example uses this to solve a 100-row triangle in 0.01 seconds. The implementation uses a well-designed virtual machine with a memory manager that garbage-collects and grows its stacks and data areas as needed.
brief.install_notes: The homepage text does not describe installation steps, hardware needs, or first-run configuration. It links to a Download section, which I did not follow. The Brew formula installs an executable named picat.
brief.standout: Picat puts explicit non-determinism, tabling with aggregate modes, and a common interface across several constraint solvers (cp, sat, mip, smt) into one language that also reads like a scripting language. Its example planner solves the Farmer's problem by tabling state transitions with best_plan rather than using a separate planner.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists a Version 3.9#12 release dated 8/28/2026, competition results at XCSP'26 and MiniZinc'26, and a news feed with recent items, including a web-based IDE and editor integrations for IntelliJ, Emacs, VS Code, and Geany.
brief.caveats: Performance and expressiveness claims (order-of-magnitude fewer lines than Prolog, faster than Prolog through pattern-matching indexing) are the authors' own assertions on the homepage, not independent benchmarks. The homepage says nothing about supported platforms or the license beyond 'Picat can be used for any fair purpose, including commercial applications'. The homepage content came from the site's HTML text; I did not read the separate documentation pages.
quotes: Simple, and yet powerful, logic-based multi-paradigm programming language
Picat is a rule-based language, in which predicates, functions, and actors are defined with pattern-matching rules.
I think Picat is like a perfect Swiss army knife that you can do anything with.

name: pict
desc: Pairwise Independent Combinatorial Tool
why: Pairwise combinatorial test generation is a genuinely interesting covering-array idea, though the tool itself is fairly plain.

brief.what_it_is: PICT is a command-line tool that generates a compact set of test cases from a plain-text model file. You list parameters and their possible values, optionally add sub-models, constraints, weights, aliases, and negative values, and PICT prints a tab-separated table of test cases. The default goal is that every pair of values across parameters appears in at least one test case, and /o raises the order to triplets or higher. The output goes to stdout and any warnings or errors go to stderr.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says PICT produces tests 'more effective than manually generated tests and in a fraction of the time required by hands-on test case design.' Its framing is that exhaustive testing of all combinations is impractical, and that 'Research shows that testing all pairs is an effective alternative to exhaustive testing and much less costly.'
brief.how_it_works: The model file has a parameter section, optional sub-model lines like { PLATFORM, CPUS, RAM, HDD } @ 2, and optional constraints written as IF ... THEN ... predicates over [Parameter] names. The engine packs value combinations into as few rows as it can with deterministic heuristics; /r:N sets a random seed and /b:N tries N seeds and keeps the smallest suite. The doc says different seeds commonly change the row count by about 5% to 10%, while coverage stays the same.

Sub-models let you set a different combination order for a group of parameters, such as hardware, which keeps the number of distinct hardware configurations down.

name: picoruby
desc: Smallest Ruby implementation for microcontrollers
why: A tiny Ruby runtime for microcontrollers, a fun look at squeezing a high-level language onto very small hardware.

brief.what_it_is: PicoRuby is an alternative mruby implementation of Ruby aimed at microcontrollers, such as the Raspberry Pi Pico and Pico 2 W. name: pixiewps
desc: Offline Wi-Fi Protected Setup brute-force utility
why: Offline WPS PIN recovery exploiting weak entropy in the protocol, a revealing look at how a Wi-Fi handshake can leak secrets.

brief.what_it_is: Pixiewps is a C command-line tool that brute-forces a Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) PIN offline, using the "pixie-dust" weakness in some implementations' low or non-existent entropy. The user feeds it values captured from a WPS exchange (public keys, hashes, authentication key, nonces) and it prints the PIN if the target is vulnerable. Since version 1.4 it can also recover the WPA-PSK from a complete passive capture (M1 through M7) on some devices, using --mode 3. The README says the tool is meant for educational purposes only.
brief.why_it_exists: The README contrasts it with online WPS brute-forcing in tools like Reaver or Bully, which can take hours; Pixiewps aims to get the PIN in seconds or minutes, if the target is vulnerable. It is based on Dominique Bongard's 2014 offline attack research and started as a community project on the Kali Linux forums.
brief.how_it_works: The offline attack works from values captured during a WPS exchange rather than by sending guesses to the access point. The README says the common usage needs a modified Reaver or Bully that prints the Authentication Session key (--authkey), and recommends reaver-wps-fork-t6x. The --dh-small (-S) option, which relies on private key 1 and public key 2, is documented as deprecated and should never be used with Reaver.

name: pkcs11-tools
desc: Tools to manage objects on PKCS#11 crypotographic tokens
why: A door into PKCS#11 hardware tokens and HSM object handling, a protocol few developers have poked at.

brief.what_it_is: pkcs11-tools is a toolkit of small command-line utilities for managing keys and objects on tokens that implement the PKCS#11 interface, including hardware tokens and HSMs. Its commands are modelled on Unix tools: p11ls, p11mv, p11rm, p11od and p11more. It also has commands that generate keys (p11keygen), generate CSRs (p11req) and self-signed certificates (p11mkcert), import certificates, public keys and data files, wrap and unwrap keys (p11wrap, p11unwrap, p11rewrap), and initialise or reset tokens (p11init). The tools work with software tokens such as SoftHSM, NSS and Kryoptic as well as vendor libraries, and there are with_xxx wrapper scripts that locate a vendor's library for you.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the toolkit is for key management tasks on PKCS#11 tokens, and that its commands are compatible with many implementations, including both IBM and Oracle JVMs. The author is Eric Devolder at Mastercard.
brief.how_it_works: Each p11* command is a small program that loads a PKCS#11 library, which can be selected with -l or the PKCS11LIB environment variable, and then selects a slot and token with -s and -t. It then works on token objects by name, such as pubk/rsa or seck/aes-128, and the README says a PIN can be supplied with -p or PKCS11PASSWORD. Wrapped keys are written to a file (p11wrap writes to stdout) with a documented grammar, and p11unwrap reads that file back in. Shell completion for bash and zsh queries the token live, and the man pages are generated from markdown by pandoc at build time.

brief.install_notes: Build from source with ./bootstrap.sh, ./configure and make install, and the README asks you to check the prerequisites in docs/INSTALL.md first. The build needs OpenSSL 3.x (libcrypto 3.0.0 or newer). Post-quantum CSR and certificate creation needs libcrypto 3.5.0 or newer, and PQC is on by default unless configured with --disable-pqc. Compiling on macOS requires brew. The README says the project builds on Linux, and older AIX and Solaris are deprecated. Windows builds use cross-compilers, and the Windows packages ship HTML docs instead of man pages. Shell completion for bash and zsh installs automatically after make install, but variables such as PKCS11LIB must be exported for the completion to see them. AWS CloudHSM support is disabled by default and needs its own setup. The brew formula's executable list includes the with_xxx wrapper scripts.
brief.standout: Most PKCS#11 tooling is a thin wrapper around one vendor's library, but this one gives you a Unix-style file-manager set (ls, mv, rm, cat, od) that works across many tokens. Its wrapped-key files are a documented format, so you can wrap a key on one token and unwrap it on another, and p11rewrap does both steps in one command, with the session key wrapped under one or more keys.
brief.status: Maintained. The README's news section has entries up to August 2026, with the 3.1.0 release described as adding a full set of man pages and a unit and integration test suite. The 3.0.0 release in July 2026 followed a gap of about three years, so release cadence is irregular. I did not check commit dates or the release page directly.
brief.caveats: Requires OpenSSL 3.x, so the older OpenSSL 1.1.1 is no longer supported. PQC CSR and certificate features need libcrypto 3.5.0 or newer. AIX and Solaris support is deprecated and may be removed. The AWS CloudHSM limits listed in the README are significant: certificates are not supported, attribute changes are not supported so p11mv and p11setattr do not work, p11od does not work, and wrap and unwrap templates are not supported. The README says ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are supported, but the CSR and certificate features depend on the OpenSSL version. The README's SoftHSM p11slotinfo sample has a stray line of shell output at the top, so treat it as illustrative. The license is Apache 2.0, and the README's section headings and the desc field tell me nothing about the project's stability beyond the news items.

name: plink1
desc: Whole-genome association analysis toolset
why: Whole-genome association toolset is real science you can run, though it is a standard, somewhat dated genetics tool.

brief.what_it_is: PLINK 1.9 is a command-line toolset for whole-genome association analysis of genotype data. It reads PLINK binary (.bed/.bim/.fam) and text (.ped/.map) filesets, plus VCF/BCF, Oxford .gen/.bgen, 23andMe text, and GCTA GRM matrices. It writes new filesets (for example via --make-bed or --recode), summary statistics such as allele frequencies, missingness, Hardy-Weinberg and LD, and association results such as --assoc, --linear, --logistic, and --pca for population structure. The homepage describes it as 'a free, open-source whole genome association analysis toolset, designed to perform a range of basic, large-scale analyses in a computationally efficient manner.'
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a comprehensive update to the original PLINK, written by Shaun Purcell, and developed by Christopher Chang with support from the NIH-NIDDK's Laboratory of Biological Modeling, the Purcell Lab, and others. The point is running standard large-scale genetic association analyses efficiently on genotype datasets.
brief.how_it_works: It is a single 'plink' executable driven by flags, each with a documented role in a pipeline: filter samples and variants, convert or merge filesets, compute statistics, then run tests and post-process reports. The homepage's index covers data management, basic statistics, LD, IBD, population stratification, association, family-based tests, epistasis, and scoring. Development builds are published alongside the stable release, and the changelog lists bug fixes per date.

name: pmdmini
desc: Plays music in PC-88/98 PMD chiptune format
why: Plays PC-88/98 PMD chiptune files, an old Japanese sound format you can listen to straight from the terminal.

brief.what_it_is: pmdmini is a C library with a simple API for playing back PMD music, the chiptune format made with the Professional Music Driver for PC-98 computers. Its README describes it as a library rather than a player. The homepage README does not document the pmdplay command-line tool that the Homebrew formula installs, so what pmdplay accepts and prints is not confirmed here. The library takes a PMD file path and renders PCM samples at a chosen rate, such as 48000 Hz. It also exposes the song length, title and composer (both Shift-JIS), track count, and the current notes per channel.
brief.why_it_exists: The PC-98 had a Yamaha YM2203 or YM2608 sound chip, and many games and songs were written for it using PMD. The README says pmdmini exists to allow playing back that music, which it describes as a library built on earlier PMD sound engines.
brief.how_it_works: The caller initialises the library with pmd_init, checks the file with pmd_is_pmd, sets the sample rate with pmd_setrate, and opens the file with pmd_play. It then calls pmd_renderer in a loop to fill a buffer of 16-bit samples, and pmd_get_current_notes for per-channel note data. The README says the library is based on PMDXMMS and PMDWin and uses the OPNA FM sound generator from M88/cisc.
brief.install_notes: The homepage README shows no build steps, dependencies, or first-run configuration. It contains only C API sample code. The brew formula lists the executable as pmdplay, but the README does not show how to run it.
brief.standout: It is a small, portable C reimplementation of a 1990s Japanese sound driver, built from several earlier engines and used in Android and other players. The README also says the library can report per-channel note data during playback, which a terminal player could show visually.

name: pngcheck
desc: Print info and check PNG, JNG, and MNG files
why: Dissects PNG, JNG, and MNG chunk structure, a useful way to see how image file formats are actually laid out.

brief.what_it_is: pngcheck is a command-line utility that checks PNG image files, including animated PNG, for validity, and prints information about the metadata inside a file (apart from the image data itself). It takes one or more image files as input and prints a chunk-by-chunk report to the terminal, with each chunk's offset and length, decoded header fields, and warnings or errors. The sample output shows it reporting dimensions, bit depth, and color profile chunks, and ending with 'ERRORS DETECTED' when it finds a problem. The README also covers JNG and MNG in the scout notes, though the README text itself focuses on PNG.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as a way to check PNG files for validity and to report their metadata, and it tracks new PNG specification editions (Third and Fourth Edition) as they add chunks.
brief.how_it_works: It walks the file's chunk structure and decodes each chunk it recognizes, printing offsets, lengths, and field values, with -v giving the verbose per-chunk detail. It flags problems such as an eXIf chunk appearing after IDAT, which the README says browsers ignore and which the Third Edition no longer permits. It also reports deprecated chunks, as in the sample where an old cLLi chunk is flagged 'do not use'.

commands_seen.context: Sample usage from the README: checks the file with -c (colorized output) and -v (verbose), printing each chunk and ending with ERRORS DETECTED for that file. The -c and -v flags are described only by this example, not by a flag reference.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the Homebrew formula was visible in the README. No runtime, account, or configuration is mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a chunk-level dissector that decodes the newest PNG features (cICP, mDCV, cLLI, animated PNG chunks, caBX content credentials, and Apple's iDOT) and flags obsolete or misplaced chunks, so it doubles as a readable map of how a PNG file is laid out. The README says all registered extension chunks are supported.
brief.status: Maintained as far as the README shows: it is at version 4.0.1 and adds PNG Fourth Edition features (caBX). It is hosted under the pnggroup organization. The README gives no release date, and I did not open the releases or commit history, so I cannot give a last-commit date.
brief.caveats: The README does not mention platform support, license, or known limitations. The README's own changelog-style text says it was derived from pngcheck 3.0.3, and the 3.0.3 README is linked but I did not fetch it. The brew description mentions JNG and MNG, but the README body discusses only PNG.

name: ponyc
desc: Object-oriented, actor-model, capabilities-secure programming language
why: An actor-model language with reference capabilities for data-race freedom, a genuinely unusual design worth exploring.

brief.what_it_is: Pony is an open-source, object-oriented, actor-model programming language that compiles ahead-of-time to native code, with no interpreter or virtual machine. Its type system uses reference capabilities, labels on data that say how it may be shared, and the compiler checks those labels so concurrent programs can be free of data races without locks. The ponyc executable is the compiler; the Homebrew package also installs pony-agent-server, pony-dep, pony-doc, pony-lint, and pony-lsp. Programs can call C libraries through a foreign function interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Pony as a "get-stuff-done" language that puts correctness first, performance second, and simplicity third. It aims to make fast, safe, highly concurrent programs easy to write, with the compiler enforcing the guarantees instead of the programmer.
brief.how_it_works: Reference capabilities are labels attached to data types that describe how data can be shared: immutable data can be shared freely, and isolated data can only be exchanged. Actors are the unit of concurrency and communicate by asynchronous messages, with behaviours declared using "be" and called as methods on other actors. The compiler verifies these labels at compile time, which is how the project claims there are no data races, locks, or deadlocks.
brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: on Windows the minimum is Windows 11 or Windows Server 2022 (build 20348), and Windows 10 is unsupported. On Linux the minimum kernel is 5.3, because process support uses pidfd_open. Building from source needs an SSL/TLS development library (OpenSSL 1.1.x, 3.0.x, or 4.0.x, or LibreSSL) because the standard library's net package depends on it; CMake detects it and configure fails if none is found. The README points to INSTALL.md, BUILD.md (per-distribution package names), and INSTALL_DOCKER.md for further setup. I did not open those files. The brew caveats field is empty.
brief.standout: Most languages that prevent data races do it with locks, borrow checkers, or runtime checks. Pony instead puts reference capabilities in the type system so that the sharing rules are checked at compile time, and the README says it has no locks or atomic operations at all. Its homepage example of three actors coordinating a party is a short way to see the model.
brief.status: Maintained, but the evidence is limited. The README says Pony is still pre-1.0 with breaking changes arriving semi-regularly, and that applications are currently used in production. The README has a current platform support matrix and recent Windows and Linux minimums. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so I could not confirm activity directly.
brief.caveats: Pre-1.0, so breaking changes happen semi-regularly. The homepage says the library ecosystem is small and there is no IDE. Windows 10 and Linux kernels older than 5.3 are unsupported. FreeBSD and OpenBSD are tested in CI but have no prebuilt binaries, and FreeBSD and OpenBSD arm64 are unsupported. Source builds need an SSL development library. The homepage explicitly says Pony is not the right choice today for projects that need a large ecosystem and stable APIs. The license is 2-Clause BSD.
quotes: Pony is still pre-1.0 and as such, semi-regularly introduces breaking changes.
Pony doesn't have locks or atomic operations. The type system ensures at compile time that your concurrent program can never have data races.
Share only immutable data. Exchange only isolated data. The compiler enforces both. No locks needed.
If you ask us, that's pretty damn cool.

name: precice
desc: Coupling library for partitioned multi-physics simulations
why: A coupling library that lets separate physics solvers run together, a real multi-physics simulation you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: preCICE is an open-source coupling library and ecosystem for partitioned multi-physics and multi-scale simulations, including surface and volume coupling. It does not solve physics itself. It takes existing solver programs, each simulating one part of a coupled problem, and connects them so they exchange data during a run. It handles transient coupling, communication, time interpolation, and data mapping between the solvers' meshes. Programs call its API (C++, C, Fortran, Python, Matlab, and others) or load an adapter for a ready-made solver such as OpenFOAM, CalculiX, FEniCS, deal.II, or Nutils. The Homebrew package installs the library plus the command-line tools listed below.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the problem as partitioned coupling: it lets separate, existing solvers that each cover a subpart of the physics run together, which keeps time-to-solution reasonable for complex coupled problems without rewriting each code. The README says preCICE stands for Precise Code Interaction Coupling Environment, and that it is an academic project developed at TU Munich and the University of Stuttgart.
brief.how_it_works: Each solver is a separate program that links the preCICE library, or uses an adapter, and calls it to read and write coupling data at each time step. The homepage describes a pure peer-to-peer design, so solvers communicate directly rather than through a central server. The library handles quasi-Newton acceleration of strong coupling, radial-basis-function data mapping between non-matching meshes, and time interpolation. The coupling scheme (for example serial-explicit) is defined in a preCICE XML configuration file.

commands_seen.context: Docs say to run this in a terminal to check the preCICE installation; it is one of the built-in tools installed with the package (the Homebrew executables list also includes precice-config-doc, precice-config-validate, precice-profiling, and precice-tools, which I did not see documented in the pages I read).

brief.install_notes: The core library is required, and bindings for Python, Fortran, Matlab, Julia, and Rust are installed separately. On Linux, binary packages exist for Ubuntu and an AUR package for Arch and Manjaro. On macOS the docs recommend Homebrew, with a Linux container as an alternative when a solver does not run natively on macOS. On Windows the docs recommend MSYS2, or Ubuntu under WSL 1 or 2. Spack is recommended for building multiple compiler, MPI, or dependency variants. Building from source is recommended for hacking on preCICE, and a demo virtual machine with preCICE and most adapters preinstalled is offered for experimenting. The Homebrew caveats field was empty.
brief.standout: The approach is partitioned rather than monolithic: it couples programs that already exist, including unmodified solvers through adapters, instead of requiring a single new multi-physics code. It also ships a fairly full ecosystem around the library (adapters, bindings, tools, a distribution that pins compatible versions, and a literature guide), and the homepage says it has been used across academia and industry.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists latest release v3.4.1 and a call for contributions to a preCICE Workshop 2027. The GitHub repository shows 984 stars, 302 forks, 5,725 commits on the develop branch, and an active docs page marked 'Updated 13 Oct 26'. I did not see the date of the latest commit or release on the pages I read.
brief.caveats: Coupling a program running on Windows with one running on Linux is described as at least complicated. Under WSL, the Windows firewall prompts on every coupled run, and GUI apps such as ParaView are awkward under WSL 1. Installing from source is easy only if all dependencies come from system packages; otherwise the docs push you to Spack. The license is LGPL-3.0, and the homepage notes that other components use compatible free licenses. The homepage also offers paid support tiers with priority access to developers, which is a business layer on top of the free project. The README is short and mostly points to the external docs site, so I did not see command-line usage beyond precice-version.

name: ppl
desc: Parma Polyhedra Library: numerical abstractions for analysis, verification

brief.what_it_is: The Parma Polyhedra Library (PPL) is a C++ library, per its README, for (not necessarily closed) convex polyhedra and other numerical abstractions. It can handle polyhedra given as intersections of rational linear equalities and strict or non-strict inequalities, plus boxes, bounded difference shapes, octagonal shapes, grids (sets of congruence relations), and finite powersets and products of these. It also solves linear programs with an exact-arithmetic primal simplex, solves parametric integer programming problems, and performs termination analysis by synthesizing linear ranking functions. The README does not describe input or output file formats. The brew package ships three executables: ppl-config, ppl_lcdd, and ppl_pips. The source tree has demos for ppl_lcdd, ppl_pips, and ppl_lpsol.

name: precomp
desc: Command-line precompressor to achieve better compression
why: Decompresses deflate streams inside files to recompress them losslessly, a neat look into how compressed data hides in formats.

brief.what_it_is: Precomp is a command-line precompressor written in C++. It takes an already-compressed file, such as a PDF, PNG, ZIP, GIF, JPG, MP3 or bZip2 file, finds the zLib/Deflate, bZip2, GIF, JPG or MP3 streams inside it, and decompresses them. If a stream can be recompressed to be bit-for-bit identical to the original, Precomp keeps the decompressed data. The output is either a smaller LZMA2-compressed .pcf file, or with -cn a file of decompressed data plus reconstruction data that a stronger compressor can then squeeze further. Precomp can also restore the original file from the .pcf.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Precomp "can be used to further compress files that are already compressed" and "improves compression on some file-/streamtypes", by reversing the compression of the streams inside those files so a general-purpose compressor can see the raw data.
brief.how_it_works: Precomp tries to decompress each stream and then recompress it with the matching codec. If the result is bit-to-bit identical to the original, the decompressed stream replaces the compressed one. For Deflate it uses preflate, which the README credits with creating reconstruction information, and for JPG and MP3 it uses packJPG/brunsli and packMP3. The default output is compressed with LZMA2 into a .pcf file.

name: primecount
desc: Fast prime counting function program and C/C++ library
why: Fast prime counting via combinatorial algorithms, real number theory software you can run to count primes far beyond brute force.

brief.what_it_is: primecount is a command-line program and C/C++ library that counts the primes up to x, for x up to 10^31. You give it a number, such as 1e14, and it prints pi(x), the count of primes less than or equal to x. It can also compute the nth prime (--nth-prime), approximate pi(x) with Riemann R or Li functions, and evaluate phi(x, a). It is built on the combinatorial prime counting algorithms, parallelized with OpenMP.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a program built on highly optimized implementations of the combinatorial prime counting algorithms, so you can count primes far beyond what brute-force sieving can reach. It also says it contains the first open source implementations of the Deleglise-Rivat algorithm and Xavier Gourdon's algorithm.
brief.how_it_works: It implements Legendre, Meissel, Lehmer, Lagarias-Miller-Odlyzko, Deleglise-Rivat and Gourdon formulas, which reduce pi(x) to a sum of phi function values and correction terms (P2, S1, S2, and others) evaluated over a small sieve bound. The default is Gourdon's algorithm. Its nth-prime method estimates the nth prime with the inverse Li or inverse R function, counts primes up to that guess, then runs a segmented sieve forward to the exact answer. A custom load balancer is shared across implementations and, per the README, scales to hundreds of CPU cores.

name: primer3
desc: Program for designing PCR primers
why: Real molecular biology software for designing PCR primers, a genuine scientific tool you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: Primer3 is a command-line C program, with Perl test scripts, that designs PCR primers from a DNA sequence. The core binary, primer3_core, reads Boulder-IO text records from stdin or a file. Each record gives a template sequence, optional target and exclusion regions, and PRIMER_ settings such as size, melting temperature, GC content and product size range. It prints ranked candidate primer pairs in the same Boulder-IO format, or a readable report when run with --format_output. The homepage says it can also design hybridization probes (internal oligos) and sequencing primers. The brew executables list also includes ntdpal, ntthal, oligotm, long_seq_tm_test, amplicon3_core and primer3_masker; the README names only primer3_core, ntdpal, oligotm and long_seq_tm_test.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes PCR as an essential and ubiquitous tool in genetics and molecular biology, and says PCR is used for many different goals, so primer3 exposes many input parameters that let the user define what makes a good primer for their goal. The README frames it as doing everything from mispriming libraries and sequence quality data to generating internal oligos.
brief.how_it_works: The manual says primer3 scores candidate primers against criteria including oligo melting temperature, size, GC content and primer-dimer possibilities, PCR product size, positional constraints within the template, and ectopic priming (amplifying the wrong sequence). Some criteria are hard constraints and others are terms in an objective function that defines the optimal pair. Thermodynamic alignment is used for oligo-oligo and hairpin checks by default from version 2.3 onward, and it needs parameter files from a primer3_config directory. The masker component (primer3_masker) masks template sequence before design.

name: prjtrellis
desc: Documenting the Lattice ECP5 bit-stream format
why: Documents the bitstream format of Lattice ECP5 FPGAs, a rare look inside how programmable chips are actually configured.

brief.what_it_is: Project Trellis is an open-source set of tools and a device database for Lattice ECP5 FPGAs. Its C++ library, libtrellis, reads and writes ECP5 bitstreams, tiles and the Project Trellis databases, with Python bindings via pybind11. The README says it provides the device database and tools for bitstream creation, and it sits between Yosys (Verilog synthesis) and nextpnr (place and route) in a fully open flow. The brew listing names five executables (ecpbram, ecpmulti, ecppack, ecppll, ecpunpack), but the README does not describe them individually, so their exact roles are unverified here.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Project Trellis documents the Lattice ECP5 bit-stream format and internal architecture, enabling a fully open-source flow for ECP5 FPGAs. It says it follows the lead of Project X-Ray, which documents the bitstream format for Xilinx Series 7 devices.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes a black-box process: Lattice Diamond is asked to generate a large number of designs, which are turned into bitstreams. The bitstreams are then cross-correlated to discover what different bits do. These generator scripts are called fuzzers, after the software-testing idea of fuzzing. The resulting database can be downloaded precompiled (prjtrellis-db) or regenerated from scratch by running the fuzzers, which the README says takes several hours.

name: primesieve
desc: Fast C/C++ prime number generator
why: Fast prime generator that lets you count primes to enormous limits and explore number theory at home.

brief.what_it_is: primesieve is a command-line program and C/C++ library for quickly generating prime numbers. You give it a range, such as primesieve 1e10 to count primes up to 10 billion, and it prints the count. With --print it lists the primes, and with --count=2 or --print=2 it counts or prints twin primes (k-tuplets up to 6 are supported). It can handle limits up to 2^64, and it also has a built-in CPU and RAM stress test.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a fast, cache-efficient way to generate primes and prime k-tuplets to very large limits, using all CPU cores when ordering does not matter. The scout notes describe it as a way to count primes to enormous limits and explore number theory at home.
brief.how_it_works: It uses the segmented sieve of Eratosthenes with wheel factorization, with run time O(n log log n) and memory O(sqrt n). For primes above 2^32 it uses the bucket sieve to improve cache efficiency. It detects the CPU's L1 and L2 cache sizes and sizes its data structures to match, using about 8 bytes per sieving prime per thread.

name: probe-rs-tools

brief.what_it_is: probe-rs is a Rust toolkit for talking to microcontrollers through hardware debug probes. You give it a debug probe (CMSIS-DAP, J-Link, ST-Link, FTDI, ESP32 USB JTAG, WLink, Blackmagic, and others) and a target chip name, and you can flash a firmware binary (ELF, BIN or IHEX), run it, and stream RTT and defmt output back to your console. It also exposes a library API for reading and writing target memory, halting, stepping and setting breakpoints, and a Debug Adapter Protocol server for VS Code and other editors. brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as 'a modern, embedded debugging toolkit, written in Rust', with the goal 'to provide a toolkit to interact with a variety of embedded MCUs and debug probes'. brief.how_it_works: The library opens a debug probe and attaches to a named chip, then talks to ARM, RISC-V and Xtensa cores over SWD or JTAG. Flash programming uses CMSIS-Pack flash algorithms, and target descriptions are generated from CMSIS-Packs with the target-gen tool. The README also says probe-rs can drive SWD directly from a Linux host's GPIO or spidev interface through a plugin crate, without a dedicated probe.

name: prog8

brief.what_it_is: Prog8 is a structured, compiled programming language for the 8-bit 6502/6510/65c02 CPU family, with a 32-bit Motorola 68000 backend as well. You write source files (.p8) in its block-and-subroutine syntax, and the prog8c compiler turns them into native machine code for a chosen target machine, such as the Commodore 64, Commodore 128, Commodore PET, Commander X16, or Amiga. The compiler relies on the external 64tass cross assembler to produce the final binary. The README and docs describe it as offering many conveniences over raw assembly while staying low-level enough for high-performance programs.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as giving "all advantages of a higher level language over having to write assembly code manually" for 8-bit home computers from the late 1970s and 1980s. The docs say it aims to provide conveniences over raw assembly, even with a macro assembler, while staying low level enough for fast programs.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler reads .p8 module source files and generates code for the selected target, with target differences handled by the compiler flag. The README says that if a program uses only standard Kernal and Prog8 library routines, the same program can be compiled for different machines by changing the target flag. The README also notes that the 64tass cross assembler must be on the shell path, and that the compiler can automatically run the program in the VICE emulator after a successful build.

Building from source needs a Java SDK and Kotlin 1.3.x, or IntelliJ IDEA with the Kotlin plugin; non-Gradle builds may need some manual steps described in the docs. You must install the 64tass cross assembler and put it on your shell path (Windows users download an .exe from SourceForge). For running programs, the compiler assumes the VICE emulator for C64, and for Commander X16 it expects x16emu R42 or newer. Box16 is an alternative with debugging features. It also includes a debugging loop with VICE breakpoints and automatic source label loading.

brief.what_it_is: Prover9 is an automated theorem prover for first-order and equational logic, and Mace4 is its companion that searches for finite models and counterexamples. brief.how_it_works: Prover9 uses resolution and paramodulation, which is the mechanism that lets it reason about equality, to search for a derivation of the goal from the given axioms. Mace4 instead searches for finite models, and a model it finds can serve as a counterexample to a conjecture. The homepage also mentions a portfolio strategy selector trained on 32 problem features that picks a search strategy, but it gives no detail on how that works.

name: prqlc
desc: Simple, powerful, pipelined SQL replacement
why: A pipelined query language that compiles to SQL is a genuinely different way to think about queries.

brief.what_it_is: PRQL (Pipelined Relational Query Language, pronounced 'Prequel') is a language for transforming data, described by its authors as a simple, powerful, pipelined SQL replacement. You write a query as a linear list of transformations (from, filter, derive, group, aggregate, sort, take, join, select), and the compiler turns it into SQL for a chosen database dialect. The tool in this entry is prqlc, the Rust compiler and CLI, which takes PRQL text and emits SQL; it can also format and annotate PRQL queries. Bindings exist for Python (prqlc-python, pyprql), JavaScript (prqlc-js) and R.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames PRQL as a readable alternative to SQL that keeps SQL's explicit, declarative style but forms a logical pipeline and supports variables and functions. The homepage says it was originally designed for analytical queries, emphasizing data transformations, development speed and readability.
brief.how_it_works: Each line of a PRQL query transforms the result of the line before it, so the query reads top to bottom starting from the table. The compiler, written in Rust, translates the pipeline into SQL for the target dialect, and s-strings let you embed raw SQL where PRQL has no equivalent. The homepage example shows 'filter' placed both before and after an aggregation, which PRQL turns into WHERE and HAVING clauses.

brief.what_it_is: Ptunnel is a small command-line program that tunnels TCP connections through ICMP echo request and reply packets, the ones ordinary ping uses. You run a proxy on a publicly reachable machine and a client on your own machine. The client listens on a local TCP port and forwards each connection, via pings, to a destination you name, so for example an ssh session to a remote host can reach that host through the proxy. Input is TCP traffic on the client's local port; output is the same TCP stream arriving at the destination, with the proxy converting between ping packets and TCP data.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it for the case of an open wireless network that lets you ping anywhere but blocks outgoing TCP and UDP, so you cannot check mail. In the author's words, 'For those times when everything else is blocked.'
brief.how_it_works: The client sends ICMP echo requests (type 8) and the proxy answers with echo replies (type 0), with ptunnel's own packet format carried in the payload, including a magic-number flag to tell its packets apart from normal pings. Each packet carries sequence and acknowledgement numbers modelled on TCP, and the sender resends the first unacknowledged packet after 1.5 seconds without an ack. Optional password authentication uses an MD5 challenge-response, and a random ICMP identifier separates multiple concurrent tunnels.

commands_seen.context: Compiling from source is just running make, with no configure step. The author says there is no ./configure, make, make install, just make. On Windows the target is make ptunnel.exe.
Starts the proxy on the remote machine. Root is needed for raw sockets.

brief.install_notes: Needs root on both ends, preferably, because raw sockets are used. On a POSIX system you need libpcap and its headers (a dev package on Ubuntu) if you want packet capture. On Windows you need mingw and WinPcap to build. Build is plain make. The README lists Debian packages from a third-party repository, RPMs, Solaris packages, an iPhone build for jailbroken devices, and a Windows binary from another site. Note that the README's Debian repository and some download links point to old third-party hosts and may be dead.
brief.standout: It is a tiny, single-purpose tunnel that uses only the ICMP echo mechanism, so it can work where only ping is allowed. The protocol is documented in unusual depth on the homepage, with the packet format, state codes, sliding window, and MD5 challenge-response all spelled out.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage says 'Last updated: 5. September 2011' and the current version is 0.72, released the same day. I did not check a source repository, so I cannot say whether there have been commits since. The brew formula still exists, so it has been packaged.
brief.caveats: Requires root for normal operation. The brew caveat and the README both say the -u unprivileged mode is not recommended, and on Linux raw sockets still need root either way. Packet capture via libpcap is sometimes needed on Mac OS X and it cuts bandwidth noticeably. The README gives measured maximums of about 150 kb/s down and 50 kb/s up for one tunnel. There is no congestion control, the window is a fixed 64 packets that needs a recompile to change, and ICMP identifier collisions between instances are not detected. Passwords can show up in ps or top output. Gateways that filter ICMP break it, and the author says nothing can be done about that. Source-IP spoofing is listed as experimental. The license is BSD. The homepage was last edited in 2011 and the author says 'I don't use Windows', so Windows support is not maintained by him.

name: pwnat
desc: Proxy server that works behind a NAT
why: A clever hack that punches through NAT using UDP and ICMP, a real door into how NAT traversal actually works.

brief.what_it_is: pwnat is a command-line proxy tool that lets a client behind one NAT reach a server behind a different NAT without port forwarding, a DMZ, or any third party. The server runs in server mode and listens on a UDP proxy port (default 2222), and the client runs in client mode with a local port to listen on plus a remote host and port to reach. Traffic is carried over UDP between the two ends, so TCP services such as HTTP or SSH can be tunnelled through. The README says the client can reach any host and port, or a fixed destination chosen by the server.
brief.why_it_exists: Samy Kamkar's framing is that NAT blocks unsolicited inbound packets, so a server behind NAT normally cannot be reached, and the README presents pwnat as a way to get NAT-to-NAT connections with 'no port forwarding, no DMZ setup, and no 3rd party involvement.' He describes it as a follow-on to his earlier chownat and to udptunnel by Daniel Meekins.
brief.how_it_works: The server repeatedly sends ICMP echo requests to a fixed, unreachable address (3.3.3.3) so that its NAT creates a translation entry. When a client wants to connect, it sends an ICMP Time Exceeded packet to the server that embeds that same echo request; the server's NAT matches it and forwards it inward, which reveals the client's public IP to the server. After that, both sides send UDP packets to each other's public addresses, and each NAT treats the inbound packets as replies to outbound ones, so the UDP session opens from both sides. A keep-alive with a zero-byte payload runs at least every 5 seconds when no other data is flowing.

commands_seen.context: Top-level usage synopsis; -s selects server mode and -c selects client mode.
Starts the server side, allowing anyone to proxy through it (no allowed-host list given).

brief.standout: It achieves NAT-to-NAT UDP connectivity without any relay or cooperating third party, using a stateful-NAT quirk: an ICMP Time Exceeded packet carrying a hard-coded echo request lets the server learn the client's address through its own NAT. The README also explains the rest of the mechanism in plain terms, which makes it a readable case study in NAT traversal.

name: pwntools
desc: CTF framework used by Gallopsled in every CTF
why: A CTF exploitation framework that opens a door into binary exploitation and running programs.

brief.what_it_is: Pwntools is a CTF framework and exploit development library written in Python. You import it into a Python script (the README example starts with `from pwn import *`), set a target context such as architecture and OS, open a connection to a remote service, and send it payloads. It can also assemble and disassemble code, including shellcode generated by its shellcraft module. It ships about 19 command-line tools alongside the library, including asm, checksec, cyclic, disasm, elfpatch, shellcraft, template and unhex.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a CTF framework and exploit development library designed for rapid prototyping, "intended to make exploit writing as simple as possible."
brief.how_it_works: Everything is driven from Python: a script imports the pwn package, configures context(arch, os), and uses helpers such as remote() to talk to a target, asm() and shellcraft to produce machine code, and interactive() to hand control to the user. Most functionality is self-contained Python, but assembling and disassembling foreign architectures calls out to non-Python binutils-style dependencies.

name: qbe
desc: Compiler Backend
why: A tiny, readable compiler backend that shows how real compilers lower code, a clean door into compiler internals.

brief.what_it_is: QBE is a compiler backend, written in C, that takes code in its own SSA-based intermediate language (IL) and emits assembly for amd64 (Linux and macOS), arm64, or riscv64. The homepage's example program is a small .ssa file that defines an add function, calls it, and calls printf. Compiling it with qbe produces assembly (out.s), which you then assemble and link with cc. The output is a normal binary that uses the local libc.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says QBE aims to provide 70% of the performance of industrial optimizing compilers in 10% of the code, to foster language innovation with a compact, user-friendly, and performant backend. The size limit is meant to keep it focused on the essentials and avoid endless diminishing returns.
brief.how_it_works: Front ends emit the QBE IL, which is the same IL used at all compilation stages. The backend then runs optimizations such as copy elimination, sparse conditional constant propagation, and dead instruction elimination, followed by register allocation. The page says the spiller and register allocator are split and use SSA form, which it calls simpler and faster than graph coloring, with a linear allocator that uses hinting and a loop-aware spilling heuristic.

commands_seen.context: Compiles the QBE IL file file.ssa into assembly out.s, then uses the system cc to assemble and link it into a runnable binary. The page says to copy the example into a file and run this.

It notes that compile time was about 2 seconds on a Core 2 Duo with CFLAGS=-O2, which suggests building from source with that flag. The brew formula's description is 'Compiler Backend'.
brief.standout: It is deliberately small and readable, with a stated size budget and a full C ABI implementation, so programs can call into C and be called from C. It is a good, compact door into how real compilers lower code, since the IL, optimizations, and register allocator are all in one small codebase.

name: qdl
desc: Flash firmware on Qualcomm-based devices via USB Emergency Download (EDL) mode
why: Talks to Qualcomm devices in USB emergency download mode, a fascinating low-level firmware door for taking phones apart.

brief.what_it_is: QDL is a command-line tool that talks to Qualcomm devices in USB Emergency Download (EDL) mode. It uploads a flash loader (a Sahara and Firehose programmer, typically prog_firehose_ddr.elf) to the device, then writes firmware images to it using the XML descriptors that come with a build (rawprogram*.xml and patch*.xml). Input is a programmer file plus XML and image files, or an installer zip, flashmap.json or contents.xml. Output is per-region flashing progress and a summary, and the same binary also reads, writes, erases, dumps and lists devices. It can also run as a dry run that never touches hardware.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it lets you flash images on Qualcomm EDL USB devices, and it notes that EDL 'provides low-level access for firmware flashing and recovery', including on unresponsive devices or those with locked bootloaders. It is maintained under the linux-msm project.
brief.how_it_works: QDL matches any USB device with Vendor ID 05c6 that exposes a vendor-specific EDL interface, without relying on Product ID, because new IDs keep appearing. It can use a libusb backend (on Windows this needs WinUSB, for example via Zadig) or, on Windows only, the Qualcomm QDLoader 9008 COM port via the qud backend; the default auto backend polls both. The README describes the Sahara protocol for loading the programmer and the Firehose protocol for writing regions, with --debug printing timestamped SAHARA: and FIREHOSE: log lines.

name: qdmr
desc: Codeplug programming tool for DMR radios
why: Programs DMR radio codeplugs over USB; a real door into amateur radio hardware and its odd file formats.

brief.what_it_is: qdmr is a free, GPL-3.0 licensed GUI and command-line tool for building and writing 'codeplugs', the configuration files that program DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) handsets. You assemble channels, zones, contacts, RX groups, scan lists, radio ID, and APRS/GPS settings for a supported radio, and it uploads them to the device, with downloads from the radio supported too. The stored result is a human-readable text file rather than a vendor binary, so it can be shared between devices. The GUI can pull nearby repeater frequencies from repeatermap.de and fetch the DMR call-sign database for contact auto-completion. The page names a command-line tool, dmrconf, which ships with a man page.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says vendor DMR programming software for cheap radios is hard to use, poorly documented, often Windows-only, and produces device-specific binaries that cannot be shared, so amateur operators must redo regional setup for every model. qdmr is meant to cut the feature set to what amateur use needs and make setup friendlier.
brief.how_it_works: Codeplugs are stored as a device-independent human-readable text file, and the tool converts that to each supported radio's own format for upload. The page says it is derived from Serge KK6ABQ's reverse-engineering of cheap Chinese DMR radio code-plug formats and communication protocols, reworked for interactive use. Repeater and call-sign lookups come from repeatermap.de (which requires an API key from its maintainer) and a downloaded DMR ID database.
brief.install_notes: The page says there are several install routes, from App-package downloads to building from source, and points to a separate install instructions page that I did not fetch. Building requires Qt6, since the page links Qt6 API docs for the GUI and command-line tools. Repeater auto-completion needs a repeatermap.de API key requested from Martin DK3ML, and location lookup uses the locator set in the settings dialog or the OS location service. Radios are connected over USB serial, which the 0.6.2 release note mentions for MacOS 11.
brief.standout: Instead of a binary blob, the codeplug is a plain text file that works across models and vendors, which makes sharing and diffing configs practical. The GUI also pulls real repeater frequencies and the DMR call-sign database, so contacts can be added by callsign instead of numeric DMR ID.
brief.status: Maintained, based on the page: the version history runs through 0.15.0 (adds AnyTone AT-D168UV), there are regular bugfix releases, and the license notice covers 2019-2026. The page gives no release dates or commit dates, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: Only a small set of radios is supported. The author owns just three (Radioddity/Baofeng RD-5R, Retevis RT3S, AnyTone AT-D878UV), and support for the rest comes from reports and testers. Features are deliberately reduced to amateur use, and Serge's dmrconfig supports more models. The support table marks the Baofeng DR-1801-A6 with 'Stay away!', and the 0.9.0-alpha3 release was an alpha after a core rewrite that may have added bugs. The version list repeats 0.12.3 twice and the license line calls it a 'GUI programming tool for Chinese DMR radios', which does not quite match the tagline. Some features (APRS, GPS, call-sign DB upload) only work on radios that support them. The page's own text mentions that DMR encryption is illegal for ham use, but does not describe how the tool handles it.

It takes compiled Tads game files for the Tads virtual machine and runs them on Linux, macOS, or Windows, with a Qt-based interface. It supports both Tads 2 and Tads 3 games, and the homepage says it is fully compatible with HTML TADS (Multimedia TADS). The GitHub README says it could in principle run on any system where Qt exists, but Linux, macOS, and Windows are the main targets.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a multimedia-capable player for TADS games, the Text Adventure Development System, a C-like object-oriented language for authoring interactive fiction. The README describes Tads as similar to Infocom or Legend Entertainment games like Zork.
brief.how_it_works: QTads does not implement the virtual machine from scratch. It builds on Mike Roberts' reference implementations of the T2 and T3 Tads VMs and adds the graphical, multimedia front end. The README says the Tads compiler produces executables for the Tads VM, and QTads runs those programs.

name: quickjs

It takes JavaScript source and runs it through an interpreter via the command-line tool qjs, or can compile JavaScript into standalone executables with qjsc. The command-line interpreter's contextual colorization is implemented in JavaScript. The project also embeds the libregexp, libunicode and dtoa C libraries, which can be reused separately.

name: radamsa
desc: Test case generator for robustness testing (a.k.a. a "fuzzer")
why: A mutation-based fuzzer that quietly generates malformed inputs, a good window into how programs break under strange bytes.

brief.what_it_is: Radamsa is a general-purpose, black-box fuzzer (test case generator) distributed as a single binary with no runtime dependencies. You feed it sample data on stdin or as files, and it emits mutated variants of that data to stdout, to numbered files, or over TCP. The README describes it as a cat-like filter that breaks data in interesting ways as it flows through. It needs no knowledge of the target program or the data format.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames fuzzing as a way to find unexpected program behavior by feeding it varied inputs, and says Radamsa solves the input-generation half of that job while a short shell script handles checking what happened. The stated selling points are that it has already found a slew of bugs in programs that matter, that it is easily scriptable, and that it is easy to get running.
brief.how_it_works: Radamsa mutates the sample data using various heuristics and change patterns that it varies between runs, from a single change to many, including bit flips and more advanced mutations. By default it takes a random seed from /dev/urandom, and a fixed seed (--seed or -s) reproduces the same output. The README suggests testing with a shell loop that flags a crash when the target's exit status is greater than 127.

name: ragel
desc: State machine compiler
why: A state machine compiler that turns regex-like descriptions into fast parsers, a deep and old-school tool for seeing how parsers work.

brief.what_it_is: Ragel is a state machine compiler. You write a machine description that mixes regular-expression operators (union, concatenation, Kleene star) with embedded actions, which are small blocks of host-language code attached to points in the machine. Ragel takes that description and emits C, C++, or x86_64 GNU assembly that runs the machine with no runtime dependencies. The page's example takes a number grammar with actions as input and outputs a chain of goto-based states, and it can also visualize the machine with Graphviz.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage positions Ragel for writing robust protocol implementations, parsing data formats, lexical analysis of programming languages, and validating user input. Its stated goal is to let developers describe recognizers declaratively and run code at exact points during recognition.
brief.how_it_works: Ragel compiles the regular expressions to a deterministic finite automaton and associates the embedded actions with the transitions of that automaton. The generated code can be table-driven or control-flow-driven, and the machine can be minimized with Hopcroft's algorithm. The page also notes operators for controlling non-determinism, building scanners, and statechart-style machines, plus jumping or calling into other parts of a machine from inside an action.

name: radare2
desc: Reverse engineering framework
why: A full reverse engineering framework for binaries, firmware, and running programs; a deep door into taking things apart.

brief.what_it_is: radare2 (r2) is a command-line reverse engineering framework: a set of libraries, tools and plugins for disassembling, analysing, emulating, debugging and patching binaries. It takes files, raw memory, or running processes (locally or via a remote gdb/windbg server) as input and produces disassembly, function lists, hexdumps, control-flow graphs, and edited binaries. The Homebrew package installs about twenty executables, including r2, radare2, rabin2, rasm2, rahash2, radiff2, rafind2, rax2, rarun2, ragg2, and the package manager r2pm.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says r2 is 'a complete rewrite of radare', and that the radare project 'started as a simple command-line hexadecimal editor focused on forensics'. The stated aim is to 'ease reverse engineering tasks' with a full-featured low-level command-line tool that can be scripted.
brief.how_it_works: r2 is a modular C framework. Its command-line shell takes short commands (for example aaa to analyse, afl to list functions, pdf to disassemble a function), and it can be scripted with an embedded JavaScript interpreter or through r2pipe from other languages. Architecture and file-format support, and extra features, come from plugins; r2pm installs third-party plugins such as the r2ghidra decompiler, r2frida, and the iaito Qt GUI.

name: rakudo

why: The main Raku implementation, a rich and idiosyncratic language with unusual ideas about grammars and laziness.

brief.what_it_is: Rakudo is the reference compiler for the Raku programming language, the most mature implementation according to its homepage. It compiles Raku source and runs it on one of three backends: MoarVM, the JVM, or JavaScript, with each backend supporting a somewhat different feature set. The executables installed are raku, rakudo, perl6 and debug or valgrind/gdb/lldb wrapper variants of each. brief.how_it_works: Rakudo is written in NQP and built with a Perl Configure.pl script that can fetch and build MoarVM and NQP for you. Its backends are MoarVM, the JVM, and JavaScript, and multiple backends can be built into one prefix, with each installed under its own name such as rakudo-m or rakudo-j. Installing with make install puts everything in a local prefix, so no administrator privileges are needed.

name: ratarmount
desc: Mount and efficiently access archives as filesystems
why: Mounts archives like tar, zip and rar as random-access filesystems, a clever trick with some depth in its indexing.

brief.what_it_is: Ratarmount is a command-line tool that mounts archives such as TAR (including compressed TAR), ZIP, RAR, 7z, SquashFS/AppImage, and many others as a read-only FUSE filesystem, so you can browse and read files inside without extracting them. It takes an archive (or a folder, or a remote URI) as input and produces a mount point whose contents are the archive's files. It builds an index of file offsets, stored as a SQLite sidecar, so later mounts are fast and reads can seek directly to a file's position. The README also describes a write overlay that tracks changes and can apply them back to the archive.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's problem statement is a large TAR such as the 1.31TB ImageNet set: you may lack the disk space, time, or a fast enough filesystem to extract all 14.2 million files. Earlier tools (archivemount, tarindexer) were slow to mount, did not support recursion or random access well, or needed a database setup.
brief.how_it_works: On first mount, ratarmount scans the archive and records every file's name, ownership, permissions, and offset in an SQLite index, stored next to the archive as <archive>.index.sqlite or in ~/.ratarmount/. For compressed streams (bzip2, gzip, xz, zstd) it also stores seek points so decompression can resume near the requested offset, and it uses parallel decoders where available. FUSE exposes the indexed tree to other programs, and nested archives can be mounted recursively into folders of the same name.

brief.install_notes: Requires Python and FUSE (macFUSE on macOS, fuse on Debian-like Linux). Plain pip is usually enough; the README says pip may need extra system packages (fuse, sqlite3, gcc, liblzo2-dev, libarchive-dev, zlib1g-dev, libzstd-dev, liblzma-dev) when no manylinux wheel exists. On macOS the README suggests brew install macfuse unar libarchive lrzip lzop lzo. Alternatives are a portable AppImage from the releases page (chmod u+x, then run) and conda install -c conda-forge ratarmount. Argument completion needs argcomplete, which is optional. Ratarmount works without the compression backends if installed with --no-deps. There is also a work-in-progress Qt GUI on the gui branch.
brief.standout: Random access to files inside compressed TARs: it stores seek points for bzip2, gzip, xz, and zstd, so reading one file in a huge archive does not require decompressing from the start. Its index is a reusable SQLite sidecar, so the same archive can be remounted in under a second, and it can mount TARs inside TARs recursively and union multiple archives and folders under one mountpoint.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub releases page shows ratarmount 1.3.0 marked Latest, built 2026-05-10, following 1.2.3 (2026-04-19), 1.2.2 (2026-03-13), and 1.2.1 (2025-11-19). The README still shows older 0.15.x examples and install commands, so parts of the docs lag behind the 1.x releases.
brief.caveats: Read-only by default; the write overlay is the only write path described. Random access for xz and zstd works only on block or frame boundaries, so ordinary xz and zstd files are not truly seekable. The README says some remote backends (Samba, Dropbox, etc.) are very experimental and may be slow. Libarchive-backed formats are not random access and must be parsed from the start. Gzip indexes grow with archive size. The README's install examples reference 0.15.x AppImages even though the latest release is 1.3.0. Platform support is Linux and macOS via FUSE; the README does not mention Windows. Licensed MIT. The README says Python 3.6+, but the 1.2.0 release notes say Python 3.7 and 3.8 support was dropped.
quotes: Ratarmount collects all file positions inside a TAR so that it can easily jump to and read from any file without extracting it.

Getting file contents of a mounted archive is generally vastly faster than archivemount and fuse-archive and does not increase with the archive size or file count resulting in the largest observed speedups to be around 5 orders of magnitude!
Ratarmount takes ~15min to create a ~150MB index and <1ms for opening an already created index (SQLite database) and mounting the TAR.
