name: radvd
desc: IPv6 Router Advertisement Daemon
why: IPv6 Router Advertisement daemon is a real door into SLAAC and NDP, the quiet protocol running every IPv6 network.

brief.what_it_is: radvd is the IPv6 Router Advertisement Daemon, a small server run on a Linux or BSD machine acting as an IPv6 router. It listens for Router Solicitation messages and sends Router Advertisement messages (RFC 4861) onto the local LAN, both periodically and when a host asks. Its input is a configuration file (radvd.conf) describing prefixes, lifetimes, DNS options and similar settings for each interface. Its output is the advertisements themselves, which let hosts configure their own addresses and pick a default router. The package also ships radvdump, a companion tool that dumps the Router Advertisements it sees on the wire.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says radvd is run by Linux or BSD systems acting as IPv6 routers and that its messages are required for IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration. The GitHub README adds that hosts can then configure addresses and other parameters automatically and choose a default router from these advertisements.
brief.how_it_works: radvd sends Router Advertisements periodically to the all-routers multicast group and answers Router Solicitations from hosts. Each advertisement carries the options the admin configured, such as prefixes, lifetimes, route information, and DNS (RDNSS and DNSSL) entries. The README's FAQ stresses the design philosophy: radvd only advertises, and it does not assign addresses, configure routes, or run a routing or forwarding daemon. Those jobs are left to the admin or init scripts.

brief.install_notes: Build from source: run ./configure (see configure --help for options), then make and make install. On BSD you may need gmake. Release tarballs (tar.gz or tar.xz) come with signatures and sha256/sha512 checksums. Root or the required privileges are needed, since it opens raw ICMPv6 and netlink sockets, but I did not read this in the pages.
brief.standout: It is a single-purpose daemon that deliberately does less than the router-config tools people expect: it advertises prefixes and options but never configures interfaces or addresses. It is also the reference implementation many Linux distributions use for SLAAC and RDNSS, and its changelog goes back to 2001.

name: ratfor
desc: Rational Fortran
why: Rational Fortran is a preprocessor from the 1970s that turns structured control flow into Fortran, a fine piece of computing history.

brief.what_it_is: Linux Ratfor is a command-line preprocessor that takes Ratfor source, a Fortran dialect with structured control flow (the README's own description is only that Ratfor is short for Rational FORTRAN), and emits FORTRAN 77 source. You then compile that output with a separate FORTRAN 77 compiler such as GNU Fortran. The README mentions a -s command-line option that changes the type of array elements generated for strings. The page says the program is derived from public domain ratfor 1.0 and has been maintained with bug fixes and buffer-overrun hardening.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames Ratfor as a way to write Fortran with rational control structures, and notes it was used in the Software Tools text by Kernighan and Plauger. This Linux version keeps the public-domain tool buildable and patched; the README does not state a broader motive.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the translation mechanism in detail. It says the preprocessor outputs FORTRAN 77, which is then compiled by a standard Fortran compiler. Its change history mentions include-file handling, string directives, and data-statement ordering, which are the parts of the preprocessor it touches most.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are source tarballs ratfor-1.07.tar.gz back to 1.01, plus binary and source RPMs from the author. You need a FORTRAN 77 compiler, such as GNU Fortran from GCC, to compile and run the generated output. The 1.01 change notes say the source was adapted for GNU autoconf, so a configure-and-make build is likely, but the README gives no explicit build steps. The page gives no Homebrew-specific notes.
brief.standout: It is a preprocessor from the Software Tools era that is still being patched: the latest release, 1.07, is dated 2025-01-13, and the recent changes are security-style buffer-overrun fixes rather than new features. Its public-domain lineage is spelled out on the page.
brief.status: maintained. The change history runs from 1.01 (2001) through 1.02 (2015), 1.03 (2015), 1.04 (2020), 1.05 (2020), 1.06 (2024-12-08), to 1.07 (2025-01-13), so the author has been releasing recently. The README contains no explicit maintenance statement, and the 2001 release note says the author considered it stable.
brief.caveats: Output is FORTRAN 77, so you need a separate F77 compiler, and the README does not describe the full Ratfor syntax. The README documents a limit of 60 characters for quoted-string include filenames. The string directive needs eos defined, and the 1.05 note says it emits a warning if that is missing. The 1970s date from the Homebrew scout note does not appear in the README; the page only says Ratfor was used in Kernighan and Plauger's Software Tools. The page calls the code public domain, and says it is still in the public domain. Contact is by email to brg at dgate.org.

name: raxml-ng
desc: RAxML Next Generation: faster, easier-to-use and more flexible
why: Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree inference is real science you can run, though it is a specialist bioinformatics tool.

brief.what_it_is: RAxML-NG is a command-line phylogenetic tool that infers maximum-likelihood trees from a multiple sequence alignment. You give it an alignment (FASTA or similar via --msa) and a substitution model, and it searches for the best-scoring tree, optionally with bootstrap replicates, branch support values, or evaluation on a fixed topology. The output is tree files and run logs. It is the successor to RAxML 8 and is installed by the brew formula as the raxml-ng executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a faster, more flexible and more user-friendly successor to RAxML (Stamatakis 2014), and says it carries over features from ExaML such as checkpointing and load balancing for partitioned alignments.
brief.how_it_works: The search heuristic repeatedly applies Subtree Pruning and Regrafting (SPR) moves to climb toward the best-known maximum-likelihood tree. Likelihood computation uses the optimized coraxlib library. Version 2.0 adds adaptive search heuristics, automatic model selection (MOOSE), and fast branch support metrics, per the README.

name: rdap
desc: Command-line client for the Registration Data Access Protocol
why: A client for RDAP, the modern successor to WHOIS, a protocol door most people never open.

brief.what_it_is: OpenRDAP is a command line client for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), written in Go. You give it a domain, IP address, AS number, entity tag, or a few other query types, and it looks up the registration record over HTTP. brief.why_it_exists: RDAP is presented as a replacement for WHOIS, returning domain and IP registration data in JSON over HTTP instead of the older plain-text WHOIS protocol. The homepage calls it a command line client for that protocol and says the same site also hosts the Go library and a public RDAP service at rdap.net.
brief.how_it_works: The client detects the query type from the input (domain, ip, asn), finds the authoritative RDAP server through bootstrap data from data.iana.org or a custom URL, and sends the query over HTTP. It can cache the bootstrap files on disk. Results come back as RDAP JSON, which it renders as text, raw JSON, or WHOIS style.

name: reaver
desc: Implements brute force attack to recover WPA/WPA2 passkeys
why: Brute-forces WPS PINs on WPA networks, a famous wireless weakness that makes the WPS protocol itself fascinating to understand.

brief.what_it_is: Reaver is a command-line tool that runs a brute-force attack against the WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) registrar PIN of a Wi-Fi access point, with the goal of recovering the WPA/WPA2 passphrase. It takes a monitor-mode wireless interface and a target BSSID (plus optional ESSID, channel and timing flags) and sends PIN guesses to the access point. When it finds the PIN, it reports the recovered PIN and passphrase. The companion tool wash scans for nearby access points and reports which ones have WPS enabled, and it can also output WPS details as JSON. This is the community fork (reaver-wps-fork-t6x) of Craig Heffner's original reaver, which adds the offline Pixie Dust attack.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the tool implements the brute-force attack on WPS PINs described by Stefan Viehbock, 'Brute forcing Wi-Fi Protected Setup: When poor design meets poor implementation', and presents it as a robust, practical attack tested against many access points. The fork exists to fix bugs, add features, and add the offline Pixie Dust attack, which the original did not have.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the online attack guesses WPS registrar PINs against the access point, which typically takes hours (it claims 4-10 hours on average, and about half that to hit the right PIN). The offline Pixie Dust mode (-K or -Z) collects values such as PKE, PKR, E-Hash1, E-Hash2, E-Nonce and Authkey, and passes them to the separate pixiewps program, which tries to work out the PIN without online guessing. The README says the offline attack can take seconds to minutes against vulnerable access points. The README does not describe the internal protocol mechanics in more detail.

Runtime extras are pixiewps (required for the Pixie Dust attack) and aircrack-ng (optional but recommended). Pixiewps must be installed separately from its own repository. You need a wireless interface in monitor mode (for example wlan0mon) before running either tool. Install with ./configure, make, then sudo make install from the src directory. The Homebrew formula only lists the executables reaver and wash. The README does not describe a Homebrew-specific setup.
brief.standout: Pixie Dust is the notable idea: it turns a days-long online PIN guess into an offline calculation that can succeed in seconds on vulnerable chipsets, using values captured during the WPS handshake. The fork also adds an option to pass an arbitrary string as a PIN (-p).

name: rdb

brief.what_it_is: A Go command-line tool and library that parses Redis RDB snapshot files, the binary on-disk dump of a Redis database. It reads an .rdb file and can output a JSON dump of every key, a CSV memory report, the biggest or hottest keys, a key-prefix size breakdown, a flame graph served on a local web port, or an AOF/RESP command stream. brief.how_it_works: It decodes the RDB binary format and streams objects (string, list, set, hash, zset, stream, aux, functions) one at a time. Memory figures are estimates based on the RDB-encoded size of each key, not Redis's live allocator numbers. For flame graphs, keys are split on separators such as ':' and grouped by shared prefix. The default prefix analysis uses a radix tree, and -prefix-sep switches to a flat map with constant memory use.

name: recoverpy
desc: TUI to recover overwritten or deleted data
why: Scans raw disks for deleted file signatures, a door into how data survives deletion, though mostly a utility.

brief.what_it_is: RecoverPy is a terminal user interface (built on Textual) for scanning a raw partition or disk image for a byte string and inspecting the disk blocks where matches appear. You select a partition, enter a search string, and start a scan. You then open a match, move through neighbouring blocks, and select and save the content you want. It takes a block device or disk image as input and writes out whatever content you choose to save. It does not reconstruct files, infer file boundaries, interpret filesystem structures, or restore filenames.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's framing is that when a file is deleted its metadata disappears first, while the underlying disk blocks often remain intact until they are reused. RecoverPy exposes what remains on disk so you can find deleted content by its bytes.
brief.how_it_works: The selected partition is opened read-only and scanned sequentially in fixed-size chunks, with a small overlap between chunks so matches spanning a boundary are not missed. For each byte-level match it records the absolute offset within the device, and block inspection and navigation use explicit offsets rather than filesystem abstractions. The scan is streaming and memory-bounded, so the full partition is never loaded into memory.

name: recutils
desc: Tools to work with human-editable, plain text data files
why: GNU recutils treats plain text files as typed databases with a query language, an unusual and underused take on data.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Recutils is a set of tools and libraries for working with human-editable, plain text databases called recfiles. A recfile holds a sequence of records, and each record has any number of named fields. Its features include typed fields (predefined types such as integer, real and date, plus user-defined types based on regular expressions), constraints such as mandatory and unique fields, joins, grouping, sorting and aggregate functions, and password-based AES encryption of individual fields. It ships converters for mdb and CSV files, report templates, and editor support for Vim and Emacs. The executables in the package are csv2rec, rec2csv, recdel, recfix, recfmt, recinf, recins, recsel and recset.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents recfiles as plain-text databases that people can edit by hand, with the structure and checks of a typed database. The README does not state a longer motivation in its own words.
brief.how_it_works: Data lives in ordinary text files as records made of named fields, so any text editor can change it. The rec* utilities and the librec C library read and write these files, and the type system and constraints are enforced on that data. The homepage does not describe the internal mechanism in more detail.
brief.install_notes: Binary packages are listed for Trisquel, Fedora, openSUSE, Debian, Arch, Mandrake, Parabola, OpenCSW for Solaris, FreeBSD, Termux for Android and Void Linux. Source tarballs come from the GNU FTP server and its mirrors. The rec-mode Emacs mode is distributed through ELPA. The homepage does not give specific build steps or first-run configuration.
brief.standout: Most database tools want a server or a binary store, but this one keeps the data as plain text that a person can edit in any editor and still gives it typed fields, constraints, joins and aggregates. Field-level encryption inside a text file is also unusual.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage was updated 2025/03/26, the manual was last updated September 23, 2024, and the README names an active maintainer, Jose E. Marchesi, who is reachable through the mailing lists. I did not find a release version or release date on the pages I read.

The manual is an index of download formats and does not show the content of the manual itself. The FSF page is licensed CC BY-ND, but the software is GPL-3.0-or-later.

The data is stored as a sequence of records, each record containing an arbitrary number of named fields.

It outputs a live terminal table of aircraft (--interactive), periodic aircraft.json files, and TCP feeds in Beast, SBS, raw, JSON, VRS and ASTERIX formats, plus an optional HTTP API and recorded flight traces and heatmaps. The README says one of its main uses is as the backend for global aircraft maps.

name: redka
desc: Redis re-implemented with SQLite
why: Redis protocol reimplemented on SQLite is a strange, appealing database twist worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Redka is an open-source Go project that reimplements the core parts of Redis on top of a relational database, keeping compatibility with the Redis API and wire protocol (RESP). It takes Redis-style commands from clients, such as strings, lists, sets, hashes, and sorted sets, and stores the data in SQLite or PostgreSQL. It can run as a standalone Redis-compatible server or be imported as a Go module for in-process use. The README also notes SQL views for analysis and reporting.
brief.why_it_exists: The README pitches it for three cases: an embedded key-value store for Go apps that already use SQLite, a lightweight stand-in for Redis test containers in local development and integration tests, and Redis-like data structures for teams that want everything in PostgreSQL with the same tools and transactions.
brief.how_it_works: Redka maps Redis data types onto a relational schema in SQLite or PostgreSQL, so data lives in ordinary tables and can exceed RAM. The server speaks the RESP wire protocol, and the README credits the Redcon RESP server library. The README does not go deeper into the schema; it points to docs/persistence.md.

The README highlights SQL views for introspection and ACID transactions, which Redis itself does not offer in the same way.

name: redo
desc: Implements djb's redo: an alternative to make
why: An implementation of djb's redo build system, a worthwhile idea about dependency tracking that is less known than make.

brief.what_it_is: redo is a Python implementation of Daniel J. Bernstein's redo build system, an alternative to make. You write a small shell script per target (for example default.o.do or myprog.do) that calls redo-ifchange on its inputs and then produces the output file, with $1, $2 and $3 supplied for target name, base name and temp output. Running `redo myprog` builds the target and records the dependencies it declared in a persistent .redo database, so later runs only rebuild what changed. The package installs eleven executables: redo, redo-always, redo-ifchange, redo-ifcreate, redo-log, redo-ood, redo-sources, redo-stamp, redo-targets, redo-unlocked and redo-whichdo.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says redo keeps the simplicity and flexibility of make while avoiding its flaws, and that it is simpler, more flexible and more powerful than make without giving up performance. djb's design existed only as terse notes with no code, so the author wrote this implementation from scratch based on those notes.
brief.how_it_works: Declaring a dependency is an ordinary shell command: redo-ifchange builds its arguments and, if any of them or their dependencies change, the current script is re-run. Dependencies can be declared after the build, for example by reading a gcc -MD dependency file, so no special make-style dependency syntax is needed. The initial build is imperative, with scripts declaring dependencies as they run, and later runs check the stored dependency data once at the start of the build, without re-running scripts that do not need it.

The homepage says the implementation is written in Python, so a Python runtime is presumably needed, but neither page states a version. The author also ships an optional pure-POSIX-sh version called do in the minimal/ directory. No accounts or hardware are needed.
brief.standout: Dependencies are declared by running ordinary shell commands inside the build script, sometimes after the target is built, rather than in a special make-style syntax. The author also says this is the only known redo variant that supports parallel builds (redo -j) and log linearization (redo-log), which he calls important for large projects.

name: redress
desc: Tool for analyzing stripped Go binaries compiled with the Go compiler
why: Recovers package and type information from stripped Go binaries, a real door into how compiled programs are taken apart.

brief.what_it_is: Redress is a command-line tool written in Go that analyzes stripped Go binaries built with the Go compiler. It reads the binary, pulls out embedded data, and rebuilds symbols, packages, types, and an approximate source layout. Its output is text on the terminal, and in radare2 mode it also sets symbol flags and type annotations inside the r2 session. The README's examples use a macOS malware sample called pplauncher.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it tries to 're-dress' a 'stripped' binary, recovering the names and structure that the build removed so the code is easier to analyze.
brief.how_it_works: The README says redress extracts data from the binary and uses it to reconstruct symbols and perform analysis. It runs in two modes: standalone, where you run it on its own, and inside radare2 via r2pipe, where it detects that it is in that environment and changes behavior. With no flags, standalone mode extracts nothing, and the README says the design is to print more than the user asks for. In r2 mode, running it with no flags performs automatic analysis: it creates symbol flags for functions and methods, extracts types and marks the matching _type symbols, and recursively analyzes main.init and main.main.

The README's examples use a real malware sample, which makes the tool's purpose concrete.

name: regipy
desc: Offline registry hive parsing tool
why: Offline Windows registry hive parsing opens a window into forensic artifacts most developers never see, though it's a fairly ordinary parser.

brief.what_it_is: Regipy is a Python library and set of command-line tools for parsing offline Windows registry hive files, meaning REGF-format files such as SYSTEM, NTUSER.DAT and amcache.hve. It takes a hive file, and optionally its transaction logs, and outputs JSON, a timeline, CSV hive diffs, a recovered hive file, or plugin results. The library exposes RegistryHive with recurse_subkeys, get_key, iter_subkeys and get_values. A plugin system extracts forensic artifacts such as amcache, shimcache, computer name, BAM and NTUser Run-key persistence, and the hive type is detected automatically.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a problem or motivation in so many words. It describes the project as a library for parsing offline registry hives, with CLI tools for dumping, diffing, recovering and running plugins against them.
brief.how_it_works: Pure-Python parsing of REGF structures, using the construct library per the README's profiling notes, with the option of an alpha Rust backend (regipy-rs) that exposes the same API via regipy.registry_rs. The CLI applies transaction logs to recover a dirty hive before comparison, and regipy-parse-header also runs checksum and transaction validation. Plugins are chosen by detected hive type and run through run_relevant_plugins.

Install from a cloned source tree in editable mode.
Opt-in install of the alpha Rust-accelerated backend, published separately as regipy-rs.
Prints the REGF header fields of a hive and warns if the hive is not clean and needs transaction logs applied.

Detects the hive type and runs the relevant plugins, writing results to JSON.
Compares two hives of the same type and writes differences to CSV; prints to screen without -o.

Use pip install regipy[full] for full functionality, which needs compilation tools; omitting [full] gives relaxed dependencies. The optional Rust backend needs pip install regipy[rust] and is imported from regipy.registry_rs instead of regipy.registry. Development setup uses pip install -e ".[full,dev]" and pre-commit install. Running the GitHub Actions workflows locally needs Docker and the act tool. No Homebrew-specific steps appear in the README.
brief.standout: The README makes an unusually specific claim for the alpha Rust backend: it is validated 1:1 against the pure-Python parser by matching SHA-256 traversal digests over a test-hive corpus, with benchmarks up to roughly 2,550x on a SOFTWARE hive. That is a self-reported figure with a disclaimer about intentional divergences on corrupted hives. The breadth of forensic plugins and the transaction-log recovery path also go beyond a bare hive reader.
brief.status: Maintained, with evidence from the README: it describes a recent v6.0.0 with breaking changes, an active alpha Rust backend, CI and lint configuration, and an OpenSSF Scorecard badge. The README shows no release date or last-commit date, so I cannot confirm a date.
brief.caveats: Requires Python 3.9+. The [full] extra needs compiler tooling and can be slow to install. The Rust backend is explicitly alpha and may raise different exception types on corrupted hives than the Python parser. The benchmark numbers and parity claims are the project's own and were not independently checked. The example header output includes a warning that the hive is not clean, so real evidence often needs transaction-log recovery first. The regipy-plugins-list executable appears in the Homebrew metadata but is not documented in the README. Licensed under MIT.

name: regldg
desc: Regular expression grammar language dictionary generator
why: A generator that produces dictionaries from regex grammars, turning a pattern language into a word list in an odd way.

brief.what_it_is: regldg is a command-line program, written in C, that takes a regular expression pattern and generates every string of text that matches it. The output is a word list, so the program works as a dictionary generator. The homepage describes it as a "regular expression grammar language dictionary generator" and gives the current version as 1.0.1. It supports a subset of Perl's regex syntax, with some differences noted on the page.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it to get a password list: he knew a password started with "omu" and was 7 characters long, and had only a very old computer. The page frames it as the reverse of normal regex use, where a pattern is used to test whether a string matches.
brief.how_it_works: You give regldg a pattern and it enumerates all the strings in the language that the pattern defines. The page describes regex as defining a grammar, and the words matching it as that grammar's language. The page does not describe the enumeration algorithm. It also says uniqueness is not guaranteed, so duplicates can appear, for example from a{2,3}a{3,2}.

commands_seen.context: Suggested on the homepage as a Perl regex tutorial to read on *nix systems. It is a man page lookup, not a regldg command.

name: reposurgeon
desc: Edit version-control repository history
why: A scriptable surgeon for version-control history that rewrites repositories as if they were dissectable specimens.

brief.what_it_is: reposurgeon is a command-line tool for editing version-control repository history. It reads a repository's history, lets you rewrite it (edit past comments and metadata, remove or merge commits, delete files or subtrees from history), and writes the result to another or the same VCS. It is driven by an interactive, debugger-like prompt or by scripts. The homepage lists five executables: repobench, repocutter, repomapper, reposurgeon and repotool. The homepage also describes conversion as its main use: Subversion to any VCS with write support.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says reposurgeon enables "risky operations that version-control systems don't want to let you do, such as editing past comments and metadata and removing commits." The man page adds that a major use is helping a human produce higher-quality conversions between VCSes than fully automated converters can.
brief.how_it_works: Rather than reading and writing repositories itself, reposurgeon parses and emits git fast-import streams, so it works with any VCS that has fast-export and fast-import utilities. For systems without such tools it uses built-in extractor code that replays history into an internal stream; repositories read this way can be read but not modified. The man page says the git fast-import format also gives it a common language of primitive operations.

commands_seen.context: Synopsis from the reposurgeon(1) man page. Invokes reposurgeon, optionally with a command to run.

brief.install_notes: The homepage links a source tarball (reposurgeon-5.12.tar.gz) with an MD5 checksum and an INSTALL.html document, which I did not fetch. The man page says reposurgeon bails out gracefully and names any missing helper tool it needs, such as git-fast-export or git-fast-import equivalents for the VCS you are converting. The GitLab page says the code is usually packaged as 'reposurgeon'. I saw no account, hardware or runtime requirements in the pages I read.
brief.standout: It treats history rewriting as surgery on a specimen: an interactive, symbolic-debugger-style interface that can also run scripted recipes. Its main trick is using git fast-import streams as a universal intermediate format, so it can rewrite history for many VCSes without a dedicated reader or writer for each.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage shows release 5.12 with a page date of 05 Oct 2026, a 'Recent Changes' list (Unity Version Control read support, Software Heritage support, timezone fixes), and a man page last updated 2026-10-03. The project is at gitlab.com/esr/reposurgeon. I did not check commit dates.
brief.caveats: Support is uneven. The man page says full read and write support covers git, hg, bzr, brz, Fossil, darcs, RCS and SRC. SCCS, CVS, svn and Software Heritage are read-side only, and Unity Version Control read support is untested. CVS lifts can need serious hand-hacking. Metadata may not survive both import and export directions. The GitLab page's plugin wording for hg, SCCS, CVS, RCS and src differs from the man page, so trust the man page. The license is in a COPYING file that I did not open, so I cannot name it. Funding is via Patreon and SubscribeStar.

The user interface of reposurgeon resembles a symbolic debugger.
In particular, this tool can be used to script the production of very high-quality conversions from Subversion to any VCS with write support.

name: remind
desc: Sophisticated calendar and alarm
why: A decades-old calendar language with moon phases, recurring rules, and sunrise computation hidden in a tiny scripting syntax worth exploring.

brief.what_it_is: Remind is a command-line calendar and alarm program for UNIX and Linux, installed as the commands rem, remind, rem2ps, and tkremind. You write reminders in its own scripting language, which handles recurring events, exceptions, and holidays. It can output plain text, PDF, PostScript, and HTML calendars, and it can produce timed reminders and pop-up alarms. It also supports Gregorian and Hebrew calendars and 12 languages, and a graphical front-end is available for people who do not want to learn the scripting language.

name: retdec
desc: Retargetable machine-code decompiler based on LLVM
why: A retargetable machine-code decompiler from Avast that turns binaries back into readable C, a strong door into reverse engineering.

brief.what_it_is: RetDec is a retargetable machine-code decompiler built on LLVM. It takes an executable or raw machine code and produces readable high-level output, either C or a Python-like language. It handles ELF, PE, Mach-O, COFF, AR archives, Intel HEX, and raw code, for x86, ARM, MIPS, PIC32, PowerPC, x86-64, and ARM64 (AArch64). Beyond decompiling, it also offers static analysis, compiler and packer detection, a disassembler, call and control-flow graphs, and statistics.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a decompiler that is 'not limited to any particular target architecture, operating system, or executable file format', so one tool can cover many binary types. The project is from Avast, and the README credits research funding from TACR (Technology Agency of the Czech Republic).
brief.how_it_works: The README gives little detail on internals beyond the feature list. It mentions loading and instruction decoding, signature-based removal of statically linked library code, use of DWARF and PDB debug info, reconstruction of instruction idioms, and recovery of C++ class hierarchies from RTTI and vtables. It also lists C++ symbol demangling for GCC, MSVC, and Borland. Optional UPX unpacking runs in a preprocessing stage.

brief.what_it_is: RGBDS (Rednex Game Boy Development System) is a free assembler and linker package for the Game Boy and Game Boy Color. It has four tools: RGBASM (assembler), RGBLINK (linker), RGBFIX (ROM checksum and header fixer), and RGBGFX (PNG-to-Game Boy graphics converter). Source assembly code and PNG art go in, and a playable ROM comes out. The homepage says each tool can be swapped for a custom one or used standalone in another process.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as giving developers complete control over the console with no middle-man, so debugging is simpler, and pushing the Game Boy's limited capabilities by writing native assembly. brief.how_it_works: Each stage of the pipeline is a separate program: RGBGFX converts images to Game Boy tile formats, RGBASM assembles source into object files, RGBLINK links those objects into a ROM, and RGBFIX patches the ROM header and checksum. The README and homepage do not describe the internal object format or language syntax in detail.

name: rocq
desc: Proof assistant for higher-order logic
why: The Coq proof assistant renamed; running formal proofs and dependent types is a real mathematical rabbit hole.

brief.what_it_is: Rocq (formerly the Coq Proof Assistant) is an interactive theorem prover and dependently-typed programming language. You write definitions, executable algorithms, theorems and proof scripts in its formal language, and it checks the proofs with a small trusted kernel. It can also extract executable programs from specifications as OCaml or Haskell source. The Homebrew description calls it a proof assistant for higher-order logic, but the homepage and README describe a dependent type theory, so the brew blurb undersells it. The installed executables include coqc, coqtop, rocq, coqchk, coqdep, coqdoc and votour.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a tool 'to write mathematical definitions, executable algorithms and theorems together with an environment for semi-interactive development of machine-checked proofs'. The homepage pitches it as a trustworthy, industrial-strength tool for mechanised reasoning in mathematics, computer science and more.
brief.how_it_works: Proofs are built interactively with tactics and checked by a kernel written in OCaml, which the homepage describes as a well-delimited, trusted core. The homepage says the core type theory is formalised in the MetaRocq project and that a verified reference checker can be extracted to shrink the trusted base. Compiled output comes from the coqc/rocq compilers, and the native conversion checker relies on the OCaml runtime.

commands_seen.context: Prints the Rocq version. The README suggests including it in bug reports.
Same as coqtop -v, using the new rocq entry point, to report the version in bug reports.

brief.install_notes: Linux: the official Rocq Platform binary installer is no longer offered, so the Platform is installed from source via its scripts, which wrap opam. Also available: the experimental Rocq Platform Starter GUI installer (it also sets up VS Code and VsRocq), opam directly, Nix, distro packages (the version may be old and external packages may be missing), and Docker. macOS: the Platform binary installer (recommended for beginners), the scripts, Homebrew (limited external packages), Nix, or Docker. Windows: the Platform binary installer, the scripts (run them first so opam environment variables are set), or WSL or a Linux VM. Editors: VsRocq is the recommended VS Code extension and needs a matching language server version; alternatives are Rocq LSP, VsCoq Legacy, Proof General plus Company-Coq for Emacs, Coqtail for Vim/Neovim, and the standalone RocqIDE. Bug reports should cite the OCaml version, Rocq version and configuration.
brief.standout: The homepage ships live code samples (fac, a lemma proved with lia, extraction to OCaml) and it is the lineage of Coq, with decades of use in the Four Colour Theorem, CompCert and HoTT. Its MetaRocq project verifies the kernel's own type theory.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists Rocq Prover 9.2.0 (2026-03-27) and Rocq Platform 2026.07.0 (2026-07-30). The GitHub README shows active GitLab and GitHub CI badges, a Zenodo DOI, and a live reference manual for master. I did not see a commit date.
brief.caveats: native_compute is only supported on some x86 setups when built with OCaml 5, according to the 9.2.0 release notes. There is no Linux binary installer for the Platform. The Homebrew route lacks many external packages and has no language server, so VS Code users need VsCoq Legacy. The VsRocq extension and language server must be the same version. The brew description ('higher-order logic') is looser than the project's own framing. I did not check the license, and the homepage text I read did not state it.

name: rizin
desc: UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset
why: A full UNIX-style reverse engineering framework that opens binaries, firmware, and running programs to inspection.

brief.what_it_is: Rizin is a free, open-source reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. You point it at a binary, firmware image, or running program, and it gives you disassembly, analysis, and inspection through an interactive shell (the `rizin` command) or through separate single-purpose tools such as rz-bin, rz-asm, and rz-hash. The README describes it as usable for analyzing binaries, disassembling code, debugging programs, forensics, and as a scriptable command-line hex editor that can open disk files. The Cutter GUI sits on top of the same backend.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Rizin takes a unique, Unix-friendly approach to reverse engineering, aiming for a shell-like environment for analyzing binaries from the command line "without unnecessary weight", while still providing a base for GUIs and scripting. The GitHub README says it was "born as a fork of the radare2, with a focus on usability, features and cleanliness."
brief.how_it_works: The `rizin` shell is built on a backend that analyzes binary formats and architectures; the homepage says the shell was redesigned using Tree-sitter for grammar parsing, with commands registered in YAML files to drive help text. A new analysis step matches unnamed functions in stripped binaries against FLIRT signatures from sigdb. Scripting goes through rzpipe, which the README says supports Python, Haskell, OCaml, Ruby, Rust, and Go.

name: root

Python bindings use the cppyy technology for on-demand, two-way C++/Python access. RDataFrame is a parallel processing framework that can use multiple cores or distributed systems to speed up analyses.

name: rpiboot
desc: Raspberry Pi USB boot tool for Compute Modules
why: Uses USB to expose a Compute Module's bootloader, a neat way into how the Pi boots over USB.

brief.what_it_is: rpiboot is a host-side command-line tool, built from C source with make against libusb, that talks to a Raspberry Pi over USB while the device is in its ROM USB boot mode. It acts as a file server, sending boot firmware and a boot image into the device's memory. The default payload is a Linux-based mass-storage-gadget, which makes the Pi's storage appear to the host as a standard USB drive. An OS image can then be written to that drive with Raspberry Pi Imager. On Compute Module 4 and newer, it is also used to update the bootloader SPI flash EEPROM.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says rpiboot 'provides a file server for loading software into memory on a Raspberry Pi for provisioning.' The aim is to get at a Pi's storage or bootloader from a host computer over USB, without needing a working OS on the device.
brief.how_it_works: The host uses libusb to talk to the Pi, and the Pi's boot ROM is put into usbboot mode, either by a nRPIBOOT/EMMC-DISABLE jumper, a GPIO set up in OTP on Pi 4B and Pi 400, or by holding the power button on Pi 5, Pi 500 and Pi 500+. rpiboot then sends the chosen firmware or initramfs payload. The mass-storage-gadget boots a Linux initramfs that scans for SD/EMMC, NVMe and USB block devices and uses configfs to expose them as USB mass-storage devices. The legacy msd firmware instead exposes the SD/EMMC device as an emulated mass-storage device, with no console and slower writes.

name: rpg-cli
desc: Your filesystem as a dungeon!
why: Turns your filesystem into a role-playing dungeon, a playful idea that makes you see directories differently.

brief.what_it_is: rpg-cli is a minimalist computer role-playing game written in Rust, played from the command line. Its CLI works as a cd replacement: as you change directories, the hero walks deeper into the filesystem, and enemies sometimes appear and battle automatically. Input is ordinary shell commands like cd, ls, buy and todo, and the output is a text status block showing HP, MP, XP, stats, equipment and gold. The hero's location is the working directory, and directories farther from home hold tougher enemies and treasure chests.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted to strip a JRPG down to its underlying mechanics, "the simplest thing that could possibly pass as a video game," and the command line was the narrowest interface he could think of. The blog post describes it as a constraint that fostered creativity and as a side project meant to yield something usable within a few months.
brief.how_it_works: The game keeps its own record of the hero's location and turns directory changes into movement, rolling for random encounters on the way. Battles are fully automatic: each side acts according to its speed stat, and the player's default action is to attack unless HP is low and a potion is available. Because a program cannot change its parent shell's directory, a small shell function forwards arguments to rpg-cli and then runs cd to the path rpg-cli pwd reports. Death is permanent, and a tombstone left in the dead hero's directory can be looted by a new hero.

name: rrdtool
desc: Round Robin Database
why: A round-robin time-series database with a fixed-size circular store; an old-school idea that still quietly underpins monitoring graphs.

brief.what_it_is: RRDtool is a data logging and graphing system for time series data, which the homepage calls "the OpenSource industry standard" for this job. It stores values in round robin databases: files created at a fixed size and pre-filled with UNKNOWN data, whose archives wrap around as new data arrives. Timestamped values go in through rrdupdate or rrdtool create and related commands, and the tool can give back fetched data, XML dumps, and graphs. The homepage says it can be called from shell scripts and from perl, python, ruby, lua or tcl applications.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a high-performance system for logging and graphing time series data that can be embedded in ordinary scripts and applications. The fixed-size design is my inference from the docs rather than the author's stated reason: files are created at their final full size, so storage stays bounded.
brief.how_it_works: Each RRD defines one or more data sources (DS) at create time, each with a type such as GAUGE, COUNTER, DERIVE or ABSOLUTE, plus a heartbeat and optional min and max. Updates arriving at arbitrary times are folded into primary data points on each step interval, and round robin archives (RRA) consolidate those with AVERAGE, MIN, MAX or LAST into a fixed number of rows that wrap around. Counter-type sources are stored as per-second rates, not running totals.

brief.standout: The fixed-size circular store means the file never grows, and the rrdcreate doc is unusually frank about trade-offs, such as COUNTER versus DERIVE and how a counter reset can be mistaken for a wrap. It also ships built-in Holt-Winters forecasting and failure flagging (HWPREDICT, FAILURES) and COMPUTE data sources that act like virtual columns.

name: rshijack
desc: TCP connection hijacker
why: A TCP hijacker is a sharp door into how TCP sequence numbers and connection trust actually work.

brief.what_it_is: rshijack is a TCP connection hijacker written in Rust, described by its author as a rewrite of shijack from 2001. You give it a network interface and the source and destination addresses and ports of an established TCP connection. It sniffs for a packet from that connection, reads the SEQ and ACK fields, and then sends a crafted packet on a raw socket that the remote server accepts as valid. The README's example injects a shell command, piped in on stdin, into a live telnet session.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it was written for TAMUctf 2018 (the brick house 100 challenge), where the target was a 2FA-protected telnet server. The team's solution was to wait until authentication finished and then inject a TCP packet into the open telnet connection.
brief.how_it_works: The tool sniffs for a packet belonging to the target connection and reads its SEQ and ACK fields. With those values it can build a packet on a raw socket that the remote end treats as part of the existing stream. The README notes that after some attempts the injected command was accepted and executed, and the server returned a packet containing the flag.

name: rtl_433
desc: Program to decode radio transmissions from devices
why: Decodes ISM-band sensor transmissions from your neighbourhood using a cheap SDR dongle.

brief.what_it_is: rtl_433 is a command-line program that decodes the data that radio devices send on the ISM bands, mainly 433.92 MHz, 868 MHz (SRD), 315 MHz, 345 MHz and 915 MHz. It takes radio samples from a software-defined radio (Realtek RTL2832 RTL-SDR dongles, or LimeSDR, PlutoSDR, HackRF and SoapyRemote through SoapySDR) or from a saved sample file. It prints decoded messages as log or key-value text, JSON, CSV, MQTT, InfluxDB, syslog, or through an HTTP API and UI. The decoder list covers weather and temperature sensors, remote controls, doorbells, car tyre pressure sensors (TPMS), energy and water meters, and more.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as "a generic data receiver" and notes that despite the name it is not limited to RTL-SDR hardware or to one kind of device. It gives no separate problem statement. Its stated goals are portability and low resource use, so it can run on embedded hardware, and it aims to support older compilers.
brief.how_it_works: The SDR captures the radio signal and rtl_433 demodulates it into pulses, then matches those pulses against a large set of per-device decoders. You can pick which decoders run with -R, or define your own with -X using a flex spec that gives modulation type and pulse timings (for example OOK_PWM, OOK_PCM, FSK_PWM). The README also documents a pulse analyzer (-A) and raw I/Q saving (-S) for debugging and building test files.

name: rtp2httpd
desc: Multicast RTP/RTSP-to-HTTP converter with web player and status dashboard
why: Bridges multicast RTP IPTV streams to HTTP, a real door into how multicast television travels over networks.

brief.what_it_is: rtp2httpd is an IPTV forwarding server written in C. It takes multicast RTP/UDP streams and RTSP streams from an IPTV network and re-serves them as ordinary HTTP unicast streams, so a normal browser or player can watch them. It can also reverse-proxy HLS sources from an internal IPTV network out to a LAN or the public internet. It includes a built-in web player, a live status dashboard at /status, and M3U playlist generation at /playlist.m3u. The README says it is a drop-in replacement for udpxy and msd_lite, and it is aimed at the Chinese mainland IPTV environment.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to get near set-top-box viewing quality on IPTV from ordinary devices, using carrier-grade FCC (Fast Channel Change) for quick channel switching. It positions itself as a lightweight, zero-dependency alternative to udpxy and msd_lite for routers, optical modems, NAS boxes and other embedded hardware.
brief.how_it_works: The server joins multicast groups, reads the RTP packets, and reorders out-of-order packets. It can apply Reed-Solomon FEC recovery where the upstream multicast supports it. It sends the result to HTTP clients over epoll-driven non-blocking IO, with multiple worker processes sharing multicast subscriptions and a preallocated buffer pool. For channel changes it uses the carrier's FCC server to get an IDR frame quickly so the player can decode immediately. The web player is pure front-end and does no transcoding, so the server's overhead is small.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no build or install commands. It points to a Quick Start guide for OpenWrt (https://rtp2httpd.com/guide/quick-start) and an installation page covering several platforms (https://rtp2httpd.com/guide/installation). I did not open those pages. Setup needs a working multicast IPTV feed on the network; the README recommends a separate IPTV setup tutorial for newcomers who are unfamiliar with DHCP authentication, routing, multicast and firewalls. The built-in player needs an M3U playlist configured first, then it is opened at http://<server:port>/player. Timeshift and catch-up need an RTSP catch-up source from the carrier. FCC fast switching needs a carrier FCC server address, and the README links a collection of regional FCC addresses. The brew formula installs an executable named rtp2httpd, and I did not verify the brew install path.
brief.standout: It is a small pure-C server with no dependencies, and the x86_64 binary is about 509KB with the whole web player bundled in. It implements FCC fast channel change, which is usually found only in carrier set-top boxes. It also reverse-proxies HLS, not just multicast. The author publishes a benchmark against udpxy, msd_lite and tvgate, claiming 25 simultaneous 1080p multicast streams at 8 Mbps each using about 25% of one core of an i3-N305 and 4MB of RAM. Those numbers are self-reported and I did not check them.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I could not confirm dates. The README is detailed and current, and its sponsor banner references a 2026 September promotion, which suggests recent activity. I did not see a release date or last commit date in the fetched pages. The GitHub page returned the README only, so I did not check the commit history or release tags.
brief.caveats: Licensed under GPL v2.0. The README spells out that modified source must be published and that binaries must ship with source. Its features are tuned to Chinese mainland IPTV, and FCC fast switching only works with a carrier FCC server. FEC needs multicast upstream support. Fast switching is only noticeable in IPTV-optimised players; the README says PotPlayer and IINA will not show the difference. The built-in web player may show no audio or a black screen on some channels because of browser decoding limits. The README's performance figures come from the author. The README and homepage carry a sponsor advertisement for Token Unlimited, which is not part of the software. The README is in Chinese, with an English documentation site at https://rtp2httpd.com/en/.
quotes: rtp2httpd 是一个 IPTV 转发服务器，支持将组播 RTP/UDP、RTSP 转换为 HTTP 流，或将 HLS 流从内网代理到外网。
本项目专为中国大陆 IPTV 环境进行优化，实现了运营商级的 FCC（Fast Channel Change）快速换台协议，可作为 `udpxy` 和 `msd_lite` 的无缝替代，为 IPTV 用户提供接近原生机顶盒的观看体验。
纯 C 语言编写，零依赖，小巧简洁，适合运行在各种嵌入式设备上（路由器、光猫、NAS 等）

name: rtptools
desc: Set of tools for processing RTP data
why: Tools for capturing, replaying and inspecting RTP streams, a direct door into how real-time audio and video travel.

brief.what_it_is: RTP Tools is a set of small command-line applications for processing RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) data. The README lists six programs: rtpdump parses and prints RTP packets and writes output files that rtpplay and rtpsend can use; rtpplay plays back sessions recorded by rtpdump; rtpsend generates RTP packets from a textual description, written by hand or produced by rtpdump; rtptrans is an RTP translator between unicast and multicast networks; multidump and multiplay start multiple rtpdump or rtpplay instances at once. Recorded or captured RTP goes in, and replayed packets, printed packet details, or translated streams come out.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no separate motivation. It describes the project only as a set of small applications for processing RTP data, and points to the individual manpages for details.
brief.how_it_works: rtpdump turns RTP traffic into a textual or file form that rtpplay and rtpsend can consume, so recording and replaying are a pair of steps. rtpsend builds packets from that textual description. rtptrans relays RTP between unicast and multicast networks. The README does not go deeper into the internals.

name: rubberband
desc: Audio time stretcher tool and library
why: Time stretching and pitch shifting audio from the command line, a useful transform that opens onto signal processing.

brief.what_it_is: Rubber Band is an open-source audio time-stretching and pitch-shifting library written in C++, plus a free command-line tool built on it. It changes the tempo and pitch of an audio stream or recording independently of each other. The command-line tool takes an input audio file (WAV, via libsndfile) plus a time ratio and a pitch shift in semitones, and writes a new audio file with the altered speed and pitch. The library itself is meant for developers embedding this in their own apps.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a way to make audio applications "stretchier than ever", offering high-quality tempo and pitch changes that are independent of each other. The README describes it as permitting "changing the tempo and pitch of an audio recording independently of one another."
brief.how_it_works: The library exposes two C++ classes in the RubberBand namespace: RubberBandStretcher for general time and pitch manipulation, and RubberBandLiveShifter for simpler block-by-block pitch shifting. It has two processing engines: R2 (Faster), the default for the rubberband binary and the only engine in 2.x, and R3 (Finer), which the README says gives higher quality on most material, especially complex mixes, vocals and bass-heavy music, at much higher CPU cost. The README says the command-line tool is an example of offline use, and the LADSPA/LV2 plugins are examples of real-time use.

commands_seen.context: The basic invocation of the command-line tool: -t sets the time ratio, -p sets pitch shift in semitones, then input and output WAV files.
Example from the README: stretches test.wav to 50% longer, raises pitch by a whole tone, and writes output.wav.
Quoted in the README prose as the way to get the full list of options for the command-line tool.

brief.install_notes: Homepage offers a source release, a Windows command-line executable, and a macOS binary for v4.0.0. Building from source is covered in COMPILING.md in the repository (not fetched). The command-line tool needs libsndfile for audio file loading. The LADSPA and LV2 plugins need the ladspa.h and lv2.h headers, and the Vamp analysis plugin needs the Vamp plugin SDK; none of these are included. The library may optionally link external resampler and FFT code, depending on build configuration. Nothing else in the README suggests accounts or runtime setup.
brief.standout: Stretch and pitch are fully independent, and the tool offers two engines so you can trade CPU for quality (-2 for R2, -3 for R3). Its free command-line tool, library, and plugins all come from one codebase, and a Vamp plugin exposes the stretch decisions the library makes, which is unusual for this kind of tool.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the evidence goes. Homepage announces v4.0 released 25 October 2024 with a new simplified pitch-shifting API. Homepage copyright reads 2025. The README says copyright 2007-2024. I could not see a last-commit date from the GitHub mirror page I fetched.
brief.caveats: Licence is GPL (v2 or later), so any application that links it must also be GPL-compatible unless you buy a commercial licence, which the README says is required for distributing it in proprietary apps and for Apple App Store distribution. Build and dependency setup is non-trivial, with optional FFTW3 (GPL with commercial option) and Intel IPP (proprietary) among the possible dependencies. Many options only affect the R2 engine. The C API is not documented separately from the C++ headers.

name: rumbledb
desc: JSONiq and XQuery query engine on Apache Spark
why: JSONiq and XQuery running on Spark is an unusual query language world, though heavy and niche.

brief.what_it_is: RumbleDB is an open-source query engine that runs JSONiq and XQuery on Apache Spark. You write a query in the JSONiq language and point it at nested or messy data such as JSON, JSON Lines, XML, CSV, Parquet, Avro, libSVM, or text, from a local disk, HDFS, S3, or Azure blob storage. Results come out as JSON, XML, CSV, Parquet, YAML, and other formats. It can run on a laptop or scale out across a Spark cluster, including Amazon EMR. The homepage calls version 3.0 'Coast Redwood'.
brief.why_it_exists: The README argues that RumbleDB exposes a query language rather than a DataFrame API, for more flexibility and productivity, and because a lot of data simply will not fit in DataFrames. The homepage pitches it as built for 'Big data. Nested data. Beautifully messy data.'
brief.how_it_works: Queries are written in JSONiq, a FLWOR-based language for nested data, and run on top of Apache Spark. The homepage says JSON navigation, FLWOR clauses, and downward XML navigation are automatically parallelized across cores or a cluster, and that count and sum-style pushdowns are applied automatically. The README does not describe the internals in more detail.

commands_seen.context: Listed on the homepage as the Python installation route ('Installation via pip install jsoniq'). Not shown as a separate code block.

brief.install_notes: The homepage lists installation via pip (the jsoniq package), Homebrew, Docker, a standalone jar, and a thin jar for use with an existing Spark installation, plus a Java API and an interactive query shell. There is a Jupyter notebook integration, and the README points to a Colab sandbox notebook (RumbleSandbox.ipynb) that can also be run locally. Running on a cluster needs Spark; the homepage says it runs on Amazon EMR (8.x) with data on S3 or HDFS. The homepage says Spark 4.0, 4.1, and 4.2 are supported. PostgreSQL and MongoDB reading is listed as Python-edition only. I saw no account or registration step; the homepage says none is needed.

name: runit
desc: Collection of tools for managing UNIX services
why: A minimal init and service supervisor from the daemontools lineage, a small door into how Unix systems boot and keep processes alive.

brief.what_it_is: runit is a cross-platform UNIX init scheme with service supervision, meant as a replacement for sysvinit and other init schemes. Its programs are runit (run as process 1), runit-init (installed as /sbin/init replacement), runsvdir, runsvchdir, runsv, sv, svlogd, chpst and utmpset. Input is a service directory of run scripts; output is supervised long-running processes, with logging through svlogd and runlevel changes via runsvchdir. It runs on GNU/Linux, *BSD, MacOSX, Solaris, and can be adapted to other Unix systems.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as a reliable, small replacement for sysvinit that handles booting, running and shutting down in three stages, and that keeps the code in process no 1 minimal. The homepage says runit is optimized for reliability and small size.
brief.how_it_works: At boot, runit-init starts runit, which runs /etc/runit/1 (one-time initialization, with full control of /dev/console for an emergency shell), then /etc/runit/2 (normally runsvdir, which should not return until halt or reboot and is restarted if it crashes), then /etc/runit/3 on halt or reboot. runsvdir starts one runsv supervisor per service directory entry, and runsv keeps each service's run script alive, with a log/ subdirectory piped through svlogd. Runlevels are handled through runsvdir and runsvchdir, and service dependencies are resolved automatically per the homepage.

Releases are tarballs (the install page names runit-2.3.1.tar.gz with a sha256sum), and you report success by mail to a listed address. Replacing init is a separate step covered by a 'How to replace init' page. name: rune
desc: Embeddable dynamic programming language for Rust
why: An embeddable dynamic language for Rust is a small, unusual language worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Rune is an embeddable dynamic programming language for Rust. You write scripts in Rune syntax (functions, structs, enums, async code, pattern matching, template literals) and run them either with the bundled `rune` command-line tool or from inside a Rust program through the `rune` crate. Source text goes in, and the compiler turns it into bytecode for a stack-based virtual machine that the host program can call into. The homepage and README do not describe the output format beyond running programs and returning values to Rust.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls it "an embeddable dynamic programming language for Rust" and the homepage says it is "easily embeddable and has support for an exciting set of language features". The stated aim is to give Rust programs a scripting layer that is dynamic, with first-class async, without leaving Rust.
brief.how_it_works: Source is compiled into a compact representation that runs on a stack-based virtual machine. The Rust host builds a Context, loads Sources, calls rune::prepare(...).build_vm(), then invokes functions by name with vm.call(["add"], (10i64, 20i64)) and converts the result back with rune::from_value. Memory safety comes from reference counting, and each function call gets its own stack frame.

name: rustpython

It can also be embedded in a Rust program as a scripting engine, or compiled to WebAssembly (WASI or the browser) to run Python in a browser or sandbox. It also cites Rust's minimal runtime as what makes WebAssembly builds practical.
brief.how_it_works: It is a from-scratch Python implementation in Rust rather than a wrapper around CPython. The README points to an architecture document for the component layout. The Lib/ directory of Python standard library files is wired in through symlinks, and the stdlib can be frozen into the binary for WASI builds.

name: rura
desc: Interactive TUI scratchpad for building shell pipelines
why: An interactive scratchpad for building pipelines live is a fresh way to watch shell data flow step by step.

brief.what_it_is: Rura is a terminal UI (TUI) for building shell pipelines. You type a pipeline such as grep | sort | uniq into an input line, and its output appears in a pane that updates as you edit. You can run the pipeline in full or only up to a chosen subcommand, inspect any stage's output, diff outputs between runs, and save commands as presets. Input can come from a file passed with --file, from piped stdin, or from an initial command passed with --command.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Rura replaces the usual loop of editing a pipe, pressing up-arrow, and rerunning it. It presents itself as a way to see shell data flow stage by stage while you build a pipeline.
brief.how_it_works: Commands run through a configurable shell (sh by default on Unix, powershell on Windows), and the README says Rura caches the output of subcommands to speed up iteration. Live modes re-execute the pipeline as you type, with a debounce delay (default 500 ms), and the Alt+\ binding runs the pipeline only up to the cursor's subcommand. Tab completion uses the system's bash, zsh, or fish tools.

name: ryelang
desc: Rye is a homoiconic programming language focused on fluid expressions
why: A homoiconic language with fluid expressions, an unusual and under-known language worth an afternoon of poking.

brief.what_it_is: Rye is a small, high-level, dynamic programming language with a Go-based interpreter and an interactive console (REPL). Programs are built from function calls and pipes, with no keywords, and most values are blocks, strings, numbers, tables, or Failures. You run it on a script file or in the REPL, and it can also be embedded in a Go program as a scripting or configuration language. It ships with many built-in modules (HTTP, SQLite, JSON, CSV, regexp, and others) and built-in dialects for validation, math, SQL and HTML.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Rye is inspired by Rebol, Factor, Linux shells, and Go, and the homepage frames it as "designed for predictable, composable programs and interactive use" and as "a programming and interaction language." The design principles on the homepage are flexibility, consistency (functions are all you need), immutability by default, explicit failure rather than null, homoiconicity, and strict scope isolation.
brief.how_it_works: Everything is a function call, including if, loop, fn and try, so a user can inspect or replace them. Code is made of Rye values, so blocks can be passed, stored, combined and introspected. Names defined with a colon are constants, and mutation requires a mod-word (::) or a function whose name ends in !. Failed lookups return a Failure value that can be handled inline with fix, for example: person -> "surname" |fix { "Doe" } |print.

name: rvvm
desc: RISC-V Virtual Machine
why: A RISC-V virtual machine that can boot real operating systems, a good way to watch a foreign architecture execute.

brief.what_it_is: RVVM is a virtual machine and emulator for RISC-V guest systems. You give it a RISC-V firmware image (for example OpenSBI plus U-Boot, bundled as fw_payload.bin), optionally a disk image, and memory, core, and display settings on the command line. It then boots the guest OS in a window with a framebuffer display, UART terminal, and keyboard and mouse input. The README also describes a userland emulation mode, still marked WIP, for running RISC-V applications on a foreign-architecture host without a guest OS.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames RVVM as an emulator that emphasizes performance, security, lean code and portability, and says it already runs many guest operating systems, including Linux, Haiku, FreeBSD and OpenBSD. It also aims to run RISC-V applications on a foreign-arch host without full OS guest and isolation.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the CPU runs through a tracing JIT with x86_64, ARM64 and RISC-V backends, and claims this is faster than QEMU TCG. It also lists an interpreter for the RV64IMAFDC instruction set in its contributor notes, and describes a librvvm library API that the rvvm binary builds on. The README does not explain the JIT or the kernel-level isolation mechanism in more detail.

name: s6
desc: Small & secure supervision software suite
why: A small init and supervision suite from skarnet with an unusual philosophy about process supervision worth reading into.

brief.what_it_is: s6 is a small suite of UNIX command-line programs for process supervision (service supervision), in the line of daemontools and runit, plus various other operations on processes and daemons. Its tools are independent and can be used inside or outside the supervision framework, then combined into larger functions. The homepage lists examples: syslogd-style logging, service readiness notification for dependency management, sudo-like privilege gain without setuid binaries, and socket-activation-like behaviour without changing application code. The executables are the s6-* programs plus ucspilogd, and the packaging list includes many of them (s6-svscan, s6-supervise, s6-svc, s6-log, s6-fdholderd, s6-sudo and others).
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes s6 as a toolbox for low-level process and service administration, meant to do a lot with very little code. The homepage has a "Why another supervision suite? Isn't runit good enough?" section, which I did not fetch.
brief.how_it_works: Two long-lived processes, s6-svscan and s6-supervise, maintain the supervision tree, and other programs act as a user interface to control them and watch service state. Readiness notification (s6-svwait, s6-notifyoncheck and related tools) is the basis for dependency management. Fifodirs and the ftrigr/ftrigw libraries provide instant notification between processes. Most programs use the documented exit codes: 111 for a temporary error, 100 for a permanent error, 127 if a program to exec is not found, and 126 if exec fails for another reason.

commands_seen.context: Clones the s6 git repository, one of the ways to get the source. The homepage also says a Codeberg, GitHub or SourceHut mirror exists. Compilation is described only as following the INSTALL file in the source.

brief.install_notes: Requirements: a POSIX-compliant system with a standard C development environment, and GNU make 3.81 or later. skalibs 2.16.0.0 or later is required at build time, and at run time if you link against its shared library. execline 2.10.0.0 or later is optional but recommended for full functionality; it is needed at build time when s6 is built with execline support (the default), and at run time for binaries that spawn execlineb scripts. On musl, nsss 0.2.1.3 or later gives nsswitch-like functionality, needed at build time and boot time. The current release on the homepage is 2.15.1.1, with checksums linked. The homepage does not mention brew, and the brew caveats field is empty. The homepage does not mention a Homebrew formula, so the install route should be checked before the entry asserts one.
brief.standout: The programs are rewrites of daemontools utilities with extras, and the suite does things that are usually done by larger systems: fd-holding (s6-fdholderd) as the sensible part of socket activation, and suidless privilege gain via s6-sudo. The author argues the tools are meant to be assembled rather than used as an all-in-one init, and the homepage's section on other init systems is opinionated about systemd and suckless init.
brief.status: unknown: the homepage names 2.15.1.1 as the current released version and lists git mirrors on Codeberg, GitHub and SourceHut, but I saw no release date or last-commit date.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a project page, not a README, so no install commands beyond git clone were shown. Installation is by building from source against skalibs (and optionally execline). The scout note calls s6 a small init; the homepage presents it as a supervision suite, and init replacement is a separate choice (s6-linux-init, s6-rc and s6-overlay are separate projects it links to). The homepage is also explicit that the Linux socket-activation article it links is one to read with caution. The man-page port, the s6-linux-init and s6-rc links, and the background pages on the mailing list, IRC and related projects were not fetched.
quotes: s6 is a small suite of programs for UNIX, designed to allow process supervision (a.k.a service supervision), in the line of daemontools and runit, as well as various operations on processes and daemons.

It is meant to be a toolbox for low-level process and service administration, providing different sets of independent tools that can be used within or without the framework, and that can be assembled together to achieve powerful functionality with a very small amount of code.
s6 is free software. It is available under the ISC license.
All-in-one init systems generally feel complex and convoluted, and when most people find out about the process supervision approach to init systems, they usually find it much simpler.

desc: Extract/Import/FUSE for 3DS save/extdata/database
why: Mounts and rewrites Nintendo 3DS save and extdata formats as a filesystem, a good door into console storage internals.

brief.what_it_is: Save3DS is a Rust project for reading and writing Nintendo 3DS save data, extdata, and title databases. It has two parts: the library libsave3ds, and the save3ds_fuse program, which extracts, imports, or mounts an archive through FUSE. Inputs are 3DS storage (NAND, SD, cartridge, or a standalone save file) plus console-specific keys and dumps such as boot9.bin, otp.bin, and movable.sed. Outputs are a browsable and editable directory tree on the host, or an extracted or re-imported archive.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit motivation. It describes the project as an 'Extract, import and FUSE program for common save format for 3DS'.
brief.how_it_works: save3ds_fuse takes an archive selector (such as --sdsave, --nandsave, --db, or --cart), a mount path, and a mode. The default mode mounts the archive as a virtual filesystem, and unmounting writes the changes back. --extract and --import move content between the archive and a host directory, and --touch opens and closes the archive to check that the resources are correct. Format parameters are passed through --format and follow the fs:USER service functions on the 3DS.

name: sby
desc: Front-end for Yosys-based formal verification flows
why: Formal hardware verification front-end for Yosys, a real and rarely seen corner of proof-based circuit checking.

brief.what_it_is: SymbiYosys (sby) is a front-end driver program for Yosys-based formal hardware verification flows. You give it a .sby file that defines one or more verification tasks, and it runs Yosys to prepare the hardware design and then hands it to solver engines. It covers bounded and unbounded checking of safety properties (assertions), generating test benches from cover statements, and liveness properties. Its output is a PASS or FAIL per task, plus counterexample traces (VCD, a Verilog testbench, and a constraints file) when a property fails.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs describe sby as the driver that runs Yosys-based formal verification flows for hardware designs, so the user does not have to assemble the Yosys steps and solvers by hand. The README points to YosysHQ's documentation for how to use it and says it is licensed under ISC.
brief.how_it_works: A .sby file is organised into sections (tasks, options, engines, script, files), and each task names its own engine and script steps. sby runs the Yosys commands in the script section (for example read -formal, hierarchy -check, prep) and passes the result to an engine such as smtbmc with boolector, which checks the properties. When a check fails, the engine writes the counterexample trace to engine_0/trace.vcd, a trace_tb.v testbench, and a trace.smtc file.

name: rqlite
desc: Lightweight, distributed relational database built on SQLite
why: A distributed SQLite with a Raft-replicated HTTP interface, an unusual database with a twist worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: rqlite is an open-source, fault-tolerant, distributed relational database built on SQLite. You run the rqlited server binary on one or more machines, and it exposes SQLite behind an HTTP and JSON API. You send SQL statements over HTTP (for example CREATE TABLE or INSERT via POST to /db/execute, and SELECT via GET to /db/query) and get JSON results back. Nodes replicate the data among themselves, so the database stays up if one node fails. The project also ships a CLI, a built-in web console, and client libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The README pitches it as a SQLite that is highly available and easy to operate, aimed at resilient cloud services and reliable edge applications. It says to think of etcd, but with relational modeling available.
brief.how_it_works: Nodes form a cluster and keep their SQLite databases in sync through replication. The README does not name the consensus protocol, but the homepage describes a Raft cluster and a Raft state view in the console. Clients talk to the cluster over plain HTTP with JSON, so no driver is needed. Read consistency and write durability can be tuned per application, and clusters can form automatically through Kubernetes, Docker Compose, Consul, etcd, or DNS.

name: scamper
desc: Advanced traceroute and network measurement utility
why: CAIDA's advanced traceroute and Internet measurement tool, a real door into how the internet's routing is probed and mapped.

brief.what_it_is: Scamper is a feature-rich active Internet probing tool from CAIDA, written by Matthew Luckie, that runs ping, traceroute and related measurements against lists of IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. It takes target addresses from the command line, from files, or from commands sent to a running scamper process over a control socket. Results are written in scamper's native warts format, or as text or JSON. The package also includes many sc_ driver programs and warts conversion tools, plus a Python module and C libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says scamper is the successor to skitter and is built to analyze Internet topology and performance by actively probing at scale. It is the prober deployed in CAIDA's Macroscopic Topology Project. The paper cited on the page describes its motivation as a scalable and extensible packet prober.
brief.how_it_works: Scamper sends probes in parallel at a rate you set with -p, from 1 to 50000 packets per second, so bulk data can be collected in a reasonable time. Simple jobs are a single method applied to a list, such as traceroute over many IPs. Complex jobs use a driver program, written against the Python API or the libscamperctrl and libscamperfile C libraries, that connects to a running scamper and decides the next measurement from earlier results. Output is stored in warts files, which hold metadata about each measurement along with the response detail.

name: scriptisto
desc: Language-agnostic "shebang interpreter" to write scripts in compiled languages

brief.what_it_is: Scriptisto is a command-line tool that acts as a shebang interpreter for single-file scripts written in compiled languages. You put a #!/usr/bin/env scriptisto line at the top of a source file, and the build steps go in a comment block between scriptisto-begin and scriptisto-end markers. On first run it builds the script, caches the result, and runs the binary. It takes a source file as input and produces a cached compiled executable, with no separate build step for the user. The README says templates exist for languages such as Rust, Go, C, Fortran, COBOL and C#.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is a tool for writing one-file scripts in languages that need compilation, dependency fetching or preprocessing, which otherwise need a separate build setup. The wiki 'Advantages' page is linked for more on use cases, but I did not fetch it.
brief.how_it_works: Scriptisto reads the build instructions (such as script_src and build_cmd) from comments in the script. If the script has changed, it rebuilds and caches the result. If a built copy already exists, it hands off to that binary with, per the README, under 1 ms of overhead. Builds can also run inside Docker so no compiler needs to be installed on the host.
