name: scryer-prolog
desc: Modern ISO Prolog implementation written mostly in Rust
why: A modern ISO Prolog in Rust opens a logic programming world most developers never touch.

brief.what_it_is: Scryer Prolog is a free ISO Prolog system written mostly in Rust. You give it Prolog source files, which it consults (loads), or type queries at its interactive toplevel, and it prints answers or bindings such as X = "Scryer Prolog!". It includes a WAM-based engine and a large library set, covering constraint solving (clp(B), clp(Z)), DCGs, tabling, TCP sockets, an HTTP server and client, and cryptography. It can also be built as a WebAssembly package or used as a library from other programs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the goal is to become to ISO Prolog what GHC is to Haskell: an open source, industrial-strength production environment that is also a testbed for bleeding-edge research in logic and constraint programming, itself written in a high-level language.
brief.how_it_works: It is an implementation of the Warren Abstract Machine (WAM) in Rust, built in phases following Warren's Abstract Machine tutorial. Its best-known internal trick is a packed UTF-8 representation of strings and partial strings, which the README says cuts memory use by up to 24-fold compared with one WAM cell per character. Tabling is implemented on top of delimited continuations (reset/3, shift/1) rather than as a separate engine mode.

brief.standout: Scryer's string representation is a packed encoding that makes character lists cheap, and the README says it is the first Prolog system to implement it. It also ships a large standard library, including CLP(Z), tabling, an HTTP server, TLS and crypto, and it claims to pass the ISO syntax conformity tests.

name: scummvm-tools
desc: Collection of tools for ScummVM
why: A toolkit for extracting and converting resources from classic adventure game data files, a good door into old game formats.

brief.what_it_is: scummvm-tools is a collection of utilities that work with ScummVM and the original data files of classic adventure games. The extraction and compression tools can run from the command line or from a GUI wizard, and the rest are command-line only. Inputs are original game data files, such as archives, disk images, and scripts. Outputs are extracted resources, recompressed audio (MP3, Vorbis, or FLAC), rebuilt data packs, or decompiled and disassembled scripts. The main entry point is scummvm-tools-cli, which auto-detects the right tool from the input file. Extraction and compression are selected with the extract or compress modes, or by naming a tool with --tool. Audio format flags (--mp3, --flac, --vorbis) and tool-specific options are passed before the input file. The script tools, such as decine, degob, and descumm, are standalone decompilers or disassemblers that take a script file and a version or type flag.

name: sdcc

brief.what_it_is: SDCC is a retargetable, optimizing ANSI/ISO C compiler suite for small microcontrollers. It takes C source and produces machine code for Intel MCS51 parts (8031, 8051, 8052 and similar), Maxim DS80C390, Freescale HC08/S08, many Zilog Z80-family chips, Padauk, STM8, MOS 6502 and WDC 65C02. The suite also bundles an assembler and linker (sdas/sdld), a preprocessor (sdcpp), a source-level debugger (sdcdb), archive tools, and about a dozen ucsim simulators. Prebuilt binaries are published for GNU/Linux amd64, Windows, and macOS amd64.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents SDCC as a portable, optimizing C compiler for 8-bit and small MCU targets, developed by volunteers and kept current by user input since it moved to SourceForge in 1999. The funding news frames the goal as making SDCC more competitive with non-free compilers and better suited to modern C standards, safety, and security.
brief.how_it_works: The page describes a compiler proper (sdcc) with MCU-specific language extensions, standard optimizations (CSE, loop optimizations, constant folding, dead code elimination, switch jump tables), a global register allocator, and a rule-based peephole optimizer. Per-target backends sit under a shared front end, and the assembler/linker derive from ASXXXX and the archive tools from GNU Binutils. The page does not describe the internal pipeline in more detail.

name: sdrmm
desc: Modular, client-server software-defined radio
why: A client-server software-defined radio system, a neat architectural idea for listening to the airwaves with real hardware.

brief.what_it_is: SDR-- (the brew formula calls it sdrmm) is a software-defined radio application for listening, decoding, and recording. You plug in a radio (the README's first example is an RTL-SDR dongle) and wire up nodes on a canvas: a Device node for the radio, channel nodes such as WFM, and displays and outputs such as a Speaker. It can run as a desktop app with a local SDR, or as a server near the antenna that you reach from a browser; both use the same receiver engine and interface. Outputs include audio, decoded messages, maps, recordings, and network IQ, and a phone remote is also offered. The brew formula's desc calls it a modular, client-server software-defined radio, which matches the server-plus-browser design the README describes.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a single application for listening, decoding, and recording radio signals, with a layout that puts connections in a Patch view and everyday controls in a Rack view. It also positions the server as something you can put near an antenna and reach remotely, rather than a desktop-only tool.
brief.how_it_works: Radios, channels, and displays are nodes you connect with wires in the Patch view; for example, Device iq is wired to WFM iq, and WFM audio to the Speaker. Nodes you use often can be pinned to the Rack view with the p key. The desktop app and the server share one receiver engine, so the browser interface and the local app behave the same. The README says Automation is available through REST, WebSocket, and MCP APIs.

name: seqwish
desc: Alignment to variation graph inducer
why: Builds variation graphs from pairwise sequence alignments; real genomics science, but a specialised pipeline piece.

brief.what_it_is: seqwish is a command-line tool and Rust library that converts pairwise sequence alignments into a variation graph. It takes FASTA or FASTQ sequences (plain or gzipped) plus alignments in PAF format, where each alignment must carry a cg:z: CIGAR tag. It writes a GFA1 graph to the file given with -g, or to standard output if -g is omitted. The README says the input is typically all-versus-all alignments, produced by aligners such as wfmash or minimap2.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says seqwish is built for very large inputs with many noisy sequences, where memory must stay bounded. It uses disk-backed sorts and passes over the alignment and sequence inputs, and the author describes the goal as a lossless conversion from alignments to a graph. The project's own framing is "These sequences wish they were squished into a graph."
brief.how_it_works: The README describes a "squish" induction algorithm. Sequences are concatenated into a coordinate space Q with a compressed suffix array and rank/select dictionaries, and alignments are sorted by position in Q. For each base, the transitive closure of aligned bases is collapsed into one graph base, and links between graph bases are derived from the rewritten input sequences. Unitigs are then compressed into single nodes, and the result is written as GFA or vg format. The README says memory is limited by sorted disk-backed arrays and succinct rank/select structures.

name: sequin
desc: Human-readable ANSI sequences
why: Turns raw ANSI escape sequences into human-readable text, a small window into how terminals actually talk.

brief.what_it_is: Sequin is a small command-line filter from Charm that takes raw text containing ANSI/VT escape sequences on stdin and prints a human-readable description of each sequence, so you can see what the escape codes are doing. It can also run a program for you in a fake TTY with `sequin -- <command>`, and its `-r`/`--raw` flag highlights sequences inline in the original text instead of describing them. The README describes it as "Human-readable ANSI sequences."
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is a utility for debugging CLIs and TUIs, for describing escape sequences you don't understand, and for exploring what TUIs do under the hood. It also mentions inspecting golden files from Bubble Tea's teatest.
brief.how_it_works: Sequin relies on the `ansi` package from Charm's `x` project (github.com/charmbracelet/x/ansi). While it walks through the input string, it pretty-prints what each sequence is and what it does. The FAQ also notes that some background-colour queries (OSC 10/11) go through to the terminal, so multiplexer version and config matter for those.

name: sequoia-sq
desc: Sequoia-PGP command-line tool
why: A modern OpenPGP implementation with a CLI; the packet format it exposes is a worthwhile door, though it is a close call.

brief.what_it_is: sq is the command-line frontend for Sequoia, a Rust implementation of OpenPGP, installed as the executable 'sq'. It covers common OpenPGP tasks: encrypt and decrypt messages, sign and verify messages or detached signatures, download a file and check its signature, generate and manipulate keys and certificates, query keyrings, look up or publish certs over the network, and inspect any OpenPGP data (similar to file(1)). Inputs are files, stdin, URLs or keyrings, in binary or ASCII-armored form, and the tool handles armor automatically. Output is ASCII-armored by default. The homepage says Sequoia is a new OpenPGP library focused on safety and correctness and written in a memory-safe language.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Sequoia as 'a new OpenPGP Library' with a focus on safety and correctness, and says improving the security of OpenPGP users 'requires more than a new implementation', so the project is also improving the surrounding ecosystem. The sq manual pitches the CLI as a tool that makes OpenPGP usable for ordinary tasks and offers a Web of Trust authentication model as an alternative to X.509 certificate authorities.
brief.how_it_works: Commands are grouped into subcommands (encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify, download, inspect, cert, key, pki, network, keyring, packet, config, toc, version). The interface is not fully stateless: it uses a default certificate store under $HOME/.local/share/pgp.cert.d and a key store server under $HOME/.local/share/sequoia/keystore, which sq starts if none is running. Verification succeeds only if there are no bad signatures and the count of good ones meets the --signatures threshold. The CLI is versioned and --cli-version can pin an interface version. The --time and --policy-as-of flags let you verify or inspect data as of a past reference time.

Default config lives at $HOME/.config/sequoia/sq/config.toml, and a config template can be created with sq config. The manual also says sq packet dump is useful as a learning tool for the OpenPGP packet format, which matches the scout's note that the packet layer is the most interesting door, though this is a close call since the other features are more conventional.

name: ser2net
desc: Allow network connections to serial ports
why: Exposes serial ports over the network, a neat bridge into physical devices hiding behind old serial lines.

brief.what_it_is: ser2net is a daemon that makes a serial port reachable over the network. It takes a YAML configuration naming an accepter (such as tcp or telnet on a port number) and a connector (such as serialdev with a device path and line settings like 115200N81), then opens a network listener and relays bytes between the socket and the physical serial device. The README describes it as allowing connections between gensio accepters and gensio connectors, and says that generally means network connections to serial ports or IPMI Serial Over LAN connections. The homepage adds that it provides serial port setup, a configuration file, a control login for changing port parameters, and port monitoring and control.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Corey Minyard, says on the homepage: "I tried all the other ones I could find and found them lacking, so I wrote my own." The aim is to let people reach serial devices, such as UPS units and old equipment, from across a network without running a cable to the machine.
brief.how_it_works: ser2net is built on the gensio library, which supplies the accepter and connector layers, so the strings in its config are passed almost directly to gensio. Optional layers add RFC 2217 remote control of port parameters (via telnet(rfc2217)), TLS/SSL, certificate-based authentication (certauth), mDNS discovery, and multiplexing. It uses epoll on modern Linux and can run with a configurable number of threads, and it handles reconfiguration in a separate thread.

brief.install_notes: The README says ser2net needs three libraries to build: libyaml, libxcrypt and gensio. The distro gensio package may be missing features or be too old, so gensio may need building from the tarball on SourceForge or from github.com/cminyard/gensio. Crypto, mDNS and IPMI features depend on how gensio was compiled. The build is standard autoconf; if you build from git rather than a release tarball, run the included reconf script first. Docker support is available from github.com/jippi/docker-ser2net. Windows builds are possible under MINGW64 or UCRT64 but need extra steps (see caveats). The config file lives at /etc/ser2net/ser2net.yaml in the README example. The Homebrew caveat says to edit $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/etc/ser2net/ser2net.yaml. The README also advises running ser2net as a dedicated user, not root.
brief.standout: Rather than being a simple socket-to-tty bridge, it sits on a general connection-stacking library, so one YAML line can add RFC 2217 remote port control, TLS with client certificates, mDNS advertisement, or IPMI Serial Over LAN as a serial source. The README also notes that a telnet-based port with rfc2217 turned on lets a client change baud and stop bits remotely.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as I can tell. The SourceForge project page shows a last update of 2026-08-14, a registration date of 2001-06-04, and a 2024 user-review reply saying multi-connection support has been added. The GitHub README is current and documents gensio-based features and a Windows build. I did not see commit dates on GitHub, so the most recent activity is the SourceForge date.
brief.caveats: The SourceForge page lists the operating systems as BSD and Linux. The README says the test suite runs only on Linux and needs a simulated serial kernel module (serialsim) plus Python bindings for gensio and, for IPMI tests, OpenIPMI. Building on Windows requires some work: libxcrypt does not build cleanly there, so you must remove -Werror from its Makefile, and the README also says it needs an Inno Setup step for the installer. Normal ssh clients do not work with ser2net encryption; you need gtlssh or gensiot. The standard telnet command cannot use RFC 2217 control; a compliant client such as gensiot or gtlssh is required. brief.what_it_is: sh4d0wup is a command-line framework, written in Rust, that runs a malicious HTTP/HTTPS update server acting as a reverse proxy in front of a legitimate update server. It takes a 'plot' (a YAML file, or a prebuilt tar.zst archive made from one) that describes request routing, how artifacts are patched or generated, and which signing key to sign them with. It can also infect ELF binaries, pacman, deb and OCI image packages directly, and generate or use signing keys, including hardware keys.

The bait subcommand serves the matching artifacts, which are patched with the infect subcommands and signed with the configured key. For development and testing, mock signing keys and certificates can be generated and marked as trusted. A plot can be compiled ahead of time with build so downloads and artifact patching don't slow startup.

name: sha1dc
desc: Tool to detect SHA-1 collisions in files, including SHAttered
why: Detects SHAttered-style crafted SHA-1 collisions by inspecting file contents, a real door into how the hash is broken.

brief.what_it_is: sha1dcsum is a C library and command-line tool that computes the SHA-1 hash of files, like sha1sum, and also checks whether the input shows signs of a cryptanalytic SHA-1 collision attack. It takes a file (or stdin via '-') and prints the hash plus a warning when a known attack pattern is found. The package includes two programs: sha1dcsum, which detects SHAttered-style and sha-mbles attacks, and sha1dcsum_partialcoll, which detects attacks against reduced-round SHA-1. The library exposes an indicator flag, and a safe-hash mode that changes the output hash when a collision is detected.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes the tool as designed to be a near drop-in replacement for common SHA-1 libraries and sha1sum, so that applications can detect known SHA-1 collision attacks without changing much code. The README frames the goal as protecting applications, such as those vulnerable to forged digital signatures built from SHA-1 collisions.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the detector looks for the disturbance vectors used by known collision attacks, and claims detection of any collision attack using the top 32 SHA-1 disturbance vectors with probability 1, with false positives below 2^-90. In safe-hash mode, an undetected file gets the real SHA-1 hash, while a detected collision gets a different, unpredictable 'safe' hash, so colliding files no longer match. The theory is in the author's CRYPTO 2013 paper 'Counter-cryptanalysis'.

name: sgn
desc: Shikata ga nai (仕方がない) encoder ported into go with several improvements
why: A polymorphic shellcode encoder that rewrites payloads to evade detection, a good window into how binaries get disguised.

brief.what_it_is: sgn is a command-line polymorphic binary encoder, the Rust port of the Shikata ga nai shellcode encoder. It takes a raw binary payload (for example shellcode in a file) and outputs an encoded binary that is wrapped in a runtime decoder stub. Each pass prepends random garbage instructions, enciphers the payload with an LFSR-style cipher, and can additionally encrypt the decoder stub itself. Options cover 32- or 64-bit architecture, number of encoding passes, bad-byte avoidance, ASCII-only output, and a register-preserving safe mode. It can also be used as a Rust library.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the original Shikata ga nai is considered the best shellcode encoder, but researchers (cited via a FireEye article) found ways to statically detect its decoder stub. The stated goal is an encoder whose output is 'identical with totally random data and not possible to detect the presence of a decoder.'
brief.how_it_works: Each encoding pass optionally appends a register-restore suffix (safe mode), prepends random value-preserving garbage instructions, and ciphers the payload with the ADFL (additive feedback loop) cipher, prepending a loop-free decoder stub that reverses it at runtime. Unless --plain is given, the stub is itself encrypted with a random per-run schema cipher (XOR/ADD/SUB/ROL/ROR/NOT over DWORDs) and prepended with a self-locating schema decoder. The --enc option repeats this with fresh seeds, and safe mode may add a register-save prefix. The README describes the LFSR as a companion-matrix construction in Fibonacci configuration.

name: shairport-sync
desc: AirTunes emulator that adds multi-room capability
why: An AirPlay receiver that reveals how AirTunes audio streams over the network, though it is mostly a practical server.

brief.what_it_is: Shairport Sync is an AirPlay audio receiver for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS and OpenBSD. It takes audio streamed from Apple devices and from AirPlay sources such as OwnTone, and sends it to a sound system (ALSA, sndio, PipeWire, PulseAudio, CoreAudio), a unix pipe, or STDOUT. It can be built for AirPlay 2 (stereo and multichannel, including lossless 24-bit stereo at 48,000 frames per second) or as classic AirPlay 1. It can also expose metadata such as artist and cover art, and accept remote control, over MQTT, an MPRIS-like interface and D-Bus.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a practical AirPlay player for Linux and other Unix-like systems, with a substantial rewrite of Shairport 1.0 as its heritage. The README says Apple's AirPlay protocols are unpublished, so the project is the result of study and analysis of how those protocols behave.
brief.how_it_works: Shairport Sync keeps the source's timestamps in step with the local machine's clock, so audio plays at the time the source specifies. When used with ALSA, sndio, CoreAudio, PipeWire or PulseAudio, it compares source timestamps with timing feedback from the audio system and resamples frames slightly to add or remove them as needed; libsoxr gives higher-quality resampling when the CPU can afford it. For AirPlay 2, a companion application called NQPTP handles PTP-based clock sync, and classic AirPlay uses a variant of NTP-style synchronisation.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no install commands; it points to BUILD.md for building from source and to CONFIGURATION FLAGS.md for build-time options, since some features need them. AirPlay 2 builds need the separate NQPTP companion app. Runtime settings are documented in scripts/shairport-sync.conf. A Docker image is on Docker Hub (mikebrady/shairport-sync), with docker/README.md. The README says it needs roughly Raspberry Pi B-class power or better. For best sync, it recommends a dedicated headless system with ALSA and a decent DAC. Updaters should read RELEASENOTES.md for breaking changes. The man page covers command-line options. The brew caveats field was empty, and I did not verify the Homebrew formula itself.
brief.standout: Full audio synchronisation: rather than just buffering, it stretches or shrinks the audio stream by resampling so that playback stays locked to the source clock on the local clock, to within a fraction of a millisecond with ALSA. It also ships its own AirPlay 2 timing daemon (NQPTP) and offers MQTT, D-Bus and MPRIS interfaces for metadata and remote control.

brief.what_it_is: Shamrock is an open-source hydrodynamics simulation code for astrophysics, described by its authors as a general-purpose HPC code focused on astrophysical contexts. It runs astrophysical fluid simulations, including particle-based SPH and grid-based methods, on GPUs or CPUs and can scale across multiple GPUs and heterogeneous clusters with MPI. Its accelerated parts are written in SYCL, so one source base can target CUDA, ROCm, OpenMP, OpenCL and others. The README does not spell out input and output file formats, so I could not confirm those.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a code that aims to be Modern, Modular, Fast, Portable, aimed at astrophysical hydrodynamics on HPC hardware. The homepage adds that it should scale from laptops to exascale supercomputers.
brief.how_it_works: The whole code is C++20 by default, and all accelerated components are written in SYCL, which compiles to native CUDA, ROCm, OpenMP, OpenCL and more. Multiple GPUs and heterogeneous clusters are supported through MPI. The homepage says the solvers include SPH, AMR and other methods, but I did not see the details of how each one is implemented.

name: shtools
desc: Spherical Harmonic Tools
why: Spherical harmonic tools for geophysics and planetary maps lets you run real science on a globe at home.

brief.what_it_is: SHTOOLS (the Python package is called pyshtools, docs show version 4.14) is a library for working with spherical harmonics on a sphere. It takes gridded data or spherical harmonic coefficients as input and returns transforms between them, spectra, and derived fields. Its stated uses are spherical harmonic transforms, multitaper spectral analyses, expansion of gridded data into Slepian basis functions, and standard operations on global gravity and magnetic field data. The core is Fortran 95, wrapped by a Python interface, and it also imports gravity, topography and magnetic datasets and makes maps via Cartopy and PyGMT. It is a code library, not a command-line tool, so it has no executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as an archive of software for spherical harmonic transforms, multitaper spectral analysis and Slepian expansions of global gravitational and magnetic field data. The reference paper is Wieczorek and Meschede (2018), SHTools: Tools for working with spherical harmonics, in Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems.
brief.how_it_works: The Fortran 95 core runs the transforms and is exposed to Python through wrappers and dedicated classes. Users can pick among normalization and phase conventions and convert between real and complex harmonics, and the README mentions a choice of backends (the native Fortran one, or DUCC0) for the heavy math. The docs also describe regularly sampled geographic grids and Gauss-Legendre quadrature grids.

name: shmcat
desc: Tool that dumps shared memory segments (System V and POSIX)
why: Dumps System V and POSIX shared memory segments, a rare look at inter-process memory living on the system.

brief.what_it_is: shmcat is a small command-line tool, written in C, that dumps the contents of shared memory segments. It handles both System V segments (created with shmget/shmat) and POSIX segments (created with shm_open). The project page also says it can dump files, like cat, and text, like echo, and that several objects can be dumped in one run. The page does not show example invocations or output.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says it is 'a simple tool that dumps shared memory segments (System V and POSIX), files and text. It might be useful when you have to debug programs that use shared memory.'
brief.how_it_works: The SourceForge page does not explain the mechanism. It lists features only: System V access through the shmget/shmat API, POSIX access through shm_open, and an optional utility that computes System V IPC keys with the ftok(3) library function.
brief.install_notes: The page gives no install steps, build instructions, or dependencies. It has a 'Download' button and an 'Add to Preferred Sources' option on the SourceForge project page. The brew entry lists the executable as shmcat. Platform support is listed as Linux and FreeBSD.
brief.standout: It is a niche debugging tool that looks at inter-process shared memory directly, which most tools don't do. It also accepts files and plain text as inputs, so it can be used like cat and echo in the same run.
brief.status: Maintained, judging by the page metadata. The SourceForge page shows 'Last Update: 2026-07-24', 'Downloads: 8 This Week', and a registration date of 2012-02-21. The page does not contain a changelog or a commit history, so this is the only evidence I have.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a SourceForge project listing, not a project site with docs. It has no README, usage examples, or command reference, and I could not see any command lines. Listed platforms are Linux and FreeBSD; the page says it 'probably' works on other un*x systems. Licence is GPL v2. The page offers no evidence on whether the tool works with recent kernels or with shared memory from containers.

name: sile
desc: Modern typesetting system inspired by TeX
why: A TeX-inspired typesetting system written in Lua, an unusual and underknown take on document layout.

brief.what_it_is: SILE is a typesetting system that takes a plain-text source document (for example, a .sil file) and produces a printed-quality PDF. It is programmable in Lua, and the README says it can also process XML directly to PDF without XSL stylesheets. Its features include page layout with frames and typesetting text on a grid. The CLI is a Rust binary with a Lua VM built in since v0.15.0, and a pure-Lua CLI is still available as sile-lua.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says SILE is conceptually similar to TeX, borrowing some of its concepts and algorithms, but is 'a new typesetting and layout engine written from the ground up using modern technologies and borrowing some ideas from graphical systems such as InDesign.' The stated aim is 'to produce beautiful printed documents.'
brief.how_it_works: The Rust CLI embeds a Lua VM and runs SILE's Lua code, so documents and extensions are scripted in Lua. Font access and shaping use HarfBuzz with fontconfig, and PDF output uses libtexpdf, a PDF library extracted from TeX. ICU handles Unicode. Third-party packages are installed with LuaRocks and found by SILE at runtime.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew does not install the default font, so install Gentium Book (brew install font-gentium-book). Fonts that matter are Gentium Book for body text, Libertinus Math for formulas, and Hack for monospace. The README says that without these fonts the examples will not work unless modified. Building from source needs a Rust toolchain and Lua sources (Lua 5.1 through 5.4 or LuaJIT are supported), HarfBuzz 2.7.4 or newer, fontconfig, and ICU (on macOS: brew install icu4c, then export PKG_CONFIG_PATH if pkg-config cannot find it). OpenSSL development headers are needed to compile luasec. Third-party plugins are installed with luarocks --lua-version $(sile -q <<< SILE.lua_version) install <package>. Docker users must mount a fonts folder to /fonts because the container has no access to host fonts by default.
brief.standout: SILE is a TeX-inspired typesetter written in Lua rather than a TeX derivative, and it can be extended in Lua. It offers frames and grid typesetting, and the README claims it can take XML straight to PDF without XSL. Since v0.15.0 the CLI is a Rust binary with an embedded Lua VM.

name: silk
desc: Collection of traffic analysis tools
why: CERT's flow-record traffic analysis suite opens a door into NetFlow-style network telemetry few developers have seen.

brief.what_it_is: SiLK (System for Internet-Level Knowledge) is a suite of command-line traffic analysis tools from CERT NetSA for querying large volumes of network flow data. Its packing system takes IPFIX, NetFlow v9, or NetFlow v5 input and converts it into a more space-efficient format, stored as service-specific binary flat files. The analysis suite reads those flat files and runs queries ranging from per-record filtering to statistical analysis of groups of records. The tools chain together through pipes. The homepage lists version 3.24.2 and about 70 executables, including rwfilter, rwcut, rwstats, rwuniq, rwsort and flowcap.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says SiLK exists to facilitate security analysis of large networks by supporting efficient collection, storage, and analysis of flow data, so analysts can rapidly query large historical traffic data sets. It is pitched as best suited to backbone or border traffic for a large distributed enterprise or mid-sized ISP.
brief.how_it_works: Flow records are collected and packed into compact binary flat files by the packing system. The analysis tools read those files and communicate through Unix pipes, so a simple query can be built up stage by stage. The homepage says most of the code is C, Perl, or Python.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no install steps. It offers downloads and a Documentation link, but I did not fetch those pages, so setup and configuration details are unknown from this brief. The tested platforms are Linux, Solaris, OpenBSD, Mac OS X, and Cygwin, and the homepage says it should be usable with little or no change on other Unix platforms.
brief.standout: Flow data is stored in a compact binary format and the tools are designed to be piped together like classic Unix utilities, which makes large historical NetFlow/IPFIX archives queryable from the shell. The tool names are terse rw-prefixed commands, and the executables list shows many of them.
brief.status: Unknown as to exact maintenance date. The homepage shows current version 3.24.2 and a copyright range running to 2026, which suggests active development, but no release date or last commit date was visible in what I fetched.

name: simgrid
desc: Studies behavior of large-scale distributed systems
why: A discrete-event simulator for studying large distributed systems, a real research tool you can run at home to model networks and clusters.

brief.what_it_is: SimGrid is a framework for building simulators of distributed computer systems. You write a program against its API (in C, C++, Python, or Java, per the homepage) that describes a platform such as clusters, networks, or data centers, plus the applications running on it. The simulator then predicts performance, including time and energy, and can also be used to debug and profile real MPI applications. It is a library, not a graphical tool or a command-line simulator that runs user scripts. The brew package also ships companion executables (graphicator, simgrid-mc, smpicc, smpicxx, smpirun, tesh, and others), but I did not see their usage in the pages I fetched.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says SimGrid exists to "prototype, evaluate and compare relevant platform configurations, system designs, and algorithmic approaches" for distributed applications. The docs add that it has been developed for about 20 years by a research community, initially in France and the U.S.A.
brief.how_it_works: Simulation models for platforms such as commodity clusters, WANs and LANs, DSL peers, and data centers are provided ready to use, and the APIs let you build a simulator on top of them. The docs describe the models as fast, scalable, and experimentally validated. The docs also mention a prototypical model checker for formally checking simple algorithms and applications.

name: sipp
desc: Traffic generator for the SIP protocol
why: A SIP traffic generator that opens a real door into the telephony protocol running behind calls and VoIP systems.

brief.what_it_is: SIPp is a free, open source test tool and traffic generator for the SIP protocol, the signalling protocol behind VoIP and call systems. It ships with a few basic SIPstone UAC and UAS user-agent scenarios that set up and tear down multiple calls with INVITE and BYE. It also reads custom XML scenario files describing call flows from very simple to complex, and it can send RTP media through RTP echo or pcap replay. Its output is live statistics on the terminal (call rate, round trip delay, message counts), periodic CSV dumps, and a passed/failed verdict when run as a single call.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says SIPp is for testing real SIP equipment such as proxies, B2BUAs, media servers, gateways and PBXes, and for emulating thousands of user agents calling your SIP system. It is aimed at traffic, stress and performance testing, though it can also run one call and exit.
brief.how_it_works: Scenarios are described in XML call flows, and the tool drives them over UDP, TCP, TLS, or SCTP, with retransmission management and adjustable call rates. Regular expressions extract protocol fields from received messages so they can be re-injected into later messages, and CSV files can inject per-user field data to emulate live users. Call-specific variables, conditional branches, and actions on message receipt (logging, running a system command, stopping the call) are also supported.

name: siril

brief.what_it_is: Siril is a desktop astronomical image processing program for preprocessing and processing telescope images. It takes raw camera frames, FITS files, and SER video sequences, applies calibration with bias, dark and flat master frames, registers and stacks many frames into one image, then offers enhancement tools such as colour calibration, deconvolution and histogram stretching. It also has science tools for star brightness variation and astrometry. It ships as a GUI app with a companion command-line binary, siril-cli. The homepage describes it as 'an astronomical image processing tool'.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the job as improving signal-to-noise ratio by combining many registered frames, and removing unwanted signal and pattern from raw images in a calibration step. It presents itself as a complete workflow from raw data to publishable image, usable manually or through scripts.
brief.how_it_works: Preprocessing writes out a new file for each step, using the SER or FITS-cube formats to keep this cheap. Stacking methods run in parallel across all cores, and registration can align on all stars, one star, or the nebulosity, which the site says helps with faint stars. Outlier rejection during stacking further reduces noise.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are offered per platform from the homepage: Linux AppImage, a third-party Flathub Flatpak (flagged with a warning), Windows 64-bit UCRT64 installer and Portable UCRT64 build, and macOS Intel and Apple Silicon builds. The homepage asks users who publish work with Siril to cite the JOSS paper.
brief.standout: It processes SER video natively, so lucky-imaging workflows with tens of thousands of frames are practical, and the site claims 10,000 images can be processed in about the time it takes to drink a coffee. The project is open source under GPLv3 and is also published as a journal article in the Journal of Open Source Software.

The -l option daemonizes it as a minimal HTTP server; the README says only the first line of each request is parsed, the file name is looked up in a skin directory, and $$command(n)?yes:no$$ control sequences in HTML pages are replaced with live outlet status or actions.

name: sleuthkit
desc: Forensic toolkit
why: A forensic toolkit for dissecting disk images and file systems, a real door into how storage is structured.

brief.what_it_is: The Sleuth Kit (TSK) is an open source collection of command-line forensic tools and a C library for analyzing disk images and file systems. It takes a raw disk or file system image, such as one made with dd, and lets an investigator inspect partitions, file system structures, files, deleted content, and hashes, and recover evidence. The tools are low-level and each does one job, so they are chained together for a full analysis. It also powers Autopsy, a GUI front end.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it lets investigators identify and recover evidence from images acquired during incident response or from live systems, and that being open source lets investigators verify what the tool does or customize it. It describes itself as independent of any commercial or academic organization.
brief.how_it_works: Tools are organized in layers, and each name's first letter shows its layer: f for file names (fls, ffind), i for metadata structures such as inodes (ils, istat, icat, ifind), and blk for content units (blkls, blkcat, blkcalc, blkstat). Its code descends from The Coroner's Toolkit file system tools, modified for platform independence, with added support for NTFS and FAT. Timelines come from fls and ils body files fed to mactime, and hfind does fast hash-set lookups including NSRL.

commands_seen.context: From the README's timeline section: used to get data on allocated and unallocated file names for a mactime body file.

brief.standout: Tool names carry their layer in the first letter, and each tool does one narrow job meant to be piped and combined, closer to Unix philosophy than to a single monolithic forensic suite. Its lineage runs back to Wietse Venema and Dan Farmer's Coroner's Toolkit.

name: skani
desc: Fast, robust ANI and aligned fraction for (metagenomic) genomes and contigs
why: Fast average nucleotide identity estimation for metagenomic genomes is real bioinformatics you can run on your own sequences.

brief.what_it_is: skani is a command-line program that calculates average nucleotide identity (ANI) and aligned fraction (AF) between DNA sequences such as genomes, MAGs (metagenome-assembled genomes), and contigs, for ANI above roughly 80%. You give it FASTA files, and it prints tab-separated results with the ANI and the fraction of each genome aligned. It has three main modes: pairwise or all-vs-all comparison (dist), searching a query against a prebuilt sketch database (search), and building a similarity matrix or edge list for a folder of genomes (triangle). The README describes it as an approximate mapping method that avoids base-level alignment, combined with a k-mer sketching filter.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says skani is meant for large-scale microbial genomics and for comparing incomplete MAGs, where it claims to be more accurate than pure sketching methods such as Mash, which 'may underestimate ANI for incomplete MAGs'. It is also aimed at speed on huge, diverse datasets.
brief.how_it_works: skani uses an approximate mapping method without base-level alignment to estimate ANI, and a fast k-mer sketching filter to make comparisons across very large collections feasible. Sketches can be saved to a database with skani sketch and searched later with skani search. The README does not go into further internal detail; the Nature Methods paper it cites describes sparse chaining.

The README says the static binary runs about 3-10% slower most of the time and can be drastically slower on some tasks. No accounts, API keys, or config files are mentioned. For searching, you either download a pre-sketched database from the wiki or build one yourself with skani sketch; the README cites about 6 GB RAM for searching a database of more than 65,000 prokaryotic genomes. The clustering script in scripts/ needs python3, seaborn, scipy/numpy, and matplotlib.
brief.standout: It reports aligned fraction alongside ANI, so you can tell how much of each genome the ANI is based on, which matters for incomplete MAGs. brief.status: Maintained, per the README. It names a single active developer (Jim Shaw), announces v0.4.0 as released with a dated note of October 2026, and links a CHANGELOG. I could not see commit history or release dates on the page itself, so this rests on the README's own statements.

The prebuilt binary is Linux x86-64 only and can be slower. The Rust API has no stability guarantee and minimal docs. The Python bindings (pyskani) are by a different author, and the README disclaims their correctness. The README does not state a license in the text I read.

name: ski
desc: Evade the deadly Yeti on your jet-powered skis
why: Eric Raymond's old terminal skiing game with a Yeti, a charming relic of classic Unix game culture.

brief.what_it_is: ski is a terminal game, written in Python per the man page, in which you ski down an endless slope while unable to see ahead, since your jet-powered skis are on backwards. The input is single-letter commands typed at a '?' prompt, one per turn (for example turn, jump, teleport, launch an ICBM, or summon the Fire Demon), and the output is an ASCII view of the slope drawn behind you. The goal is to avoid trees, ice, bare ground and the Yeti for as long as possible. The run ends when something bad happens, and the final score reflects distance skied, jumps, Yetis melted, and remaining health.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as a silly, fun game that shows you do not need fancy graphical user interfaces to have a good time. It is a revival of a classic Unix-era game, originally by Mark Stevans for Roy's Games, Inc., with the Python implementation, colour support and the invisible shell monster added by Eric S. Raymond.
brief.how_it_works: The slope is shown as characters: '.' snow is safe, 'Y' trees hurt, ' ' bare ground can make you fall, '#' ice stops turning, and 'A' is the Yeti, which crawls toward you at one space per turn and grabs you within one space. name: slirp4netns
desc: User-mode networking for unprivileged network namespaces
why: A user-mode TCP/IP stack that gives unprivileged containers networking, a neat door into how network namespaces and NAT work.

brief.what_it_is: slirp4netns is a user-mode networking program for Linux network namespaces that an unprivileged user can create. You run it on the host with the PID of a process in the namespace and a TAP device name, such as tap0. It attaches that TAP device to a user-space TCP/IP stack (libslirp, the "slirp" stack), which gives the namespace outbound internet access without root. The namespace ends up with a tap0 interface (the README example shows 10.0.2.100/24) and can reach the Internet through the host. It runs as a separate process alongside the namespace rather than as a library.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that since Linux 3.8 unprivileged users can create network and user namespaces, but those namespaces were not very useful because creating veth pairs across the host and namespace still needs root, so a namespace had no internet connection.
brief.how_it_works: slirp4netns connects a TAP device inside the target network namespace to the user-mode TCP/IP stack from libslirp. The README says it is optimized to avoid copying packets across namespaces, and it benchmarks faster than vde_plug and VPNKit on an iperf3 test from 2018. The example sets up a resolver by pointing resolv.conf at the 10.0.2.3 nameserver that slirp provides.

commands_seen.context: Terminal 1: creates user, network, and mount namespaces as an unprivileged user, the first step of the quick start.
Terminal 2: starts slirp4netns against the namespace PID saved in /tmp/pid and creates a tap0 device with the given MTU.
Run inside the namespace: writes a resolv.conf that points at the slirp DNS address 10.0.2.3.
Run inside the namespace: bind-mounts the custom resolv.conf over /etc/resolv.conf so name lookups work.
Run inside the namespace as a final check that outbound internet access works.
Prints the slirp4netns version and the linked libslirp version, shown in the maintenance section.

If unshare fails, the README says some distros (Debian, Arch, old CentOS 7) may need sysctl changes: set user.max_user_namespaces=28633 and, where present, kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1, then run sudo sysctl --system. Building from source needs libglib, libslirp (v4.1.0 or later), libcap, and libseccomp development packages. For a static build, configure with LDFLAGS=-static. name: slowhttptest
desc: Simulates application layer denial of service attacks
why: Slowloris-style attacks reveal how HTTP servers handle partial requests, a useful and slightly unsettling look at a protocol weakness.

brief.what_it_is: SlowHTTPTest is a command-line tool that simulates Application Layer denial-of-service attacks by holding HTTP connections open for as long as possible, in several different ways. You point it at a web server with a target and tuning options (the README mentions connection counts and per-connection behaviour), and it reports on how the server copes. The README also lists a companion beta, slowhttptest-ng, a C++ rewrite that installs alongside the classic binary and adds HTTP/2 attacks and a JSON availability verdict. The README's own description of the classic tool is that it simulates some Application Layer DoS attacks by prolonging HTTP connections in different ways.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is for testing your own web server for DoS vulnerabilities, or for finding out how many concurrent connections it can handle. It frames the work as defensive: availability testing, capacity planning, and checking that HTTP-layer DoS mitigations do what you think they do.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals of the classic tool beyond saying it prolongs HTTP connections in different ways. The ng README table names the techniques: slow headers (-H), slow body (-B), range (-R), and slow read (-X) for the classic tool, plus HTTP/2 slow read, rapid reset, and CONTINUATION flood in ng. The classic report is a CSV of socket states, and ng's report is a verdict (served, slow, or denied) with a list of other possible explanations.

commands_seen.context: Fetches the latest official classic image from Docker Hub, the README's suggested way to try the tool without building it.
Example run of the beta slowhttptest-ng binary from the ng image against a placeholder target, with 1000 connections (-c 1000) and the slow-headers mode (-H).

brief.install_notes: The README points to the Wiki for installation and usage details, which I did not fetch. It says the tool works on most Linux distributions, OS X, and Cygwin, and it ships a Dockerfile. The Docker Hub image is the simplest route. The v1.10.0 release notes (fetched from the releases page) mention ./configure, an OpenSSL requirement, and a --with-openssl=DIR option for non-standard OpenSSL locations, so building from source needs OpenSSL development headers. Those release-note details are not from the README.
brief.standout: The beta ng report is built around availability rather than socket counts. It states whether service was actually denied, lists what else could explain the result, and uses distinct exit codes so an unreachable host does not look like a clean run in CI. Its HTML report is self-contained inline SVG, while the classic report loads Google Charts from the web at view time.

Its notes say it is the first release since v1.9.0 (July 2022), and the page shows 71 commits on master since that release. name: smlnj
desc: Compiler and programming system for Standard ML
why: Standard ML's long-running compiler; an old-school functional language with a serious pedigree.

brief.what_it_is: Standard ML of New Jersey (SML/NJ) is a compiler for the Standard ML '97 programming language, shipped with associated libraries, tools, and documentation. You give it Standard ML source code and it produces compiled programs, and you can also use its interactive top level (the `sml` command). The distribution also includes companion tools: asdlgen, heap2exec, ml-antlr, ml-build, ml-burg, ml-makedepend, ml-ulex, ml-yacc, and sml. The homepage says it is free, open source software.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes SML/NJ simply as a compiler and toolset for Standard ML '97. The README gives no broader motivation beyond that.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals in detail. It does say the code generator moved from MLRISC to LLVM in the 2021 release, and that the development repository includes a customized LLVM library as a git submodule. Building from source goes through a build.sh script, and the system bootstraps itself from pre-compiled boot files.

commands_seen.context: Installs SML/NJ via Homebrew; dependencies are installed automatically. This is the simplest route.
Source build step 2: clones one commit of the development repo at a chosen version tag, including the LLVM submodule. VERSION is set beforehand, for example VERSION=2026.2.
Source build step 3: run inside the smlnj directory to build and install. Afterwards bin/sml is the interactive system. Use build.sh -h to list options.
Recompiling step 1: switch to the system directory before running cmb-make.
Recompiling step 1: recompiles the system with cmb-make. The path argument is optional; if omitted, the sml on PATH is used.
Recompiling step 2: bootstraps the system.
Recompiling step 3: installs the system. -boot is optional and replaces the boot files in the root directory with newly generated ones.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew (brew install smlnj) is the easiest route on macOS and Linux. Building the development version from source needs a C++17 compiler (clang or gcc), CMake 3.23 or later, and GNU autoconf 2.71 or later; the macOS installers avoid these. As of 2025.1, build.sh downloads pre-compiled boot files if they are missing. config/targets can be edited to add or remove components. The README gives no account or licence requirements beyond that.

The project also runs two tracks: a stable 110.99.x legacy line and a 20xx.x development line.

name: snapcast
desc: Synchronous multiroom audio player
why: Synchronised multiroom audio over the network is a clever timing problem, though the core is fairly conventional.

brief.what_it_is: Snapcast is a client-server audio system that plays the same audio in several rooms at once, with all clients time-synchronized to the server. It is not a standalone player. It extends an existing player: the server reads PCM audio from stream sources such as a named pipe (/tmp/snapfifo), ALSA capture, TCP, or a process's stdout. It encodes the audio (PCM, FLAC by default, Vorbis, or Opus), tags each chunk with local time, and sends it over TCP to the snapclient programs, which play it through the OS audio API. Binaries are snapserver and snapclient. A bundled web app (Snapweb) and a JSON-RPC API control volume, mute, naming, streams, and groups.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to turn an existing audio player, such as MPD or Mopidy, into a Sonos-like multiroom system without buying proprietary hardware. The README's own framing is 'Synchronous audio player' and a multiroom solution that stays generic across players.
brief.how_it_works: The server reads PCM chunks from a configured source, encodes them, and stamps each with the local time. Each client continuously synchronizes its clock with the server, decodes incoming chunks into a buffer, and plays each one at the correct server-time moment through a low-level audio API such as ALSA. Clock drift is corrected by playing slightly faster or slower, by removing or duplicating single samples, and the README claims typical deviation stays below 0.2 ms.

commands_seen.context: Homebrew install on macOS and Linux, as the README's recommended package route besides Linux distro packages.
Test step: pipes random noise into the server's fifo so connected clients should play noise, confirming the chain works.
Raspberry Pi only: switches audio output to the 3.5mm jack (the README notes 2 is HDMI and 0 is auto).

Example /etc/snapserver.conf [stream] line configuring a named-pipe source with a name, sample format, and codec.
Example /etc/snapserver.conf [stream] line that makes the server play a WAV file, used as an alternative test.

brief.install_notes: Linux packages exist for Debian, OpenWrt, Alpine, Arch, and Void. macOS and Linux users can use Homebrew. Building from source has separate guides for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Android, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Raspberry Pi, webOS, and Windows (vcpkg). Configuration: after install, snapserver and snapclient read their options from /etc/default/snapserver and /etc/default/snapclient, and the server config lives in /etc/snapserver.conf. You must feed it audio: point a player (MPD, Mopidy, mpv, VLC, Spotify, AirPlay, and so on) at the fifo. The client needs an audio backend chosen with --player, and you can list ALSA/PulseAudio devices with -l or --list and pick one with -s or --soundcard. Accounts and runtimes beyond the OS audio stack are not mentioned in the README.
brief.standout: The sync trick is distinctive: instead of resampling, the client corrects clock drift by dropping or duplicating individual samples, which is inaudible at 48 kHz. The server also aggregates many input types (fifo, ALSA, TCP, process stdout, librespot, AirPlay, PipeWire, JACK) and a large ecosystem of third-party controllers (Home Assistant, Music Assistant, Android app, ESP32 client).

However, the fetched text gave no release date, last-commit date, or version number, so I could not confirm recent activity. I did not fetch the releases page.
brief.caveats: Not a standalone player: it needs an upstream player feeding the fifo or another source. Client audio backends are OS-specific (ALSA and PulseAudio on Linux, CoreAudio on macOS, WASAPI on Windows, Oboe and OpenSL on Android). Building from source requires per-platform guides, which signals some build effort. The README's 0.2 ms sync figure is the author's claim and I did not verify it. Mixed inputs and some integrations are third-party and labeled unofficial.

name: snap7
desc: Ethernet communication suite that works natively with Siemens S7 PLCs
why: Opens a door into Siemens S7 industrial PLC protocols over Ethernet, letting you talk to real factory controllers from your laptop.

brief.what_it_is: Snap7 is a multi-platform Ethernet communication library for talking to Siemens S7 PLCs (industrial controllers) from a PC or small board. Per the SourceForge listing it has three components, Client, Server and Partner, and offers wrappers for C/C++, .NET/Mono, Pascal, LabVIEW and Python. Your program makes calls to read and write PLC data over the network; the PLC side is the real controller on the factory network. It is licensed LGPLv3. The official homepage is a frameset with no readable content, so this description comes from the SourceForge project page.
brief.why_it_exists: It lets ordinary PC software exchange data with Siemens S7 controllers over Ethernet without buying Siemens' own communication software. The SourceForge summary says it is designed to transfer large amounts of high-speed data in industrial facilities.
brief.how_it_works: The library implements the S7 communication protocol over Ethernet in native code, with no third-party dependencies. It offers synchronous and asynchronous data transfer, and both polling and unsolicited flows, where the PLC pushes data when it chooses. Its own description also says it adapts endianness at runtime and needs no compiler switch.
brief.install_notes: No install step is documented in the pages I could read. The SourceForge listing says it needs no installation and no configuration and has no third-party library dependencies. It also says ready-to-run projects and makefiles are included for rebuilding in many platforms without being a C++ expert. Downloads are on SourceForge as snap7-full zip, 7z and tar.gz archives; the search-term list mentions versions 1.4.2 and 2.0.2-x64. I did not find brew-specific instructions, and I saw no commands. Real use needs a Siemens PLC reachable over Ethernet.
brief.standout: It runs on Linux, Windows, Mac, BSD and Solaris, down to small ARM boards such as the Raspberry Pi, with the client and server both in the same library. Its own description says a full working server example is no bigger than a 'Hello world'.

Snap7 is a community project by Davide Nardella rather than an official Siemens product, even though the repo is named SiemensAG in my guess. It talks to live industrial controllers, so mistakes can affect real machinery; test against a simulator or a bench PLC first. Supported models per the listing are S7-300/400/1200/1500, WinAC, LOGO 0BA7/0BA8, S7-200 and SINAMICS. Newer or other PLC families may not be covered.

name: sng
desc: Enable lossless editing of PNGs via a textual representation
why: Turns PNGs into a textual representation you can edit losslessly, a transform that opens the file format up.

brief.what_it_is: SNG (Scriptable Network Graphics) is a small text language that describes the full contents of a PNG file: its chunks, pixel data, and ancillary metadata. The sng program is a compiler and decompiler that converts PNG to SNG and back. Input is a PNG or an SNG text file, and output is the other format. Per the manual, the conversion is meant to be lossless, so you can edit the text with ordinary text tools and compile it back to PNG. The homepage is a SourceForge resource page for version 1.1.2, not a GitHub repository.
brief.why_it_exists: Graphics editors don't handle many obscure PNG ancillary chunks, so SNG exposes them as editable text. The README also says SNG is easy to generate from scripts, so sng can finish a pipeline that programmatically produces PNG images.
brief.how_it_works: An SNG file starts with #SNG and a colon, then a series of chunk blocks such as IHDR, PLTE, IDAT, and tEXt that mostly map one-to-one onto PNG chunks. The IMAGE block is translated into IDAT, with interlacing and compression handled automatically. Pixel data can be written as a string, hex, base64, or P1/P3 PBM/PPM text. With no file arguments, sng reads stdin and picks a direction by checking whether the first character is printable.

commands_seen.context: Synopsis from the man page. Translates each named file, choosing direction by extension (.png or .sng), and writes the result with the opposite extension.
From the README. Runs a basic regression test on the source distribution.

brief.install_notes: Packaged as 'sng' in many distributions. Building from the sng-1.1.2.tar.gz source tarball is documented, and the README says it requires libpng-1.2 or later. The README also states that older libpng versions may work but are untested and unsupported. The distribution has a Makefile and a regression harness called sng_regress. I did not find any account, runtime, or hardware requirements.
brief.standout: It is a lossless text round-trip for the entire PNG container, including exotic chunks that editors drop, and the author is Eric S. Raymond, a libpng contributor. The same format is meant to be both hand-edited and script-generated.
brief.status: Maintained, judging by recent activity. The homepage is dated 16 Mar 2026 and lists version 1.1.2. The man page was last updated 2026-02-03 and the README on 2026-01-29. The recent-changes section lists fixes for buffer overruns and dimension checks, and says the code was hardened with ChatGPT 5.2.
brief.caveats: The -i option is documented as not working yet in the man page BUGS section, pending libpng support for suppressing special IDAT handling. Base64 encoding is only usable when every byte is below 64, so it is limited to small bit depths or small palettes. Named colours come from the X rgb.txt database, which the man page says is not portable across hosts or displays. The README says testing covered the non-broken images of the PNG test suite. brief.what_it_is: Snort is an open source network intrusion detection and prevention system. It inspects network packets against a set of rules that describe malicious activity, and it generates alerts when packets match. It can run inline to stop matching packets, or work as a packet sniffer or packet logger for traffic debugging. Rules come in a Community Ruleset, freely available and QAed by Cisco Talos, and a Snort Subscriber Ruleset, developed and approved by Cisco Talos and delivered in real time to subscribers. The Snort 3 config is a Lua file (snort.lua), and the README says the rules are pulled in automatically once an Oinkcode is entered.

name: snowflake
desc: Pluggable Transport using WebRTC, inspired by Flashproxy
why: Pluggable transport routing Tor traffic through volunteer WebRTC browsers, a fascinating censorship-circumvention protocol door.

brief.what_it_is: Snowflake is a pluggable transport for Tor, written in Go, that lets Tor traffic travel through volunteer-run WebRTC proxies. A blocked user's Tor client finds an available volunteer proxy through a broker, which is reached over a domain-fronted signalling channel. The client and the proxy then open a WebRTC peer connection, and the proxy relays the Tor traffic on to a Tor relay. The repository contains four programs: snowflake-broker, snowflake-client, snowflake-proxy and snowflake-server. The volunteer side can be a browser extension or a standalone proxy.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Snowflake as combining the advantages of flashproxy and meek: the convenience of meek, but able to support far more users at negligible CDN cost, and the unlimited volunteer proxies of flashproxy without manual port forwarding.
brief.how_it_works: Volunteers visit websites that host the snowflake proxy, as in flashproxy. Tor clients locate available browser proxies through the Broker, which is a domain-fronted signalling channel, and then establish a WebRTC peer connection with the proxy. The proxy connects to a relay and Tor traffic flows over that DataChannel. Domain fronting is only used for brief signalling and NAT piercing, not for carrying the traffic itself.

brief.standout: Volunteers can run a proxy just by leaving a browser tab open, and Snowflake disguises Tor traffic as a WebRTC video or voice call. Because domain fronting only handles signalling, it avoids the CDN cost that made meek hard to scale.

name: soapyremote
desc: Use any Soapy SDR remotely
why: Lets one machine's SDR hardware be used across the network, a neat way into remote radio sensing.

brief.what_it_is: SoapyRemote is a SoapySDR plugin module plus a server executable that lets any SoapySDR-supported SDR be used over a network. You run SoapySDRServer on the machine that has the hardware, and the SoapyRemote client plugin on another machine finds and opens those devices through the standard SoapySDR API, SoapySDRUtil, and applications built on it. Device discovery and control go over a TCP RPC protocol, and sample streams go over UDP by default, with TCP available as an option. The client sees the remote radio as a local device.
brief.why_it_exists: The wiki pitches it as a way to turn any SDR into a network peripheral: sharing one device across a network, using it from several processes or hosts, adapting an IPv4-only SDR for an IPv6 network, aiding embedded-device development, or working around software issues.
brief.how_it_works: SoapyRemote has two parts: the server, which runs on the remote machine, and the client, which is an ordinary SoapySDR plugin. The server runs a simple RPC protocol over reliable TCP for discovery, creation, and configuration, and streams use a separate windowed-datagram protocol over UDP, with flow-control messages so the sender never sends more than the receiver's socket buffers can hold. Discovery of servers on the local network is automatic unless you name a host with the remote key.

brief.install_notes: Pre-built installers are available through the Pothos SDR environment (downloads page on the PothosCore wiki). Otherwise, build from source with CMake, after installing SoapySDR; the SoapyRemote build must be installed on both the remote (hardware) and local (client) machines. On Ubuntu, avahi-daemon and libavahi-client-dev are recommended for discovery. No extra runtimes or accounts are needed. On Linux, optional tuning includes raising the socket buffer limits with sysctl and granting the user rtprio 99 in /etc/security/limits.conf so forwarding threads can get elevated priority. The server can run under systemd; enable it with sudo systemctl enable SoapySDRServer to start at boot.
brief.standout: The server is a transparent transport for the whole SoapySDR API, so existing SDR applications, UHD and GrOsmoSDR users included, can use a remote device with only extra device arguments. Stream tuning is exposed as per-stream keys such as remote:format (for example CS16 or CS8 on the wire), remote:scale, and remote:prot, and the wiki explains the reasoning behind each.

name: sollya
desc: Library for safe floating-point code development
why: A rigorous floating-point toolkit with its own language for polynomial approximation and certified error bounds.

brief.what_it_is: Sollya is a tool environment and a library for developing safe floating-point code. It has its own scripting language, adapted to analysing numerical programs in the way a computer algebra system is. It computes certified infinity-norm error bounds, runs a fast Remez algorithm for minimax polynomials, and evaluates composed functional expressions with multi-precision, faithful rounding on top of MPFR. It can also generate CRlibm-style C code for approximation polynomials along with a Gappa proof. The homepage describes it as particularly aimed at automated implementation of mathematical floating-point libraries (libm). The brew entry lists a single executable, sollya.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it is targeted at the automatized implementation of mathematical floating-point libraries (libm), where approximation error has to be bounded safely rather than estimated.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage names the main pieces but does not explain the internals: a certified infinity (supremum) norm for safe error bounds, a fast Remez algorithm for minimax polynomials, a multi-precision evaluator for composed expressions that extends MPFR, and a polynomial implementer that emits CRlibm-style C code with a matching Gappa proof. It also offers interfaces for extending Sollya with your own code.
brief.install_notes: Building from source needs a C compiler (e.g. gcc), a C++ compiler (e.g. g++), GMP, MPFR, MPFI, FPLLL and libxml2. Bison and Flex are also needed to build from the git repository. Gnuplot is strongly recommended for the plot and externalplot commands but is optional. The site says Sollya is packaged directly for Debian and Ubuntu. A weekly git snapshot is offered as an alternative to stable releases, and a third-party Python interface exists (see the GitLab link on the homepage, which I did not open).
brief.standout: It is a numerical-analysis language and toolkit rather than a library you call from C: you write scripts that search for polynomial approximations and prove their error bounds, and it can emit C code and Gappa proofs for libm-style functions. The homepage also offers an explicit citation (Chevillard, Joldeş and Lauter, ICMS 2010).

desc: Strict subset of Go with transpiler that translates to regular C
why: A strict Go subset that transpiles to plain C is a neat idea for exploring language design and C output, though it's a close call.

brief.what_it_is: Solod is a strict subset of Go that transpiles to readable C11. You write ordinary Go source, using Solod's own packages (solod.dev/so/...) instead of the standard library, and the `so` tool emits a C header and implementation file for each package. The README says it supports structs, methods, interfaces, slices, maps, multiple returns and defer, with limited generics. Concurrency comes from the standard library rather than from language syntax. The output has no garbage collector or reference counting, and memory is stack-allocated unless you opt into the heap through the standard library.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants Go developers to get systems-level control without learning a new language, and wants C programmers to get Go's safety, structure and tooling. The homepage headline is "Solod: Go can be a better C".
brief.how_it_works: The `so` command translates a Go module into C11, producing main.h and main.c for each package, and calls the C compiler set by CC (default cc) when you ask for a binary. The README says the generated code relies on GCC/Clang extensions such as statement expressions, __auto_type and alloca/VLAs. It also says C interop needs no CGO, and that the sobind tool can generate bindings from C headers.

commands_seen.context: Installs the Solod command-line tool `so` using the standard Go toolchain.
Creates a new Go module, the first step of starting a Solod project.
Adds the Solod standard library as a dependency of the module.
Transpiles the module in the current directory to C, writing the output to the generated directory.
Transpiles and compiles to a binary named main in one step, using the C compiler from CC.
Transpiles, compiles and runs the module without saving the binary. The README says commands take a module, not a single file, so use `so run .` rather than `so run main.go`.

brief.install_notes: Install with `go install solod.dev/cmd/so@latest`, which needs a Go toolchain. You also need a C compiler: the default is `cc`, and you can override it with the CC environment variable. Supported compilers are GCC, Clang, Emscripten and zig cc, and MSVC is not supported. To use the Solod standard library in your own project, run `go mod init` and `go get solod.dev@latest`. Use `main` or a commit hash instead of `latest` to get the development version. There is no account or runtime to set up beyond these.
brief.standout: The generated C is meant to be read: the README's example shows a Go method turning into a plain C function that takes a void pointer and a named struct type, with no runtime library. Concurrency is a thread pool and atomics in the standard library, not language keywords. The Go tests remain ordinary Go and are never transpiled, so `go test` still works next to `so test`.
brief.status: Quiet. The latest tagged release is v0.4, which the homepage describes as shipping an automatic binding generator and a freestanding mode. The roadmap says "There are no more releases planned at this time." I did not see a last-commit date, so I cannot say whether development continues. The homepage says the project is not ready for production yet.
brief.caveats: The homepage says "Solod isn't ready for production yet." Generics are limited. MSVC is not supported, so Windows builds depend on a GCC or Clang toolchain (the README links a Windows doc). The generated code depends on GCC/Clang extensions. The README calls the project "highly opinionated", so it may not suit anyone who wants the full Go language. The license is BSD 3-Clause, and the README credits the Go stdlib code to the Go Authors. Benchmarks and FAQ pages were linked but not fetched.

Zero runtime. No garbage collection, no reference counting, no hidden allocations.
Solod is highly opinionated. Simplicity is key. Heap allocations are explicit. Strictly Go syntax.
Even though Solod isn't ready for production yet, I encourage you to try it out on a hobby project or just keep an eye on it if you like the concept.

name: sparse
desc: Static C code analysis tool
why: Linux kernel's semantic C checker, built on annotations; a window into how the kernel polices itself.

brief.what_it_is: Sparse is a semantic C parser and static analysis tool. It takes C source files, including most of ANSI C and many GCC extensions, and builds a complete parse tree for each whole file. It ships with sample compiler backends, one of which is a static analyzer also called sparse. The analyzer checks type-level semantics, such as which address space a pointer points to or which locks a function acquires or releases, using annotations in the source. The brew formula installs two executables, cgcc and sparse. I did not verify what each one does.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Linus Torvalds began Sparse in 2003 to catch problems such as mixing pointers into user address space with pointers into kernel address space. The GitHub mirror README describes it as a small library whose one mission is to create a semantic parse tree for further analysis, not a tokenizer or a generic parser.
brief.how_it_works: The GitHub mirror README says parsing runs in five phases: full-file tokenization, preprocessing (which can trigger tokenization of another file), semantic parsing, lazy type evaluation, and inline function expansion with tree simplification. Type details are computed only when a back end asks for them. The README stresses that a whole file is parsed before any result is available, with no partial results.

brief.what_it_is: Spglib is a C library that finds and handles crystal symmetries. The feature list covers finding symmetry operations, identifying the space-group type, assigning Wyckoff positions, refining a structure, finding a primitive cell, and searching irreducible k-points. brief.how_it_works: The caller supplies a structure and a tolerance so that small distortions in the atomic coordinates still count as symmetric. The library searches for symmetry operations under that tolerance, then identifies the space group from them. name: spigot
desc: Command-line streaming exact real calculator
why: Streaming exact real calculator by Simon Tatham that prints digits of pi, e and others forever without ever rounding, a real door into exact arithmetic.

brief.what_it_is: spigot is a command-line streaming exact real calculator by Simon Tatham. You give it a mathematical expression, and it prints digits of the result one at a time, including constants such as pi and e, and keeps going until you stop it. It can also read numbers from a file or a pipe and start producing output once it has read enough input to know how the output begins.
brief.why_it_exists: Ordinary calculators need to know in advance how many digits you want, and rounding errors pile up across successive operations so the last digits can be wrong. spigot's author frames it as a tool that outputs no digit until it is sure that digit is right, and that is useful when you need very many digits or want a cross-check on other calculating systems.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage names the core algorithm as Jeremy Gibbons's unbounded spigot algorithm for the digits of pi, which spigot extends to more output modes and many more input numbers. The page does not explain the internals beyond that. Its streaming behaviour means output starts as soon as enough input has been read to determine the start of the result.

name: spot

brief.what_it_is: Spot is a C++20 library for LTL and ω-automata manipulation and model checking. It handles LTL in several syntaxes plus a subset of the linear fragment of PSL, and it reads automata in five formats (HOA, never claims, LBTT, DSTAR, PGsolver). Most of its algorithms are also exposed as command-line tools (the brew package installs 16 executables, including ltlfilt, autfilt, ltl2tgba, ltlsynt and ltlcross) and as Python bindings. Formulas and automata go in; simplified formulas, translated or transformed automata, test results, benchmark results, and synthesis outputs come out.

brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes the mechanism only at the feature level: formula algorithms (simplification, implication and equivalence checks, stutter-invariance tests, translation to automata) and automata algorithms (products, emptiness checks, simulation-based reduction, determinization, SAT-based minimization, and similar) are exposed through the C++ API and the command-line tools. It supports Emerson-Lei acceptance conditions, and state-based acceptance is handled by reduction to transition-based acceptance. It also covers safety and parity games and reactive synthesis and model checking applications.

name: sqlancer
desc: Detecting Logic Bugs in DBMS
why: Automatically finds logic bugs in database engines via generated queries, a fascinating look at how DBMS correctness is tested.

brief.what_it_is: SQLancer is a command-line Java tool that automatically tests database management systems for logic bugs, meaning cases where the DBMS returns an incorrect result set, such as silently omitting a record. It generates schemas, data, indexes, views, and queries in several phases, then checks the results with test oracles such as TLP, NoREC, PQS, DQP, and CODDTest. The input is a target DBMS, and the output is bug reports with log files containing the statements needed to reproduce each bug. It also covers performance issues via CERT and crash bugs. It supports many DBMSs, including SQLite3, DuckDB, H2, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and TiDB.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says SQLancer finds bugs in the DBMS implementation itself, not in user-written queries, and it presents logic bugs as its main focus. It states that it has found hundreds of bugs in mature, widely known DBMSs.
brief.how_it_works: SQLancer uses hand-written generators that work in phases: create a schema, insert data, add other database state, then generate queries. Each query is validated by a test oracle that compares results, for example by checking that a TLP partition or a NoREC rewrite matches the original query's result set. An optional feedback-guided mode (--qpg-enable, from QPG) mutates database state when no new query plans appear, to exercise more distinct plans. An experimental reducer (--use-reducer) applies delta debugging to shrink bug-inducing inputs.

Builds the SQLancer JAR with Maven, skipping the test suite.
