name: sylph
desc: Ultrafast taxonomic profiling and genome querying for metagenomic samples
why: Metagenomic taxonomic profiling is real science you can run on sequencing data, though the appeal to a general reader is narrow.

brief.what_it_is: Sylph is a command-line tool for taxonomic profiling of metagenomic shotgun reads. It takes sequencing reads from a sample and reports which species are present and their abundances, measured against reference databases such as GTDB (about 200k genomes). It also supports containment ANI querying, where you search a single reference genome against your reads and get an estimated average nucleotide identity for any matching strain. It works with short reads and with nanopore or PacBio long reads.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as fast and precise species-level profiling. It claims to be more than 50x faster than other methods and to have fewer false positives than Kraken, while matching marker-gene methods such as MetaPhlAn and mOTUs on precision and sensitivity.
brief.how_it_works: The docs describe sylph as a k-mer containment method. Its stated novelty is a statistical technique for estimating k-mer containment at low genome coverage, which the authors say gives accurate results for low-abundance organisms. The docs point to a newer database format, syl2db, for more efficient profiling.
brief.install_notes: The README and docs point to sylph-docs.github.io for installation and usage. I did not reach the install or quick-start pages, so I have no install commands. The docs mention pre-built databases for prokaryotes, viruses and eukaryotes, and custom databases built from your own MAGs. Brew installs the executable named sylph.
brief.standout: Rather than relying on marker genes or exact k-mer classification, sylph uses containment with a statistical correction for low coverage. The README also offers ANI estimates for a reference genome down to about 0.1x coverage, which is a different question from 'what species is here'.

I did not see a last-release or last-commit date, so the exact maintenance state is unknown.

name: sysdig
desc: System-level exploration and troubleshooting tool
why: Captures and inspects live system calls, a genuine window into how running programs behave, though now a bit commercial.

brief.what_it_is: Sysdig is an open-source Linux system visibility tool with native container support. It installs into the Linux kernel, captures system calls and other OS events from a machine, and can save that activity to trace files for later analysis. Two command-line programs ship with it: sysdig, the general tool, and csysdig, a curses-based interactive UI. The README describes it as strace + tcpdump + htop + iftop + lsof + ...awesome sauce. The homepage at sysdig.com is a commercial cloud security marketing page for the Sysdig Secure platform, not documentation for this tool; the open-source project lives at github.com/draios/sysdig.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says system-level monitoring and troubleshooting still means SSH-ing into machines and using many dated tools with inconsistent interfaces, and that many of those tools break down in containerized environments. Sysdig aims to unite that toolkit into one consistent interface, with deep inspection of containers without instrumenting the containers themselves.
brief.how_it_works: Sysdig instruments physical and virtual machines at the OS level by installing into the Linux kernel and capturing system calls and other OS events. It can write these captures to trace files, similar to how tcpdump and Wireshark handle network traffic, so problems can be analysed later. The README says the trace files store rich system state so captured activity can be put into full context.

name: t2sz
desc: Compress a file into a seekable zstd with per-file seeking for tar archives
why: Compresses tar archives into seekable zstd so you can jump into a single file without decompressing everything, a neat format trick worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: t2sz is a command-line tool that compresses a file into a seekable zstd archive by splitting the input into multiple zstd frames. Given a tar archive, its default mode gives each file in the archive its own independent frame, so one file can be pulled out without decompressing the whole archive. Given any other file, or with -r, it runs in raw mode and cuts the input into blocks. Output is a .zst file (for example archive.tar.zst), written to a path set with -o or to stdout. The README says any Zstandard tool, including zstd, can decompress the result.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as tar 2 seekable zstd: the goal is fast seeking and extraction of a single file from a compressed archive without decompressing everything before it. The README does not give a longer origin story.
brief.how_it_works: In tar mode, each file in the archive becomes its own zstd frame, unless -s or -S changes the grouping. With -s SIZE, small files are packed into one frame until the block reaches at least SIZE, and a file is never split; with -S SIZE, large files are split into SIZE-length blocks. A seek table is written by default (-j turns it off). Seeking itself is done by separate reader projects that the README links: libzstd-seek (C/C++), indexed_zstd (Python), and ratarmount (FUSE mount).

Read stdin in raw mode (-r) and write to out.zst.
Read a tar stream from stdin and write it to out.tar.zst in tar mode.

macOS build prerequisite: install zstd from Homebrew before building from source.

brief.install_notes: Packaged on Homebrew, AUR (pamac build t2sz), and Snap, plus a .deb and source tarball on the GitHub release page. Source builds need CMake and libzstd-dev on Linux, or zstd from Homebrew on macOS, followed by make and sudo make install; cpack makes a .deb. The Snap build runs in strict mode and only reaches the home directory by default; removable media needs sudo snap connect t2sz:removable-media, and --devmode grants access to every file. Windows executables can be cross-compiled from macOS or Linux with a Docker command in the README, or downloaded from the release page. No accounts or runtime services are needed.
brief.standout: Each tar member is its own zstd frame with a seek table, so ordinary zstd tools still decompress the output while seeking-aware readers can jump straight to one file. The -s and -S options give a tunable tradeoff between archive size and seek granularity.

name: tailcat
desc: Netcat-like tool over Tailscale's data plane, without its control plane
why: Netcat-style pipes over Tailscale's WireGuard data plane, minus the control plane, is a revealing look at how the overlay actually moves packets.

brief.what_it_is: Tailcat is a netcat-style command-line tool and Go library that pipes data between two machines over an encrypted Tailscale-style tunnel, without needing a Tailscale account or the Tailscale control plane. One side runs a server (listener) that prints a short tailcat address, and the other side passes that address to the client. Data in and out is ordinary stdin/stdout, TCP port forwarding, SOCKS5, SSH, SFTP, file drop boxes, or a throughput test, depending on the service chosen. Traffic is WireGuard-encrypted end to end, bootstrapped through a DERP relay, and upgraded to a direct UDP path when NAT traversal succeeds.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as Tailscale's data plane without its control plane: point-to-point WireGuard tunnels between two machines, with connection metadata exchanged out of band however you like. It also describes itself as "Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale".
brief.how_it_works: The server generates a WireGuard keypair (and by default a pre-shared key) and encodes them, plus DERP region info, into a tailcat address (a "tc" prefix followed by base64 CBOR). The client parses that address, connects to the same DERP relay, and sends a "Meow" discovery message; the server adds it as a WireGuard peer, and the WireGuard handshake runs over DERP at first while magicsock hole-punches toward a direct UDP path. The userspace stack uses WireGuard, magicsock, and gVisor netstack, so no TUN device, routes, DNS changes, or root access are needed.

commands_seen.context: Starts a server (listener). It prints a selected bootstrap relay region and a line like '🐈 Server listening with new address: tc...', then waits for a client.
Client side: pipes stdin into the tailcat address given as the argument; the server's stdout receives 'hello'.
Serves local TCP ports 8080 and 8443 through the tunnel (the README also lists 'tailcat serve all').
Client side: makes the server's port 8080 appear on local port 18080 and the server's port 3306 on local port 3306.
Runs an SSH server that accepts keys from a local authorized_keys file (other sources, including user@github, can be comma-separated).
Runs an SSH server with no client authentication, so the tailcat address itself is the credential. The README warns strongly against sharing it publicly.
Runs a write-only drop box that receives files into ~/inbox; senders share the printed tailcat address.
Sender side: copies a file to the drop box by running the system scp with the connection routed through tailcat.
Client side: runs an iperf-like throughput and latency test against a server started with 'tailcat serve perf'. It refuses to run through a shared DERP relay unless --via-derp is given.
Pings the server and keeps trying until a direct (non-DERP) path works, exiting non-zero if none does.
Generates a saved key named 'default' pinned to the nyc region, so the server address stays stable across restarts.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt static binaries are listed for Linux and Windows, .deb and .rpm packages, Homebrew (macOS), Scoop (Windows), Snap, a container image, Nix (Linux and macOS), AUR (Arch), and conda-forge (Linux, macOS, Windows). FreeBSD and OpenBSD are only covered by building from source with the Go toolchain, as is the js/wasm browser build. The README points to INSTALL.md for details, which I did not fetch. No Tailscale account, root or admin access, or configuration is needed. By default it uses Tailscale's free rate-limited DERP relays via the derpmap at https://tailcat.dev/derpmap.json, and you can run your own derper with a hostname and TLS certificate.
brief.standout: It reuses Tailscale's WireGuard, magicsock, and gVisor netstack as a userspace library, so you get NAT traversal and encryption without a TUN device or root, and the address itself carries a WireGuard pre-shared key. The README also has a neat safety feature: 'tailcat ssh' probes DNS-named destinations as a stranger would and refuses to connect if the SSH server accepts that login.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no version number, release date, or last commit date. The History section says it was open-sourced in August 2026 at the TailscaleUp conference, and it describes recent work (a refactor into a regular Go module client, and open issues such as #4 and #7). The README also says there are no API or CLI stability promises, so it is clearly actively developed but not a stable release.
brief.caveats: No API, CLI, or wire-format stability promises. The public DERP relays have no uptime SLA or throughput targets and may be revoked at any time. The web demo is experimental and browser traffic goes over DERP only, with no direct connections until WebRTC support lands (issue #4). no-auth-ssh makes the address a full shell credential, so it must not be published in DNS. Addresses published in DNS TXT records need --allow or --ssh-authorized-keys. Compression is not used for transfers. The perf command refuses to run through Tailscale's shared relays. Installation is uneven: no macOS static binary, and FreeBSD and OpenBSD require building from source. The README does not give a license, and I did not check one.

You don't need a Tailscale account, root/admin access on the machine (it doesn't alter your machine's routing tables, DNS, etc.). It's just a userspace library and CLI tool.

name: tarantool
desc: In-memory database and Lua application server
why: An in-memory database that doubles as a Lua application server, a database with a twist worth poking at.

brief.what_it_is: Tarantool is an in-memory computing platform made of a database and an application server, distributed under BSD 2-Clause. The database keeps data in RAM, with WAL-based persistence, and offers HASH, TREE, RTREE and BITSET indexes, MessagePack data and client-server protocol, and ANSI SQL. The application server runs Lua (LuaJIT 2.1 with a tracing JIT) inside the same process, with cooperative multitasking and non-blocking IO, plus built-in persistent queues, sharding, and a cluster management framework. Data goes in through the database API, SQL, or Lua code, and results come back to clients or to the application logic running alongside the data.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a fast in-memory store that also fixes the usual weakness of RAM-only databases, which is losing data on failure or restart. The README frames it as a platform for data-enriched parts of scalable web architecture, such as queue servers, caches, and stateful web applications.
brief.how_it_works: Code and data share one address space, so Lua logic runs next to the stored data instead of across a network hop. Writes go to a write-ahead log and the transaction result returns only after it is saved to disk. The homepage also describes synchronous and asynchronous replication, and an MVCC transaction mode.
brief.install_notes: The README points to the download page for binary packages for your OS and to Docker images, and to the Tarantool documentation for building from source. Supported platforms are Linux (x86_64, aarch64), macOS (x86_64 and M1), and FreeBSD (x86_64). Extra modules and connectors come from the rocks repository, the connectors page, and the Awesome Tarantool list. I did not read the install page itself, so there are no first-run steps or config details in these notes.
brief.standout: It is a database and an application server in one process: the Lua code and the data share an address space, and the database is a C extension that can be switched off. Most in-memory stores are only a cache or a key-value store, so this combination is the unusual part.

Enterprise-only products, such as Tarantool Enterprise, Data Grid, and Cluster Manager, are mixed into the same navigation, so check which features are in the Community build. Platform support is limited to Linux, macOS, and FreeBSD, with no Windows listed in what I read.

brief.how_it_works: You run 64tass on a source file and it makes multiple passes over the source to resolve forward references and optimize addressing modes. Addressing modes are chosen from the instruction type and the .dpage, .databank and program counter settings. The manual's Makefile examples show it feeding a cruncher such as pucrunch, so the output can be a PRG file for a real or emulated machine.

desc: Replay saved tcpdump files at arbitrary speeds
why: Replays captured packets onto live networks at chosen speeds, a hands-on way to watch traffic and protocols act out again.

brief.what_it_is: Tcpreplay is a suite of GPLv3 command-line utilities for UNIX (and Windows under Cygwin) that takes a capture file (.pcap, from tcpdump, Wireshark or similar), optionally rewrites its Layer 2-4 headers, and sends the packets back onto a live network. The main tcpreplay binary replays at the original timing, at a target rate in packets/sec or Mbps, or as fast as the hardware allows. The suite also includes tcpreplay-edit (replay with rewriting in one pass), tcprewrite, tcpprep, tcpbridge, tcpliveplay and tcpcapinfo. Output is packets on the wire, plus replay statistics.
brief.why_it_exists: Real network traffic is messy, bursty and hard to reproduce on demand. Tcpreplay lets you capture a slice of traffic once and replay it deterministically as often as you like, with the same packets and timing, to benchmark throughput, reproduce a bug, regression-test a firewall rule, or drive a NetFlow appliance to its limits.
brief.how_it_works: A capture goes in and packets come out on the wire. tcpprep and tcprewrite are optional pre-processing stages that can be used alone, together, or not at all; tcpprep writes a cache file that classifies packets as client or server, which is what a two-NIC in-line test needs. tcpreplay-edit folds tcprewrite's rewriting options into the replay so headers are changed in a single pass, while plain tcpreplay stays a lean, edit-free engine. tcpliveplay replays a captured TCP session against a real server so the full stack up to the application responds, rather than staying at Layer 2.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: a release tarball needs only a C compiler and libpcap. Building from a git checkout needs python3 and asciidoctor to generate CLI parsers and man pages (AutoGen is no longer needed for most of this). CMake 3.16+ is the recommended build. Optional fast paths: io_uring needs liburing-dev on Linux; AF_XDP needs libxdp-dev and libbpf-dev plus an eBPF-capable driver; netmap needs netmap-patched drivers and a netmap source tree pointed to with -DWITH_NETMAP. Injecting packets requires root (sudo) because it uses raw sockets. The test suite needs test NICs configured with --with-testnic and --with-testnic2 under autotools.
brief.standout: The suite can replay traffic into a device with real timing and at high rates, including up to hundreds of thousands of flows per second for NetFlow appliance testing, and tcpliveplay replays a TCP session so a real server answers, which plain replay tools usually cannot do. The 4.6 release also ships libtcpreplay, a static C library, so programs can embed the replay engine instead of parsing its output.
brief.status: maintained. The README describes 4.6 as the current release with a changelog, CI and CodeQL badges, and the homepage and GitHub repo are both up. I did not see an explicit release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so the timing of the latest activity is unconfirmed.
brief.caveats: GPLv3 license, and some bundled files carry other licenses marked in-file. UNIX-focused; Windows is supported only under Cygwin. netmap is the most invasive option: the network stack goes dark on that interface while it is active, so the README warns not to test on the interface you SSH in on. The test suite sends live traffic. Non-IP packets such as ARP fail on L3 interfaces, and --io-uring is not supported there. Autotools is being phased out in favor of CMake. The homepage and README are slightly inconsistent about whether tcpreplay-edit is built by default, saying it exists only 'when built with editing support'.
quotes: Edit and replay captured network traffic — at the original timing, a fixed rate, or as fast as the hardware allows.
Take a .pcap file, optionally rewrite its Layer 2–4 headers, and push it back onto the wire.
Tcpreplay lets you capture a slice of it once and replay it deterministically as often as you like — the same packets, the same timing, at whatever speed your test calls for.

name: tcpflow
desc: TCP/IP packet demultiplexer
why: Reassembles raw TCP streams into per-flow files, a useful look at the wire that is a close call against plenty of packet tools.

brief.what_it_is: tcpflow is a command-line program that captures or reads TCP traffic and reassembles each TCP connection into its own file, with one file per direction. It takes live packets from a network interface (via libpcap, with tcpdump-style filter expressions) or stored tcpdump captures, and writes out per-flow byte streams named after the source and destination IP and port. It can also write a DFXML summary report listing each flow's addresses, ports, byte and packet counts, and optionally an MD5 of each stream.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Jeremy Elson wrote it to capture data from programs that use undocumented protocols so they could be reverse engineered, and it was later used for HTTP protocol analysis. Simson Garfinkel took over maintenance after leaving Sandstorm and used it as a flow-reassembly tool. The stated use is network forensics and protocol debugging, where you want to see many connections in context rather than individual packets.
brief.how_it_works: It tracks TCP sequence numbers so it can rebuild each byte stream correctly despite retransmissions or out-of-order delivery. Output file names follow a template that encodes an optional timestamp, source IP.port, destination IP.port, VLAN, and a connection counter; -F and -T change the template. With -a it post-processes HTTP responses into separate -HTTP and -HTTPBODY files, and a -GZIP file when the body is gzip-compressed. IP fragments are not handled.

Building from git requires --recursive and bootstrap.sh. The README also covers a CMake route (cmake/README.md), an RPM build, and a mingw cross-build for Windows from Fedora. Packet capture usually needs root or capture privileges, which the README does not spell out.
brief.standout: Instead of showing packets or one connection at a time, as Wireshark does, it turns a capture into a directory of per-connection files that you can grep, hash, or feed to other tools. Its -a option also decodes HTTP into header and body files, which makes it a quick way to pull web pages or drive-by malware out of a capture.
brief.status: Maintained by one author, with a CI badge and a dated status note. The README is labeled TCPFLOW 1.5.0, and an October 18, 2020 status report says a 1.6 rewrite to C++17 is underway and roughly three quarters done. I did not see a release date or last commit date, so the exact activity level is unknown. Leaning quiet rather than active.
brief.caveats: Does not understand IP fragments, so flows that contain fragments are recorded incorrectly; the README calls this rare. The README's build instructions are tied to older distros (Ubuntu 16.04, Fedora 18 and 26, Arch 17.8). The autotools build is involved, and the README says it needs a complete recursive checkout and bootstrapping. Licensing was not stated in the README I read. Its statements on platform support are limited to Linux, Amazon AMI and Windows-via-mingw.
quotes: tcpflow is a program that captures data transmitted as part of TCP connections (flows), and stores the data in a way that is convenient for protocol analysis and debugging.
tcpflow understands sequence numbers and will correctly reconstruct data streams regardless of retransmissions or out-of-order delivery.
Unlike programs such as WireShark, which show lots of packets or a single TCP connection, tcpflow can show hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of TCP connections in context.

name: tcptraceroute
desc: Traceroute implementation using TCP packets
why: Traceroute using TCP SYN packets, a clean door into how routers and firewalls treat different traffic.

brief.what_it_is: tcptraceroute is a traceroute implementation that sends TCP packets instead of the ICMP or UDP probes that classic traceroute uses. You give it a destination host, and it reports the routers along the path to it. The README describes it only as 'A traceroute implementation using TCP packets', and the README I read does not show the output format. It is a single C program, and Homebrew installs it as the executable tcptraceroute.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no motivation beyond the one-line description. The practical point is that TCP probes can get through firewalls that drop ICMP or UDP probes, so the path they reveal can differ from a classic traceroute.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the mechanism. Its dependencies, libnet (packet crafting) and libpcap (packet capture), suggest it builds raw TCP packets and captures the replies to see which hop answered. The SYN-packet detail comes from the scout notes, not from the README.

name: teamtype
desc: Peer-to-peer, editor-agnostic collaborative editing of local text files
why: Peer-to-peer, editor-agnostic collaborative editing is a neat look at how real-time sync works without a server.

brief.what_it_is: Teamtype is a command-line daemon, `teamtype`, that gives you real-time collaborative editing of plain local text files without a server. You run `teamtype share` in a directory, and another person runs `teamtype join` with the printed join code in their own directory. Edits sync between the two directories, and you edit through your usual editor via a plugin (Neovim, VS Code/Codium, or a community plugin for JetBrains, TeXstudio, and others). Peers see each other's cursors, selections, and edits, and it works on whole directories, not just single files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as the missing real-time complement to Git and other version control systems, aimed at pair programming, brainstorming, and note-taking. The project says it is built by people who want to use it themselves and share it with others, and that it is not a company and has nothing to sell.
brief.how_it_works: Two peers connect over encrypted peer-to-peer connections, with no server required, and the content stays on disk so you keep full access even offline (a local-first model). The README credits Automerge, Iroh, and Magic Wormhole as the underlying pieces. Editors talk to the local daemon through a simple JSON-RPC protocol, which is what plugin authors implement. The README does not go deeper on the sync mechanism beyond these pointers.

name: teip
desc: Masking tape to help commands "do one thing well"
why: Masks parts of a stream so a command only touches selected regions, a clever pipeline trick that is close to plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: teip is a command-line filter written in Rust. It reads standard input, selects parts of it (by character, field, line number, regex match, or the output of another command), and passes only those selected parts, called holes, to a command you name after --. The targeted command's output replaces the holes, and the unselected text passes through unchanged. Input is text on stdin, and output is the same stream with the holes processed.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as helping commands "do one thing well" by letting a command act on only a chosen part of a stream. The author's post on dev.to is linked as the origin story.
brief.how_it_works: teip marks the selected ranges on the input like masking tape, with each hole shown as [...] by default. It sends only the hole contents to the targeted command, line by line, and splices the command's output back into the original positions. With -s it runs the command once per hole, and with -e the selection comes from a shell pipeline that receives the same stdin, whose output gives line numbers to act on.

brief.install_notes: macOS and Linux: install Homebrew, then brew install teip. Linux also has .deb and .rpm packages on the GitHub releases page (dpkg, apt, dnf, yum examples given), and the README asks you to check the sha256 on the release page. Windows (x86_64) has an installer .exe from the releases page, with more detail in the wiki page 'Use on Windows'. Other architectures: use the release page or build from source with cargo install teip. For the -G Oniguruma regex option, build with cargo install teip --features oniguruma, which needs cargo, clang and libclang available (apt, dnf, or choco install llvm on Windows). Optional environment variables: TEIP_HIGHLIGHT, TEIP_GREP_PATH, TEIP_SED_PATH, TEIP_AWK_PATH. No accounts or hardware are needed.
brief.standout: Teip can chain with itself and with any other command, so one teip can select regions that a second teip selects inside. Its -e option hands the selection to an arbitrary shell pipeline that also gets the same stdin, so you can select with grep -n -A, sed '/A/,/B/=', or nl | tail. Compared with awk or sed, which apply one script to a whole stream, teip lets an ordinary tool like tr or sed run only on the chosen spans.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The README points to the v2.3.3 release, has a passing-test CI badge, and shows a crates.io version badge. I did not see a last commit or release date, so the exact recency is unknown. Small inconsistency: the deb/rpm filenames in the install commands say teip-2.3.2 while the URL path says v2.3.3.
brief.caveats: Some features have real costs. -s (solid mode) and -I spawn a process per hole, so the README says they are unsuitable for large files. The targeted command must print one output line per input line, or teip fails with 'Output of given command is exhausted'; grep is the usual example. With -z, commands that cannot handle NUL bytes can produce unintended output. The -A, -B, -C, --sed and --awk options are labelled experimental and may be discontinued. -G needs a libclang build. The logo is licensed CC BY-NC 4.0, which is non-commercial, while the code is MIT. Parts of the cut list code come from uutils/coreutils and parts of the CSV parser from BurntSushi/rust-csv, each under its own license, which the README notes.

name: tenyr
desc: 32-bit computing environment (including simulated CPU)
why: A minimal 32-bit architecture with one instruction format and a simulated CPU, a strange and delightful environment to explore.

brief.what_it_is: tenyr is a 32-bit computer architecture and computing environment, described as focused on simplicity of design and implementation. It has three parts: an instruction set architecture, a Verilog hardware definition for FPGAs, and a set of software tools (assembler tas, linker tld, simulator tsim). Assembly source goes in, linked images come out, and tsim runs them on a simulated CPU. The README also ships a standard library of tenyr code and example programs such as Conway's Game of Life, a random snakes screensaver, and a recursive Fibonacci generator.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames tenyr as a simple 32-bit computer whose design and implementation are kept deliberately small. It does not state a broader motivation beyond that.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives no detailed mechanism. It names the pieces: an assembler (tas), a linker (tld), and a simulator (tsim), with the ISA documented in the project wiki. The Verilog hardware definition has been run on a Lattice ECP5 FPGA (ULX3S board) and a Xilinx Spartan6 FPGA (Nexys3 board), with VGA text output at 64x32.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no install steps and no commands. Running on real hardware requires an FPGA development board: the ULX3S (Lattice ECP5) or the Nexys3 (Xilinx Spartan6) have been demonstrated. The software tools are said to run on Mac, *nix, and Windows on multiple architectures. The homepage offers ZIP and TAR downloads, and the wiki holds the assembler, linker, and simulator docs.
brief.standout: The whole stack is small and self-contained: a custom ISA, a hand-rolled assembler, linker and simulator, and Verilog that runs on real FPGA boards, with example programs that have been shown running both in the simulator and on hardware. The homepage describes it as a simple environment, not a toy.
brief.status: Maintained as far as the pages show, but not confirmed. The GitHub page shows a C-language CI badge and a Codecov badge, and the project keeps a changelog from v0.9.4 onward. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in the fetched content, so recent activity is unverified.

name: testdisk
desc: Powerful free data recovery utility
why: Recovers lost partitions and files by reading raw disk structures, a satisfying look under the filesystem layer.

brief.what_it_is: TestDisk is a free, open-source (GPL v2+) data recovery utility from CGSecurity. It reads the raw structures of a disk (partition tables, boot sectors, backup superblocks, filesystem metadata) and tries to repair them or rebuild lost partitions. It can also undelete files from FAT12/16/32, exFAT, NTFS and ext2/3/4, and copy them out. Input is a physical disk, USB device, or disk image such as a .dd or .E01 file. Output is a repaired partition table or boot sector, or recovered files. The package also ships PhotoRec (signature-based file carving for when filesystem-level recovery fails) and fidentify.
brief.why_it_exists: The wiki says TestDisk was primarily designed to recover lost partitions and make non-booting disks bootable again when the cause is faulty software, certain viruses, or human error such as accidentally deleting a partition table. It also aims to serve novices, who can collect detailed information about a non-booting drive and send it to a tech, and experts doing onsite recovery.
brief.how_it_works: TestDisk scans the disk for partition structures and filesystem signatures, including backup boot sectors (FAT32, NTFS), backup superblocks (ext2/3/4) and other partition types, then lists what it finds so the user can choose which partitions to keep, mark as deleted or logical, and write back to the partition table. The Deeper Search option scans each cylinder for backups. Boot sectors can be restored by copying the valid backup over the damaged one. PhotoRec works differently: it identifies files by their content signatures rather than by reading the filesystem.

commands_seen.context: Unix/Linux/BSD: TestDisk needs root, so the static binary is launched with sudo (example from the step-by-step guide, which uses an older 6.13 build path).

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers binary executables and source for DOS, Win32, macOS and Linux. Brew installs the executables fidentify, photorec and testdisk. Physical-device work needs elevated rights: Administrator on Windows (Run as administrator on Vista and later), root on Unix/Linux/BSD, and on macOS TestDisk restarts itself under sudo after you confirm. OS/2 only handles disk images. No account, runtime or configuration is mentioned.
brief.standout: It works at the level below the filesystem: it reads partition tables and backup boot sectors directly and can often bring back a whole partition, not just individual files. It pairs that with PhotoRec, which carves files by signature when the filesystem is too damaged to read. The step-by-step guide walks through a real recovery in menus, which is a good way to see the raw structures.

name: tfel
desc: Code generation tool dedicated to material knowledge for numerical mechanics
why: Generates material-behaviour numerical code for mechanics, a real scientific tool that is obscure and worth a closer look.

brief.what_it_is: TFEL/MFront is a code generator. MFront takes short domain-specific language files that describe material knowledge and translates them into plain C++ built on the TFEL library. The languages cover material properties (such as Young's modulus or thermal conductivity), mechanical behaviours (constitutive laws for finite element and FFT solvers), and simple point-wise models such as fuel swelling. The bundled MTest tool can test a material's local behaviour by imposing constraints on strain or stress components. The homepage lists interfaces for Cast3M, Code-Aster, Abaqus Standard and Explicit, CalculiX, ANSYS APDL, ZeBuLoN, ElmerFEM, and the AMITEX_FFTP and TMFFT FFT solvers.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to manage material knowledge in numerical mechanics: write a behaviour once in a readable DSL and get optimised C++ for several solvers. The project is a collaboration of CEA and EDF, and the citation section points to a 2015 paper in Computers & Mathematics with Applications introducing it as part of the PLEIADES fuel element modelling platform.
brief.how_it_works: You write a behaviour or property in MFront's DSL. The MFront code generator translates it into plain C++ that links against the TFEL library, and the generated code is then used inside a solver's interface. MTest runs the behaviour locally under imposed strain or stress conditions, which the README says is much faster than a full finite element run, by a factor of ten to several hundred depending on the test.
brief.install_notes: Neither fetched page gave install commands. The homepage links to an Installation Guide covering Linux, Windows, macOS and FreeBSD, and to a CMake Options page and a Compiling MFront page. The README says the current official version is built on the C++-20 standard, so expect a modern C++ compiler. I did not open those linked pages, so build dependencies are unverified.
brief.standout: It is a code generator for material constitutive laws that targets many commercial and research finite element solvers from one source, and the README says its generated code is competitive with the solvers' native implementations. MTest's local testing is a practical way to check a behaviour before running a full simulation.
brief.status: Maintained, judging by the README and homepage. The README says the latest official version is TFEL-5.1.0 and that the rliv-5.1 branch is recommended for most users. The homepage release notes list up to 5.2.0, so the README may be slightly behind. The homepage's own publication date reads 15/08/2014, which looks stale, and I saw no commit or release dates to confirm activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage says it is a work in progress. The tfel-unicode-filt and tfel-config tools are in the executables list but I saw no usage for them. Licensing is GPL or CECILL-A from version 2.x onward (the README notes a linking exception added to GPL in 2023), and earlier versions had other terms. AMITEX_FFTP is distributed under a free licence for research and education only. The domain is specialised, so the DSL and solver interfaces assume prior knowledge of computational mechanics.

name: testssl
desc: Tool which checks for the support of TLS/SSL ciphers and flaws
why: A shell script that pokes TLS handshakes cipher by cipher, a revealing door into how servers actually negotiate crypto.

brief.what_it_is: testssl.sh is a free command-line TLS/SSL checker written as a bash script. You point it at a host, host:port, or HTTPS URL, and it probes the service for supported protocols and cipher suites, plus a set of known TLS flaws and misconfigurations. It also covers STARTTLS services (SMTP, IMAP, XMPP and others), MX records, and HTTP security headers. Output is colour-coded good/bad text, with optional CSV, JSON, HTML and log files.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as a tool that checks a server's service on any port for TLS/SSL cipher and protocol support, along with recent cryptographic flaws and more. Its stated aims are clear output, no installation burden, and privacy: 'It's only you who sees the result, not a third party.'
brief.how_it_works: Most checks run over raw bash sockets, which the homepage says is true of almost every check since version 2.9.5. OpenSSL is still used for some core functions such as openssl verify, ocsp and pkey, and any OpenSSL or LibreSSL binary can serve as the helper. The docs say the bundled OpenSSL is recommended because it supports features like IPv6, proxy and STARTTLS for MySQL/PostgreSQL.

commands_seen.context: The normal use case per the homepage: a default full run against a host (the README says the default run covers everything except -E and -g).
STARTTLS check against a POP3 service on port 110, using the -t flag to name the protocol.
STARTTLS check against an SMTP submission port.
Tests a domain's MX records from highest to lowest priority via STARTTLS on port 25; the homepage notes outbound port 25 must be open.
Lists locally available OpenSSL ciphers matching the hex code x14. Use -V CBC to search by name instead.
Tests only the ECDH ciphers offered by the target server, and also lists ones it does not offer.
Mass testing: reads one testssl.sh command line per line from a file. Blank lines and # comments are allowed.
Checks HTTP response headers for HSTS and other security headers, colour-marked by strength, and can help fingerprint proxies.
Routes the openssl and bash-socket connections through an HTTP proxy. Proxy authentication is not supported.
Recommended install: a shallow clone of the 3.3dev development branch, then run the script from that directory.

brief.install_notes: No package manager or runtime is needed beyond /bin/bash. Clone the repo, or download a release tarball from testssl.sh (3.2.3 is the current stable tarball; each has a .asc signature). Works out of the box on Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, WSL/MSYS2/Cygwin; OpenBSD only needs bash installed. The homepage says System V Unix probably needs GNU grep. The README says bash >= 3.2 plus sed and awk are expected. Docker: 'docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/testssl/testssl.sh <your_cmd_line>'. The older Docker Hub name drwetter/testssl.sh also appears on the homepage. Homebrew is a packaging route noted in the README. The homepage also lists curl -L https://testssl.sh for a stable-code download. Some features need the files in etc/ present alongside the script.
brief.standout: It is a full TLS scanner in plain bash, with almost all handshake work done over bash sockets rather than delegating to an OpenSSL binary, so it can test cipher suites one at a time, including ones the local OpenSSL does not ship with. It also covers STARTTLS across many protocols and adds ROBOT and Opossum checks alongside the usual flaw list.
brief.status: Maintained. Its homepage lists 3.2.3 released February 12, 2026, a 3.3dev snapshot on February 13, 2026, and directory timestamps into 2026. The README says the project supports only the current dev branch and the one before it (n-1), and that 3.0.10 was the final 3.0.x release. The GitHub page shows 9.2k stars, 1.2k forks and about 5,590 commits.
brief.caveats: Licensed GPLv2. The README includes a no-warranty clause and says it is meant as a standalone CLI tool, not a web service. Windows support goes through WSL, MSYS2 or Cygwin, and the homepage calls MSYS2/Cygwin slow. Some core functions still need an OpenSSL binary, and the bundled one is old. The homepage says 3.2 will get no new features and 3.0.x support is paid. The dev branch is expected to change output and features, so scripts that parse output may break. The homepage's screenshots come from an older version. name: thrax
desc: Tools for compiling grammars into finite state transducers
why: Compiles grammar rules into finite state transducers, a rare look at how text normalisers and morphology engines are built.

brief.what_it_is: Thrax is a set of command-line tools from the OpenGrm project that compile grammars into weighted finite-state transducers (FSTs). You write grammar source files (.grm) that combine regular expressions and context-dependent rewrite rules. The compiler turns them into an FST archive (.far), which you can test with thraxrewrite-tester or sample with thraxrandom-generator. The README's example grammar tokenises English text, for instance turning "Well, I can't eat muffins" into "Well , I ca n't eat muffins", and it also spells out numbers, so it works as a text normaliser. It builds on the OpenFst library.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the tools "compile grammars expressed as regular expressions and context-dependent rewrite rules into weighted finite-state transducers". It is named after Dionysius Thrax, "the reputed first Greek grammarian".
brief.how_it_works: A .grm file has an Imports section and a Body of functions and statements, and each source file compiles to a .far archive that other grammars can import by alias. The language provides operators for concatenation, union, composition, rewrite (cross product) and CDRewrite for context-dependent rules, plus Feature, Category and Paradigm tools for morphology. For nested or copying structure, the README describes pushdown (PDT) and multi-pushdown (MPDT) extensions, with the MPDT example handling reduplication such as "kidongo" to "kididongo".

commands_seen.context: Installs the library and its dependencies from conda-forge; the homepage says this is for Linux (x86) and Mac OS X users who already have conda.
Generates the Makefile for a grammar, from the Quick Tour's step for copying and building the sample grammar.
Builds example.far from the grammar, after thraxmakedep has created the Makefile.
Runs the TOKENIZER rule from the built archive interactively on input strings, with sample input and output shown in the Quick Tour.
Tests a pushdown transducer rule together with its parenthesis transducer; the README notes ":" can replace "$" as a bash-friendly form.
Tests a multi-pushdown reduplication rule with its parenthesis and assignment transducers; example outputs are kidongo to kididongo and fungus to fungungus.

brief.install_notes: The homepage gives conda-forge as the easy route (conda install -c conda-forge thrax) for Linux x86 and Mac OS X users who already have conda. Building from source is implied by the Quick Tour: the sample grammar is installed to /usr/local/share/thrax/grammars and you copy it to a writable directory before running make. Writing a function in C++ means overloading thrax::function::Function, registering it in src/lib/loader.cc, and rebuilding the libraries. Optional GNU readline support is enabled with --enable-readline at configure time. I did not fetch a separate download or install page, so details beyond these are unknown.
brief.standout: The grammar language is unusually approachable for FST work: a short, readable script with named functions, imports and tokenised string literals, and the README shows a working text normaliser and morphology tools. Pushdown and multi-pushdown extensions let the same toolkit express context-free patterns and copying such as reduplication, which plain finite-state rewriting cannot.
brief.status: Probably maintained. The homepage was edited on 2025-09-09 by KyleGorman, it announces version 1.3.10 as available for download, and it says Thrax is on conda-forge. The Quick Tour page was last edited in 2019, so some of its docs may lag the current release. I did not see a release date for 1.3.10 itself.
brief.caveats: The README states that thraxrewrite-tester only works with grammars compiled to standard (tropical) arcs. Temporary symbols are not handled well by thraxrewrite-tester. Symbol tables must match across a multi-file grammar when --save_symbols is used, and byte-mode compilation splits non-ASCII characters into byte sequences that are hard to read. The conda-forge route is only mentioned for Linux x86 and Mac OS X. The homepage is a TWiki page with older documentation links, and I did not find the licence in what I read. The brew caveats field was empty.

It is named after Dionysius Thrax (Διονύσιος ὁ Θρᾷξ, 170 BC – 90 BC), the reputed first Greek grammarian.

name: tile38
desc: In-memory geolocation data store, spatial index, and realtime geofence
why: A geofence database with realtime hooks and a Redis-like protocol, a neat niche but mostly a server you configure rather than explore.

brief.what_it_is: Tile38 is an in-memory geolocation data store and spatial index, with a server (tile38-server) and a command line client (tile38-cli). You load it with objects such as lat/lon points, bounding boxes, geohashes, GeoJSON, QuadKeys and XYZ tiles, grouped into named collections. You then query it with Nearby, Within and Intersects, filter results by field values or object id, or turn any search into a geofence that streams enter, exit, inside, outside or cross events. Results come back as JSON over HTTP and websockets, or as RESP over telnet and Redis-compatible clients.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as an open source server for location-based applications that need fast geospatial queries and realtime geofence notifications. The homepage says it lets you 'simplify your architecture' by handling geofencing in the database rather than in application code.
brief.how_it_works: Objects are stored in named collections, each with an id, a geometry and optional double-precision fields, and a spatial index serves the search commands. A search becomes a geofence when you add the FENCE keyword; the connection then stays open and the server pushes JSON messages as objects move in or out of the area. Notifications can also go to pub/sub channels (via setchan) or to webhooks (sethook), and the README says the data is in memory and persists on disk.

commands_seen.context: Adds a lat/lon point named truck1 to the collection fleet, from the README's basic CLI example.
Searches fleet for objects within 6000 meters of a point; the README says this returns one truck.
Turns the same radius search into a geofence that keeps the connection open and streams detection messages.

commands_seen.context: Same geofence, limited to enter and exit detections.

commands_seen.context: Creates a static geofence that publishes notifications for buses within 200 meters of a point to the busstop pub/sub channel.

Starts the server with the Prometheus metrics endpoint enabled on localhost port 4321; the flag is disabled by default.

brief.install_notes: No account or external service is needed. The README offers prebuilt binaries for OSX, Linux, FreeBSD and Windows on the GitHub releases page, plus a Docker image and a Homebrew formula (macOS). To build from source you need Go installed; the README says 'make' builds everything and 'make test' runs the tests, and that both 32-bit and 64-bit systems are supported. Run ./tile38-server -h for options. The CLI connects to localhost:9851 by default. Prometheus metrics are off unless you set --metrics-addr. The README's docs are mostly on tile38.com, with examples in the GitHub wiki.
brief.standout: Queries and geofences share one syntax: a plain search becomes a live monitor by adding fence, and enter, exit, inside, outside and cross come built in. It also speaks the Redis RESP protocol natively, so most Redis client libraries can talk to it.
brief.status: unknown. The README is current enough to mention Discord and the Redis RESP docs, and the homepage is live, but neither the fetched pages nor the brew metadata show a release date or last commit, so I can't confirm recent activity.

The scout notes describe it as mostly a server you configure rather than explore, which matches the README's focus on running the server and its protocols.

name: tinc
desc: Virtual Private Network (VPN) tool
why: A mesh VPN daemon with an unusual decentralised design, a fair door into tunnelling protocols.

brief.what_it_is: tinc is a Virtual Private Network daemon, named tincd. It uses tunnelling and encryption to create a private network between hosts on the Internet. The VPN appears to the IP-level network code as an ordinary network device, so existing software needs no changes. Encryption uses LibreSSL or OpenSSL, with message authentication codes and sequence numbers, and traffic can optionally be compressed with zlib or LZO. The homepage lists Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, OS X, Solaris, and several Windows versions as supported platforms.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way for sites to share information over the Internet without exposing that information to others. It also presents tinc as a way to link Ethernet segments so that LAN-only applications and games can run across the Internet.
brief.how_it_works: Nodes run the tincd daemon and connect to each other, and the homepage says VPN traffic is always sent directly to the destination when possible, without passing through intermediate hops. NAT traversal works as long as one node accepts incoming connections on a public IP address, even a dynamic one. Adding a node means adding a configuration file, with no new daemons, devices, or interfaces needed. The documentation contents list a UDP tunnel, a meta-connection, a meta-protocol, and an authentication protocol, but I did not read those sections.
brief.install_notes: The documentation table of contents lists these preparation steps: configure the kernel for your OS (Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Solaris, Darwin, Windows), install the LibreSSL or OpenSSL, zlib, and lzo libraries, then build and install tinc. Windows builds are described under Cygwin and MinGW environments, and Darwin has its own build environment section. Configuration covers main and host config files, generating keypairs, and network interface setup, with a worked example. I only saw section titles, not the steps themselves, so no commands were read.
brief.standout: Its design is a decentralised mesh in which every node can route directly to every other node, rather than funnelling traffic through a central hub. Adding a node means dropping in one config file, without starting new daemons or creating new devices.
brief.status: The homepage lists 1.0.37 as the latest stable release and 1.1pre18 as the latest prerelease from the 1.1 branch, and says 1.0.37 'will most likely be the last version of tinc 1.0'. No release date or commit date was visible, so recent activity is unknown, but the project is clearly still publishing news and releases.
brief.caveats: The supported-platforms list on the homepage names Windows 2000 through Windows 8, which looks dated. The 1.0.37 news item says Linux ethertap device support was dropped. Building from source needs kernel TUN/TAP configuration and three libraries, and Windows needs Cygwin or MinGW. I did not read the platform support page or the license text beyond the homepage's GPL v2-or-later statement.
quotes: tinc is a Virtual Private Network (VPN) daemon that uses tunnelling and encryption to create a secure private network between hosts on the Internet.
Regardless of how you set up the tinc daemons to connect to each other, VPN traffic is always (if possible) sent directly to the destination, without going through intermediate hops.
When you want to add nodes to your VPN, all you have to do is add an extra configuration file, there is no need to start new daemons or create and configure new devices or network interfaces.

name: tkey-ssh-agent
desc: SSH agent for use with the TKey security stick
why: Routes SSH authentication through a hardware security stick with open firmware, an interesting look at how key material gets isolated.

brief.what_it_is: tkey-ssh-agent is an OpenSSH-compatible SSH agent that uses the Tillitis TKey, a compact USB-C security token, to make SSH signatures. It runs as a daemon that listens on a Unix socket (or a named pipe on Windows), and OpenSSH clients reach it through the SSH_AUTH_SOCK environment variable. The agent loads a signer app onto the TKey, which performs the signing, so the private key stays on the stick. The agent also prints the public key with --show-pubkey, which you can paste into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The README calls it the TKey SSH Agent and says it is for use with the TKey USB security token.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no separate problem statement. The homepage frames TKey as a device that provides a secure and isolated environment for specialized applications, with Authentication among its named uses, and says applications run one at a time in complete isolation. This agent is one application built on that idea.
brief.how_it_works: The agent auto-detects the TKey, or takes a serial port via --port. It loads the signer device app onto the TKey and derives the key pair from the signer app binary, the USS (User-Supplied Secret) and the UDS in the USB stick, so changing any of those changes the key pair. Signatures need a physical touch on the TKey by default, and the agent shows touch notifications. The README says the agent does not keep its own key material, but its own description of the mechanism is brief and it does not spell out the wire protocol.

name: topiary
desc: Uniform formatter for simple languages, as part of the Tree-sitter ecosystem

brief.what_it_is: Topiary is a uniform code formatter for simple languages, built on the Tree-sitter parsing ecosystem and written in Rust by Tweag. Formatter authors describe a language's style in a simple DSL, and Topiary's engine applies that style to source code, so authors do not need to write their own formatting engine or parser. End users get one formatter tool that can apply a consistent style across several languages. brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the problem as subjective personal style choices that waste hours of review time. brief.how_it_works: The README says the style is defined in a simple DSL and that Topiary relies on Tree-sitter for parsing, so a formatter author does not write a grammar. name: toxiproxy
desc: TCP proxy to simulate network & system conditions for chaos & resiliency testing
why: A TCP proxy that injects latency and failures; a useful lens on how networks break, though it leans toward testing tooling.

brief.what_it_is: Toxiproxy is a TCP proxy written in Go, paired with an HTTP API and a CLI. You point your application's test connections at a Toxiproxy listen address, and Toxiproxy forwards them to the real upstream (Redis, MySQL, a web app). You then add toxics over HTTP or the CLI to add latency, cut bandwidth, drop packets, reset connections, or take the whole service down. The inputs are proxy definitions (name, listen address, upstream address) and toxic definitions; the output is the same traffic with the injected faults applied. Client libraries exist in many languages, with Ruby as the original.
brief.why_it_exists: Shopify built it to prove with tests that an application has no single points of failure, and has used it in all development and test environments since October 2014. The README says existing tools lacked the dynamic API needed for integration and unit testing, and that Linux tools like nc are not cross-platform and require root.
brief.how_it_works: Each proxy is a listener that forwards bytes between a client and an upstream. Toxics sit on a stream (upstream or downstream) and alter the data: latency adds a delay of latency +/- jitter, bandwidth limits KB/s, packet_loss drops chunks, and down disables the proxy by setting enabled to false. Toxics can be applied with a toxicity probability, so only a fraction of connections are affected. The server listens for HTTP on port 8474, and clients change proxies and toxics through that API.

Faults are switched on and off from inside a test through a client API, and the Ruby client can wrap a block so the fault lasts only for that block. name: tracebox
desc: Middlebox detection tool
why: Reveals middleboxes that silently rewrite TCP packets by comparing what you sent against what came back, a real door into hidden network behaviour.

brief.what_it_is: Tracebox is a command-line tool for detecting middleboxes (devices that modify packets in transit) on a network path between a source and any destination. It is similar to traceroute in that it reports hop by hop, but instead of just listing routers it uses ICMP replies to spot changes made to the packets it sent. Input is a destination address (plus options such as -j for JSON output, -m for maximum hops, and -v for verbose detail). Output is a per-hop report of modifications, additions and deletions, or a JSON document with a Hops array. The distribution includes a Lua API (luatracebox) alongside the tracebox executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to detect middleboxes on any path, which is hard to do with ordinary traceroute. Its core observation is that ICMP messages often do not follow RFC 792: routers that return the full original datagram in Time-to-Live exceeded messages reveal what the packet looked like when it reached that hop.
brief.how_it_works: Tracebox sends probes with increasing TTL, as traceroute does, and compares the packet it sent with the quoted packet in the ICMP reply from each hop. Differences in the quoted headers or payload show where a middlebox changed, added or removed fields. The README says this works because some operating systems (Linux, Cisco IOS-XR) and MPLS routers return the full datagram, as well as through the ICMP Multi-Part Messages extension.

name: trealla-prolog
desc: Compact and efficient ISO Prolog interpreter written in plain old C
why: A compact ISO Prolog in plain C is a genuinely old-school logic language worth an afternoon of queries and backtracking.

brief.what_it_is: Trealla Prolog is a compact ISO Prolog interpreter written in plain C99 and built with a plain Makefile. You give it Prolog source files or queries, either on the command line with tpl or at its REPL, and it runs them and prints answers. The README also lists a C embedding API (libtrealla.a and trealla.h), a WebAssembly build, and a Python bridge marked experimental. The feature list covers unbounded integers and rationals, UTF-8 atoms and strings, DCGs, freeze/dif/when, CLP(B) and CLP(Z), tabling, threads, engines, actors, sockets, and SQLite via an FFI-backed module.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a compact, efficient ISO Prolog interpreter that runs on very many platforms, including bare boards and bare metal. It is also meant to be embeddable from C and usable in Jupyter notebooks.
brief.how_it_works: Trealla runs as a single tpl executable that loads files, consults .pl sources, and drops into a REPL with history when given no goal. Double-quoted text defaults to a packed UTF-8 byte array that behaves like a char list, and open/4 with mmap(Ls) gives a memory-mapped file view as a string. Tabling memoizes each call variant so left-recursive predicates terminate, and the table can be declared incremental or mode-directed (min/max).

name: treecc
desc: Aspect-oriented approach to writing compilers
why: An aspect-oriented tree compiler generator from the DotGNU project, a rare look at how compilers get built from declarative specs.

brief.what_it_is: Treecc is a compiler-compiler from the DotGNU project that generates C (or C++) code for building and walking compiler parse trees. You write a declarative spec in treecc's own rule-based syntax, listing node types with their fields and abstract superclasses, plus 'operation' definitions that give per-node-type code for things like type inference. Embedded C code supplies the details. Treecc emits the node structures, the '*_create' constructor functions, and the operation dispatch code, and it reports an error when an operation lacks a case for some node type.
brief.why_it_exists: The manual argues that lex and yacc stop at parsing and leave semantic analysis and code generation to hand-written tree code, which is error-prone. Adding a node type means finding every walker that must handle it, and the Visitor pattern makes adding node types painful. Treecc aims to catch coverage gaps automatically.
brief.how_it_works: The yacc grammar's semantic actions call the generated '*_create' functions to build the tree, and the parameters match the node's fields in type and order. Each operation is declared once, with a case per node type, and abstract types such as 'binary' let one case cover all subclasses. A more specific case, such as one for 'power', overrides the inherited one. Treecc checks that every concrete node type is covered and raises an error if one is missing, so a newly added node type that an operation does not handle is caught at translation time.
brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the brew install was visible in the pages I read. Section 3 of the manual, 'Invoking treecc from the command-line', was listed in the table of contents but I did not fetch it, so I have no command syntax from the manual.
brief.standout: Treecc applies aspect-oriented ideas to compiler trees. Each operation is a cross-cutting aspect that gets woven across all node types, and the generator checks coverage globally, which the manual says ordinary OO and Visitor designs do not do. It also keeps the spec declarative and yacc-like rather than inventing a new language.

name: tsshd
desc: UDP-based SSH server with roaming support
why: A UDP-based SSH server with roaming, a neat look at how SSH can ride a different transport and survive IP changes.

brief.what_it_is: tsshd is a server-side program that behaves like sshd but listens on UDP, so an SSH session can keep working when the client's IP or network changes or the link drops. The client, tssh (trzsz-ssh), first logs in over ordinary SSH, which starts a fresh tsshd process on the server. That process picks a random UDP port in 61001-61999, hands the port number and session keys back through the SSH channel, and then the client talks to it over QUIC or KCP. The README says it aims to stay compatible with OpenSSH and supports UDP port forwarding, both local and remote.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says it was inspired by mosh and aims for the same roaming and sleep/wake survival, while keeping ordinary SSH behaviour. The README states that tssh and tsshd 'work exactly like ssh', with no plans for mosh-style local echo and line editing.
brief.how_it_works: tssh logs in normally over TCP SSH, and the server then spawns a per-session tsshd that listens on a random UDP port and sends the port and session secret keys back over the SSH channel; the SSH connection is then closed and traffic moves to UDP. On the client, a proxy implementing net.PacketConn sits between the KCP or QUIC client and the network, so when heartbeats stop it can re-authenticate to the server proxy from a new address while the transport above it never sees an interruption. Authentication packets are AES-256-GCM encrypted with a session key, with a strictly increasing sequence number to block replays; the transports are kcp-go or quic-go (QUIC uses TLS 1.3).

name: tup
desc: File-based build system
why: A file-based build system that tracks real file access; an unusual design, though it is mostly build plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: Tup is a file-based build system for Linux, OSX, and Windows, written by Mike Shal. Per its homepage, it takes a list of file changes and a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies as input, then runs the commands needed to bring dependent files up to date. The homepage does not say what the build description looks like beyond the Tupfile name it links to, and it does not describe the output in detail.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches tup as a faster, lower-friction alternative to make and its derivatives: quick edit/compile/test cycles on large projects, running a build from any directory in the tree, and no clean builds or stale files to worry about. The author frames it humorously, and the README says it is 'so fast that your chair mounted jousting might suffer.'

name: twoping
desc: Ping utility to determine directional packet loss
why: Measuring directional packet loss reveals asymmetric network behaviour that ordinary ping hides, a good door into ICMP.

brief.what_it_is: 2ping is a command-line ping utility written in Python 3 that reports which direction packet loss happens, outbound or inbound, rather than only whether packets were lost. You run the 2ping client against a host, and that host runs a 2ping listener (started with 2ping --listen). The output is per-ping lines marked as outbound lost, inbound lost, or received, followed by summary counts of outbound, inbound, and undetermined losses along with round-trip min/avg/max. The 2ping6 executable is listed alongside it for IPv6.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a bi-directional ping: ordinary ping cannot tell you whether a lost packet was lost on the way out or on the way back. The author built 2ping to make that split visible.
brief.how_it_works: Each probe uses a three-way exchange akin to TCP SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK. Afterward, the client and listener compare their state to work out which direction each loss occurred. The protocol is documented in a separate specification and is described as version-agnostic, so clients and listeners of different versions are meant to interoperate.

commands_seen.context: Example run against the public test listener; the sample output shows outbound and inbound losses labelled per sequence number and a statistics block with an outbound/inbound/undetermined breakdown.
Starts a listener on a stable remote host so that a client can test against it.

brief.install_notes: Needs Python 3.5 or higher. Beyond the package manager, nothing special is required on the client side, but a useful test needs a 2ping listener at the far end, which you either run yourself (2ping --listen on a stable host) or borrow from one of the public test listeners (test.2ping.net, ipv4./ipv6.test.2ping.net, and several secondary servers including cromulent.colobox.com and Finnix mirrors in Dallas, London and Tokyo). Windows is installed from source with pip3 rather than from a package. The page says tested on Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Mac OS X and Windows.
brief.standout: Most ping tools only count losses. 2ping uses a three-way exchange and compares state after the fact, so it can label each lost probe as outbound or inbound, which exposes asymmetric paths that plain ping hides.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists source release 2.ping 4.6.1 dated 2026-03-02 with an OpenPGP signature, and it points to an active GitHub issue tracker and pull requests. The author is Ryan Finnie. I did not check commit history directly.

Public listeners must not be flooded: the page asks for no interval faster than 0.2 seconds, no excessive periods of pinging, and no constant large padded packets. Distribution packages may lag the latest release, and the official release tarballs differ from tagged git checkouts. Windows support depends on installing Python and using pip. The copyright line says 2010, but the release is recent. The license is the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

name: twtxt
desc: Decentralised, minimalist microblogging service for hackers
why: A decentralised microblogging format built on plain text files over HTTP, a quietly odd corner of the web.

brief.what_it_is: twtxt is a command-line tool and a plain-text format for microblogging. You publish short posts by appending lines to a publicly reachable text file, and the URL of that file serves as your identity. twtxt then fetches the text files you follow, much like a feed reader, and merges them into a single timeline. The README describes it as a CLI tool plus a format specification for self-hosted, flat-file microblogging.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as an alternative to signing up at a closed or regulated microblogging platform: you put status updates in a publicly accessible text file instead. It also aims to be simple, human readable, and easy to combine with UNIX command-line utilities.
brief.how_it_works: Each user hosts a plain text file over HTTP, and each line is a timestamped post. The client acts like a feed reader that polls the files you track with asynchronous HTTP requests (asyncio/aiohttp) and builds a timeline from them. Posting can be as simple as appending a line to the file with a shell command.

commands_seen.context: README's example of posting without the official client: appends a tab-separated ISO timestamp and a message to twtxt.txt, the publicly hosted file.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no installation steps. It names Python 3, click for the CLI, and asyncio/aiohttp for HTTP. The PyPI badge indicates a pip-installable package named twtxt, and the Homebrew formula installs the twtxt executable. Hosting your feed requires a publicly accessible URL for the text file.
brief.standout: The identity model is a single text file at a URL, with no server or account. Posts are plain lines that a shell one-liner can write, and the timeline is built by polling other people's files as a feed reader would.

name: txr
desc: Lisp-like programming language for convenient data munging
why: A Lisp-like language for data munging with pattern matching in both directions; an unusual, underknown corner worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: TXR is a programming language with two parts: a whole-document pattern matching and extraction language for pulling information out of arbitrary text, and TXR Lisp, a general data-processing Lisp dialect. It takes text or structured data as input and produces extracted or transformed data as output. The homepage says many tasks can be done as one-liners from the shell prompt. It also includes an Awk implementation as a Lisp macro.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes TXR as a convenient tool for daily hacking and data munging, aimed at messy, loosely structured text that is hard to handle with regexps or Awk-style field splitting. The project values brevity: programs should be short and clear.
brief.how_it_works: The pattern language uses nested, recursive pattern matching that binds variables, rather than imperative statements. Each construct ends by matching, failing, or throwing an exception, and searching and backtracking are implicit. TXR Lisp is a new dialect, not an implementation of Common Lisp or Scheme, and it compiles to a register-based virtual machine bytecode with an optimizing compiler.
brief.install_notes: Packaged by GNU Guix, NixOS, Chimera Linux, Alpine Linux, Void Linux, EasyBuild and T2. Binary downloads are available for several platforms, and 32-bit and 64-bit Windows installers exist for TXR 302. The source build needs only GNU Make, GCC or Clang, and a few shell utilities for configure. It has no external dependencies except libffi. The homepage explicitly says not to install it through Homebrew, so the suggested brew install should not be used.
brief.standout: Its pattern language matches whole documents with nested, recursive bindings instead of working line by line like Awk, and it still handles simple one-liners. The project is also small: the executable is about 1.7 MB, and peak memory when compiling its standard library is around 18 MB.
brief.status: Unknown from the homepage alone. The page is active and refers to TXR 302 and a Git repository, and says the project started in 2009, but it gives no release date or last-commit date. I did not fetch the release notes or repository to check.
brief.caveats: The homepage warns: 'Do not use TXR via Homebrew.' It says Homebrew packages contain an unstable, unreliable executable, that some users could not build the Homebrew formula, and that the formula does not run make tests. The project suspects Homebrew's compiler code generation flags. The Homebrew package is the one listed in the scout notes, so it should be avoided. The reference manual is very long, about 900 pages as a man-page-style PDF, so the learning curve is steep. The page itself says the language is 'no longer a small language'. The license is the two-clause BSD license.

TXR is a pragmatic, convenient tool ready to take on your daily hacking challenges with its dual personality

name: uade

It runs the original Amiga player code for each format inside a 68k CPU emulator built on the UAE project, and it reimplements the Eagleplayer and Delitracker player APIs so those players can run outside AmigaOS. It takes Amiga music files as input and plays them as audio. The GitLab project page describes it as playing 200+ Amiga computer music formats. The homepage says it is designed to run from the command line or as a player plugin. The brew metadata lists three executables: uade123, bencat, and mod2ogg2.sh.

brief.how_it_works: Rather than reimplementing each format's parser, UADE emulates the Amiga's m68k code and runs the original player routines in that environment. A free implementation of the Eagleplayer and Delitracker APIs supplies the surrounding infrastructure. The homepage describes the design as a cmdline tool or a player plugin.

name: ucspi-tcp
desc: Tools for building TCP client-server applications
why: D. J. Bernstein's tcpserver and tcpclient toolkit is a sharp, strange door into how TCP servers are built from the shell.

brief.what_it_is: ucspi-tcp is a set of small command-line UNIX tools by D. J. Bernstein for building TCP client-server applications. tcpserver listens on a host and port and, for each incoming connection, runs a program of your choice with the network on its stdin and stdout, plus environment variables describing the local and remote host names, IP addresses and ports. tcpclient makes an outgoing TCP connection and runs a program the same way. The package also ships sample clients built on tcpclient (who@, date@, finger@, http@, tcpcat, mconnect), plus recordio for logging a server's input and output, and rules tools (tcprules, tcprulescheck) that compile access-control rules into a cdb hash file.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a replacement for inetd, which the author says is unreliable under high loads, has no effective resource management, and has a listen() backlog that is typically only 5 or 10. The stated aim is easy-to-use command-line TCP tools with a concurrency limit and fast, hashed access control.
brief.how_it_works: For each accepted connection, tcpserver forks the program given as prog, wiring descriptor 0 to read from the network and descriptor 1 to write to it. It defers accepting new connections once the concurrency limit (default 40, set with -c) is reached. Access rules compiled by tcprules into a cdb file (passed with -x) can reject sources or set environment variables, and can be recompiled while the server runs.

commands_seen.context: Install step: decompress the downloaded 0.88 tarball (the page lists this as the latest published package).
Install step: unpack the source tree.
Install step: enter the unpacked source directory.
Install step: compile the ucspi-tcp programs.
Install step, run as root: installs the programs under /usr/local and runs checks.

Interface summary from the tcpserver page: opts are getopt-style options, host is an IP or host name (0 for any local address), port is a name or number (0 picks a free port), and prog is the program to run per connection.
Option: cap simultaneous connections at n; new connections are deferred while n copies of prog are running. Default 40.
Option: follow access rules and environment settings compiled into cdb by tcprules; rules can be rerun while tcpserver runs.
Option: write banner to the client immediately on connect, to cut latency for protocols where the client waits for a greeting.
Option: give up on the TCPREMOTEINFO lookup after n seconds (default 26).

brief.install_notes: UNIX only. Download the ucspi-tcp package (latest listed as ucspi-tcp-0.88.tar.gz), unpack, run make, then as root run make setup check to install under /usr/local. The install page asks users who succeed to report it by piping their name and the SYSDEPS file to a mailing list address (djb-sysdeps@cr.yp.to). No accounts, runtimes or hardware are mentioned. Homebrew users get a packaged version with no brew-specific caveats recorded.
brief.standout: Access control is compiled into a cdb hash so the lookup stays fast even with thousands of host rules, and the tool passes connection metadata to an ordinary program through environment variables instead of requiring a server-side plugin model. The tool is a small, Unix-style alternative to inetd, xinetd, netcat and netpipes.

The homepage's scout note calls it strange, which is editorial; the page itself is terse and assumes Unix background.
