name: wabt
desc: Web Assembly Binary Toolkit
why: WebAssembly binary toolkit that lets you disassemble, inspect, and rewrite .wasm binaries into readable text and back.

brief.what_it_is: WABT (the WebAssembly Binary Toolkit) is a suite of command-line tools for working with WebAssembly files. It converts the text format (.wat/.wast) to the binary format (.wasm) with wat2wasm and back again with wasm2wat, and it can disassemble and inspect binaries with wasm-objdump and wasm-stats. It can also validate, strip sections from, and interpret binaries (wasm-interp, spectest-interp), convert binaries to C with wasm2c, and convert spec test files to JSON with wast2json. Inputs are .wat, .wast, .wasm, and spec-test JSON files; outputs are binaries, text, C source, JSON, or console reports.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says these tools are "intended for use in (or for development of) toolchains or other systems that want to manipulate WebAssembly files." They are written in C/C++ so they are easier to integrate than the spec interpreter, and they aim for full spec fidelity rather than optimization.
brief.how_it_works: Each tool is a separate executable built from one C/C++ codebase. The README says the tools aim for "1:1 round-trips with no changes to instructions," so converting a binary to text and back should preserve the instructions. The project also says it has been compiled to JavaScript with emscripten to power the online demos.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt packages: brew install wabt on Homebrew, sudo apt install wabt on apt-based Linux, or download binaries from the GitHub releases page. To build from source you need CMake, plus Ninja if using the top-level Makefile. Clone with --recursive, or run git submodule update --init afterward, to get the test submodules. For CMake directly, create a separate build directory, because running cmake from the repo root will not work. On Windows you need CMake and either Visual Studio 2015 or newer or MinGW. Building gperf is only needed if you add new lexer keywords.
brief.standout: Unlike Binaryen, which is an optimizer and higher-level compiler target, WABT is built for fidelity: it promises byte-exact, instruction-preserving round-trips and treats the spec as the target. The proposal table tracks which WebAssembly proposals each tool supports, with a flag for each, so you can see exactly which features are on by default.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a passing CI badge and a proposal table that includes recent proposals such as wide-arithmetic and custom-page-sizes, but it shows no release date or last-commit date, and I did not fetch the releases page to check.

Several proposals (threads, custom-page-sizes, compact-imports, function-references, wide-arithmetic) are not default-on, and some are not supported by interpret or wasm2c. The README has no explicit licence statement, and I did not check the LICENSE file.

name: waon
desc: Wave-to-notes transcriber
why: Transcribes a recording into musical notes by analysing the waveform, a strange and genuinely clever audio-to-symbol transform.

brief.what_it_is: WaoN is a command-line 'wave-to-notes' transcriber that reads a WAV file and writes a standard MIDI file (format 0) containing the notes it detects. Input can be a WAV file, or any format SoX can decode if SoX is installed; input and output can both be stdin/stdout. Its version 0.11 also ships pv, a phase vocoder for time-stretching and pitch-shifting, and gwaon, a GUI for waon and pv. The README describes it as the inverse of timidity.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted to pick out the voicing of harmony from recordings of favourite pianists, and said that no functional application of this kind existed on Unix as far as he knew, so he started writing WaoN.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives few internals. It uses FFT analysis with selectable windows (default hanning, 2048-sample frames) and a phase-vocoder correction to refine frequency estimates. Note selection is controlled by cutoff, peak-threshold and pitch-range options, with optional drum-removal and octave-removal filters.

name: wasm-micro-runtime
desc: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR)
why: A tiny WebAssembly runtime for embedded targets, a interesting window into running bytecode on small devices.

brief.what_it_is: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR) is a lightweight, standalone WebAssembly runtime. It loads Wasm modules and runs them, either interpreted, ahead-of-time compiled (AOT), or JIT-compiled. Its command-line product, iwasm, takes a .wasm file (or an AOT file produced by the wamrc compiler) and runs it with WASI support. The VMcore is also meant to be embedded as a C/C++ library, with Python, Go and Rust bindings. The scout note calls it tiny and aimed at embedded targets; the README does say small footprint and embedded/IoT, but it also covers Linux, macOS, Windows, Android and cloud and TEE uses, so 'embedded' is only part of the picture.
brief.why_it_exists: The README pitches WAMR as a runtime for applications "from embedded, IoT, edge to Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), smart contract, cloud native and so on", with small footprint and high performance as the main goals. The README does not spell out a separate problem statement beyond that.
brief.how_it_works: The VMcore offers several execution modes: a fast interpreter, a classic interpreter, AOT (wamrc compiles a .wasm to an AOT file that iwasm loads), LLVM JIT, Fast JIT, and a multi-tier JIT. Multi-tier starts a module on Fast JIT right away and compiles LLVM JIT functions on background threads, switching over as they finish. Build-time choices are made with cmake flags such as -DWAMR_BUILD_JIT=1 and -DWAMR_BUILD_FAST_JIT=1.

Ahead-of-time compile a Wasm file into an AOT file using the wamrc compiler, which must be built first.
Run the AOT file produced by wamrc.

Configure a build that enables multi-tier JIT, which starts on Fast JIT and tiers up to LLVM JIT.

brief.install_notes: Building iwasm from source is the normal route; the README has no Homebrew-specific steps. Linux needs build-essential, cmake, g++-multilib, libgcc and ccache (Ubuntu) or glibc-devel.i686 (Fedora). macOS needs Xcode and cmake. Windows needs MSVC and cmake. The default build is fast interpreter, AOT and libc WASI, with JIT off. LLVM JIT needs the LLVM library built first (build_llvm.sh, which takes a long time). Embedded targets each have their own steps: Zephyr, ESP-IDF (at least 4.3.1), NuttX (Kconfig), RT-Thread (menuconfig), and Android (SDK and NDK). A Docker route exists via ci/build_wamr.sh. The README does not explain the iwasm-2.4.5 executable name from the brew formula.
brief.standout: One runtime that offers an interpreter, AOT, and two JIT tiers, with a Fast JIT that moves to LLVM JIT while the program runs. It also ships a small libc option alongside full WASI, and its README gives per-part size figures measured on a Cortex-M4F (about 21.4K for WASI libc, 3.7K for builtin libc).
brief.status: unknown. The fetched pages show no release date or last-commit date. The README has a recent-looking notice that the project moved to a new GitHub organisation and that CI/CD is being rechecked. It also lists a current TSC roster and a wiki of adopters, which suggests active upkeep, but that is inference rather than a dated signal.
brief.caveats: The README lists some hard limits. MinGW builds have WASI disabled, and hardware bounds checking is turned off there, so wamrc needs --bounds-checks=1. VxWorks is only validated on SR0620. Cosmopolitan Libc supports only x86_64 and interpreter modes. LLVM JIT needs a large LLVM build. The wamr.dev domain has not moved yet. The license is Apache 2.0 with the LLVM exception. The README does not say which version the brew formula's iwasm-2.4.5 corresponds to.

name: wasm-tools
desc: Low level tooling for WebAssembly in Rust
why: Swiss-army knife for WebAssembly binaries, letting you dissect, validate and convert the format by hand.

brief.what_it_is: wasm-tools is a Bytecode Alliance command-line program and set of Rust libraries for working with WebAssembly modules and components at a low level. The single wasm-tools binary has subcommands that take a .wasm binary or a .wat text file as input. They validate it, print it as text, parse text back to binary, mutate or generate test modules, strip or demangle sections, dump binary structure, and build or inspect components and WIT interface files. Output goes to stdout or to a file with -o.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes the project as 'CLI and Rust libraries for low-level manipulation of WebAssembly modules,' and says the CLI 'contains useful tools for debugging WebAssembly modules and components.' It also states that the repository 'strives to implement any standardized proposal to WebAssembly.'
brief.how_it_works: Each CLI subcommand wraps a library in the same repo, such as wasmparser for validate, wat for parse, wasmprinter for print, wasm-smith for smith, and wasm-mutate for mutate. Commands follow shared conventions: stdin is read when no file is given, output goes to stdout unless -o is passed, -t emits text format, and -v adds log verbosity. Commands can be piped together. Proposal support is switched by a --features flag, and stage 4+ proposals are on by default in validation.

name: wasm3
desc: High performance WebAssembly interpreter
why: A tiny WebAssembly interpreter that shows how portable bytecode actually executes, a good way to watch a VM run.

brief.what_it_is: Wasm3 is a WebAssembly interpreter written in C. It takes a WebAssembly module (portable bytecode) and executes it directly, without generating native machine code. It is also distributed as a library that other programs can embed, with bindings listed for Python, Rust, Go, Zig, .NET, Arduino and others. The README describes it as a fast interpreter and the most universal WASM runtime, and says it runs on Linux, Windows, macOS, the BSDs, Android, iOS, routers, single-board computers and microcontrollers. The README mentions a minimum footprint of about 64 KB of code and 10 KB of RAM.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a research project: it asks whether WebAssembly is a practical portable, sandboxed alternative to Lua, JS, Python or Lisp on microcontrollers, for uses like edge computing, plugin systems and IoT rules. It also argues that an interpreter is the better trade-off over a JIT when size, memory, startup latency, portability and security matter.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the interpreter approach gives small executables and low memory use, and that it avoids the need to generate executable code at runtime. This matters on platforms such as iOS and WebAssembly itself, where a JIT is unavailable. The README does not describe the internal design in detail; it points to docs/Interpreter.md for architecture.

commands_seen.context: From docs/Installation.md: makes the downloaded Linux prebuilt binary executable. Wasm3 ships as a static binary with nothing to install alongside it.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt static binaries are on the latest GitHub release page: wasm3-win-x64.exe or wasm3-win-x86.exe on Windows, wasm3-linux-x64.elf on Linux (needs chmod +x), and wasm3-linux-other.tar.gz for Arm, AArch64, MIPS, PowerPC, RISC-V, s390x, LoongArch, m68k, MicroBlaze and SH4, built against musl. There is also a Cosmopolitan Actually Portable Executable (wasm3-cosmopolitan.com) that runs across several OSes. Homebrew is available on macOS. Arduino, PlatformIO and Particle libraries are installed through their library managers, and OpenWRT has its own instructions. Embedding is done through the language bindings. The README itself contains no shell commands to run the interpreter; usage details are in docs/Cookbook.md and docs/Demos.md, which I did not fetch.
brief.standout: The same small C engine runs from a Linux prebuilt binary up to microcontrollers such as ATmega1284P with 16 KB RAM (per the author's tweet), and the README claims it can run itself (self-hosting) and can be compiled to WebAssembly for browsers. The feature list also includes gas metering, suspend and resume snapshots, a deterministic profile and structured execution tracing, which are unusual for a tiny interpreter.
brief.status: Minimal maintenance, per a note at the top of the README. The author says he cannot add new features but will review and merge pull requests. The pinned tweet announces v0.9.0 as the first major update in five years, and a v0.9.1-beta.1 followed on Sep 14 of the same year. The tweets are not dated with a year in the fetched page, and I did not see a last-commit date or latest-release date, so the exact recency is unclear.
brief.caveats: The README says the project is in minimal maintenance and that new features will not be added. It is an interpreter, so it is slower than JIT runtimes, which the README concedes ('Your mileage may vary'). JIT is unavailable on platforms such as iOS and in browsers. The feature list marks garbage collection, threads and fixed-width SIMD as not applicable, and threads are listed as atomics only. The scout note calls it tiny, which fits the README's minimum-size claim but is not a measured figure.

name: wayland
desc: Protocol for a compositor to talk to its clients
why: The Wayland protocol is a real door into how display servers talk to clients, though the formula is mostly libraries and the famous name lowers its surprise.

brief.what_it_is: Wayland is a protocol and system architecture for graphical display, meant to replace the X11 window system protocol. Applications (clients) use the Wayland protocol to talk to a display server (a compositor) to make themselves visible and to receive user input. The page describes it as a language rather than a single program: there is no common Wayland server like Xorg, and each graphical environment ships its own compositor implementation. The core library, libwayland, translates protocol definitions written in XML into a C API, and it only encodes and decodes messages.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says Wayland is a replacement for the X11 window system protocol and architecture, aimed at being easier to develop, extend, and maintain.
brief.how_it_works: Protocol definitions are written in XML, and libwayland converts them into a C language API for encoding and decoding messages between compositor and clients. The compositor and the applications are separate processes that talk over that protocol. Window management and user experience are often tied to the compositor rather than swappable parts.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps, accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration. The formula's listed executable is wayland-scanner, which the homepage does not mention.
brief.standout: Unlike X11, there is no single canonical server: the protocol is the shared contract, and every desktop environment brings its own compositor. The page also notes Wayland can run nested inside another X11 or Wayland session, and that some web browsers use it for internal communication between application parts.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows no release date, last commit, or maintenance note. It does list releases, git repositories, a mailing list, IRC channel #wayland on OFTC, and a bug tracker, which suggests an active project, but I did not verify recency.
brief.caveats: The formula is a library and protocol toolkit, not a standalone application, so installing it gives you little to run directly. The page says libwayland 'does not implement Wayland'; the real behaviour lives in compositors and toolkits. The homepage has no platform or licensing details.
quotes: Wayland is a replacement for the X11 window system protocol and architecture with the aim to be easier to develop, extend, and maintain.
Wayland is the language (protocol) that applications can use to talk to a display server in order to make themselves visible and get input from the user (a person).
There is no single common Wayland server like Xorg is for X11, but every graphical environment brings with it one of many compositor implementations.

judge.reason: Wayland is well known, but its protocol-first design—where each desktop supplies its own compositor—makes a genuinely interesting system to explore.

name: wcslib
desc: Library and utilities for the FITS World Coordinate System
why: Astronomy coordinate transform library for FITS images, real science you can run at home on sky data.

brief.what_it_is: WCSLIB is a C library, with FORTRAN wrapper functions, that implements the coordinate transformations defined in the FITS World Coordinate System papers. It works with the WCS keywords in a FITS image header and the coordinate systems they describe (celestial, spectral and time). The homepage lists several bundled utilities. HPXcvt converts 1D HEALPix pixelization data stored in FITS (ring or nested order in a binary table extension) into a 2D primary image array with HPX or XPH coordinate representation. The package also includes PGSBOX, a curvilinear axis drawing routine for PGPLOT that can optionally interface to WCSLIB. The homepage does not describe the other installed executables (fitshdr, sundazel, tofits, wcsware) beyond their names in the brew metadata.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as the reference implementation for the FITSWCS standard, which defines keywords and usage for describing astronomical coordinate systems in a FITS image header. WCSLIB is presented as a C implementation of the coordinate transformations those papers define.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal mechanism. It says the library implements the transformations defined in the FITS WCS papers (Papers I to VII, including the HEALPix/HPX projection from Paper V and the XPH butterfly projection from Paper VI). It also points to a doxygen-generated programming manual in HTML and PDF, which I did not fetch.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps. It says WCSLIB is distributed as releases (the current one is 8.10, with older releases also available), and that the distribution includes RCS version files back to v1.0 from release 8.5 on. It also says test data is available: example FITS files for each projection in Paper II and for spectral representations from Paper III, plus a 13MiB bzip'd WMAP 3-year ILC map example for HPXcvt. Nothing on the page covers build requirements, accounts or runtime configuration.
brief.standout: It is the reference C implementation of the FITS WCS standard, which the homepage says was honoured with the 2025 ADASS software prize. It also ships a HEALPix-to-image converter (HPXcvt) and bundled test data for every projection in the standard, so you can check the transforms against known files.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage was last modified 2026-09-27, the same date as the announced WCSLIB 8.10 release with enhancements and bug fixes. The author's contact address is listed. The page's dates are as stated; I did not check a release page or repository commit history.
brief.caveats: Installation details, build requirements and the full list of commands are not on the homepage, so the brief does not cover them. The homepage is a literature and download page rather than a user guide. Based on the homepage, the library is C with FORTRAN wrappers, so it is aimed at people writing code, not at interactive use. The homepage gives no licence information. The brew description calls it a library for the FITS World Coordinate System, and the scout note calls it real science that can be run at home on sky data. The homepage does not say anything about running it that way.
quotes: WCSLIB is implemented in C, with support for FORTRAN via a set of wrapper functions.

Utility program HPXcvt is included with WCSLIB. It converts 1D HEALPix pixelization data stored in a variety of forms in FITS, including ring or nested organization in a binary table extension, into a 2D primary image array with HPX or XPH coordinate representation.
WCSLIB was honoured with the ADASS software prize for 2025 for which I gave the invited conference talk remotely by video.

name: wcstools
desc: Tools for using World Coordinate Systems (WCS) in astronomical images
why: Old astronomy tools for world coordinate systems in FITS images, a real science workflow you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: WCSTools is a set of command-line C programs and a utility library for reading and setting the world coordinate system (WCS) stored in the header of an astronomical image. It works on FITS and IRAF .imh files. Given an image, its tools convert between pixel positions and sky coordinates (sky2xy, xy2sky), match image stars to reference catalogs and fit a WCS to the image (imwcs, immatch), and do header and pixel manipulation (gethead, sethead, getpix, imrot, imsmooth and so on). The README lists about 55 programs, and the executables list in the brief has 50 entries.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says astronomers need to relate positions on an image to positions on the real sky, to identify catalogued objects, tell others where to find them, and compute motions of planets, satellites, asteroids, or comets. The software grew out of the impending standardization of WCS keywords in FITS, discussed at the 1994 ADASS conference. The author says the subroutines came first, then the utilities that use them, then the programs for catalog search and WCS fitting.
brief.how_it_works: The WCS lives in standard keywords in the image header, which relate pixel position to sky position. The library reads those keywords and does the projection math, using WCSLIB by Mark Calabretta plus the SAO WCSTools library. Catalog programs such as imcat, scat and imstar read reference catalogs from CD-ROM or online files, or local Starbase, ASCII, or SAO TDC binary files, with paths set by environment variables. imwcs matches detected stars to catalog stars and fits a new WCS into the header.

commands_seen.context: Builds the entire WCSTools package from the source tree, per the README's installation instruction.

brief.install_notes: The README says to build with make all. The homepage says the code is portable C and needs only a C compiler. A full source tarball (wcstools-3.9.7.tar.gz) and a smaller subset for WCS conversion only (wcssubs-3.9.7.tar.gz) are offered. Catalog-based tools need reference catalogs, either CD-ROM or online copies of USNO, GSC, 2MASS, Tycho-2 and similar, and the catalog location is set through environment variables. The package can also be installed as an IRAF package. At CfA-managed systems, a prebuilt bin directory is available to add to the search path. Full installation directions are in the README and on the documentation site.
brief.standout: The WCS fitting and projection code is the same library used by SAOimage, SAOtng, ds9 and skycat, so the header conversions match what those image viewers do. It is also a long-lived, single-author toolkit, with the package described in ADASS papers from 1996 to 2018.
brief.status: Maintained at a low level, leaning quiet. The current version is 3.9.7, dated April 26, 2022, and the homepage says it was last updated 26 April 2022 by Jessica Mink. A 2018 ADASS paper by Mink is cited on the homepage. I did not find a later release or commit, and I did not check a repository commit log, so the date is the only evidence.
brief.caveats: No license was visible in the pages I read, so check the tarball before reuse. Catalog access needs catalog files that you must obtain yourself, and the online catalog access depends on network services that may have changed since 2022. The homepage's brew-listed executables differ from the README list: the README includes httpget, filedir, fixhead and isdate, which are not in the brief's executables list, and the brief's list includes wcstools, which is not in the README's program list. Several program names are unusual, like getdate or char2sp, and the older docs predate most modern tooling, so expect the interface style and documentation to be dated. Nothing on the pages shows a warning about build failures.

This software is all written in very portable C, so it should compile and run on any computer with a C compiler.
The subroutines to translate between sky and image coordinates came first, then the utilities to use them, and then the programs to search catalogs and fit a world coordinate systems to images.

name: weave
desc: Entity-level semantic merge driver for Git using tree-sitter
why: Entity-level merging via tree-sitter is a clever angle on version control, but it is a git plumbing add-on with limited strangeness.

brief.what_it_is: Weave is an entity-level semantic merge driver for Git. It plugs into `git merge` and, instead of comparing lines, parses the base, ours, and theirs versions of a file with tree-sitter into functions, classes, and keys, then merges those entities. Two edits to different functions in one file merge cleanly, while two incompatible edits to the same entity still conflict. It takes source files in about 38 languages and formats (including JSON, YAML, TOML, CSV, and Markdown) and writes one merged file, with conflict markers that name the entity and the reason where a conflict remains. Files it can't handle fall back to Git's line merge. It ships as the `weave` CLI, the `weave-driver` binary that git invokes, and a `weave-mcp` server for AI agents.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage argues that Git merges by line, so two independent changes to different functions in the same file still produce a conflict, which is common when several AI agents edit one codebase. The README frames it as Git 'declaring a conflict' on changes that are 'completely independent'.
brief.how_it_works: Weave runs as a git merge driver (configured through `.gitattributes` and git config, with `%O %A %B %L %P` arguments). It parses all three revisions into entities, matches them by identity (file, type, name, parent, including renames), then resolves each entity: one-side changes win, and when both sides change the same entity it attempts an intra-entity three-way merge and conflicts only if that fails. The merge is a pure, stateless function over three file revisions, not a CRDT. A separate Automerge-based layer (`weave-crdt`) tracks live agent claims, but the merge path does not depend on it.

Building from source requires Rust and two cargo install commands (one per binary). Jujutsu (jj) users can add a [merge-tools.weave] block to their jj config and run `jj resolve --tool weave`. For agents, add the weave-mcp server to an MCP client; the live CRDT coordination tools appear only with WEAVE_EXPERIMENTAL=1. `weave stats` only accumulates counters if WEAVE_STATS=1 is set. brief.standout: It refuses on purpose: when two branches add different decorators to the same Python or TypeScript function, weave declines to pick a stacking order, because decorator order is semantic. It also publishes a benchmark page and a README that disclose regressions against Git and against real repos, rather than only headline wins. The conflict markers carry entity names and the internal guard that refused the auto-merge.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the README shows. The README contains a benchmark note dated 2026-09-01 for the 0.5.3 engine, and it describes a small team that reviews incoming PRs. I did not see a release date or last-commit date on the pages I read, so the evidence is the README's own dating rather than repo activity.
brief.caveats: Vue, Svelte, ERB, and Haskell are deliberately not merged by weave and fall back to Git's line merge. Files over 1MB and binary files fall back too. The homepage and README disagree on current numbers: the homepage says 0 regressions on C, Python, and Go, while the README's 0.5.3 table shows 23 regressions on git/git (C), 37 on Go, and 1 on Flask, with 86 regressions total across five repos, which the README says is partly by design. The 31-scenario benchmark is the author's own corpus. Live claims are advisory and a crashed agent's claims are not released automatically. The `weave-github` crate is a hosted-service component and not an installable binary. The homepage's 'Every time' promise is marketing; the README is more hedged. License is MIT OR Apache-2.0.

name: weggli
desc: Fast and robust semantic search tool for C and C++ codebases
why: A semantic code search that matches C patterns by structure, a neat way to query code like syntax trees.

brief.what_it_is: weggli is a command-line search tool for C and C++ source code. You give it a query written in a C-like pattern language, plus a file or directory, and it reports the places where code matches that structure. It parses the source into abstract syntax trees and matches the query against them, so it finds code by shape rather than by plain text. Output shows matching snippets with configurable lines before and after each match.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is designed to help security researchers identify interesting functionality in large codebases. It is inspired by Semgrep, Coccinelle, joern and CodeQL but makes different design choices, mainly first-class C++ support, minimal setup, interactive speed, and greedy matching.
brief.how_it_works: weggli is built on the tree-sitter parsing library and its C and C++ grammars. Queries are parsed with an extended version of the grammar, and the resulting AST is transformed into a set of tree-sitter queries (in builder.rs). Matching is done by query.rs, a small wrapper around tree-sitter's query engine that adds weggli-specific features.

name: websocketd
desc: WebSockets the Unix way
why: Exposes ordinary stdin and stdout programs as WebSockets, a charming door into a protocol nobody looks at.

brief.what_it_is: websocketd is a single command-line binary that wraps an ordinary program and serves it over a WebSocket. The program reads lines from stdin and writes lines to stdout, and websocketd turns each incoming WebSocket message into a stdin line and each stdout line into an outgoing WebSocket message. Each browser connection gets its own process, which websocketd starts on connect and stops on disconnect. It also includes a static file server, a classic CGI server, and a built-in developer console for inspecting frames.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that any program that can read stdin and write stdout can become a WebSocket server, with no networking library, framework, or change to the program. The README says 'WebSocket-capable applications can now be built very easily.'
brief.how_it_works: On startup websocketd listens on a port. When a client connects, it forks the configured program and pipes each client message to the program's stdin followed by a newline. Each newline-terminated line the program prints to stdout is sent to the client as a WebSocket message. When the socket closes, the process is shut down, and teardown signals the whole process group. The homepage describes the model as 'CGI's idea, applied to WebSockets.'

name: whosthere
desc: LAN discovery tool with a modern TUI written in Go
why: LAN discovery TUI that surfaces ARP and mDNS chatter, a readable door into local network protocols.

brief.what_it_is: Whosthere is a Local Area Network discovery tool written in Go, with an interactive terminal UI. It runs mDNS and SSDP scanners concurrently, sweeps the local subnet with TCP/UDP connection attempts so the OS fills the ARP cache, then reads that cache to list devices. Each device is enriched with a manufacturer name from OUI lookups. It can run as the TUI, as a one-shot CLI scan that prints results (optionally JSON), or as a background daemon with a small HTTP API. Devices can be given aliases, stored in a local bbolt database.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a friendly way to answer the question every network administrator asks: "Who's there on my network?" It says it was created primarily for educational purposes and home network exploration.
brief.how_it_works: The mDNS and SSDP scanners listen for multicast service announcements. For ARP, the sweeper opens TCP/UDP connections to each address in the subnet, which triggers ARP resolution by the OS without elevated privileges, and then reads the ARP cache to find live hosts. Optional port scanning checks a configurable list of TCP ports on found devices.

name: wiggle
desc: Program for applying patches with conflicting changes
why: Patch application that tolerates conflicting context is clever diff-matching work, though it is still a fairly niche utility.

brief.what_it_is: Wiggle is a command-line C program that applies patches whose context no longer matches the target file exactly, the cases where GNU patch would reject a hunk. It can also do word-wise diffs and three-way merges. Its inputs are one, two, or three files (use - for stdin), which can be patch files, merge output, or whole files. Output is the patched or merged text, with unresolvable conflicts marked, or a diff-style report. The help text describes four functions: merge (the default), diff, extract, and browse.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a tool to 'apply patches that patch rejects', and the repository's own description is 'apply rejected patches and perform word-wise diffs'. The problem is a patch whose surrounding lines have drifted, so a line-based tool gives up on the hunk.

name: wiiuse
desc: Connect Nintendo Wii Remotes
why: A library for talking to Wii Remote Bluetooth hardware, a fun door into poking at a physical device's protocol.

brief.what_it_is: Wiiuse is a C library that connects to Nintendo Wii Remotes over Bluetooth and exposes them to your own program. Per the README it supports motion sensing, IR tracking, the Nunchuk, the Classic Controller, the Balance Board, and the Guitar Hero 3 controller. It runs on Linux, Windows, and Mac and builds as a shared library (libwiiuse.so, or wiiuse.dll on Windows). Input is the controller's Bluetooth reports and output is state your application reads through the API, which is single-threaded and nonblocking.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is for developers who want to add Wii Remote support to a third-party application. It is a community-maintained fork: the original author's upstream stopped being maintained, and the maintainers say the fork was made to replace scattered ad-hoc forks with one project that has real infrastructure.
brief.how_it_works: Wiiuse talks to the controller through each OS's Bluetooth stack (BlueZ on Linux, the Microsoft stack on Windows, the Mac OS X Bluetooth stack on Mac). The README says it is single-threaded and nonblocking, and the application calls wiiuse_poll or wiiuse_update in a loop to pump events. Expansions such as the Nunchuk and Motion Plus are initialized and calibrated over time after connection, which is why the README asks you to keep polling for 10 to 15 seconds before enabling Motion Plus.

To use the library, include include/wiiuse.h, link libwiiuse.so (-lwiiuse) on Linux or wiiuse.lib on Windows, and ship wiiuse.dll with the program. On Mac, the controller must be in discoverable mode (press the button inside the battery cover), and it must be unpaired from the OS Bluetooth preferences first, since disconnecting is not enough.
brief.standout: It is a small, C, nonblocking library that predates most Wii hacking tooling and still covers the Balance Board and Guitar Hero 3 controller, which many newer tools skip. Its acknowledgements credit the wiibrew.org reverse-engineering community as the source of the protocol knowledge.

name: wimlib
desc: Library to create, extract, and modify Windows Imaging files
why: Opens Windows Imaging files up for inspection and modification, a decent look inside a closed file format.

brief.what_it_is: wimlib is an open source, cross-platform C library for creating, extracting, and modifying Windows Imaging (WIM) archives. Its command-line frontend, wimlib-imagex, is the tool most people will use, and the brew package installs it as many separate wim* executables such as wimapply, wimcapture, wimdir, wiminfo, and wimverify. WIM files go in and extracted files, directory listings, or new or modified WIM archives come out. It also handles ESD (.esd) archives, which are WIM archives that use solid LZMS compression.
brief.why_it_exists: WIM is a Windows archive format that is somewhat like ZIP but also stores Windows-specific metadata, holds multiple images in one file, and deduplicates content. wimlib is pitched as a free, cross-platform alternative to Microsoft's WIMGAPI, ImageX, and DISM, so non-Windows systems can read and write these files.
brief.how_it_works: Each distinct file content is identified by its SHA-1 digest and stored only once per archive, even when it is referenced by several images, duplicate files, hard links, or named data streams. wimlib performs this deduplication automatically when creating or updating an archive. It implements XPRESS, LZX, and LZMS compression, with LZX as the default, and can use solid mode. On Windows it uses native API calls to handle NTFS features; on UNIX it handles hard and symbolic links and can optionally store uids, gids, modes, and extended attributes.

brief.standout: The homepage stresses that wimlib writes NTFS-correct archives (ACLs, attributes, links, named streams) and can deploy Windows from Linux, including capturing NTFS block devices through NTFS-3G. It also says its LZX and LZMS compressors typically beat Microsoft's own implementations, and offers them as standalone libraries for other formats.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists wimlib-1.14.5 as the current release, dated January 29, 2026. Copyright runs through 2026 and the source is on git and GitHub with pull requests accepted.
brief.caveats: Mounting a WIM (wimmount, wimmountrw) is Linux-only and relies on FUSE. wimlib cannot decrypt Microsoft's partially encrypted ESD archives. The Windows ARM64 build is marked EXPERIMENTAL. Block-device capture and apply depend on NTFS-3G on UNIX. The homepage does not list a license beyond saying a COPYING file ships with the software.

Provides independent, high quality open source compressors and decompressors for several compression formats used by Microsoft which are not as well known as more open formats.

name: witr
desc: Why is this running?
why: Explains why a process is running by tracing its causes; a neat look at process ancestry, though a niche small tool.

brief.what_it_is: witr is a command-line tool (with an interactive terminal dashboard) that explains why a process, port, container, or file is running by tracing it back to the chain of things that started it. You give it a process name, PID, port, file path, or container name, and it prints a narrative of the ancestry chain (for example systemd → pm2 → node), the source that supervises it, the working directory, sockets, and warnings. Output can be human-readable text, a short or tree view, or JSON for scripts. It is distributed as a single static binary for Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, and Windows.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says existing tools like ps, top, lsof, ss, systemctl, and docker ps show what is running but leave the user to infer why by correlating output across tools. witr's stated aim is to make that causality explicit in one readable answer.
brief.how_it_works: witr maps a target (name, port, file, container, or PID) to a PID, then builds a causal ancestry chain for that PID and picks one primary source, such as a systemd unit, launchd job, container, pm2, cron, SSH session, or tmux session. Per the README it reads /proc on Linux, uses ps, lsof, sysctl and pgrep on macOS, uses procstat, ps and lsof on FreeBSD, and calls Win32 APIs directly on Windows. If the original parent has exited, the chain marks the break rather than guessing. Exit codes (0 clean, 1 warnings, 2 not found, 3 permission denied, 4 invalid input, 5 internal error, 6 cause unknown) let scripts act on the result.

The install script verifies a SHA256 checksum optionally. On Windows the PowerShell script adds the bin directory to the user PATH. name: wllvm
desc: Toolkit for building whole-program LLVM bitcode files
why: Builds whole-program LLVM bitcode from ordinary builds, a useful trick for analysing programs at the IR level.

brief.what_it_is: WLLVM is a set of Python compiler wrappers that stand in for gcc or g++ (as CC and CXX) in an ordinary C or C++ build. Each wrapper runs the real compiler as normal, then also produces LLVM bitcode for each object file. The companion tool extract-bc pulls the bitcode out of a finished executable, library, or archive. Input is an unmodified C or C++ source package; output is a single whole-program LLVM bitcode module (or a bitcode archive). The README says it runs on *nix systems such as Linux, FreeBSD, and Mac OS X.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the two-phase design is needed to be a drop-in replacement for gcc or g++ in any build system. It says gcc's LTO with the gold linker plugin works in many cases but fails when static libraries are involved, and that WLLVM's approach produces working binaries when a build step needs them.
brief.how_it_works: The wrappers first invoke the compiler as normal, then call a bitcode compiler to make LLVM bitcode for each object file. They also store the location of that bitcode file in a dedicated section of the object file, and those sections are concatenated when objects are linked. After the build, a WLLVM utility (extract-bc) reads that section and links all the bitcode into one whole-program bitcode file.

commands_seen.context: Installs WLLVM from PyPI; the README also shows sudo pip install wllvm for system-wide installs.

brief.install_notes: Install with pip install wllvm (or sudo pip install wllvm). For development, git clone the repo and run pip install -e . inside it, optionally in a virtualenv. Before use, set LLVM_COMPILER to clang or dragonegg. If using dragonegg, you must also set LLVM_GCC_PREFIX (may be empty) and LLVM_DRAGONEGG_PLUGIN (full path to the plugin); these are ignored for clang. Optional variables include LLVM_CC_NAME, LLVM_CXX_NAME, LLVM_LINK_NAME, LLVM_AR_NAME (for suffixed binaries like clang-3.7), LLVM_COMPILER_PATH, WLLVM_BC_STORE (directory to keep copies of the bitcode), and LLVM_BITCODE_GENERATION_FLAGS. The Homebrew formula lists seven executables (extract-bc, wfortran, wllvm, wllvm++, wllvm-as, wllvm-sanity-checker, wparse-args), but the README only documents four: wllvm, wllvm++, extract-bc, and wllvm-sanity-checker. The README does not describe wfortran, wllvm-as, or wparse-args.
brief.standout: Instead of trying to make the linker do the work, it hides bitcode paths inside object-file sections, so ordinary build systems can be used unchanged and the real binaries still get produced. Extraction later gives one whole-program bitcode module for analysis.

name: wmbusmeters
desc: Read wired or wireless mbus protocol to acquire utility meter readings
why: Decodes wireless M-Bus utility meter telegrams from cheap radio dongles, letting you read your neighbourhood's water and power meters.

brief.what_it_is: wmbusmeters is an open-source program that reads utility meter readings from wired M-Bus or wireless wM-Bus (OMS-compatible) meters. It takes in raw telegrams from radio dongles (im871a, iu891a, amb8465/Metis, amb3665, cul, rc1180, or rtl-sdr software-radio sticks), from serial M-Bus master converters, or from files, pipes, stdin, or MQTT topics. It decodes them with meter drivers into key-value pairs and outputs them as human-readable text, CSV fields, or JSON, which can be published via MQTT, posted to a REST API, inserted into a database, or written to log and meter files. The README's example turns the hex telegram 1844AE4C4455223368077A55000000_041389E20100023B0000 into a line showing a water meter's id, total m3, flow and timestamp.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the problem as getting utility meter readings out of wired or wireless M-Bus meters, and points out that a raw value like a 32-bit signed volume in storage slot 1 means nothing without knowing what it measures (last month's billing reading, last year's gas delivered, and so on). The drivers supply that meaning.
brief.how_it_works: Dongles or serial ports deliver telegrams to the program, which matches each one to a meter by id and selects a driver, either auto-detected or named in the config. Drivers translate manufacturer-specific bytes into named fields; since version 2.0 many drivers are written as declarative xmq/ixml text files rather than C++, and the README says new drivers should be written in that form. Users can also add calculated fields with formulas that track SI units, and run a shell command with METER_ environment variables for each reading.

Search the built-in list of meter drivers by keyword.
List the fields a given driver can output, for use with --selectfields.

brief.install_notes: Distribution packages: dnf install wmbusmeters on Fedora 31 or newer, and a Debian package that is in Experimental. Docker and Snap images are marked experimental. Building from source is recommended by the README because development is fast: remove any wM-Bus dongle or rtl-sdr stick from the computer first, then run ./configure; make; sudo make install. Config lives in /etc/wmbusmeters.conf and /etc/wmbusmeters.d (or a directory passed with --useconfig). Each meter gets a file with name, id, key and driver. For rtl-sdr, the rtl_sdr and rtl_wmbus binaries must exist in /usr/bin or next to the wmbusmeters binary. Serial M-Bus needs a bus alias such as MAIN=/dev/ttyUSB0:mbus:2400. The wiki at wmbusmeters.github.io covers the snap and more.
brief.standout: Drivers are being moved out of C++ into a declarative xmq/ixml format that can be edited as text, and the maintainer says new drivers should be written that way and will not be accepted as C++. The project also gives an explicit upgrade promise: if a meter is pinned to a named driver, the JSON keys will not change incompatibly on upgrade, and the README spells out that rule.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub releases page shows 3.0.0 as latest, dated 2026-06-17, with 2.0.0 on 2026-03-01 and 1.20.0 on 2026-01-27, so releases are frequent. The README's usage text prints version 3.1.0, which is ahead of the latest tagged release, so the README may be slightly ahead of the tags. The README also says development progresses quickly.
brief.caveats: Runs on GNU/Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and Raspberry Pi. make install is GNU/Linux only. Hardware is required: a supported wM-Bus dongle, an rtl-sdr stick, or a serial M-Bus converter. The cul dongle is limited to shorter telegrams unless a firmware fix is applied. The rc1180 listens only to T1. Encrypted meters need that meter's own key, so this reads meters you have keys for, not arbitrary neighbours' meters. Plain /dev/ttyUSB0 no longer works and the device has to be named with its type. Auto-probing of serial ports is slow, and the README advises a full device path in production. Using a driver of auto in production is discouraged. Driver licensing is GPLv3 or later per the --license option; the README does not state a licence on the page I read. The README was truncated at 40000 characters, so later sections were not read.

I am not accepting new drivers as C++ code.
So wmbusmeters strives to guarantee that if you have specified the driver name, then wmbusmeters can be safely upgraded at any time.

name: woxi
desc: Interpreter for a subset of the Wolfram Language
why: A from-scratch Wolfram Language subset interpreter is an unusual, under-the-radar way to play with symbolic computation in a terminal.

brief.what_it_is: Woxi is an interpreter for a subset of the Wolfram Language, written in Rust. You give it Wolfram Language source, either as a one-line expression through `woxi eval`, as a script file through `woxi run`, or interactively in a REPL or Jupyter notebook, and it evaluates the code and prints the result. The README says it is aimed at CLI scripting and notebooks. It also ships a Language Server Protocol server for editors and a Woxi Studio notebook editor, and it has a WebAssembly build with npm and Python bindings.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the initial focus is to implement a subset of the Wolfram Language so that it can be used for CLI scripting and notebooks. It also positions Woxi against WolframScript: it runs faster because it does not start a kernel or verify a license.
brief.how_it_works: Woxi is a from-scratch interpreter rather than a wrapper around a Wolfram kernel. The README says the CLI tests in tests/cli define the supported commands and expected output, and that all of them must pass with both Woxi and WolframScript. The functions.csv file tracks the implementation status of each Wolfram Language function. The language server takes its hover docs and completions from the same symbol registry the interpreter uses, and it warns on symbols the interpreter does not implement.

brief.what_it_is: WuppieFuzz is a coverage-guided fuzzer for REST APIs, built on LibAFL and developed by TNO. You give it an OpenAPI specification (YAML) and a running target service, and it generates and mutates HTTP requests against that API, using coverage feedback to steer the search. Output goes to a timestamped subdirectory under reports/ when you pass --report: endpoint coverage (from the spec alone) and, for JaCoCo targets, code coverage. A database of request data is also written, which can be explored in a Grafana dashboard.
brief.why_it_exists: TNO says it targets a wide audience of end-users, with a strong focus on ease-of-use, explainability of the discovered flaws and modularity. The README says it supports black box, grey box and white box testing.
brief.how_it_works: The OpenAPI spec tells WuppieFuzz how to build and mutate requests, and the target must already be running (instrumented, if you want code coverage). Coverage from the target, such as a JaCoCo agent or LCOV for Python, feeds back into the fuzzing loop. Endpoint coverage needs only the spec; code coverage needs a mapping from coverage data to source files.

name: x3270

brief.what_it_is: x3270 is an IBM 3270 terminal emulator for the X Window System and Windows. It runs over a TELNET connection and emulates either an IBM 3279 (color) or 3278 (monochrome) terminal, so it lets a desktop act as a mainframe terminal. It runs on most Unix-like systems, including Linux, macOS, Solaris and Cygwin, and natively on Windows. It is distributed as source code and is free to use. The homepage describes several front ends: x3270 (X display), wx3270 (Windows GUI), c3270 (curses, for dumb terminals and consoles), wc3270 (Windows console), s3270 (displayless, for screen-scraping scripts), tcl3270 (s3270 integrated with Tcl), and pr3287 (printer emulation). It also mentions x026, an IBM 026 keypunch emulator.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit problem statement. It presents x3270 as a way to reach IBM 3270 mainframe applications over TN3270/TELNET from Unix, X and Windows machines.
brief.how_it_works: It connects over TELNET and speaks the 3270 data stream, including the full TN3270E protocol, with optional SSL/TLS via OpenSSL. Beyond interactive use it offers printer session integration, IND$FILE file transfer, a pop-up keypad for 3270-specific keys, and scripting and debugging facilities. The s3270 variant has no display and is meant for scripts that read screens. The homepage says it does not yet support graphics.

The homepage says it is distributed as source code, so a source build is implied for Unix-like systems. Windows has a native build (wx3270, wc3270). Nothing on the homepage mentions accounts, runtimes or first-run configuration. The brew executables list suggests the package installs b3270, c3270, pr3287, prtodir, s3270, x3270, x3270a and x3270if, but the homepage does not document them.
brief.standout: It is one of the few open-source emulators that covers the full 3270 family, including TN3270E, IND$FILE transfer, APL2 and DBCS (Chinese and Japanese) character sets, and a scripting-oriented headless variant (s3270) alongside the GUI and curses front ends. Its scripting and screen-scraping angle is the part that differs most from simple terminal emulators.

name: xdelta
desc: Binary diff, differential compression tools
why: A binary diff and delta compression tool that reveals how files can be encoded as differences.

brief.what_it_is: Xdelta 3 is a C library and command-line tool for delta compression using the VCDIFF (RFC 3284) format. Given an old file and a new file, the encoder writes a small delta file that describes how to turn the old file into the new one. Given the old file and that delta, the decoder rebuilds the new file. The CLI resembles gzip, takes its input from files or stdin, and writes the delta or reconstructed file to a named output or stdout. The Homebrew executable is xdelta3.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a library and tool for delta compression using the VCDIFF/RFC 3284 standard, rather than giving a broader motivation. The scout note describes it as a tool that reveals how files can be encoded as differences.
brief.how_it_works: The encoder matches strings between the source and the target and emits VCDIFF instructions that copy from the source or insert literal bytes. An optional secondary compressor (LZMA, DJW, or FGK where compiled in) can then compress that output. Armor mode, on by default when compiled in, embeds BLAKE3 digests of the logical source and target and verifies them on decode. The inspection commands (printhdr, printhdrs, printdelta) dump the delta's headers, windows, and instructions as readable text.

Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows (x86, x86-64, ARM64) are attached to GitHub Releases. Xdelta 3 release binaries statically link liblzma and BLAKE3, so no separate runtime is needed. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned. Running xdelta3 config shows which features and compressors a given build has. The Homebrew caveats field was empty.
brief.standout: It is a standards-based format (VCDIFF/RFC 3284), not a private one, so deltas are meant to be decodable by other VCDIFF implementations. Armor mode adds whole-file BLAKE3 verification, and the merge command collapses an ordered chain of deltas (1→2, 2→3, 3→4) into a single 1→4 delta, checking digests along the way.

name: xbyak
desc: C++ JIT assembler for x86 (IA32), x64 (AMD64, x86-64)
why: A C++ JIT assembler for x86 hints at generating machine code at runtime, though it is mainly a library.

brief.what_it_is: Xbyak is a C++ header-only library for generating x86 and x64 machine code at runtime. You write C++ calls that look like assembly mnemonics, such as mov(eax, x) or ret(), and it emits the encoded instructions into a memory buffer. You then call getCode() to get a function pointer and invoke the generated code. The input is C++ calls naming instructions and operands, and the output is executable machine code in memory. The README calls it a JIT assembler, and it is a library rather than a standalone tool.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes it as a JIT assembler for x86/x64 that supports the latest instruction set extensions, such as AVX10.2 and ACE, using mnemonics. The name comes from the Japanese word kaibyaku, meaning 'the beginning of the world' or 'creation'.
brief.how_it_works: You subclass Xbyak::CodeGenerator (or pass an instance to a function) and call instruction methods in C++ that mirror MASM/NASM syntax, with parentheses for operands. Labels, jumps, and memory addressing are supported through Label objects and ptr[...] expressions. Calling getCode<T>() returns a callable pointer to the generated code. Memory is set to Read/Write/Exec by default, and you can opt into Read/Exec with DontSetProtectRWE and setProtectModeRE().

commands_seen.context: Usage example: a CodeGenerator subclass emits mov eax, x followed by ret() to return a value.
Obtains a callable function pointer from the generated code, then the example invokes f().

brief.install_notes: Copy xbyak.h, xbyak_mnemonic.h and xbyak_util.h into your compile include path. On Linux, make install copies them into /usr/local/include/xbyak. Alternatively, install through vcpkg by cloning Microsoft/vcpkg, running ./bootstrap-vcpkg.sh, ./vcpkg integrate install, then ./vcpkg install xbyak. No accounts, hardware, or runtimes are needed beyond a C++ compiler. The README mentions -fno-operator-names for gcc/clang if you want to use and() or or() as names. Brew installs the headers only, and the brew entry lists no executables.
brief.standout: It is a header-only JIT assembler that writes instructions as ordinary C++ method calls with MASM-like syntax, and it covers very recent extensions such as APX, AVX10.2, AMX, and ACE. It also has an optional StackFrame helper for automatic register save and restore, and forks exist for AArch64 and RISC-V.
brief.status: Maintained, by inference. The README's header shows version 7.43 and the News list covers recent additions such as ACE 1.15, AVX10.2, and APX support. I could not see a release date or last-commit date in the fetched pages, so I cannot confirm the recency of the last commit.
brief.caveats: Supported OS is Windows, Linux, and macOS on Intel CPUs only. The README notes that and(), or(), and similar names clash with C++ operators unless you use and_() or -fno-operator-names. Some APX and AVX10.2 features need the defaults set carefully, since encodings are selected by setDefaultEncoding functions. Omitted-destination forms such as vaddps(xmm2, xmm3) are deprecated and only work with XBYAK_ENABLE_OMITTED_OPERAND. The disp32 address check changed, and XBYAK_OLD_DISP_CHECK is slated for removal. Generated code runs from memory that is writable and executable by default unless you opt out. The README mentions a few APX instructions are not yet supported. Licence is BSD-3-Clause.

name: xidel
desc: XPath/XQuery 3.0, JSONiq interpreter to extract data from HTML/XML/JSON
why: Full XPath, XQuery and JSONiq interpreter in one binary, an unusual and underknown way to query documents.

brief.what_it_is: Xidel is a command-line tool that downloads and extracts data from HTML, XML, and JSON. It takes a URL, file, or stdin as input and runs XPath 3.0, XQuery 3.0, CSS 3 selectors, pattern matching, or JSONiq queries against it. Results print in a human-readable form or as XML, HTML, JSON, or shell variables. The homepage says it is a single binary with no external dependencies beyond standard system libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes the point of the tool as making it easy for anyone to parse any webpage, and says he would rather people learn to query with Xidel than ask him how to scrape a particular site. It began as the backend of the VideLibri library service and was released as a standalone command-line tool in 2012.
brief.how_it_works: Xidel fetches the page over HTTP or HTTPS, following redirects while keeping cookies, and then evaluates the query expression against the parsed document. Query languages include CSS selectors, XPath and XQuery, pattern matching against an annotated sample of the page, and JSONiq. Output can be piped onward or, with --output-format bash, eval'd into shell variables.

brief.install_notes: Download a release from SourceForge: zip for Windows, tar.gz for Linux and Android, deb for Debian, or source tarball. Usually you extract it and put the binary on your PATH. HTTPS on Linux needs OpenSSL and libcrypto, including openssl-dev. Unicode collations need libicu. To build from source with FreePascal, run ./build.sh in a Unix shell or call fpc xidel.pas with -Fu and -Fi paths. Lazarus users install components/pascal/internettools.lpk and then open programs/internet/xidel/xidel.lpi. Mac binaries are not current: the page lists only an externally built 0.9.6 for Mac 10.8. The homepage does not mention Homebrew.
brief.standout: It is a single binary that bundles a full XPath/XQuery 3.0 interpreter, CSS selectors, pattern matching, and JSONiq, so one command line can fetch, follow links, fill and submit forms, and run Turing-complete scripts. The pattern-matching syntax, which uses an annotated sample of the page as the query, is a less common approach.

name: xlispstat
desc: Statistical data science environment based on Lisp
why: A Lisp-based statistics environment from the 1990s, an old-school environment with real oddity value.

brief.what_it_is: Lisp-Stat is an extensible statistical computing environment for data analysis, teaching, and research, built on a subset of Common Lisp. It extends standard Lisp arithmetic to work element-wise on lists and vectors, and adds basic statistical and linear algebra functions. Its main emphasis is dynamic graphics, delivered through a portable window system meant to behave the same across Mac OS, X Window System, and Microsoft Windows. The homepage does not spell out input or output formats beyond data analysis and graphics.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a statistical computing environment for data analysis, statistical instruction and research, with an emphasis on providing a framework for exploring dynamic graphical methods. Extensibility is achieved by building on Lisp, and many design choices were motivated by the S language.
brief.how_it_works: A prototype-based object-oriented programming system implements the graphics system and lets users customize and adapt it. The same object system is the basis for statistical model representations, including linear and nonlinear regression and generalized linear models. Element-wise arithmetic on lists and vectors is added on top of standard Common Lisp.

name: xmount
desc: Convert between multiple input & output disk image types
why: Converts between forensic disk image formats, a window into how disk images and their containers are structured.

brief.what_it_is: Xmount is a command-line tool that converts disk images between formats on the fly. It takes forensic and virtual disk images as input (Raw/DD, Expert Witness EWF, AFFv3, VirtualBox VDI, QEMU QCOW2) and presents the converted image as a virtual file system built with FUSE. Output formats are Raw/DD, Apple DMG, Microsoft VHD, VirtualBox VDI, and VMware VMDK. It can also apply morphing functions that combine several input images into one output or reconstruct RAID0 sets, and it can extract unallocated sectors from FAT or HFS filesystems.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a way to convert between harddisk image types without making a full converted copy, and to let acquired images be used directly. Its stated example is booting acquired harddisk images in QEMU, KVM, VirtualBox, VMware or similar.
brief.how_it_works: Xmount mounts a FUSE virtual file system that exposes the converted input image as a file in the requested output format. Write access is supported by redirecting changes to a cache file, so the original acquired image is not modified. The morphing functions (Combine, Raid, Unallocated) sit on top of the same input handling.
brief.install_notes: The homepage lists Debian and Ubuntu packages through a package repository, plus source downloads of the latest releases and a Git repository. It does not give build steps, dependency lists, or a first-run walkthrough, and no command lines appear on the page. Because it relies on FUSE, a working FUSE setup is needed to mount the virtual file system.
brief.standout: Few small tools combine forensic container reading (EWF, AFFv3) with writable, copy-on-write style access to the result and with morphing operations such as RAID reconstruction and combining several images into one. The cache-file approach lets an evidence image be booted in a hypervisor without changing the original.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows no version number, release date, or changelog, and the fetched page did not link to a dated release or commit history. The Git repository and release pages it links to were not followed.
brief.caveats: The page gives no list of supported platforms; the FUSE dependency suggests Unix-like systems. RAID support is limited to RAID0. Unallocated extraction supports only FAT and HFS. Output formats do not include EWF or AFF, so forensic containers are input-only. Licensed under GPL v3 or later. The Homebrew description is short and the page does not mention macOS specifically.

You can for example combine multiple input images into one output image, or reconstruct raids on-the-fly.
This makes it for example possible to boot acquired harddisk images using QEMU, KVM, VirtualBox, VmWare or alike.

name: xmp
desc: Command-line player for module music formats (MOD, S3M, IT, etc)
why: Plays tracker module formats like MOD and S3M, a window into the old demoscene music world that most developers never touch.

brief.what_it_is: xmp, the Extended Module Player, is a portable command-line player for tracker music files. You give it a module file such as an Impulse Tracker .it or a Protracker .mod and it renders the song to audio. The homepage says it plays many mainstream and obscure formats, including Protracker MOD, Scream Tracker 3 S3M, Fast Tracker II XM and Impulse Tracker IT. Its terminal screen shows the module name, type, pattern and channel counts, duration, and a live position readout, and single keypresses move between patterns and songs, mute channels, and show instrument and sample lists. The player is a front end to libxmp, a separate library that renders module audio as linear PCM.
brief.why_it_exists: The project is framed as preservation and playback of tracker music: the homepage calls the Amiga and PC trackers of the demoscene and related formats 'classic, rare or otherwise interesting' and lists archives such as Modland and Aminet. The author also wants libxmp to be reusable by other programs, for example players, information extractors, module-to-mp3 renderers and game music.
brief.how_it_works: Since release 4.0 the project is split into libxmp, a library that loads a module and renders it to PCM at a rate and format the caller chooses, and xmp, the player application built on it. The homepage says xmp can read compressed modules using built-in depackers for formats such as zip, gzip, xz and LHA, or external helpers (unmo3 for MO3, unrar for RAR). In archives only the first module is played. The README says xmp -L lists supported formats.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: the homepage describes xmp as the player that sits on top of libxmp, so the player release needs libxmp 4.4.0 or newer and recommends 4.7.0 or newer. The brew formula is named xmp and installs an xmp executable. Playback uses the audio system the homepage example shows (ALSA on Linux). Interactive mode can be turned off with --nocmd. No accounts, API keys or special hardware are mentioned. I did not check the Homebrew formula itself, so I cannot confirm its exact dependencies.
brief.standout: It handles a very wide range of formats, including obscure Amiga, Atari, Acorn and game-specific ones, with a long supported-formats list and dozens of packer and depacker variants. Its interactive controls (pattern skip, song skip, per-channel mute, instrument and sample dumps) work like a tracker's own view of a song, which is unusual for a command-line tool.

name: xnvme
desc: Cross-platform libraries and tools for efficient I/O and low-level control
why: Low-level NVMe I/O library that talks directly to storage hardware; a close call for a catalogue of hardware doors.

brief.what_it_is: xNVMe is a set of C libraries and command-line tools for programming NVMe storage devices from user space, on Linux, FreeBSD, macOS and Windows. Its core, libxnvme, exposes one C API for memory allocation, synchronous and asynchronous NVMe command submission, and device geometry and parameter queries. The API sits on top of a swappable backend: Linux io_uring, io_uring_cmd, libaio or block-layer IOCTLs; the native NVMe driver on FreeBSD, macOS and Windows; SPDK; or the uPCIe user-space driver. The command-line tools (xnvme, lblk, zoned, kvs, xdd) and the libraries for NVM, Zoned and KV command sets are built on top of it, and there is a Fio IO engine for benchmarking. Input is an NVMe device or namespace; output is I/O results and device management actions.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the problem as a combinatorial one: without a unified API, supporting n platforms and m I/O interfaces costs n*m implementations, and xNVMe aims to reduce that to 1. Its stated goal is to let tool builders, application developers and anyone wanting host software to run on more than one platform talk to NVMe devices through a single C API.
brief.how_it_works: The backend is chosen at runtime, so the same application code runs unmodified across backends. The library provides a memory API for DMA-transferable buffers and a command interface for sync and async submission and completion, plus helpers such as maximum transfer size and a device geometry concept. The README also describes homi, a daemon that lets several host processes and accelerator compute kernels run I/O directly against one NVMe controller, which it likens to SR-IOV, and qublk, a ublk server that lets kernel I/O and file systems work alongside the user-space drivers.
brief.install_notes: The homepage (the Sphinx docs site) lists sections for building and installing, toolchains per OS (Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Windows), and troubleshooting, but I did not open those pages, so build steps and the first-run flow are unverified. From the release page: source tarballs are published as xnvme-0.7.5.tar.gz (without subprojects) and xnvme-fat-0.7.5.tar.gz (including SPDK sources). Language bindings are available as a Python package on PyPI (ctypes based), a Rust crate (xnvme-sys) on crates.io, and libxnvme on conda-forge. Changelog entries show that the build uses Meson, that SPDK became optional in the build, and that liburing is taken from the system via pkg-config rather than bundled, so the build depends on what is installed on the host. Using the tools against real hardware requires access to NVMe devices; the README does not describe privileges or permissions, and the Linux backends and the uPCIe backend need device access (uPCIe is noted as Linux only).
brief.standout: One C API hides several very different I/O paths (io_uring, libaio, SPDK, a user-space PCIe driver with peer-to-peer data movement to CUDA and HIP accelerators) and chooses between them at runtime. The homi daemon, which the README compares to SR-IOV for sharing one NVMe controller among host processes and accelerator kernels, is also an unusual idea for a user-space library.
brief.status: Active. The README says the project is 'in active development' and names Simon A. F. Lund as maintainer. The latest release, v0.7.5, has assets timestamped 2024-09-17 on the releases page. The v0.7.4 release is dated 4 Feb and v0.7.3 is dated 21 Nov, with the year not shown on the page. The release notes list a steady stream of merged pull requests. I did not see a last-commit date, so I cannot give one.
brief.caveats: The README does not state supported hardware or kernel versions. The changelog for v0.7.5 includes 'drop support for WPDK (SPDK on Windows)', so SPDK on Windows is no longer supported; the Windows backend uses the native driver instead. The uPCIe backend is Linux-only and is described as compatible with CUDA and HIP (ROCm). The tool descriptions are brief, and the README points to the website for the rest. The homepage I fetched was the docs site landing page and showed only the table of contents for the tools, so I have no command examples from it. The brew description says 'Low-level NVMe I/O library', and the scout note calls it a close call for a catalogue of hardware doors. The project is BSD-3-Clause licensed according to the SPDX header in the README.
quotes: Reduce your code-complexity from n * m (where n is the number of platforms and m are the number of I/O interfaces on the platform.) to 1.
xNVMe provides APIs, libraries, and tools for user space programming of NVMe devices on Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, and Windows, through a single C API backed by the `libxnvme` library.

`homi`, the software equivalent of SR-IOV: a daemon enabling multiple users, different processes on the host as well as compute kernels on accelerators, to run I/O directly against a single NVMe controller

name: xorriso
desc: ISO9660+RR manipulation tool
why: Manipulating ISO9660 images in place, including bootable hybrid structure, is a satisfying look inside a file format most people never open.

brief.what_it_is: xorriso is a command-line tool for reading, creating and changing ISO 9660 disc images with Rock Ridge extensions. It can copy files from a normal POSIX filesystem into an image, edit an existing image session by session (add, rename, delete, change permissions), and copy files back out of an image. It writes the result either to optical media (CD, DVD, BD) or to ordinary files and block devices. It is also the engine behind the mkisofs- and cdrecord-style emulation commands (xorrisofs, xorrecord) and has a Tcl/Tk GUI frontend, xorriso-tcltk.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes xorriso as an ISO 9660 + Rock Ridge manipulator that keeps the management information of an existing image and writes changes as new sessions, so an image can be updated incrementally rather than rebuilt. It is a GNU project, and it is part of the libburnia family of libraries (libburn, libisofs, libisoburn).
brief.how_it_works: xorriso loads the directory tree of an existing ISO image (or starts an empty one), applies a list of text commands to that in-memory model, and then writes the result as a new image or as an add-on session. It is driven entirely by text commands given as arguments, in batch files, or on standard input in dialog mode, and it can be given a frontend process that reads its state and sends commands. Multi-session behaviour on overwritable media is emulated. Bootable structures (El Torito, MBR, EFI System Partition) are added with -boot_image.

Optional libraries add features: libreadline (nicer dialog), libacl (ACLs), zlib (zisofs, gzip, Jigdo), libbz2, and Tcl/Tk >= 8.4 with BWidget for xorriso-tcltk. Optional libjte (jigit-1.22) must be installed before libisofs and libisoburn are built if you want Jigdo. A 1.5.9 development tarball and git builds from libburnia are also listed. Hardware: any CD/DVD/BD recorder made in roughly the last twenty years. Linux 2.4 needs ide-scsi for PATA drives, but 2.6+ does not. Ordinary users need read-write permission on the /dev/srN node (on Solaris, read permission plus the basic,sys_devices privileges). Running as superuser avoids most of these problems.
brief.standout: It treats an optical disc as a sequence of sessions and edits an existing image in place, including its bootable structure, instead of rebuilding it from scratch. The same engine is exposed as a text command language, a mkisofs/cdrecord emulator, and a GUI frontend, which is an unusual combination for a disc tool.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage shows the 1.5.8.pl02 stable tarball released 22 May 2026, a 1.5.9 development snapshot with change notes, and a copyright range running to 2026. The site lists a support mailing list and a maintainer who responds to bug reports. No commit history was checked.
brief.caveats: The page says it has been tested only on GNU/Linux, FreeBSD, Solaris and NetBSD; other systems need the maintainer's help. Without direct drive access, optical media writing is less reliable on CD-R, DVD-R, DVD+R and BD-R (DVD-RAM, DVD+RW and BD-RE are said to work better). xorriso does not write audio CDs and does not produce UDF filesystems for official video DVD or BD. Building from git needs autotools >= 1.7 and a chain of libburnia libraries that are development versions and not safe to ship dynamically linked. Writing to /dev/ paths requires the stdio: prefix, and a wrong target can overwrite a hard disk. The licence is GPL version 3 or later. Brew caveats were empty.

name: xroar
desc: Dragon and Tandy 8-bit computer emulator
why: A Dragon and Tandy 8-bit emulator lets you run and poke at vintage machine code and hardware behaviour.

brief.what_it_is: XRoar is a free emulator of Dragon and Tandy 8-bit home computers. The homepage says it emulates the Dragon 32/64, Tandy Colour Computers 1, 2 and 3, the Tandy MC-10, and some similar machines or clones. It runs on several platforms, with source code, Mac OS X, Windows, and Debian/Ubuntu packages offered. Its inputs are firmware ROM images and emulated disk or tape media, and its output is the emulated machine's display and sound. The homepage does not spell out the input and output formats in detail.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage does not give a stated motivation. It presents XRoar as a maintained emulator for the Dragon and Tandy Colour Computer families, and it also links to a 6809 assembler, asm6809, for writing machine code for the Dragon.

commands_seen.context: Clones the XRoar git repository from the author's site, given in the Git repository download section.

brief.install_notes: Firmware ROM images are required to run the emulator usefully. The homepage says these can be extracted from a real Dragon, CoCo or MC-10, or obtained from the Dragon Archive or the Color Computer Archive. Other routes are a source tarball (xroar-1.12.1.tar.gz), prebuilt Windows ZIP or MSI installers in 32-bit and 64-bit, a 64-bit x86 Mac OS X binary, Debian snapshot builds in an Apt repository, and an Ubuntu PPA on Launchpad. Building from source has its own page in the manual, and there is a note on running under Wayland.
brief.standout: The homepage offers XRoar Online, a version that runs in a browser, so you can try a Dragon without installing anything. The version 1.12 notes also add GDB remote-debugging support for the emulated CPU, including MC-10 support, which suits people who want to inspect 6809 code and hardware state.
