name: xplanet
desc: Create HQ wallpapers of planet Earth
why: Renders planets as wallpapers from real astronomical data, a pleasant old-school trick, though the output is mostly pretty.

brief.what_it_is: Xplanet is a free, GPL-licensed program that renders an image of a planet, moon, or the Sun and either draws it to an X window, saves it to a file (gif, jpg, png, ppm, tiff), or sets it as the desktop wallpaper. Its inputs are command-line options and an optional configuration file, along with map and star images and, for precise positions, JPL ephemeris or SPICE kernel files. The output is a rendered picture of the chosen body as seen from a chosen observer position, date, and projection. Earth is the default body.
brief.why_it_exists: Xplanet was inspired by Xearth, which renders an image of the earth into the X root window. The author's homepage says all of the major planets and most satellites can be drawn, similar to the Solar System Simulator.
brief.how_it_works: The program places an observer at a chosen location and time relative to a target body, then computes the view and shading. Position data comes from a built-in model or from JPL ephemeris or SPICE files, and the view can be a globe or one of many map projections (azimuthal, Lambert, Mercator, Mollweide, orthographic, rectangular and others). Background stars come from a star map file, and output can be rerun on a timer with -wait or -num_times.

commands_seen.context: Centers the field of view on NAIF ID -82, which the README says is the Cassini orbiter. Requires SPICE support compiled in and the kernels present.
Centers the field of view on NORAD ID 20580, which the README says is the Hubble Space Telescope. Requires the appropriate TLE files.
Places the observer at the center of the Sun while targeting Earth. The README notes that -origin -sun instead places the observer on the far side of Earth from the Sun.
Places the observer where the Moon appears 3 degrees to the left of Earth.
Uses the given date (assumed GMT) instead of the current time.
Writes to a file instead of a window. The format comes from the extension and the default size is 512 by 512 pixels.
Sets the image geometry in X syntax, for example 256x256-10+10. The README uses this with -window or -output.
Runs a command before each render. The README example is xplanet.exe -prev_command ./prev.bat on Windows.
Selects a map projection such as mollweide or mercator. The README says multiple bodies are not shown when this option is used.
Rotates the globe counterclockwise. The README says -rotate 180 suits Southern Hemisphere viewers.

brief.install_notes: The homepage's own description implies a compile step: it lists several optional features that depend on build-time libraries or kernels, including the X Screensaver extension (for -idlewait and -hibernate), Pango (for -pango), SPICE (for -body naif-N), and image format libraries. Satellite and SPICE use needs extra data files: JPL ephemeris files (DE200, DE405 or DE406) for -ephemeris_file, SPICE kernels with a README in the spice subdirectory, and TLE files for norad IDs. Input files are found by searching the current directory, then -searchdir, then ~/.xplanet on X11, ~/Library/Xplanet on macOS, and DATADIR/xplanet, where DATADIR defaults to /usr/local/share. The homepage links to Maps & Scripts and Cloud Maps pages, which I did not fetch, so I can't say what map images are needed. I did not check the Homebrew formula.
brief.standout: It descends from Xearth but reaches further: many bodies, a wide range of projections, real ephemeris and spacecraft-tracking input, and cloud-overlay map generation. Its option set is large enough to work as a small astronomy visualizer rather than only a desktop picture.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage and option reference describe old platforms (FreeBSD 5.1, Sparc Solaris, Cygwin, Mac OS X Aqua) and have no release date or changelog visible in what I fetched. The sourceforge hosting and the Homebrew formula suggest it still packages, but I found no last-release or last-commit date.
brief.caveats: The homepage's tested platforms are old (i386 GNU/Linux, Sparc Solaris, FreeBSD 5.1, Cygwin, Darwin, Mac OS X Aqua). The README warns that -pango appears to leak memory, so it should not run indefinitely. -fork on Windows can leave multiple processes running unnoticed. Only TrueType fonts are supported. Satellite and SPICE features need extra data files and a build with those options. License is GPL, per the homepage.

My friends in the Southern Hemisphere can use -rotate 180 to make the earth look like it should!

name: xwpe
desc: Borland-style IDE clone with LSP/DAP support (terminal UI)
why: A Borland-style IDE in the terminal is a nostalgic old-school environment with a fun retro twist.

brief.what_it_is: xwpe is a terminal and X11 programming editor and IDE modelled on the Borland C and Pascal environments. It has syntax highlighting, project management, function-key driven menus, mouse support, and Emacs cursor keys (Ctrl-P/N/F/B/A/E). It runs compilers and debuggers for 12 languages from inside the editor (F9 builds with error navigation, Ctrl-G R starts a debugger). Through an Alt-Q prefix it also acts as an LSP client (hover, go-to-definition, references, rename, diagnostics) for C/C++, Python, Go, Rust and Scala, and as a DAP client for source-level debugging of Go and Rust. The binaries are wpe (ncurses terminal mode) and xwpe (graphical mode, native Wayland or X11).
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a revival: the original Borland-style editor by Fred Kruse (1993), continued by Dennis Payne (1997-2006), was untested for nearly 20 years and was taken up again in 2026 by Juan Manuel Mendez Rey. Its stated aim is a discoverable Borland-style UX with no per-project config and no heavy GUI runtime, that works over SSH or on a plain console, while adding modern language servers and debuggers.
brief.how_it_works: It is a C program that draws its own text interface: ncurses in the terminal, and Cairo/Pango/Xft rendering in X11 or on Wayland, with a double-buffered screen model. Language servers and debug adapters are spoken to over the same protocols VS Code and Neovim use (LSP and DAP), so existing servers such as clangd, Metals and Delve plug in. The README says the LSP client attaches to one open file at a time.

name: yaf
desc: Yet another flowmeter: processes packet data from pcap(3)
why: A flowmeter that turns raw packet captures into IPFIX flow records, a good door into how network traffic is summarised.

brief.what_it_is: YAF (Yet Another Flowmeter) is a sensor that reads network traffic, either live from an interface or from PCAP files, and turns the packet stream into flow records describing each connection it observed. It examines payloads for supported application protocols and exports protocol-specific fields alongside the flow, which the site calls deep packet inspection. Output is IPFIX, a binary format that is much smaller than the original packets. The brew executables include yaf, yafMeta2Pcap, yafscii, yafcollect, airdaemon, filedaemon and getFlowKeyHash.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says YAF is the data collection component of the CERT NetSA Security Suite, whose purpose is to turn packets into network flows for downstream tools such as Analysis Pipeline, SiLK and Mothra. It began as an experimental implementation tracking IETF IPFIX work on bidirectional flows, archival formats and structured DPI export.
brief.how_it_works: YAF groups observed packets into bidirectional flows and writes IPFIX records using templates suited to the data, discarding most packet payload. Application-level fields (DNS, SSL, HTTP(S), SMTP and so on) are added only when a protocol is recognised through regular-expression or plug-in labelling, which must be enabled. For PCAP input it can split captures with --pcap and --max-pcap and write a metadata file of flow key hash, millisecond start time and capture file name, so flows can be located across captures.
brief.install_notes: The homepage does not give install steps. It links to an 'Installation Instructions & Dependencies' page, which I did not fetch, so hardware, runtime and dependency details are unknown. The homepage also describes running on commodity or low-end single-board hardware, with specialty hardware recommended at scale.
brief.standout: The packet-per-flow mode turns each packet into a one-packet flow, keeping per-packet volume and timing without the full capture, which the homepage proposes for covert timing channel and session hijack analysis. The flow key hash metadata index, which lets analysts find the same flow across multiple capture points and then pull matching packets back out of the original PCAPs, is also unusual.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage lists 3.0.0.alpha4 as the current download and 3.x as pre-release, with 2.x as the stable line. Copyright runs to 2026. I saw no release date or last-commit date on the page.
brief.caveats: The current 3.x line is labelled pre-release (3.0.0.alpha4), and the stable line is 2.x. DPI fields appear only when application labelling is enabled and the protocol is recognised. The installation page, license and FAQ were not read, so the license and platform support are unknown. The homepage was reachable, but the brief is based on it alone.

YAF is the data collection component of the CERT NetSA Security Suite.
Flow records use a binary format, so they are much smaller than full packet captures or textual representations of the data.

name: yacas
desc: General purpose computer algebra system
why: A general purpose computer algebra system with its own scripting language, an old-school environment worth exploring.

brief.what_it_is: Yacas (Yet Another Computer Algebra System) is a general-purpose computer algebra system for symbolic manipulation of mathematical expressions. You type infix-notation expressions and it manipulates them symbolically, with arbitrary-precision arithmetic in the core engine. The distribution ships a small library of mathematical functions, but the README says its main strength is the scripting language, where you write your own symbolic manipulation rules and algorithms. It is aimed at mathematicians, engineers, and students, and is usable from a command-line interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a free, open-source alternative to commercial CAS software, suitable for research, education, and recreational mathematics. The project's own framing is that it was built for a broad audience, not only specialists.
brief.how_it_works: A parser built on an infix-operator grammar reads expressions. The core engine applies user-defined rules to mathematical objects to carry out symbolic transformations, and it supports arbitrary-precision arithmetic. The README does not go deeper into the internals; the docs index lists a Reference Manual, a Programming in Yacas guide, and a Book of Algorithms, which I did not open.
brief.install_notes: The homepage and README point to a Downloads page (http://www.yacas.org/getting_started/downloads/) for binary packages and installation instructions across platforms. I did not fetch that page, so I have no verified per-platform steps. Nothing in the README mentions accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration. The brew formula exposes a single executable named yacas.
brief.standout: The scripting language is the point, not the built-in function library: the README says the real strength is in writing your own symbolic manipulation algorithms. It is an older, self-contained, LGPL-licensed CAS with its own language, rather than a wrapper around another system, and it has a browser demo on the homepage (Yacas Online) and a Visual Studio Code syntax highlighting post on the blog.
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage lists release 1.9.1 (also 1.8.0 and 1.7.0) under recent articles, but I saw no release dates. The docs page I fetched was only a table of contents. The brew description and scout note are consistent with an active, released project, but I could not confirm recency.

The README's own intro is somewhat promotional in its "who is yacas for" section (it claims under 1% of the population are math enthusiasts), which is a tone note rather than a limitation. I did not verify platform support beyond the README's statement that it is available for a variety of platforms. The homepage 'More' links for blog articles and release notes were not followed, so release dates and changelog details are missing from these notes.

name: yara-x
desc: Tool to do pattern matching for malware research
why: VirusTotal's Rust rewrite of YARA pattern matching, a real window into how malware signatures scan binaries.

brief.what_it_is: YARA-X is a pattern-matching tool for malware researchers, a Rust rewrite of VirusTotal's YARA. You write rules that describe a malware family or anything else, built from textual or binary patterns plus a boolean condition over them. A rule is run against files, and the output is which rules matched. The README's example rule matches any file containing one of three byte or text patterns and reports it as silent_banker. The homepage says the library has C/C++, Python and Go APIs. The brew executable is named yr, but I did not find that name or any usage in the pages I read.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the goal is to replace YARA as the default pattern matching tool for malware researchers, with a new incarnation that is faster, safer and more user-friendly than its predecessor. It also says YARA itself is still maintained, but new large features and modules will now go to YARA-X.
brief.how_it_works: Each rule has a strings section with named patterns ($a, $b, $c) written as hex byte sequences or quoted text, and a condition section that combines them with boolean operators such as or. The README says patterns can use wildcards, case-insensitive strings and regular expressions. The homepage says it is 99% rule compatible with YARA, so most existing YARA rules should run unchanged.
brief.install_notes: The fetched pages contained no install steps, no shell commands and no first-run instructions. The docs page at /docs/intro/console/ returned 404, so I could not check how the yr command is used.
brief.standout: It is a drop-in-compatible rewrite of YARA, meaning most existing YARA rule sets should run unchanged, and it is the same engine VirusTotal runs in production. The README says it has been used to scan billions of files with tens of thousands of rules.
brief.status: Probably maintained. The README calls YARA-X mature and stable and says VirusTotal runs it in production. It is published on Crates.io, and the repo has CI, coverage and MSRV badges. I did not see a release date or last commit date in the pages I fetched, so the exact recency is unknown.

name: yara
desc: Malware identification and classification tool
why: Pattern-matching language for classifying binaries; a real door into malware analysis, though well known in security.

brief.what_it_is: YARA is an open-source pattern-matching tool that malware researchers use to identify and classify samples. You write rules that describe a family, or anything else you want to describe, as a set of textual or binary strings plus a boolean condition over those strings. You point it at files, and it reports which rules match. The homepage says it runs on Windows, Linux and Mac OS X, and it can be driven from the command line or from Python scripts through the yara-python extension. The README's example rule matches files containing any of three strings (two hex byte patterns and one text string) and reports them as silent_banker.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes YARA as 'The pattern matching swiss knife for malware researchers (and everyone else)' and says it is aimed at, but not limited to, helping researchers identify and classify malware samples.
brief.how_it_works: A rule has a meta section, a strings section that names patterns ($a, $b, $c) as hex byte sequences or quoted text, and a condition section with a boolean expression such as '$a or $b or $c'. The homepage says richer rules can use wildcards, case-insensitive strings, regular expressions and other operators, which are covered in the documentation. Rules are applied to files to produce matches.
brief.install_notes: Neither page showed build or install steps. The README says the tool runs on Windows, Linux and Mac OS X, offers a command-line interface, and has a separate yara-python extension for Python use. The homepage also lists a 'Latest release' download and the GitHub repository, which the brief did not fetch. For compressed-file scanning, the homepage recommends the separate yextend extension from Bayshore Networks.
brief.standout: The rule language is the real product: a small, readable, declarative format that many security vendors and sandboxes have adopted, and the homepage lists dozens of organisations using it. The 'swiss knife' framing and the readable example rule make it an approachable way into malware analysis.
brief.status: Maintenance mode, according to an IMPORTANT notice at the top of the GitHub README, which points to the YARA-X project as stable and as the successor. I did not find a last release date or last commit date in the fetched pages, so I cannot give a date from the evidence I saw. The README still lists active CI badges and links to current docs.
brief.caveats: The GitHub README says the project is in maintenance mode and points to YARA-X (https://virustotal.github.io/yara-x/blog/yara-x-is-stable/), so new work is likely to happen there. The homepage lists supported platforms as Windows, Linux and Mac OS X. The brief did not check licensing, the install process, or whether the YARA-X rules are compatible with the classic language. name: yaz
desc: Toolkit for Z39.50/SRW/SRU clients/servers
why: Z39.50 and SRU are old library-catalogue protocols nobody looks at, and yaz opens that door, though the toolkit itself is plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: YAZ is a programmers' toolkit, written in C, for building Z39.50, SRW and SRU clients and servers. Per the README and the user's guide, it supports Z39.50-2003 (version 3) and SRU 1.1 through 2.0 in both client and server roles, and the Solr webservice in the client role through the ZOOM API. It is a library plus a set of command-line tools (yaz-client, yaz-ztest, zoomsh, yaz-marcdump, yaz-iconv, yaz-url and others) that work with protocol traffic and library records. Developers feed it queries and get back search results, records and scan output. The docs describe it as a compact toolkit covering the protocol layer and higher-level client and server tools. Note that the brew metadata lists the executables but I did not verify them against the docs beyond the guide's reference index.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents YAZ as the way to build Z39.50/SRW/SRU clients and servers without writing the protocol from scratch, and says it has been the leading toolkit for these since its first release in 1995. It says that most library software vendors use it for protocol support, and that many others use it for interoperability testing and data conversion.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the primary output of the source is the YAZ library, which provides support functions for implementing the server or client role of Z39.50 and SRU. The user's guide says the ZOOM API is the recommended high-level route for writing clients, and that YAZ can also be used directly from C. Language bindings are separate projects: YAZ++ for C++, PHP/YAZ for PHP, SimpleServer for Perl servers, NET::Z3950 for Perl clients, and yaz4j for Java clients (client only at the moment). The homepage also mentions a hosted commercial service called MasterKey Connect, which wraps resources that lack Z39.50 access with SRU or Z39.50 connectors.

name: yosys
desc: Framework for Verilog RTL synthesis
why: Open-source Verilog synthesis lets you turn hardware descriptions into real netlists, a genuine door into circuit design.

brief.what_it_is: Yosys is a framework for Verilog RTL synthesis, driven from a command-line binary with an interactive shell or from synthesis scripts. It takes Verilog-2005 designs, and per the GitHub README also an informally defined synthesizable subset of SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800-2017 or 2023), via the sv-elab and slang libraries. It outputs gate-level netlists mapped to ASIC standard cell libraries in Liberty format or to Xilinx 7-Series, Lattice iCE40 and ECP5 FPGAs, and it can also convert designs to BLIF, EDIF, BTOR, SMT-LIB or simple RTL Verilog. It has built-in formal methods for property and equivalence checking.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Yosys as a foundation and front-end for custom flows: "Yosys can be adapted to perform any synthesis job by combining the existing passes (algorithms) using synthesis scripts and adding additional passes as needed by extending the Yosys C++ code base." It also serves as the backend for formal tools such as sby and mcy.
brief.how_it_works: You chain named passes in a script or the interactive shell. Typical steps are read_verilog, hierarchy -top, proc and opt to turn always blocks into netlist elements, techmap to map to the internal cell library, dfflibmap -liberty for flip-flops, abc -liberty for combinational logic, then write_verilog. The synth command bundles a good default script that you can build on.

name: yaze-ag
desc: Yet Another Z80 Emulator (by AG)
why: A Z80 emulator lets you run and step through old 8-bit machine code and CP/M software.

brief.what_it_is: YAZE-AG (Yet Another Z80 Emulator by AG) is a Z80 CPU emulator, written by Andreas Gerlich, that runs inside a host UNIX, Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Cygwin or Raspberry Pi system. It is a CPU emulator, not a CP/M emulator: it runs an original CP/M or a replacement such as the CP/M 3.1 replacement ZPM3N10 or the CP/M 2.2 replacement Superdos. Its inputs are the emulated machine's boot files and disk images (.ydsk files, up to 64 MB), plus host directories that can be mounted as CP/M drives. Its output is the emulated CP/M session on the terminal, with serial-line access to real PC serial ports.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it to provide an exact simulation of the Z80 microprocessor so that old 8-bit software can run. The homepage says it is 'designed to provide an exact simulation of the Z80 microprocessor', and it grew out of yaze-1.10 with added CP/M 3.1 support.
brief.how_it_works: The emulator is a Z80 core with an emulated Memory Management Unit (MMU), which the author developed from Michael Haardt's page-table idea. A BIOS (ybios.c and BIOS3 *.Z80 files) provides CP/M 3.1 features such as date, disk-change, xmove and multi-I/O. Disk images are .ydsk files managed with the cdm utility, and the import/export utilities R.COM and W.COM move files between the host and the emulated system.

name: yices2
desc: Yices SMT Solver
why: An SMT solver you can throw logic puzzles and constraints at, a real math engine that rewards an afternoon of tinkering.

brief.what_it_is: Yices 2 is an SMT solver from SRI International that decides satisfiability of formulas over uninterpreted functions with equality, real and integer arithmetic (linear and nonlinear), bitvectors, scalar types, and tuples. You feed it a problem written either in SMT-LIB (versions 2.0 and 1.2) or in Yices' own specification language, and it reports sat or unsat, plus a model of variable values when satisfiable. It ships as command-line tools (yices, yices-sat, yices-smt, yices-smt2) and can also be used as a library through a C API with bindings for Java, Python, Go, and OCaml.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a general-purpose engine for SMT problems, which are satisfiability questions that combine logical structure with arithmetic, bitvectors and other theories. The homepage describes it as a formal-methods tool from SRI's Computer Science Laboratory, developed with funding from SRI, NSF, NASA and DARPA.
brief.how_it_works: You write constraints as assertions over declared variables, then call check-sat and get-model. The example runs show the solver returning concrete witnesses, such as x = 2.0 and y = -1.0 for a linear real problem, or 32-bit vectors for a bitvector problem. Nonlinear arithmetic is handled by MC-SAT, which is not enabled in a default source build.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew and apt packages are the easy routes on macOS and Debian/Ubuntu, and the homepage also offers prebuilt Linux (64-bit) and macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon) binaries. Building from source needs GCC 4.9 or newer (or clang 3.3 or newer), gperf 3.0 or newer, GMP 4.1 or newer, and GNU make, then autoconf, ./configure and make install. Nonlinear MC-SAT from source additionally needs SRI's libpoly and the CUDD BDD library, and you pass --enable-mcsat. Thread-safe builds use --enable-thread-safety. Windows is supported through Cygwin, or natively via MinGW cross-compilers as described in doc/COMPILING. No accounts or runtime setup are mentioned.
brief.standout: Yices is a full SMT solver with SMT-LIB input, its own specification language with tuples and scalar types, and bindings for several languages, and it comes from a formal-methods lab. The bundled parallel portfolio script that races several configurations is a practical extra.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage lists Yices 2.7.0 as the current release, dated 2025-07-16. The homepage says Yices 1 is no longer maintained, and the GitHub README shows active CI and coverage badges. I did not check commit history.
brief.caveats: Yices is GPLv3, and the homepage says alternative license terms can be discussed with fm-licensing@csl.sri.com. A source build does not include nonlinear MC-SAT by default, and it needs extra libraries (libpoly and CUDD) to enable it. The library is not thread-safe unless built with --enable-thread-safety. Native Windows needs MinGW cross-compilation, and Cygwin is the recommended route. The README says MC-SAT is being extended to handle bitvector constraints, which suggests that support is still growing.

name: zeek
desc: Network security monitor
why: A network monitor that turns traffic into structured logs and scripts, a real window into protocols most people never inspect.

brief.what_it_is: Zeek is an open-source network security monitor, formerly called Bro. It passively watches live network traffic on a sensor (hardware, software, virtual, or cloud) and analyzes application-layer protocols such as HTTP, DNS, SSL/TLS, and SSH. What goes in is raw network traffic; what comes out is structured transaction logs, file contents, and customizable data outputs for manual review or for feeding into a SIEM. The site says Zeek is not an active defense mechanism like a firewall or intrusion prevention system. Monitoring policy is written in Zeek's own domain-specific scripting language.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Zeek was developed by Vern Paxson in the 1990s under the name Bro to give deep insight into network activity at university and national lab networks. The README frames it as 'a powerful framework for network traffic analysis and security monitoring.'
brief.how_it_works: Zeek observes traffic without interfering with it and keeps extensive application-layer state about the network. Site-specific behavior is set by scripts, and the README says this means it is not restricted to any particular detection approach. The README does not go deeper into internals, so this is as far as the sources go.

name: z80dasm
desc: Disassembler for the Zilog Z80 microprocessor and compatibles
why: A disassembler for Z80 binaries, a doorway into retro hardware and the machine code of classic computers and game consoles.

brief.what_it_is: z80dasm is a command-line disassembler for the Zilog Z80 microprocessor and compatible chips. It takes a binary file, such as a ROM dump or program image, and writes out Z80 assembly source. It can read label names from a symbol file and use code and data section information to produce a cleaner listing. The output can be reassembled to the same binary with z80asm, zasm, or the original Zilog assembler.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it can be used to reverse engineer programs and operating systems for 1980s microcomputers that used the Z80, such as the Sinclair ZX81 and Spectrum. It was developed to produce the Galaksija ROM disassembly.
brief.how_it_works: The core is based largely on dz80 3.0 by Jan Panteltje, and the README says z80dasm fixes multiple bugs in it and adds features. It guesses label locations from jumps and similar instructions, unless a symbol file supplies names. The README says it handles undocumented instructions, illegal sequences and partial opcodes correctly.

name: zfind
desc: Search for files (even inside tar/zip/7z/rar) using a SQL-WHERE filter
why: Searching inside tar, zip and rar archives with SQL WHERE filters is a neat twist on find.

brief.what_it_is: zfind is a command-line file finder written in Go. You give it a filter written in SQL WHERE-clause syntax, plus optional paths, and it prints matching files. Unlike find, it also looks inside tar, zip, 7z and rar archives, treating archive contents as searchable entries with properties such as name, size, date, ext, type and archive. Output can be a plain list, a long listing with -l, CSV with --csv or --csv-no-head, or NUL-separated with -0 for piping into xargs. The README says it does not implement find-style actions and expects you to pipe results into other commands.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that if you know SQL you should not have to learn or remember any new syntax to find files. It presents the SQL-WHERE filter as the main idea and archive search as the added capability.
brief.how_it_works: Each filter is parsed into a WHERE-style expression over file properties (name, path, container, size, date, time, ext, ext2, type, archive) and evaluated against every entry found. Archive contents are read directly, so you can filter inside them without extracting, though the README notes that 'not archive' in a query still makes zfind open the archive. The -n or --no-archive flag turns archive support off.

name: zfp
desc: Compressed numerical arrays that support high-speed random access
why: Lossy compression for floating point arrays with random access, a real scientific-computing idea you can run on your own data.

brief.what_it_is: zfp is an open-source C and C++ library, with Python and Fortran bindings, for compressing multidimensional floating-point and integer arrays. It provides compressed-array classes that allow fast read and write access to individual elements, and it also compresses whole arrays serially or in parallel (OpenMP, CUDA) for large data sets read from and written to disk. It is aimed mainly at 2D, 3D, and 4D arrays with spatial correlation, such as physics simulation fields and images. Its output is a compressed array, and it can be lossy with an optional error bound, or bit-for-bit lossless.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes zfp as providing 'compressed floating-point and integer arrays that support high throughput read and write random access,' aimed at saving memory and storage for numerical work such as differential equation solvers, data analysis, and visualization. The README says zfp is 'designed to achieve high compression ratios' and is 'loosely based on' Peter Lindstrom's 2014 fixed-rate paper.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the mechanism in detail; it points to the online documentation's algorithm page. The homepage says the data is partitioned into small blocks, which is visible in its figure. Each block is compressed separately, which is what allows random access to individual elements without decompressing the whole array.

name: zmap
desc: Network scanner for Internet-wide network studies
why: An Internet-wide scanner that sweeps the whole IPv4 space, a striking way to see how the public internet actually responds.

brief.what_it_is: ZMap is an open source command-line network scanner that sends single probe packets across the public IPv4 address space, or a chosen part of it, to find which hosts answer on a given port or protocol. You give it a target port and probe module, and it prints the responding IP addresses to stdout, with a live progress line on stderr. The homepage zmap.io is an umbrella page for the wider ZMap Project, which also covers ZGrab, ZDNS, LZR, ZCrypto, ZLint and others; the Homebrew formula installs the zmap binary plus zblocklist, ziterate and ztee helpers.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a tool for 'Internet-wide network surveys', so researchers can measure the hosts and services that make up the public internet. The README says it is designed to scan the whole IPv4 space on one port in under 45 minutes on a gigabit connection.
brief.how_it_works: ZMap is described as stateless: it sends one packet per target, such as a TCP SYN, and records replies without keeping per-connection state, which is what makes the speed possible. The companion tool ZGrab 2 handles stateful application-layer handshakes when deeper detail is needed. The README mentions optional netmap or PF_RING for 10GbE speeds, and the 2025-era release notes mention an optional JA4TS fingerprint of SYN-ACK replies and RTT measurement on TCP SYN probes.

commands_seen.context: README's first example: a simple scan of the entire IPv4 space on TCP port 80. It needs root privileges.

Optional high-speed capture needs netmap or PF_RING on a 10GbE link. No account or API key is mentioned.
brief.standout: Unlike a typical port scanner such as nmap, ZMap is built for sweeping the entire IPv4 space in minutes, using stateless single-packet probes and a random permutation of addresses. name: zlint
desc: X.509 Certificate Linter focused on Web PKI standards and requirements
why: A linter that checks X.509 certificates against Web PKI rules, a rare window into how certificate standards are enforced in practice.

brief.what_it_is: ZLint is an X.509 certificate linter written in Go. You give it a certificate (PEM file) and it runs a set of checks against it, reporting where the certificate departs from RFC 5280, CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements, root store policies, and ETSI standards. It runs as a command-line tool (the bundled zlint executable) or as a Go library that CA software can call. The lints are grouped by source, and you can include or exclude whole sources or individual lints by name. It also handles certificate revocation lists (CRLs) in PEM form. On the ZMap homepage it appears as one tool in a family of Internet-measurement utilities, described as checking 'conformity with X.509 RFCs, CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements, root store policies, and ETSI standards.'
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the Mozilla root program strongly recommends pre-issuance linting, so CAs can catch certificate errors before they go out. ZLint started focused on RFC 5280 and v1.4.8 of the CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements, and was restructured so lints from other sources could be added more easily.
brief.how_it_works: Each lint is a named check tied to a source document, and all lints sit in a global registry that can be filtered by source or name. A certificate is parsed with ZCrypto's x509 package (a lenient parser: if parsing fails, the certificate counts as rejected), then the applicable lints run against it. Lints that need settings read them from an optional TOML configuration file, which the CLI can print as a full example with -exampleConfig.

brief.what_it_is: libzita-convolver is a real-time C++ convolution library that uses FFT-based convolution with non-uniform partition sizes, small ones at the start of the impulse response and larger ones further on. It takes audio input and impulse responses and produces the convolved audio output. The homepage describes it as able to do zero-delay processing of very long IRs such as reverbs at moderate CPU load. brief.how_it_works: Partitions are sized non-uniformly, and the calculations are spread over up to five threads, one per partition size, running at priorities equal to or just below the calling thread's priority. The homepage says this lets CPU be allocated well when several instances run at once. Sparse and diagonal matrices skip empty cells and empty partitions.

name: zsync
desc: File transfer program
why: Delta-based file syncing over HTTP using rsync-like rolling checksums, a neat protocol idea behind an obscure tool.

brief.what_it_is: zsync is a command-line file transfer program that downloads a new version of a file over HTTP while reusing a copy of the older version you already have. It fetches only the changed parts, using a .zsync metadata file that the distributor generates once on the server. The input is a .zsync file plus your existing local copy; the output is the updated file. The Homebrew package installs two executables, zsync and zsyncmake.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says zsync fills a gap in large-scale file distribution: it brings rsync-style delta transfers to plain web hosting, with the rsync algorithm run on the client so the server carries no extra load. The stated target is one file on a server distributed to thousands of downloaders.
brief.how_it_works: The distributor builds a .zsync file, which holds precalculated rsync-algorithm checksums and a simple text header that can be edited, such as to change the download URL. The .zsync can point to a relative URL on the same server or to one or more absolute URLs, so third parties can offer it while still pointing at the original site. The client compares its old copy against those checksums and downloads only the new parts. The homepage does not give a command-level walkthrough.
brief.install_notes: The homepage and download index only list source tarballs (zsync-0.8.0.tar.gz is the newest, with older .tar.bz2 releases back to 0.5). They describe no build steps, dependencies, or configuration. The server-use page that would cover creating and offering .zsync files returned HTTP 404, so server setup details could not be read. A .zsync file must be generated by someone who already has the file before any client can use it.
brief.standout: Instead of the server running rsync, the client does the rsync-style work against precomputed checksums in a static .zsync file, so any plain HTTP/1.1 web server or shared hosting account can serve delta downloads. The metadata file can also be mirrored or produced by a third party.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage says the author does not do much active development these days but still reviews bug reports and pull requests on GitHub and will cut releases for interesting changes. The download index shows releases as recent as zsync-0.8.0.tar.gz (2026-08-15), with 0.7.x and 0.8.0 as rewrites. The original release was 2004 and the project never reached v1.0.
brief.caveats: Never reached v1.0. The homepage says 0.7.0 is a rewrite that is less mature than the 0.6.x line, so bugs and incompatibilities are more likely. Multiple-file (directory) support is explicitly not planned. Look-inside-compressed-file support was removed in the latest release; users who need it must use 0.6.4. It only works for files where someone has already generated a .zsync file. Licence is version 2 of the Artistic License per the homepage. The homepage was reachable but the server-use subpage was not.
quotes: zsync is a file transfer program. It allows you to download a file from a remote server, where you have a copy of an older version of the file on your computer already.
zsync requires no special server software — just a web server to host the files — and imposes no extra load on the server, making it ideal for large scale file distribution.
Client-side rsync — zsync uses the rsync algorithm, but runs it on the client side, thus avoiding the high server load associated with rsync.

name: zvbi
desc: Vertical Blanking Interval (VBI) decoding library
why: Decodes Vertical Blanking Interval data like teletext and closed captions hidden in analog TV signals, a door into forgotten broadcast protocols.

brief.what_it_is: ZVBI (libzvbi) is a C library for capturing and decoding data carried in the vertical blanking interval of analog TV signals. It reads raw VBI from Linux V4L/V4L2 and FreeBSD BKTR capture devices, from Linux DVB devices, or through a VBI proxy that shares devices between applications. It demodulates raw VBI into sliced data in software and decodes services such as Teletext and Closed Caption. It also has a Teletext cache with search and text export and rendering functions. It ships a few command-line tools, including zvbi-ntsc-cc for NTSC closed captions. The README says it offers everything a VBI application needs except the user interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the VBI is the interval where the screen's electron beam returns to the top, so data sent there would not be displayed, and it can carry test signals, closed captioning and other digital data. The library was written for the Zapping TV viewer and is meant to supply the decoding layer so applications only need a UI.
brief.how_it_works: The library reads raw VBI frames from capture devices (V4L, V4L2, BKTR, DVB) or through the zvbid proxy. It demodulates them in software into sliced VBI data, then runs decoders for services like Teletext and Closed Caption. The README does not go into more detail than that.

name: zork
desc: Dungeon modified from FORTRAN to C
why: A faithful C port of the 1970s text adventure that started it all, a piece of computing history you can actually play.

brief.what_it_is: Dungeon, also called Zork, is a text adventure game whose source code is in the public domain. The repository holds a C version of the mainframe game, converted from the FORTRAN source of Zork 2.6. You type commands at a prompt and the game replies with text describing the world. The README's startup banner, which appears in the fetched page, reads: "Welcome to Dungeon. This version created 11-MAR-91." It then shows the opening scene, a field west of a white house with a boarded front door.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the project's primary design goal is code preservation. It aims to keep the logic and behavior of the game as accurate as possible while updating the code to compile and run on modern C compilers and operating systems.
brief.how_it_works: The C code was generated from the f77 version with f2c, the FORTRAN-to-C translator, and then modified to remove the FORTRAN I/O library, add simple more processing, and change the format of the database file. The lineage runs from MDL (MUDDLE) at MIT, to DEC FORTRAN for the PDP-11 by Bob Supnik, to f77 on UNIX, and then to C. The README also notes that Dungeon differs from Zork I, which is a microcomputer adaptation covering about a third of the original map and puzzles.

commands_seen.context: Installs the package on Fedora Linux from the official repositories, per the README's Fedora section.
Builds the game from the source files in the repository, per the README's Building from Source section.

brief.install_notes: On Fedora, the package is in the official repositories. From source, run make in the repository. The README gives no further requirements such as a compiler version, runtime, or configuration. No first-run steps are documented in the fetched text.
brief.standout: It is a faithful, machine-translated descendant of the original MIT game, with a documented chain of translations from MDL to FORTRAN to f77 to C. The README also credits the people at each step, so the port reads as a piece of computing history you can play.
brief.status: Maintained, per the README. It lists three current maintainers and describes the modern maintenance period as running from 2013-12 to present, and the Fedora packaging is mentioned. I did not see a last release date or last commit date in the fetched content, so I cannot confirm recent activity beyond that.
brief.caveats: The README describes this as a preservation project, so it aims to keep the original behavior rather than add features. The fetched text does not mention a license beyond the public-domain claim, and it does not describe platforms beyond Fedora, make builds, and the MS-DOS and Microsoft C port mentioned in the history section. Dungeon is not the same game as Zork I, which the README stresses.

The primary design goal is code preservation.

name: zxcc
desc: CP/M 2/3 emulator for cross-compiling and CP/M tools under UNIX
why: A CP/M emulator under UNIX lets you run eight-bit era toolchains and binaries, a true old-school environment.

brief.what_it_is: ZXCC is a CP/M 2/3 emulator that runs on UNIX, with the stated purpose of letting Hi-Tech C for CP/M be used as a cross-compiler under UNIX. It also lets the CP/M build tools (MAC, RMAC, GENCOM, LINK) run under DOS or UNIX. It is built on two libraries: CPMIO handles terminal emulation (VT52, VT100, or native), and CPMREDIR maps host directories to CP/M drives. The homepage does not describe command-line usage, so the executables listed in the package metadata (zxas, zxc, zxcc, zxlibr, zxlink) are not confirmed from the page.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants eight-bit-era CP/M development tools to keep working on modern machines, so that CP/M compilers and build tools can be used for cross-compiling without a real CP/M system.
brief.how_it_works: CPMREDIR makes directories on the host system appear as CP/M drives, and ZXCC uses it for all drives. CPMIO provides terminal emulation, with multiple emulation modes modelled on MYZ80 under DOS. The page says the two libraries are LGPLed and can be used separately, and that CPMREDIR is also used in the JOYCE PCW emulator.
brief.install_notes: The stable 0.5.7 release is distributed as zxcc-0.5.7.tar.gz and builds with the GNU Autotools. It bundles development versions of CPMIO and CPMREDIR, so they do not need to be downloaded separately. CPMIO 1.1.1 and CPMREDIR 1.1.1 are also published as separate tarballs. The page gives no download URLs beyond these filenames, and no runtime or configuration steps.
brief.standout: It is a CP/M emulator built for toolchains rather than games or retro nostalgia, and its terminal and filesystem layers are split into reusable LGPL libraries. The author notes that CPMREDIR is also used in his JOYCE PCW emulator.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage footer is dated 2013-12-28 and is signed by John Elliott. The page shows no later release or commit information, so the current state is unknown beyond that.
brief.caveats: Version 0.5.7 has not been built or tested on DOS, according to the author. The older 0.4.0 release is free for non-commercial use only and needs CPMIO and CPMREDIR compiled separately. The GPL/LGPL split between versions is a licensing consideration. The homepage describes no features beyond terminal emulation and filesystem mapping, and no documentation beyond this single page was fetched. Homebrew reported no caveats.

name: zyre
desc: Local Area Clustering for Peer-to-Peer Applications
why: Zero-configuration peer discovery and clustering on a LAN, a real protocol idea, though it is a library rather than something to poke.

brief.what_it_is: Zyre is a C library for local network group messaging between peers. A program creates a Zyre node, starts it, and joins named groups; the node finds other nodes on the same LAN by UDP beacons (or optionally by a gossip service) and connects to them directly. Applications receive events such as ENTER, EXIT, JOIN, LEAVE, WHISPER and SHOUT from zyre_recv, and send messages with zyre_whisper or zyre_shout. The brew package ships one executable, zpinger, which the README says to run on two or more PCs to test; the README does not describe its output.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Zyre provides reliable group messaging over local area networks with no administration or configuration, and that peers talk to each other without any central broker or server. Its listed use cases are local service discovery, clustering services on one Ethernet network, controlling smart devices (Internet of Things), and multi-user mobile apps such as smart classrooms.
brief.how_it_works: Each node broadcasts UDP beacons on a port (default 5670) to find peers and heartbeats them, following the RFC 36 ZRE protocol. Once discovered, nodes interconnect using a Dealer-Router pattern over ZeroMQ, which the README says avoids losing messages unless a peer application terminates. An alternative gossip discovery mode, set up with zyre_gossip_bind and zyre_gossip_connect, replaces UDP beaconing for networks where broadcast is unsuitable.

Prerequisites include build-essential or Visual Studio, uuid-dev and libpcre3-dev, plus git. name: zzuf
desc: Transparent application input fuzzer
why: A transparent input fuzzer that mutates file bytes under a program is a classic door into how software breaks on malformed input.

brief.what_it_is: zzuf is a transparent application input fuzzer. It runs a target program and corrupts the data that program reads, by intercepting file and network operations and flipping random bits in the input. The program then sees malformed input, and crashes or memory faults it hits are the output. The Homebrew entry lists two executables, zzuf and zzat. The homepage is an old Trac wiki page; the README is short and sends readers to the wiki and manual page for usage.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames it as a way to find bugs in applications by corrupting user-supplied data, which often comes from untrusted sources on the Internet. The homepage says the idea of fuzzing is barely new, and the main goal is to make it easier and automated.
brief.how_it_works: zzuf intercepts file and network operations and changes random bits in the program's input. Its behaviour is deterministic, so a bug found with a given seed can be reproduced. The homepage lists three uses: quality assurance and test suites, security (segfaults and memory corruption as possible holes), and code coverage analysis.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are on GitHub releases (https://github.com/samhocevar/zzuf/releases). The tutorial says it requires zzuf 0.11 or later. Nothing else about accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration appeared in the pages I read.
brief.standout: zzuf is aimed at real-world targets such as media players, image viewers and web browsers, rather than only unit tests. It is transparent: the target program is not modified, because the tool intercepts its I/O. The homepage says CERT's Basic Fuzzing Framework (BFF) is based on it.
brief.status: unknown. The Trac wiki page says it was last modified on 06/09/2015. The GitHub README has a Travis CI badge but no release or commit date showed in what I fetched. The tutorial is marked WORK IN PROGRESS.
brief.caveats: Support is listed as: Linux (glibc), FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Mac OS X and OpenSolaris fully supported; NetBSD almost working; Windows not ready. The tutorial is marked WORK IN PROGRESS, and its advanced sections are only partly described on the pages I read. The homepage notes that zzuf is full of black magic and difficult to hack on. Licensing was not visible in the pages I read.
quotes: zzuf is a transparent application input fuzzer.
zzuf's behaviour is deterministic, making it easy to reproduce bugs.
zzuf is not rocket science: the idea of fuzzing input data is barely new, but zzuf's main purpose is to make things easier and automated.
